Patient note:
A 70-year-old woman who resides in her own bungalow and still gardens most mornings was brought to the emergency department by her husband shortly after lunchtime because of forty-eight hours of feverish chills, a productive cough yielding yellow-green sputum, and new right-sided chest discomfort that worsened whenever she tried to lie flat; she deliberately skipped her usual morning prescriptions—carvedilol, low-dose bumetanide, and nadolol prescribed for portal-related variceal prophylaxis—so that, in her words, “the numbers won’t be watered down.” She had eaten only dry toast at dawn and drank no coffee, alcohol, or acetaminophen before arrival, and she used neither her home incentive spirometer nor the salbutamol metered-dose inhaler she keeps for occasional winter wheeze. Past medical background includes longstanding congestive pump dysfunction following an anthracycline-based chemotherapy course in early adulthood for Hodgkin disease (she has had no malignant recurrence and has routine oncology surveillance that remains clear) and biopsy-confirmed non-alcoholic steatohepatitis with compensated portal hypertension; her last hepatology clinic visit three months earlier documented normal synthetic markers, occasional esophageal varices managed endoscopically, and no ascites. She has never required renal replacement therapy and her primary-care records show an estimated glomerular filtration rate consistently above 60 mL/min; she denies any history of stroke, transient neurologic events, carotid surgery, or focal deficits. Immunizations are current, including both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza injection, and she quit a fifteen-pack-year cigarette habit nearly two decades ago. On ambulance roll-in she sat upright, conversed in full sentences, correctly recited the date and the names of her three grandchildren, and followed multi-step commands without hesitation. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic, sclerae were anicteric, and nail beds were pink with brisk capillary refill. First-pass, untreated vital signs obtained while she breathed ambient air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.05 °C, regular radial pulse 75 beats per minute confirmed on telemetry, non-invasive right-arm blood pressure 103/61 mm Hg verified manually, respiratory rate counted over a full minute at 20 breaths per minute with mild intercostal effort but no accessory muscle use, and fingertip pulse oximetry varying between 93 % and 94 %. Jugular venous contour was mildly elevated at the angle of Louis, similar to her cardiology baseline, and trace bilateral ankle edema was noted. Cardiac auscultation revealed an S3 gallop already documented in previous notes as well as crisp S1 and S2 without new murmurs or rubs. Pulmonary examination demonstrated dullness to percussion and absent breath sounds over the dependent half of the right posterior hemithorax with coarse inspiratory crackles and egophony just above that zone; the left lung transmitted vesicular airflow throughout. Abdomen was soft, non-tender, and mildly distended; a smooth liver edge was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and no splenomegaly was appreciated. A focused neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, fluent speech, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. Capillary glucose checked immediately prior to phlebotomy read 93 mg/dL. Within ten minutes of bay entry—before any fluids, antimicrobials, vasodilators, or supplemental oxygen—peripheral venous blood and a right radial arterial sample were drawn. The basic metabolic panel returned sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. A complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 15.1 × 10⁹/L with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 33 %, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, and platelets 189 × 10⁹/L. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, PaO₂ 86 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 21 mEq/L, consistent with mild hypoxemia and near-physiologic acid–base balance. Serum lactate was 1.7 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin I fell below the analytical threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy demonstrated a dense consolidation within the posterior segment of the right lower lobe accompanied by a crescentic fluid collection layering laterally that blunted the ipsilateral costophrenic angle; cardiac silhouette matched prior films and there was cephalization of pulmonary vasculature similar to previous images. Electrocardiography displayed sinus rhythm at 74 beats per minute with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes unchanged from tracings in her cardiology file. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, a nurse-assisted expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory prior to any antibiotic, diuretic, vasodilator, bronchodilator, corticosteroid, or oxygen order. Up to the moment this narrative is completed she has received only the minimal heparinized saline needed to maintain patency of one 18-gauge peripheral catheter, ensuring that every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding reported above represents her untreated state at presentation.

Patient note:
A 28-year-old woman with no known medical history, no prescription medications, and a social history limited to occasional weekend alcohol use was air-lifted by helicopter EMS after being thrown from a downhill mountain bike during a regional race at 11:12 this morning; bystanders stated she lost control on a loose gravel berm at approximately 30 km/h, struck an overhanging pine trunk with the right side of her helmet, and tumbled another six meters before coming to rest face-up on a shaded slope. Race medics reached her within four minutes, applied a rigid cervical collar, immobilized her on a scoop stretcher with head blocks, and inserted a single 18-gauge catheter into the right antecubital vein that was flushed with 5 mL of normal saline only. They delivered 12 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather mask because of reports of transient wheezing but withheld all opioids, benzodiazepines, paralytics, dextrose, vasopressors, antiemetics, antihypertensives, hyperosmolar agents, antiepileptics, and intravenous crystalloid boluses in order to preserve a baseline neurologic examination. Capillary glucose measured 104 mg/dL in the field, and three-lead telemetry showed sinus tachycardia between 96–102 beats/min without ectopy during the nine-minute flight to our level-I trauma center. She was transferred directly from the aircraft pad to our resuscitation bay at 11:31, still secured on the scoop stretcher, racing jersey glazed with coarse dirt and cedar needles, full-face helmet removed but a cracked visor taped to the side for forensic photography. Prior to any hospital therapy, simultaneous automated vital signs recorded were blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg in the left brachial artery, heart rate 100 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min with shallow abdominal excursion, pulse oximetry 98 % on the prehospital mask, and core temperature 36.8 °C by aural probe. Airway assessment revealed intact dentition, moist oropharyngeal mucosa, and a brisk gag when a Yankauer catheter touched the posterior pharynx; there was no soot, emesis, or blood pooling, and cough was strong. Both pupils measured 3 mm, were round, equal, and briskly reactive to direct and consensual light; corneal reflexes and blink to threat were present, and oculocephalic testing was deferred secondary to the collar. During a forty-second period of silent observation her eyelids remained naturally parted, irides wandering between overhead lights, the trauma clock, and the movement of staff without any prompting or painful stimulus. When asked, “Can you tell us where you are?” she replied in a clear voice yet produced tangential statements—initially “I’m still on the trail, need to finish my lap,” then “Mom’s birthday cake is chocolate”—failing to recognize the hospital environment despite coaxing. She provided her first name accurately but misidentified the month as “August” (current date April) and insisted the year was “next season.” Further simple orientation questions elicited similarly incongruent answers spoken with appropriate articulation and normal prosody, devoid of slurring or dysarthria, but clearly disconnected from context. Baseline limb tone was normal in all extremities, and no spontaneous abnormal posturing was observed. When instructed to squeeze the examiner’s fingers or lift her right leg, she stared quizzically and made no purposeful movement. A firm supra-orbital ridge pressure applied on the left for five seconds prompted her left hand to rise, cross midline, and push at the examiner’s gloved knuckles with moderate force before settling back once the stimulus ceased; an identical maneuver to the right trapezius produced a mirrored response with the contralateral arm deliberately reaching toward the discomfort. Nail-bed compression of either great toe provoked directed knee flexion and an attempt to grasp the examiner’s hand near the foot, confirming purposeful localization rather than mere withdrawal or extensor posturing. Deep tendon reflexes were 2 + and symmetric at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles; plantar responses were flexor bilaterally, and no clonus was present. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; distal pulses were 2 + with brisk capillary refill. Lungs were clear to auscultation, percussion note resonant, and chest wall demonstrated symmetric expansion without crepitus or paradox. Abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender with active bowel sounds; pelvis was stable to gentle compression, and rectal tone was intact. Log-roll inspection disclosed a 6 × 3 cm occipital scalp hematoma without palpable step-off, scattered superficial abrasions over both shoulders, and no vertebral tenderness or deformity. Extremities were aligned with no long-bone deformities, though mild ecchymosis circled the right iliac crest. Point-of-care arterial blood gas on current oxygen flow revealed pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 39 mm Hg, PaO₂ 192 mm Hg, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Rapid serum panel returned sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, and glucose 108 mg/dL. Hematocrit measured 38 % with platelets 230 × 10⁹/L, INR 1.0. Up to this point no sedative, opioid, paralytic, hyperosmolar solution, vasopressor, antiepileptic, antihypertensive, or additional intravenous fluid beyond the initial saline flush has been administered, ensuring that the unprompted lid opening, the disoriented yet fluent speech, and the consistent purposeful reaching toward noxious stimuli reflect her untreated neurologic status at first hospital contact while neurosurgery, trauma surgery, and radiology teams assemble for emergent non-contrast head CT, cervical spine CT, and full trauma imaging.

Patient note:
A 14-month-old Congolese male child with oculocutaneous albinism visited the Mbujimayi pediatric clinic with fever and fatigue. He was originally from Kasai Oriental, a region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He was the youngest in a family of five children, three of whom had oculocutaneous albinism. He himself has sickle cell disease and the rest of the siblings have a sickle cell trait (Fig. ). He was born at term with a birth weight of 3000 g, and presented with spontaneously resolutive neonatal jaundice. The other significant history was episodes of fever with a monthly frequency of two episodes. No vaso-occlusive crisis was clearly diagnosed, in particular no dactylitis episode was reported. The vaccination schedule according to the expanded program of immunization in the DRC was respected with Bacille Calmette et Guérin (BCG) vaccine against tuberculosis; diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP) vaccine; oral polio vaccine (OPV) against polio; hepatitis B and haemophilus influenzae vaccine (HepB-HiB1); rotavirus vaccine (Rotasiil1); pneumococcal vaccine (Prevenar); measles vaccine (VAR); and yellow fever vaccine (AAV). The patient has never been hospitalized and has always been treated on an outpatient basis in health centers during febrile episodes such as malaria or typhoid fever. The siblings reported no particular clinical history.
His parents are not albinos and have no specific medical history; they never benefited from a prenuptial test. They reported their fear of the judgment of others because they have albino children when they are not affected.
The patient was wide awake with good contact and interaction. Generalized pallor was noted with subicteric conjunctivae, and the irises were bluish gray and translucent, thus appearing red with nystagmus (Fig. ). The patient’s skin was pinkish white, depigmented, without any particular lesions or bruises.
On physical examination, weight and height were at the third and tenth percentile for age, respectively. There was no fever (temperature 36.5 °C), the respiratory rate was high (53 cycles/minute), as well as the heart rate (176 beats/minute), but the latter was regular with the presence of a 1/6 systolic murmur at the mitral focus. The oxygen saturation was 94%. The oral examination was normal. The lymph nodes were free, without lymphadenopathy. The lung examination was normal. The abdomen was supple and painless. There was stage III splenomegaly according to the Hackett classification. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 48 g/L and white blood cells at 13,200/μl (complete blood count performed with the Sysmex poch-100i; Sysmex, Norderstedt, Germany).
The diagnosis of SCD has been suggested on the basis of pallor, jaundice, and severe anemia. It was confirmed first by a positive rapid test (BioMedomics, Inc, Morrisville, USA) and then by hemoglobin electrophoresis.
The diagnosis of albinism was proven by molecular genetics on a blood sample and identification of the mutation involved, that is homozygosity for the 2.7 kb deletion of OCA2 (laboratory “Centro Nacional de Biotecnologia CNB-CSIC Campus de Cantoblanco, Darwin 3, 28049 Madrid, Spain). A family investigation was then performed (see Fig. ).
Given the very low hemoglobin level, the patient’s age, and SCD, a blood transfusion was indicated. Antibiotic treatment (ceftriaxone and amikacin) was started in the hospital. The evolution was favorable. On discharge from hospital, routine prophylaxis with folic acid and oral penicillin was initiated, and advice on crisis prevention and medical monitoring was given to the parents.
A dedicated patient monitoring program has been set up for sickle cell anemia and albinism with hygiene advice and sun protection measures. The patient received a hat, sunglasses, and sun protection cream. Ophthalmologic follow-up has also been set up. The evolution remains dermatologically stable, no skin lesion was observed. For SCD, the patient received treatment with hydroxyurea since early 2020. It is still too early to objectify the benefit of this therapy but he had only one infectious episode, one vaso-occlusive crisis, and did not require blood transfusion for over a year.

Patient note:
A 60-year-old male patient was admitted with myalgia and fatigue for 2 days. The patient had no fever, cough, sore throat, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.
The patient had no previous history of chronic diseases such as kidney disease, hypertension, and an endocrine disorder; muscle diseases such as muscular dystrophy and neuromuscular disorders; or a statin class of drug use that could lead to muscle breakdown. There was no trauma and no history of medication. The patient reported no alcohol intake and smoking.
Blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/minutes, heart rate 93/minutes, temperature 36.7°C, and arterial oxygen saturation 98% in room air. The patient was conscious and had a clear mind. He was in a regular heart rhythm without any obvious murmur. There were obvious moist crackles during auscultation of inferior lobes in the lung.
Routine blood test results were as follows: white blood cells, 2.91 × 109/L; neutrophils, 55.7%; lymphocytes, 30.2%; total number of lymphocytes, 0.88 × 109/L; C-reactive protein (CRP), 35.1 mg/L; potassium, 4.3 mmol/L; sodium, 138 mmol/L; urea, 21 mg/dL; D-dimer, 210 ng/mL; alanine aminotransferase (ALT), 52 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST), 117 U/L; lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), 575 U/L; ferritin, 428 ng/mL; international normalized ratio, 1.07; prothrombin time, 11 minutes; total bilirubin, 0.5 mg/dL; and direct bilirubin, 0.2 mg/dL. Cardiac acute damage marker values such as creatine kinase myocardial band (CK-MB: 3.80 U/L) and troponin (13.6 pg/mL) were among normal reference values at the time of hospital admission.
The patient’s baseline serum creatinine (Cr) level was 0.91 mg/dL and baseline serum CK level was 4,267 U/L. Changes in CK, CRP, AST, ALT, LDH, ferritin, and D-dimer during the patient’s hospitalization are presented in .
Blood tests for rapid detection of influenza A, influenza B, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B were all negative. Electrocardiogram was normal; no significant cardiac arrhythmia was detected.
The patient, who was admitted with frequent complaints of myalgia and fatigue, was diagnosed in the emergency department. Considering the clinical features, physical examination, and chest radiography, the patient was hospitalized with the diagnosis of suspected viral infection. However, considering COVID-19 infection to the epidemic area, atypical pneumonia virus infection had to be ruled out. On the same day, a chest computerized tomography (CT) scan was performed, and small ground-glass nodules were seen, suggesting viral pneumonia scattered across the two lungs (). Two days later, a real-time reverse transcription–PCR (RT-PCR) analysis of the patient’s throat swab sample indicated SARS-CoV-2 infection.
We hospitalized the male patient diagnosed with COVID-19. When we evaluated according to the WHO classification, we found that our patient had severe pneumonia. During hospitalization, hydroxychloroquine (first day 2 × 400 mg loading + 4 days 2 × 200 mg maintenance), oseltamivir (2 × 75 mg, 5 days), and azithromycin (first day 1 × 500 mg loading + 4 days 1 × 250 mg) therapy were used as recommended in the COVID-19 guidelines. The patient was quickly treated with a combination of IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate for alkalization. After five days of treatment, the patient’s clinical condition deteriorated, and the patient’s respiratory rate was 30 breaths/min; severe respiratory distress developed, and SpO2 was ≤ 93% on room air. Favipiravir (first day 2 × 1,600 mg loading + 4 days 2 × 600 mg) antiviral treatment was added to the treatment of the patient, who was thought to develop severe pneumonia. The length of hospital stay of our patient was 10 days between April 9, 2020 and April 19, 2020. After 11 days of treatment, the patient’s symptoms improved significantly, and he recovered with a negative RT-PCR test.

Patient note:
A 55-year-old male patient without a prior medical history was admitted to the emergency room of our university hospital for treatment of a severe headache and vomiting on May 12th, 2010. His vital signs included blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg, pulse rate of 88/min, respiratory rate of 24/min, and body temperature of 36.0℃. An initial head computed tomography (CT) scan revealed an acute extensive subarchnoid hemorrhage filling the basilar cisterns. Subsequent CT angiography showed an anterolaterally-directed ruptured aneurysm on the left mid-cranial artery bifurcation. As a result of these findings, microsurgical clipping was proposed. During the left pterional craniotomy and dural reflection, an intraoperative rupture was encountered and a rapid corticectomy with a retraction of the temporal lobe made the aneurysm clipping amenable.
Post-operatively, the patient was stuporous and responded only to basal stimuli. On post-operative day 2, a controlled mandatory ventilation mode mechanical ventilator was applied along with intravenous sedatives. The patient's neurologic status was stationary. Around post-operative day 5, the patient's body temporal temperature elevated to 38.1℃, and the arterial oxygen saturation levels dropped to 90%. Additional laboratory examinations revealed elevated C-reactive protein (27.0 mg/dL), leukocytosis (20,990/mm3) with a high neutrophil percentage (93%) and a left-shift. A chest CT discovered diffused bilateral lower lobe interstitial infiltrates with pleural effusion, consistent with a diagnosis of ARDS. Following this, the patient was placed on a regimen of IV teicoplanin (200 mg every 12 h), moxifloxacin (400 mg every 24 h) and meropenem (0.5 g every 12 h). On post-operative day 7, a culture of a sputum specimen was found to be positive for multi-drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, but they were not isolated later. Consequently, the administration of meropenem was changed to colistimethate sodium (160 mg every 12h). However, oxygenation deteriorated further (PaO2/FiO2 90-150 mmHg) and the patient became hemodynamically unstable despite the use of volume resuscitation and mechanical ventilation.
Despite the previous 10 days of regimented intravenous antibiotics and inotropics, the patient's condition worsened and progressed into severe sepsis. On May 27, lab results revealed a white blood cell count of 18,400/mm3, hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 111 mg/dL, alanine transaminase 116 IU/L, aspartate transaminase 88 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 183 IU/L, sodium 155 mEq/L, potassium 4.7 mEq/L, and chloride 116 mEq/L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 75 mm/hr and C-reactive protein was 23.5 mg/L. At this point, the patient's arterial oxygen saturation levels had dropped to 86%. In response, in addition to the existing assist-controlled mechanical ventilation, the patient was treated with 2 liters of IV normal saline, dopamine (3 µg/kg/min) and dobutamine (7 µg/kg/min). On post-operative day 17, gram-positive bacilli were detected in the patient's blood cultures. Blood was drawn from peripheral veins on both arms and feet, and six isolates could be obtained from six blood cultures. Of these, isolate 100604-2 was subjected to species identification, but it could not be identified using conventional methods in the clinical microbiology laboratory, including VITEK2 (bioMerieux, Hazelwood, MO, USA) and Microscan (Dade-Microscan, West Sacramento, CA, USA) analyses. On post-operative day 23, it was ascertained that there was little hope of recovery and his family requested the patient be transferred to a hospital located closer to their house. As a result the patient was discharged and transferred to the requested hospital. The patient died 3 days later.
The isolates including the isolate 100604-2 formed translucent, flat colonies of gram-positive bacilli, and showed no hemolysis on blood agar. To identify isolate 100604-2, 16S rRNA gene analysis was performed. A portion of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified and sequenced using the primer set fD1/rp2 []. Determined sequences (1,425 bp) were compared with the GenBank public database using the BLASTN program () and the EzTaxon public database () []. Sequences showing high similarities were retrieved from the database and were aligned using the CLUSTALX program. A phylogenetic tree was also constructed by the neighbor-joining method and bootstrap values were evaluated from 1,000 replications.
The 16S rRNA gene sequence (1,425 bp) of the isolate 100604-2 showed the highest similarity (99.6%) with a sequence of P. pasadenensis SAFN-007T (AY167820), followed by P. humicus PC-147T (AM411528) (98.0%), P. kobensis DSM 10249T (AB073363) (95.0%), and P. pinihumi S23T (GQ423057) (94.7%). Thus, the isolate 100604-2 was identified as P. pasadenensis. The constructed phylogenetic tree also indicated that isolate 100604-2 clustered with P. pasadenensis SAFN-007T (AY167820), which was supported strongly by bootstrap analysis ().
In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by the broth microdilution method according to the guidelines of the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) []. Isolate 100604-2 showed a low minimum inhibitory concentration for several antimicrobial agents that included ceftazidime (1 mg/L), imipenem (≤0.06 mg/L), penicillin (≤0.06 mg/L), polymyxin B (1 mg/L), vancomycin (0.12 mg/L), and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (0.06/1.18 mg/L).

Patient note:
A previously independent 29-year-old woman with a five-year history of biopsy-proven focal segmental glomerulosclerosis complicated by steadily declining glomerular filtration—she receives thrice-weekly outpatient hemodialysis but underwent her most recent session the afternoon before presentation—was brought to the emergency department by her roommate after awakening late this morning markedly confused and repeatedly asking why the bedroom looked unfamiliar. According to the roommate, the patient had complained of feverish chills, right-sided chest discomfort when taking deep breaths, and a hacking dry cough that turned thick and blood-flecked over the preceding forty-eight hours; she had taken no antipyretics, cough suppressants, inhalers, supplemental oxygen, or over-the-counter decongestants, wanting “to let it run its course.” The roommate denied illicit drug use, accidental ingestions, or carbon-monoxide exposure in the apartment and confirmed that the patient was last in her usual state of alertness the night before while streaming a movie. Past medical records retrieved electronically list only chronic kidney impairment managed by nephrology, secondary renal anemia treated intermittently with darbepoetin, and iron supplementation; there is no documentation of cerebrovascular accidents, chronic liver disorders, malignancies, or cardiac pump failure. She finished a two-year vocational program in graphic design and works remotely, climbing two flights of stairs to her walk-up unit daily without baseline limitation. She quit smoking cigarettes six years ago after a short three-pack-year exposure, takes no alcohol, and denies recreational drug use. Vaccination history notes completion of both pneumococcal series and last autumn’s inactivated influenza dose. Emergency medical services found her sitting on the edge of her bed, skin flushed and hot to touch, mumbling the wrong month, and breathing rapidly with shallow excursions; they established a saline lock but withheld fluids, antipyretics, nebulized medication, or oxygen so that initial vitals would reflect her untreated physiology. On arrival to the resuscitation bay she appeared ill, eyes wandering intermittently, oriented only to self, and following single-step commands sluggishly but purposefully; Glasgow Coma Scale summed to 14, with spontaneous eye opening, confused verbal output, and localizing motor response. Capillary refill was brisk, mucous membranes were dry and sticky, and no peripheral edema was evident around her permanent upper-arm arteriovenous graft site. Pre-intervention vitals documented an oral temperature of 102.4 °F, a thready yet regular radial pulse racing at 134 beats per minute, a non-invasive blood pressure of 98/54 mm Hg confirmed manually, and a markedly elevated respiratory rate of 58 breaths per minute with faint intercostal retractions; pulse oximetry on ambient air at sea-level fluctuated between 93 % and 95 %. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination showed markedly reduced breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion over the lower half of the right posterior hemithorax, with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles just superior to that zone; the left lung was clear. Abdominal examination demonstrated a soft, mildly distended abdomen with diffuse tenderness to deep palpation but no rebound or guarding; the peritoneal catheter scar from a childhood therapy was well healed. Neurological screening beyond her clouded sensorium showed equal and reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, symmetric facial expression, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. A finger-stick glucose performed before any intravenous flushes registered 170 mg/dL. Peripheral venous blood and an arterial sample from the left radial artery were obtained within ten minutes of triage, prior to any therapy. Laboratory results returned sodium 162 mEq/L, potassium 4.9 mEq/L, chloride 110 mEq/L, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 61 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 7.1 mg/dL, values comparable to her routine pre-dialysis measurements except for the pronounced hypernatremia. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 17.4 × 10⁹/L with 89 % segmented neutrophils, an alarmingly low hematocrit of 22 %, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, and platelets 238 × 10⁹/L. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated a pH of 7.18, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, PaO₂ 98 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, indicating severe metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation and preserved oxygen tension. Serum lactate was 3.1 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin and bedside ultrasound of the inferior vena cava showed no evidence of volume overload or myocardial ischemia. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph performed before any medication revealed dense consolidation involving the right middle and lower lobes accompanied by a large meniscus-shaped opacity blunting the costophrenic angle, consistent with a sizable fluid collection; the cardiac silhouette and mediastinum were unremarkable for age. Electrocardiography obtained simultaneously showed sinus tachycardia at 132 bpm with peaked T waves identical to previous dialysis-unit tracings and no new ischemic changes. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, pleural fluid aspiration kits, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigen assays for common bacterial pathogens, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched to the laboratory before antibiotics or dialysis orders were initiated. At the time this note is written, she has received no antimicrobial agents, intravenous crystalloid, antipyretics, vasopressors, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen, ensuring that all physiologic observations, imaging findings, and laboratory values above represent her untreated state on presentation.

Patient note:
A 60-year-old female who resides in a skilled nursing facility secondary to longstanding functional decline and mild cognitive aging was brought to the emergency department in early winter for progressive shortness of breath, pleuritic chest discomfort, productive cough with yellow–green sputum, and subjective fevers over the preceding three days. Staff at the facility reported that her oral temperature at the bedside had ranged as high as 38.9 °C overnight despite scheduled acetaminophen, and that she had become increasingly tachypneic, requiring frequent rest during transfers. Past medical history is notable for stage 3 chronic kidney disease related to hypertensive nephrosclerosis, well-documented chronic hepatitis C with compensated cirrhosis but no prior episodes of hepatic decompensation, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin alone, and osteoarthritis of the knees. She has never been treated for any malignancy and has no prior cerebrovascular accidents. Baseline functional status involves ambulating short distances with a walker; she is continent of bowel and bladder and makes her own decisions. There is no prior diagnosis of heart failure and she denies orthopnea or lower-extremity edema prior to this illness. No recent antibiotic exposure was recorded, and no residents around her have had confirmed influenza. She does not smoke, drinks alcohol only on special occasions, and has never used illicit drugs.

On arrival to the ED she appeared ill, sitting bolt upright on the stretcher, breathing through pursed lips, but remained alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Initial vital signs obtained before any interventions revealed a rectal temperature of 39.0 °C, heart rate of 115 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, blood pressure of 90/54 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute with shallow excursions, and an oxygen saturation of 84 % on room air that improved to 91 % with 4 L/min oxygen delivered via nasal cannula. Her skin was warm and flushed; no rash or jaundice was present. Examination of the chest disclosed dullness to percussion and inspiratory crackles over the right middle and lower lung fields without audible pleural rub. Cardiac auscultation revealed tachycardia with normal S1 and S2 and no murmurs. Abdominal exam demonstrated a soft, non-tender abdomen without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. She had trace pedal edema bilaterally but no calf tenderness. Neurologic exam showed intact cranial nerves, symmetrical strength, normal sensation, and no nuchal rigidity.

Blood was drawn before antibiotics or fluids. Arterial blood gas on 2 L nasal cannula showed pH 7.29, PaO₂ 50 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 32 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation. Complete metabolic panel revealed sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 97 mEq/L, bicarbonate matching the ABG, BUN 35 mg/dL, creatinine 2.0 mg/dL (baseline 1.6 mg/dL), glucose 180 mg/dL, AST 48 U/L, ALT 42 U/L, and total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL. Complete blood count showed white blood cells 15.2 × 10⁹/L with 88 % neutrophils, hematocrit 35 %, and platelets 160 × 10⁹/L. High-sensitivity troponin and BNP were within normal limits. Blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and Legionella urinary antigen were sent. A portable upright chest radiograph demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms; the costophrenic angles were sharp without layering fluid, and no cavitation or mass was seen. There was no obvious cardiomegaly. Bedside ultrasound of the thorax, performed by the emergency physician, showed lung hepatization but no anechoic stripe suggestive of an effusion.

Electrocardiogram displayed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Point-of-care lactate was 3.2 mmol/L. Urinalysis was unremarkable. Given her living situation and comorbid renal and hepatic conditions, the team considered her at elevated risk for adverse outcomes. She remained hemodynamically borderline; systolic pressures fluctuated in the low 90s mm Hg range while diastolic pressures hovered in the 50s, and she had cool extremities but preserved capillary refill. Over the next thirty minutes, she continued to maintain mental clarity, correctly reciting the date and the reason for presentation, and followed commands without hesitation. No focal neurologic deficits emerged. The plan at this stage, prior to initiation of intravenous fluids, vasopressors, or antimicrobial therapy, included blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, careful volume resuscitation mindful of her renal impairment, and admission to a monitored step-down setting with escalation to intensive care if oxygenation worsened.

Patient note:
The patient, a 32 year old female, had ingested approximately 12.5 g of 70% oxalic acid mixed in a glass of water in an attempt at deliberate self harm. Immediately after ingestion, she experienced abdominal pain and profuse vomiting and was brought to the local rural hospital within 2 hours of ingestion. After intravenous access was established and an initial assessment was done, she was immediately transferred to the regional hospital. On arrival, 4 hours after ingestion, she was found to be drowsy but alert (Glasgow coma scale 15), but with a pulse rate (PR) of 50/min and a blood pressure (BP) of 80/60 mmHg. Oxygen saturation on air (SpO2) was 92%. Immediate volume resuscitation was done and the patient required inotropic support during the first 24 hours. Vomiting continued throughout the day, with two episodes of blood stained vomitus.
Her urine output was maintained subsequently, but by the 3rd day she developed worsening generalized oedema with a reduction of urine output to approximately 20 ml/hr. There was gradual elevation of serum creatinine (S.Cr) levels (up to 704 umol/dl) and blood urea (BU) levels (up to 43.5 mmol/dl). She was transferred to our hospital on the 3rd day after oxalic acid ingestion. On admission, she was febrile (temperature 99.6°C), nauseous, with stable vital parameters (PR 82/min, BP 120/80 mmHg, SpO2 99% on air) and mild tachypnoea. There was generalized oedema with bilateral fine basal crepitations in the lungs. S.Cr level was 493 umol/dl, with serum potassium (S.K+) of 4.8 mEq/l and a white blood cell (WBC) count of 22,500/ul with 87% neutrophils. Urinalysis revealed active sediment (70–80 red cells, 1–2 pus cells/hpf). Arterial blood gases (ABG) showed a metabolic acidosis, with a pH of 7.328, PaCO2 of 33.2 mmHg, PaO2 of 84.2 mmHg, BE of −6.2 and a HCO3 of 18.9 mmol/L.
The patient underwent hemodialysis on the 3rd day, with symptomatic improvement. Post dialysis ABG revealed a respiratory alkalosis (pH of 7.479, PaCO2 of 34.9 mmHg, PaO2 of 91.9 mmHg, BE of 2.5 and a HCO3 of 26.2 mmol/L). The urine output remained low and she required a second dialysis on the 7th day. Urine output increased by day 9, but the S.Cr level remained high.
Renal biopsy was performed on the 8th day revealed acute tubulointerstitial nephritis associated with diffuse moderate acute tubular damage with refractile crystals seen in some tubules (Figure
). This was reported as being consistent with oxalic acid poisoning. After day 9, the renal functions and urine output gradually improved. No further dialysis was required. She was prescribed antacids and mucoprotective agents and upper gastrointestinal symptoms settled. Blood picture was reported as mild normochromic normocytic anemia (Hb: 9.1 g/dl) with normal WBC and platelets. She was transferred back to the local hospital on 12th day and subsequently discharged on day 14.
On follow up (Day 28), she was asymptomatic with a normal S Cr. Level (114umol/L).

Patient note:
An 83-year-old woman with a history of autoimmune thrombocytopenia, arterial hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus was admitted to the hospital with extensive hematoma of the left hemithorax following trauma. Blood tests revealed anemia (Hbg: 10 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (PLT: 24 × 10³ µL). A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the thorax proved contrast blush in the region of left pectoralis major muscle; hence, an urgent angiography and embolization were requested.
Because of thrombocytopenia, the patient had a high risk of bleeding and vascular complications related to the FA, so we decided to perform a TRA, but the Barbeau test showed a type D waveform. DRA diameter (2 mm) was suitable for puncture at US examination. The patient gave her informed consent before the interventional procedures.
The DRA access was obtained with the same technique already described. A diagnostic angiography of left axillary and subclavian arteries was performed using a 100-cm 4-French Berenstein catheter. It showed contrast extravasation of left lateral thoracic artery (LLTA). A microcatheter was introduced for a superselective angiography of the LLTA and we used Spongostan to embolize the LLTA. A final diagnostic angiogram demonstrated the success of the procedure. An occlusive pressure of the DRA was obtained in the same way as described. The evaluation of the RA patency, using a color Doppler examination, was performed in the same way as in case 1, which gave similar results.

Patient note:
A 68-year-old man with a twelve-year history of cirrhosis that developed after three decades of chronic hepatitis B infection presented on a Tuesday morning to the walk-in liver clinic at 09:10 because his spouse observed that over the past ten days he had paused longer than usual before answering routine questions, misplaced his cell phone twice in one afternoon, and seemed more sluggish balancing the household ledger; the patient himself reported that fastening his belt by late evening felt “a notch tighter” yet he did not think his weight had changed, and he admitted to noticing a faint yellowish hue in the bathroom mirror. He denied vomiting blood, black or maroon stools, hematochezia, frank abdominal pain, early satiety, nausea, fever, chills, dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, chest discomfort, lower-extremity swelling, pruritus, or changes in urine volume or color beyond a slightly darker shade. His prior liver-related complications included small esophageal varices discovered on surveillance endoscopy two years earlier that did not require band ligation, and a single hospital stay eight months ago for community-acquired pneumonia but never for gastrointestinal bleeding, renal dysfunction, or tense abdominal fluid collection. He had never undergone paracentesis, transjugular portosystemic shunt placement, or liver transplantation evaluation. Current medications—reconciled with pharmacy records—are entecavir 0.5 mg nightly for viral suppression, losartan 50 mg each morning for stage 1 hypertension, metformin 1000 mg twice daily for type 2 diabetes, and over-the-counter vitamin D3 2000 IU daily; he takes no diuretics, β-blockers, lactulose, rifaximin, anticoagulants, vitamin K, herbal preparations, or sedatives. He does not drink alcohol since diagnosis, quit smoking fifteen years ago after a 20-pack-year exposure, and denies recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a father who died from myocardial infarction at 69 and no known hereditary liver disease. The patient previously worked as an accountant, now retired, and lives in a single-story home where he remains independent in basic activities of daily living, exercising by walking a half-mile loop most mornings. On arrival—before intravenous access, blood draw, imaging, or administration of any medication—vital signs recorded were temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. He ambulated to the examination table unaided, answered his full name and location correctly, but required a four-second pause to state the exact date and made one error subtracting serial sevens from 100; he recalled two of three objects after five minutes and produced a low-amplitude irregular flap in both hands within ten seconds of sustained arm extension. Speech was slightly slowed but coherent and goal-directed. Breath carried a barely sweet odor. Sclerae were lemon-tinged, conjunctivae pink, and oral mucosa moist without ulceration. The neck was supple with jugular venous pulsation at 5 cm H₂O while reclined 30 °. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; peripheral pulses were symmetric. Lungs were clear to auscultation. Abdominal inspection showed a mildly protuberant contour with the umbilicus remaining inverted; no visible collateral veins or tense drum-like distention were seen. Percussion revealed tympany over the epigastrium transitioning to a thin ribbon of dullness along both flanks that shifted subtly when the patient rolled onto his side, and a faint fluid impulse traversed the abdominal wall despite the examiner’s stationary palm—suggesting only a small volume of free intraperitoneal fluid. The abdominal wall was soft and non-tender, and on deep inspiration a firm nodular liver edge was palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen tip was not felt. There was no ankle edema. Skin survey disclosed half-a-dozen spider angiomas scattered over the anterior chest and mild palmar erythema; no bruises, scratch marks, or caput medusae were present. Neurologic examination otherwise demonstrated intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation, and physiologic reflexes. A bedside capillary glucose measured 114 mg/dL. Five minutes later—still prior to any therapeutic intervention—an 18-gauge antecubital venous sample was drawn, and initial laboratory results returned total bilirubin 2.88 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.23 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 52 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 84 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 201 U/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL (estimated GFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m²), hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.8 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 104 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 2.57. A portable 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained immediately afterward showed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min with a QTc of 422 ms, and a supine anteroposterior chest radiograph displayed elevated hemidiaphragms but clear lung fields without pleural effusion. Focused abdominal ultrasonography performed at the bedside by the hepatology fellow—still before any fluids, laxatives, diuretics, antibiotics, or vitamin K—revealed a shrunken heterogeneous liver with an irregular capsule, patent portal vein with hepatopetal flow measuring 15 cm/s, spleen length 16.4 cm, and anechoic free fluid averaging 1.5 cm in depth along the right paracolic gutter and pelvis; kidneys appeared normal in size and echogenicity, and there was no biliary dilation or portal vein thrombosis. Up to completion of this note the patient has received no pharmacologic or procedural therapy, ensuring that all findings and laboratory values recorded reflect his untreated physiologic state at initial presentation for subtle cognitive slowing and slight abdominal fullness in the context of long-standing hepatitis B–related cirrhosis.

Patient note:
A 61-year-old man is reviewed in the ambulatory procedure bay while nursing staff complete a timeout for a planned arthroscopic debridement and rotator-cuff anchor repair of the dominant right shoulder, an operation the orthopedic team estimates will occupy the glenohumeral joint for roughly ninety minutes under general anesthesia with an interscalene nerve block and same-day discharge if he meets recovery criteria. He arrived on foot from the parking deck, negotiated two flights of stairs without pausing, and matter-of-factly reports that he still bicycles four miles along a canal towpath most mornings despite chronic shortness of breath from long-standing tobacco-related lung disease; he keeps a rescue inhaler in his jersey pocket but has not required systemic steroids or emergency visits this season. Pulmonary clinic letters in the electronic chart document moderate airflow obstruction on spirometry, a baseline oxygen saturation of 94 % on room air, and no need for supplemental oxygen outside acute exacerbations. He has not been hospitalized for pneumonia, bacteremia, or any infection meeting sepsis criteria within the past thirty days. Sixteen days ago, during evaluation of purulent sputum and wheeze that never progressed to systemic hypotension or organ dysfunction, hospitalists placed a single-lumen peripherally inserted central catheter in the right basilic vein for a planned fourteen-day course of intravenous levofloxacin; that catheter remains tunneled to the mid-upper arm today beneath an intact occlusive dressing, flushes freely with saline, and shows no erythema, induration, or tenderness along its course. He has otherwise avoided operating rooms, endoscopy suites, or interventional radiology in the past year and confirms that he has not undergone any procedure requiring general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care in the last thirty days. He denies recent fractures of the hip, pelvis, or lower extremities, has not worn any immobilizing casts or braces, and has had no spinal cord injuries, strokes, or transient neurologic attacks over the same period. Review of recent events is negative for fever, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, calf cramping, unilateral leg swelling, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, transient neurological deficits, abdominal pain, traumatic injury, or prolonged immobilization. Past medical history is notable for diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, hypertension managed with lisinopril, and a heterozygous mutation in the prothrombin G20210A gene identified five years ago after his younger sister developed an unprovoked iliofemoral clot while on a transpacific flight; although he himself has never experienced venous or arterial thrombosis, he recalls that both his mother and an aunt required blood thinners during pregnancy-related clotting events. He specifically denies physician-diagnosed lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, platelet factor-4 antibodies, or other named coagulation disorders, and states he has never had heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. There is no history of inflammatory bowel disease, malignant tumors, myocardial infarction, or heart-failure admissions. He quit a 40-pack-year smoking habit eight years ago, enjoys a single whiskey on Friday evenings, and does not use recreational drugs. Current medications include tiotropium once daily, albuterol as needed, lisinopril 20 mg, and over-the-counter fish-oil capsules; no glucocorticoids, hormone therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, or antiplatelet drugs are taken. Vital signs obtained ten minutes ago reveal temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 95 % breathing ambient air; body-mass index is 26 kg m⁻². He is alert, oriented, and converses easily without accessory-muscle use. Airway assessment shows Mallampati class II, more than three finger-breadth mouth opening, thyromental distance six centimeters, and good cervical extension. Cardiovascular examination displays a nondisplaced apical impulse and crisp S₁/S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous contour is below the sternal angle at 30°. Lung fields reveal bilateral scattered end-expiratory wheezes that clear with coughing, no crackles, and symmetric excursion. Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and without organomegaly or surgical scars. Inspection of both lower extremities shows normal color, temperature, and hair distribution; there are no tortuous superficial veins, pitting edema, calf tenderness, or side-to-side circumference difference measured ten centimeters below the tibial tuberosity (both 35 cm). Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+/4 bilaterally. Neurologic screening demonstrates 5/5 strength in all muscle groups, intact sensation to light touch, and a smooth tandem gait witnessed when he walked unassisted to the restroom moments ago. The right shoulder exhibits visible supraspinatus wasting and painful arc above 90°, while the contralateral joint has full painless motion. A 20-gauge peripheral IV in the left antecubital fossa runs lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate in addition to the dormant PICC line. Morning laboratory values drawn through the catheter at 05:45 show hemoglobin 14.0 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 42 %, platelets 248 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 7.2 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 137 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.0 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.90 mg dL⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 22 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram acquired on arrival shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats min⁻¹ with nonspecific ST-T changes identical to previous tracings. Postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs from yesterday demonstrate hyperinflated lung fields without focal infiltrate or mass and confirm the PICC tip at the cavo-atrial junction. Sequential intermittent pneumatic compression devices are at the foot of the stretcher awaiting activation after induction; pharmacologic prophylaxis has been deferred until surgical hemostasis is confirmed. He has been nil per os since midnight, last voided at 0600, removed his dental bridge, and demonstrates clear understanding of the operative plan, post-anesthesia expectations, and the importance of continuing range-of-motion exercises once the sling is discontinued.

Patient note:
A 67 years old woman, premorbidly bed ridden due to stroke was brought in from nursing home after complaining of left knee pain and swelling for a week. She denied any history of fever, fall or trauma. Her other medical illnesses include mixed connective tissue disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension and chronic atrial fibrillation. She was also on long term oral prednisolone 15 mg OD for autoimmune hemolytic anemia and vasculitis.
On admission, she was septic looking and in severe pain. The left knee was swollen, tender, warm and erythematous, extending proximally to mid thigh. There were multiple inguinal lymph nodes palpable. Other systems examinations were unremarkable.
Her total WBC was 19.3 x 109/L with neutrophilia of 18.2 x 109/L. Her ESR was 86 mm/hour and C-reactive protein was 16.8 mg/dL. Ultrasound of the left knee showed hypoechoic collection at the suprapatella region with some internal echos and septation within the lesion. The collection was seen within the muscular striation and appears to be continous with the subpatellar knee joint region. Left knee x-ray showed soft tissue swelling at suprapatellar region with reduced joint space and osteophytes. Aspiration from the joint revealed thick, turbid fluid. There were more than 500 white blood cells/mm3 and more than 500 red blood cells/mm3 in the synovial fluid and culture grew Pseudomonas Species. Blood culture grew Bacillus Species and urine culture grew Klebsiella ESBL. She responded well with intravenous Meropenam and oral steroid was reintroduced slowly.
She underwent arthroscopic knee wash out at day 14 of admission and repeat synovial fluid, blood and urine culture were negative.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old man with a medical history of hypertension presented with dyspnea that had worsened during the past 3 weeks. He had been experiencing mild dyspnea on exertion for the past 6 months. On admission, he had a cough but denied other symptoms. His vital signs were as follows: respiratory rate, 20 bpm; temperature, 36.7°C; pulse, 77 bpm; and blood pressure, 130/70 mmHg. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a partial oxygen pressure of 65 mmHg, partial carbon dioxide pressure of 39 mmHg, pH of 7.44, and oxygen saturation of 93% while resting in room air. Laboratory data included a D-dimer level of 0.44 µg/mL (reference range, 0.00–0.50 µg/mL) and an N-terminal B-type natriuretic peptide level of 15 pg/mL (reference range, 0–500 pg/mL). A chest radiograph indicated no active lesions in the lung (). Contrast-enhanced chest CT was performed to exclude pulmonary thromboembolism or other lung disease and revealed no evidence of filling defects in vessels, thus suggesting pulmonary thromboembolism. Transthoracic echocardiography indicated a mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 47 mmHg (reference range, 10–22 mmHg). On further evaluating the chest CT through the bone setting, however, we identified several hyperdense linear lesions in both peripheral pulmonary arteries that could not be identified using the lung or soft tissue windows, and this raised suspicion for PCE (). We confirmed that the patient had undergone PVP with a diagnosis of vertebral compression fracture at another hospital 14 months previously. During hospitalization, his symptoms resolved slightly after starting treatment with diuretics.
This study was a case report involving only one patient and only involved observation of the clinical effects. Therefore, approval by an ethics committee was not required. We obtained verbal consent from the patient for publication of this case report and images.

Patient note:
A 46-year-old man is evaluated this morning in the orthopaedic theatre holding bay for an urgently arranged left knee arthroscopy that the sports-medicine consultant estimates will last 40 minutes under general anaesthesia; the intention is to trim a displaced bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus that has repeatedly locked the joint in 30 degrees of flexion. Since sustaining an anterior-chest squeezing pain nineteen days ago that proved to be an ST-segment elevation infarction of the inferior wall, he has remained on the cardiac telemetry ward, and nursing documentation shows he has not taken more than a handful of assisted pivot transfers to a bedside chair during the entire admission—physical therapy has deferred hallway ambulation until after today’s procedure because of his ongoing reliance on continuous ECG monitoring and intravenous nitroglycerin during the first week. Coronary angiography performed on the day of the infarct revealed an acute thrombotic occlusion of the mid-right coronary artery successfully treated with a drug-eluting stent; ventricular function is preserved with an ejection fraction of 55 %, and he has had no episodes of pulmonary congestion, orthopnoea, or lower-extremity oedema since the event. The cardiology team transitioned him from heparin to dual antiplatelet therapy three days after the intervention, and his most recent high-sensitivity troponin has trended down to 24 ng L⁻¹ from a peak of 7,800 ng L⁻¹. The current orthopaedic problem predates his cardiac event by several months but became intolerable during convalescence when he could no longer compensate with quadriceps strength or bracing. His oncologic history includes a resected stage II sigmoid adenocarcinoma four years ago for which he completed twelve cycles of adjuvant FOLFOX; surveillance colonoscopy six months ago was clear, CT chest–abdomen–pelvis last quarter showed no recurrence, and he has been off chemotherapy for over three years, carrying no implanted ports or catheters at present. He has not required any surgical procedures since that colon resection, and there have been no operations within the past 30 days. He denies fevers, rigors, sputum production, or any diagnosed pneumonia or bloodstream infection during the current stay, and there have been no recent splints, casts, or traction devices on either lower limb. Review of systems is negative for paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, wheeze, chronic cough, exertional syncope, transient focal neurologic deficits, bowel disturbance suggestive of inflammatory disease, or chronic steroid use. Patient note:

During an initial thirty-second interval of quiet observation her eyelids remain gently closed with no flutter, and extremities lie still. When the charge nurse addresses her by surname in a clear conversational tone, both lids part halfway, hazel irides track toward the speaker, and she immediately articulates, “Yes, I’m here at Memorial Hospital, it’s Thursday morning, and you’re asking me questions.” She is able to state her full name, date of birth, the current month, and the city without hesitation, then volunteers, “My head hurts on the left.” Requests to “lift both arms toward the ceiling” and “wiggle your toes” are met with no purposeful movement beyond a faint twitch of the right fingers; she stares back as if attempting to comply but nothing follows. A similar targeted reach is elicited when supra-orbital pressure is applied on the same side, confirming reproducible localization rather than generalized withdrawal, while she grimaces and verbalizes “that hurts” but still fails to execute commanded tasks. Patient note:
A 76-year old obese woman presented to the intensive care unit for acute NSTEMI. Her medical history included poorly-controlled insulin-dependent diabetes and systemic hypertension. Two hours before the admission, pain in the substernal area developed suddenly. The first electrocardiogram obtained showed normal sinus rhythm with a rate of 85 beats per minute and ST-segment depression of 3 mm in the inferior leads. Serum levels of hematocrit, creatinine and electrolytes were all within the normal range. The troponin I level was 6.4 ng per milliliter (normal range < 0.05 ng per milliliter). Nitroglycerin, morphine, loop diuretics, unfractioned heparin and tirofiban IV were administered and the patient became asymptomatic shortly thereafter. Oral therapy with clopidogrel 75 mg, simvastatin 20 mg and metoprolol 50 mg bid was added.
Trans-thoracic echocardiography showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% in the absence of segmental wall motion abnormalities, mild hypertrophy of the left ventricle, mild left atrial enlargement (transverse diameter 4.4 cm) and moderate mitral regurgitation.
Continuous ECG monitoring showed multiple episodes of sustained, self-terminating paroxysmal AF () symptomatic for dizziness, hypotension and palpitations. All AF episodes were triggered by short-coupled (280 msec coupling interval) ventricular monomorphic couplets with 1:1 ventriculo-atrial (VA) retrograde conduction. The ventricular ectopic beats showed left bundle-branch block (LBBB) morphology with inferior axis (, arrows) and retro-conducted P waves were detectable in aVL and inferior leads (, arrows). Intravenous metoprolol (5 mg) and amiodarone (900 mg) were administered and in one hour stable sinus rhythm was achieved.
The day after a coronary angiography was performed, which showed severe right coronary ostial stenosis. Balloon angioplasty of the lesion was performed and a bare-metal stent was successfully deployed.
The patient was discharged home four days later in therapy with acetyl-salicylic acid 100 mg, clopidogrel 75 mg, furosemide 25 mg, metoprolol 50 mg bid, enalapril 20 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg and insulin. A pre-discharge echocardiography was unchanged. At 1 month follow-up visit she was in stable NYHA functional class II, asymptomatic for angina and palpitations and in sinus rhythm.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease suffered cervicalgia and a stiff shoulder after engaging in farm work. He was a chicken farmer and produced a fertilizer that utilized cow and poultry manure. He went to a nearby clinic 2 days after the onset of symptoms as he experienced difficulty swallowing. Tetanus was strongly suspected from his clinical condition, and he was transferred to the emergency room 3 days after the initial symptoms began. His vital signs were as follows: Glasgow Coma Scale score, 15 (E4V5M6); blood pressure, 144/63 mmHg; heart rate, 79 b.p.m.; respiratory rate, 24 breaths/min; and body temperature, 36.5°C. The level of oxygen saturation showed 96%. Painful contracture of the neck was observed. Trismus, risus sardonicus, and strong muscle spasms in the platysma and sternocleidomastoideus were observed (Fig. ). Laboratory tests revealed slight inflammation and rhabdomyolysis (white blood cell count, 12,600 cells/mm3; C-reactive protein, 0.04 mg/dL; lactase dehydrogenase, 276 U/L; creatine kinase, 340 IU/L; blood urea nitrogen, 25.5 mg/dL). A computed tomography scan showed emphysematous bulla in the lung and patchy pneumonia in the right upper lobe. Tetanus was clinically diagnosed and he was admitted into the intensive care unit (Fig. ). Polyethylene glycol-treated human anti-tetanus immunoglobulin (3,000 units) was injected and benzylpenicillin potassium (8,000,000 units/day) was administered. Both KT (7.5 g/day) and SKT (7.5 g/day) were given by nasogastric tube to release muscle tension. One to three packages of each Kampo extract was dissolved in tap water (20 mL). Trismus and generalized convulsions were temporarily improved 30 min after treatment with KT and SKT (Fig. B). Fluctuation of systolic blood pressure (100–170 mmHg) was observed for the first 3 days of hospitalization. It was most severe on day 1 (70–180 mmHg). On day 3 of hospitalization, mechanical ventilation was introduced to treat the complications of pneumonia. Blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.47, PaO2 87 mmHg, PaCO2 41 mmHg, base excess (BE) 5.6 mEq/L (FIO2 0.6, synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilaton (SIMV) 13/min, pressure control (PC) 10 cmH2O, pressure support (PS) 8 cmH2O, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) 4 cmH2O). After 11 days of hospitalization, doses of KT and SKT were reduced to 5.0 g/day, as the tetanic convulsions were controlled without the use of muscle relaxants. After 17 days of hospitalization, the patient was weaned from the ventilator. The patient was discharged from the intensive care unit after 25 days; after 27 days, treatment with all Kampo medicines was terminated. After 30 days of hospitalization, he was discharged from the hospital without sequelae.
The blood culture at the time of the patient's admission showed negative results; however, on day 4 of hospitalization, Klebsiella oxytoca was detected from the sputum culture.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old man was evaluated late this afternoon in the orthopedic pre-admission clinic prior to next week’s scheduled right total knee arthroplasty, a procedure anticipated to last under two hours with regional anesthesia and short-term pneumatic tourniquet use; he has exhausted conservative measures for tricompartmental osteoarthritis documented on recent radiographs and wishes to return to recreational cycling by summer. He arrives walking without assistive devices, breathing comfortably, and converses easily, stating that he can mow his modest lawn and climb two flights of stairs while pushing a toolbox without stopping, but pain in the knee—not shortness of breath—limits his distance. Ten years ago he suffered an anterior-wall myocardial infarction while shoveling snow and underwent emergent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with deployment of two drug-eluting stents to the mid-left anterior descending artery; he completed cardiac rehabilitation, has had no recurrent chest pressure, syncope, or exertional diaphoresis since, and follows annually with cardiology. A treadmill echocardiographic stress test done nine months earlier for routine surveillance achieved 9 metabolic equivalents with no ischemic wall-motion abnormality, and the most recent transthoracic echocardiogram described a left ventricular ejection fraction of 58 % with normal diastolic filling and no valvular pathology. He has never required loop diuretics, has not experienced orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or ankle swelling, and has had no emergency visits for fluid overload. Diabetes mellitus type 2 was diagnosed in his early forties; despite lifestyle efforts, oral agents no longer sufficed, and for the past three years he has administered 24 units of insulin glargine each evening as well as mealtime insulin aspart dosed on a sliding scale before breakfast and supper. Portable glucometer records he brings today display pre-prandial values ranging from 110–160 mg/dL during the past week. Other medical problems include stage 3b chronic kidney disease attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis and contrast exposure at the time of his infarction, essential hypertension well managed with lisinopril 20 mg once daily and a long-acting beta-blocker, mixed dyslipidemia controlled with rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and hyperuricemia for which he takes allopurinol. He quit smoking a pack per day twelve years ago, consumes two beers on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Family history notes premature coronary disease in a brother at 54 and metabolic syndrome in both parents; no relatives are known to have undergone joint replacement. Current medications also include low-dose aspirin, omega-3 supplements, and topical diclofenac for the knee. He has no known drug allergies. Review of systems is otherwise negative for palpitations, claudication, transient vision changes, dizziness, fever, or unintentional weight loss. Vital signs in clinic: blood pressure 128/70 mm Hg in the right arm while seated, heart rate 64 beats per minute in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, and body mass index 29 kg/m². Neck veins are not distended, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, precordial palpation reveals a discrete point of maximal impulse in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line, and auscultation discloses crisp S1 and S2 without additional sounds or murmurs. Lungs are clear to bases, abdomen is soft and nontender with no hepato-splenomegaly, and distal pulses are 2+ throughout without edema. The operative knee is enlarged with crepitus on passive flexion but no overlying erythema or warmth. Neurologic examination demonstrates intact cranial nerves, full motor strength, and normal sensation in all extremities. Pre-operative laboratories drawn two hours before the visit reveal hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 7.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL, consistent with long-standing baseline; estimated glomerular filtration rate is 30 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose is 134 mg/dL, and HbA1c measured last month by his endocrinologist was 7.3 %. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows normal sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute, Q-waves in V1-V3 compatible with prior infarction, and no acute ST-T segment abnormalities; corrected QT interval is 410 ms. Chest radiograph exhibits a normal cardiac silhouette and clear lung fields. The airway appears Mallampati class II with good cervical movement, and dentures will be removed prior to induction. He is instructed to continue his beta-blocker and aspirin up to and including the morning of surgery, to hold his evening statin the night before, to reduce the glargine dose by 30 % prior to midnight, and to omit rapid-acting insulin on the day of admission unless finger-stick glucose exceeds 180 mg/dL, in which case a protocolized dextrose-insulin infusion will be employed by anesthesia. The orthopedic team has discussed postoperative thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin and early mobilization; renal-adjusted dosing will be arranged. After reviewing risks of bleeding, infection, myocardial injury, renal impairment, and thromboembolism, the patient verbalizes understanding and remains keen to proceed with the joint replacement next Tuesday.

Patient note:
A 64-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of symptomatic drug refractory PeAF. The patient was admitted for catheter ablation of AF. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed normal ejection fraction of 55-60% with mildly enlarged LA of 43.8 mm in the anterior-posterior diameter. A transesophageal echocardiogram prior to ablation showed no visible intracardiac thrombus or shunt. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging revealed late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in 20% of the LA surface including the anterior and posterior wall.
After PVI, AF was still sustained. CFAEs in the LA were mapped for 6 seconds using EnSite NavX® system three-dimensional automated software (Endocardial Solutions, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA). The CFAEs were predominantly located at perimitral, septal area and left atrial appendage base (). Activation pattern at the high clustering of CFAE was mapped using high density 20-pole catheters (AFocus II; St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA). The activation patterns obtained from three AF beats of unipolar recordings at each CFAE site were classified into four categories: 1)complete reentry, 2) incomplete reentry, 3) wave collision, and 4) wave breakup with conduction block. We preferentially targeted CFAE areas with complete or incomplete reentry pattern because these sites might play an important role as rotor. In this case, only the perimitral area had re-entrant, rotor-like electrical activity (). Based on the activation pattern, we assumed that the perimitral area could be the critical site for AF perpetuation. Therefore, we decided to infuse ethanol into the VOM as an add-on to radiofrequency ablation.
At first, cannulation into coronary sinus was performed by ablation catheter (Therapy CoolFlex; St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA) and 8 Fr sheath (SL1 sheath; St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA). To confirm the existence and feasibility of VOM, occlusive coronary sinus (CS) venogram was done (). A multipurpose A-1 guiding catheter (7 Fr; Cordis, Miami, FL, USA) was subselectively engaged into the VOM and then a Hi-Torque Floppy II angioplastic guidewire 0.014 (Abbott, Santa Clara, CA, USA) was advanced into the VOM as far as possible. A Ryujin Plus OTW 2.0×20 mm angioplasty balloon catheter (Terumo, Tokyo, Japan) was advanced into the VOM over the angioplastic wire and inflated at the ostium of VOM. Engagement of the balloon catheter into the VOM was confirmed by injecting contrast medium into the VOM (), and 1 cc of 100% ethanol was injected into the VOM three times (). Each injection was delivered over 1 minute through a balloon lumen and flushed with normal saline. Within 30 seconds after the first ethanol injection, AF was organized to AT (). LA local activation time mapping demonstrated macro-reentrant AT, the circuit of which involved reentry around the mitral annulus in a counterclockwise fashion (). Radiofrequency ablation at PMI for only 40 seconds terminated AT (). Bidirectional block of PMI line was achieved after ablation within CS adjunct to PMI ablation (). The repeated induction test confirmed no inducibility. The patient has been followed at outpatient clinic without recurrence of AF/AT.

Patient note:
A 62-year-old woman underwent a right mastectomy with axillary node dissection for a poorly differentiated ductal carcinoma. One month later she underwent left nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma. After 14 days, she received her first cycle of CMF as a part of her breast cancer treatment. Two weeks later, she developed progressive shortness-of-breath, dry cough, and mild fever, for which she was started on antibiotics for possible pneumonia. Two days later, her respiratory status deteriorated and she required intubation and mechanical ventilation. Because of hemodynamic instability and hypotension, she was started on inotropes and transferred to the intensive care unit. On examination, her blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, pulse of 104 beats per minute, normal temperature, and her jugular venous pressure was 8 cm above the sternal angle. Chest examinations revealed bilateral bronchial breathing and diffuse crackles. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Her initial chest x-ray showed bilateral mixed alveolar and interstitial infiltrates with volume loss (). Her arterial blood gases on room air prior to intubation, were partial pressure of oxygen 47torr, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 32torr, pH 7.49, bicarbonate 21, O2 saturation was 85%. The PAP was 36/21 mm Hg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 12 mm Hg, central venous pressure 20 cm H2O, cardiac index of 2.0 L/min/m2, and calculated PVR was 560 dynes sec/cm-5 (). A spiral CT of the chest showed a non-occlusive saddle pulmonary embolism with multiple bilateral pulmonary emboli (Figures ). She was treated with thrombolytics (100 mg rt-PA) followed by heparin without complications. She improved hemodynamically, and the inotropes were discontinued. Doppler ultrasound of the legs confirmed bilateral deep vein thrombosis. Because of persistent pulmonary infiltrates (Figures ), she underwent a fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage, which was negative. This was followed by open lung biopsy that showed loose organizing granulation tissue in the small airways consistent with BOOP (). She was treated with a pulse of steroids (1 g of methylprednisolone intravenously daily for 3 days followed by 1 mg/kg of prednisone daily). She was extubated 8 days later. She was transferred to the medical ward and was discharged home on long-term anticoagulation and steroids 2 weeks later. She had a chest x-ray before discharge, which showed near resolution of the infiltrate and restoration of lung volumes ().

Thumb pressure applied for ten seconds over the mid-anterior tibial surface of the left leg produced a 3-mm depression that persisted for 15 seconds, whereas identical pressure on the contralateral side rebounded immediately. The skin of the affected calf was warm but retained normal color, with no erythema, brawny hyperpigmentation, stasis dermatitis, blistering, or visible serpiginous superficial channels; hair distribution was symmetric, and there were no varicosities. Gentle palpation along the expected track of the femoral, popliteal, and posterior tibial vessels elicited only a diffuse dull ache without a sharply localized point of tenderness, and no palpable cord, crepitus, fluctuance, or popliteal mass was detected. Passive ankle dorsiflexion reproduced a stretching sensation but not sudden pain. Hip, knee, and ankle ranges of motion were full, distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill to all toes was under two seconds, light-touch sensation remained intact, and motor strength graded 5/5 throughout. He works as a city bus driver and had completed three consecutive double shifts earlier in the week, each involving long stretches of sitting punctuated by short walks to the depot lounge; afterward he noticed a vague heaviness in the posterior thigh that he dismissed as fatigue from climbing the yard’s metal stairs.
