A 4-year-old male was brought to the outpatient clinic complaining of vision loss. The mother noticed clumsiness, constant eye rubbing, head tilting and covering one eye, holding things close to his face, and occasional ocular pain. He was diagnosed at birth with 47, XYY syndrome by clinical findings and karyotyping. Other comorbidities were asthma diagnosed at 2 years, under control, the rest was unremarkable. There was no family history suggestive of any genetic diseases. On exam, macroscopically there were no conjunctival injection or epiphora; the ocular range of movements was normal. The pupils were round and reactive with normal reflexes. Right-eye refraction was −6.00 −1.00 × 30°, and left-eye was −5.00 −1.50 × 20°. We did not perform visual acuity and peripheral vision exams due to an underaged uncooperative patient. Under anesthesia, we observed a translucent right cornea with a horizontal diameter of 12.5 mm, a well-formed narrow anterior chamber (depth 1.04 mm), closed iridocorneal angle in 360°, round translucent crystallin protruding anteriorly, and intraocular pressure of 26 mm Hg (Fig. , ). Left eye examination evidenced a corneal horizontal diameter of 11.5 mm with an open iridocorneal angle in all four quadrants. Additionally, multiple iridian processes with a posterior embryotoxon in the temporal sector were present. The intraocular pressure on tonometry was 14 mm Hg. Fundoscopic examination revealed an excavated papilla of 90% OD and 40% OS with no other retinal or macular changes. Based on these findings, we diagnosed right microspherophakia with phacomorphic glaucoma. We performed phacoemulsification and aspiration of the lens with posterior capsulotomy and anterior vitrectomy. An intraocular lens (IOL) was implanted in the capsular bag. Despite a successful IOL position, the patient continued with increased right intraocular pressure postoperatively. Three weeks later, we decided to place an Ahmed valve implant for intraocular pressure control. During follow-up, the right intraocular pressure remained within normal limits. No additional intraocular pressure-lowering drugs were required as an adjuvant.

Patient note:
A 38-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 3, was admitted to the emergency room at the university hospital of Hassan II. She presented with a 2 day history of extreme right iliac fossa pain. She experienced heavy bleeding for one day. The last reported menstrual period was 10 weeks before presentation. She denied fevers, chills, vomiting, constipation, and diarrhea. Past medical, obstetric, gynaecological, and surgical histories were remarkable only for 3 uncomplicated live births and no history of sexually transmitted diseases or pelvic inflammatory disease. On examination, she was found to have a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, a pulse rate of 80 beats/min and a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min; she was mildly pyrexial at 37.5°C. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa. Gynaecological examination revealed a closed cervix and a right adnexal mass.
Serum level of β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) was 3175 IU/ml and complete blood cell count was significant for a leukocyte count of 14,000/mm3 with 80% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, hematocrit of 0.30, and a platelet count of 300,000. A pelvic sonogram revealed echogenic mass in the right adnexa measuring 4×5 cm with empty uterine cavity. An abdominal sonogram showed a thickening of the appendix wall associated with a free intraperitoneal fluid.
Diagnoses of appendicitis and ectopic pregnancy were entertained preoperatively, but neither could be excluded by history, physical, laboratory, and radiology examinations.
Because of the uncertainty in diagnosis, emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed through a subumbilical incision, leading to the surprising finding of concurrent ruptured ectopic pregnancy and appendicitis. She was found to have 400 ml of blood free in the pelvis with a perforated right-sided tubal pregnancy and a grossly inflamed appendix. Right salpingectomy, appendectomy and evacuation of blood clot were performed without complications. Post-operatively the patient received intravenous antibiotics; she made an excellent recovery. She was discharged from the hospital in stable condition 3 days later with a prescription for oral antibiotics. Pathologic examination of the resected segment of appendix revealed edema and inflammation of the appendix without abscess formation, consistent with early appendicitis. Pathology of the resected right fallopian tube revealed immature placental tissue and villi consistent with ectopic pregnancy.

Patient note:
An 82-year-old female with secondary post-herpetic uveitic glaucoma of the right eye presented at the Department of Ophthalmology for an elective trans-scleral laser cyclophotocoagulation. She had a history of chronic heart failure, arterial hypertension, hyperlipidemia, depression and Hodgkin’s lymphoma in remission. Her regular medications included acetylsalicylic acid, bisoprolol, isosorbide mononitrate, telmisartan, atorvastatin and escitaloprame. The patient denied having any allergies. On preoperative assessment she weighed 62 kg, her height was 162 cm and her blood pressure (BP) was 166/83 mmHg with 70/min heart rate (HR). Physical examination was unremarkable.
The patient’s orbit was anatomically normal. She was given a retrobulbar block to the right eye with 2 mL of 0.5% levobupivacaine and 2 mL of 2% lidocaine. No mydriatic agent was used. She did not move her eye during the procedure. Aspiration for blood was negative. Upon injection, no resistance was felt. 2-3 minutes after the injection, she started yawning and feeling progressively drowsy; anaesthesiology team was immediately called. 5-8 minutes after the injection she became unresponsive to verbal and tactile stimuli; her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 3. On arrival of the team she had developed bradycardia with hypotension, her HR was 40/min, BP 50/30 mmHg and blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) 85%. 10 mg of ephedrine was promptly administered intravenously (i.v.) with no significant effect, continued by 3 i.v. doses of 0.1 mg adrenaline 2 minutes later. Concurrently the patient developed respiratory arrest, her SpO2 had fallen to 54%, BP was 163/100 mmHg with HR 93/min. A bolus of 200 mL intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) was given. Anaesthesia was induced with 50 mg of propofol, the patient was intubated and mechanically ventilated, and her vitals had stabilized (SpO2 98%, BP 113/60 mmHg, HR 92/min). She was additionally sedated with 5 mg of midazolam. Because of persistent hypotension (RR 92/58), 500 mL of hydroxyethyl starch (HES 130/0.4) in isotonic sodium chloride solution was also administered.
Surgery was cancelled and the patient was relocated to the ICU. She was additionally sedated with midazolam and propofol, then gradually shifted through supportive ventilation techniques to spontaneous ventilation and extubated 6 hours after admission. There was no need for vasoactive support, oxygen or fluid replacement therapy. Blood test results were within normal range. Her BP was 140/60 mmHg, HR 71/min, SpO2 95%, without additional oxygen. Her GCS score was 15. The next day she was discharged to the Department of Ophthalmology, where the intended procedure was performed under general anaesthesia. The patient was discharged home 6 days later, she was stable and had not suffered any consequences from the adverse reaction.
Informed consent has been obtained from the patient to use the data presented in this case report.
The research has been complied with all the relevant national regulations, institutional policies and in accordance the tenets of the Helsinki Declaration.

Patient note:
An 86-year-old man who lives alone in a one-story bungalow and still insists on mowing his own lawn was brought to the medical intensive care intake area by advanced life-support ambulance after a neighbor noticed him sitting on his porch looking pale and slightly breathless late this afternoon; according to the neighbor he had complained earlier of a “touch of the flu,” took two acetaminophen tablets, and lay down but received no prescription medications, inhalers, intravenous fluids, or supplemental oxygen until the paramedics arrived. His past history, obtained from a well-kept wallet card and verified by electronic chart review, lists treated hypertension and cataract extraction only; he has never required organ transplantation, dialysis, chemotherapy, chronic corticosteroids, or biologic agents and has no record of cirrhosis, chronic lung disease, advanced heart failure, or immunodeficiency. Paramedics found him seated upright, conversant though mildly confused about the exact date, with an initial automated blood pressure of 142/82 mm Hg that was reproduced on a second cuff; pulse oximetry on ambient air showed 90 %, so they placed a simple face mask attached to the truck blender delivering 38 % inspired oxygen, started one peripheral line without running fluids, and gave no bronchodilators, diuretics, antibiotics, analgesics, or vasopressors during the eight-minute transport. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—and before any emergency department intervention—the first complete set of vitals was captured: oral temperature 98.5 °F, non-invasive blood pressure 140/80 mm Hg confirmed with the manual sphygmomanometer, regular pulse 95 beats per minute displayed on telemetry, and a visually counted respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute without accessory-muscle use. The patient opened his eyes to voice, answered most orientation questions but stumbled on the month, and obeyed two-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 14 in the absence of ethanol or sedatives. Skin was warm and dry with brisk capillary refill; no mottling or peripheral cyanosis was present. Neck veins were not distended at 30°, cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1, single physiologic S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Breath sounds were vesicular throughout with a few scattered end-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases; percussion remained resonant and there was no wheeze. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender with active bowel sounds, and there was no flank costovertebral angle pain. Extremities showed no edema, clubbing, or tenderness, and a brief neurologic screen demonstrated equal pupils, symmetric strength, and intact coordination when he touched his nose. A right radial arterial specimen drawn nine minutes after stretcher placement—while the face mask continued to deliver the same 38 % oxygen—yielded a pH of 7.43, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 79 mm Hg; end-tidal CO₂ on waveform capnography was 34 mm Hg. Point-of-care basic metabolic panel returned sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, the last value matching his outpatient baseline recorded at a primary-care visit two months earlier. A complete blood count drawn from the same stick showed white blood cells 12 800 /mm³ with 80 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 34 %, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, and platelets 206 000 /µL. Venous lactate measured 1.9 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before any hospital therapy revealed mild bilateral bibasilar infiltrates and elevated hemidiaphragms without pleural effusion, cardiomegaly, or pneumothorax. Twelve-lead electrocardiography performed during the arterial draw demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 96 beats per minute, PR interval 180 ms, QRS 94 ms, and nonspecific lateral T-wave flattening but no acute ST-segment elevation or depression. Bedside focused cardiac ultrasound showed a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle with an inferior vena cava diameter of 1.4 cm that collapsed more than 50 % on inspiration, suggesting euvolemia rather than congestion. Bladder scan revealed 120 mL of urine, and he reported having voided shortly before the ambulance arrived. Importantly, during the thirty minutes between EMS arrival and acceptance by the critical-care team, he received no intravenous crystalloids, antibiotics, bronchodilators, diuretics, vasopressors, corticosteroids, or transfusions; thus the physiologic and laboratory data—temperature 98.5 °F, systolic pressure 140 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 80 mm Hg, heart rate 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, arterial pH 7.43, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, hematocrit 34 %, white blood cell count 12 800 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 38 %, and arterial oxygen tension 79 mm Hg—represent his untreated presentation for what is presumed to be early community-acquired pneumonia complicated by mild hypoxemia and transient confusion.

Patient note:
A 64-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with pulmonary valve stenosis (PVS) in childhood underwent open surgical commissurotomy and infundibulectomy at the age of 35. Significant residual pulmonary regurgitation (PR) was documented at follow-up. After remaining asymptomatic for years, she was referred to our centre following rapid progression of exertional dyspnoea and recent onset of effort-related chest pain.
Physical examination revealed good general condition, mild hypertension (147/81 mmHg), heart rate of 80 b.p.m., and oxygen saturation of 98%. There were no signs of heart failure and the cardiovascular examination showed a short, low-pitched diastolic murmur over the left upper sternal border.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, right bundle branch block, and frequent supraventricular premature complexes. A chest X-ray revealed signs of dilated right heart and a prominent PA (Figure ).
Our differential diagnosis included progressive PR with right ventricular (RV) failure, RV restrictive physiology with diastolic dysfunction, exercise desaturation in the presence of a patent foramen ovale, progressive PH with RV failure, and LMCA or compression of the left mainstem bronchus by PA dilatation.
To evaluate these potential diagnoses, we first performed an echocardiogram that showed moderate right ventricle and atrial dilatation with normal RV systolic function (TAPSE of 19 mm and fractional area change of 43%), significant PR with diastolic retrograde flow from the main PA, pressure half-time of 209 ms and a PR index (ratio of PR duration/diastole duration) of 80%, normal RV outflow gradient (see , Videos S1 and S2), mild tricuspid regurgitation with an estimated RV systolic pressure of 34 mmHg, and a normal-sized inferior vena cava. No evidence of RV restrictive physiology was observed.
We then performed cardiopulmonary exercise testing. The patient did not develop any symptoms and oxygen saturation remained constant throughout the test, but functional capacity was poor, achieving 1.2 METS. Age-predicted maximal heart rate attained was 65%, and percent-predicted peak oxygen consumption was 23%. During the test, she developed frequent exercise-induced ventricular premature beats. Consequently, we performed a 24-h Holter monitor, which showed frequent atrial and ventricular premature beats and a short run of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) (Figure ).
We next performed a coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) to evaluate potential mechanical complications caused by PA dilatation. No compression of the left main bronchus was seen. Coronary artery anomalies and significant coronary artery disease were ruled out. However, the CCTA showed extrinsic compression of the proximal segment of LMCA caused by an enlarged PA (60 mm diameter in systole) (Figure ), and a takeoff angle of the LMCA of 26° (defined by a line parallel to the border of the left coronary sinus and a line parallel to the LMCA) (Figure ). A coronary angiogram confirmed the diagnosis and the right-sided heart catheterization showed normal PA pressure (see , Video S3).
The patient underwent surgical PAA repair along with pulmonary valve replacement with a conduit constructed intraoperatively composed of a 25 mm bioprosthetic Carpentier-Edwards valve within a Dacron tube graft. As complete decompression of LMCA was visually documented intraoperatively, coronary revascularization surgery was unnecessary. Intraoperative findings showed a thickened, trileaflet pulmonary valve, and the anatomopathological examination of the PA wall showed changes suggestive of cystic medial necrosis.
A second CCTA, performed 2 weeks after surgery, showed the PAA had decreased in size (Figure ) and LMCA compression had disappeared (Figure ). An exercise stress test performed 4 months after surgery showed functional capacity had improved, and no ventricular premature beats were observed. Over a 9-year follow-up, the patient has remained asymptomatic and functional capacity is good.

A 37-year-old, active Caucasian man was admitted to our hospital’s acute medical unit with a 1-week history of erythematous painful swelling of his right elbow and arm. He had no history of fever and rash. His systemic review was generally unremarkable. He worked as an engineer but also did judo tutoring in the evenings. He was normally fit and well, had no family history of thrombosis, and had not undergone surgery recently or in the past. He was not on any regular medication, denied any current or previous history of recreational drug use, and had no known history of drug allergy.
After a routine judo training session, he noticed acute onset of a red, swollen, and painful right arm. He presented to his general practitioner (GP), who made a diagnosis of cellulitis with possible trauma-related musculoskeletal injury. He was subsequently commenced on analgesics and antibiotics. About 1 week later, he attended a follow-up examination with his GP, who immediately referred him to the hospital because he showed no improvement. On admission, his temperature was 37.3 °C, his blood pressure was 124/74 mmHg, his pulse rate was 80 beats/minute, his respiratory rate was 16 breaths/minute, and his oxygen saturation was 96 % on room air.
His physical examination revealed noticeable swelling and redness from his right elbow to his shoulder as well as mild erythema and tenderness of the affected area. No superficially engorged vein was noted on his chest. All of his systemic examinations were essentially within normal limits. All of his blood workup results, including the coagulation profile, were unremarkable, except for a slightly elevated C-reactive protein level of 26 mg/l (normal range <5 mg/l).
The working differential diagnoses of possible olecranon bursitis and right arm cellulitis to rule out DVT were made. The patient was then commenced on parenteral antibiotics and low molecular weight heparin pending further investigations. The x-rays of his right elbow, right arm, and chest showed no abnormalities; however, venous Doppler ultrasonography revealed a right axillary DVT with extension into the cephalic and brachial veins.
Thrombophilia screening was performed, and the patient was started on warfarin with a plan to discharge him to home with community-based anticoagulant clinic follow-up. While waiting for discharge, he was moved to a medical outlier ward on the diabetes ward due to bed pressures. The consultant on the ward reviewed the patient’s case and made a diagnosis of PSS, and an urgent requests for consultation was sent to the vascular surgical team for review of further management.
The vascular team organized catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) to clear the patients’ extensive thrombosis. A prethrombolysis venogram (Fig. ) with extensive thrombosis showed marked reduction in thrombus load within the axillary and subclavian veins after a postlysis venogram (Fig. ) was performed. Following thrombolysis, an early thoracic outlet decompression via a transaxillary first rib resection was undertaken to reduce the risk of recurrent thrombosis and long-term morbidity. The BMJ Best Practice treatment guideline for thoracic outlet syndrome [] provides a good illustration of this procedure. The patient had an uneventful postoperative recovery. He was subsequently anticoagulated and was discharged to home with a target international normalized ratio of 2–3. A few weeks after his surgical procedure, the patient was followed in the outpatient clinic. The swelling of his right arm had completely almost resolved. The patient reported no postoperative complications.

Patient note:
A 38-year-old female patient was diagnosed with clinical Stage IIIC (cT2cN3M0) infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the left breast with left supraclavicular lymph nodes metastases. She was treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy consisting of docetaxel and doxorubicin. After six cycles of chemotherapy, the supraclavicular lymph node was not palpable with a partial response of the breast cancer and the axillary nodes. She underwent a curative resection for the breast cancer, and the final pathologic stage was ypStageIIIC (ypT2N3M0). Immunohistochemistry showed negative staining for the estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epithelial growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). Histological and nuclear grades were III/III and 3/3, respectively, and extensive endolymphatic tumor emboli were present. Adjuvant chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, and 5-fluorouracil (CMF) was commenced, but on her visit for the third cycle she complained of sudden-onset right chest pain and cough. Her chest X-ray was within normal limits (). Ten days later, she felt right inspiratory chest pain and was referred to the emergency department. She complained of dyspnea on exertion (DOE), cough, and a mild febrile sense, however, she denied the high fever, sputum, pitting edema, or orthopnea. Her initial vital signs were a heart rate of 97 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20 per minute, blood pressure of 133/68 mmHg, body temperature of 36.5℃, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Signs of respiratory distress were not definite. Fine crackles in the right upper lung field were present on chest auscultation but a pleural friction rub was not present. A chest X-ray demonstrated patchy consolidation on the right upper lung field () and computed tomography (CT) showed right upper lobe (RUL) patchy consolidation with ill-defined small ground glass opacities (GGO) in the RUL and right lower lobe (RLL) (, respectively). The differential diagnosis from the radiological study was pneumonia with a fungal etiology but we could not rule out a bacterial etiology. The white blood cell count was 5,800/mm3, and the segmented neutrophil portion was 76.4%. The C-reactive protein level was 0.86 mg/dL (reference range, 0-0.5 mg/dL) and there was no evidence of pulmonary thromboembolism on chest CT.
We started empirical antibiotics with third generation cephalosporin and macrolide under the impression of community acquired pneumonia, but the follow-up chest CT at 1 week showed an increased extent of RUL patchy consolidation (, ). Furthermore, subjective symptoms of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain rapidly aggravated. No microorganisms were identified on the initial respiratory specimen culture. Findings from chest X-rays and chest CT suggested fungal pneumonia, however, the patient had not experienced severe neutropenia for several months, and there were no predisposing clinical factors favoring a diagnosis of fungal pneumonia. We considered the probability of lymphangitic metastatic carcinoma or a fungal infection such as aspergillosis or mucormycosis. Therefore, we performed a video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy for an accurate pathological diagnosis before administering antifungal agents. We thought it might be difficult to obtain a differential diagnosis using a percutaneous needle biopsy, because the nature of the lesion was infiltrative consolidation, not a mass.
We performed a wedge resection of the RUL. The specimen was 6×3×3 cm, and a gross examination of the sections showed focal brownish discoloration of lung parenchyma without definite evidence of necrosis, tumor, hemorrhage, or a calcified area. A microscopic examination showed metastatic carcinoma with extensive endolymphatic tumor emboli and hemorrhagic infarctions (, ). In contrast, Gram staining revealed no microorganisms and Gomori's methenamine silver and periodic-acid Schiff stains revealed no fungal hyphae. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis-polymerase chain reaction result was also negative.
We confirmed that the patient was not under infection, so we discontinued antimicrobial agents, enrolled the patient to the clinical trial and started first-line palliative chemotherapy consisting of ixabepilone (Ixempra™; Bristol-Myers Squibb, New York, USA) and capecitabine (Xeloda®; Roche, Basel, Switzerland), as the disease had relapsed just 4 months after neoadjuvant docetaxel and doxorubicin and during adjuvant CMF chemotherapy (). This study was supported by a grant of the Korean Health Technology R&D Project, Ministry of Health & Welfare, Republic of Korea (A110448). After chemotherapy, the size of the consolidative lesion in the RUL and the extent of focal GGO in RUL and RLL decreased markedly. The pleuritic chest pain and DOE also improved. Currently, after 17 months, she is under palliative chemotherapy and regular follow-up with partial response to the disease ().

A 55-year-old man with known longstanding hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2 presented with acute onset of dizziness, slurred speech, and unsteady gait. Meanwhile, he also showed spasmodic crying and laughing on examination. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain performed 36 hours after the onset of symptoms revealed acute, bilateral, symmetric, cerebral peduncular infarcts (BCPI), which showed increased signal intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with low values on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map (Figures and ), in line with acute infarction. T1-weighted images (T1WI) demonstrated the lesion mainly involving the central portion of the cerebral peduncle with low signal intensity (). Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) disclosed the vertebrobasilar artery occlusion and the absence of flow signals of bilateral PCA without collateral patency of the posterior communicating artery (). The patient was given antiplatelet and hypervolemic therapy, with no further deterioration of his condition. He was transferred to the rehabilitation ward for rehabilitation treatment of swallowing function twenty days after his admission.

Patient note:
A 61-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease managed with inhaled tiotropium, poorly controlled hypertension, and compensated alcoholic fatty-liver disease was found by his roommate at dawn sitting upright in bed, tachypneic and complaining of sharp pleuritic discomfort along the right lower hemithorax that had worsened overnight after two days of productive cough streaked with rust-colored sputum. The roommate attempted to bring him to the bathroom but noted the patient became light-headed and briefly leaned against the wall, prompting activation of emergency medical services. Paramedics arrived eight minutes later to discover him speaking in short sentences, using accessory muscles, and saturating 86 % on room air; they attached a snug-fitting oronasal interface connected to a portable blower that generated a fixed distending pressure of 8 cm H₂O while entraining wall oxygen through a blender set to 0.38, after which the pulse oximeter rose into the low nineties. No endotracheal instrumentation, bag-mask ventilation, intravenous crystalloid, vasopressor, bronchodilator, steroid, or antibiotic was administered during the twelve-minute transport. On stretcher arrival to the emergency department—and before any hospital interventions—the patient remained seated forward, hands braced on the rails, breathing spontaneously through the same positive-pressure circuit with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute. Initial vitals obtained via automated cuff and confirmed within three minutes by a right radial arterial line showed blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg with a mean of 87 mm Hg, heart rate 102 beats per minute in regular rhythm, temperature 38.1 °C temporal, and peripheral saturation oscillating between 91 % and 93 % on the documented 38 % inspired oxygen. Skin was warm without mottling, capillary refill two seconds, and jugular veins were flat at 45°. Neurologic assessment prior to any analgesic or sedative revealed that he opened eyes spontaneously, conversed but was intermittently disoriented to date, and obeyed commands briskly, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 14 (E4 V4 M6); pupils were 3 mm and briskly reactive, and there were no lateralizing deficits. Chest examination revealed asymmetric expansion with diminished breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower lung zone, faint wheezing throughout expiration, and adequate chest rise around the mask seal; measured peak airway pressure on the transport device was 12 cm H₂O during inspiration. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was soft and nontender with the liver edge palpable two fingerbreadths below the costal margin; no splenomegaly, shifting dullness, or hepatomegaly was present. Extremities showed scattered ecchymoses over the forearms from recent falls but no petechiae; pedal pulses were 2+. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the secondary survey immediately returned 70 mL of concentrated amber urine. The roommate, who keeps meticulous fluid logs because of the patient’s prior nephrolithiasis, provided documentation indicating three voids totaling approximately 1 120 mL over the preceding twenty-four hours. Five minutes after arterial cannulation, while ventilatory settings and inspired fraction remained unchanged, the first blood gas revealed pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, bicarbonate 21 mEq/L, lactate 2.4 mmol/L, and PaO₂ 77 mm Hg. Simultaneous laboratory studies—drawn before any bronchodilator, corticosteroid, antibiotic, antipyretic, intravenous fluid, or vasoactive agent was started—demonstrated sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, glucose 148 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL compared with a baseline of 1.2 mg/dL from a primary-care visit three months earlier. The complete blood count returned leukocytes 17.6 × 10³/µL with 11 % band forms, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, and a platelet count of 94 000 /µL indicating moderate thrombocytopenia without prior documentation of such. Hepatic panel showed aspartate aminotransferase 65 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 172 U/L, total bilirubin 1.48 mg/dL with predominantly conjugated fraction, and an international normalized ratio of 1.2. High-sensitivity troponin was undetectable, and C-reactive protein measured 156 mg/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained while he remained on the non-invasive circuit depicted a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, hyperinflated lung fields consistent with emphysema, and no pleural effusion; no tracheal tube or gastric tube was seen. Focused cardiac ultrasound showed a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle without pericardial effusion, and the inferior vena cava collapsed more than 50 % with inspiration, suggesting relative euvolemia. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram recorded sinus tachycardia at 104 beats per minute with low-voltage QRS complexes but no ischemic changes. Up to the precise moment all physiologic measurements and laboratory data above were captured, the patient had received neither antimicrobial therapy nor systemic steroids, remained awake and interactive, maintained spontaneous ventilation through the positive-pressure mask supplying 0.38 inspired oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 77 mm Hg, preserved an arterial pressure of 116/72 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, exhibited moderate thrombocytopenia, mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, early renal insufficiency yet non-oliguric daily urine output, and demonstrated mild encephalopathy likely multifactorial from hypoxemia, infection, and chronic alcohol use.

Patient note:
A 65-year-old woman was seen in the peri-operative consultation clinic ten days before a scheduled elective laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy with primary anastomosis for recurrent uncomplicated diverticulitis that has caused three admissions over the past eighteen months; the colorectal surgeon anticipates a two-hour pneumoperitoneum under general anesthesia with an overnight stay on the surgical floor if bowel function returns promptly. She arrived unaccompanied after parking in the adjacent garage, walked the 150 m corridor to the examination suite at her usual pace, and stated that she routinely completes a two-mile loop around her neighborhood each morning pushing a lightweight stroller for her grandchild without pausing for breath, chest tightness, or lower-extremity swelling. Twelve years ago she experienced a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction attributed to an 80 % lesion in the mid–left anterior descending artery that was treated with a drug-eluting stent; since then there have been no emergency visits for cardiac symptoms, and a pharmacologic sestamibi stress study performed six months earlier as part of routine surveillance demonstrated a small fixed anterior scar without inducible ischemia at 8 metabolic equivalents. Her current cardiovascular medications include metoprolol succinate 50 mg each morning, aspirin 81 mg daily, and rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly; she has never required nitrates, ranolazine, or revascularization beyond the index stent. Four years ago she had a transient episode of expressive aphasia and right hand numbness that resolved within one hour; magnetic resonance imaging suggested a left frontal cortical ischemic focus, carotid duplex showed mild (<40 %) bilateral internal carotid plaque, and she was started on clopidogrel 75 mg daily in addition to intensified lipid management. Since that event she has had no further focal neurologic complaints, dizziness, visual disturbance, or gait imbalance, and she continues to perform daily crossword puzzles without difficulty. Other chronic conditions include well-controlled primary hypertension diagnosed in her fifties and treated with amlodipine 5 mg, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus with a most recent hemoglobin A1c of 6.3 % managed on metformin 500 mg twice daily (she has never been advised to start injectable glucose-lowering agents), post-menopausal osteoporosis on weekly alendronate, and seasonal allergic rhinitis. She does not recall ever being told she had a weak heart, has never used loop diuretics, and denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or needing extra pillows. Surgical history is notable only for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 40 without complications. She quit cigarette smoking 20 years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of red wine on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Family history reveals a father who underwent coronary bypass at 72 and a mother with a stroke at 79; there is no familial colon cancer. Review of systems today is negative for palpitations, syncope, claudication, melena, weight loss, or fevers. After five minutes seated, vital signs are temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg in the right arm, pulse 64 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing room air; body mass index is 29 kg/m². Neck veins are not distended at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, and auscultation reveals a crisp S1 and S2 without gallops, murmurs, or rubs. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. Abdomen is soft with mild left lower-quadrant tenderness but no rebound, guarding, or masses; there is a well-healed right subcostal scar from her prior surgery. Extremities show no clubbing or edema, and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ bilaterally. Focused neurologic examination demonstrates intact cranial nerves, fluent speech, 5/5 strength, normal sensation, symmetric reflexes, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour before the visit document hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 243 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 58 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose sampled concurrently is 112 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram performed today shows normal sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute with Q waves in V2–V3 consistent with prior infarction and no ST-segment deviations or T-wave inversions. Upright posteroanterior chest radiograph reveals clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Airway assessment by anesthesia identifies a Mallampati class II oropharynx, inter-incisor distance of 4.2 cm, full cervical extension, and stable dentition. She has been instructed to continue beta-blocker, aspirin, clopidogrel, antihypertensive agents, and statin through the morning of surgery, to withhold metformin only on the day of operation, and to stop solid food eight hours before induction while allowing clear liquids until two hours pre-procedure. The operating team reviewed the potential need for conversion to an open approach, postoperative ileus, anastomotic leak, and cardiovascular or neurologic complications; the patient demonstrated understanding, voiced no additional concerns, and is eager to proceed.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old male was admitted to the Department of Cardiology, Daejeon St. Mary’s Hospital (Daejeon, Korea), for the evaluation of exertional dyspnea (New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class III), palpitations, and bilateral leg pitting edema for several months. His electrocardiography and Holter monitoring showed atrial fibrillation and rare premature ventricular complexes. He underwent transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), which showed RCM with biatrial enlargement and small pericardial effusion (A–D). His coronary artery angiogram was normal and other secondary causes of RCM were not found. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images revealed normal left ventricle (LV) chamber size, borderline diffuse left ventricular hypertrophy and very large atria. Contrast enhanced CMR images demonstrated extensive transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in the apical wall and mid myocardial patchy LGE in the ventricular septum (E–H).
We recommended clinical evaluation and genetic counseling for his family members because he presented a family history of heart disease, with two affected daughters. The proband’s second daughter had mild exertional chest discomfort. Her TTE showed asymmetric septal hypertrophy of the LV and a mildly dilated left atrium (LA) (A–D). Her diastolic dysfunction was grade I according to the American Society of Echocardiography and the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging criteria []. The proband’s fourth daughter also had asymmetric septal hypertrophy of the LV, with mild enlargement of the LA (E–H). CMR images of the two daughters showed asymmetric septal hypertrophy of the LV, consistent with a diagnosis of HCM. LGE was not found in either daughter.
To resolve the potential genetic cause of cardiomyopathy in a Korean family (I-1, II-2, and II-4 in A), the proband’s genomic DNA was analyzed by whole exome sequencing (WES). The exomic DNA of the proband was enriched using Agilent’s SureSelect XT Human All Exon v5 (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), and paired-end sequencing was conducted on an Illumina HiSeq2500 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) for the detection of variants, given the suspicion of familial disease. Base calling, alignment, variant calling, annotation, and quality control reporting were performed using a GATK Best Practices workflow for germline short variant discovery and were manually reviewed by medical laboratory geneticists. In particular, the annotation of the identified variants with respect to the results of their mutation in the reported genes was estimated using the dbNSFP [] and Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor []. By estimating sequence quality along all sequences, 5973 million reads were generated from the proband. A percentage of bases above the average of 30× was achieved for 92.3% of the target region, and the mean read depth (×) was 110. WES of the proband identified five heterozygous variants within the coding region of each gene as candidate causes of autosomal dominant inherited heart diseases with a population allele frequency within the Genome Aggregation Database < 0.001. To determine which variant was the cause of cardiomyopathy in the affected family members, Sanger sequencing was performed additionally. As a result, Sanger sequencing confirmed the presence of a heterozygous frameshift mutation (NM_000256.3:c.3313_3314insGG; p.Ala1105Glyfs*85) in MYBPC3 in the proband (I-1) and his affected daughters (second (II-2) and fourth (II-4)), but not in his unaffected granddaughter (III-3) (B). The variant is not listed in public genome databases from gnomAD (; accessed on 8 November 2020) and the Korean Reference Genome Database (; accessed on 8 November 2020). Although the four remaining variants (KALRN: NM_007064.5: c.1702C>T, p.Pro568Ser; KCNH2: NM_000238.4:c.442C>T, p.Arg148Trp; SKI: NM_003036.4: c.30T>G, p.Cys10Trp; TTN: NM_133378.4: c.54293T>C, p.Ile18098Thr) were the likely candidates, there was no exact correlation between the genotype of these variants and the clinical phenotype in the proband and his family members as determined by Sanger sequencing. Therefore, the MYBPC3 frameshift mutation seemed to be the pathogenic variant.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman is evaluated in the pre-operative bay just before transfer to the operating theatre for an elective four-port laparoscopic fundoplication to treat long-standing, proton-pump-inhibitor-refractory gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She walked from the visitor garage unaided, climbed a flight of stairs to registration, and has spent the morning seated in the waiting room reading the newspaper, reporting that she continues to manage household chores, garden for an hour most afternoons, and complete a two-kilometre stroll after dinner with her spouse; thus her baseline activity remains intact. The forthcoming procedure will be her first in more than a decade, and she confirms that she has not undergone any operation or endoscopic intervention in the past four weeks. Review of her recent medical course reveals that twenty-one days ago she awoke with transient slurred speech and mild facial droop; brain MRI demonstrated a small right pontine diffusion-positive lesion without large-vessel occlusion, and her deficits resolved within forty-eight hours after antiplatelet therapy was started. She required no thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, or rehabilitation stay and was discharged home on day three with favourable neurologic examination. No additional cerebrovascular events have occurred since, but the episode places today’s surgery within the thirty-day window of an ischaemic stroke. Past medical history is also notable for moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributed to a forty-pack-year smoking history; she quit twelve years ago and now uses a tiotropium inhaler each morning plus salbutamol as needed, reporting one mild exacerbation last winter that was managed in the outpatient setting. She denies any history of systolic dysfunction, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, peripheral oedema, or prior echocardiograms suggesting reduced ejection fraction. There have been no recent chest infections, and she has been afebrile with stable respiratory symptoms over the past several months. Skeletal integrity has been intact: she has never fractured her hip, pelvis, or long bones, never worn a cast or brace, and has suffered no multi-system trauma. She has not been confined to bed for any reason and remains fully ambulatory at home and in the community. Vascular access consists only of a single 18-gauge peripheral cannula placed this morning in the left dorsum of the hand; she has never had a peripherally inserted central catheter, chemo port, or tunnelled dialysis line. Examination of the lower limbs shows equal calf circumferences, warm skin, easily compressible pretibial tissue without pitting, and an absence of tortuous superficial channels. She recalls no episodes of spontaneous leg swelling, pleuritic chest pain, or imaging-confirmed venous or pulmonary clot, and there is no family lore of thrombotic disease in first-degree relatives. Nevertheless, five years ago a haematology consultation for mildly prolonged prothrombin time uncovered heterozygosity for the G20210A mutation in the prothrombin gene; lifelong anticoagulation was not advised given the absence of clinical thrombosis, but the finding is documented on her problem list. Serologic testing at that time was negative for factor V Leiden, lupus anticoagulant, or anticardiolipin antibody, and homocysteine concentration was within reference limits. She carries no diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, myocardial infarction, connective-tissue disorder, or endocrine abnormality, and her only chronic medications are omeprazole 40 mg twice daily for reflux, tiotropium 18 µg inhaled once daily, salbutamol 100 µg two puffs as needed (last use three days ago), low-dose aspirin started after the recent pontine infarct, and cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily. She abstains from alcohol, denies illicit drug use, and has maintained a body mass index of 29 kg m⁻². On arrival her vital signs were temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 96 % breathing ambient air. Airway evaluation reveals a Mallampati class II view, full cervical range of motion, three-finger thyro-mental distance, and secure dentition. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, cardiac auscultation discloses crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs or gallops, and peripheral pulses are 2+ bilaterally. Lungs exhibit scattered end-expiratory wheezes that clear with forced exhalation and no crackles. Abdomen is soft and non-tender with mild epigastric fullness but no organomegaly. Neurological screening confirms intact cranial nerves, symmetric strength in all extremities, normal heel-to-shin testing, and no residual facial weakness or dysarthria. Laboratory studies drawn two hours ago show haemoglobin 13.2 g dL⁻¹, platelet count 210 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 7.1 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.84 mg dL⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 24 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, and international normalised ratio 1.1, consistent with prior results; activated partial thromboplastin time is 31 s. Twelve-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats min⁻¹ with preserved intervals and no acute ST–T changes. Two-dimensional echocardiogram [Figures and ] revealed a giant LA measuring 15.2 cm × 10.1 cm, an area of 170 cm2, and a volume of 1326 mL. RA was 13.1 cm × 7.05 cm, with a volume of 760 ml. The mitral valve was thickened with a planimetered mitral valve area of 1.2 cm2. The mean LA-left ventricular diastolic gradient was 4.5 mm Hg. The left ventricular size was small with an ejection fraction of 60%. The right ventricle was small with right ventricular dysfunction which was evident from a reduced tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion of 10 mm and a right ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. Tricuspid valve was thickened with noncoaptating leaflets and severe tricuspid regurgitation as evident from vena contracta width of 0.8 cm and hepatic vein systolic flow reversal [Video –].

Patient note:
A 55-year-old right-handed male presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He was teaching a karate class when a coworker saw him fall to the ground. He spontaneously regained consciousness after a few seconds but was confused for ∼15–20 min. He had no recollection of the event, and was hemodynamically stable and neurologically intact. He denied illicit drug use. Vitals, physical examination and laboratory studies were within normal limits. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with normal PR and QT intervals and no ST-T wave changes. He was on no AV blocking agents. Head CT showed no intracranial bleed or mass lesion.
He had a history of five similar episodes in the past. During the last episode, he had been noted to have sinus arrest on telemetry and underwent single atrial lead pacemaker placement. The pacemaker was programmed to AAI mode. AV conduction was tested and was normal. Coronary angiogram showed no evidence of coronary artery disease. EEG had been minimally abnormal with left temporal theta slowing, suggestive of an area of neurophysiologic dysfunction, but no epileptiform activity was noted. He had no history of febrile seizures, central nervous system infection or cranial trauma.
The patient was admitted for further work up. Continuous EEG monitoring was ordered to evaluate for seizure activity. At ∼7 min and 36 s, the patient started to have recurrent automatisms and became unresponsive, with the EEG showing complex partial seizure activity emanating from the left anterior temporal region with continued post-ictal right temporal delta slowing. The seizure lasted ∼1 min. The simultaneous ECG lead demonstrated heart rate slowing toward the end of the seizure episode, with the rhythm changing from sinus to atrially paced at 60 beats min−1 with 1:1 conduction, to atrially paced with 2:1 AV block, followed by complete heart block for 4 s, followed by resumption of the baseline atrially paced rhythm with 1:1 conduction (Fig. ).
Cardiac electrophysiology recommended treating the seizure episodes before considering upgrade of the pacemaker to a dual-chamber device. The patient was started and subsequently discharged on levetiracetam. More than 15 months later, he has had no seizures or syncopal events.

Patient note:
A 54-year-old man with a background of well-controlled mild hyperlipidemia, no chronic cardiac, pulmonary, renal, or hepatic illness, and no history of immunosuppressive conditions or therapies (including HIV infection, malignancy, chemotherapy, organ transplantation, or long-term corticosteroid use) was brought to the high-dependency area of the emergency department after collapsing at home with sudden onset pleuritic right-sided chest discomfort, a dry cough, and lightheadedness that had begun roughly six hours earlier while trimming hedges; he denied antecedent trauma, recent surgery, long-haul travel, immobilization, or use of anticoagulants and takes only a daily statin. According to the patient and his spouse, he had been completely well the previous evening, ate dinner normally, and went to bed at his usual time; he awoke at dawn with mild substernal tightness that progressed to sharp pain on inspiration and he became increasingly short of breath while walking from the driveway to the kitchen. Emergency medical technicians found him sitting upright on the porch, speaking in full sentences but visibly anxious, with fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 82–85 % while breathing ambient air. They applied a Venturi mask that, when checked on arrival, was delivering approximately 47 % inspired oxygen, established a single peripheral 18-gauge cannula but administered no intravenous fluids, bronchodilators, analgesics, antipyretics, or anticoagulants during the twelve-minute transport. Upon stretcher placement in the resuscitation bay—and before any hospital therapy was initiated—vital signs were documented as oral temperature 37.9 °C, automated blood pressure 130/73 mm Hg corroborated by a manual cuff, radial pulse 93 beats per minute in regular sinus rhythm, and respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute without audible wheeze or stridor though mild intercostal retraction was noted. He was alert, oriented to time, place, person, and situation, answered questions appropriately, opened his eyes spontaneously, and obeyed complex commands, establishing a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 in the absence of sedatives, intoxicants, or neurologic deficit. Skin examination revealed warm, dry extremities without cyanosis or mottling; capillary refill was under two seconds, and no peripheral edema was present. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a crisp S₁ and single S₂ with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lung fields were clear to percussion; breath sounds were slightly diminished on the right posterior base with a faint late inspiratory crackle but no bronchial breathing or pleural rub. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and without organomegaly; bowel sounds were present. There was no spinal or costovertebral angle tenderness, and distal pulses were symmetric and strong. A radial arterial sample drawn within ten minutes of bay entry while he remained on the 47 % mask revealed a pH of 7.46, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 65 mm Hg, indicating a mild respiratory alkalosis accompanied by significant hypoxemia relative to the delivered oxygen fraction. Laboratory studies obtained from the same arterial stick showed serum sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 3.3 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.85 mg/dL, the latter essentially unchanged from a routine employment screen eight months earlier and arguing against intrinsic or acute prerenal dysfunction. Hematologic indices demonstrated a hematocrit of 40 % with hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, white blood cell count 10 100 cells/mm³ with 74 % neutrophils and no bandemia, and platelets 248 000/µL; coagulation parameters were within reference range. High-sensitivity troponin measured on arrival was undetectable, and serum D-dimer was pending at the time the decision to admit was made. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before any anticoagulation or diuretic therapy showed a subtle wedge-shaped opacity in the right lower lobe without cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, or obvious infiltrate; the pulmonary vasculature appeared mildly pruned and the hemidiaphragms were sharp. Electrocardiography performed fifteen minutes after arrival demonstrated sinus rhythm at 92 beats per minute with an incomplete right bundle-branch block pattern and T-wave inversion in V₁ through V₃ but no ST-segment elevation or depression. Focused bedside cardiac ultrasound revealed a normal-sized left ventricle with preserved systolic function, a mildly dilated right ventricle with interventricular septal flattening during systole, and no pericardial effusion; inferior vena cava diameter measured 2.1 cm with less than 50 % collapse on inspiration, and no deep venous thrombus was visualized in the bilateral femoral veins. Lower-extremity examination showed no calf swelling, tenderness, or Homan sign. Urine output was not available because no Foley catheter had been placed prior to imaging, and the patient had voided spontaneously once at home earlier in the morning. No analgesics, anticoagulants, thrombolytics, vasopressors, intravenous crystalloids, antibiotics, corticosteroids, bronchodilators, or antipyretic agents had been administered at the time the above physiologic and laboratory data were captured, ensuring that the blood pressure of 130/73 mm Hg, heart rate 93 beats per minute, temperature 37.9 °C, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, arterial pH 7.46, serum sodium 135 mmol/L, serum potassium 3.3 mmol/L, serum creatinine 0.85 mg/dL, hematocrit 40 %, white blood cell count 10 100 /mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 47 %, and arterial oxygen tension 65 mm Hg represent his untreated presentation at the moment of intensive care unit admission request for suspected acute pulmonary embolism with preserved hemodynamics but significant gas-exchange impairment, and that there is no evidence of acute or chronic renal failure.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman with a six-year history of biopsy-proven cirrhosis related to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis came to the liver clinic for an unscheduled evaluation because over the preceding two weeks she noted her waistband felt marginally tighter and that when lying flat her lower flanks seemed to curve outward a bit more than usual, although she could still zip her jeans without difficulty and denied any shortness of breath, early satiety, ankle swelling, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, melena, pruritus, or recent weight change beyond one pound. She remained fully functional at her job as a legal proofreader, completed crossword puzzles nightly, and had no trouble balancing the household budget or recalling remote or recent events; family members had not observed personality change, irritability, purposeless movements, or spells of staring. Her past medical history also included well-controlled hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 75 µg daily and stage 1 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL; she had never consumed alcohol, had no history of viral hepatitis, and did not use herbal preparations. Previous upper endoscopy showed small portal hypertensive gastropathy without varices, and she had never required diuretics, paracentesis, lactulose, rifaximin, or hospitalization for gastrointestinal bleeding or infection. Home medications were levothyroxine, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, and omega-3 fatty acids; she reported no drug allergies. She walked briskly for thirty minutes each morning, followed a 2 g sodium diet recommended by her dietitian, and had lost 15 lb three years earlier through lifestyle modification; body mass index now measured 27 kg/m². There was no family history of chronic liver disease; her mother had type 2 diabetes and her father died of bladder cancer. She never smoked and denied recreational drug use. At presentation—before any intravenous access or medication—vital signs were temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 15/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. She was alert, oriented, conversant, performed serial threes promptly, and spelled “planet” backwards without hesitation. Sclerae were anicteric, conjunctivae pink, and the breath carried no sweet or musty odor. Skin exam revealed three scattered spider angiomata over the upper chest and mild palmar erythema; there were no bruises or xanthomas. Jugular venous pulsation was normal, cardiac auscultation showed a regular rhythm without murmurs, and lungs were clear throughout. Abdominal inspection showed a softly rounded contour with barely perceptible fullness of the lower flanks; the umbilicus remained inverted and the abdominal wall was not tense. Percussion uncovered a narrow crescent of dullness in the dependent right flank that migrated when she rolled leftward, and with one hand exerting firm midline pressure a faint impulse was felt on the contralateral side; bowel sounds were present and the abdomen was nontender. The liver edge was firm, finely nodular, and palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration; the spleen was not appreciated. Lower extremities were free of edema, and neurologic examination showed brisk, symmetric reflexes, intact coordination, and absence of a flapping tremor after 20 seconds of sustained wrist extension. Point-of-care ultrasonography performed prior to phlebotomy demonstrated a coarse, nodular hepatic surface, patent main portal vein with antegrade flow at 16 cm/s, no portal vein thrombosis, and a thin anechoic stripe of free fluid measuring up to 1.2 cm along the right paracolic gutter; kidneys were normal in size and echogenicity, and no biliary dilation or focal hepatic mass was visualized. Initial laboratory studies drawn immediately thereafter—before any diuretic, albumin, or vitamin K administration—revealed: total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, serum albumin 4.4 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 34 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 46 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 126 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 138 U/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, fasting glucose 104 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.4 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 142 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.42. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody remained negative, alpha-fetoprotein was 4 ng/mL, ceruloplasmin was normal, and anti-mitochondrial antibody remained positive as on prior testing. A screening electrocardiogram displayed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min with no ischemic changes, and upright chest radiography demonstrated clear lung fields with mildly elevated hemidiaphragms but no pleural effusions. No therapeutic interventions had yet been instituted at the time these findings were documented.

Patient note:
A 48 years old woman, mother of two children with normal menstruation and insignificant prior history, presented with abdominal pain. Ultrasound examination and MRI of the abdomen revealed a solid mass, 20 cm of maximum diameter in the pelvis (), with no sign of peritoneal or nodal metastasis. Tumor markers were negative. The patient underwent laparotomy, and intraoperative gross inspection confirmed the presence of a solid mass originating from the mesentery. A uterine tumor with maximum diameter of 6 cm was also inspected. The mesenteric tumor was completely excised and was followed by frozen section examination which revealed a spindle cell neoplasm. Nuclear atypia, increased mitotic index, or tumor cell necroses were not observed. Because of the coexistence of the uterine tumor, hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy was performed. Infracolic omentectomy was also performed, and peritoneal biopsies were taken. Thorough counseling was made, and informed consent was taken preoperatively from the patient concerning the possibility of hysterectomy.
Paraffin-embedded sections of the mesenteric tumor revealed that it was a smooth muscle tumor, composed of anastomosing fascicles of smooth muscle cells with no atypia, mitosis, or tumor cell necrosis. Immunohistochemically, the smooth muscle cells were positive for SMA and desmin and negative for CD117 (Figures and ). Peritoneal biopsies and omentum were disease free. The uterine tumor was a typical benign leiomyoma.
The patient was discharged four days later. The postoperative course was uneventful. Because of the dilemma regarding the biologic behavior of the mesenteric tumor, long-term close followup was decided. Nine months after surgery, no recurrent disease has been noted.

Patient note:
A 46-year-old man with morbid obesity, insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension, and longstanding obstructive sleep apnea normally treated with a home auto-titrating device was brought in from his workplace after suddenly developing severe shortness of breath while climbing one flight of stairs; coworkers noted he became diaphoretic, cyanotic about the lips, and unable to speak full sentences. Emergency medical technicians arrived within ten minutes to find him sitting forward in a chair, tachypneic at 30 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 83 % on room air, and speaking only in two- or three-word phrases but following commands. They applied a tight-fitting oronasal circuit that provided continuous distending pressure of 10 cm H₂O through an air-oxygen blender set to 0.43 inspired fraction; after five minutes the saturation rose to 92 %, and he remained on that interface throughout transport. No sedatives, diuretics, nitrates, bronchodilators, steroids, pressors, or intravenous fluids were administered in the field. On arrival to the resuscitation bay, before any hospital therapy was begun, he was seated upright, still wearing the same positive-pressure mask, drawing his own breaths, and able to answer questions but intermittently pausing for air. A right radial arterial sample obtained within three minutes revealed pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 41 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and a PaO₂ of 84 mm Hg while the delivered oxygen concentration remained 43 %. Simultaneous vital signs documented temperature 37.0 °C tympanic, heart rate 106 beats per minute in regular sinus rhythm, blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute with moderate accessory-muscle use, and pulse oximetry fluctuating between 91 % and 93 % on the mask. He opened eyes spontaneously, answered orientation questions accurately but complained that “everything feels fuzzy,” and obeyed commands without hesitation, giving an overall Glasgow Coma Score of 14. Pupils were 3 mm bilaterally and briskly reactive, extraocular movements were full, and no focal motor deficits were discerned on quick pronator-drift testing. Skin was warm, mottling absent, and capillary refill under two seconds. Cardiac examination demonstrated a regular rhythm with a prominent S3 gallop but no murmurs; jugular venous distension to the angle of the mandible at 45° suggested volume overload. Breath sounds revealed diffuse fine crackles up to mid-scapula bilaterally without wheeze, and percussion was dull at the bases. The abdomen was protuberant yet soft, nontender, and without hepatosplenomegaly. Lower extremities displayed bilateral pitting edema to the mid-shin but no calf tenderness. A 16-gauge peripheral intravenous catheter and right radial arterial line were placed, though no medications or fluids had yet been infused when laboratory draws were sent. Initial complete blood count showed white-cell count 11.8 × 10³/µL, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, and a platelet count of 118 000 /µL. Serum chemistry returned sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, anion gap 14, blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.75 mg/dL compared with a baseline of 1.2 mg/dL from six months earlier. Total bilirubin was 1.25 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 38 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 35 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 104 U/L, and international normalized ratio 1.1. Venous lactate measured 2.2 mmol/L. A bedside cardiac ultrasound performed before any pharmacologic intervention revealed an ejection fraction around 35 %, concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, and a plethoric inferior vena cava with less than 10 % respiratory variation. Lung ultrasound demonstrated multiple B-lines in every scanned zone, supporting pulmonary congestion. Portable chest radiograph obtained moments later showed bilateral symmetrical perihilar hazy opacities consistent with edema, mild cardiomegaly, and no focal consolidation or pleural air. A 14-French Foley catheter inserted during the secondary survey immediately evacuated 90 mL of clear yellow urine; review of the patient’s digital glucose-monitoring log, which he uses to track fluids, along with his wife’s report indicated approximately 1 150 mL of urine over the preceding 24 hours. Electrocardiogram displayed sinus tachycardia at 108 beats per minute with left-ventricular strain pattern but no acute ischemic changes. At the moment all the above physiologic and biochemical data were captured, the patient remained spontaneously breathing on the same mask delivering 10 cm H₂O continuous pressure and 43 % oxygen, maintained a blood pressure of 114/72 mm Hg without vasoactive support, demonstrated mild thrombocytopenia, modest renal impairment with creatinine 1.75 mg/dL, near-normal total bilirubin of 1.25 mg/dL, a PaO₂ of 84 mm Hg under those conditions, and had produced just over a liter of urine in the past day.

Patient note:
A 30-year-old woman who works as a warehouse inventory coordinator and coaches a community girls’ basketball team after hours was referred to the combined hematology–pulmonary clinic this morning for a pre-induction assessment of recently diagnosed precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and concurrent review of her long-standing respiratory and metabolic conditions before she begins an intensive chemotherapy protocol next week. She reports that for the past fifteen years she has carried rescue albuterol wherever she goes, originally prescribed during high-school track meets when exercise routinely provoked chest tightness and audible wheeze; over the last five years spirometry has demonstrated a persistently reduced FEV1/FVC ratio with only partial reversibility after bronchodilator, most recently measuring a pre-bronchodilator FEV1 of 2.1 L (68 % predicted), FVC of 3.6 L (87 % predicted), and FEV1/FVC of 0.58, improving to 0.62 fifteen minutes after administration of 400 µg salbutamol, and her outside pulmonologist labeled the pattern consistent with chronic airway limitation related to a combination of childhood asthma and cigarette exposure from a brief two-pack-year history in college. Maintenance therapy has included budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 µg two inhalations twice daily plus montelukast nightly, with flares requiring short prednisone tapers roughly twice per winter; she has never required hospital admission or intubation, and today she arrives breathing comfortably, speaking in full sentences, and saturating 97 % on room air. Cardiovascular review is otherwise silent: she denies squeezing substernal pain, diaphoresis out of proportion to exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, palpitations, or syncope, and a screening echocardiogram obtained by the oncology team last week displayed normal chamber sizes, a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 63 %, and no valvular abnormality; N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide measured 42 pg/mL, and a high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I level was <6 ng/L, with a contemporaneous 12-lead ECG showing normal sinus rhythm without Q waves or ischemic changes. She similarly recounts no episode of unilateral weakness, slurred speech, facial droop, visual blackout, or gait imbalance. Endocrine history reveals that at age twenty-seven, during an employee wellness fair, fasting plasma glucose measured 145 mg/dL on two separate occasions and hemoglobin A1c was 7.4 %; her most recent hemoglobin A1c two weeks ago was 6.8 %, and since then she has taken metformin 1000 mg twice daily, logs carbohydrate intake on a smartphone application, and brings finger-stick readings that cluster between 100 and 150 mg/dL before breakfast; a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio last month was 12 mg/g. She denies visual blurring, numbness in the feet, change in vibration sense, renal colic, or non-healing ulcers, and an ophthalmology note from six months ago documented a clear retina without microaneurysms. The leukemia was discovered three weeks ago when she sought care for prolonged bruising on her shins, fatigue after climbing one flight of stairs, and intermittent low-grade fevers; complete blood count at an urgent-care clinic showed white cells 85 × 10⁹/L with 80 % lymphoblasts, hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, and platelets 38 × 10⁹/L. Bone-marrow aspirate confirmed the diagnosis and revealed a t(12;21) translocation; she has received no cytotoxic agents yet, only allopurinol for tumor-lysis prophylaxis and a single dose of dexamethasone for laryngeal edema after mediastinal biopsy. Baseline hepatic panel drawn yesterday demonstrated alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0. An abdominal ultrasound performed at diagnosis described a mildly enlarged, diffusely echogenic liver without nodularity, patent portal and hepatic veins, no splenomegaly, and absence of ascites; she has never manifested jaundice, encephalopathy, gastro-intestinal bleeding, pruritus, or abdominal distention. Kidney function today is intact—sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 112 mL/min/1.73 m², and urinalysis is bland. She denies heartburn, coffee-ground emesis, melena, or prior ulcer therapy, uses ibuprofen only during menses, and takes no proton-pump inhibitor. An HIV antigen/antibody screen obtained at the time of leukemia work-up was non-reactive. Current medication list therefore includes metformin, budesonide–formoterol, montelukast, albuterol as needed (one inhaler lasts about two months), allopurinol 300 mg daily since last week, and a combined ethinyl-estradiol/levonorgestrel oral contraceptive to regulate irregular cycles exacerbated by systemic corticosteroid bursts; she reports no drug allergies. Socially, she lives in a small apartment with her twin sister, jogs two miles three times weekly when fatigue allows, quit smoking eight years ago, consumes two glasses of wine per month, and has never used recreational drugs. Family pedigree reveals a father with type 2 diabetes diagnosed in his forties, a mother with childhood-onset asthma, and no relatives with leukemia, cirrhosis, myocardial infarction before age sixty, or stroke. Vital signs on arrival: temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg seated, heart rate 92 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body-mass index 26 kg/m² (height 165 cm, weight 70.8 kg). Examination finds a well-oriented woman with scattered petechiae over the forearms, supple neck without lymphadenopathy, brisk carotid upstrokes, jugular venous pulsation estimated at 3 cm above the sternal angle, normal first and second heart sounds without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, lungs clear at bases with faint expiratory wheezes in upper fields, abdomen soft with a smooth liver edge palpable 1 cm below the costal margin and no splenic tip, and extremities without edema. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, full strength, symmetric reflexes, preserved sensation, and steady tandem gait. She seeks clarification regarding timing of induction chemotherapy relative to her glucose control, guidance on preventive inhaler adjustments during expected neutropenic isolation, and counselling on hepatoprotective measures while receiving potentially hepatotoxic agents.

Patient note:

The patient has not entered an operating theatre, endoscopy suite, or interventional radiology bay in recent months, there have been no hospitalizations, emergency visits, or urgent care encounters for any reason during that interval, and she has not undergone any major surgical procedure in the past month. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-extremity edema that indents with pressure, exertional chest discomfort, exercise intolerance, or episodes of sudden weight gain; the most recent transthoracic echocardiogram, obtained five years ago during a murmur evaluation, showed normal chamber sizes and preserved left-ventricular ejection fraction. Patient note:
A 52-year-old male was brought to the emergency department (ED) via emergency medical services (EMS) with complaints of chest pain and pressure after a motor vehicle collision. The patient was the restrained driver in a collision while traveling at approximately 45 miles per hour when a car turned in front of him at an intersection. His airbags deployed; he did not lose consciousness and was able to self-extricate from the vehicle. After extrication, he started to experience substernal chest pressure, which was not present prior to the accident. When EMS arrived he was placed in a cervical collar and given aspirin, and an electrocardiogram (ECG) was obtained (). He was transported to the ED.
On arrival, a repeat ECG was performed, and the emergency physician alerted a cardiac activation given concern for an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). He complained of substernal chest pain and pressure that was non-radiating and exacerbated by deep inspiration. Additional review of systems was negative.
On examination in the ED, the patient’s temperature was 36.6° Celsius, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respirations 15 breaths per minute, blood pressure 102/60 millimeters mercury, and an oxygen saturation of 97%. He was in no acute distress. He had tenderness to palpation over the sternum with no evidence of contusion or seatbelt sign on chest or abdomen. He had no abnormalities on cardiac, lung, or abdominal exams. He had no bony point tenderness of extremities and had full range of motion of all extremities.
He had no prior medical history but had not had regular medical care in the prior 30 years. He had smoked 1.5 packs per day of cigarettes for many years, consumed alcohol on social occasions, and denied recreational drug use. He had no known drug allergies. He had never had surgery. He denied any family history of coronary artery disease and denied any personal history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or coronary artery disease.
Chest radiography demonstrated only mild left lung base atelectasis. Point-of-care echocardiography by the cardiology service was limited by difficult windows and pain on transducer pressure, but demonstrated a relatively preserved ejection fraction, no pericardial effusion, and no obvious wall motion abnormalities. Initial troponin-I was elevated at 0.045 nanograms per milliliter (ng/mL) (reference range 0.02–0.04 ng/mL), and B-type natriuretic peptide was 10 picograms (pg)/mL (<=99 pg/mL).
While the diagnosis of cardiac contusion was entertained, the field ECG could not be ignored. With no contraindications to angiography identified, the patient was fully anticoagulated and taken emergently for coronary angiography. Coronary angiogram demonstration 100% occlusion of the mid left anterior descending artery (LAD) without dissection (). There was also a mid-right coronary artery (RCA) ragged 70–90% lesion. After intervention on the LAD lesion, the patient’s pain subsided. The next day, he complained of chest pain on deep inspiration and chest heaviness. He had a staged intervention of the RCA the following day. In the interim, he was discovered to have a sternal fracture by computed tomography ().
