Patient note:
A 63-year-old woman who lives alone in a single-story house and still drives herself to weekly church choir practice presented to the emergency department early this morning after three days of gradually worsening cough and exertional breathlessness that culminated in an episode of lightheadedness while walking from her bedroom to the kitchen; she denied syncope, and she had taken no over-the-counter medications, used no home nebulizers, and received no supplemental oxygen before arrival because she “wanted the doctors to see the real picture.” Her medical history includes an anterior wall myocardial infarction five years ago that left her with systolic dysfunction (most recent echocardiogram six months earlier showed an ejection fraction in the mid-30s with mild left atrial enlargement) and a small right parietal cerebrovascular event two years ago from which she recovered full strength but remains on low-dose aspirin. She follows a cardiologist, takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily and sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily, has never required dialysis, has no history of chronic kidney disease or renal insufficiency, has normal liver enzymes on prior panels and has never been diagnosed with cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis, or any chronic liver disorder, and has no record of malignant disease. She quit smoking two decades ago after a ten-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of red wine with Sunday dinner only, and denies any recreational drug use. Vaccination records retrieved from the state registry confirm completion of both pneumococcal series and an influenza vaccine given at her local pharmacy last autumn. On EMS arrival to her home she was sitting upright on the couch in moderate respiratory distress but answering questions lucidly; the crew transported her without intravenous access, fluids, or oxygen so as not to confound initial measurements. In triage she appeared alert, oriented, and anxious to cooperate, speaking in full sentences but pausing for breath after every few words. Skin was warm and dry, conjunctivae were pink, and capillary refill was brisk. Untreated vital signs on ambient air at sea-level were: oral temperature 99.8 °F, regular but thready pulse 145 beats per minute confirmed on telemetry, non-invasive blood pressure 119/72 mm Hg verified manually, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute with mild suprasternal retraction, and fingertip pulse oximetry 96 % while seated upright. Jugular venous pulsation was estimated at 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, identical to notes from her cardiology visit. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid S1 and S2 with a soft third sound and no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Lungs transmitted coarse inspiratory crackles over the right mid-lung field posteriorly and faint scattered rhonchi on the left; percussion remained resonant throughout, and costophrenic angles were sharp. The abdomen was flat, soft, and nontender with no hepatosplenomegaly; there was no pedal edema. A focused neurologic screen showed equal pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, symmetric facial expression, 5/5 strength in all extremities, and fluent speech, without dysmetria or aphasia. Finger-stick glucose performed before venipuncture measured 141 mg/dL. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of arrival—before any saline flushes—returned sodium 142 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, values very close to those in her primary-care records. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 13.6 × 10⁹/L with 86 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 44 %, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, and platelets 248 × 10⁹/L. A right radial arterial sample obtained while she continued to breathe room air revealed an alkalemic pH of 7.73, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, PaO₂ 107 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, consistent with a primary respiratory alkalosis from tachypnea and no hypoxemia. Serum lactate was 1.3 mmol/L. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 146 bpm with nonspecific ST-T wave flattening but no acute ischemic pattern compared with prior tracings. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph acquired before any treatment displayed a patchy consolidation in the right middle lobe with air bronchograms, preserved diaphragmatic contours, and no blunting of the costophrenic angles or layering fluid. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for common bacterial pathogens, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched to the laboratory prior to antibiotic initiation. Up to the time of this note she has received neither intravenous crystalloids, vasopressors, bronchodilators, diuretics, nor supplemental oxygen beyond the ambient 21 %, and she has not been given antipyretics or analgesics; therefore every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding detailed above reflects her untreated presentation.

Patient note:
We present the case of an 80-year-old female patient known to have ischemic heart disease, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and atrial fibrillation. Almost 20 years before her current presentation, the patient had a history of ascending cholangitis post endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, complicated by an iatrogenic esophageal perforation requiring surgical repair and cholecystectomy. In 2015, the patient had another abdominal perforation secondary to an ischemic bowel due to arterial emboli.
The patient presented with a one-week history of abdominal pain, dysuria, and fever. Her vitals showed a blood pressure of 86/55 mmHg and a heart rate of 127 beats per minute, which recovered after 500 mL of normal saline. Her urine dipstick revealed 100 leukoestrase and positive nitrites. Basic blood investigations were normal, and cultures were sent. She was started on Ceftriaxone 1 g once a day to treat her urinary tract infection. The cultures came back negative apart from blood cultures which grew V. cholera within a day of incubation (Table shows the antibiotics' sensitivity).
The patient was clinically improving but to identify the bacteremia source, a stool culture was sent, and abdominal computed tomography (CT) was arranged. The stool culture was negative, and the CT showed a common bile duct dilatation with a heterogeneous enhancement of the liver, representing cholangitis, but no obstruction was observed (Figure ).
Since the patient was improving and her CT findings were related to her previous surgeries, no intervention was done.
She completed a seven-day course of Ceftriaxone, and repeated blood culture did not grow any organism. She was discharged home, but a few days later, she returned with severe sepsis without a clear focus. Cultures were sent, and the results showed Clostridium perfringens bacteremia. She was started on an intravenous metronidazole loading dose of 750 mg, and then she was kept on 375 mg every 6 hours as a maintenance dose. The patient's condition worsened as her level of consciousness and blood pressure dropped, requiring norepinephrine infusion and intubation. Her intensive care unit stay was complicated with ventilator-associated pneumonia. After two days, the patient's condition deteriorated, and she passed away.

Patient note:
A 54-year-old woman with a background of well-controlled systemic lupus erythematosus on hydroxychloroquine, hypertension managed with amlodipine, and a remote Roux-en-Y gastric bypass was air-lifted to the emergency department after being thrown from a quarter horse during a cross-country event at 14:05 this afternoon; by witness report her helmet struck a low tree branch as she cleared a ditch, she somersaulted forward over the saddle, and landed supine on compacted dirt without further trampling. On arrival of flight medics at 14:17 she was breathing spontaneously, maintained a palpable radial pulse, and displayed no obvious long-bone deformity, yet her eyes were closed and she uttered nothing despite repeated questioning. To preserve the neurologic examination the crew placed a rigid cervical collar, secured her to a vacuum mattress, established two 18-gauge antecubital saline locks without running fluids, and withheld analgesics, sedatives, anticonvulsants, paralytics, vasopressors, dextrose, and hyperosmolar therapy. Capillary glucose was 108 mg/dL and no alcohol odor was noted. She received humidified oxygen at 12 L/min by non-rebreather during the thirteen-minute flight but no other intervention. On touchdown at 14:38 she remains immobilized on the vacuum mattress, riding breeches caked with loam, face spattered with dried dust, and a 6-cm crescent laceration arches along the right parietal scalp with slow venous ooze. Immediately prior to any hospital treatment, simultaneous vital signs record blood pressure 142/86 mm Hg in the left arm, heart rate 88 beats/min in regular sinus rhythm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min with symmetric chest rise, oxygen saturation 99 % on the pre-hospital mask, and core temperature 36.5 °C by esophageal probe placed in flight. Airway survey shows intact dentition, midline uvula, moist mucosa, and a vigorous cough when a Yankauer catheter traverses the posterior pharynx; no stridor or gurgling is heard. Pupils are 3 mm bilaterally, round, and brisk to direct and consensual light. During a silent thirty-second observation her eyelids remain firmly shut, lashes motionless; when the trauma nurse speaks her first name at conversational volume adjacent to either ear both lids spring open to three-quarters aperture, gaze steadies on the speaker for several seconds, then drift closed again once questioning ceases. The behavior recurs each time verbal prompting is repeated but never occurs spontaneously. Despite sustained attempts—questions about identity, date, location, and commands to speak—she produces no phonation; exhalations are quiet and unaccompanied by grunt, moan, or word. Baseline tone is low to intermediate, limbs lying loosely at her sides. Cranial nerve testing elicits a symmetric grimace to supra-orbital ridge pressure and intact corneal reflexes. Motor assessment reveals that simple instructions such as “lift your right hand” or “wiggle your toes” generate no movement. A focused painful stimulus—firm trapezius squeeze on the left—provokes an immediate purposeful reaction: the right arm arcs across midline, shoulder flexes, elbow bends to roughly 90 degrees, and the hand purposefully seeks and makes contact with the examiner’s pinching fingers in an apparent attempt to push them off; lower extremities simultaneously flex slightly at the hips without posturing. Identical localization occurs when nail-bed pressure is applied to the right great toe, with the ipsilateral hand reaching toward the examiner’s grasp at the foot, demonstrating reproducible, directed defensive motion that ceases once the noxious input stops. No abnormal flexor or extensor postures are observed, and there is no myoclonus or tremor between stimuli. Deep tendon reflexes are 2 + at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles; plantar stimulation yields down-going toes bilaterally. Oculocephalic testing is deferred due to the cervical collar. Cardiovascular examination reveals a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses are 2 + with capillary refill under two seconds and warm, well-perfused extremities. Lungs are clear to auscultation with resonant percussion and no rib step-off. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender; bowel sounds are present. Pelvis is stable to gentle compression, and rectal tone is preserved. Secondary survey identifies scattered ecchymoses over both shoulders, minor abrasions along the left forearm, and no vertebral step-off or long-bone deformity. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained within five minutes shows clear lung fields, intact clavicles, and appropriate collar position; pelvic radiograph is unremarkable. Point-of-care arterial blood gas on current oxygen flow reveals pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 39 mm Hg, PaO₂ 198 mm Hg, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, and base excess −1 mEq/L. Rapid chemistry panel returns sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, calcium 8.9 mg/dL, and glucose 112 mg/dL. No sedative, narcotic, paralytic, anticonvulsant, antihypertensive, hyperosmolar, or reversal agent has yet been administered in the department, ensuring that the observed eyelid opening only after verbal address, the complete absence of speech, and the deliberate reaching toward painful stimuli accurately represent her untreated neurologic baseline at presentation while neurosurgery, trauma surgery, and critical care services are paged and stat non-contrast head CT with cervical spine reconstruction is arranged.

Patient note:
A 28-year-old woman with no recorded medical history and taking only a combined oral contraceptive pill was transferred by rural ground EMS after being discovered at 13:40 lying prone on a rocky riverbank beneath a collapsed bouldering wall; companions stated she had fallen roughly four meters, struck the left parietal region on limestone, and was briefly motionless before emitting incoherent phrases such as “where are my shoes” and “the water’s upside-down,” then lapsed into silence with her eyes shut. Paramedics arrived nine minutes after the call, placed a rigid collar, rolled her onto a scoop stretcher with head blocks, established a single 18-gauge IV in the right antecubital vein but left it saline-locked, checked a capillary glucose of 112 mg/dL, and delivered 10 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather mask; no crystalloid bolus, analgesic, sedative, paralytic, dextrose, naloxone, anticonvulsant, or vasoactive medication was administered en route during the fifteen-minute transport so the neurologic examination would remain unaltered. She arrived in our resuscitation bay at 14:09 still secured to the scoop, clothing damp from river spray and lightly dusted with chalk, a 3-cm ragged scalp laceration oozing along the superior margin of the left pinna. Pre-intervention vital signs recorded simultaneously with the first in-hospital neurologic survey are blood pressure 142/88 mm Hg in the right brachial artery, heart rate 102 beats/min in regular sinus rhythm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min with shallow thoracoabdominal excursion, oxygen saturation 97 % on the same mask, and tympanic temperature 37.1 °C. Airway inspection reveals intact dentition, minimal dried blood on the hard palate, no pooled secretions, and a Yankauer sweep to the oropharynx prompts a brisk cough and gag. During an initial 30-second period of quiet observation she lies motionless, eyelids fully closed without fluttering and no spontaneous limb activity. When her given name is called at conversational and then shouted volume adjacent to either ear, there is no lid separation, no verbal reply, and no extremity movement. A firm supra-orbital ridge pressure applied for five seconds, however, causes both eyelids to spring open half-way; pupils 3 mm bilaterally constrict briskly to direct light, gaze drifts past the examiner, and the lids fall shut within two seconds once the stimulus stops. Immediately after eye opening she utters slurred but intelligible phrases—“I’m late for the train,” “don’t let the cats out”—that do not correspond to questions about her identity or location, and she becomes intermittently querulous, asking “why is it snowing?” despite being indoors. When asked her name she provides a childhood nickname, gives the month as “Octember,” and cannot recall the accident, demonstrating obvious disorientation though sentence structure remains intact. Upper extremities at rest display normal bulk and baseline tone. Nail-bed compression of the right index finger elicits rapid adduction of both shoulders, elbows flex to approximately 90 degrees with forearm pronation, and wrists curl inward; lower limbs simultaneously extend slightly at the knees with plantar flexion. The posture persists two seconds beyond removal of the stimulus before the limbs relax. A sternal rub reproduces an identical flexor pattern without any purposeful reach toward the examiner’s hand. No spontaneous purposeful movement is observed between stimuli, and she fails to follow simple commands such as “show two fingers” or “stick out your tongue.” Deep tendon reflexes are 3 + at biceps and patellae, 2 + at Achilles; there is no clonus and plantar responses are mute. Cranial nerve assessment confirms symmetric corneal reflexes, midline tongue when the jaw is passively opened, and facial grimace present with nail-bed pain. Cardiovascular exam reveals a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs; distal pulses are 2 +, capillary refill under two seconds. Lungs are clear to auscultation with equal breath sounds and resonant percussion; no paradoxical chest wall motion is noted. Abdomen is flat, soft, nontender, with active bowel sounds; pelvis is stable. Log-roll inspection shows mild ecchymosis over the left scapular ridge but no step-off; spine palpation is midline and non-tender. Extremities demonstrate no deformity, and distal neurovascular status is intact. Skin is warm and well perfused; aside from the scalp laceration there are superficial abrasions over the right forearm and left knee. Point-of-care venous blood gas on current oxygen flow reveals pH 7.37, pCO₂ 39 mm Hg, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Portable anterior-posterior chest radiograph obtained within five minutes shows clear lung fields and normal mediastinal silhouette; pelvic X-ray is unremarkable. Blood for complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, coagulation studies, serum ethanol, and type-and-screen has been drawn but not yet resulted. No pharmacologic agents or intravenous fluids other than the prehospital saline lock have been given in the department, ensuring that the ocular, verbal, and motor behaviors detailed above represent her untreated neurologic baseline. Neurosurgery and trauma surgery have been paged; urgent non-contrast CT of the head, maxillofacial CT, and cervical spine CT are being arranged, and nursing staff have instituted fifteen-minute neurologic checks while airway equipment for possible rapid-sequence intubation stands ready should her mental status deteriorate.

Patient note:
A 76-year-old woman with a history of HIT-T was admitted to our department for unstable angina pectoris (UAP); coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) was indicated. Her first admission by the cardiologist was 7 years prior for UAP with congestive heart failure, and diagnosed with three-vessel coronary artery disease. She was mechanically ventilated; intra-aortic balloon pumping (IABP) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with a bare-metal stent to the right coronary artery (RCA) were performed. Post-intervention, continuous hemodiafiltration (CHDF) with heparin was continued. Repeated heparin use caused gangrene and amputation of four fingers; she was subsequently diagnosed with HIT-T, and a temporary tracheostomy was required. Moreover, due to her poor general condition, PCI for residual coronary disease was not performed.
Other comorbidities included insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c = 6.4%), chronic kidney disease (eGFR = 15 ml/min/1.73 m2), pulmonary hypertension, and peripheral artery disease (left carotid artery and left radial artery stenosis). There was no family history of coronary disease, allergy, or history of smoking.
Her left ventricular function was moderately impaired (left ventricular ejection fraction, 44%). The preoperative platelet count was 18.0 × 104/μl, and platelet factor PF4/H Ab was negative; thus, she was diagnosed with ‘‘remote’’ HIT [, ]. The estimated postoperative mortality by Japan SCORE II (which does not include entry for the thromboembolism) was 4.9%, and the estimated risk of mortality and morbidity was 28%.
On admission, aspirin and clopidogrel were substituted for argatroban, and argatroban was used during coronary angiography. Target activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) was twice the baseline; thus, argatroban was administered until 9 h prior to the operation. Surgery was performed under general anesthesia, and a median sternotomy approach was used. Simultaneously, the right femoral artery and vein were secured by introducing peripheral mechanical circulatory support, avoiding central cannulation for cardiopulmonary bypass establishment.
A bolus of 5000-unit unfractionated heparin was administered when anastomosis was started, and activated clotting time (ACT) was maintained between 189 s (control score) and 429 s (Fig. ). After all coronary anastomoses (RITA-LAD, LITA-LPL, SVG-4PD) were completed, 100 mg protamine was administered; however, the ACT did not normalize fully (Fig. ). The surgery was uneventful, and the patient was extubated in the operating theater. The intra and postoperative blood losses were 495 cc and 358 cc/16 h, respectively.
Furthermore, the postoperative anticoagulation regimen was based on the ACCP guideline []. Argatroban was initiated at 0.2µg/kg/min (this value is in accordance with the Japanese standard []) 3 h postoperatively and continued until postoperative day (POD) 6. (Fig. ) Warfarin was also started when platelet count exceeded 10 × 104/μl on POD 4 and continued for 3 months. The postoperative course was uneventful, and there were no signs of thromboembolism. PF4/H Ab was positive on POD 8 (examined by latex flocculation turbidimetry; 2.8 U/ml: the threshold is < 1.0) and negative by POD 91.
Informed consent was obtained from the patient for the reporting of this case.

Patient note:
A 64-year-old African American man presented to a university hospital with one-week history of worsening dyspnea, cough, and lower extremity edema. He endorses frequently forgetting to take his medications as well as nonadherence with dietary and fluid restrictions. Past medical history is pertinent for morbid obesity, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (prior radiofrequency ablation, currently anticoagulated), coronary artery disease (prior stent to mid-left anterior descending (LAD) artery), hypertension, ventricular septal defect (VSD), and previous motor vehicle collision approximately ten years prior.
Upon arrival to the emergency department, he was noted to have blood pressure of 106/77 with heart rate of 94 and respirations of 23. He was saturating at 86% on 4-5 L nasal cannula and was subsequently started on Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure (BiPAP) to improve respiratory status. Physical exam was notable for bibasilar crackles, grades II/VI holosystolic murmur, mildly elevated jugular venous pressure, and 1+ bilateral lower extremity edema. Admission labs were unremarkable (including normal B-natriuretic peptide, troponin-I, and albumin). Chest X-ray demonstrated interstitial pulmonary vascular congestion (), and EKG was sinus tachycardia with first-degree AV block. He was admitted to the cardiology inpatient service for continued management of presumed acute decompensated heart failure.
Given the persistent hypoxemia, transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) and computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) were ordered. TTE demonstrated normal biventricular systolic function, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, and a small, 5 mm distal inferoseptal/apical VSD (). CTPA was without evidence of pulmonary embolism but did demonstrate a 6.4 × 4.3 cm calcified lesion concerning for giant LAD coronary artery aneurysm (), though image quality was limited by lack of gating. Diuresis was continued with symptomatic improvement, but given these findings, the decision was made to proceed with invasive angiography.
Heart catheterization revealed elevated right-sided (right atrium (RA) 9 mmHg, right ventricle (RV) 52/12 mmHg, pulmonary artery 71/29 mmHg (mean 45 mmHg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 14 mmHg), and left-sided pressures (left ventricle 183/31 mmHg, systemic arterial pressure 171/97 mmHg (mean 128 mmHg)) without evidence of step-up intracardiac RV shunt (RA 59%, RV 61% saturation). There was elevated cardiac output (Fick—11.1 L/min (index 4.39 L/min); Thermodilution—14.4 L/min (index 5.73 L/min). Coronary angiography revealed mild luminal irregularities only, with normal ejection fraction and no evidence of LAD aneurysm (). There was no apparent mass lesion evident with fluoroscopy and ventriculogram showed normal left ventricular wall motion.
Follow-up imaging was performed to elucidate these findings, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) clarified the anomaly as a 5.4 × 4.1 × 4.9 cm pseudoaneurysm arising from the mid-apical free wall of the RV with a 9 mm neck (). Cardiac CT angiogram was well performed and confirmed pseudoaneurysm arising superiorly from the mid-apical free wall of the RV measuring up to 6.1 cm in maximal diameter with a 15 mm neck as well as 4 × 11 mm mid-apical VSD (). A review of the previously performed CTPA was conducted at this point and revealed a previously healed rib fracture anterior to the pseudoaneurysm ().
Given the high output heart failure noted on angiography, an abdominal ultrasound was performed and revealed evidence of a cirrhotic liver. Upon further questioning, our patient admitted to prior longstanding alcohol abuse, now in remission. Remote motor vehicle accident was the presumed etiology to the rib fracture, and in the subsequent years, our patient developed RV pseudoaneurysm as well as VSD from the penetrating fracture. The patient was seen by cardiothoracic surgery for further evaluation, with plan to continue close surveillance per patient preference.

Patient note:
A 61-year-old woman presented to the peri-operative medicine clinic at the request of orthopedic surgery for risk assessment before a scheduled right total knee arthroplasty to address end-stage osteoarthritis that has limited her walking radius to three city blocks. She still works part-time as a librarian, drives herself, and supervises grandchildren after school, but she wishes to be certain that her chronic health issues are sufficiently stable for an inpatient joint replacement. She reports a 28-pack-year cigarette history, quitting six years ago after her second episode of winter bronchitis required oral prednisone; pulmonary function testing performed last month showed an FEV1 of 64 % predicted with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58 and no significant bronchodilator response, consistent with moderate fixed airflow limitation. She uses umeclidinium once every morning, a fluticasone-vilanterol combination each evening, and albuterol two puffs before climbing stairs, typically replacing the rescue inhaler every three months. Patient note:
A sixty-one year old man, came to our emergency department because of a long episode of chest pain. He had a story of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia under statin therapy, type II diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycaemic therapy, and he was a smoker in the past. He referred previous saphenectomy and haemorrhoidectomy operations, no other comorbidities.
He reported, for several days, the appearance of episodes of chest pain in the back that occur at rest for about five to ten minutes each
The first ECG showed sinus rhythm with ST segment depression in leads V2-V6, not evident at the repeated ECGs done in the absence of chest pain.
Repeated cardiac enzymes (CK-MB fraction and Troponin I) were slightly elevated with a typical trend (peak values CK-MB 23,7 ng/dl; Troponin I 4,83 ng/dl).
Echocardiographic (ECO) evaluation showed good right and left ventricular global function with ipo-akinesia of postero-lateral medium-basal wall. Non valvular diseases.
After the diagnosis of acute coronary syndromes (NSTE-ACS) non-ST-Segment Elevation the patient was admitted to hospital for the evaluation of suspected coronary artery disease and began a pharmacological anti-ischemic therapy complete with Ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose e, second ischemic and bleeding risks, fondaparinux (2.5 mg sc per day).
Twenty hours from hospital admission, the patient was referred to the haemodynamic laboratory and a coronarography was performed via right radial artery approach. Angiography revealed small left anterior descending with diffused luminal irregularities, not significant stenosis, intermediate artery of small calibre, with 99% proximal stenosis; normal Circumflex artery; right coronary artery, dominant, without stenosis.
In view of this and in agreement with the patient, it was decided to attempt interventional revascularization and stenting of the intermediate artery. An Ipercoat run-through guide wire was chosen for revascularization.
Pre-dilatation with Maverick 2 x 20 mm (8 ATM) balloon was done and the artery was stented with Supraflex 2 x 16 mm (14 ATM).
Finally post-dilation with Hiryu 2,25 x 10 mm balloon was done.
Angiography after wire retraction demonstrated a small depot of contrast evolving around the stented vessel segment, referred to coronary perforation of distal tract of third branch of intermediate artery.
The operator decided to achieve the haemostasis by sealing the coronary artery perforation with repeated balloon inflations lasting 5 minutes for each one. Administration of protamine for heparin neutralization, was prescribed. A later angiographic control displayed disappearance of images related to perforation, TIMI 3 flow.
ECG did n’t shows new ischemic changes
An echocardiography exam showed slight, stable, pericardial effusion.
Due to stable haemodynamic condition the patient was transferred to the coronary care unit, but the following hours the patient had a sudden haemodynamic evolution with a drop of blood pressure and increase of heart rate. An echocardiography exam revealed a severe pericardial effusion with compression of the right ventricle.
This situation was initially managed with rapid volume supply and vasopressor to maintain sufficient end-diastolic right atrial and ventricular pressure.
During the pericardiocentesis, sudden cardiac arrest occurred due to asystole, which required cardiopulmonary resuscitation. The ACLS protocol was performed for 15 minutes, with the administration of Epinephrine 3 mg which involved ROSC.
Pericardiocentesis, by a subxyphoid approach, was then performed emergently at patient’s bed and 500 ml of blood was removed from the pericardial space. Echocardiography was repeated 10 minutes later, having found a new pericardial effusion despite pericardial drainage. Due to persistent haemorrhage and progressive hemodynamic collapse an urgent surgery management was required .The pericardium was opened via median sternotomy and a significant amount of clot and blood was removed (about 1,5 L) with immediate hemodynamic benefit. Exploration showed an intramural ventricular haematoma of the inferior-lateral wall (site of coronary perforation) of the left ventricle with parietal haemorrhagic infarction.
Extracorporeal circulation (CEC) and cardioplegic arrest with ante-grade hot blood cardioplegia was done.
A composite Dacron with autologous pericardium patch (Resorcinol-Formol type glue) was used for left ventricular free wall rupture repair and the geometry of the left ventricle was restored. Subsequently aorta was declamped; the patient was weaned from CEC with a good haemodynamic recovery.
The postoperative evolution was characterized by bilateral decline of visual acuity. Angio-CT cerebri was negative for alteration of intracranial vessels. Retinal fluoroangiography and computerized optical tomography (OCT) were also negative for retinal ischemia and other alterations. Encephalic RMN didn’t detect significant changes. In the following days the patient showed progressive improvement and slow recovery of visual capacity. No complex arrhythmic events have been recorded and good ventricular global function was maintained. The patient was then discharged after twenty days of hospitalization and started cardiovascular rehabilitation.

question:
Patient note:
A 37-year-old man presented to the emergency department this afternoon after experiencing three days of worsening fatigue, exertional shortness of breath, and a new cough productive of green-yellow sputum that began the previous night. He drove himself from home, pausing only to gather a list of medications supplied by his dialysis center; he deliberately avoided taking any over-the-counter antipyretics or inhalers and did not receive supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, or nebulized therapy en route so that hospital staff could evaluate his unmodified physiology. The patient was diagnosed eight years ago with non-ischemic systolic dysfunction attributed to viral myocarditis, with a most recent echocardiogram three months prior demonstrating an ejection fraction near 30 % and mild biatrial enlargement; carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and low-dose torsemide are part of his usual regimen. Five years ago he developed progressive glomerulosclerosis complicated by uremia, requiring thrice-weekly hemodialysis—his last session ended the evening before presentation; the nephrologist’s notes document persistent metabolic acidosis between treatments and intermittent symptomatic hyponatremia, but he has never started peritoneal dialysis or been evaluated for transplant. He denies any prior cerebrovascular accidents, seizures, chronic liver disorders, or malignant disease, and his vaccination record confirms receipt of pneumococcal conjugate and annual influenza injections. He works remotely as a software engineer, lives with his partner in a second-floor apartment, climbs a flight of stairs daily without baseline limitation, and has never smoked; alcohol intake is limited to an occasional glass of wine, and he abstains from illicit drugs. Upon arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, conversing in full sentences without confusion and accurately stating the date, location, and reason for visit. Skin was warm and dry with no peripheral edema beyond trace pitting at the ankles—unchanged from his cardiology baseline. Untreated triage vitals were as follows: oral temperature 99.2 °F, regular pulse 80 beats min⁻¹, automated blood pressure 152/86 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 11 breaths min⁻¹ with tidal volumes judged adequate, and pulse oximetry 97 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude. Neck veins were estimated at 5 cm above the sternal angle while he sat at 45°, similar to previous examinations. Cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and S2 with a soft third heart sound but no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Lung examination disclosed markedly reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower posterior hemithorax with faint egophony just superior to that zone; vesicular breath sounds were preserved elsewhere without wheezes or crackles. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with a palpable left forearm arteriovenous fistula bruiting briskly; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites was appreciated. Neurologic screening showed equal and reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, symmetric facial expression, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. Bedside glucometer read 116 mg dL⁻¹ immediately before phlebotomy. Venous chemistries obtained within ten minutes—prior to any saline flushes except those required to maintain catheter patency—revealed profound hyponatremia at 110 mEq L⁻¹, potassium 4.8 mEq L⁻¹, chloride 92 mEq L⁻¹, bicarbonate 14 mEq L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 54 mg dL⁻¹, and serum creatinine 7.0 mg dL⁻¹, all representing typical inter-dialytic values for him except for the lower than usual sodium. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 13.9 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 21 %, hemoglobin 7.1 g dL⁻¹, and platelets 265 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. An arterial sample drawn from the left radial artery while he continued to breathe room air demonstrated pH 7.14, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, PaO₂ 104 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 11 mEq L⁻¹, confirming a severe metabolic acidosis with only partial respiratory compensation and no hypoxemia. Serum lactate measured 2.0 mmol L⁻¹. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any medications or fluids displayed a homogeneous opacity obscuring the right costophrenic angle with a classic meniscus sign and associated basilar consolidation, while the cardiac silhouette appeared mildly enlarged but unchanged from a film six months earlier. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm at 82 beats min⁻¹ with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes identical to prior tracings. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigen assays for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a respiratory viral panel were dispatched prior to antibiotic administration. As of this documentation he remains seated comfortably on the gurney breathing ambient air, has not yet received antimicrobials, intravenous crystalloids, diuretics, vasopressors, antipyretics, bronchodilators, or dialysis, and therefore every physiologic observation, imaging finding, and laboratory value cited above reflects his presentation before any hospital intervention.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old man was sent from a skilled nursing facility to our acute care clinic late this afternoon because the nursing staff observed a new asymmetric fullness of his left calf that had appeared over the past 18 hours when they first stood him at the bedside for physical therapy. Five days earlier he had been admitted to that facility after a community-acquired influenza A pneumonia that had required four days of inpatient intravenous antibiotics; during the first three days of the nursing-home stay his oxygen requirements and generalized fatigue were such that he remained in bed except for brief trips to the bathroom, eating his meals in the supine position and skipping the initial scheduled ambulation sessions. By yesterday his respiratory status had improved and rehabilitation was initiated, at which point the therapists noted that the left trouser leg seemed tighter than the right. The patient himself reports a dull sensation of heaviness confined to the posterior calf when he lowers the limb but denies sharp or focal pain, burning, numbness, tingling, groin mass, fever, chills, color change, or drainage from the skin. He has never been diagnosed with blood clots in the legs or lungs, has no known thrombophilia, and recalls no similar episodes in the past. Medical history is notable for stage 2 chronic kidney disease, well-controlled hypertension on lisinopril 10 mg daily, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes; he has not undergone any surgical procedure in the last year and wears no splints, casts, or braces. Medications are lisinopril, a multivitamin, and as-needed acetaminophen; he is not taking systemic corticosteroids, hormonal therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antithrombotic drugs. He quit smoking three decades ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of whisky on holidays, and does not use illicit substances. There is no family history of venous thrombo-embolism. He recalls bumping the same calf against the wheelchair footrest two evenings ago and wonders whether he might have strained a muscle while coughing vigorously during the pneumonia, both of which he believes could explain the swelling. On arrival to our unit—before receiving analgesics, intravenous fluids, compression, or anticoagulant therapy—he was sitting in a recliner with the legs dangling. Nursing triage vitals were temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 126/72 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats min⁻¹ and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 96 % on 2 L min⁻¹ nasal cannula, identical to his baseline flow at the facility. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed a normal S₁ and S₂ without murmurs or gallops and clear breath sounds except for faint inspiratory crackles at the left base that have been stable since discharge from the hospital. The abdomen was soft and nontender; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites was appreciated. Inspection of the lower extremities showed that the left calf appeared subtly more convex posteriorly than the right, while the thigh, knee, ankle, and foot contours were symmetric. A cloth tape placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 41.7 cm on the left versus 38.1 cm on the right, documenting a 3.6 cm difference. Fifteen centimeters above the patella both thighs measured 55.0 cm, and around the malleoli the girths were 27.4 cm left and 27.0 cm right. After the leg hung dependent for 30 seconds a lattice of straight, bluish superficial vessels became prominent along the posteromedial calf and collapsed completely when the limb was elevated, distinguishing them from chronic varicosities. The skin was warm but retained a uniform pink color with no erythema, brawny discoloration, or weeping; there was no induration, crepitus, or fluctuance, and thumb indentation over the tibial crest rebounded immediately without leaving a pit. Gentle palpation tracing the expected course of the femoral, popliteal, and posterior tibial veins elicited no discrete point tenderness or palpable cord; squeezing the gastrocnemius reproduced only a dull stretch sensation. Knee and ankle ranges of motion were full and painless, straight-leg raise provoked no discomfort, and distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were 2 + bilaterally with capillary refill to all toes under two seconds. Sensation to light touch and pinprick was intact, and motor strength in the lower extremities was 5/5 except for mild deconditioning-related fatigue. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was appreciated. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained before blood sampling demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats min⁻¹ without ST-T abnormalities. Point-of-care laboratory analysis drawn prior to any intervention showed hemoglobin 13.2 g dL⁻¹, leukocytes 7.0 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, platelet count 234 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, serum sodium 138 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 1.32 mg dL⁻¹ (baseline 1.28 mg dL⁻¹), AST 21 U L⁻¹, ALT 18 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph ordered by the facility earlier today showed persistent mild bibasilar infiltrates but no new consolidation or pleural effusion. Given the recent prolonged bed rest followed by sudden asymmetric calf enlargement exceeding three centimetres, yet with the possibility of a post-traumatic muscular hematoma or localized soft-tissue injury from coughing or the wheelchair incident appearing equally credible in the absence of focal deep venous tenderness, the decision was made to obtain a comprehensive duplex ultrasound of the left iliac, femoral, popliteal, and infrapopliteal venous segments while the patient remains hemodynamically stable and prior to any administration of anticoagulation.

Patient note:
A 54-year-old man presented this morning to the peri-operative internal medicine service at the request of his urologic surgeon for evaluation prior to an elective laparoscopic left adrenalectomy scheduled in two weeks for a 3.2-cm hormonally inactive incidentaloma discovered on imaging of the abdomen performed to investigate vague flank discomfort; he reports no catecholamine-associated spells, cushingoid features, or electrolyte disturbances, and surgical planning anticipates a brief overnight stay if there are no complications. He arrived on foot from the parking lot, carrying his medical records without assistance, and states that during a typical workday as a postal carrier he walks several city blocks, climbs two flights of stairs to sort mail, and lifts parcels weighing up to 20 lb without dyspnea, palpitations, or chest pressure. His only cardiometabolic illness of significance is long-standing diabetes mellitus first diagnosed at age 14; he self-manages with a hybrid basal-bolus insulin strategy consisting of 28 units of insulin degludec subcutaneously each evening and correction doses of insulin aspart with meals guided by a continuous glucose sensor. Review of his downloads over the past month demonstrates fasting glucose values varying between 95 mg/dL and 160 mg/dL, with no nighttime hypoglycemia alarms. He denies any episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis since adolescence. Hypertension is present and treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, yielding home blood pressures in the 120s/70s. Hyperlipidemia is managed with rosuvastatin 40 mg nightly. There is background mild non-proliferative retinopathy followed by ophthalmology but no visual impairment, and he wears custom-molded insoles for sensory neuropathy manifested by diminished vibration sense in his toes. He categorically denies hospitalizations or emergency visits for fluid overload, has never been told he had a murmur or cardiomyopathy, and has not experienced orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, unexplained weight gain, or exercise intolerance. He similarly reports no prior episodes suggestive of myocardial ischemia such as exertional chest discomfort, jaw pain, or radiation to the arm, and he has never undergone coronary angiography, stress testing, or revascularization procedures. Respiratory history is notable only for well-controlled mild intermittent asthma requiring albuterol two or three times per month during pollen season; he has never smoked cigarettes or used vaping devices. There is no personal or family history of premature atherosclerotic events; his father died at 82 of colon cancer, and his mother is alive at 80 with osteoporosis. He consumes one or two light beers on weekends and does not use recreational drugs. Allergies are limited to seasonal grasses; he tolerates contrast media and latex. Systems review is otherwise unrevealing for syncope, transient neurologic symptoms, claudication, night sweats, fevers, bleeding diathesis, or easy bruising. After five minutes seated, vital signs are: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg in the right arm, pulse 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air; body mass index is 27 kg/m². He appears well hydrated and in no distress. Jugular venous contour is not elevated at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruits, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced. Heart sounds are crisp S1 and S2 with no S3, S4, murmurs, clicks, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout with good air movement. Abdomen is soft; a firm but non-tender left adrenal fullness is not palpable, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Extremities show no edema; peripheral pulses are 2+ and symmetric. A focused neurologic examination reveals intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups, normal light touch, diminished vibratory sense in the distal toes, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratories drawn one hour before the encounter demonstrate hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, elevated from a baseline of 1.7 mg/dL six months ago but stable for several years and attributed to long-standing diabetic nephropathy with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 41 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose in the same sample is 142 mg/dL; albumin-to-creatinine ratio from last month was 220 mg/g. Liver enzymes, bilirubin, and coagulation studies are within reference limits. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram performed today shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, normal intervals, and no pathologic Q waves, ST-segment deviations, or T-wave inversions. A transthoracic echocardiogram obtained nine months earlier for baseline diabetic evaluation recorded left ventricular ejection fraction of 60 %, normal wall thickness, and no valvular pathology. Chest radiograph this morning demonstrates clear lung fields and normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Anesthesia examination notes Mallampati class II airway, full cervical extension, and an inter-incisor distance of 4.5 cm. He has been instructed to continue all usual antihypertensive and statin therapy up to the day of surgery, to reduce the evening basal insulin dose by 20 % the night before the procedure, omit rapid-acting insulin on the morning of surgery unless fasting glucose exceeds 200 mg/dL, and monitor point-of-care capillary glucose upon arrival to the pre-operative holding area. He verbalizes understanding of nil-per-os instructions after midnight, postoperative incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and the importance of glycemic control to wound healing.

Patient note:
A 16-year-old previously healthy male presented to the emergency department with chills, abdominal pain, worsening nausea, and shortness of breath. He was noted to have increased work of breathing. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the periumbilical area, but no rebound guarding. His oral temperature was 38.6°C, heart rate 123 beats/min, blood pressure 121/69, and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. He was noted to have poor perfusion with capillary refill of 4 seconds, which improved after fluid resuscitation. Complete blood count showed a white blood cell count at 18,300 mm3, platelet count at 78,000/mm3, and hemoglobin of 14.3 g/dL (14-17 g/dL). Blood chemistry demonstrated high blood urea nitrogen at 27 mg/dL, high creatinine at 2.3 mg/dL, high alanine aminotransferase at 442 IU/L, high aspartate aminotransferase at 343 IU/L, and high total bilirubin at 2.8 mg/dL. The patient received one dose of ceftriaxone in the emergency department. He was placed on vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam.
The patient was admitted to pediatric intensive care where he underwent abdominal ultrasound to investigate the acute renal and liver injury. Ultrasound revealed a complex 9.3 x 9.2 cm heterogeneous-appearing mixed soft tissue and cystic lesion within the dome of the right hepatic lobe (). After discussion with surgical and infectious disease teams, a CT-guided 10 French pigtail percutaneous drainage catheter (PD) was placed in the abscess and drained purulent brown fluid.
The drained fluid grew Streptococcus anginosus, which was penicillin susceptible, and antibiotic regimen was changed from piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin to ampicillin monotherapy. Metronidazole was added later in his hospital course. Following drainage of the abscess, he became hypotensive, necessitating norepinephrine infusion. He developed respiratory failure requiring noninvasive positive pressure ventilation. Minimal fluid was drained from PD in the first 3 days. Follow-up ultrasound two days after the PD placement demonstrated abscess enlargement (18.4 × 117 cm) (). After multispecialty discussion, open surgical drainage was deferred. Instead, tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) was instilled into the PD. Four milligrams tPA was diluted in 50 mL saline, capped for one hour, and then drained to gravity. This was performed every 6 hours for total of five doses. Following instillation of tPA, catheter drainage significantly increased, and the patient's respiratory status and fever curve improved significantly (). Follow-up ultrasound after 5 doses of tPA therapy demonstrated a decrease in abscess size to 11.3 × 6.2cm (). The patient was discharged home on amoxicillin/clavulanate and metronidazole, with the drain in place, after 14 days of hospitalization. Ultrasound performed eleven days after hospital discharge demonstrated further decrease in size of abscess to 7 × 4.9 cm. The PD was removed 34 days after initial placement.

Patient note:
A 39-year-old male office worker without a previous history of specific diseases and symptoms underwent a scheduled colonoscopy as part of a medical check-up. The patient underwent colonoscopy in another institute 3 years ago, and did not experience any specific symptoms from the use of sodium phosphate bowel purgative (Solin oral solution, Korea Pharma Co. Ltd., Seoul, Korea) as a colonic cleansing agent. Other examinations also indicated no abnormal findings.
One day prior to the colonoscopy, the patient received a dose of PEG agent (Colyte powder, Taejoon Pharma Co. Ltd., Seoul, Korea). About 5 minutes later, he experienced a generalized rash, itching, swelling and tingling feeling in his arms, dizziness, dysphagia, and dyspnea, and therefore, he visited our emergency room (ER). The patient did not have a history of chronic diseases (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis, and hepatitis), or any allergic disorders such as bronchial asthma and food allergies. He had been smoking for over 10 years and drinking at least once per week. In addition, no specific family history was noted, including any known occurrence of CRC.
Within 30 min, the patient was transferred to the ER by ambulance. When admitted to the ER, he was in a state of shock, with a blood pressure of 41/31 mmHg, heart rate of 102 beats/min, respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min, and body temperature of 36.0℃. Even though the patient showed acute symptoms, he was still conscious. No specific findings were noted on chest and abdominal examinations. The liver and spleen were not palpable. Blood tests revealed leukocytes, hemoglobin, and platelet levels of 6,700/mm3 (92.9% neutrophils, and 0.0% eosinophils), 15.5 g/dL, and 238,000/mm3, respectively, which were all within normal ranges. Electrolyte tests showed that sodium, potassium, and chloride levels were 141 mEq/L, 3.1 mEq/L, and 106 mEq/L, respectively.
Other results on biochemical and urine analyses were found to be within normal ranges. In arterial blood gas analysis, levels of pH, pCO2, pO2, and bicarbonate were 7.427, 35.2 mmHg, 84.0 mmHg, and 23.2 mEq/L, respectively. Cardiac enzyme tests revealed a CK-MB level of 0.7 ng/mL and a Troponin I level of 0.012 ng/mL, both of which were within normal ranges. The heart rate was found to be 82 regular sinus rhythms per minute on electrocardiography, and no significant findings were revealed on chest and abdominal radiography. The patient was interviewed completely and thoroughly several times regarding food allergens, medications, exercise, and occupational exposure to hazardous substances that can cause anaphylaxis. However, no cause other than the administration of the PEG agent could be identified.
As anaphylactic shock by PEG was suspected, oxygen was supplied via a nasal cannula at a rate of 4 L/min. Although the patient was administered with 1 L of saline as well as an intravenous injection of 0.1 mg of epinephrine (epinephrine injection solution, Daihan Pharm Co., Seoul, Korea), 3 mg of piprinhydrinate (Plakon®, Yungjin Pharm Co., Seoul, Korea), and 125 mg of methylprednisolone (Salon®, Hanlim Pharm Co., Seoul, Korea), his hypotension was not alleviated after 10 minutes. Therefore, 1 mg of epinephrine was dissolved in 0.5 L of glucose injection solution (5%) and then injected with the constant rate of 1 µg/min. Most symptoms (e.g., difficulty in breathing, hives, itching, and other symptoms) improved 1 hour after treatment, and vital signs returned to normal (blood pressure, 120/78 mmHg; heart rate, 92 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min). The continuous injection of epinephrine and oxygen supply were subsequently discontinued. In order to confirm whether the PEG agent was responsible for the anaphylaxis, a skin prick test was planned but not performed because the patient firmly refused to undergo the test owing to a fear of experiencing another anaphylactic shock.
Three hours after admission to the ER, the patient only showed edema on both arms, but all other symptoms were attenuated or they disappeared. After 20 hours, his vital signs were stable and no further evidence of exacerbation and recurrence were noted. The patient was informed about the possibility of anaphylaxis caused by the PEG agent, and advised to avoid such substances in the future. After discharge, no evidence of recurrence or after-effects was observed on subsequent outpatient follow-ups.

Patient note:
A 72-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with a chief complaint of palpitations due to drug-refractory AF to undergo RFCA. She underwent a total right lung excision due to bronchiectasia at an age of 23 years old. Her physical examination and laboratory analysis yielded no abnormalities. Her 12 lead electrocardiogram exhibited normal sinus rhythm, but a counter clockwise rotation (Figure A). Her echocardiograms yielded no evidence of clinically overt structural and/or organic heart disease including right ventricular dysfunction and dilation, and pulmonary hypertension, and a normal ejection fraction of 70% and left atrial (LA) dimension of 30 mm. Her chest X-ray (Figure B) and computed tomography (CT) (Figure C) revealed a severely right-sided dislocation of the heart. The CT also revealed that the area of the atrial septum was small and parallel in the 40° left anterior oblique (LAO) view and perpendicular to the 50° right anterior oblique (RAO) view (Figure C). Thus, before the transseptal puncture, right atriography was performed in those views (Figure A,B). A temperature probe (SensiTherm™, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA) for monitoring the esophageal temperature and a guidewire were inserted and placed between the level of the left superior and inferior pulmonary veins (PVs) and in the ascending aorta, respectively. Then, a double transseptal puncture was carefully performed under guidance of an intracardiac echogram (Ultra ICE catheter; EP Technologies, Boston Scientific Corporation, San Jose, CA, USA) (Figure C). After an open irrigated 3.5-mm-tip ablation catheter (FlexAbility™, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA) and circular mapping catheter (Optima™, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA) were positioned in the LA, the LA was reconstructed by a 3D mapping system (EnSite NavX/Velocity™ Cardiac Mapping System, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA). The left atriography (Figure D) and EnSite voltage map (Figure E,F) revealed that the right PVs had a blind edge, but had PV potentials. The left PVs’ stenosis or occlusion might be fatal complication in this present case. Thus, to prevent those complications, a circumferential PVAI was performed and the radiofrequency energy did not deliver in the PV, especially left PVs, under electroanatomic guidance with the 3D mapping system (Figure H,I) until the achievement of bidirectional conduction block between the LA and PVs under the administration of isoproterenol (Figure G). Because the run of the phrenic nerve was unknown, the procedure was performed while confirming the diaphragmatic movement by fluoroscopy. Because firing from the superior vena cava (SVC) was induced under an intravenous administration of isoproterenol, an SVC isolation was additionally performed. Then, program stimulation could no longer induce any arrhythmias including AF. She has remained well without any symptoms or medications for 1 year after the RFCA.

Patient note:
A 56-year-old man with a background of poorly controlled essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia treated sporadically with atorvastatin, and active tobacco use of one pack per day was rushed in by airport EMS after collapsing while disembarking from a red-eye flight that landed at 07:02. Witnesses-—a gate agent and two passengers seated behind him-—reported that he had complained of a “sudden exploding headache” while the aircraft was still taxiing, put a hand to the right occipital region, then slumped forward in his seat without striking the cabin interior. He never lost respiratory effort and did not seize or vomit during the brief interval before medics arrived at 07:07. Field personnel secured a chin-lift airway, applied 15 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather mask, placed a rigid cervical collar as a precaution, obtained a capillary glucose of 118 mg/dL, and inserted a single 18-gauge IV in the right antecubital fossa that was flushed only with 5 mL normal saline; no crystalloids, no analgesics, no sedatives, no paralytics, no vasopressors, and no reversal agents were given in the jet bridge or during the eight-minute transport to the hospital so his neurologic examination would remain unaltered. He is rolled into the resuscitation bay at 07:21 still strapped to the airline transfer sled, suit coat draped across his abdomen and shirt collar stained with a small patch of dried sweat. Pre-intervention vital signs at the moment of arrival are blood pressure 198/104 mm Hg in the left brachial artery, heart rate 76 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min with shallow thoracoabdominal excursions, oxygen saturation 99 % on the prehospital mask, and an esophageal temperature of 37.0 °C measured by the EMS probe that remains in place. The airway is patent; dentition is intact, the tongue is midline, and a Yankauer tip passed to the posterior oropharynx provokes a brisk cough but no intelligible speech. Pupils are 3 mm bilaterally and briskly reactive. During a silent thirty-second watch his eyelids rest shut without flutter. When the trauma nurse leans close and calls his surname at normal conversational volume, both lids immediately separate to half aperture, hazel irides drift past the ceiling fixtures, and his gaze fails to fix on the examiner before the lids slide closed again within three seconds; no spontaneous eye opening recurs thereafter. At baseline he issues a low, throaty moan unaccompanied by discernible words; repeated questions regarding name, location, or discomfort elicit only guttural vowel sounds that rise and fall in pitch but never form syllables. Muscle tone between stimuli is low throughout. Nail-bed compression of the left middle finger for five seconds produces a dramatic reaction: both upper limbs adduct, elbows lock in near full extension, forearms pronate, wrists flex slightly, and fingers curl; simultaneously the lower extremities extend at hips and knees with plantar flexion of the ankles. This rigid extensor pattern persists two seconds beyond removal of the noxious stimulus, then fades back to flaccid repose. An identical response follows trapezius squeeze and supra-orbital ridge pressure, with no attempt to withdraw, localize, or shield the affected region. Based on these findings the Glasgow Coma Scale totals 7/15 (E3, V2, M2). Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ at biceps and patellae, 2+ at Achilles, and there is unsustained two-beat clonus at both ankles; plantar stimulation leads to equivocal big-toe movement. Corneal reflexes are present and symmetric, oculocephalic testing shows conjugate deviation, gag and cough remain intact, and facial muscles are symmetric at rest. Cardiovascular examination reveals a loud S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses are 2+ radially and dorsalis pedis with capillary refill under two seconds. Breath sounds are vesicular and equal bilaterally, percussion is resonant, and there is no accessory muscle use. The abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender; bowel sounds are present. Pelvis is stable on gentle compression, and rectal tone is preserved. Skin inspection finds no trauma aside from faint seat-belt erythema over the right shoulder; spine palpation is non-tender without step-off, and long bones are straight with full passive range. Point-of-care arterial blood gas on current oxygen flow shows pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, PaO₂ 210 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Rapid chemistry panel returns sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, and glucose 120 mg/dL. A bedside electrocardiogram records normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats/min with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria but no acute ischemic changes. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained within five minutes reveals clear lung fields and normal mediastinum; pelvic X-ray is unremarkable. No medications or intravenous fluids beyond the initial saline flush have been administered since hospital arrival, ensuring that the described pattern-—brief lid opening only when spoken to, primitive vocalizations devoid of words, and bilateral extensor posturing in response to painful stimuli-—represents his untreated neurologic status at presentation. Neurosurgery, neurocritical care, and interventional neuroradiology have been paged; emergent non-contrast CT of the head and CT angiography of intracranial vessels are being expedited while airway equipment for possible rapid-sequence intubation stands ready at the bedside and nursing staff commence fifteen-minute neurologic checks.

Patient note:
A 31-year-old male, airline pilot, with no clinical history or cardiovascular risk factors, was admitted to the emergency room with 12 h history of retrosternal chest pain radiating to the jaw and upper extremities, during a trans-Atlantic flight, which did not improve with analgesia. Because of persistent pain, he came to our hospital. Upon arrival to the emergency room, his vital signs were stable and he had a normal physical examination but complained of precordial pain. The cardiac enzymes were elevated and the EKG detected S-T changes consistent with MI (Fig. ). A multidetector CT coronary angiography was performed showing left main trunk dissection with 50% stenosis (Fig. ).
The patient underwent emergent coronary revascularization with saphenous vein grafts to the first obtuse marginal and the left anterior descending artery (LAD). His postoperative course was uneventful and the patient was discharged home 7 days later. Control CT coronary angiography was performed 2 months later revealing patent aorto-coronary grafts (Fig. ).

Patient note:
Prior to COVID-19 vaccination becoming widely available, a previously healthy, 20-year-old Caucasian male with no significant past medical history presented with two weeks history of progressive dyspnea. About four days prior to presentation, he was evaluated at the emergency department with dyspnea, nonproductive cough, malaise, emesis, diarrhea, intermittent fever with a temperature max of 103°F, and found to have leukocytosis of 20,000 and negative COVID-19 test. Chest X-ray (CXR) showed bilateral interstitial patchy opacities and he was prescribed a five-day course of azithromycin for possible atypical pneumonia. He failed to improve after four days of treatment with azithromycin. He presented with worsening hypoxemia associated with fever, cough, emesis, and diarrhea.
On presentation, vitals showed temperature of 100.8°F, heart rate 99, blood pressure 129/81, respiratory rate 40, SpO2 85% on room air which improved to >90% on 4L nasal cannula. The patient was not in respiratory distress and a physical exam showed crackles over right lung fields and left lingula with expiratory wheezes in the same distribution. Labs were significant for leukocytosis (18x10^3/uL) with eosinophilia (7%). CXR demonstrated diffuse bilateral airspace and interstitial opacity concerning for infection or inflammatory process including COVID-19 (Figure ). Azithromycin was continued and ceftriaxone was initiated for possible community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).
The patient was placed in isolation for CXR findings, as mentioned above, which was concerning for COVID infection. Repeat testing for COVID came back negative. Further workup was significant for elevated ferritin 1,258 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 734 units/L, c-reactive protein (CRP) 27.20 mg/dL, procalcitonin 0.58 ng/mL suggestive of possible false-negative COVID-19 infection vs. CAP. Eosinophilic pneumonia vs. allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) was considered for eosinophilia and it was noted on initial complete blood count (CBC); further workup with IgE was unremarkable with 9.7 U/ml. Extensive infectious work up with influenza, mycoplasma, chlamydia nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), sputum culture, urine antigen testing for legionella, Histoplasma, blastomycosis, aspergillus all came back negative. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and QuantiFERON (QFT-G, Cellestis Limited, Carnegie, Vi Australia) were both negative.
On further evaluation, the patient reported living in his parent’s basement around the time of dyspnea onset but denied being exposed to mold. He moved out to go to college within a few days of symptoms onset and he has been living with three housemates since then. The patient initially denied tobacco use, recreational drug use, or being sexually active, and later admitted to binge drinking and vaping (dapping, use of nicotine, and delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) products) once a week during social gatherings, and the last time he vaped was two days prior to the onset of dyspnea. The urine drug screen came back positive for cannabinoids.
Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) acutely worsened while on empiric therapy for CAP requiring a high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) with 35 to 45 L/min O2 and 0.4 to 0.6 FiO2, and he was started on treatment with methylprednisolone 40 mg every six hours and albuterol-ipratropium nebulizers. Infectious disease and pulmonology were consulted. Work up with CT chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral lower lobe predominant ground-glass opacities with relative sparing of the subpleural regions and associated interstitial thickening (Figure ). Suspicion of COVID infection remained high but he had a few more negative tests. An echocardiogram showed normal size lateral ventricles and normal systolic function with an ejection fraction of 63%; left pleural effusion was noted. AHRF improved significantly to 2L of nasal cannula after two days of receiving methylprednisolone. The patient was diagnosed with EVALI as a diagnosis of exclusion and AHRF resolved with steroid therapy.
Infectious disease recommended discontinuing all antibiotics for low concern of infectious etiology. Pulmonology service recommended checking antinuclear antibodies (ANA), vasculitis panel with ANA, anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) for initial eosinophilia. All these labs were negative, and eosinophilia was later resolved. He underwent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial biopsy. Infectious work-up on the BAL sample was unremarkable for viral, fungal, and bacterial pathogens and cytology demonstrated small clusters of atypical cells with a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio. The patient briefly required being on HFNC after bronchoscopy, but he was back on room air the third day after initiating methylprednisolone. Repeat CXR showed marked improvement in bilateral interstitial and soft tissue opacities (Figure ).
The patient was hospitalized for a total of seven days, and he was discharged on prednisone 60 mg tapered dose over two weeks and supplementary oxygen (3 L of O2 with exertion). Five weeks after the hospital admission, the patient was evaluated at the pulmonary clinic for follow-up. He has been asymptomatic and AHRF has completely resolved.

Patient note:
A 44-year-old male with a history notable for a bicuspid aortic valve that was repaired 19 years ago via a Ross procedure (pulmonary autograft replacement of the aortic valve and cadaveric allograft replacement of the pulmonary valve) was admitted for evaluation of 2-3 months of persistent daily fevers up to 39.4°C, headaches, night sweats, and marked fatigue of unknown origin. Review of systems was remarkable for a week of mild painless hematochezia. He was using aspirin frequently for control of his fevers. His family and social history were unremarkable beyond owning a pet dog. He reported a dental cleaning approximately 5 months prior to presentation. At the time of presentation, he had undergone extensive infectious and rheumatologic evaluations for persistent but undifferentiated fevers. Blood cultures obtained three months prior to admission, and again one week prior to admission at a separate facility in Bactec Plus aerobic and anaerobic FAN bottles, processed in a Bactec 9120 system (Becton Dickinson), were negative after 5 days of incubation.
On physical examination the patient was febrile to 38.8°C. He was diaphoretic but otherwise well appearing. He had no evidence of dental or periodontal disease and no visible oropharyngeal abnormalities. Cardiovascular examination was notable for an old III/VI holosystolic murmur greatest at the left lower sternal border, radiating to the back, and an old II/VI diastolic murmur best appreciated over the RUSB. The pulmonary exam was unremarkable. Abdominal exam was notable for slight tenderness to palpation in the RLQ. On rectal exam, no perianal lesions were noted and there were no masses in the rectal vault; he had brown, guaiac positive stools but no melena. No other findings of endocarditis were appreciated.
Laboratory evaluation revealed a hematocrit that was decreased to 30.7% from a preillness baseline of 48%, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 44 mm/hr, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 55 mg/L, and creatinine of 1.01 mg/dL. His white blood cell count was 6,000 per mcL. A urinalysis with sediment was notable for 1+ blood, and 2 red blood cells per high-powered field on microscopy. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed mild, diffuse thickening of the mitral valve with trace mitral regurgitation and focal thickening of the pulmonic valve homograft, which were highly suggestive of a valvular vegetation. There was stable, severe dilation of the aortic root. These findings were confirmed with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.
Blood cultures were sent on the day of admission and processed with the BacT/ALERT system (bioMerieux) and on day 2 grew thin, tapered Gram-variable rods from an anaerobic FAN bottle. Subcultures grew only on Brucella agar plates incubated within an anaerobic chamber, and Gram stain of the culture revealed thin Gram-negative rods with tapered ends. This isolate was negative for oxidase and spot indole testing. The patient was started on vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole for empiric coverage. Multiple blood cultures continued to be positive for Gram-negative rods from anaerobic FAN bottles, and Gram-variable rods were also subsequently isolated from both aerobic and anaerobic FAN bottles over the following 2 days during which the patient was taking antibiotics. Despite the positive blood cultures, the patient defervesced and felt better following the administration of antibiotics. Blood cultures drawn on day 3 of antibiotic treatment were negative and remained negative after 5 days. At discharge, the isolate was still not identified.
Additional work-up with gas-liquid chromatography revealed a large peak for lactic acid and a small peak for acetic acid. The appearance on Gram stain, aerotolerance noted on further passage, and lactic acid production were most consistent with Leptotrichia species. A RapID ANAII test, which uses conventional and chromogenic substrates for species identification, did not reveal any satisfactory matches. Isolates were sent for 16S rRNA sequencing as a definitive diagnosis was unattainable via conventional phenotypic methods. Following 16S rRNA sequencing, a search of the Isentio RipSeq 16S database yielded a match with a 99.9% identity for L. goodfellowii and 7.3% difference separating it from another related species.
The patient was discharged on piperacillin/tazobactam and metronidazole as these antibiotics had demonstrated clinical effectiveness in a previous case report []. Antibiotic susceptibility testing of the isolates via Etest showed sensitivity to ceftriaxone (MIC 0.016 μg/mL), clindamycin (MIC 0.016 μg/mL), metronidazole (MIC 0.25 μg/mL), and penicillin (MIC 0.125 μg/mL). Following the availability of susceptibility data, the patient was switched to ceftriaxone and metronidazole and in total completed a 6-week course of antibiotics. He was then started on chronic suppressive therapy with penicillin V potassium, which was complicated by elevated liver transaminases and discontinued. He was then started on cefpodoxime, which he has tolerated well. Cardiac surgery was under consideration but ultimately deferred as he has been otherwise asymptomatic and with stable cardiac imaging since his hospitalization.
