Patient note:
A 70-year-old retired accountant, biologically male, was brought to the acute-care clinic by his spouse on the fifth morning of a gradually progressive respiratory illness characterized by a dry cough that had become productive of yellow sputum overnight, low-grade chills, pleuritic discomfort along the left posterior thorax, and new limitation of exertion such that he became winded after climbing one flight of stairs—an activity he normally tolerated despite chronic, medically managed cardiomyopathy. His medical background included long-standing hypertension, an ischemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction (last outpatient echocardiogram four months earlier showed an EF of 35 %), paroxysmal atrial fibrillation controlled on metoprolol, and a remote lacunar infarct eight years earlier that left no residual weakness but prompted daily clopidogrel therapy; his primary physician followed serum creatinine and cystatin C semi-annually, and both had remained within reference limits, with no prior diagnosis of intrinsic renal pathology. He had never been diagnosed with any malignancy and had no history of liver inflammation, alcohol-related disease, or viral hepatitis. The patient lives with his spouse in their own single-level home and remains fully independent in dressing, bathing, cooking, and driving; he explicitly denied any recent stays in skilled-nursing facilities, rehabilitation centers, or congregate living environments. Two weeks before presentation he completed his seasonal influenza vaccination and had not taken antibiotics during the current illness. On arrival he was seated upright on the examination table, conversing coherently and oriented to date, location, and situation without confusion, lethargy, or agitation. His initial vital signs recorded by nursing staff were: oral temperature 37.8 °C, pulse 108 beats/min with an irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with known atrial fibrillation, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min with mild accessory muscle use, and automated blood pressure 125/68 mm Hg; pulse oximetry on ambient air registered 92 %. Conjunctiva appeared mildly injected but not icteric, and oral mucosa was moist. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated above the clavicle at 45° positioning. Cardiac auscultation revealed the irregular cadence of atrial fibrillation, a soft S3 gallop similar to previous examinations, and no new murmurs. Pulmonary examination noted coarse crackles superimposed on diminished breath sounds throughout the left lower lobe without wheezes or egophony on the right, and percussion remained resonant bilaterally. There was no peripheral edema or calf tenderness. Neurologic screening showed full strength, symmetric reflexes, intact speech, and steady gait. Point-of-care finger-stick glucose measured 110 mg/dL before breakfast. Laboratory studies obtained within the first 20 minutes showed a hematocrit of 39 %, leukocyte count 11.3 × 10⁹/L with left shift, serum sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 101 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL—consistent with his baseline. Serum troponin I was undetectable. An arterial blood gas drawn on room air revealed pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 75 mm Hg, producing an A–a gradient elevated for age. Portable postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs demonstrated a dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and preservation of both costophrenic angles; no layering or meniscoid density suggested pleural fluid. Cardiothoracic ratio was unchanged from prior imaging, and pulmonary vasculature did not appear congested. Electrocardiogram confirmed chronic atrial fibrillation without new ST-T abnormalities. Prior to any pharmacologic therapy the patient had received only acetaminophen for skeletal discomfort earlier that morning and had not yet been given bronchodilators, diuretics, vasodilators, antibiotics, or supplemental oxygen beyond the arterial puncture. The clinical picture at presentation therefore reflects unaltered baseline physiology aside from the suspected infectious process involving the left lower lung field.

Patient note:
An otherwise healthy 18-year-old woman was referred to our outpatient clinic because of a 2-week history of sore throat, high fever, and mild neck tenderness. Ten days before, she had been diagnosed with acute pharyngotonsillitis and had started a 7-day amoxicillin/clavulanic acid course (1 g bid), obtaining only partial relief of the throat pain. On examination, the patient was febrile (38.2°C); neck palpation revealed tender lymph nodes in the right anterior cervical chain. The tonsils were enlarged but not erythematous; breath sounds were diminished over the right lung base. Examination of the abdomen revealed slight splenomegaly. The diagnostic suspicion was oriented toward infectious mononucleosis and, after the collection of blood samples for laboratory tests, the patient was discharged home with the prescription of paracetamol. Laboratory tests showed neutrophilic leukocytosis (white blood cells count 11.56 × 109/L, neutrophils 93%), low platelet count (61.00 × 109/L), and elevated C-reactive protein (25.9 mg/dL). Serological tests for EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative. An unexpectedly high procalcitonin value (294 ng/mL) raised the suspicion of bacterial sepsis and elicited an urgent hospitalization in our internal medicine ward for diagnostic and therapeutic management. On presentation, the patient was alert, hypotensive (BP 100/60 mmHg), and tachycardic (115 bpm); body temperature was 38.7°C; respiratory rate was 17, with oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. A chest X-ray showed a faint retrocardiac opacity and raised the suspicion of a community acquired pneumonia. After drawing two sets of blood culture (aerobic, anaerobic), an empirical treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin was started. Two days later, the patient was still febrile and mildly lethargic, with toxic appearance. Blood cultures grew gram negative bacilli, and amikacin was added to ceftriaxone. The next day, Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic gram negative rod, was identified as responsible for the bloodstream infection, and the antibiotic treatment was changed to intravenous metronidazole and meropenem. Based on this microbiological finding, a neck ultrasound exam was performed, showing a nonoccluding parietal thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein. Diagnosis of Lemierre's syndrome was ultimately confirmed by a contrast enhanced CT scan of the neck and the thorax. This showed a small right parapharyngeal abscess, thrombosis of the right internal jugular vein (), and multiple peripheral lung nodules, expression of septic embolization (Figures , , and ). Anticoagulation with subcutaneous enoxaparin was prescribed (4,000 UI bid); subsequently, the patient was transferred to the High Dependency Unit for haemodynamic monitoring. Five days later, the body temperature became steadily normal and blood tests showed a sharp decline of procalcitonin (2.11 ng/mL) and C-reactive protein (2.3 mg/dL), an increase of platelet count (428.00 × 109/L), and the negativization of microbial cultures. The patient was discharged home after a 2-week course of intravenous antibiotic treatment. She received an outpatient oral treatment with metronidazole and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid for 14 days and a 3-month course of enoxaparin, experiencing an uneventful recovery. A control CT scan showed the complete resolution of lung opacities and pleural effusion (Figures , , and ).

The pain was dull in quality, radiated to her right shoulder, worsened with meals, taking a deep breath, and moving. She described the severity of pain as 8/10; it was associated with nausea and vomiting of ingested matter for the past three days. She denied any alleviating factors. Furthermore, the patient complained of dry cough and gradual worsening of shortness of breath which started seven days ago. Shortness of breath was both at rest and while walking. The patient also had intermittent low-grade fever with a T-max of 100.8°F in the past three days. Otherwise, she denied chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, yellowish discoloration of the eye, change in stool color, diarrhea, or constipation.
Upon initial evaluation and physical exam, the patient was fully awake and oriented to person, place, and time. Initial vitals were as follows: respiratory rate of 23 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 86% on room air which later improved to 94% with 2 L of oxygen via nasal cannula, blood pressure of 127/87 mmHg, pulse rate of 89 bpm, and temperature of 98.6°F. Head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat (HEENT) exam revealed pink conjunctiva and nonicteric sclera, dry tongue, and buccal mucosa. On respiratory system exam, she had mild tachypnea with a respiratory rate of 23 breaths/min and bilateral coarse crackles with rhonchi. Heart sounds were irregularly irregular, S1 and S2 well heard no murmur or gallop. Jugular venous pressure (JVP) was flat, and no distended neck veins. The abdomen was slightly distended abdomen which moved with respiration. The patient had marked right upper quadrant tenderness on both superficial and deep palpation with significant guarding and rigidity, and murphy’s sign was positive. She had no costovertebral angle tenderness or suprapubic tenderness. Extremity exam revealed mild pretibial and pedal trace edema. Inflammatory markers were elevated with C-reactive protein (CRP) of 68 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 278 u/L, and D-dimer of 0.77 mg/L FEU (fibrinogen equivalent units)​​​​​​. ​Procalcitonin was within normal limits (0.20 ug/L). Blood cultures showed no growth in two bottles. COVID-19 nasal swab test was positive. Chest X-ray showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates typical of viral interstitial pneumonia (Figure ). Ultrasound of the gallbladder showed gallbladder wall thickness with mild pericholecystic fluid collection and no gallstone suggestive of acalculous acute cholecystitis (Figures , ). The most recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 50%.
The patient was admitted to the COVID-19 unit with the diagnosis of acute hypoxic respiratory failure due to COVID-19 pneumonia and acute acalculous cholecystitis. She was treated with dexamethasone, remdesivir, and vitamin supplements. The patient also received supportive care with oxygenation via nasal cannula. Anticoagulation with Eliquis from her home medication was continued for the atrial fibrillation and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis. Abdominal pain was significantly resolved, and oral feeding was resumed on the third day of her admission. Eventually, she was discharged home with oral Augmentin and the remaining dose of dexamethasone as well as vitamin supplements. Patient note:

Patient note:

She ambulated from the parking structure without assistance and reports that she routinely walks her dog briskly for 30 minutes each evening and manages household chores, including carrying laundry up one flight, without shortness of breath or lower-extremity swelling. Twelve years ago, while on vacation, she experienced sudden substernal pressure radiating to the left jaw while climbing a hill; coronary angiography at that time revealed a 90 % mid-left anterior descending lesion successfully treated with a drug-eluting stent, after which she completed cardiac rehabilitation and has remained free of chest discomfort, unplanned cardiology visits, or repeat revascularization. Follow-up exercise treadmill imaging performed eight months ago to investigate atypical palpitations demonstrated excellent functional capacity to 9 metabolic equivalents without inducible perfusion defects, and a contemporaneous transthoracic echocardiogram described a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60 % with normal diastolic filling and no valvular abnormalities. She has never been hospitalized for fluid overload, uses only one pillow at night, and denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or ankle edema. Past medical history is notable for well-controlled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diet-managed type 2 diabetes first diagnosed five years ago after an elevated screening hemoglobin A1c of 6.8 %; she has never required injectable glucose-lowering therapy. There is no personal history of stroke, transient neurologic symptoms, carotid procedures, peripheral arterial interventions, or chronic kidney disease. Her daily medications include metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril 10 mg, rosuvastatin 20 mg, low-dose aspirin, vitamin D, and a calcium supplement; she takes no insulin or other injectable agents and has no drug allergies. She quit smoking more than three decades ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, enjoys a glass of white wine with dinner twice weekly, and denies illicit substance use. Family history reveals a brother with coronary bypass surgery in his fifties and a mother who died of colon cancer in her seventies. Vital signs seated in the right arm are blood pressure 124/68 mm Hg, heart rate 62 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air, and oral temperature 36.5 °C. Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated, carotid pulses are brisk without bruits, the apical impulse is localized and nondisplaced, and auscultation reveals crisp S1 and S2 without gallops, murmurs, or rubs. Lungs are clear to bases, the abdomen is soft and nontender with no organomegaly, and distal pulses are 2+ without edema. Neck examination demonstrates a well-circumscribed thyroid nodule that moves on deglutition and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves, normal strength, and symmetrical reflexes. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn an hour before the visit reveal hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.95 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate exceeding 60 mL/min/1.73 m². Patient note:

Facility staff, who are equipped only with basic respiratory aides, reported that the patient had been using his home portable oxygen concentrator set at 2 L/min until midnight, but by 03:00 he was unable to complete sentences, and saturation on their finger probe read 78 % despite escalation to 6 L/min via simple mask. Because the facility has a standing protocol against field intubation unless airway reflexes are lost, the nurse fitted a full-face non-invasive circuit delivering continuous distending pressure of 12 cmH₂O through a turbine unit; an in-line analyzer connected to the wall blender recorded an inspired oxygen fraction of 0.57, and this configuration accompanied him in the ambulance. He remained spontaneously breathing throughout the twenty-minute transport, never received a paralytic or sedative, and no bag-mask ventilation was attempted. Intravenous access consisted of a single 18-gauge cannula through which only a keep-open rate of normal saline ran; no vasopressors, bronchodilators, or antibiotics were begun en route. On arrival to the emergency department—and before any hospital-based therapy was initiated—he was found seated upright on the stretcher, leaning into the mask cushion with visible sternocleidomastoid recruitment, respiratory rate 32/min, pursed-lip expiration, and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower thorax. Cardiovascular examination disclosed a gallop over the apex, no new murmurs, and jugular veins that were difficult to appreciate because of laboured breathing; extremities were cool to touch and mottled to the mid-shin. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, with mild epigastric tenderness but no guarding. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the primary survey produced 40 mL of dark amber urine; review of the nursing-home intake-output sheet confirmed only 700 mL over the preceding twenty-four hours. Liver profile demonstrated aspartate aminotransferase 68 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 176 U/L, total bilirubin 1.85 mg/dL with predominantly conjugated fraction, and an international normalised ratio of 1.4. Up to the moment these data were captured, he had not been exposed to any intravenous fluid bolus, pressor agent, antimicrobial, or corticosteroid, remained unsupported by an endotracheal tube or invasive ventilator, continued to require continuous positive airway pressure at 12 cmH₂O with a 57 % oxygen blend, persisted with a systolic pressure no higher than 92 mm Hg in the absence of pharmacologic support, exhibited mild thrombocytopenia, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, an acute creatinine elevation with oliguria totaling only 700 mL over twenty-four hours, and demonstrated moderate encephalopathy while struggling against severe right-sided community-acquired pneumonia complicated by early septic physiology.

Patient note:
A 60-year-old Caucasian man presented with 2 weeks of back pain with drenching night sweats 20 days after undergoing laparotomic sigmoidectomy for severe diverticulitis. One week after his discharge, the patient developed right sided lower back pain and severe drenching night sweats that prompted him to change his clothing and bed sheets multiple times every night. The patient described the pain as a 7/10 throbbing, sharp pleuritic pain that was better in supine position and was initially responsive to nonsteroid anti-inflammatory drugs. The patient experienced mild shortness of breath on exertion. He denied any nausea, vomiting, chest pain, or chills or fevers. He had a 12-pound weight loss starting 3 weeks prior to presentation. His medications were silodosin, atorvastatin, diazepam, docusate, and as needed acetaminophen, naproxen, and oxycodone. Patient never smoked and lived an active life prior to his surgery.
On physical examination he was afebrile, resting in bed comfortably. Heart rate was 100 beats/minute, blood pressure was 144/91 mmHg, respiratory rate was 20 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation level was 97% on room air. He had no palpable lymph nodes and had bibasilar dullness to percussion with decreased breath sounds. Auscultation of the heart revealed tachycardia, but regular and normal heart sounds. The right lower back was tender to palpation. The abdominal surgical scar was intact with no signs of inflammation.
The laboratory findings were hemoglobin level: 13.1 mmol/L; white blood cell count: 10.4 × 103/mL; platelet count: 354 × 103/mL; troponin: 0.01 ng/mL. Basic metabolic profile values were all within normal limits. Our initial differential diagnosis list included PE, pneumonia, pericarditis, and pneumothorax. As the patient presented with pleuritic back pain after recent surgical intervention, PE was very high on our differential diagnosis. Chest radiography revealed bilateral basilar opacities and no pneumothorax. CT imaging of the chest demonstrated PE involving the main pulmonary arteries (). Transthoracic echocardiogram showed no sign of pericardial effusion.
Therapy was initiated with subcutaneous enoxaparin injections. The back pain resolved after the first day, but night sweats continued. Further diagnostic workup showed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 53 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP): 19.34 mg/dL, normal thyroid-stimulating hormone, and normal procalcitonin. CT of abdomen and pelvis was performed to rule out abdominal abscess and showed postsigmoidectomy state with intact anastomosis. MRI of the spine revealed no epidural mass or collection. Based on clinical guidelines the patient was discharged home on 3 months of rivaroxaban treatment []. Patient's night sweats completely resolved after discharge, verified by a 3-month follow-up visit and by a 9-month follow-up call.

Patient note:
An 88-year-old-female presented to our emergency department with complaints of abdominal discomfort associated with nausea and vomiting for one day. Upon arrival, she was afebrile with a blood pressure of 120/54 mmHg, a pulse rate of 40 beats per minute (bpm) (), and a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. She denied any chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations. She denied any recent illnesses, had no history of recent travel, and denied any sick contacts, or recent change in medications. Her medical comorbidities included hypertension (HTN), diabetes, CAD, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypothyroidism, and a history of cerebrovascular accident (CVA) without any residual deficits. Her prescription regimen included amlodipine (10 mg), furosemide (20 mg OD, same dose for past 1 year), isosorbide mononitrate (30 mg OD), levothyroxine (37.5 mcg OD), metformin (500 mg BID), omeprazole (20 mg OD), and ranolazine (500 mg BID, same dose for the past 1 year). Physical examination was remarkable for bradycardia and decreased breath sounds in the left lower lung field, and she was euvolemic on exam. Laboratory studies were significant for a serum potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L and a serum creatinine level of 1.6 mg/dL and eGFR of 32 ml/min/m2 (increased from baseline creatinine of 0.9 mg/dl, eGFR 68 ml/min/m2). Thyroid studies were within the normal range. Chest radiography revealed minimal left pleural effusion. She received an intravenous fluid bolus for her acute renal injury and was administered sodium polystyrene sulfate, calcium gluconate, albuterol, intravenous insulin, and a dextrose injection to treat the hyperkalemia. Over the next few hours, her bradycardia worsened despite correction of the hyperkalemia. A 12-lead electrocardiography (ECG) showed junctional bradycardia at 32 bpm, a normal QRS complex, and a prolonged QTc of 532 milliseconds. There was no demonstrable peaking of the T waves. Atropine was administered without any significant chronotropic response. She was admitted to the cardiac care unit for close monitoring. The following day, her serum creatinine reached a maximum of 2.2 mg/dL. Ranolazine was discontinued. Metabolic derangements were treated appropriately. After 48 hours from presentation, potassium and renal function returned to baseline and her heart rate improved to a range of 60–100 bpm. She was discharged the next day with an outpatient cardiology follow-up. Ranolazine treatment was not continued upon discharge.

Patient note:
A 54-year-old woman with an eight-year history of biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis that evolved into macronodular cirrhosis despite previous courses of prednisone and azathioprine was brought to the liver clinic by her adult son after she noticed progressive tightness of her clothing, visible abdominal enlargement, and a new need to loosen the watchband around each ankle over the last three weeks. She denied fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, dysuria, rash, or recent travel. Alcohol use had been negligible since college, and she had never injected drugs. Other medical conditions included well-controlled Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with levothyroxine 100 µg daily and mild essential hypertension on lisinopril 5 mg daily. Surgical history consisted of laparoscopic hysterectomy fifteen years earlier without complications. She was allergic to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, developing hives when exposed. The family pedigree was notable for a mother who required liver transplantation in her mid-sixties for cryptogenic cirrhosis and a father with coronary artery disease; no siblings had autoimmune disease. She worked as a high-school art teacher, did not smoke, and exercised by walking her dog two miles each morning until the abdominal distention curtailed her pace last week. At intake her vital signs prior to any intervention were temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 116/70 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. She sat comfortably upright but leaned back slightly to accommodate a rounded abdomen. Sclerae were anicteric, conjunctivae pink, oral mucosa moist, and there were a few telangiectasias scattered over the upper chest; no palmar erythema, jaundice, or bruising was present. Neck veins were not distended and carotid upstrokes were brisk. Cardiac auscultation revealed a regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear to percussion and auscultation at the apices but breath sounds were slightly diminished at bilateral bases. Inspection of the abdomen showed a protuberant contour with bulging flanks, an inverted umbilicus, and several superficial veins tracking toward the epigastrium. On percussion there was tympany centrally that transitioned to dullness laterally, and shifting dullness was clearly elicited when she rolled to her side. A fluid impulse transmitted across the abdominal wall confirmed the presence of a sizable peritoneal collection, yet the skin remained soft without tautness or shininess. The liver edge was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, firm and nodular, non-tender, while the spleen tip was not appreciable. There was 2 + pitting edema up to the mid-shins but no sacral edema. Extremities otherwise showed normal capillary refill and intact peripheral pulses. Cutaneous examination found no excoriations. The remainder of the systemic examination, including cranial nerves and deep tendon reflexes, was deferred to focus on abdominal assessment. Baseline laboratory studies obtained immediately on arrival, prior to administration of diuretics, albumin, or paracentesis, demonstrated: white blood cell count 5.4 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, platelet count 112 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.82 mg/dL, glucose 97 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 38 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 55 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 140 U/L, and gamma-glutamyl transferase 118 U/L. Synthetic function tests revealed a total bilirubin of 1.0 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.7 g/dL, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.25. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was within therapeutic range at 2.1 µIU/mL. Serologic screening for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody remained negative, immunoglobulin G level was 1950 mg/dL (chronically elevated), and alpha-fetoprotein measured 6 ng/mL. A focused point-of-care ultrasound performed before any therapeutic tap visualized a nodular, coarsely echogenic liver, patent portal and hepatic veins with antegrade flow, and anechoic fluid layers measuring up to 5 cm depth in the right paracolic gutter and around the spleen, findings consistent with a moderate volume ascites; no discrete focal mass or portal vein thrombosis was identified, and the gallbladder appeared unremarkable. Chest radiography showed mild elevation of both hemidiaphragms but clear lung fields, while electrocardiography recorded normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats per minute with a QTc of 422 ms. Given the objective findings of a significant fluid burden within the peritoneal cavity consistent with a moderate-grade ascites, preserved serum protein synthesis reflected by a near-normal albumin, minimal bilirubin elevation, and only a slight prolongation of coagulation indices, the impression was progressive decompensation of known autoimmune cirrhosis manifested by abdominal volume accumulation in the absence of overt infection or gastrointestinal hemorrhage at presentation.

Patient note:
A 45-year-old male with no history of ischemic heart disease presented to the emergency department 45 min after the onset of retro-sternal chest pain which radiated to the left arm and accompanied with cold sweating. His past medical history was only indicative of cocaine and tobacco abuse for several years. Initial physical examination demonstrated a blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg, heart rate of 94/min, respiratory rate of 18/min, oral temperature of 37.4°C and oxygen saturation 95% while he was breathing ambient air. Heart and lung examinations were unremarkable.
On admission, the electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm and elevated ST segment in V1-V4 leads and depressed ST segment in II, III, AVF, V5 and V6 leads, well-suited with the diagnosis of acute antroseptal myocardial infarction. Bed-side echocardiography showed ejection fraction of about 35% and antroseptal akinesia.
The patient was immediately transferred to the intensive care unit for cardiac monitoring and thrombolytic therapy. Pain was alleviated with nitroglycerine and morphine. An intravenous infusion of 1.5 million units of streptokinase over 50 min, followed by heparin at 900 U/h and one 325 mg tablet of aspirin and one 75 mg tablet of clopidogrel were administered.
Results of laboratory evaluation included normal levels of electrolytes and glucose. The blood urea nitrogen level was 16 mg/dl and the creatinine level was 1.3 mg/dl. The alanine aminotransferase level was 64 U/l (reference range: 8-40), the aspartate aminotransferase level 180 U/l (reference range: 8-30), the alkaline phosphatase level 130 U/l (reference range: 35-125), total bilirubin level 0.8 mg/dl (reference range: 0.2-1.2 mg/dl), the albumin level 4.4/dl (reference range: 3.7-5.5), and the total protein level 7.3 g/dl (reference range: 6.0-8.0). The white blood cell count was 11,000/mm3, the hematocrit was 45.9% and the platelet count was 218,000/mm3. Also, creatinine kinase myocardial bound/creatinine kinase equal to 597/8932 U/l and elevated troponin-I level equal to 29 ng/ml were recognized.
After 8 hours of admission, the patient gradually developed shortness of breath, hypoxemia and fever (38.5°C) and after 3 h later, cough and hemoptysis developed. Bed-side chest X-ray showed bilateral basal alveolar infiltrates. Finally, endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation was necessitated when hypoxemia (SaO2= 78%) and symptoms of respiratory distress were present with a respiratory rate of 40/min. Laboratory tests showed a fall in the hemoglobin level from 15.8 to 12 g/dl within 20 h, and to 9 g/dl within 48 h; so two units of packed cell were administered. Activated partial thromboplastin time was 99 s. In addition, he received four units of fresh frozen plasma and eight units of cryoglobulin with the purpose of pulmonary hemorrhage control. There was no sign of hematuria or melena. The lab tests of admission time showed normal coagulation, liver and kidney functions tests. No other bleeding site was discovered.
On the next day, the patient remained febrile (39.0°C) with constant and moderate hemoptysis. Due to the increased blood urea nitrogen and creatinine during the 72 h after admission, bed-side hemodialysis according to the nephrology consult was done for him with the impression of acute renal failure. Bronchoscopy on the 3rd day showed no lesion in the bronchial tree and broncho-alveolar lavage was positive for hemosiderin laden macrophages (90%) and negative for acid fast bacillus. Computerized tomography of the chest on the 3rd day revealed diffuse alveolar infiltrates []. The results of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody, antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid antibody, peripheral antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA), and cytoplasmic ANCA were all negative.
The patient was intubated for 9 days with no significant improvement in his condition and in the 10th hospital day his blood pressure was not detected and cardiac rhythm became asystole; in spite of cardiopulmonary resuscitation for 60 min he remained pulseless and eventually expired.

Patient note:
A 52-year-old man with a background of ischemic cardiomyopathy complicated by chronic systolic dysfunction (most recent outpatient echocardiogram three months earlier showed an ejection fraction in the mid-30s) and a remote left parietal infarct that required a brief course of inpatient rehabilitation two years ago was transported to the emergency department by family after he awoke at dawn speaking incoherently, unable to recall the month, and insisting he was in a hotel rather than at home. According to his spouse, he had complained of progressive cough over the preceding five days, initially dry but now producing small amounts of yellow-green sputum, intermittent shaking chills, and a sensation of “burning” behind the sternum whenever he drew a deep breath. He normally works as an accountant from a home office, performs all activities of daily living independently, and has not been hospitalized in more than a year. His routine laboratory panels during cardiology and primary-care visits have consistently shown normal serum creatinine and stable liver transaminases. Home medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, low-dose furosemide only as needed for ankle swelling (none taken over the past week), aspirin 81 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly; he is a lifelong non-smoker, drinks two glasses of wine per week, and denies recreational drug use. He has no prior diagnosis of chronic kidney disease or liver disease, has never required dialysis, and denies any history of hepatitis, cirrhosis, or other hepatic disorders. He received an influenza vaccine in the autumn but has not yet obtained the current season’s pneumococcal booster. Emergency medical services reported that he was seated on the sofa when they arrived, answering questions slowly and misidentifying the day of the week, with no focal motor deficit or seizure activity en route; no intravenous line, oxygen, or medications were administered before arrival. In triage, prior to any antipyretics, fluids, or antimicrobial agents, vital signs were: oral temperature 38.1 °C, pulse 94 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 119/74 mm Hg with a palpable systolic of 119 mm Hg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute with quiet chest excursions, and pulse oximetry 92 % on ambient air. He appeared flushed and slightly diaphoretic, sitting upright but confused; he recognized his spouse but was unsure of the hospital name and answered only one of three orientation questions correctly. Mucous membranes were moist, sclerae anicteric, and no cervical adenopathy was palpable. Jugular venous contour was at the level of the clavicle at 45°, similar to baseline. Cardiac examination revealed a displaced point of maximal impulse and a soft third heart sound without new murmurs or pericardial rub. Lung auscultation disclosed diminished breath sounds with inspiratory crackles over the right lower posterior zone; percussion was dull in the same area, and tactile fremitus was moderately increased, but there was no stony dullness or asymmetry of diaphragmatic excursion to suggest fluid accumulation. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge was not palpable. Extremities were warm with 2+ distal pulses and no peripheral edema or clubbing. Neurologic screening showed equal pupils, symmetric facial movements, 5/5 strength throughout, intact cerebellar finger-to-nose testing, but he was oriented only to person and exhibited short-term memory gaps, consistent with acute encephalopathy rather than residual stroke deficit. A finger-stick glucose measured 124 mg/dL. Venous blood draw and arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival, before any therapeutic intervention. Initial laboratory results revealed hematocrit 30 %, white blood cell count 13.6 × 10⁹/L with 82 % neutrophils, serum sodium 145 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated pH 7.46, PaCO₂ 36 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 82 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, and an A-a gradient mildly above age-predicted norms. High-sensitivity troponin I was undetectable, lactate 1.5 mmol/L. A portable posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph obtained minutes later showed a dense alveolar opacity with air bronchograms localized to the right lower lobe; the diaphragmatic costophrenic angles were sharp, and there was no meniscus sign or shift of mediastinal structures. Cardiothoracic ratio was unchanged from an outpatient film six months prior, and pulmonary vasculature was not engorged. Electrocardiography displayed sinus rhythm at 92–94 beats per minute with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria and nonspecific ST-T changes but no acute ischemia. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and a rapid viral panel were sent while the patient remained on room air, seated upright, and he had not yet received intravenous crystalloids, diuretics, supplemental oxygen, or antibiotics at the time this note was completed.

Patient note:
An HIV-infected 32-year-old male presented to Mulago National Referral Hospital, Uganda with a 2-week history of headache with fevers and a 1-day history of confusion (
). He had been on ART (zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz) and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for 5 years. 5 months prior, he was diagnosed with pulmonary TB by positive sputum Xpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA). He had completed 2 months of induction TB therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) and was 3 months into continuation phase (rifampicin, isoniazid). He endorsed poor adherence to both ART and anti-tuberculous medications.
On examination, the patient was febrile (38.6°C). His blood pressure was 112/71 mmHg, pulse 94 beats/minute, respiratory rate 48, and oxygen saturation 98%. He was wasted, dehydrated, and had overt rigors. His Glasgow Coma Scale was 14/15 with nuchal rigidity and positive Kernig’s sign. Cranial nerves were intact. He had normal tone and power in all limbs. A clinical diagnosis of HIV-associated meningitis was suspected and he was recruited into the ‘Improving Diagnostics and Neurocognitive Outcomes in HIV/AIDS-related Meningitis’ study (registration:
). Whilst awaiting further investigations, he received empiric therapy of ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily for possible bacterial meningitis.
A finger stick cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay (CrAg LFA) (IMMY, Norman, Oklahoma, USA) was negative. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure was elevated to 33 cm CSF (normal <20 cm CSF), CSF white cells 590 /µl, protein 419 mg/dl (normal range 15–45 mg/dl), CSF lactate 9.5 mmol/L (normal range <2.5 mmol/l). CSF glucose was unavailable.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis in CSF was confirmed on Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra; there was no evidence of rifampicin resistance. On day 2, he was initiated on dexamethasone at 0.4 mg/kg/day and induction TB-medications were re-commenced (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) for TBM. The IV ceftriaxone was stopped, his ART was continued. He continued to spike high-grade fevers (39.6°C.) with tachycardia (pulse 118 beats/min). A peripheral blood smear showed
P. falciparum parasites (1+ trophozoites), despite a negative malaria histidine rich protein-2 (PfHPR2)-based rapid diagnostic test (Malaria
Plasmodium falciparum Rapid Test Cassette, Vaxpert, Florida, USA). Given his ongoing neurological symptoms, which could be compatible with cerebral malaria, the decision was made to treat for severe malaria. Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) between rifampicin and artemisinin compounds, and rifampicin and quinine are recognized (
); a decision was made to treat with IV artesunate as the most efficacious anti-malarial for severe malaria
. He received three doses of IV artesunate (3 mg/kg), after which a repeat peripheral blood smear showed no malaria parasites. He then completed 3 days of oral artemether/lumefantrine. His fevers subsided on day 6. He was discharged on day 8; medication adherence counselling was provided for the patient and his guardian and outpatient follow-up was arranged for the following week.

Patient note:
A 47-year-old man with a decade-long history of alcohol-related chronic liver injury—biopsy three years ago showed stage-3 fibrosis with mild portal tract inflammation and his last hepatology follow-up six months back documented mild thrombocytopenia without encephalopathy—presented to the emergency department after noticing three consecutive jet-black, shiny bowel movements that glued to the toilet porcelain over the preceding twelve hours, accompanied by foul, tar-like odor and a dull epigastric squeeze that intensified whenever he tried to lie flat. He denied dizzy spells, blackout, chest pressure, palpitations, cough, or lower-extremity swelling, and stated that he walked into the hospital unaided but felt “weak and soaked in sweat” while waiting at triage. His regular medications are limited to 40 mg oral furosemide each morning, lactulose as needed for constipation, and an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor he takes sporadically when heartburn flares; he has never been prescribed beta-blockers, anticoagulants, dual antiplatelet therapy, or corticosteroids, and he last ingested non-steroidal anti-inflammatory pills “a couple of months” ago for a dental extraction. Alcohol intake averages four shots of whiskey nightly, though he says he abstained for the last two days because of nausea; he denies intravenous drug use since college, has smoked one pack per day for twenty years, and uses no illicit substances currently. Family history is notable only for a mother with type 2 diabetes; no relatives have bleeding disorders or congestive cardiomyopathy. Review of systems revealed early satiety, occasional right upper-quadrant fullness, easy bruising on the shins, and stable body weight; there were no orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or exertional limitations beyond his usual baseline. On arrival—prior to intravenous access, fluid bolus, antiemetic, vasoactive infusion, blood product administration, or acid suppression—he sat forward on the stretcher, pale, with beads of sweat on the forehead but fully oriented and answering in complete sentences. Manual vital signs obtained by nursing staff showed a narrow pulse pressure with a systolic blood pressure of 90 mm Hg and diastolic of 56 mm Hg, a brisk tachycardia clocked at 128 beats per minute that was regular on the monitor, respiratory rate 24 per minute, oral temperature 37.1 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing ambient air. Conjunctival pallor was evident; sclerae were anicteric; oral mucosa appeared tacky with a trace of dried coffee-ground material at the uvula. Spider angiomas peppered the upper chest and there was faint palmar erythema; no digital clubbing or leukonychia was seen. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated at 30°, and there was no peripheral edema. Cardiac auscultation identified a rapid but otherwise unremarkable S1 and S2 without gallops or murmurs. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was scaphoid, soft, and mildly tender in the epigastrium on deep palpation, with a firm, 15 cm liver edge palpable two fingerbreadths below the costal margin and a splenic tip just felt on inspiration; percussion suggested a shifting dullness of less than 2 cm and no obvious fluid wave. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. Digital rectal examination produced a smear of black, tarry stool that turned the bedside guaiac card an immediate dark blue. Two 18-gauge antecubital intravenous lines were placed solely for sampling at this juncture, and a type-and-screen was sent but no therapies had yet commenced when initial labs resulted: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 27 %, mean corpuscular volume 90 fL, platelet count 109 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.6 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 52 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.4, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, and glucose 98 mg/dL. A portable single-view chest radiograph performed concurrently showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette; an abdominal upright film revealed a nonspecific gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. Twelve-lead electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia at 130 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic ST-T changes. At this point he had received no crystalloid resuscitation, proton pump inhibitor infusion, vasoactive medications, octreotide, or transfusion; he was placed on continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring, kept nil per os, an emergent gastroenterology consult was initiated for possible endoscopic hemostasis of presumed upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of chronic hepatic injury, and cross-matched packed red blood cells were requested while serial hematologic indices and vital signs were arranged for close surveillance.

Patient note:
An 89-year-old woman who ordinarily knits in the activity room of her long-term-care facility and manages her own daily medications for hypertension and osteoarthritis—without any history of chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, advanced heart or lung failure, malignancy, HIV infection, or ongoing immunosuppressive therapy—was transferred directly from the emergency department to the medical intensive care unit for closer monitoring after a morning of intractable, bilious emesis and crampy epigastric pain that had left her too weak to stand; according to her caregiver, the gastrointestinal upset began the previous afternoon, but overnight she became progressively lethargic, produced only a trickle of dark concentrated urine, and stopped drinking the bedside water kept within reach. The paramedics found her seated on the edge of the bed, pale but alert, with a fingertip oxygen saturation in the mid-80s on ambient air, so they placed a clear Venturi mask delivering 40 % inspired oxygen, established a single peripheral line that remained capped, and provided no fluids, antiemetics, analgesics, bronchodilators, vasopressors, or antibiotics during the twelve-minute transport. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—before anyone altered the oxygen settings or initiated therapy—the first complete set of observations registered an oral temperature of 36.9 °C, non-invasive blood pressure cycling reproducibly at 126⁄72 mm Hg, a regular pulse of 87 beats min⁻¹ on three-lead telemetry, and a respiratory rate visually timed at 20 breaths min⁻¹ without accessory-muscle recruitment. She opened her eyes spontaneously, conversed appropriately, and obeyed multistep commands, confirming an intact Glasgow Coma Score of 15 in the absence of sedatives, ethanol, or head trauma. Skin was cool and slightly doughy with capillary refill just over two seconds; mucous membranes were dry and fissured, and jugular veins were difficult to appreciate at 30°, suggesting intravascular depletion. Cardiovascular examination revealed a crisp first heart sound, physiologic splitting of the second, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses were thready but symmetrical. Chest auscultation disclosed faint basilar crackles likely atelectatic, otherwise breath sounds were vesicular. The abdomen was distended, tympanitic, and diffusely tender to light palpation but without guarding; high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds accompanied intermittent visible peristaltic waves, raising concern for a proximal small-bowel obstruction. There was no hepatosplenomegaly, surgical scar, or flank ecchymosis. A bladder scan performed during the primary survey read less than 50 mL. Six minutes after stretcher placement, a right radial arterial specimen obtained while she remained on 40 % oxygen revealed an alkalemic pH of 7.62 with an arterial oxygen tension of 57 mm Hg; end-tidal capnography displayed 27 mm Hg, implying a component of respiratory hypocapnia layered on a metabolic disturbance from volume loss and chloride depletion. Simultaneously drawn chemistry showed sodium 145 mmol⁄L, potassium 3.9 mmol⁄L, chloride 90 mmol⁄L, bicarbonate 36 mmol⁄L, glucose 118 mg⁄dL, blood urea nitrogen 46 mg⁄dL, and serum creatinine 1.9 mg⁄dL—markedly higher than her documented baseline of 0.9 mg⁄dL two months earlier—corroborating an acute decline in renal filtration likely prerenal in origin rather than an exacerbation of chronic insufficiency. Complete blood count returned a white-cell concentration of 12 200 mm³ with 80 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 30 %, hemoglobin 10.0 g⁄dL, and platelets 210 000 µL⁻¹. Point-of-care lactate measured 1.9 mmol⁄L. A supine abdominal radiograph acquired before decompressive maneuvers demonstrated multiple dilated jejunal loops with air-fluid levels and paucity of colonic gas; upright chest film taken concurrently showed low lung volumes with bibasilar atelectasis but no free sub-diaphragmatic air. Focused cardiac ultrasound revealed a vigorously contracting small left ventricle and an inferior vena cava measuring 0.9 cm in expiration that collapsed completely on inspiration, reinforcing the impression of volume depletion. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram printed during the arterial puncture displayed normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats min⁻¹, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 88 ms, QTc 430 ms, and diffuse ST-T wave flattening without acute ischemic change. Capillary blood glucose checked by nursing matched the laboratory value, and bedside ketone testing was negative. Importantly, by the time the critical-care team assumed responsibility—less than twenty minutes from ambulance arrival—she had still received no intravenous crystalloid, vasoactive infusion, antiemetic, proton-pump inhibitor, nasogastric decompression, or antimicrobial therapy; the sole ongoing intervention remained the Venturi device fixed at 40 % inspired oxygen. Thus, the contemporaneous physiologic and laboratory data—temperature 36.9 °C, systolic pressure 126 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 72 mm Hg, heart rate 87 beats min⁻¹, respiratory rate 20 breaths min⁻¹, pH 7.62, serum sodium 145 mmol⁄L, potassium 3.9 mmol⁄L, creatinine 1.9 mg⁄dL, hematocrit 30 %, white-cell count 12 200 mm³, fractional inspired oxygen 40 %, and arterial oxygen tension 57 mm Hg—accurately capture her untreated presentation for suspected high-grade mechanical bowel obstruction complicated by profound metabolic alkalosis, prerenal azotemia, mild hypoxemic respiratory compromise, and borderline anemia.

Patient note:
An 89-year-old man who still resides in the bungalow he built after returning from military service and who remains largely self-sufficient—he prepares his own breakfast, manages his medications, and tends a small vegetable garden—was brought to the emergency department by his adult grandson late this morning after three days of progressively deeper cough, scant rusty sputum, and fevers that peaked overnight high enough to drench the bedclothes; he insisted on skipping the acetaminophen his daughter offered so the hospital team could “see the numbers straight.” He observed that climbing the five steps from his porch required two pauses today and that he felt “winded just walking to the mailbox,” shortness of breath not present at baseline. Past history is notable for a left middle cerebral artery ischemic event four years ago that left a mild expressive aphasia now barely perceptible, and for chronic systolic dysfunction attributed to idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 30 % on an echocardiogram six months earlier; he takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, low-dose furosemide most mornings, and sacubitril-valsartan 24-26 mg twice daily with good refill adherence. He has never been told he has chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, or any form of malignancy, and his last outpatient basic metabolic panel two months ago documented a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL and sodium 139 mEq/L. He quit smoking cigarettes three decades ago after a 40 pack-year exposure, drinks one glass of red wine with Sunday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Immunization records at his primary clinic confirm both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza shot. He lives with his wife, does not receive home health aide services, and has never spent time in a skilled-nursing facility. The grandson drove him the 35 minute trip with windows cracked; no supplemental oxygen, nebulizers, intravenous fluids, or antipyretics were given en route. On arrival the patient sat bolt upright on the stretcher, lips pursed, speaking in brief phrases but clearly oriented to name, place, date, and current events. Skin appeared flushed and dry with poor axillary sweat; mucous membranes were tacky, and capillary refill remained under two seconds. Pre-intervention vital signs on ambient air at this sea-level institution revealed an oral temperature of 38.45 °C (101.2 °F), an irregular but rapid radial pulse that averaged 139 beats per minute over a full minute and was confirmed on three-lead monitoring as sinus tachycardia, a non-invasive right-arm blood pressure of 151/76 mm Hg verified manually, respirations counted at 63 breaths per minute with pronounced intercostal and suprasternal recruitment, and pulse oximetry fluctuating between 92 % and 94 %. Jugular venous contour was 4 cm above the sternal angle while upright—unchanged from cardiology notes—and there was trace bilateral ankle edema. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a crisp S1 and S2 with a soft third heart sound already documented previously, no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination demonstrated coarse crackles throughout the right mid-zone and lower posterior lung field with bronchial breath sounds over the right apex, preserved resonance to percussion bilaterally, and no stony dullness or egophony at either costophrenic angle. Abdomen was scaphoid and nontender; the liver edge was not palpated below the costal margin, and no splenomegaly or shifting dullness was appreciated. Neurologic screen showed equal reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, a mildly labored but fluent speech pattern identical to his previous baseline, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. A bedside glucometer prior to venous access read 157 mg/dL. Two large-bore peripheral lines were placed, flushed only with minimal saline to maintain patency, and venous samples together with a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival—before any crystalloid, diuretic, antipyretic, antibiotic, vasodilator, or oxygen therapy was given. The basic metabolic panel returned sodium 169 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 115 mEq/L, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 67 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, revealing severe hypernatremia and azotemia out of proportion to his preserved filtration baseline. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 17.4 × 10⁹/L with 90 % segmented neutrophils, a striking hematocrit of 68 %, hemoglobin 22.1 g/dL, and platelets 255 × 10⁹/L, consistent with significant hemoconcentration. The arterial blood gas on room air revealed a pH of 7.16, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, PaO₂ 109 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, indicating a severe metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory alkalotic compensation yet preservation of oxygen tension. Serum lactate measured 3.1 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin was below the assay threshold, and NT-proBNP returned at 3,500 pg/mL, similar to prior clinic values. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes into the visit, before any therapeutic intervention, showed a dense consolidation occupying the right upper and middle lobes with air bronchograms, sharp costophrenic angles, and a cardiac silhouette unchanged from films six months earlier; no layering fluid or meniscus was visualized. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 138 bpm with nonspecific ST-T flattening but no acute ischemic pattern compared with a tracing on file from last year. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an induced sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any empiric antibiotics or intravenous therapy were ordered. Up to the moment this narrative is documented he remains seated upright on 21 % inspired oxygen, has received no intravenous fluids beyond the saline used to lock the lines, no diuretics, no vasoactive drugs, no bronchodilators, and no antipyretics, such that every vital sign, laboratory datum, and imaging finding above reflects his untreated physiologic state on presentation.

Patient note:
A 55-year-old woman developed generalized urticaria, itching, and a subsequent coma within 5 minutes of ingesting yacon roots. At the time, she was in a steam bath. She was treated at a regional hospital, and her systolic blood pressure was 60 mmHg. She was then referred to our clinic to determine the cause of her problem.
She had a 20-year history of hypothyroidism and had been taking amlodipine (5 mg) for hypertension for 3 years. There was no history of bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis, although she frequently developed pruritus when preparing Codonopsis lanceolata. She did not smoke or consume alcohol. She reported that her one son developed urticaria and angioedema when he ingested shrimp, apple, or pear.
On physical examination, she appeared acutely ill, but her consciousness was clear. Her blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg; respiratory rate, 20/minute; pulse, 81/minute; and body temperature, 36℃. Her conjunctivae were not anemic, and no jaundice was observed in her sclera. On auscultation, no rales or stridor were heard. There were no abnormal findings in the abdomen or extremities.
Routine blood tests revealed a white blood cell count of 5,350/µL, 182/µL eosinophils (3.4% of all white blood cells), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 2 mm/hour. Thyroid function tests showed TSH at 5.99 mIU/L (normal range, 29-4.2 mIU/L), free T4 at 0.86 ng/dL (normal, 0.93-1.70 ng/dL), total T3 at 96.14 ng/dL (normal, 80-200 ng/dL), and anti-TPO antibody at 278.3 IU/mL (normal, 0-314 IU/mL). No abnormalities were observed by biochemical or serologic testing, urinalysis, stool examination, electrocardiography, and simple chest X-rays.
She refused skin prick tests with common inhalant allergens, although skin prick and intradermal tests were performed using juice extracted from cut raw yacon root. The skin prick test showed a 3.5×4.0/+ reaction to histamine (H), -/- reaction to normal saline, 4.5×7.0/+ reaction to yacon extract (allergen A), and a 3+ A/H ratio (positive reaction) (). An oral food provocation test was performed using 1-g pieces of yacon root. The patient complained of tingling, pain, and numbness in the oral cavity and around the lips at about 5 minutes after ingesting 2 g of the root. Headache, chest tightness, dizziness, and pruritus/urticaria extending to the neck and face developed about 10 minutes after ingesting the root. At that time, her blood pressure was 85/50 mmHg and her pulse was 115/minute. The oral provocation test was stopped because the patient complained of chest tightness and dizziness. The patient was given epinephrine (1:1,000, 3 mL, intramuscularly), dexamethasone (5 mg, intravenously), and fluids. Her symptoms improved immediately and her blood pressure normalized. She was definitively diagnosed with anaphylaxis to yacon root based on the oral provocation test results. She was instructed not to ingest yacon roots and to carry a portable epinephrine kit for use in an emergency. Levothyroxine (50 µg) was prescribed for her hypothyroidism.

Patient note:
An 85-year-old woman with a past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, cerebrovascular accident (CVA), and left lower lung lobectomy presented to the ER due to intermittent abdominal pain, dysuria, and nausea for one day. Physical exam was significant for diffuse tenderness to palpation, worse in the suprapubic region. Her vitals were blood pressure of 167/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 16 per minute, pulse rate 87 beats per minute, and temperature of 95.9 °F. Relevant laboratory workup is mentioned in Table .
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous (IV) contrast was suggestive of proximal ureteral/ureteropelvic junction rupture and a large amount of fluid in the left retroperitoneum and surrounding the left kidney in the pelvis (Figure ). No clear obstructive etiology was identified on the CT scan. There was no evidence of stone or mass on the CT scan.
The patient received broad-spectrum antibiotics in ER. While the patient was in the ER, she was noted to have an atrial flutter with rapid ventricular rate and systolic blood pressure dropped to 89 mm Hg. She was given an amiodarone bolus and she reverted to normal sinus rhythm. Norepinephrine infusion was also planned to be given but once she reverted to sinus rhythm, her blood pressure was noted to improve. She was also noted to drop her oxygen saturation to 70% and was placed on two liters of oxygen through a nasal cannula.
Urology consultants were consulted and the recommendations were to admit the patient to the intensive care unit (ICU) and placement of percutaneous nephroureteral catheter tube (PNCT). This was done successfully (Figure ). The patient was monitored in ICU and continued on antibiotics.
Over the course of her stay, the patient clinically improved, and she was transferred out of ICU to medicine service. Due to persistent leukocytosis, a CT scan abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast was repeated, which did not show any clear infectious etiology (Figure ). The infectious disease was also evaluated and antibiotics were switched to ceftriaxone as per blood culture sensitivities.
Eventually, the patient's leukocyte count down trended. Clinically she was noted to improve significantly. Urology recommended that PNCT should be kept in place for at least three weeks. She was discharged on oral antibiotics and recommendations were given to follow-up outpatient with urology and IR specialists.

Patient note:
A 47-year-old woman with medically refractory temporal-lobe epilepsy, obesity class II, and quiescent systemic lupus controlled on hydroxychloroquine was discovered at 05:40 by her overnight home-health aide lying supine on the kitchen floor after what sounded like “a series of loud thuds” followed by gurgling respirations; empty pill blisters for her evening levetiracetam dose were accounted for, and no witnessed overdose or trauma was reported. The aide noted tonic–clonic movements of all extremities lasting roughly two minutes, copious oropharyngeal secretions, and cyanosis of the lips, prompting immediate activation of emergency medical services. Paramedics arrived six minutes later to find the patient unresponsive, apneic, and still pulsing at 88 beats per minute; bag-mask ventilation with 100 % oxygen was begun, and after a single attempt a 7.0-mm cuffed endotracheal tube was placed at 21 cm at the incisors using etomidate 20 mg and succinylcholine 100 mg for rapid-sequence induction. A portable ventilator was programmed to volume assist-control mode with a tidal volume of 480 mL, a rate of 16 breaths per minute, 5 cm H₂O of positive end-expiratory pressure, and an inspired oxygen fraction of 0.40, settings that remained unchanged during the thirteen-minute transport. No crystalloid bolus, vasopressors, benzodiazepines, antiepileptics, or other medications were administered in the field. On entry to the resuscitation bay—and before any hospital therapy was initiated—the patient was secured to a transport backboard, mechanically ventilated on the documented 40 % FiO₂, and exhibiting bilaterally equal chest rise without cuff leak. Initial vital signs recorded by the trauma monitor showed heart rate 94 beats/min in sinus rhythm, respiratory rate 16/min delivered by the ventilator, non-invasive blood pressure 135/82 mm Hg confirmed moments later by a right radial arterial line waveform, oxygen saturation fluctuating between 97 % and 98 %, and core temperature 37.4 °C by esophageal probe. The arterial catheter placed within two minutes furnished an immediate blood gas revealing pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, and a PaO₂ 120 mm Hg on the unchanged 0.40 inspired oxygen fraction. Neurologic assessment after the paralytic had worn off showed pupils 3 mm equally brisk, a gaze deviated slightly to the left, eyes opening only to deep trapezius squeeze, incomprehensible expiratory phonation around the tube, and purposeful localization of a supra-clavicular pinch with both arms, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 7; corneal, cough, and gag reflexes were present, plantar responses were flexor bilaterally, and tone was symmetrically increased. Head and neck inspection disclosed no scalp lacerations or battle sign; the cervical collar remained in place pending imaging. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular S₁ and S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, capillary refill <2 seconds, and jugular veins not distended. Lung fields were clear to auscultation with equal air entry, and peak airway pressure measured 18 cm H₂O on the ventilator. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, and nontender; no organomegaly was palpated. Skin survey demonstrated several lateral thigh ecchymoses consistent with peri-ictal falls but no petechiae. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the primary survey immediately drained 130 mL of straw-colored urine; the aide, who keeps strict intake/output charts because the patient is enrolled in a lupus nephritis surveillance program, provided a handwritten log confirming 2 100 mL of urine in the preceding twenty-four hours. Peripheral blood drawn concurrently with the arterial sample—before any antiepileptic loading, antimicrobial therapy, corticosteroids, or intravenous fluids—returned sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, unchanged from nephrology clinic three weeks prior. Total bilirubin measured 0.6 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 34 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 96 U/L, and the international normalized ratio was 1.1. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 11.2 × 10³/µL with 5 % band forms, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, and a platelet concentration of 154 000 /µL. Serum lactate was 2.1 mmol/L, high-sensitivity troponin was below the limit of detection, and serum ammonia was pending. A non-contrast head CT obtained while the ventilator and FiO₂ remained fixed demonstrated no acute intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect but diffuse cerebral edema compatible with post-ictal hypoxia. Chest radiograph taken at the same time showed the endotracheal tip 4 cm above the carina, clear lung fields, and normal cardiac silhouette. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound displayed a well-contractile left ventricle with an inferior vena cava diameter of 1.8 cm collapsing 40 % during inspiration. Importantly, throughout the prehospital period and the interval needed to collect the above data, the patient maintained an arterial pressure of 135/82 mm Hg without any vasopressor or fluid support, remained on controlled mechanical ventilation rather than spontaneous modes, delivered a PaO₂ of 120 mm Hg on 40 % inspired oxygen, exhibited normal platelet and bilirubin values, preserved renal function with robust urine output quantified at 2 100 mL per day, and demonstrated a severely depressed level of consciousness reflected by a Glasgow Coma Score of 7 in the setting of a probable status-epilepticus–related hypoxic insult.

Patient note:
A 50-year-old female with a past medical history of SLE diagnosed 20 years ago, ESRD on hemodialysis and atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. The patient was sitting on the side of her bed when she suddenly lost consciousness falling to the floor striking the right side of her face. She sustained significant facial trauma; however there were no signs of intracranial hemorrhage on CT scan of the brain. She described palpitations with chest pressure prior to the event. Initial electrocardiogram (ECG) reported by emergency medical services did not reveal any acute arrhythmias, such as TdP. Due to the complaints of chest pressure she was evaluated for cardiac ischemia utilizing cardiac biomarkers, CKMB and Troponin I. A total of three sets were completed every eight hours apart; all studies were reported within normal limits ruling out cardiac ischemia. Troponin I values were less than 0.045 ng/mL and CKMB values were all less than 0.5 ng/mL. ECG on presentation revealed 1st-degree AV block with corrected QT (QTc) interval of 689 ms (). Patient's ECG from two years prior showed a baseline prolonged QTc interval of 500 (). She was evaluated for reversible causes of QT interval prolongation including electrolyte derangements, medications, and SLE flare. Her electrolytes were within normal limits including potassium (3.9 mmol/L), magnesium (2.3 mg/dL), phosphorous (4.2 mg/dL), and calcium (9.0 mg/dL). C3 levels were low, with normal C4 and ESR, and anti-dsDNA was negative making SLE flare unlikely. Patient continued to have dialysis on her normally scheduled days.
After evaluation by electrophysiology there was concern for presumed TdP due to her clinical presentation and grossly abnormal QTc interval. She was placed on mexiletine 150 mg BID and was initially recommended to have defibrillator implantation to protect against sudden cardiac death from cardiac arrhythmias. Evaluation of the patient's medications revealed that she was taking HCQ for the past two years for treatment of refractory SLE. HCQ was discontinued and the patient's QT interval slowly decreased to a QTc interval of 500 over the next 7 days (). She was monitored on the telemetry unit for one week and did not have any further arrhythmic events. After further discussion with the patient's Cardiologist and Rheumatologist she had been noted to have a prolonged QTc interval of approximately 500 ms while on therapy with HCQ. She was trialed off the medication for two months without resolution of the QT interval abnormality, possibly due to undiagnosed underlying SLE cardiomyopathy. The patient's ejection fraction on echocardiography one year prior was estimated at 65% with Doppler parameters consistent with abnormal relaxation suggesting heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Implantable defibrillator placement was discussed with the patient prior to admission due to the prolonged baseline QTc interval. However, she was reluctant to proceed as she did not want indwelling devices due to concern for possible Permacath placement in the future for dialysis if her arteriovenous fistula malfunctioned.
The risks and benefits of continuing HCQ were discussed with the patient, and she decided she wanted to continue the medication due to well controlled SLE flares. She had noted adverse reactions to steroid therapy and limited treatment options for SLE due to her underlying renal failure. We discussed the risks of recurrent syncopal episodes if she was to continue HCQ therapy, and the high risk for intracranial bleed while on anticoagulation if she was to have another syncopal episode. Final recommendations were made to proceed with defibrillator placement if she was to continue with HCQ to protect against life threatening arrhythmias. She had a subcutaneous defibrillator placement and was to be restarted on HCQ as an outpatient with dose reduction and close monitoring of QTc interval.
At three-month follow-up the patient remained off HCQ as after discussion with her Rheumatologist the risks related to syncope and possible intracranial bleed while on anticoagulation treatment greatly outweighed the benefits of HCQ therapy. She continues to be closely monitored for SLE flares, and treatment decisions are to be strategized as clinical issues arise. Subcutaneous implantable defibrillator interrogation showed no recorded events at three months. Her ECG continues to show a prolonged QTc interval of 508 ms. Due to the prolonged QTc interval she is still at high risk of ventricular arrhythmias despite discontinuation of HCQ. Therefore, the subcutaneous implantable defibrillator is providing secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death due to prolonged QT interval.

Patient note:
A 32-year-old woman living in North Carolina but under the care of a local physician in Washington DC for symptoms attributed to chronic Lyme disease presented to George Washington University Hospital with fever, shortness of breath, and increasing confusion. Two years prior to the current presentation, the patient had been given a diagnosis of chronic Lyme disease after she developed multiple symptoms including confusion, photophobia, arthralgia/ myalgia, headaches, constipation, and seizures. A computed axial tomography (CT) scan of the chest at the time showed patchy infiltrates and she underwent a bronchoscopy, which did not detect any abnormality including negative acid-fast bacilli smear and culture. Subsequent imaging showed resolution of those infiltrates. She was treated with multiple oral regimens including rifabutin, pyrimethamine, leucovorin, metronidazole and ivermectin. One year prior to her current presentation she had a subclavian CVC implanted for administration of intravenous antibiotics including meropenem, clindamycin, and tigecycline. Most recently, she had completed a three-week course of ciprofloxacin and meropenem every other day, ending several weeks prior to her presentation. After development of her current symptoms, she sought treatment in an emergency department in North Carolina, where she was diagnosed with pneumonia and treated with azithromycin without improvement. She then traveled to Washington, DC for evaluation by her local physician, and subsequently presented to our institution.
In the emergency department the patient was noted to be febrile to 39.5°C, blood pressure 125/73 mmHg, heart rate 85 beats/minute. Physical exam revealed fatigued appearance with decreased breath sounds bilaterally, and a CVC with port access in the left chest wall without evidence of infection. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (white blood count 11,370 cells/mL, 85% neutrophils). Contrast CT chest showed bilaterally symmetric opacification with bronchovascular distribution and innumerable pulmonary nodules (). Multifocal pneumonia due to septic emboli was suspected, and vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam were started. A trans-thoracic echocardiogram (TTE) found no evidence of valvular vegetations. No other foci of infection were apparent on physical examination. After 72 hours anaerobic blood culture bottles (BACTEC Plus Aerobic/F, Becton Dickinson, Sparks, Maryland) revealed growth of beaded Gram-positive, acid-fast rods suggestive of mycobacterial species.
After lengthy discussion with the patient and her family, the CVC was removed. Culture of initial blood cultures and the CVC tip revealed growth of M. goodii. The patient’s antibiotics were empirically changed to azithromycin 500 mg intravenously daily, ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours, and meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours. The patient clinically improved on this regimen. The patient returned to North Carolina before the identification and sensitivities of the mycobacterial species was available. Therefore, she was empirically switched to an oral regimen of trimethoprim/ sulfamethoxazole 800 mg/160 mg twice daily, azithromycin 250 mg once daily, and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for two-weeks from time of line removal. The patient was counseled extensively to avoid future placement of a CVC in the absence of a clear medical indication. Blood cultures drawn after CVC removal were negative at the time of her discharge but subsequent to discharge also grew M. goodii. The patient cancelled her follow-up appointment in our Infectious Diseases clinic and she was lost to follow-up.
The mycobacterial isolate was sent to Quest Diagnostics Labs (San Juan Capistrano, California) for the beta subunit of RNA polymerase (rpoB) and 16S rDNA sequencing which revealed the organism to be genetically consistent with M. goodii with an identity match of 99.86%.
