Surgical drain ultrasonography showed no significant intra-abdominal fluid collection. Twelve-lead electrocardiography printed concurrently displayed sinus tachycardia at 109 beats per minute, normal intervals, and no ischemic ST-T changes. No broad-spectrum antibiotics, antipyretics, stress-dose steroids, vasoactive drips, or additional crystalloids had been started in the forty-five minutes between ICU admission and completion of the diagnostic work-up, so the recorded physiologic and laboratory values—temperature 102.6 °F, systolic pressure 117 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 66 mm Hg, pulse 111 beats per minute, respirations 23 per minute, arterial pH 7.39, serum sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, hematocrit 31 %, white-cell count 12 300 / mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 68 %, and A-a gradient 313 mm Hg—faithfully represent her untreated status immediately upon transfer for surveillance of suspected peri-operative infectious complication in the setting of immunosuppressive therapy and chronic kidney disease.

Patient note:
The index case, 36 year old man, lived with his wife, two daughters and his son. He presented to a clinic with fever (37.8°C) and cough on April 16. He felt well after taking compound paracetamol tablets (II), Ibuprofen Tablets and Radix Isatidis on April 17. On April 18, he continued fever and developed pneumonia and was admitted to Zaozhuang City Hospital on April 21. Due to progressive respiratory distress and suspicion of impending acute respiratory distress syndrome, he was transferred to intensive care unit on the day of admission. Bilateral ground-glass opacities and pulmonary lesions were observed on chest radiography (Figure ). The index patient recovered and was discharged on May 16. The positive throat-swab collected on April 21 was confirmed by Chinese Center for disease Control and Prevention on April 23 and virus was A/Shandong/01/2013(H7N9) (SD/01). The antibody titers was 1:80 for the serum sample collected on May 21st compared with 1:5 on April 24 by the micro-neutralization assay [].
The second case was the index patient’s 4 years old son. He began to have fever (37.8°C) and cough on April 14. He was given domiciliary care before April 18. From April 18 to 20, he was treated for common cold at the clinic with his father and recovered. On 21st April, when the index case was hospitalized, the boy separated with him and was under medical observation till April 27 when the fever (38.3°C) and cough started again. After taking antipyretic granules and cephalosporin on the morning, the temperature decreased to 37°C in the afternoon. On 28th morning, he was hospitalized with fever (37.2°C) and was treated with oseltamivir (5 mg). Initial testing identified leucopenia and multiple patchy shadows in the lungs bilaterally. He was discharged on May 6. The throat swab collected on April 23 was negative for H7N9. On April 27, PCR test from throat swabs was H7N9 positive and virus was A/Shandong/0068A/2013(H7N9) (SD/0068A). The antibody titers was 1:20 for the serum sample collected on May 21st compared with 1:5 on April 24 and May 1st.
Table summarized the demographic and clinical characteristics of the two cases.
The index case lived in rural–urban fringe zone in Zaozhuang City. There were several living chicken in the cage and vegetable gardens fertilized with fences in the living community away 10 meters from their apartment. And there were two living poultry slaughter sites in the Mazhuang Farm Market located 500 and 1000 meters from the residential district (Figure ).Interviews with the family members, other close contacts and the first case after recovery constructed the timeline of the two cases onset of ill and treatment (Figure ). From April 6 to 16, the index case always stayed at home except taking his two daughters to school on the morning and picking them up after school every day by car with his wife and his son, while they passed the poultry slaughter sites in the Mazhuang Farm Market. Two days before the onset of illness, the index case had visited a village with several large poultry farms in the other city, but he didn’t enter the poultry farms. At the same time, his son didn’t go to the kindergarten and stayed at home since April because he always got sick and had a cold on April 14.
Furthermore, the index case was not in charge of purchase the foodstuff and his family members didn’t buy poultry from the two living slaughter sites in the Mazhuang Farm market and the other markets. None of the members of his family raised poultry or other animals, none brought live poultry to their home, none had direct contact with sick or dead poultry, and none played with the living chicken in the living community.
After the index case fell ill, his family, including his son had prolonged, close, unprotected contact with him, including eating together. Furthermore his son was the nearest to him when they ate, watched TV and slept till April 20. His son also accompanied the index case while seeking medical care from April 18 to 20. After the index case hospitalization, his son was under the medical observation till April 27 in his apartment and didn’t go out.
11 close contacts of the two H7N9 cases were identified and followed up daily for 7 days. Of these, seven were family members or relatives, two were health care workers and two were index case’s friends. All the throat swabs collected on April 23 were negative for H7N9 virus. Four close contacts of the second case were the same as those of index case, all being family members (the index case’s wife, his two daughters and mother in law), whose specimens collected on April 28 were negative for H7N9. No micro-neutralization antibodies against A (H7N9) virus were detected from paired serum samples of all close contacts. To trance the infectious source, 96 environment samples were collected and only one chopping block swab from Jinniu living poultry market located 10 kilometers away from the living community was positive for H7N9 by rRT-PCR and virus was A/environment/Shandong/01/2013(H7N9) (Ev/SD/01),while the samples from the surrounding areas of the living community including the slaughter sites were negative.
Complete genomic sequencing of SD/01, SD/0068A and Ev/SD/01 were analyzed. The homologous analysis showed that they were 97.92% to 100% identical in all eight gene segments and the two human A (H7N9) viruses were 100% identical in HA, PB1, PA, NS and M genes (Table ). There are only four amino acid substitutions between the two human A (H7N9) viruses, two in the PB2 (E341K and R427Q substitutions), one in NA (L399S substitution) and one in NP (M191V substitution), respectively. The full-length gene sequence number in GISAID are EPI 1447715–1447721 and 1447618 [SD/01], EPI 1457428–1457435 [SD/0068A], EPI1447645-651 and 1447628 [Ev/SD/01].

Patient note:
A 30-year-old female was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and altered mental status. The patient had a past medical history of treatment-naïve Hepatitis C and remote intravenous drug abuse that was complicated by MRSA tricuspid valve (TV) endocarditis. She underwent a bioprosthetic TV replacement 16 months previously, however, suffered a heroin relapse 6 months later that was complicated by recurrent endocarditis; she was medically managed with 6 weeks of intravenous gentamycin, cefazolin, and rifampin. She was doing well until this presentation and taking no medications.
Her vital signs upon presentation were significant for fever of 40.5°C, blood pressure 70/30 mmHg, heart rate 134 b.p.m., and respiratory rate of 34 breaths per minute with appropriate oxygen saturation. Physical exam was remarkable for jugular venous distention of 10 cm and grade II/VI holosystolic and diastolic murmurs at the left lower sternal border. Skin had a livedo reticularis appearance with numerous tattoos. Electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia with rightward axis deviation and right atrial enlargement. Admission labs were significant for white blood cell count of 23.4 × 109/L (3.7–11.0 × 109/L), platelet count of 37 000/µL (150–400 × 103/µL), lactic acidosis of 6.9 mmol/L (0.5–2.2 mmol/L), PT INR of 1.8 (0.9–1.3), D-dimer >35 200 ng/mL (<500 ng/mL), and fibrinogen 234 mg/dL (200–400 mg/dL). The patient was empirically started on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam due to concern for septic shock; blood cultures subsequently grew MRSA and piperacillin-tazobactam was discontinued. Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiograms demonstrated thickened bioprosthetic TV leaflets with severe stenosis (peak/mean gradient 20/14 mmHg) and regurgitation and a large mobile echodensity consistent with vegetation (Figure). Chest computed tomography demonstrated numerous subpleural nodules concerning for embolic phenomena.
She was supported with aggressive volume resuscitation, maximal doses of three vasopressors (norepinephrine 50 mcg/min, epinephrine 50 mcg/kg/min, and vasopressin 0.04 units/min), and continuous venovenous haemodialysis due to acute renal failure with haemodynamic improvement by hospital day 3. However, her skin lesions progressively worsened and, by hospital day 5, included (i) violaceous discolouration of distal nose and ears, (ii) large purpuric plaques on arms and legs, most severe distally and of all digits, and (iii) haemorrhagic bullae scattered within purpuric plaques with large areas of grey discolouration suggestive of necrosis (Figure). Our leading differential diagnosis was vasopressor-induced skin necrosis given her significant exposure to vasopressors. However, the exposure was not prolonged and the appearance of the rash was atypical. The haemorrhagic appearance of the rash raised a concern for a vasculitic process such as catastrophic anti-phospholipid syndrome, levamisole-mediated vasculitis given a history of substance abuse, or antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis in light of significant renal dysfunction. The differential also included cryoglobulinaemia or a viral-mediated process such as Hepatitis B or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) given a history of untreated Hepatitis C and previous intravenous drug abuse. Finally, our differential included PF given a severe septic state with profound coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia despite no evidence of underlying liver dysfunction at baseline. Further work-up noted: C3 86 mg/dL (86–166 mg/dL), C4 14 mg/dL (13–46 mg/dL), negative lupus anticoagulant, serum levamisole, cryoglobulins, and negative serologic testing for active Hepatitis B, HIV, and anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies. Function of protein C was 45% (76–147%), protein S 31% (59–131%), and antithrombin 54% (84–138%). Factor VIII: C of 441 suggested appropriate liver synthetic function. This constellation of findings was consistent with PF with secondary bullae formation and skin necrosis.
On hospital day 7, intravenous human protein C concentrate (Ceprotin) was initiated with 100 units/kg bolus followed by 50 units/kg infusion every 6 h. With this, skin lesions rapidly improved and thrombocytopenia resolved (Figure). Blood cultures remained positive on repeated cultures and ultimately cleared following transition from vancomycin to ceftaroline on hospital day 16. She was taken to the operating room on hospital day 19 with findings notable for obstructive vegetation involving all three TV leaflets, abscess cavity around the annulus, and vegetations extending into the right ventricle and subvalvular space. She underwent debridement and removal of the infected valve (FigureA) followed by bioprosthetic TV replacement. Movat staining showed a pericardial tissue valve with marked acute inflammation and fibrinous vegetation (FigureB). Gomori methenamine silver stain showed bacterial cocci which on Gram stain revealed Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Post-operatively she did well though remained dialysis dependent. Dry gangrene of her left foot and several right toes persisted. For this, she has followed with Vascular Surgery. She was ultimately discharged to a skilled nursing facility after completion of ceftaroline for 6 weeks for rehabilitation given a prolonged hospital stay. She has been seen in follow-up and is doing well.

No mask-based positive-pressure support had been attempted prior to intubation, and no intravenous fluids, antimicrobials, or vasopressors were started during the 12-minute ride. On arrival to the resuscitation bay, before any hospital-initiated therapy, she remained intubated on the same settings, eyes opening only to painful supraorbital pressure, uttering incomprehensible groans around the cuff, and withdrawing her right arm from a nail-bed pinch while the left remained flaccid, yielding a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 9 without overt lateralizing deficits; pupils were 3 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive, corneal reflexes intact, and plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Initial automated cuff pressure read 89/47 mm Hg and was confirmed by a left radial arterial line placed immediately afterward; skin was cool, mottled to the knees, and capillary refill exceeded four seconds. A radial arterial blood gas drawn within five minutes showed pH 7.27, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, and PaO₂ 86 mm Hg on the aforementioned 0.65 FiO₂. Simultaneous venous sampling demonstrated white-cell count 18.7 × 10³/µL with 14 % bands, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, and a platelet count of 112 000/µL. Comprehensive metabolic panel returned sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, bicarbonate matching the arterial value, blood urea nitrogen 58 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, representing a marked increase from a baseline of 1.1 mg/dL documented three months earlier. Total bilirubin measured 2.3 mg/dL (direct fraction 1.6 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 92 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 76 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 212 U/L, consistent with a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern atop chronic hepatic dysfunction. Point-of-care lactate was 6.1 mmol/L. Coagulation profile revealed an international normalized ratio of 2.0 and partial thromboplastin time 48 seconds. Bedside abdominal ultrasound showed diffuse colonic wall thickening in the sigmoid region with adjacent hyperechoic foci suggestive of intramural gas, moderate ascites, and a sonographically small, collapsible inferior vena cava. A nasogastric tube returned 300 mL of coffee-ground fluid, and rectal examination yielded dark maroon stool. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the secondary survey drained scant amber urine; review of the daughter’s home intake log and paramedic documentation suggested an aggregate output of approximately 620 mL over the preceding 24 hours, far below the patient’s usual 1.5 L baseline. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST-T changes, and a portable chest radiograph confirmed appropriate endotracheal tube placement 3 cm above the carina, bilateral basal atelectasis, and no overt consolidation. No crystalloid bolus, antibiotics, vasopressors, corticosteroids, renal replacement therapy, or sedation beyond the single induction dose had been administered at the time the above data were captured. The working impression at this un-resuscitated moment was perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with feculent peritonitis leading to distributive shock, early renal injury, hepatic decompensation, thrombocytopenia, and compromised oxygenation necessitating invasive mechanical ventilation on high inspired oxygen.

Patient note:
An 83-year-old male was brought to the outpatient medicine clinic by his daughter because of gradually worsening pain in the right calf with walking two short city blocks and a non-healing shallow ulcer over the dorsum of the same foot that has been present for about three weeks. He reports that the discomfort is cramp-like, begins reliably after ambulating a similar distance, and is relieved with rest; he does not feel chest tightness, dyspnea, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea during or after these episodes. He has lived independently in a single-story home, manages his own finances, cooks simple meals, and remains fully oriented to date, place, and situation without any memory lapses noted by family or the primary caregiver. His past medical history is notable for an ischemic stroke affecting the left hemisphere six years ago, from which he recovered fully without residual weakness or speech difficulty; he completed a course of dual antiplatelet therapy at that time and has remained on low-dose aspirin alone since. He also carries a long-standing diagnosis of type 2 diabetes that was discovered twenty years earlier during an employment physical; the condition has been controlled with metformin 1 g twice daily, and his most recent primary-care record, dated six months ago, documented an HbA1c of 6.8 %, normal monofilament sensation in both feet, and no evidence of retinopathy on annual ophthalmologic screening. Two years ago, a surveillance abdominal ultrasound done for mildly elevated aminotransferases demonstrated a coarsened hepatic echotexture without nodularity, and subsequent laboratory work revealed a normal synthetic profile (albumin 4.2 g/dL, INR 1.1, platelet count 200 000/µL) and no bilirubin elevation, leading his gastroenterologist to attribute the findings to non-alcoholic fatty infiltration; he has never developed ascites, variceal bleeding, or hepatic encephalopathy. He denies any prior myocardial infarction, valve surgery, cardiac stents, or episodes of decompensated heart muscle weakness. He has never experienced transient focal neurological deficits suggestive of a transient ischemic attack. He also denies chronic lung conditions such as COPD or asthma, has no history of peptic or duodenal ulcer disease or gastrointestinal bleeding, and has not been diagnosed with any solid-organ or hematologic malignancy, including lymphoma. He has never tested positive for HIV and has no history of AIDS or other immunodeficiency. His only surgical procedure has been an endovascular balloon angioplasty of the right superficial femoral artery performed eight years ago for similar calf claudication, after which his symptoms improved for several years. He stopped smoking 35 pack-years ago, drinks red wine on special occasions only, and has never used illicit drugs. Family history is significant for hypertension and diabetes in first-degree relatives but no premature coronary disease or malignancy. He is allergic to penicillin (rash). Medications include metformin as noted, low-dose aspirin, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and vitamin D. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, weight loss, hemoptysis, chronic cough, wheezing, ankle swelling, transient vision loss, double vision, or seizures. On examination, he is a thin older gentleman appearing stated age, blood pressure 124/64 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.8 °C, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Mental status is intact with fluent speech, appropriate naming, and normal short- and long-term recall. Cardiovascular exam reveals a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Lungs are clear bilaterally to auscultation and percussion. Abdomen is soft, nontender, with no hepatosplenomegaly and no fluid wave. Peripheral vascular assessment shows normal brachial and radial pulses symmetrically, diminished right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses compared with the left, and an ankle-brachial index measured by Doppler of 0.52 on the right and 0.78 on the left. The right foot ulcer is 1.2 cm in diameter with a pale base and minimal serous drainage, surrounded by hairless, cool skin; there is no surrounding cellulitis. Sensory examination with a 10-g monofilament is intact at all plantar surfaces, and motor strength is full in all extremities. Laboratory data obtained this morning show hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 78 mL/min/1.73 m²), fasting glucose 132 mg/dL, AST 54 U/L, ALT 62 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 112 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, INR 1.0, LDL 82 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 3 mg/L. Urinalysis is unremarkable with no proteinuria or hematuria. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without Q-waves or ST-T abnormalities. A duplex ultrasound of the right lower extremity ordered today demonstrates significant atherosclerotic plaque with 70 % stenosis in the superficial femoral artery and monophasic flow in the distal popliteal segment; no acute thrombosis is visualized. Given the progressive exertional calf pain, diminished distal pulses, and non-healing ulcer, the working diagnosis is lower-extremity ischemia on the background of established systemic atherosclerosis. The patient will be scheduled for vascular surgery consultation and noninvasive imaging to delineate the arterial tree further, while attention to glycemic control, lipid lowering, antiplatelet therapy, and walking exercise will continue.

Patient note:
A 23-year-old African-American man with past medical history of G6PD-deficiency and obesity presented with dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain that improved upon leaning forward and scant hemoptysis of two weeks duration. He was notably hypertensive to the 220/110 s mmHg and tachycardic to the 120 s, but had a preserved respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. Physical exam was remarkable for bilateral diffuse wheezing throughout all lung fields. Other parts of the exam including cardiovascular, nasopharynx, skin and musculoskeletal systems were unremarkable. Additional pertinent history was remarkable only for marijuana smoking. Electrocardiogram was unremarkable except for left atrial enlargement. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, cardiomegaly, and mediastinal enlargement suggestive of bulky hilar adenopathy. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest with contrast was performed which was negative for pulmonary embolism, but revealed bilateral centrilobular opacities, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and a trivial pericardial effusion (Fig. a). Initial laboratory diagnostics were significant for acute kidney injury with a serum creatinine of 2.03 (mg/dL), trace proteinuria, troponin elevation to 0.232 (ng/mL), and a D-Dimer of 1.3 (mcg/mL). Complete blood count revealed no leukocytosis, but concomitant eosinophilia, with no evidence of anemia. The patient was subsequently admitted to the medicine wards and a therapeutic regimen of antihypertensive agents as well as intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin for presumed community acquired pneumonia was initiated.
Additional diagnostic evaluation demonstrated marked elevation of CRP (80 mg/L) and ESR (67 mm/hr). Pheochromocytoma screening with serum catecholamines and metanephrines was negative. An echocardiogram revealed an ejection fraction of 40%, moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, and trivial pericardial effusion without evidence of tamponade or pulmonary artery hypertension. Despite continuation of antibiotics for pneumonia and adjunctive heart failure management, the patient’s clinical status failed to improve. In the setting of an unremarkable infectious workup and concern for an autoimmune etiology, the patient was started on oral prednisone 60 mg daily. The patient remained symptomatic, experiencing episodic chest pain and shortness of breath, with blood pressure lability. Repeat chest X-ray showed worsening bilateral infiltrates. Subsequently, ANA resulted weakly positive (1:160) with a homogenous pattern and rheumatoid factor (RF) returned negative.
On the fifth day of admission, antibiotics were discontinued in light of negative cultures and lack of significant clinical improvement. The patient’s blood pressure was noted to be slightly improved with addition of prednisone however remained poorly controlled on multiple medications (Fig. ). Autoimmune panel including ANCA (MPO/p-ANCA, and PR3/c-ANCA), anti-double-stranded DNA antibody, anti-Smith antibody, C3 and C4 complements, anti-histone antibody, as well as other autoimmune related factors and infectious serologies returned negative or within normal limits (Table ). Renal ultrasound and renal artery duplex were performed which did not reveal any evidence of hydronephrosis or renal artery stenosis, respectively. A repeat high-resolution chest CT scan was obtained, both in supine and prone positions, to help differentiate early interstitial lung disease from intra-alveolar processes, which showed persistent intra-alveolar opacities without any change on prone position (Fig. b). Over the course of the following days, the patient reported improvement in his symptomatology and his blood pressure improved, therefore he was taken off prednisone on the sixth day. Pulmonary function testing was performed in the setting of bilateral hilar adenopathy and fixed infiltrates, which revealed a mixed obstructive and restrictive pattern. He eventually underwent lung biopsy by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with right medial lobe wedge resection and was subsequently discharged with instructions to follow up with rheumatology for planned initiation of rituximab. The histopathological results of his lung biopsy demonstrated extensive intra-alveolar hemorrhage with linear polymorphonuclear (PMN) cell collections in alveolar septa and capillaritis without any evidence of granulomatous changes, indicative of microscopic polyangiitis (Fig. ). Immunohistochemistry on lung biopsy samples was not performed and renal biopsy was deferred to outpatient rheumatology.
Unfortunately, the patient was lost to follow up, failing to attend any of the scheduled appointments. He was subsequently readmitted six months later with similar symptoms, and once again found to be in hypertensive emergency, complicated by acute decompensated heart failure. Repeat echocardiogram revealed a further decline in his ejection fraction to 25% and a trivial pericardial effusion. Rheumatology was consulted and recommended pulse steroid therapy with methylprednisolone 250 mg four times a day for three days, which led to significant improvement in symptoms and blood pressure. Repeat ANCA and autoimmune serological workup remained negative. Following initiation of pulse steroid therapy, he underwent renal biopsy. The biopsy contained forty glomeruli, six of which were globally sclerotic. One glomerulus had segmental sclerosis. There were changes suggestive of microangiopathic injury in some arteries and glomeruli, such as bloodless glomeruli and mild intimal myxoid changes in arteries, with associated acute tubular injury. Focal tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis were estimated to involve approximately 10% of the cortex. No evidence of crescents or granulomatous changes were observed. Immunofluorescence was unremarkable, with only non-specific linear glomerular and tubular basement membrane staining for IgG, kappa, lambda, and albumin, indicative of pauci-immunity. Electron microscopy demonstrated segmental effacement of podocyte foot processes (40%) with vacuolation and microvillous transformation of the podocyte cytoplasm, ischemic-type capillary wall wrinkling, and subendothelial electron lucent widening (Fig. ). He was subsequently discharged on a steroid taper with plans for outpatient rituximab. Despite extensive education about his condition he was once again lost to follow up and missed appropriate treatment.
Over the course of the next year, he was readmitted on multiple occasions and eventually progressed to dialysis-dependent end-stage renal disease. His two most recent admissions were characterized by pancreatitis with pancreatic pseudoaneurysm complicated by retroperitoneal hematoma and cardiac tamponade, respectively. With respect to his pancreatitis, he presented in the context of acute onset abdominal pain with associated nausea and vomiting. Laboratory diagnostics demonstrated an elevated lipase (3400), normal triglycerides, and a negative IgG4 serology. Abdominal CT was significant for peripancreatic fat stranding and inflammatory changes without evidence of gallstones or biliary ductal dilation. He denied recent alcohol use. Pancreatitis course was further complicated by retroperitoneal hematoma, which was found to be secondary to a 7 mm pancreatic pseudoaneurysm rupture, as revealed on repeat abdominal CT angiography (Fig. ). He was managed conservatively and subsequently discharged. One month later he presented with dyspnea, chest pain and nausea, and was found to have large pericardial effusion with an acute decrease in ejection fraction to 10% (Fig. ). He underwent pericardiocentesis with removal of one liter of serosanguineous fluid. Fluid analysis was indicative of hemorrhagic etiology and negative for malignancy. On review of most recent outpatient records, the patient has been maintained on high-dose suppressive steroid therapy with plans for initiation of Rituximab or Cyclophosphamide.

Patient note:
A 77-year-old female patient with a past medical history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia who presented to our emergency room (ER) due to worsening of respiratory distress. Four days prior to admission, the patient was hospitalized for management of community acquired pneumonia and upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleed and was later discharged to a rehab center. During a physical therapy session at the rehab facility, the patient developed severe shortness of breath and was found to be hypoxic with an oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 75%, she was placed on a nasal cannula. Presenting vitals in the ER showed a blood pressure of 152/83 mmHg, pulse 137 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/min and SpO2 97% on a 15 litre nonrebreather, and the patient was found to be COVID-19 positive using the RT-PCR test. Initial computed tomography (CT) of the chest pulmonary embolism protocol found multiple small bilateral pulmonary emboli as well as elevated right ventricular to left ventricular ratio of 1.4 indicating right heart strain (). The patient was noted to have expressive aphasia and left sided flaccid paralysis, and an initial CT scan of the head without intravenous (IV) contrast showed no evidence of acute intracranial abnormality. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head with and without gadavist intravenous (IV) contrast () done later on Day 1 found a large acute right middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory infarct. The patient was started empirically on IV dexamethasone, antibiotic therapy, aspirin, atorvastatin, and therapeutic enoxaparin. On Day 2, a CT angiography of the head and neck with IV contrast showed an abrupt vessel cut off of the right internal carotid artery at the level of the supraclinoid right ICA, and nonvisualization of the distal right internal carotid artery as well as the right M1 due to a non-occlusive thrombus ().
The patient was transferred to an acute care facility, and a transthoracic echocardiogram () showed moderately dilated right ventricle with moderately reduced systolic function, right atrial thrombus in transit and hypermobile atrial septal aneurysm. The thrombus was managed with thrombectomy using the Inari FlowTriever device () and was started on continuous IV infusion of unfractioned heparin. On day 3, a venous doppler of the lower extremities showed a thrombus in the right femoral vein of the distal thigh, gastrocnemius veins, posterior tibial, and peroneal veins. At this point, COVID-19 related hypoxic respiratory symptoms were mild and required only nasal cannula for supplemental oxygen. Patient remained hemodynamically stable until day 10 her condition was complicated by an upper GI bleeding in the form of melanotic bowel movement, she subsequently underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and found a clot in the anterior bulb, which was treated with epinephrine, clot removal and cautery of a non-bleeding vessel. She was then treated with pantoprazole IV infusion and transfused two units of packed red blood cells (PRBC), while anticoagulation therapy was held. An interdisciplinary decision was made to restart anticoagulation on day 13. On Day 18, the patient had a hemorrhagic conversion of right middle cerebral artery ischemic infarct which was detected on CT of the head (), and heparin infusion was discontinued. Neurosurgery evaluated the patient and she was deemed not a candidate for any surgical intervention. Given her grave prognosis, the patient was transitioned to hospice care on Day 20.

Patient note:
A 72-year-old woman with a decade-long history of ischemic cardiomyopathy (left-ventricular ejection fraction most recently 28 % on guideline-directed medical therapy of carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril–valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, and furosemide 40 mg each morning) arrived in the emergency department at 05:25 after being awaken at her retirement apartment by a sudden urge to evacuate what she described as “inky, tar-slick” stool that stained the commode and produced a strong metallic odor; wiping required several passes before the tissue lightened, and a second bowel movement of similar character occurred during the 15-minute ride in her daughter’s car, necessitating a towel on the seat. She reports three days of vague epigastric discomfort and new fatigue climbing a single flight of stairs, which she attributes to recent pollen season, yet she denies any vomiting of blood, coffee-ground emesis, bright red rectal bleeding, or hematemesis of any color. The patient has stage III chronic kidney disease (baseline serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL) and long-standing hypertension managed with amlodipine 5 mg nightly; an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was placed six years ago and has not discharged in the past twelve months. She has never been diagnosed with any form of hepatitis, cirrhosis, fatty liver, or other chronic hepatic condition, and prior routine hepatic panels have been unremarkable. She has taken no aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs since a gastric ulcer was treated endoscopically three years earlier, uses no anticoagulant because warfarin was discontinued after paroxysmal atrial fibrillation ablated two years ago, and her only over-the-counter products are a daily multivitamin and alternating calcium carbonate and magnesium oxide for nighttime leg cramps. She quit smoking 18 years ago after a 30-pack-year exposure, drinks half a glass of red wine at Sunday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Her mother died of congestive heart failure at 84 and her older brother has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; there is no family history of bleeding disorders or gastrointestinal malignancy. Review of systems is negative for fever, chills, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, rash, pruritus, dysphagia, chest pain beyond her stable exertional pressure, orthopnea in excess of baseline two pillows, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or leg swelling beyond her chronic trace ankle edema. When she arrived in triage—prior to any intravenous cannulation, crystalloid infusion, vasoactive support, blood products, proton-pump inhibitor, antiemetic, or octreotide—she was seated upright on the stretcher, conversant but noticeably pale, clutching an emesis bag “just in case.” Manual vital signs taken with the left arm at heart level documented a systolic blood pressure of 150 mm Hg with a diastolic of 92 mm Hg; the cardiac monitor displayed an irregular tachycardic rhythm fluctuating around 134 beats per minute that matched the radial pulse, respirations were 20 per minute, oral temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Capillary refill was approximately three seconds, conjunctivae were moderately anemic, sclerae anicteric, and oral mucosa moist without petechiae. Jugular venous pulsation measured 10 cm H₂O at 45°, peripheral pulses were 1+ but symmetric, and there was trace bilateral pitting edema to the mid-malleoli. Cardiac examination revealed a displaced, diffuse apical impulse with a soft S3 and no new murmurs or pericardial rub; lung fields disclosed bibasilar end-inspiratory crackles that cleared with coughing. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, tympanitic on percussion; gentle palpation produced mild tenderness in the epigastrium without guarding, rebound, organomegaly, or palpable masses, and bowel sounds were hyperactive. No spider angiomas, palmar erythema, or telangiectasias were seen on skin survey. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated an alert individual oriented to person, place, time, and recent events, with equal and reactive pupils, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength throughout, and steady finger-to-nose performance. Digital rectal examination performed immediately after obtaining consent yielded copious thick, jet-black stool that turned a guaiac card deep blue within seconds. A single 16-gauge catheter was placed solely for laboratory sampling and type-and-screen; at that exact snapshot she had not yet received any therapy. Initial laboratory results returned within ten minutes showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, hematocrit 30 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, platelet count 189 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 9.8 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 69 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (above her known baseline), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.11; alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase were pending. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained simultaneously revealed atrial flutter with variable block at a ventricular rate of 136 bpm, left bundle branch block unchanged from prior tracings, and no acute ST-T deviations. Upright chest radiography displayed cardiomegaly with mild pulmonary vascular congestion but no focal consolidation or effusion, while a supine abdominal radiograph demonstrated a nonspecific bowel gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. The patient remained nil per os on continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring as gastroenterology was paged for expedited esophagogastroduodenoscopy to localize and manage the presumed upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage that manifested as tarry stools in the context of chronic systolic dysfunction and progressive azotemia, all before any resuscitative measures had begun.

Patient note:
A 69-year-old Caucasian woman presented to outside hospital with complaints of chest pain and shortness of breath. Chest pain started approximately a week ago and lasted for about 5 days but then subsided for a day. Next day, the patient was experiencing continuous chest tightness both on right and left side. She was also having dyspnea on exertion. The patient had a past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and severe degenerative joint disease. Past surgical history was significant for hysterectomy. She denied any history of smoking cigarettes or using illicit drugs. The patient had a history of occasional alcohol intake. Medications at home included amlodipine/benazepril 10/20 mg daily, raloxifene 60 mg daily, celecoxib 200 mg BID, clonazepam 1 mg daily, fenofibrate 145 mg daily, a multivitamin tablet daily, a calcium tablet 600 mg daily, glucosamine 1500 mg daily, tramadol/acetaminophen 37.5/325 mg BID, and hydrocodone/acetaminophen 10/300 mg as needed for pain.
On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was tachycardic with a heart rate of 114/min, tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 24/min. She was normotensive at that time. Within the next few minutes, the patient became significantly hypotensive. Vitals at that time were blood pressure 78/52, heart rate 109/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and saturation of 96% on 3 L of oxygen via nasal cannula. On physical examination, the patient appeared to be in acute distress. On cardiovascular assessment, S1 and S2 were audible with no added murmur or gallop. She had bilateral pitting lower extremity edema. On lung examination, the patient had bilateral rhonchi and increased respiratory effort.
EKG showed sinus tachycardia with q waves and ST segment elevations of almost 2 mm in leads III and aVF. There was also left atrial enlargement (). Radiograph of chest showed interstitial edema. Laboratory results from admission included a basal metabolic panel that showed blood urea nitrogen of 40 mg/dL (6–20 mg/dL), creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL (0.7–1.2 mg/dL), and potassium of 4.2 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L). First set of troponin levels were found to be 1.60 ng/mL (0.0–0.3 ng/mL) and first set of CK was 118 U/L (29–200 U/L). A Doppler echocardiogram was done in the emergency room, which showed normal ejection fraction of 60–65% with RV hypokinesis, which was consistent with RVI.
The patient was started on vasopressors and emergently transferred to our facility to undergo cardiac catheterization. Left heart catheterization revealed 99% stenosis to mid-right coronary artery and subsequently the patient underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to the right coronary artery. An intra-aortic balloon pump was placed during cardiac catheterization as the patient was in cardiogenic shock. After successful PCI, the intra-aortic balloon pump was removed as her vitals seemed to have stabilized. Two days later, again the patient developed hypotension and worsening shortness of breath. Urgent bedside Doppler echocardiogram showed a new left-to-right shunt in the ventricle, which was noted to be a muscular VSD. The patient was transferred to a tertiary care medical center for surgical repair. At the tertiary care hospital, transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was done, which revealed large VSD with a dimension of 1.38×0.9 cm2 and an area of 0.9 cm2 located in the posterior wall of ventricle (). TEE also showed mildly reduced RV systolic function and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation ( and ).
The patient subsequently developed S. aureus bacteremia and Clostridium difficile colitis, which were successfully treated with intravenous antibiotics. She underwent cardiothoracic surgery for possible surgical versus percutaneous repair of the VSD. Based on the location of the VSD, the patient was considered to be an excellent candidate for percutaneous repair with amplatzer postinfarct VSD occluder device. After placement of the amplatzer VSD device, significant reduction in left-to-right shunt was noted on TEE. Also, hemodynamically the patient improved and her hypotension resolved, so the intra-aortic balloon pump was discontinued. Eventually, the patient developed sepsis secondary to C. difficile colitis, which resulted in development of disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemodynamic collapse, and death.

Patient note:
A 59-year-old woman was admitted to the department of Neurology for a sudden confusion with loss of vision. Her past medical history comprised of a total hysterectomy twenty-five years earlier (fibroma). She also complained of headaches and chronic asthenia for 5 years: at that time, medical investigations only found a chronic seromucous maxillary sinusitis treated by antibiotherapy, then endoscopic sinus surgery (the pathological study objective a nonspecific inflammation); however, she still complained of chronic headaches despite this treatment. At the age of 55, she had also developed refractory arterial hypertension and renal failure leading to the diagnosis of right renal artery stenosis and left renal artery occlusion: she was treated by surgery (stenting of the left renal artery, then right aortorenal bypass).
On clinical examination, there was cortical blindness, anosognosia for blindness, amnesia, and topographical disorientation suggestive of a Dide-Botcazo syndrome. There was no pyramidal sign nor cerebellar ataxia or cranial nerves involvement. No other clinical abnormality was reported. She still complained of chronic headaches.
Bilateral cerebral posterior infarction and hypodensity in the territory of the right postero-inferior cerebellar artery have been observed on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (and magnetic resonance angiography), with a severe narrowing of the basilar artery (closed to 90%) and a mild stenosis of the M1 and M2 segments of the left middle cerebral artery (Fig. A and 1B). Transcranial Doppler confirmed a severe stenosis of the basilar artery. Electrocardiogram and 24 hours electrocardiography were normal. Echocardiography (transthoracic and transesophageal) demonstrated a hypertrophic cardiopathy (with severe left ventricular hypertrophy and circumferential dilatation of the left atrium). No valvulopathy was observed, but there was a heterogeneous thickening of the interatrial septum (1.5 cm) and a hyperechogeneous thickening next to the right atrium (1.9 × 1.3 cm). Cardiac computed tomography angiography (and cardiac MRI) confirmed a right periatrial infiltration, and also found thickening of the wall of the whole aortic arch (with tardive enhancement of media) and pericardial effusion (Fig. ). Whole-body 18fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (18FDG PET) found contrast-enhancement on the right and left atria, whole aorta, iliac arteries, and femoral arteries (Fig. E). Ophthalmological examination was normal, except a grade I hypertensive retinopathy.
Ancillary tests found hyperleukocytosis (13,000/mm3, with 8890 neutrophils/mm3), biological inflammation (C-reactive protein was 24 mg/L), with no monoclonal gammopathy. Viral and bacterial serologies, immunological (antinuclear, anticardiolipin, and anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 antibodies) and metabolic (cholesterol, triglyceride, glycosylated hemoglobin, homocysteine, thyroid stimulating hormone, and transaminases) tests were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal (1 white cells/mm3; protein level at 46 mg/dL, for a normal value <45 mg/dL; normal glucose level). A bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormality.
Plain radiographs showed bilateral and symmetric cortical osteosclerosis of the diaphyseal and metaphyseal regions of the lower limbs; 99Technetium bone scintigraphy revealed a symmetric tracer uptake by the long bone of lower extremities (and also in maxillary and frontal bones) suggestive of the diagnosis of ECD (Fig. ). After a second biopsy of the maxillary sinus, pathological study finally demonstrated a xanthogranulomatous infiltrate mainly composed by foamy histiocytes accompanied by fibrosis (stains for CD1a and S-100 were negative), confirming the diagnosis of ECD.
She was treated with interferon-α (3 million IU 3 times weekly, then a gradual increase of the dose up to 9 million IU 3 times weekly over the following months), with not only an improvement of the cognitive function (particularly visual function and memory) but also of headaches. A treatment by clopidogrel (75 mg/d) was proposed for stroke. After 3 months of treatment with interferon-α, we observed reduction of the stenosis of the basilar artery (50%) on MR-angiography (with a quite total recanalization 2 years after the onset of the treatment; Fig. ). After 4 years, the neurological examination was still stable, but she developed insipidus diabetes (successfully treated with desmopressin).

Patient note:
36 year old female patient weighing 36 kgs, height 152 cm, admitted to our hospital with diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease, severe mitral stenosis (MS), severe aortic stenosis (AS), and severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR). The patient had dyspnea on exertion for the last 1½ years, with recent deterioration to dyspnea of New York Heart Association Class III. She was admitted with CHF 7 months back and managed conservatively. On examination, the patient had a pulse rate of 100 beats/min (bpm) in atrial fibrillation rhythm, mild pallor, and icterus, and pedal edema was present. Cardiovascular examination findings were suggestive of MS and AS. Hepatomegaly was present.
She was started on tablet furosemide 40 mg once daily (OD) along with tablet metoprolol 25 mg twice a day.
She was operated and mitral valve was replaced with size 27 St. Jude's mechanical valve and aortic valve with size 17 regent mechanical valve. Tricuspid commissurotomy was performed. Immediate postoperative period was uneventful and all predischarge investigations were within normal range. She was discharged on the postoperative day (POD) 9 with prescription of tablet furosemide 40 mg OD, tablet aldactone 100 mg OD, tablet ramipril 5 mg HS, and tablet amiodarone 200 mg OD, and ecosprin 150 mg OD. On discharge, the patient did not have pedal edema or hepatomegaly.
On POD 28, her medication was changed to furosemide with spironolactone 40/25 mg BD, tablet acenocoumarol, tablet aldactone 100 mg OD, and tablet digoxin 0.25 mg OD. High dose of diuretics was used for a short while as the patient still had features of fluid overload. Postoperative echocardiography showed normal prosthetic valve function with normal biventricular function and moderate TR.
On POD 33, she presented in the emergency department with complaints of loose stool and vomiting (3 episodes) with severe muscular weakness. On examination, pulse was 36 bpm, irregular, systolic BP 60 mmHg, extremities were cold and clammy, signs of dehydration present, peripheral pulses not palpable, valve click present, and tender hepatomegaly present. Serum electrolytes showed hyperkalemia with serum potassium of 7.87 meq/L, hyponatremia with serum sodium 129 mmol/L and hypocalcemia, hemoglobin 9.6 gm% and hematocrit 38%, pH 7.28, base deficit-11, serum osmolality 252 mmol/L, serum creatinine 1.1 mg%, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 17 mg/dl. Electrocardiograph (ECG) showed heart rate of 30 beats/min, broad QRS complex, tented T-wave, and impending sine wave pattern. When detailed history was elicited from her husband, he revealed that apart from her medication, she was taking 7–8 bananas every day as part of her regular diet for the last 3 weeks.
She was managed with aggressive antihyperkalemic treatment with intravenous (IV) calcium gluconate, glucose-insulin drip, soda-bicarbonate, loop diuretics, K+ binding resins, and IV fluids. Over 24 h, she was stabilized in the intensive care unit (ICU) with same treatment. Hemodialysis was not required, she recovered hemodynamically and maintained good urine output. Potassium levels were serially monitored and were on a decreasing trend and finally levels decreased to 4.5 meq/L. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, rate of 80–90 bpm. She was discharged from ICU after 2 days. She was advised to eat 1–2 bananas every day and the dose of potassium-sparing diuretics was reduced. She remained in a regular follow-up and no such incidence recurred.
8 years old child weighing 21 kgs, height 130 cm, admitted to our hospital with diagnosis of tetralogy of Fallot physiology for intracardiac repair. Examination showed a cyanotic child with pulse rate of 78 bpm in sinus rhythm and blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg. Preoperatively, the patient was continued on tablet propranolol 10 mg 8th hourly.
Perioperatively, dacron patch closure of ventricular septal defect, infundibular resection done, and transannular bovine pericardial patch placed. On POD 1, the patient developed complete heart block and was treated with temporary pacing, and injection dexamethasone was started, which was tapered off gradually and stopped on POD 10. Other medications included tablet furosemide 20 mg OD and tablet captopril 12.5 Mg 8th hourly. For nutrition, he was adviced to include banana in the diet. Gradually over next week, the patient developed hepatomegaly and weight gain of 4 kg and was started on tablet aldactone 25 mg BD. The patient was then discharged on POD 15 after features of CHF were relieved.
On POD 21, he presented in the emergency department with nausea and vomiting, electrolytes showed K+ of 7.12 meq/L, Na+ 121 meq/L, serum creatinine 1.2 mg%, and BUN 15 mg%. ECG showed hyperkalemic changes. He was shifted to ICU and antihyperkalemic treatment started that included IV calcium gluconate, sodium bicarbonate, glucose-insulin drip, and potassium-binding resin. He was maintaining good hemodynamics with adequate urine output. Potassium levels were serially monitored and after 24 h of aggressive management, his K+ level was 4 meq/l. Dialysis was not required. He was discharged from ICU after 2 days. Retrospectively on interrogating further his father said that the boy was eating at least 6–7 bananas every day for the last 15 days. He was advised to eat a single banana every day and he remained in regular follow-up and had no such episode again.

Patient note:
A 62-year-old man with a history of chronic atrial fibrillation managed on warfarin, stage 2 chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.4 mg/dL), and remote alcohol use disorder was brought to the metropolitan trauma center by subway police after commuters noticed him crumpled at the base of a concrete stairwell leading from the platform at approximately 21:05; no one witnessed the fall, and security footage reviewed later confirms only that he lost footing on the third step from the top and tumbled head-first to the landing without striking any bystanders. Rail EMTs arrived at 21:11, found him breathing on his own, placed a cervical collar, log-rolled him onto a scoop stretcher with head blocks, established a single 16-gauge catheter in the right antecubital vein that was flushed with 5 mL normal saline, and recorded a capillary glucose of 118 mg/dL. They administered no crystalloid bolus, opioid, benzodiazepine, paralytic, antihypertensive, reversal agent, anticoagulant, hyperosmolar therapy, anticonvulsant, antiemetic, vasopressor, or dextrose so as not to cloud the neurologic picture during the nine-minute transport. On entry to our resuscitation bay at 21:23 he remains immobilized on the scoop, clothing damp with light rain from a broken skylight, scalp matted with blood but without active arterial spurting. Simultaneously obtained pre-intervention vital signs show blood pressure 156/88 mm Hg in the left brachial artery, heart rate 96 beats/min in irregularly irregular rhythm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min with shallow thoracoabdominal excursion, oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing ambient air, and a rectal temperature of 36.6 °C. The airway appears patent; dentures are absent, the tongue lies midline, there are no pooled secretions, and a brief sweep with a Yankauer catheter elicits a single explosive cough without gagging. His lids are already parted to full palpebral width on arrival, hazel irides drifting slowly beneath fluorescent lighting and occasionally blinking but never closing for more than a second. He does not seem to track faces; the gaze wanders across ceiling fixtures and then fixes on nothing in particular. When the trauma nurse asks, “Can you tell me what happened?” he blurts in a clear voice, “yellow bicycle… Tuesday tickets… the dog is late,” then falls silent; posed with follow-up questions regarding his name, location, or the current year, he repeats unrelated phrases such as “door number five” and “coffee train,” never forming truly conversational speech or appropriate answers. No slurring or dysarthria is present—consonants and vowels are articulated cleanly—yet the content bears no relevance to the queries. Between prompts he utters no spontaneous words. Upper and lower extremities lie flaccid at his sides with normal bulk. When five-second nail-bed pressure is applied to the left great toe, both shoulders adduct, elbows flex to roughly ninety degrees, forearms pronate, and wrists curl inward with fingers clawed toward the sternum; hips and knees simultaneously flex but do not fully extend afterward, and there is no purposeful attempt to brush away the examiner’s hand. The posture relaxes three seconds after the nociceptive stimulus ceases and recurs identically with supra-orbital ridge pressure on the opposite side. Based on these findings, his Glasgow Coma Scale is calculated at 10 (E4 V3 M3) on arrival. No extensor posturing, localization, or withdrawal beyond the described patterned flexion is observed. Tone between stimuli is otherwise low, deep tendon reflexes are 3 + at biceps and patellae, 2 + at Achilles, and plantar responses are mute bilaterally. Pupils measure 3 mm, are round, and constrict briskly to direct and consensual light; corneal and cough reflexes remain intact, though oculocephalic testing is deferred pending imaging because of possible cervical injury. No rhinorrhea or otorrhea is noted; the left parietal scalp harbors a 5 × 2 cm stellate laceration with clotted blood but no palpable depression. Cardiovascular examination discloses an irregularly irregular S1/S2 without murmurs or rubs; peripheral pulses are 2 + radially, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial, with capillary refill under two seconds and warm, dry skin. Lungs are clear to auscultation with symmetric breath sounds and resonant percussion; no subcutaneous emphysema or tracheal deviation is present. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender to gentle palpation; bowel sounds are present, and the pelvis is stable on compression. Log-roll inspection reveals scattered ecchymoses along the thoracic spine but no step-off; rectal tone is preserved. No long-bone deformity is detected, and distal neurovascular status of all extremities is intact. A point-of-care venous blood gas drawn prior to any medication reveals pH 7.35, pCO₂ 41 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L; rapid serum electrolytes are sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, glucose 122 mg/dL, and an INR of 3.1 consistent with his home anticoagulation. A portable anteroposterior chest film obtained within four minutes shows clear lung fields and normal mediastinum; pelvic radiograph is unremarkable, and extended FAST demonstrates no intraperitoneal or pericardial free fluid. To ensure the neurologic examination remains uncontaminated, no sedatives, analgesics, paralytic agents, reversal drugs, hyperosmolar solutions, or intravenous fluids other than the initial saline flush have yet been administered. Neurosurgery, trauma surgery, and neurocritical care services have been paged; stat non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine along with CT angiography of neck vessels are in progress, continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring has been initiated, and airway equipment for rapid sequence intubation is staged at the bedside should his protective reflexes deteriorate further.

Patient note:
A 46-year-old woman with a background of symptomatic gallstones awaiting elective cholecystectomy, well-controlled asthma, and no known chronic liver or kidney disease was brought to the emergency department by her spouse after waking at dawn with intense right upper-quadrant pain radiating to the interscapular region, two episodes of emesis described as “coffee-brown,” and a brief syncopal spell at the bathroom sink. Emergency medical technicians arrived within eight minutes to find her sitting on the floor, skin clammy and faintly icteric, speaking in full sentences but clutching her abdomen. They applied a nasal cannula at 3 L/min—felt to deliver approximately 0.29 inspired oxygen—because the prehospital oximeter intermittently read 92 % on room air; no bag-mask ventilation, endotracheal tube, or noninvasive positive-pressure interface was used en route. Intravenous access was obtained in the left antecubital fossa, yet no crystalloid bolus, antiemetic, or analgesic had been administered before hospital arrival. On entry to the resuscitation bay, still breathing quietly through the same cannula and before any emergency department intervention, she appeared pale but alert, answering questions appropriately and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. A single set of vitals captured on transfer showed a temperature of 38.3 °C tympanic, pulse 116 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, respirations 20 per minute with unlabored effort, and a non-invasive blood pressure of 85/50 mm Hg confirmed by a repeat manual reading; capillary refill was three seconds, and distal extremities were cool without mottling. Sclerae were notable for yellow discoloration, and there was mild conjunctival injection. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed tachycardia without murmurs, clear breath sounds throughout, and no accessory-muscle use. Abdominal inspection demonstrated a mildly distended epigastrium; palpation elicited exquisite tenderness under the right costal margin with a positive Murphy sign, but no rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds were present and hypoactive. There was no ascites, spider angioma, or palmar erythema. Neurologic assessment revealed equal 3-mm pupils briskly reactive to light, intact extraocular movements, normal speech cadence, strength 5/5 in all extremities, and rapid alternating movements performed without hesitation, consistent with a Glasgow Coma Score of 15. A 16-gauge radial arterial catheter was placed within five minutes of arrival, and the first arterial blood gas—drawn while she remained on the unchanged 3 L/min nasal cannula—showed pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 39 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and a PaO₂ of 93 mm Hg on the documented 29 % inspired fraction. Laboratory samples obtained simultaneously and resulted before any antibiotics, fluids, or analgesics were started demonstrated sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, glucose 124 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL, matching a value from a primary-care visit four months earlier. Total bilirubin returned at 2.3 mg/dL with a predominantly direct component; aspartate aminotransferase was 112 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 98 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 356 U/L, and international normalized ratio 1.3. The complete blood count revealed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit 37 %, white blood cell count 14.0 × 10³/µL with 10 % band forms, and a platelet count of 230 000 /µL. High-sensitivity troponin was undetectable, and serum lactate measured 2.6 mmol/L. A 14-French Foley catheter inserted during the secondary survey immediately drained 210 mL of dark yellow urine; the patient’s spouse, who keeps meticulous intake and output records because of prior nephrolithiasis, reported three voids totaling approximately 1 900 mL in the preceding twenty-four hours. Point-of-care right-upper-quadrant ultrasound revealed a contracted gallbladder with multiple shadowing calculi, a thickened wall measuring 6 mm, and common bile duct diameter of 9 mm without intrahepatic ductal dilation. The portal vein was patent with normal flow, and the inferior vena cava measured 1.6 cm collapsing more than 50 % with inspiration. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained while she sat upright on the stretcher showed clear lung fields, intact costophrenic angles, and normal cardiac silhouette. An electrocardiogram recorded concurrently displayed sinus tachycardia at 114 beats/min with no ischemic changes. At the moment all the above data were captured, she remained seated, breathing spontaneously through low-flow supplemental oxygen, with persisting low arterial pressure yet without vasoactive medication or intravenous resuscitation, fully alert, carrying a modestly elevated bilirubin, normal platelet count, preserved renal function, and documented non-oliguric urine output.

Patient note:
A 79-year-old male patient presented to the ED complaining of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Medical history includes type-2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and aortic dissection. Additionally, surgical history was remarkable for thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) that was done five years ago.
During physical examination, the patient was found to be hemodynamically stable and his abdomen was soft and lax with mild tenderness on the left flank. Laboratory tests showed significant elevation of lactic acid (4.16 mmol/L) and white blood cells (WBC) (13.4 K/uL) with neutrophils 80.8%. CT angiography showed occlusive thrombus at distal superior mesenteric artery (SMA) (measuring about 2 cm) and obliterated origin of both celiac trunk and SMA with collateral from inferior mesenteric artery (Figure ). In addition, thrombus at the proximal part of the abdominal aorta (Figure ).
The patient was admitted as a case of superior mesenteric artery (SMA) ischemia, and managed by thrombolytic therapy using tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) (alteplase 0.05 mg/kg/h for 12 hours) with stent on the same day through inferior mesenteric artery. There were no complications from the procedure. However, SMA stenting failed. The patient was improving and was discharged home on apixaban 2.5 mg.
Four days later, the patient presented to the ED with diffused sharp abdominal pain. The physical examination is unremarkable except for a mild central abdominal tenderness. Laboratory findings revealed lactic acid to be 2.19 mmol/L. CT angiography showed re-demonstration of near occlusion thrombus at distal SMA with a refill of distal branches from collaterals at the portal venous phase with no frank signs of bowel ischemia. The patient stayed in a regular ward and received heparin 1200 U/h; five days later the patient recovered and was discharged in good condition.
Six days later, the patient returned to the ED with the same complaint and diagnosed with MI; he was vitally stable and afebrile; the abdomen is soft and lax with no tenderness. Laboratory tests revealed high lactic acid (2.94 mmol/L), lipase (48 U/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (28 mm/h). Angiography confirmed the presence of occlusive thrombus at distal SMA. The patient underwent a retrograde right common ilio-mesenteric artery bypass (Figure ). He made an uneventful recovery and was discharged in a good condition.

Patient note:
A 56-year-old man with a fifteen-year history of untreated chronic hepatitis C infection complicated by progressive nodular cirrhosis and known portal hypertension was brought to the emergency department by his sister after she noticed that over the preceding three days he had become increasingly forgetful, slept most of the daytime hours, and answered questions a beat slower than usual, occasionally misplacing common objects such as his wallet and house keys. He denied frank gastrointestinal bleeding, vomiting, or recent alcohol use—he last drank beer six years earlier—but admitted to poor oral intake, intermittent nausea, and having missed several doses of his prescribed lactulose because he “didn’t feel up to it.” He also reported needing to loosen his belt one notch at the end of the day and awakening once overnight with a mild crampy sensation in the right upper abdomen that resolved spontaneously. Past medical history is notable for treated hypertension, well-controlled with amlodipine 5 mg daily, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. He has never undergone variceal band ligation, is not on non-selective beta-blockers, and has no known drug allergies. Vital signs on arrival showed blood pressure 108/62 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing room air, and temperature 37.4 °C. He appeared tired but was arousable to voice, could state his name and location, but guessed the day of the week incorrectly and required cueing to recall recent events; his speech was coherent, and when he extended his hands, a barely perceptible flapping movement occurred after several seconds. Pupils were equal and reactive, extraocular movements intact, and there were no focal motor deficits. Sclerae were deeply icteric, oral mucosa was dry, and the breath emitted a faint musty odor. The chest was clear to auscultation, and cardiac examination revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs or gallops. Inspection of the abdomen showed mild distension with a small bulge of the flanks; the umbilicus remained concave. Percussion identified an area of dullness that shifted toward the dependent side when he rolled, yet no prominent fluid wave was produced. Palpation detected a firm nodular liver edge two centimeters below the costal margin; the spleen was not palpable. There was trace ankle edema but no tenderness, erythema, or skin breakdown. Several spider angiomata dotted the upper chest, and palmar erythema was present. Extremity strength was full, reflexes symmetric, and sensation intact. Bedside capillary glucose measured 98 mg/dL. Laboratory studies drawn prior to any therapy revealed total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.6 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 64 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 78 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 186 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 210 U/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, platelet count 82 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.3 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 2.9. Serum ammonia collected concurrently was 88 µmol/L. Urinalysis showed trace protein and no evidence of infection. A portable right upper quadrant ultrasound performed at the bedside demonstrated coarse parenchymal echotexture, patent portal and hepatic veins with sluggish hepatopetal flow, a small rim of anechoic fluid less than 2 cm deep tracking along the right paracolic gutter, and no focal hepatic masses. Doppler interrogation confirmed absence of portal vein thrombosis, and gallbladder walls appeared thin without stones. Chest radiograph revealed elevated right hemidiaphragm with minimal blunting of the costophrenic angle but no infiltrates. Electrocardiogram documented normal sinus rhythm at 94 beats per minute with nonspecific T-wave changes. Given the elevated bilirubin, marked hypoalbuminemia, significantly prolonged coagulation parameters, subtle cognitive slowing with asterixis, and only modest peritoneal fluid accumulation, the working impression was an acute decompensation of chronic hepatitis C–related cirrhosis precipitated by interrupted ammonia-lowering therapy, possible occult infection, and recent dietary indiscretion. The patient was placed on fall precautions, intravenous access secured, and further diagnostic studies including diagnostic paracentesis and blood cultures were arranged while awaiting hepatology consultation and consideration of transplant referral.

Patient note:
A 44-year-old man, right-hand dominant and previously working as an air-traffic-control technician, was sent to the cardio-oncology consultation service this afternoon by his primary medical oncologist because of progressive exertional breathlessness, early satiety, and intermittent confusion that have complicated ongoing systemic therapy for an advanced malignancy. He was diagnosed eighteen months ago with a sigmoid adenocarcinoma after presenting to an outside emergency department with iron-deficiency anemia and a positive fecal immunochemical test; staging at that time already revealed multiple bilobar hepatic deposits on contrast-enhanced CT as well as two sub-centimeter pulmonary nodules, and he ultimately underwent laparoscopic segmental colectomy followed by six cycles of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, after which disease assessment showed stable liver lesions but interval enlargement of the lung nodules. Pembrolizumab was initiated nine weeks ago in an effort to control the metastatic spread, and his most recent PET–CT obtained last month demonstrated persistent FDG uptake in the liver coupled with several new foci within the L2 vertebral body. Throughout the past year he has noticed progressive lower-extremity edema, nocturnal cough relieved by extra pillows, and a 15-pound unintentional weight gain, findings that were attributed to anthracycline exposure during an earlier short-lived clinical-trial regimen. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed two weeks ago documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 32 % with global hypokinesis and mild mitral regurgitation; there is no history of sudden chest pressure, diaphoresis, emergent catheterization, or enzyme-positive infarction, and serial electrocardiograms remain free of Q waves or dynamic ST–T changes. He denies calf cramping when walking the grocery aisles, has never undergone vascular bypass or endovascular stenting, and ankle–brachial indices measured at a community health fair last summer were 1.04 bilaterally. Respiratory review is notable only for occasional dry cough thought to be medication-related; he has never smoked, never required inhalers, and baseline spirometry performed before chemotherapy revealed normal lung volumes with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.81. Over the past six months family members have become concerned that he repeats questions, forgets scheduled laboratory appointments, and misplaces personal electronics around the apartment; neuropsychologic testing arranged by occupational medicine last week disclosed deficits in recent memory and executive function out of proportion to his educational background, with preserved language comprehension and visuospatial skills, raising suspicion for treatment-accelerated neurocognitive decline on a background of presumed early-onset degenerative disease first hinted at by subtle word-finding pauses three years earlier. He follows a predominantly plant-based diet after receiving nutritional counseling during oncology visits; fasting plasma glucose at last week’s clinic draw was 99 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.7 %, and he has never taken metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin. Previous electronic records contain no episodes of gastroduodenal hemorrhage, Helicobacter pylori therapy, or chronic proton-pump-inhibitor use, and he has not endorsed dyspeptic pain, melena, or occult blood on recent fecal testing beyond the tumor-related bleed that led to diagnosis. Liver function panels obtained this morning show aspartate aminotransferase 34 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 118 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.1, values essentially unchanged from baseline despite the extensive parenchymal replacement by tumor. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 92 mL/min/1.73 m², blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, indicating preserved renal handling. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg seated in the left arm, pulse 96 beats/min irregularly irregular at times, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air; body-mass index is 26 kg/m². He appears younger than stated age yet fatigued, with periorbital puffiness and mild temporal wasting. Jugular venous pulsation rises to 7 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, the point of maximal impulse is displaced laterally, and auscultation reveals a soft S3 with no murmurs or pericardial rub. Bibasilar lung fields are clear to mid-back but mild scattered crackles emerge on forced expiration. The abdomen is soft and nondistended with a well-healed infra-umbilical laparoscopic port scar; the liver edge is smooth, palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and moderately firm, while the spleen tip is not felt. There is 2 + pitting edema to mid-shin without skin discoloration, and pedal pulses are full. Neurologic examination shows an alert man oriented to person and place but uncertain of the exact date; mini-cog testing yields recall of one out of three objects at five minutes, and clock-drawing depicts misplaced numbers despite correct circle size. Cranial nerves II–XII are intact, strength is 5/5 throughout, coordination is preserved, deep-tendon reflexes are 2 + and symmetric, plantar responses are flexor, and tandem gait is performed slowly but without deviation. Current medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily started after the low-ejection-fraction finding, furosemide 40 mg each morning, lisinopril 5 mg daily, pembrolizumab every three weeks, vitamin D3 1000 IU daily, and ondansetron as needed for chemotherapy-related nausea; he reports no drug allergies, does not consume alcohol, and never used illicit substances. The referring oncologist requests guidance on optimizing volume status, adjusting cardioprotective therapy in the face of ongoing immunotherapy, and assessing capacity to participate in consent discussions for future metastatic-disease clinical trials, while the patient expresses hope to continue part-time remote work and maintain autonomy in daily living despite worsening forgetfulness and cardiorespiratory limitations.
