Patient note:
A 97-year-old retired civil engineer who spent five decades inspecting suspension bridges was brought to the outpatient perioperative medicine office this morning by his granddaughter after a urology team requested a comprehensive evaluation before scheduling image-guided brachytherapy for a recently discovered, organ-confined neoplasm of the prostate (transrectal biopsy three weeks earlier showed a single focus of acinar adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 3 + 4 = 7, magnetic-resonance imaging demonstrates capsular integrity and no nodal enlargement). The patient walked in with a polished mahogany cane he fashioned himself, greeting staff by name and accurately recalling the height of the center span of the last bridge he certified, testimony to an intact memory and sharp executive function; during history taking he recited his medication list without hesitation and named the current head of state, the clinic address, and today’s date. Musculoskeletal history is notable for long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed in his late sixties after an episode of painful morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal joints lasting more than an hour; he has taken methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid for the past two decades, supplemented by low-dose prednisone bursts during winter flares, and follows regularly with rheumatology where the most recent Disease Activity Score was in the low range. Despite occasional ulnar deviation at the hands, he buttoned his shirt unassisted this morning and continues to spend afternoons carving chess pieces, describing only mild aching controlled by acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Gastrointestinal review reveals a cratered duodenal lesion noted on esophagogastroduodenoscopy twelve years ago after dark, tarry stools; Helicobacter testing was positive and triple therapy administered, followed by eight weeks of pantoprazole until complete mucosal healing was documented. Since that episode he avoids non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, takes omeprazole 20 mg each dawn, and denies subsequent hematemesis, melena, coffee-ground emesis, or iron-deficiency anemia. He has never experienced jaundice, encephalopathy, fluid retention, or evidence of portal hypertension, and a right-upper-quadrant sonogram performed last month to evaluate biliary colic showed a smooth hepatic contour, patent hepatic and portal veins, and no ascites. Endocrine screening one week ago revealed fasting plasma glucose 96 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.6 %, values that have remained stable for years without pharmacologic intervention; no clinician has labeled him diabetic, and he follows a breakfast routine of oatmeal and fruit and records his weekly weights on graph paper taped near the pantry. The patient firmly denies ever feeling crushing or squeezing substernal discomfort, radiation to jaw or arm, diaphoresis disproportionate to exertion, or syncope; he has never been hospitalized for myocardial infarction, and no clinician has informed him of coronary artery occlusion. He climbs the eight steps to his front porch carrying the morning newspaper without dyspnea and sleeps flat on a single pillow; he has also never received a diagnosis of congestive heart failure. Cardiologist notes from his annual wellness visit six months ago document a normal stress echocardiogram reaching 8 METS with no ischemic changes, preserved global systolic performance, and trivial aortic sclerosis appropriate for age. He similarly reports no episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, orthopnea, or unexplained weight gain; his daughter confirms that socks do not leave indents around the calves at bedtime. Vascular review is silent for calf cramping, hip or buttock pain on walking, cold extremities, or prior vascular interventions, and he has never been told he has peripheral arterial disease; pulses were graded 2 +/4 at all peripheral sites during today’s examination. Neurologic inquiry reveals no sudden unilateral weakness, slurred speech, facial droop, blurred vision, gait imbalance, seizure activity, or sensory loss, and he continues to beat his grandson at rapid-fire chess without oversight. He reports no prior cerebrovascular accident or transient ischemic attack and has never experienced paralysis or hemiplegia. Respiratory history is remarkable only for childhood pertussis; he never smoked, has no chronic cough or wheeze, has never carried a diagnosis of asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or other chronic lung disorder, and lung fields were clear at the last chest radiograph obtained during prostate work-up. His medication list includes methotrexate and folic acid as noted, a daily 81-mg aspirin recommended by his primary practitioner for vascular prophylaxis, omeprazole nightly, acetaminophen as needed, and a multivitamin; he reports hives after a sulfonamide injection in the 1940s but no other drug allergies. He drinks a small glass of red wine with Sunday dinner, abstains from liquor, has never used illicit substances, and lives independently in a single-story cottage equipped with grab bars he installed himself. Family pedigree shows longevity—both parents surpassed ninety—with no early coronary events, cerebrovascular accidents, or cirrhotic complications. Vital signs recorded after five minutes of seated rest read temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/72 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 68 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air; body mass index is 23 kg/m². Physical examination reveals an alert, pleasant gentleman sitting upright without distress; sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa moist. Carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, jugular venous pulsation rises 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, the apical impulse is nondisplaced in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line, first and second heart sounds are crisp with a soft midsystolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border, no gallops, rubs, or peripheral edema. Lungs are resonant to percussion, breath sounds vesicular throughout, no wheezes or crackles. Abdomen is flat, bowel sounds normoactive, liver edge smooth and palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, no splenic tip, no tenderness, masses, or fluid wave; digital rectal examination deferred to urology. Extremities are warm with capillary refill under two seconds, radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses symmetrical; nail beds show no clubbing. Hands reveal mild ulnar deviation and Swan-neck deformities but no active synovitis. Neurologic testing finds orientation to person, place, time, and situation intact, clear and fluent speech, cranial nerves II–XII grossly normal, symmetric strength 5/5 in all extremities, deep tendon reflexes 2 +/4, intact light-touch and vibration sense to the great toes, and a steady tandem gait executed without aid. Recent laboratory data reviewed today: sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73 m²), alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 30 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.0, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, white blood cell count 5.8 × 10⁹/L with a normal differential, and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L. Complete blood counts over the years have shown no leukocytosis, blasts, or cytopenias, and he has never been diagnosed with leukemia or other hematologic malignancies. He tested negative for human immunodeficiency virus during routine blood donor screening in his eighth decade and has had no exposures or illnesses suggestive of immunodeficiency. Electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, axis 20°, no pathologic Q waves, and nonspecific ST-T changes unchanged from prior tracings. He seeks counsel on peri-procedural management of methotrexate, gastric acid suppression around planned radiation, and confirmation that his cardiovascular and pulmonary status present no contraindication to the proposed curative therapy.

question:
Patient note:
A 51-year-old man presented to the university outpatient electrophysiology clinic for a midyear review of his chronic oral anticoagulation, which had been initiated fourteen months earlier for persistent, non-valvular atrial fibrillation discovered incidentally during an annual work physical. He reports that the irregular heartbeat itself has become less noticeable since he began a supervised exercise and weight-loss program, yet he remains anxious about the possibility of another hemorrhagic episode like the upper gastrointestinal bleed he experienced nine months ago: while on a weekend holiday he developed sudden hematemesis, was transported to a regional hospital, received three units of packed red blood cells, and underwent emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy that identified a bleeding duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel successfully treated by dual endoscopic therapy. He required intravenous proton-pump inhibitor infusions for 72 hours but suffered no hemodynamic collapse, and after eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori the gastroenterologist declared the lesion healed at six-week follow-up endoscopy. Since that hospitalization he has used a protective acid-suppressive regimen and has had no further episodes of melena, coffee-ground emesis, bright red blood per rectum, epistaxis, hematuria, or easy bruising beyond fingertip discoloration at the capillary INR checks. He acknowledges long-standing high blood pressure first noted in his late thirties; despite maximally titrated lisinopril 40 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, his home cuff routinely records morning readings between 156/92 mm Hg and 168/96 mm Hg. In clinic today three seated measurements taken after five minutes of rest averaged 162/94 mm Hg with an irregularly irregular pulse of 82 beats per minute. He denies headaches, visual disturbances, chest pain, dyspnea, or claudication but admits that lifestyle modifications have been only partially successful because of his demanding job as a restaurant manager. He has never suffered a transient ischemic attack, ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, myocardial infarction, deep-vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss, abdominal distention, jaundice, pruritus, confusion, flank pain, foamy urine, or peripheral edema. Socially, he stopped cigarette smoking fifteen years ago after a 12-pack-year exposure and denies illicit drug use; however, he continues to consume large quantities of alcohol, estimating two pints of beer with lunch on weekdays, two glasses of whiskey with dinner each evening, and a mixed cocktail every hour over a four-hour poker game each Saturday night, totaling approximately 34 alcoholic drinks per week. He feels “relaxed” with this pattern, has never experienced withdrawal tremors or morning drinking, but recognizes that cutting back could benefit both his blood pressure and bleeding risk. Current medications include warfarin dosed at 7 mg on odd calendar days and 5 mg on even days, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, omeprazole 20 mg each morning for ulcer prophylaxis, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly for dyslipidemia; he takes a daily multivitamin but no herbal supplements. A neatly organized log from his community laboratory lists 18 consecutive INRs over the past six months ranging from 2.2 to 2.8, with a calculated time-in-therapeutic-range of 81 %, and the point-of-care test obtained 30 minutes before the appointment reads 2.5. Family history reveals a father with coronary artery bypass grafting at 58 years and a mother with poorly controlled hypertension complicated by heart failure, but no inherited bleeding disorders. On examination he appears well developed and in no acute distress, body mass index 30 kg/m², afebrile, respirations 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air. Sclerae are anicteric, conjunctivae pink, oral mucosa moist without petechiae, and the neck is supple with no jugular venous distention. Cardiac auscultation discloses the characteristic variable first heart sound of atrial fibrillation without murmur, rub, or gallop; lung fields are clear to percussion and auscultation. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no hepatosplenomegaly, spider angiomata, or caput medusae; bowel sounds are normal. Extremities are warm with brisk capillary refill, no edema, and no ecchymoses larger than 1 cm. Neurologic screening demonstrates intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation, and steady tandem gait. Laboratory studies drawn the same morning show hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, platelet count 240 × 10⁹/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 92 mL/min/1.73 m², aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, and albumin 4.3 g/dL. A 12-lead electrocardiogram confirms atrial fibrillation with an average ventricular response of 80 beats per minute, normal axis, QRS duration 96 ms, and no acute ST-T abnormalities. Transthoracic echocardiography performed three months ago demonstrated a mildly enlarged left atrium measuring 4.4 cm, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, and preserved ejection fraction of 58 % without significant valvular pathology. He is eager for counsel regarding whether his persistently elevated blood pressure, remote duodenal ulcer bleed, and consumption of roughly 34 alcoholic beverages each week substantially heighten the likelihood of a future major hemorrhage while he continues warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation, and he expresses interest in targeted strategies—pharmacologic or lifestyle-based—that might mitigate the modifiable components of that risk.

Patient note:
A 62-year-old female with a history of ESRD and on hemodialysis was referred to our electrophysiology department due to paroxysmal AF. Anticoagulation therapy with warfarin was started because her CHADS2-VASc score was 4 (hypertension, diabetes, congestive heart failure, and female gender), as well as amiodarone therapy for rhythm control. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated enlarged left atrium (LA) with a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (25%). The coronary angiogram demonstrated no significant stenosis at the epicardial coronary artery. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed a thrombus in the LAA ( & ). We targeted an INR of 2.0–2.5 with a monthly check up; however, labile INR was documented with time in a therapeutic range (TTR) of 45.8%. With maintaining warfarin and amiodarone, the patient experienced syncope. Tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome was documented, and therefore, a catheter ablation was planned. However, after approximately 2 years of warfarin anticoagulation therapy, TEE detected remaining thrombus (). Therefore, warfarin was switched to a direct factor Xa inhibitor, apixaban at 5mg bid. Patient’s PT and INR values were 19.4 and 1.78, respectively, at the time of replacement. Apixaban was initially prescribed at 2.5 mg bid as opposed to 5 mg bid recommended by the package labeling for fear of bleeding complications, and it was increased to 5 mg bid a month later. After 4 months of apixaban treatment, TEE revealed complete resolution of the LAA thrombus ( & ). Finally, catheter ablation was performed without complications, and the patient has since been in the sinus rhythm under continued anticoagulant treatment with apixaban. No thromboembolic or bleeding event occurred during the 26 months of the follow-up after the catheter ablation.

Patient note:
A 59-year-old diabetic and hypertensive male patient presented to our department with acute onset chest pain radiating to the left arm. His blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, pulse rate was 68 beats/min, the respiratory rate was 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. His 12-lead electrocardiography revealed QS complexes in the inferior leads (). Two-dimensional echocardiography showed the absence of regional wall abnormality of the left ventricle and normal valvular function. His high-sensitivity troponin T (Elecsys Assay, Roche diagnostics, MA) level was 5.16 ng/mL (N < 0.014 ng/mL). The patient had undergone CABG 7 years back in another hospital for stable angina. One arterial graft, that is, LIMA to left anterior descending (LAD) artery and two venous grafts, one each to the first obtuse marginal (OM1) and the posterior descending artery (PDA) were implanted at that time. His previous left ventricular ejection fraction was also normal. He was doing well on guideline-directed medical therapy since then. He was compliant to drugs. His blood sugar levels were under control with oral hypoglycemic agents. His estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) by the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) equation was 65.87 mL/min/1.73 m2. Other hematological and biochemical parameters were within normal range.
He was taken upon coronary angiogram with an intention to revascularize. His native coronary angiogram revealed severe triple vessel disease with total occlusion of the right coronary artery in mid part ( and ). To our surprise, both venous grafts were patent ( and ). To our dismay, LIMA graft to LAD graft was 100% occluded proximal to distal anastomotic site ( and ). Therefore, we considered LIMA graft as the culprit lesion and decided to intervene. However, the patient refused any intervention and opted for medical therapy. During his hospital stay, he demonstrated hemodynamic stability and pain-free status for the next 72 hours. He was discharged on dual antiplatelet (aspirin plus ticagrelor) regimen supplemented by other drugs for secondary prevention after myocardial infarction as directed by the guidelines. At first and second follow ups at 15 days and 1 month thereafter, he was symptomatic free on optimal medical therapy.

Patient note:
A 66-year-old man arrived to the emergency department by private automobile in the late morning after three days of progressively wetter cough, right-sided pleuritic chest discomfort, and new dyspnea climbing the single flight of stairs to the bedroom of his split-level home. He reports intermittent shaking chills that had him layering extra blankets overnight and an axillary temperature at home reaching 38 °C earlier today, but he declined antipyretics, inhalers, or any rescue medications so that the clinical team could evaluate an unaltered presentation. His partner confirms that the drive was uneventful and that he conversed normally, correctly reciting the date and the route they planned to take. Past health history is notable for a stage II left-sided colonic adenocarcinoma resected two years ago followed by six months of adjuvant capecitabine; surveillance colonoscopy six months earlier and recent carcinoembryonic antigen levels have been unremarkable, and he has no current weight loss or night sweats. In addition, he follows cardiology for long-standing ischemic systolic dysfunction diagnosed after an anterior wall myocardial infarction seven years ago; the most recent outpatient echocardiogram three months prior documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 35 % with mild biatrial enlargement and trace mitral regurgitation. Home medications taken yesterday morning include carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 5 mg daily, low-dose furosemide 20 mg each morning, low-dose aspirin, rosuvastatin, and a daily multivitamin. He monitors his weight each day and had not noticed any sudden gain preceding this illness. There is no chronic kidney impairment, his last recorded serum creatinine being 1.0 mg/dL at a clinic visit six weeks ago, and he has never required dialysis. He denies chronic liver problems, tuberculosis, or connective-tissue disease. Immunizations are up to date, including both pneumococcal formulations and last season’s influenza vaccine. He quit a 30-pack-year cigarette habit a decade earlier, drinks red wine with dinner twice weekly, and denies illicit drug use. Upon arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences with mild breaks for breath, appearing uncomfortable but alert and oriented to person, place, time, and circumstance. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic; mucous membranes were slightly dry with brisk capillary refill. Pre-intervention vital signs measured by triage nursing staff on room air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.0 °C, regular pulse 104 beats min⁻¹ confirmed with three-lead telemetry, non-invasive blood pressure 109/64 mm Hg verified manually, respiratory rate 26 breaths min⁻¹ with moderate use of intercostal muscles, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 90 % and 92 % while breathing ambient air. Jugular venous distention was estimated at 4 cm above the sternal angle while the patient reclined at 45°, consistent with his chronic cardiology baseline, and trace bilateral ankle edema was present. Cardiac auscultation revealed a soft S3 in addition to normal S1 and S2 without new murmurs. Lung examination showed decreased breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion at the right posterior base with fine inspiratory crackles just superior to that area; the left lung had scattered coarse crackles in the lower field but remained resonant overall, and no wheezes were appreciated. The abdomen was soft, nontender, with normoactive bowel sounds, and the post-surgical midline scar from prior colectomy was well healed. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, fluent speech, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. Capillary blood glucose obtained before phlebotomy registered 112 mg dL⁻¹. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of arrival—prior to any intravenous fluid, oxygen supplementation, or medications save for minimal heparinized saline used to lock the catheter—returned a basic metabolic panel of sodium 133 mEq L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mEq L⁻¹, chloride 101 mEq L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mEq L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 23 mg dL⁻¹, and creatinine 1.0 mg dL⁻¹. Complete blood count showed leukocytosis to 14.0 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 88 % neutrophils, hematocrit 37 %, hemoglobin 12.4 g dL⁻¹, and platelets 245 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. An arterial sample taken from the right radial artery while the patient remained on room air demonstrated pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, PaO₂ 70 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 20 mEq L⁻¹, reflecting mild hypoxemia with an acid–base status near physiologic. Serum lactate measured 1.7 mmol L⁻¹. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 106 beats min⁻¹ with old anterior Q waves and nonspecific T-wave flattening unchanged from previous tracings. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy revealed a moderate right-sided fluid collection layering above the diaphragm with a concave meniscus sign, obscuring the costophrenic angle, along with a patchy consolidation of the adjacent right lower lobe; the cardiac silhouette was borderline enlarged, and pulmonary vasculature appeared mildly cephalized compared with prior imaging. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an expectorated sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched prior to antibiotics or diuretics. At the instant this note is dictated the patient has received no antipyretics, bronchodilators, supplemental oxygen, intravenous crystalloids, vasopressors, or other medications, so every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding recorded above reflects his untreated presentation.

Patient note:
A 93-year old man was brought to the emergency room for recent neurological deterioration. His past medical history was relevant for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease, chronic atrial fibrillation and mild memory loss. He had no history of kidney disease. His chronic medication included clopidogrel, acenocoumarol, amlodipine, atorvastatin, molsidomine and furosemide; he was on levofloxacin since two weeks for pneumonia. On admission, the patient’s physical examination revealed obnubilation with episodes of agitation, a blood pressure of 160/80 mmHg, an irregular heart rate of 50 beats per minute (bpm), jugular venous distention, decreased bilateral basal breath sounds, no fever and no leg edema. He was not obese. Initial abnormal serum laboratory results included: white blood cell (WBC) count of 12630/mm3 (84 % neutrophils), international normalized ratio (INR) of 4.5, creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL (203 μmol/L), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 80 mg/dL (28.5 mmol/L), albumin of 3.2 g/dL (32 g/L), phosphorus of 5.9 mg/dL (1.96 mmol/L) and gamma glutamyl transferase of 275 UI/L. He had a positive troponin I of 0.27 ng/mL but normal CPK and CPK-MB. C-reactive protein was 19 mg/L. He had no electrolytes’ disturbance (potassium 4.9 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, chloride 110 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L), no hypocalcemia (corrected calcium 8.9 mg/dL) nor anemia (hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %). Urinalysis showed 3+ protein.
Further investigations revealed left lung basal consolidation with bilateral effusion on chest X-ray. The arterial blood gas (ABG) showed: pH 7.27, PaO2 91 mmHg, PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3ˉ 23 mmol/L. Electrocardiogram (ECG) on admission showed a slow atrial fibrillation of 55 bpm (Fig. ). Brain computed tomography (CT) scanning ruled out possible ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke.
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). An echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 40 %, ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary arterial pressure of 40 mmHg, dilated right ventricle and slightly enlarged left atrium. Renal ultrasound was normal.
Empiric antibiotics were started combining ceftriaxone and levofloxacin; fluconazole was added at day 2 after sputum cultures grew Candida albicans. Urine culture was sterile.
During cardiac monitoring in the ICU, episodes of extreme bradycardia were noticed as low as 32 bpm with maintained systolic blood pressure at 100–120 mmHg and very low diastolic blood pressure of 30–40 mmHg.
On day 3, the patient became unconscious and developed severe respiratory acidosis with ABG showing: pH 7.16, PaCO2 64 mmHg, PaO2 75 mmHg, HCO3ˉ 22 mmol/L and he was intubated. He concomitantly became oligoanuric and serum creatinine started to increase. A spot urine test revealed a sodium (Na) of 22 mmol/L and potassium (K) of 34 mmol/L with a ratio Na/K <1. He received sodium bicarbonate whenever his bicarbonate level was less than 22.
Complete AV block was then identified on ECG. A temporary pacemaker was implanted on day 5 and the patient was extubated. Serum creatinine decreased and urine output improved considerably. Table illustrates the heart rate (HR), urine output, systolic and diastolic blood pressure values, serum creatinine and potassium variations before and after the pacemaker insertion.
The patient finally got a permanent single chamber pacemaker VVIR and improved considerably his consciousness and renal function. At discharge he had a serum creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL and he was conscious, alert and well oriented.

After that, a left-sided chest tube was inserted with immediate drainage of 700 cc of bloody output. It was then placed on negative 20 mmHg suction. A chest x-ray confirmed a good chest tube placement with decreased left hydropneumothorax (Figure ).
The patient was then monitored with daily chest x-rays. Chest CT angiogram was performed on hospitalization day two that was negative for vascular aneurysms, dissection, or extravasation. It also showed significant improvement in left-sided hydropneumothorax with a small residual pneumothorax and significantly decreased residual pleural fluid (Figure ).

A morning chest x-ray on hospital day four showed a new small left apical pneumothorax, this was treated with high flow oxygen therapy (Figure ).
On the day of discharge, the patient was feeling well and denied any more shortness of breath or chest pain. The last chest x-ray on the day of discharge showed stable left-sided pleural effusion and trace left-sided pneumothorax (Figure ).

Patient note:
We present a 77-year-old Caucasian man with history of multiple comorbidities including coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, pacemaker placement, and 40-pack-years of smoking who presented with complaints of speech disturbance and left-sided numbness and tingling which resolved within couple of hours of the hospitalization. He was diagnosed with transient ischemic attack (TIA). His pacemaker had been implanted for tachy-brady syndrome 36 months prior to this presentation. He was on warfarin, aspirin, and beta blocker for atrial fibrillation. His pulse rate was 105 beats/min, blood pressure 121/51 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on 3 L of oxygen. Physical examination revealed irregularly irregular tachycardia, bilateral rhonchi, wheezes, and mild pedal edema. His international normalized ratio (INR) was subtherapeutic at 1.2. Computer tomographic scan of the head was negative for acute process. His electrocardiogram (ECG) showed paced rhythm with right bundle-branch block, rather than the typical pattern of left bundle-branch block (). His chest X-ray in lateral projection showed ventricular lead with an abnormal turn (). Given the abnormal ECG and chest X-ray findings, pacemaker lead malposition was suspected. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed the pacemaker lead position in the left ventricle apex instead of right ventricle, passing through the interatrial septal defect (). Cardiac chambers were nondilated with ejection fraction of 65%. There was no associated thrombus. Doppler color-flow showed normal peak flows along with mild mitral regurgitation. Carotid ultrasound did not reveal any significant stenosis. Neurology service was on board and did the standard workup for TIA/stroke, which was negative.
We explained the possibility of recurrence of stroke/TIA in the setting of the malpositioned pacemaker lead to him. In view of his multiple co-morbidities, he refused surgical removal of the lead or any invasive procedures, including transesophageal echocardiogram. We increased his warfarin dose and educated him to maintain his INR between 2.5 and 3.5. Two years after the clinical follow-up, there was no evidence of further thromboembolic phenomenon.

question:
Patient note:
A 36 year-old woman with no significant past medical history complained of crushing chest pain followed by collapse while deboarding a cruise ship. She received immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) at the scene and was found to be in ventricular fibrillation. Heart rhythm was recovered after defibrillation. However, she sustained a second episode of ventricular fibrillation requiring CPR for 15 minutes. She was successfully defibrillated with resumption of sinus rhythm and normal blood pressure.
The patient was air-lifted to our hospital, where her electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with no ST elevation. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed ejection fraction of 35 to 40%, with severe apical-septal hypokinesis and moderate to severe anterior wall hypokinesis. She underwent emergent cardiac catheterization, which showed SCAD involving the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery ().
There were considerable multidisciplinary discussions with cardiologists, surgeons and interventionists as to the best approach to treat this patient. Several factors were considered: her young age, complexity of the LAD dissection, the risk of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) if acute occlusion occurred during insertion of the stent, and stent stenosis in this young patient. Due to her previous two episodes of ventricular fibrillation, and the nature of the dissection of the LAD, it was decided to proceed with emergent off-pump coronary artery bypass graft. The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) was anastomosed to the LAD, and high diastolic flow, via flowmeter, was confirmed at the time of chest closure ().
A 12-lead electrocardiogram performed on post-op day one showed normal sinus rhythm. The patient made an uneventful recovery and was discharged on post-op day four wearing a cardioverter defibrillator LifeVest (ZOLL, Pittsburgh, PA), until evaluation by an electrophysiologist at her one month follow up. At follow up, there were no indications for insertion of an automated implantable cardioverter defibrillator, as she had no arrhythmias and normal left ventricular function, and the LifeVest (ZOLL, Pittsburgh, PA) was discontinued.

Abdominal inspection revealed a soft abdomen with a barely perceptible bulge of the lower flanks that did not shift markedly with position change; percussion demonstrated a fluid wave only when the assistant applied firm pressure on one flank, suggesting a small volume of free intraperitoneal fluid rather than a tense collection. At that same hospitalization he suffered a small left frontal ischemic stroke manifested by transient expressive aphasia and right facial droop; mechanical thrombectomy was not required, and after a brief inpatient rehabilitation course he recovered fully, now reporting only occasional word-finding pauses when fatigued. Warfarin 5 mg nightly was started on discharge with a target international normalized ratio of 2.0–3.0, and his community anticoagulation clinic provides a printed log showing 22 INR measurements in the past six months, ranging narrowly between 2.3 and 2.9 with a calculated time in therapeutic range of 86 %, no dose holds, no oral vitamin K rescue, and no emergency visits or hospitalizations for supratherapeutic values. He has never experienced epistaxis, hematuria, melena, hematochezia, gingival oozing, subconjunctival hemorrhage, or easy bruising, nor has he ever required transfusion or reversal agents. Because of the prior cerebrovascular event, his neurologist recommended enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg daily for secondary stroke prevention, and for chronic lumbar radiculopathy he takes over-the-counter naproxen 440 mg once or twice per week before long bike rides; three months ago his primary clinician prescribed sertraline 50 mg each morning to address situational anxiety related to a job transition. He denies any history of peptic ulcer disease, inflammatory bowel disease, hereditary coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension, jaundice, or hepatotoxic medication exposure, and his most recent hepatic panel drawn by his primary physician last month documented alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 72 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, and albumin 4.4 g/dL, findings unchanged from prior annual wellness visits. He states he has never been told his blood pressure is elevated; in fact, he keeps a home cuff out of curiosity and shows smartphone screenshots demonstrating values that hover in the low-120s systolic and high-70s diastolic, corroborated today by three seated manual readings of 118/72 mm Hg, 120/70 mm Hg, and 116/74 mm Hg with an irregularly irregular pulse of 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 per minute, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Other medical history includes childhood tonsillectomy and seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with cetirizine as needed; he has no coronary artery disease, diabetes, sleep apnea, chronic lung pathology, malignancy, or connective tissue disorder. He works as a commercial airline pilot, lifts weights thrice weekly, and cycles 40 miles on weekends. Social history is notable for consistent alcohol intake: he drinks two pints of craft beer after evening flights on weekdays and four cocktails spread across each weekend day, estimating approximately 28 alcoholic drinks per week; he denies binge patterns, morning drinking, blackouts, pancreatitis, or prior counseling for reduction, though he admits his spouse has urged moderation. He has never smoked cigarettes and has never used illicit drugs. Review of systems is negative for chest pain, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-extremity swelling, abdominal pain, pruritus, dark urine, confusion, new focal neurologic deficits, visual disturbance, vertigo, or gait instability. Transthoracic echocardiography performed six weeks earlier demonstrated a mildly enlarged left atrium measuring 4.6 cm, normal left ventricular ejection fraction of 63 %, and no significant valvular lesions. The patient requests discussion of whether continuation of warfarin, transition to a direct oral anticoagulant, or consideration of left atrial appendage occlusion would best balance stroke prevention with the possibility of gastrointestinal or intracranial hemorrhage in light of his regular use of aspirin, intermittent naproxen, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor therapy, steady consumption of 28 alcoholic beverages each week, and otherwise stable anticoagulation profile.

Patient note:
A 76-year-old woman arrived for her semiannual visit to the hospital-based anticoagulation clinic seeking counsel on the safety of continuing oral vitamin K antagonist therapy that had been started eighteen months earlier after asymptomatic, non-valvular atrial fibrillation was documented on a home blood-pressure monitor with an irregular pulse alarm and confirmed on a 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained by her primary clinician. She lives independently, gardens daily, and walks a mile to the local market, but admits growing concern that her “borderline high blood pressure,” regular use of several over-the-counter pain and mood medications, the memory of a frightening gastrointestinal hemorrhage three years ago, and her nightly alcohol routine could converge to create a dangerous bleeding scenario while she remains on anticoagulation. Printed logs supplied by the pharmacist-run monitoring service list nineteen international normalized ratio (INR) measurements over the preceding six months ranging from 2.1 to 2.8 with a calculated time-in-therapeutic-range of 82 %, no gaps in testing, no dose holds, and no vitamin K rescues, suggesting consistently stable control. Her current regimen is warfarin 4 mg each evening taken from a pillbox, enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg every morning prescribed by cardiology after percutaneous coronary intervention to a right coronary artery stent nine years ago, sertraline 50 mg at bedtime for long-standing dysthymia, and naproxen sodium 220 mg one or two tablets most afternoons when her osteoarthritic knees ache after prolonged pruning; she denies use of glucocorticoids, ginkgo, fish oil, or herbal supplements. Blood-pressure treatment was initiated four months ago with amlodipine 10 mg nightly, yet the home upper-arm cuff she brought today shows readings over the past two weeks that average 158/86 mm Hg, and three seated auscultatory measurements in clinic after five minutes of rest are 162/88 mm Hg, 166/92 mm Hg, and 160/90 mm Hg; pulse during those checks is irregularly irregular between 70 and 78 beats per minute, respirations 16 per minute, temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. She has never experienced a transient ischemic attack, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, intracranial aneurysm, or spinal hemorrhage, and she reports no family history of such events. The major bleed that continues to worry her occurred three years earlier when dual antiplatelet therapy and frequent naproxen for shoulder pain culminated in a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed from a bleeding gastric ulcer; she required hospitalization, endoscopic hemostasis with dual therapy, and transfusion of three units of packed red blood cells, after which high-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy and Helicobacter pylori eradication were completed with no recurrence of melena or anemia. Since that hospitalization she has had no episodes of epistaxis requiring packing, hematuria, retroperitoneal bleeding, hemarthrosis, or transfusion, but bruises “the size of quarters” appear on her forearms after minor bumps while gardening. She denies jaundice, pruritus, abdominal distention, encephalopathy, easy fatigue, or prior abnormal liver enzyme panels. Indeed, a hepatic panel ordered by her internist last month documented alanine aminotransferase 25 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 23 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 71 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and albumin 4.2 g/dL, values unchanged from annual physicals over the past decade, and a prothrombin time performed after holding warfarin for a dental extraction six weeks ago yielded an INR of 1.0, suggesting preserved synthetic capacity. Review of systems today is negative for black stools, red vomitus, coughing up blood, gum bleeding, vision changes, new focal weakness, headache, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, abdominal pain, dark urine, or leg swelling. Social history is notable for substantial yet regimented alcohol use: two glasses of red wine with lunch, two 12-ounce bottles of lager at dinner, and a nightcap of two ounces of bourbon every evening, with a weekend bridge club adding four additional mixed drinks on Saturdays, totaling approximately 38 alcoholic beverages per week; she denies morning drinking, blackouts, tremors, or prior counseling to cut down but acknowledges that the routine “may be too much.” She quit cigarettes at age 42 after a 20-pack-year history and has never used illicit substances. Physical examination reveals a well-groomed, alert woman, body mass index 24 kg/m², in no acute distress. Conjunctiva are pink without pallor, sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa moist with scattered ecchymoses on the buccal surface but no petechiae. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruits, heart sounds are irregularly irregular with variable first heart sound and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and lung fields are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, nontender with no hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, abdominal wall collaterals, or spider angiomata. Extremities show warm skin, symmetric distal pulses, several yellow-green resolving bruises on the forearms, and no edema or palpable purpura. Neurologic examination demonstrates an oriented individual with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, symmetric strength, normal coordination, and steady tandem gait. Point-of-care capillary hemoglobin today is 13.4 g/dL, platelet count from last week’s complete blood count was 232 × 10⁹/L, and a finger-stick INR prior to warfarin dosing reads 2.4, consistent with her documented range. A same-day echocardiogram performed by sonography confirms mild left atrial enlargement, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 61 %, and no significant valvular lesions. She seeks detailed discussion of how to balance ongoing stroke prevention with the possibilities of gastrointestinal or intracranial hemorrhage in light of her age of seventy-six years, persistently elevated arterial pressures despite monotherapy, the prior ulcer bleed, the daily use of aspirin, sertraline, and intermittent naproxen, her stable anticoagulation profile, and her regular consumption of 38 alcoholic drinks each week.

Patient note:
A 72-year-old male patient presented as an outpatient for a routine checkup and was admitted due to acute kidney failure. He had been diagnosed with ulcerate nodular melanoma 10 months earlier. His further medical history included atrial fibrillation and prostatic hyperplasia. At the time of admission, his medication consisted of methylprednisolone (16 mg daily), bisoprolol, and pantoprazole. In June 2020, he had received double immunotherapy with nivolumab (1 mg/kg) plus ipilimumab (3 mg/kg). Fourteen days later, the patient was admitted with high fever (39°C) that was accompanied by mild prerenal AKI or hemoconcentration (fractional sodium excretion <0.1%, otherwise normal urinalysis, and SCr max 1.4 mg/dL). Renal function recovered within 4 days (SCr 1.1 mg/dL) upon volume expansion (Fig. ) before steroid exposure. Three days later, the patient developed grade 3 autoimmune colitis. In accordance with the recommendations of the “American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO),” steroid therapy was initiated at 1 mg/kg/day methylprednisolone for the colitis, which was tapered over 5 weeks []. After clinical stabilization, the therapy was resumed with a single dose of 480 mg nivolumab. The asymptomatic patient presented for a routine follow-up after 2 weeks. As SCr had drastically increased from 1.01 mg/dL to 4.93 mg/dL, he was immediately admitted to the hospital. Mildly elevated urinary protein excretion (protein to creatinine ratio 0.22 mg/mg) as well as mild hematuria was observed. The urinary sediment revealed sparse leukocyturia without cylinders or signs of acute tubular necrosis, while fractional excretion of sodium now indicated renal AKI (4.4%). In face of the rapid and unexplained AKI, a percutaneous renal biopsy was performed that revealed a severe, acute, and partly granulomatous tubule-interstitial nephritis with signs of a parenchyma destruction, while there were no signs of glomerular damage (shown in Fig. ). A CD3-positive T-cell infiltrate was found interstitially. CD4-positive cells predominated over CD8-positive cells, being accompanied by sparse B lymphocytes (shown in Fig. ). We escalated steroid therapy to 250 mg methylprednisolone intravenously over 2 days. However, kidney function continued to decline, with an SCr of 5.7 mg/dL. A significant improvement in kidney function was only achieved after further escalation to 500 mg intravenous methylprednisolone for 1 day. The steroid therapy was switched to oral prednisone, and treatment with nivolumab/ipilimumab was discontinued. In a follow-up visit 5 weeks after discharge, a gradual decline of the SCr to 2.23 mg/dL was recorded. Over the course of 3 months under steroids, a continuous decline of SCr levels to 1.74 mg/dL was noted. After 5 weeks during steroid tapering to 40 mg/day, an acute elevation of alanine transaminase (AST) to 474 U/L was observed, suggesting grade 3 autoimmune hepatitis. AST rapidly fell to 83 U/L upon transient steroid escalation to 80 mg. Steroid tapering was resumed and the regime switched to hydrocortisone for this purpose. However, a dose of 30 mg hydrocortisone was maintained. Seven months after the renal biopsy, the patient was readmitted due to progressive disease with disseminated metastatic spread, and therapy was limited to palliative care. In contrast, a decrease of SCr to 1.38 mg/dL indicated further recovery of renal function.

Patient note:
An 85-year-old female patient presented to the emergency department 3 h after receiving hemodialysis, with severe left loin pain and dizziness. Her blood pressure was 70/40 and pulse was 110 not responding to bolus infusions of normal saline. Serum hemoglobin was 60 g/L. Examination revealed a left hypochondrial tender mass, with clinical evidence of hemorrhagic shock. An emergent CT of the abdomen and pelvis was done and showed extensive left retroperitoneal hemorrhage and heterogeneous left kidney. The patient was on warfarin and had end-stage renal disease (ESRD) secondary to diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure, diastolic dysfunction, coronary artery bypass grafting, and hypertension.
She was positioned with left flank elevated 45° and left retroperitoneal subcostal transverse lateral lumbotomy was done. The retroperitoneal cavity was full of blood clots that were removed; this was rapidly followed by kidney dissection using blunt dissection and Ligasure vascular control. The renal pedicle was soon accessible and Hem-o-lok clips were used for pedicle control. The kidney was safely removed and the whole procedure was completed in 35 min. The patient vitals were stabilized and she was transferred to ICU for 24 h observation.
Pathology showed extensive sclerosed glomeruli, marked interstitial inflammation, severe arteriosclerosis, perirenal and renal parenchymal hemorrhage, severe renal artery atherosclerosis, and ACKD. and show the enlarged left kidney with massive retroperitoneal hemorrhage on CT scan.

Patient note:
A 46-year-old woman was urgently presented to a nearby hospital because of a femur fracture caused by an accident. Although she was alert on arrival, she began to experience sleepiness approximately 5 hours later. A follow-up helical computed tomography (CT) of the brain revealed the absence of any additional severe lesions or skull fractures. Chest CT confirmed an exudative lesion, and a pulmonary vascular computed tomography angiography (CTA) revealed no obvious abnormalities. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, the patient was suspected to have CFE. After 2 days, the patient was moved to our neurology department to receive the appropriate care. Immediate physical examination on arrival revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4, a positive bilateral Babinski sign, a positive Kernig sign, and neck stiffness. The patients left thigh presented bruising and swelling and had been fixed with external fixation with restrained movement in the previous hospital (Fig. A). She presented an arterial pressure of 148/80 mm Hg, heart rate of 124 bpm, and partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) of 64 mm Hg. Her blood gas analysis revealed a pH value of 7.4. Total body CT revealed a left femoral comminuted fracture with dislocation (Fig. B). Her bilateral lung presented an exudative lesion as well as pleural effusion (Fig. A). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed diffuse abnormal signals in the bilateral cerebral hemisphere, brainstem, and cerebellum, which were suggestive of embolization (Fig. ). Combined with the patients trauma history and imaging findings of the lung and brain, the patient was initially diagnosed with FES, whose corresponding treatment is mainly supportive. Regarding the closed fracture of the left femur, the external fixation that had been performed at the previous hospital was appropriate, and no further treatment was applied. Subsequent cardiovascular screening, including echocardiography, cervical artery ultrasound and bilateral lower extremity vascular ultrasound, was performed, and all the findings were negative. Four days after the femur fracture, the patient presented with moderate dyspnea, and her arterial blood gas analysis retrieved a pH value of 7.4. PO2 was 35 mm Hg, partial pressure of carbon dioxide was 126 mm Hg, and arterial oxygen saturation was 97.5% under nasal oxygen. Fourteen days after the fracture, both the lung symptoms and lung CT findings were considerably improved (Fig. B). Transthoracic echocardiography ultrasound was performed again, and shunts through a PFO were observed (Fig. ). On the following day, there was a gradual improvement in consciousness. However, the patients speech indicated dysphasia. Under active supportive care and hormone therapy, the patient was finally discharged with dysphasia and an untreated closed fracture.

Patient note:

He reports that mechanical knee pain has curtailed his weekend pickle-ball games over the past four months, but he continues to walk his dog two miles each evening and perform light yardwork, climbing a flight of stairs at home without dyspnea or assistance. He has not been hospitalized, undergone any operative or endoscopic procedures, or worn splints, casts, or braces in the current calendar year, and the last time he entered an operating room was seven years ago for an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. Pulmonary history is notable for tobacco-related chronic obstructive lung disease diagnosed in his early fifties after a 35-pack-year exposure; he quit cigarettes nine years ago and now uses once-daily tiotropium in combination with as-needed albuterol, has never required home oxygen, and has avoided oral steroids for more than eighteen months. He denies winter hospital admissions, mechanical ventilation, or nebulizer dependence. Cardiovascular review is benign for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, or recent episodes of sudden weight gain, and a transthoracic echocardiogram performed during hypertension work-up last summer documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 60 % with normal valves. He denies chest pain, exertional angina, palpitations, syncope, and there is no history of coronary intervention or myocardial infarction. He has never experienced unilateral calf tenderness, asymmetric leg girth, unexplained shortness of breath, or hemoptysis, and prior imaging of the lower extremities and chest has never demonstrated venous or pulmonary clot. Lifelong bowel habits are regular, he has never been told he has Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, and colonoscopy three years ago was normal aside from two small hyperplastic polyps. A review of the electronic chart confirms no malignancies, no cerebrovascular events, no spinal injuries, and no fractures of the hip, pelvis, or long bones. Regarding thrombosis risk, the patient recalls that his older sister spent a week in the intensive-care unit with a “blood clot in the lungs” after elective gynecologic surgery in her forties and that his father received anticoagulation for proximal leg thrombosis following a long trans-Atlantic flight; prompted by that pedigree, his primary physician ordered a hypercoagulability panel five years ago which was negative for common genetic mutations but did reveal mildly elevated fasting plasma homocysteine, for which he now takes daily folic acid and vitamin B12. He does not take estrogenic or selective estrogen receptor–modulating drugs, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or chronic systemic glucocorticoids. Current outpatient medications include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled every morning, albuterol 90 µg two puffs as needed, lisinopril 20 mg once daily for blood-pressure control, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, over-the-counter folic acid 1 mg, cyanocobalamin 1,000 µg, and a multivitamin; he discontinued low-dose aspirin one week ago per anesthesia instructions. He drinks one or two beers on weekends, denies illicit drug use, and has remained abstinent from nicotine since quitting. Physical examination finds an alert, well-nourished man sitting comfortably with a body mass index of 27 kg/m². Vital signs obtained ten minutes ago show temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, pulse 82 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 15 per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Neck veins are not distended, carotid upstrokes are brisk, and heart sounds are normal without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear except for faint end-expiratory wheezes over the right mid-lung but no crackles. The abdomen is soft and nontender with active bowel sounds. Inspection of both lower limbs reveals no dilated superficial veins, no edema, and equal calf circumferences; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and Homan-like maneuver elicits no discomfort. The right knee exhibits a small joint effusion, crepitus on flexion past 90 °, and medial joint-line tenderness, while the contralateral knee is unremarkable. Skin integrity is intact throughout and there are no active ulcers or hematomas. Neurologic screening shows full orientation, symmetrical strength, and intact sensation distally. A portable chest radiograph reviewed by radiology this morning shows mild hyperinflation consistent with his chronic lung disease but otherwise clear fields and normal cardiac silhouette; spirometry from clinic last month recorded an FEV₁ of 78 % predicted without significant bronchodilator response. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram displays normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min with nonspecific T-wave flattening in the inferior leads unchanged from prior tracings. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II, full cervical extension, and intact dentition, suggesting straightforward intubation. Patient note:
A 68-year-old man with a background of chronic atrial fibrillation managed on apixaban, stage-3 chronic kidney disease, and remote left total hip arthroplasty was brought in by advanced life support after his spouse heard a thud in the upstairs bathroom at 06:40 and discovered him sprawled on the tile floor, vomitus on his chin, right arm twitching for several seconds but no prolonged convulsion; she reports he had complained of a “splitting” headache for twenty minutes prior, took no new medication, and remained upright until the collapse. Fire-rescue arrived within eight minutes, immobilized the cervical spine with a rigid collar, placed him supine on a scoop stretcher, delivered 10 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather because respirations were shallow but unlabored, and established two large-bore peripheral IV lines that were flushed only with saline locks; point-of-care glucose was 112 mg/dL, and out of concern for preserving the initial neurologic assessment they administered neither benzodiazepine, opioid, antiemetic, antihypertensive, paralytic, nor hyperosmolar agent during the ten-minute transport. On roll-in to the resuscitation bay he remains secured to the EMS backboard in pajamas damp with emesis, no tubes beyond the oxygen mask and saline locks present. Vital signs recorded simultaneously with the first hospital examination—before any medication or crystalloid—are blood pressure 168/94 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 92 beats/min in irregularly irregular rhythm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min with symmetric chest rise, oxygen saturation 97 % on the mask, and rectal temperature 36.4 °C. Airway inspection shows intact upper dentition, midline tongue, minimal residual vomitus suctioned with Yankauer, brisk gag when the catheter contacts the posterior pharynx, and no audible stridor; breath sounds are vesicular bilaterally without crackles or wheeze. Cardiac auscultation reveals variable S1 intensity consistent with his known arrhythmia but no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses are 2 + and skin perfusion is warm. Abdomen is scaphoid, soft, nontender; pelvis is stable. A meticulous head-and-neck survey uncovers a 3-cm contusion over the left parietal scalp without step-off, pupils equal at 3 mm and briskly reactive, and no periorbital ecchymosis. During a silent observation period his eyelids remain fully closed, lashes motionless; when his surname is spoken in a normal tone beside his ear both lids part to mid-palpebral height, the globes align with the examiner, and he maintains that gaze for several seconds before blinking and letting the lids drift shut, repeating the same behavior each time his name is called yet never opening them spontaneously in between. Speech is limited to low-pitched moans and guttural phonation without discernible words regardless of prompting about orientation, though the quality and volume fluctuate appropriately with respiratory effort. Despite the paucity of intelligible language, he demonstrates purposeful cooperation: upon request he squeezes the examiner’s fingers with equal strength, releases on cue, raises his right leg off the mattress and holds it for five seconds, and protrudes his tongue when asked; when instructed to give a thumbs-up he does so correctly, and he tracks the examiner’s moving hand with his eyes once the lids are open. Accordingly, his Glasgow Coma Scale is assessed at 11 (Eye 3, Verbal 2, Motor 6). Noxious stimuli are therefore unnecessary for limb assessment, but passive tone is evaluated and found normal; deep tendon reflexes are 2 + at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles, plantar responses are flexor, and no clonus is elicited. Sensation to light touch appears symmetric; he withdraws appropriately when a cold towel is applied to either foot. Cranial nerve examination is otherwise limited by the nonverbal state, yet corneal reflexes are present, face is symmetric at rest, palate elevates midline, and cough is forceful with tracheal palpation. A focused secondary survey reveals no long-bone deformity, jugular venous distention, or thoracic tenderness; lungs are clear to percussion. Portable supine chest radiograph obtained within five minutes shows clear fields and good collar position, while an ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response and no ischemic changes. Blood has been drawn for complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, cardiac troponin, serum ethanol, and anti-factor Xa level but results are pending. No pharmacologic agents, intravenous fluids, or osmotic therapies have yet been administered since hospital arrival, ensuring that the documented ocular reaction only after verbal prompting, the non-speech vocalizations, and the reliable execution of specific commands represent his untreated neurologic baseline at presentation. Neurosurgery and stroke neurology have been paged; emergent non-contrast head CT and CT angiography of the cervical and intracranial vessels are underway, and serial neurologic checks every fifteen minutes have been ordered while airway equipment for rapid-sequence intubation stands ready should his protective reflexes wane.

Patient note:
A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department after one week of repeated bouts of crampy abdominal pain and diarrhea, which became bloody on the day of arrival. There was no fever, nausea, or vomiting.
He was evaluated several times in the Emergency Medicine Department during the previous three months, with various abdominal complaints that resolved after symptomatic relief without further investigation. The patient reported no additional symptoms or relevant personal or familial medical history. He worked as a bus driver, smoked cigarettes for many years, and did not drink alcohol regularly.
The patient reported daily usage of “Mr. Nice Guy” for the last few months but denied use of any other drugs or supplements. Consumption of SCs was via smoking, and he denied other means of administration such as oral or intravenous. This information was validated by collateral anamnesis of visiting friends.
In the emergency department, the patient was hemodynamically stable with initial BP recordings of 159/100 mmHg, regular heart rate of 99 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 99% on ambient air. Physical examination was unremarkable except for intense borborygmi and mild abnormal tenderness. Initial blood work showed leukocytosis of 20,000 cells/mcL with neutrophilia (80%) and normal hemoglobin (15.1 grams/dL). Biochemistry, including electrolytes, kidney function tests, liver, and pancreatic enzymes, were all within normal limits. Urinalysis was unremarkable, and urine toxicology screen was slightly positive for amphetamines and benzodiazepines but negative for other screened drugs including THC, opiates, and cocaine. Upon repeated questioning, patient once again denied use of any other stimulant including amphetamines, besides “Mr. Nice Guy.” White cell count increased to 28,000 cells/mcL six hours later, and an abdominal computed tomography (CT) performed without IV or PO contrast enhancement was unremarkable. Over the next four days the patient continued to complain of intermittent episodes of crampy abdominal pain with episodic diarrhea, followed by pain-free periods during which he strolled freely around the hospital, admitting that he was still smoking “Mr. Nice Guy,” provided to him by his friends. Additional toxic screens were not performed during hospitalization due to lack of the patient's cooperation. Leukocytosis gradually resolved. Blood, stool, and urinary cultures were negative and other laboratory data were unremarkable, with the exception of hypophosphatemia (0.5 mmol/L, normal = 0.8–1.4) and increasing C-reactive protein (22 mg/dL, normal < 0.5 mg/dL). During his hospitalization we abstained giving the patient medications from the family of benzodiazepines, potent opiates, and any medications which involve potential future addiction.
On the fifth hospitalization day, an abdominal X-ray, taken during a bout of abdominal pain, demonstrated dilated small bowel loops without features of intestinal obstruction or perforation, consistent with paralytic ileus. Later that day, the pain subsided and the patient requested to take a walk around the hospital, as our internal medicine ward regulations permit stable patients to leave their rooms. Obviously, hospitalized patients are not permitted to use any form of drug or medication not provided to them by hospital staff.
However upon returning from his walk, the patient admitted that he had once again consumed “Mr. Nice Guy” with one a friend who came to visit him. Routine checkup of vital signs revealed elevated blood pressure 180/110 mmHg with a heart rate of 120/min, without fever. Six hours later, he developed sudden extreme abdominal pain and was found to be in profound shock vomiting “coffee ground” material. Physical examination revealed abdominal guarding and rebound tenderness compatible with peritonitis, and laboratory evaluation disclosed hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, thrombocytopenia, and worsening kidney function. An emergent surgical intervention was considered for an evolving abdominal catastrophe, but the patient quickly went into pulseless electrical activity with subsequent cardiac arrest.
A request for autopsy was declined by the patient's family, but a postmortem CT scan one hour after death revealed extensive pneumatosis intestinalis of the entire small bowel, right colon and sigmoid, gas in the portal system, and blood vessels, with free air and unclear fluid in the peritoneal cavity (Figures and ). These findings were consistent with acute intestinal perforation most probably due to a nonobstructive mesenteric infarction (NOMI) as the cause of death. There was no evidence of single vessel infarction, rather of diffuse ischemia, possibly due to splanchnic vasospasm. Air in the aorta, right ventricle, and biliary tract were conceivably postmortem changes. Urinary toxic screen sampled during hemodynamic resuscitation was positive for methadone, THC, and benzodiazepines, but negative for cocaine, opiates, and amphetamines. Unfortunately, due to technical failure, the final urine sample was not sent for confirmatory mass spectrometry testing.

Patient note:
A 71-year-old male with a history of gastric MALT lymphoma status post H. pylori treatment and confirmed eradication presented with progressively worsening shortness of breath and productive cough. He had noticed the dyspnea two months prior to presentation and reported exertion as the main trigger. There was no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, fever, chest pain, or appetite changes. However, he reported a 13-pound unintentional weight loss over six months. The patient has a past medical history that is significant for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with chronic respiratory failure requiring supplemental home oxygen, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and deep vein thrombosis. The patient is an active smoker with more than 50 pack-year tobacco use. He has no history or risk factors of tuberculosis. There was no history of alcohol use or illicit drug use. Medications prior to admission were furosemide, lisinopril, pantoprazole, tiotropium bromide monohydrate inhaler, and albuterol inhaler.
The patient was diagnosed with gastric MALT a year prior to the current presentation and underwent eradication of H. pylori infection with amoxicillin, clarithromycin with a proton pump inhibitor with resolution of the gastric tumor.
On physical examination, his temperature was 36.8 °C, his blood pressure was 121/72 mm Hg, his pulse rate was 78 beats per minute, and his respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute. He had scattered wheezing and decreased breath sounds over the right lung base. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. A chest X-ray with posteroanterior and lateral views revealed a large right pleural effusion which was confirmed on thoracic ultrasonography (Figures -).
The patient underwent thoracentesis with the removal of 750 milliliters of exudative fluid based on Light’s criteria (Table ). Cytologic assessment of the pleural fluid revealed 90% lymphocytes with no malignant cells. The pleural effusion recurred within three days and the pulmonary team elected to pursue medical pleuroscopy, pleurodesis, and pleural biopsy for further evaluation and prevention of further recurrence. The procedure was followed by chest tube placement which was removed four days later.
The biopsy of the right pleura demonstrated fibroadipose tissue with multiple poorly defined lymphoid aggregates (Figure ). The lymphocytes within these aggregates were small in size, with predominantly round nuclear contours, condensed chromatin, no identifiable nucleoli, and moderate amounts of pale-staining cytoplasm. Focally, the lymphocytes displayed a so-called “monocytoid” appearance, a histologic finding typical of marginal zone lymphoma. By immunohistochemistry, the majority of the lymphocytes were cluster of differentiation (CD)20-positive B-cells, with few infiltrating small CD3-positive T-cells. Flow cytometric immunophenotyping performed on a concurrent pleural fluid specimen identified a monotypic B-cell population that expressed CD19, CD20, CD22, and kappa surface light chains, but not CD5 or CD10. Given the patient’s known history of gastric extranodal marginal zone lymphoma, the morphologic and immunophenotypic findings in the pleural biopsy and pleural fluid were interpreted as representing pleural involvement by extranodal MALT lymphoma.
The patient responded to pleurodesis with minimal recurrence of the pleural effusion after chest tube removal and improvement in dyspnea (Figure ). However, the hospital course was complicated with a complete heart block. In light of advanced disease and multiple comorbidities, the patient declined any intervention and elected to pursue comfort care measures. He was discharged to home with hospice care.

Patient note:
A 68-year-old man attended the Accident and Emergency department with increasing breathlessness but no chest pain, sputum production or haemoptysis. He had recently returned from holiday in Spain and his general practitioner prescribed amoxicillin for a presumed chest infection. He was a diet-controlled type 2 diabetic on treatment for hypertension. He had a 40-pack-year smoking history and had lost 4 kg in weight. Examination revealed an obese man with normal blood pressure, sinus tachycardia at 100 beats⋅min−1, with a respiratory rate of 26 breaths⋅min−1. His oxygen saturation was 96% on air. His white cell count was 11×109 cells⋅L−1 and C-reactive protein was 92 mg⋅L−1. Renal function and coagulation studies were normal.
The admitting medical team felt that there was a “complete whiteout” of the left hemithorax and initially treated him for suspected severe community-­acquired pneumonia with intravenous antibiotics and fluids, while arranging a respiratory opinion. Prophylactic low molecular weight ­heparin (LMWH) was also started. The respiratory team felt that an underlying malignancy may have been responsible for the radiographic appearances of left upper lobe collapse and suggested a ­computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax. shows a “veil-like” opacity projected over the left lung field, a raised left hemidiaphragm with blunting of the left costophrenic angle consistent with left upper lobe collapse, volume loss and an associated pleural effusion.
The CT scan showed a large left hilar mass coalescing with the left upper lobe collapse. There were associated large para-aortic, subcarinal, mediastinal and supraclavicular nodes, a single liver metastasis and a second separate mass in the right lung. Lung cancer staging was T4N3M1b.
It was interesting to note that a separate mass was present in the right lung (c). He did have metastatic disease but this might represent a synchronous primary, although by strict definition, to diagnose this, we needed to prove that the second mass was of different histology to the primary mass or that it was of the same histology but with no mediastinal or metastatic spread [].
While awaiting a bronchoscopy, the patient coughed up ∼600 mL of fresh blood in 12 h, with worsening hypoxia. Repeat full blood count and coagulation studies were normal.
The patient was having massive haemoptysis, defined as coughing up anything between 100 mL and 600 mL of fresh blood in 24 h [].
He was seen by the on-call medical team and sat upright. Two large-bore cannulae were inserted in case of exsanguination. Sitting upright runs the risk of the blood spilling over into the normal lung. “Drowning” by filling up the bronchial tree with blood tends to occur before any true haemodynamic instability due to volume loss. As such, the mainstay of treatment in massive haem­optysis is to protect the normal lung and try to stop the bleeding [, ].
The respiratory team felt that a palliative approach was too premature, but it was explained to him that his prognosis was poor with limited treatment options available. He agreed to a “do not resuscitate” plan. A treatment escalation plan was agreed to ensure his treatment was limited to level 2 care. Hypoxia precluded a bronchoscopy or transfer to the local cardiothoracic centre. Bronchoscopic strategies to control pulmonary haemorrhage include balloon tamponade, iced saline lavage, administration of a topical vasoconstrictor or coagulant, laser therapy and electrocautery [].
The patient pointed to his left hemithorax when asked which side he felt the bleeding was coming from. Anecdotal experience suggests that patients with haemoptysis can often accurately indicate the side of the bleeding lesion. He was therefore positioned on his left side and tranexamic acid was administered intravenously. A pilot study evaluating the effect of tranexamic acid and the related antifibrinolytic agent aminocaproic acid included three patients with haemoptysis due to lung cancer []. All three patients experienced cessation of bleeding within 1–4 days without any recurrence. Patients received 1.5 g of intravenous tranexamic acid initially, followed by 1 g three times per day for a week after cessation of bleeding. The use of tranexamic acid in bleeding has been recognised for a long time [] and tranexamic acid may reduce both the duration and volume of bleeding, with low risk of short-term thromboembolic complications [].
His haemoptysis and hypoxia improved over the ensuing days, and at bronchoscopy an organised clot was visualised in the left upper lobe bronchus with no endobronchial masses and a normal right bronchial tree. Left upper lobe lavage revealed no malignant cells on cytology. At endobronchial ultrasound examination, a large paratracheal node was sampled and histology demonstrated a poorly differentiated necrotic squamous cell carcinoma.
The patient’s clinical condition slowly improved until 15 days into his admission, when overnight he developed acute dyspnoea with tachycardia at 120 beats⋅min−1. Arterial blood gas sampling measured his arterial oxygen tension (PaO) at 7.0 kPa on high flow oxygen via a reservoir bag, and an arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO) of 5.1 kPa. A repeat chest radiograph showed no change.
The PA–aO is a measure of the difference between the alveolar concentration (A) of oxygen and the arterial (a) concentration of oxygen. In room air (inspiratory oxygen fraction of 0.21) at sea level (atmospheric pressure of 760 mmHg) assuming 100% humidity in the alveoli, a simplified version of the equation is 21−((PaCO/0.8)−PaO), 0.8 being the respiratory quotient.
High flow oxygen delivers ∼85% oxygen, so 85−(5.1/0.8)−7=71.625, which is significantly raised. While his PA–aO was likely to be raised due to his cancer/effusion, such a disparity and the clinical picture points towards the possibility of a pulmonary embolus. The use of the PA–aO is a useful adjunct in diagnosis []. There are numerous case reports about tranexamic acid increasing the risk of pulmonary emboli [, ]. In this case, the patient had other significant risk factors such as disseminated malignancy and a prolonged period of immobility.
The patient understood that if left untreated, a large pulmonary embolus may prove fatal, but by treating it with anticoagulation, a major fatal haemoptysis was also more likely. He agreed to receive LMWH together with morphine for symptoms of dyspnoea and agitation. 6 h later, he had improved clinically and was able to safely lie flat briefly for a CT pulmonary angiogram. This confirmed large right-sided pulmonary emboli with associated right heart strain with reflux of contrast into the venous circulation (). The option of inferior vena cava filter insertion to prevent further embolic events was not available in our hospital, and he was too unstable to be transferred to an appropriate tertiary hospital. Over the following 2 days, urgent palliative radiotherapy to the left-sided tumour was arranged. After he had received a single fraction, further large volume haemoptysis recurred. LMWH was stopped and tranexamic acid restarted. The bleeding settled once more and he completed five fractions of radiotherapy. Slowly his oxygen saturations improved to 93% on air and he was discharged home on long-term full-dose LMWH with no recurrence of the haem­optysis.
He presented 3 weeks later with progressive respiratory failure and his symptoms were palliated according to his wishes.
