Patient note:
A 47-year-old Caucasian female with a known medical history of essential hypertension being treated with labetalol came to the emergency department (ED) with complaints of non-exertional, intermittent (lasting one to two minutes), 3/10, left-sided chest pain which started three days ago. At the time of presentation, the patient was asymptomatic. She was afebrile with a blood pressure of 188/90 mmHg, heart rate of 73 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 16 per minute and normal oxygen saturation levels. Physical examination revealed a faint 1/6 systolic murmur which accentuated to 2/6 in intensity when she was made to go from crouching to standing. The remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. The patient denied any pertinent family history. She was a former smoker and reported no allergies. Laboratory studies disclosed normal serum chemistry with normal troponin and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels. Electrocardiogram (EKG) showed normal sinus rhythm with no ST-T wave changes. A chest radiograph identified borderline cardiomegaly with no evidence of infection or pulmonary vascular congestion.
A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was pursued, which revealed normal left ventricular (LV) size and function. LVOT appeared normal without sub-valvular ridge or asymmetric septal hypertrophy. Mitral valve demonstrated normal-appearing leaflets; however, there was a large centrally echolucent sub-valvular chordal cyst greater than 1 cm in the largest diameter (Figure ). Due to concerns of possible exertional LVOT obstruction, an exercise stress echocardiography was scheduled. Labetalol was switched to carvedilol due to the latter’s negative inotropy and better heart rate control. During exercise stress echocardiography, the patient exercised to stage five Bruce protocol achieving 14.5 metabolic equivalents (METs). There was no suggestion of obstruction on doppler at rest however, transient LVOT obstruction was noted with exercise. The patient had an appropriate heart rate and blood pressure response to stress with no signs of coronary ischemia or regional wall motion abnormalities. (Figures -).
A cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no evidence of increased enhancement confirming the diagnosis of a benign subvalvular blood cyst of the mitral apparatus. In light of asymptomatic nature of the condition, mild to moderate LVOT obstruction at peak exertion in a beta-blocker deprived state, a conservative strategy was opted after multidisciplinary discussion with cardiothoracic surgery. The patient was resumed on carvedilol and was advised to maintain adequate hydration to avoid worsening of LVOT obstruction due to dehydration. A surveillance stress echocardiogram done during six months follow-up visit showed stable exertional hemodynamics.

Patient note:
Our patient is a 28-year-old male with a past medical history of EGE, duodenal ulcers, and stricture who presented to the hospital with chief complaints of 3 episodes of dizziness and melena for one day. The patient reported that before coming to the hospital, he was shopping at a mall, where he experienced dizziness and then had a dark black colored bowel movement. The patient recently came from Canada. He denied any other past medical history or any past surgical history. He reported allergy to peanuts. His home medications included prednisone, montelukast, and pantoprazole daily.
On admission, his vitals were obtained and he was found to be tachycardic with a heart rate of 150. Initial lab workup done in the emergency department showed hemoglobin (hgb) of 9.3. Soon after admission, the patient had an episode of large volume hematemesis >1.5 L and brief loss of consciousness for which a code rapid response was called. Between days 1 and 2, his hgb dropped from 9.3 to 5.7. The Patient was initially stabilized by intravenous crystalloids and was transferred to the ICU. The patient received blood transfusions and his hgb improved significantly. The patient was managed conservatively with continuous monitoring in the ICU. Emergent endoscopy (EGD) revealed high-grade duodenal stenosis, severe pyloroduodenal deformity and a duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel. Two clips were deployed blindly during the EGD (figure -).
Epinephrine could not be injected due to hard and fibrotic tissue around the duodenal stenosis. The Interventional radiology (IR) service was consulted. The patient was taken for angiography which revealed active bleeding from a branch of the gastric artery. Coiling and subsequent embolization were done by the IR service. The patient received 5 units of RBCs total and continued on pantoprazole intravenous twice daily. For his known duodenal stricture, surgery was consulted with a recommendation of no acute surgical intervention in the hospital was provided. On discharge, he was sent home with pantoprazole and prednisone and close follow up with gastroenterology, surgery and primary care doctor.

Patient note:
A 63-year-old Caucasian male with a history only significant for daily marijuana use received the J&J COVID-19 vaccine on May 7, 2021. One day later, he developed intractable nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, watery diarrhea, chills, sweats, and heavy chest pain. In the emergency department (ED), the patient was tachycardic at 120 beats per minute, hypoxic with oxygen 88% on room air, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) 3421 pg/ml, elevated troponins at 1.29 ng/ml, procalcitonin 25 ng/ml, lactic acid 5.0 mmol/L, white blood cells 19 K/UL, thrombocytopenia at 101 K/UL, and creatinine 1.91 mg/dL. Initial chest X-ray showed bilateral airspace opacities consistent with atypical pneumonia. The patient was intubated because he was in severe respiratory distress with use of accessory muscles and decreased oxygen saturation. Ventilator settings are presented in Table .
Echo showed an ejection fraction (EF) of 25% with global hypokinesis and grade 3 diastolic dysfunction. A right heart catheterization was performed, showing severe pulmonary hypertension. An intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted, but his condition continued to decline, so a left-sided Impella device (Impella Cardiosystems AG, Aachen, Germany) was placed and milrinone and norepinephrine were started.
The patient was worked up for infectious causes and all were negative including two negative COVID-19 results, viral panel, blood cultures, urine cultures, sputum cultures, and urine legionella. A chest X-ray five days after presenting to the ED is shown below (Figure ).
Throughout his nine-day hospital stay, he continued to have rapid cyclical fluctuations of hypertension (260s/130s) and hypotension (40s/20s), persistent fevers up to 40.2 °C, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)-like picture. His other problems included acute tubular necrosis (ATN) from an acute kidney injury (AKI), hypernatremia, arterial catheter-associated thrombosis in mid left radial artery leading to gangrene of left 1st and 2nd digits, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) with cardiogenic shock (on May 10, 2021, EF was 55% with no diastolic dysfunction), subclinical hyperthyroidism, and electroencephalogram (EEG) showed diffuse slowing, with no epileptiform activity. Echo on May 15, 2021 showed EF of 43% with mild global hypokinesis.
Neuroendocrine crisis was suspected, and the patient was worked up for pheochromocytoma and carcinoid syndrome (Table ).
The results of retroperitoneal ultrasound are shown below (Figures -).
The first step in the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma is to discontinue medications that may interfere with metanephrine levels such as norepinephrine. Due to our patient's labile blood pressure measurements, he was on and off of vasopressors (such as norepinephrine) and anti-hypertensive medications (nitroglycerin). The results of significantly elevated 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines or elevated fractionated plasma metanephrines confirms the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. Imaging with CT or MRI is done to localize the tumor. Our patient was not stable enough for these imaging tests and thus we had to do an ultrasound. There were no previous imaging studies on record for this patient or a family history that could explain the etiology of his tumor.
The patient was transferred to the University of Michigan (U of M) hospital for mass resection on May 21, 2021. A CT was performed that day to confirm the ultrasound finding of a 7 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass. The patient continued to suffer from acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and a tracheostomy was performed on June 07, 2021 due to prolonged intubation. His stay at U of M hospital was also complicated by episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) that responded well to synchronized cardioversion. He was also placed on amiodarone. On June 18, 2021, an open right adrenalectomy was performed and on June 22, 2021, repeat plasma metanephrine was <0.2 nmol/L, and normetanephrine was 0.9 nmol/L. An echo performed on June 22, 2021 revealed a left ventricular EF of 63%, normal overall left ventricular systolic function, normal overall right ventricular systolic function, and no significant valvular dysfunction. Multiple upper and lower extremity deep vein thromboses (DVTs) were found on June 24, 2021. The patient was treated with blood thinners and stabilized for transfer to inpatient rehabilitation on July 02, 2021. The patient was then discharged on July 12, 2021 to stay with his sister. He has continued outpatient therapy and is now able to walk on his own and perform all of his activities of daily living independently. He will follow up with endocrine genetics for the etiology of his pheochromocytoma, cardiology, and physical medicine and rehabilitation. He will continue amiodarone for NSVT and rivaroxaban for the DVTs until the end of September 2021. The patient is doing very well overall.

Patient note:
A 47-year-old woman with a seven-year history of autoimmune hepatitis that progressed to biopsy-proven cirrhosis despite adherence to azathioprine and low-dose prednisone was brought to the tertiary-care emergency department by her adult son after he found her mid-morning sitting at the kitchen table staring vacantly at a bowl of cereal, mumbling phrases that did not match the conversation, and unable to dial her home healthcare nurse; he reported that over the preceding forty-eight hours she had slept through multiple medication alarms, addressed him by his late father’s name twice, and attempted to exit the house wearing mismatched shoes on the wrong feet. One week earlier she had driven herself to a neighborhood grocery store without incident, paid bills online, and cooked dinner, so the abrupt cognitive decline was striking for the family. She denied fever, chills, vomiting, abdominal pain, chest discomfort, palpitations, shortness of breath, hematemesis, melena, bright red blood per rectum, pruritus, or new rashes during sporadic but coherent moments of the prehospital interview. Past medical history included hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 88 µg daily, iron-deficiency anemia treated with oral ferrous sulfate, and remote laparoscopic cholecystectomy; she had never experienced gastrointestinal bleeding, required large-volume paracentesis, or undergone band ligation. Medications in the pill organizer delivered by her son were azathioprine 100 mg nightly, prednisone 5 mg each morning, levothyroxine, ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice daily, and a daily multivitamin; no lactulose, rifaximin, diuretics, benzodiazepines, anticoagulants, or herbal supplements were present. She drank no alcohol since her diagnosis, had never smoked, denied recreational drug use, and worked part-time from home as a graphic designer. Family history was notable for a mother with systemic lupus but no other liver disease; her father died of myocardial infarction at 62. The patient lives in a single-story home with her son, follows a moderate-sodium diet prepared by a visiting dietician, and usually walks around the block once daily. Upon arrival—before intravenous access, blood draws, or administration of any medication—the initial triage vitals were temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % while breathing ambient air. She appeared somnolent, opened eyes only to loud verbal stimulus, produced incomprehensible syllables, and localized pain when the nail bed was pressed, but could not sustain a conversation; the sweet, earthy odor characteristic of advanced liver dysfunction wafted with each exhalation. Pupils were equal at 3 mm and briskly reactive, extra-ocular movements showed slow pursuit without nystagmus, and funduscopic exam revealed no papilledema. When asked to extend her arms, she was unable to follow the command; spontaneous movements were slow and uncoordinated, and intermittent irregular flapping of the hands emerged as her arms drifted off the stretcher side rails. Cranial nerves II through XII were otherwise grossly intact, strength was 4/5 diffusely, tone mildly increased in both upper limbs, deep-tendon reflexes were symmetrical, and plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. Mucous membranes were moist, sclerae were definitely yellow, and conjuctivae appeared pale. Neck veins were flat with the head of bed at thirty degrees. Cardiac examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear on auscultation across all fields. The abdomen was soft and nondistended, bowel sounds present in all quadrants, and the liver edge—firm and nodular—was just palpable at the right costal margin on deep inspiration; no tenderness or rebound was elicited, and no shifting dullness or fluid wave was appreciated. Extremities exhibited trace bilateral ankle pitting edema, and chronic excoriations were seen over both shins. Skin inspection disclosed scattered spider angiomas over the upper chest and mild palmar erythema. Capillary glucose obtained by nursing staff at the bedside measured 106 mg/dL. Within five minutes of physical examination, but still before any therapeutic intervention, venous blood was drawn revealing a total bilirubin of 4.3 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.05 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 96 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 184 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 266 U/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.9 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 94 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.88. Serum ammonia, blood cultures, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and acetaminophen level were sent but results were pending. A portable chest radiograph obtained concurrently showed elevated hemidiaphragms with patchy bibasilar atelectasis but no infiltrate or effusion, and a 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 90 beats/min with a QTc of 436 ms. Bedside focused ultrasonography performed by the emergency physician just prior to intravenous cannulation depicted a shrunken heterogeneous hepatic parenchyma with coarse nodularity, patent portal and hepatic veins exhibiting hepatopetal flow measuring 14 cm/s, splenomegaly to 17 cm, and no sonographic evidence of ascites; kidneys appeared normal in size and echogenicity, and the gallbladder was absent from prior surgery. At the time of this note the patient remained hemodynamically stable, still had not received any lactulose, rifaximin, vitamin K, antibiotics, sedatives, intravenous fluids, or other medications, and was awaiting urgent consultation from the on-call hepatology service for further evaluation and management of her profound alteration in consciousness against the backdrop of decompensated autoimmune cirrhosis.

Patient note:
A 54-year-old man presented to our Accident and Emergency (A&E) department complaining of pain in his right knee. The patient has slipped off the bottom two steps of the staircase, without suffering any direct impact to his knee. He was still able to mobilize for 10 yards afterwards, before hearing a ‘pop’ and immediately experienced pain to his right knee.
There was no previous injury to patient's right knee. His past medical history included atrial fibrillation and squamous cell penile carcinoma of the glans penis, requiring partial penectomy and urethral reconstruction, and subsequent radical right inguinal lymph node (ILN) dissection 16 years ago (limited to borders of the femoral triangle) for lymphatic metastases, with clear dissections margins. Patient has never received any radiotherapy or chemotherapy treatment. He has been free from disease recurrence since, and continued to have annual surveillance follow-up. Following ILN dissection, patient developed right lower limb lymphoedema, with episodes of intermittent swelling of his right thigh, which became more frequent over the last 3 years. Patient was on warfarin, paracetamol and codeine. There was no family history of musculoskeletal, autoimmune disease, diabetes or other systemic disease.
Physical examination showed knee swelling, a high riding patella with a palpable gap below the patella. The patient was unable to weight bear and could not perform active knee extension on his right knee. There was no obvious laceration or injury to the knee. Neurovascular examination was normal. Apart from ectopic ossification of the patellar tendon, plain radiograph showed no evidence of acute fracture or joint effusion (Fig. ). Because of the unusual mechanism of injury and the initial ultrasound performed in A&E which suggested a rupture of the quadriceps and patella tendon, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed and demonstrated complete rupture of the patellar tendon from the inferior pole of patella, an almost complete shearing of quadriceps tendon off the patella and chronic tendinosis in the mid-portion of patellar tendon (Fig. ).
Surgery was performed on the knee. A midline longitudinal incision was made, revealing a complete rupture of the patellar tendon from the inferior pole of the patella, torn medial and lateral retinacular fibres, and near complete shearing of 90% of the quadriceps tendon (Fig. ). The patellar tendon was anchored trans-osseously with 5 TiCron™ (Covidien) sutures, and further strengthened with 2/0 vicryl sutures using the Kessler technique. Both the quadriceps tendon and retinaculum were primarily repaired using 2/0 vicryl sutures. Postoperatively, the knee was immobilized in a long leg back slab for 2 weeks, followed by cylinder cast for 4 weeks. Patient was gradually worked towards full weight bearing afterwards. At 8 weeks post-surgery, patient was able to fully extend his knee, and perform straight leg raise against gravity. His range of flexion improved with physiotherapy from 30° to 100° at 3 months following surgery.

Patient note:
A 57-year-old woman is interviewed in the orthopedic holding bay this morning just before transport to the laminar-flow suite for a planned left total hip replacement that the attending surgeon anticipates will last about two and a half hours under general anesthesia with cemented fixation and postoperative weight-bearing as tolerated. Three weeks ago she was in a different operating room for an open abdominal myomectomy that required a midline infra-umbilical incision and an overnight stay; convalescence from that procedure went smoothly, and she resumed her usual eight-block dog-walks within ten days, climbing the two flights to her apartment without pauses, so baseline ambulation has returned to normal and she arrives today on her own two feet carrying a small canvas tote. Her medical history is notable for a nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed five years ago after a viral syndrome; resting echocardiography last month showed an ejection fraction of 38 %, and nine days ago dietary indiscretion led to five pounds of fluid weight with nocturnal orthopnea that prompted an emergency-department visit where intravenous furosemide and a single dose of intravenous nitroglycerin were administered with rapid symptom relief; she has had no breathlessness or lower-extremity edema since and takes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg, and a morning dose of torsemide 20 mg. Ten years earlier, following a transatlantic flight, she developed aching behind the right knee and duplex ultrasonography revealed an occlusive thrombus in the popliteal vein; she completed six months of warfarin and has remained clot-free since, although chronic serpiginous superficial veins are visible along both medial calves, more pronounced after prolonged standing but never treated with ablation or stockings. She denies prior pulmonary embolism, stroke-like episodes, spinal cord injury, recent fractures, casts, splints, or high-energy trauma. No relative has been told of an inherited clotting disorder, and she herself has never tested positive for lupus anticoagulant, prothrombin mutation, or similar. She has never carried diagnoses of chronic lung disease, inflammatory bowel pathology, active or historical cancer, or systemic infection requiring intensive care; her last chest radiograph six months ago for routine surveillance was clear. She has not had any respiratory infections—including pneumonia—nor any systemic infectious episodes suggestive of sepsis within the past month. Medications stopped five days ago per protocol include her daily 81 mg aspirin; she has never taken hormone replacement therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, glucocorticoids, or selective estrogen-receptor modulators. She quit smoking two decades ago after a 15-pack-year history, drinks a glass of wine on holidays, and her body mass index this morning is 26 kg m⁻². On inspection she appears comfortable, answers questions in full sentences, and is oriented; Mallampati class II airway with intact dentition and full cervical extension is noted. Vital signs recorded ten minutes ago show temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, respirations 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, carotid pulses are brisk, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs, and lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen bears a well-healing 12-cm midline scar with intact staples and no tenderness. Examination of the lower limbs reveals warm skin, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 2+, thin-walled tortuous veins coursing over both calves, calf circumferences symmetric at 34 cm, and no pitting or brawny edema; the left hip demonstrates painful restriction of internal rotation consistent with end-stage osteoarthritis, while motor strength in all other muscle groups is 5/5. Neurologic screen shows intact sensation and reflexes. Only a single 18-gauge peripheral IV in the right forearm is running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; there are no ports, tunneled catheters, or peripherally inserted central lines. Morning laboratory studies reveal hemoglobin 12.8 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 236 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.4 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 137 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.88 mg dL⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 18 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.2 s with international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats min⁻¹, QRS duration 92 ms, and no acute ST-T changes compared with the tracing from her heart-failure follow-up. Posterior–anterior chest radiography obtained on arrival depicts clear lung fields and a stable cardiomediastinal silhouette without vascular congestion. Sequential calf compression sleeves are already wrapped but remain uninflated pending induction, and no pharmacologic antithrombotic has yet been given while the anesthesia team completes sign-in and formulates an intra-operative hemodynamic plan. She has been nil per os since midnight, removed jewelry and contact lenses, last voided an hour ago, and articulates understanding of the operative steps, potential need for transfusion, and the importance of early postoperative mobilization.

Patient note:
A 41-year-old previously healthy female was admitted to the Department of Neurology, Taizhou People’s Hospital in March 2012, for two transitory episodes of syncope during a 5-h period. The patient had an unhealthy lifestyle of physical inactivity. No urinary and fecal incontinence, general fatigue, chest pain, breathing difficulty, hemoptysis or fever were observed during the course of disease. Following admission, physical examinations revealed a body weight of 75 kg, body height of 159 cm, body temperature of 36.0°C, pulse of 80 bpm, respiratory rate of 23 bpm and blood pressure of 120/60 mmHg. The patient had a slightly haggard expression, no cyanosis of the lips and no jugular vein distention. Bilateral respiratory movements were identical and vocal fremitus was equal. Dullness was heard in the right lower lung on percussion. Breath sounds were diminished and no moist rales were heard. The patient’s heart rhythm was regular, P2>A2 (pulmonary second sound was higher than aortic second heart sound) and there was no edema in the lower extremities.
A complete blood test revealed a white cell count of 11.21×109 cells/l and the percentage of large white blood cells was 57.2%. Biochemical tests revealed 1.4 mmol/l triglycerides, 0.75 mmol/l high-density lipoprotein and 3.61 mmol/l low-density lipoprotein. Blood gas analysis revealed a pH of 7.471, 61.1 mmHg PaO2, 23.5 mmHg PaCO2 and 18.2 mmol/l HCO3− (under the condition of a low flow rate of oxygen inhalation). Chest radiographs revealed pulmonary hilar enlargement and a broadened shadow on the right superior pulmonary artery. An electrocardiogram revealed a flat V1–V3 T wave and magnetic resonance angiography of the head revealed ∼60% luminal stenoses of the right posterior cerebral artery and the left external carotid artery.
After admission, ‘reflex syncope’ was suspected and the patient was administered oral calcium antagonists (Nimotop 30 mg qd) and intravenous Alprostadil for injection (Alprostadil 10 μg qd) to boost the cerebral circulation, without effect. A further episode of syncope occurred during the 18 h after admission and the patient was transferred to the Department of Respiratory Medicine for a D-dimer assay, which indicated a value of 1,200 μg/l. An enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed filling defects in the right main pulmonary and left inferior pulmonary arteries, as well as bilateral pleural effusion (). Color ultrasonography of the heart revealed a dilated right ventricle and right heart overload, severe tricuspid regurgitation and severe pulmonary hypertension and the systolic pulmonary arterial pressure was 130 mmHg (). The patient was finally diagnosed with MPE.
Following confirmation, the patient underwent interventional mechanical thrombectomy combined with local and systematic thrombolytic therapy with low-dose urokinase.
Following the above therapies, digital subtraction angiography (DSA) of the deep veins of the lower limbs and the inferior vena cava demonstrated unobstructed blood flow, with no apparent thrombosis. A 4–5F double J tube was inserted through the right femoral vein to the main pulmonary artery for DSA of the pulmonary artery, to confirm the filling defect in the right main pulmonary artery (). An exchange guide wire was then inserted to coordinate with the tube for twists and drags to disintegrate the embolus. Following disintegration of the embolus, 500,000 units urokinase were injected into the tube for thrombolysis over 30 min. Subsequent DSA of the pulmonary artery indicated an improvement in the filling defect compared with before treatment (). The patient’s condition was significantly alleviated and the anoxia was reduced. A blood gas assay performed 2 h after surgery indicated a pH of 7.51, 72 mmHg PaO2, 29 mmHg PaCO2 and 23.1 mmol/l HCO3− (under the condition of a low flow rate of oxygen inhalation).
A postoperative intravenous drip of low-dose urokinase (200,000 units) was initiated and the patient was also treated with 5,000 units low-molecular-weight heparin, administered subcutaneously once every 12 h for three consecutive days. Warfarin (2.5 mg) was administered orally once every 12 h on a daily basis. The prothrombin time (PT) and international normalized ratio (INR) were monitored; when the PT and INR were twice and 2.5 times their respective normal levels, warfarin therapy was administered singly, plus anti-infective, supportive and oxygen therapies.
Three days after surgery, the patient demonstrated a distinctly improved mental condition with no further syncopal attacks. An enhanced chest CT scan 10 days after surgery revealed evident improvement of the thrombosis in the right main pulmonary artery and left inferior pulmonary artery branch, as well as disappearance of the pleural effusion, compared with the previous chest CT scan (). Color ultrasonography revealed a significant decrease of pulmonary artery pressure and right heart load; the systolic pulmonary arterial pressure was 71 mmHg. The patient was discharged from hospital 26 days after admission, with continued daily administration of 2.5 mg warfarin. Based on the monitoring of PT and INR, the doctor suggested discontinuation of warfarin 3 months after hospital discharge. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Taizhou People’s Hospital, Jiangsu, China and according to the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient.

Patient note:
A 46-year-old woman with a background of cholelithiasis awaiting elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, poorly controlled dyslipidemia, and episodic alcohol use was discovered by a co-worker at 05:30 lying on the locker-room floor clutching her upper abdomen beside a bucket half-filled with bilious vomitus; the colleague reported the patient had left work early the previous evening because of “knife-like” epigastric pain but declined urgent care, instead driving home to drink ginger tea and take two over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg tablets. When emergency medical services arrived ten minutes later, they found her diaphoretic, retching, and obtunded, responding only to loud verbal stimulus with incomprehensible sounds; the gag reflex was markedly diminished and she was repeatedly aspirating small amounts of dark green fluid. Given the combination of altered mentation and ongoing emesis, the field crew performed rapid-sequence intubation with etomidate and succinylcholine, advancing a 7.0-mm cuffed endotracheal tube on the first pass and securing it at 22 cm at the incisors. She was placed on a transport ventilator in volume-assist control delivering a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, a positive end-expiratory pressure of 5 cm H₂O, and an inspired oxygen fraction of 0.53; no non-invasive interface had been tried prior to tube placement, and no intravenous fluids, vasopressors, antibiotics, proton-pump inhibitors, or analgesics were administered during the 14-minute transfer. Upon arrival in the resuscitation bay—still on the same ventilator settings and without having received any hospital therapy—initial vital signs showed a cuff pressure of 106/68 mm Hg confirmed by automated oscillometry, heart rate 132 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, respiratory rate synchronous with the ventilator, temperature 37.4 °C tympanic, and pulse oximetry fluctuating between 89 % and 91 % on the recorded 0.53 inspired oxygen. Capillary refill was two seconds, skin was warm without mottling, neck veins were flat at 30°, and distal pulses were bounding. A right radial arterial catheter inserted three minutes after stretcher transfer yielded a blood gas revealing pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 39 mm Hg, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, and a PaO₂ of 69 mm Hg while ventilator parameters remained unchanged. During a brief interruption of sedation to assess neurologic function, she opened her eyes to pain, made incomprehensible vocalizations around the cuff, and flexed purposively to trapezius squeeze in all four extremities, totaling a Glasgow Coma Score of 9; pupils measured 3 mm bilaterally and were sluggishly reactive, corneal reflexes were intact, and there were no focal asymmetries. Lung examination through the ventilator circuit demonstrated equal air entry with scattered coarse crackles at both bases, peak inspiratory pressure was 24 cm H₂O, and plateau pressure 18 cm H₂O. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs or gallops. The abdomen was distended and exquisitely tender in the epigastrium with minimal palpation, guarding but no rebound, absent tympany, and hypoactive bowel sounds; Grey Turner and Cullen signs were absent. A 16-French Foley catheter placed immediately drained 40 mL of concentrated amber urine, and collateral history obtained from the patient’s spouse, who monitors fluid intake because of prior nephrolithiasis, indicated a cumulative urine output of approximately 780 mL during the preceding twenty-four hours, far lower than her usual baseline of nearly two liters. Simultaneous laboratory studies drawn from the arterial line, all resulted before any crystalloid, opioid, antibiotic, anticoagulant, or vasopressor was delivered, showed sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, glucose 168 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 46 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 2.05 mg/dL compared with a clinic baseline of 0.9 mg/dL three weeks earlier. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 18.8 × 10³/µL with 12 % band forms, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, and a platelet concentration of 102 000 /µL indicating moderate thrombocytopenia without prior record of such. Serum lipase returned markedly elevated at 3 780 U/L, amylase 1 240 U/L; hepatic profile demonstrated aspartate aminotransferase 88 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 71 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 178 U/L, and a total bilirubin of 2.65 mg/dL with predominantly direct fraction. International normalized ratio measured 1.3, fibrinogen 320 mg/dL, triglycerides 238 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 205 mg/L. A portable supine abdominal radiograph obtained before any morphine or antiemetic showed a sentinel loop in the left upper quadrant without free air, and a quick focused bedside ultrasound revealed an edematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid, gallstones within a thin-walled gallbladder, and a common bile duct measuring 9 mm; the inferior vena cava collapsed more than 50 % with inspiration, arguing against hypervolemia. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound demonstrated a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle without pericardial effusion. Twelve-lead ECG displayed sinus tachycardia at 128 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T changes but no acute ischemia. Chest radiograph performed while she remained intubated on the original settings confirmed appropriate endotracheal-tube position 4 cm above the carina, bibasilar patchy opacities consistent with aspiration, no pleural effusion, and a normal cardiac silhouette. At this point—prior to any fluid bolus, analgesia, anti-secretory therapy, broad-spectrum antibiotics, calcium gluconate, insulin drip, or renal replacement strategy—the patient remained invasively ventilated on 53 % inspired oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 69 mm Hg, maintained a spontaneous systolic pressure of 106 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, displayed evolving acute kidney injury with oliguria, moderate hyperbilirubinemia, and consumptive thrombocytopenia in the setting of severe gallstone-associated necrotizing pancreatitis complicated by aspiration and systemic inflammatory response.

Patient note:
A 64-year-old man, a 30-year-long cigarette smoker (30 pieces per day), was admitted with syncope twice on one day to our hospital emergency department in Oct 17, 2013. The patient has two years of high blood pressure history while without any medicine treatment. He had no diabetes mellitus history. In the past two months, he felt chest discomfort sometimes. In the morning of Oct 14, 2013, he suddenly lost consciousness with incontinence while walking in the park. He felt pericardium discomfort before losing consciousness. After regaining consciousness several minutes later, he felt dyspnoeic and sweaty. In the afternoon, syncope occurred again while he was watching TV. His electrocardiogram showed a slight sinus bradycardia of 47 bpm. 24-hour Holter indicated the average heart rate was 66 bpm, the slowest heart rate 47 bpm, the fastest heart rate 129 bpm, and the longest R-R interval 1.6 second. Cranial CT produced no unusual findings (). Moderate ST-segment depression was determined in lead II and aVF on treadmill exercise ECG. Ultrasound cardiography (UCG) indicated normal function with the left ventricular ejection fraction 69.4%. No unusual finding was found in chest X-ray. Blood myocardial enzyme, renal function, electrolytes, and D-dimer values were all within normal ranges.
Five days later, the patient had coronary angiography examination. Coronary angiography revealed 80% stenosis of proximal segment and 85% stenosis of distal segment in left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery, 90% stenosis of middle and distal segment in left circumflex (LCX) coronary artery, 50% stenosis of proximal segment, and 80% stenosis of middle segment in right coronary artery (RCA). The patient refused to have coronary artery bypass grafting surgery. So we decided to perform percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). After balloon predilatation, 3.0 × 24 mm EXCEL rapamycin-eluting stent (Jiwei, Shandong, China) was implanted in RCA. A 2.5 × 14 mm EXCEL rapamycin-eluting stent and a 3.0 × 21 mm Partner sirolimus-eluting stent (Raisedragon, Peking, China) were implanted in distal and proximal segment of LAD, respectively. The further PCI was scheduled one week later for LCX. Unexpectedly, syncope occurred again. On the afternoon while sitting 2 days later, symptoms of dyspnea and palpation accompanied with hypotension occurred. Electrocardiogram monitor indicated that the heart rate was serious sinus bradycardia of nearly 30 bmp. Blood pressure was below 80/40 mmHg. The symptom disappeared after atropine and dopamine were infused. Consider the patient is a 64-year-old person with 30-year-long cigarettes intake history. We put a serum marker screen. Unexpectedly serum tumor marker results indicated that carbohydrate antigen 19-9, carbohydrate antigen 72-4, and alpha fetoprotein are all within normal ranges whereas cytokeratin-19-fragment (CYFRA21-1) and neuron-specific enolase (NSE) values elevated slightly (CYFRA21-1 3.75 ng/mL, normal <3.3 ng/mL; NSE 16.62 ng/mL, normal <16.3 ng/mL).
Examination of enhanced chest CT led to suspicion of central lung cancer (). PET-CT confirmed the leaf of central type lung cancer (4.2 × 3.7 × 2.6 cm) of left lung with multiple lymph node metastasis and the tumor infiltration of adjacent thoracic aorta and left pulmonary artery and vein. No brain metastasis or heart metastasis was found on PET-CT examination. Immunohistochemical examination of the specimens collected with bronchoscopy revealed the following: CKpan(+), CKL(+), Syn(+), CgA(+), CD50(+), CD30(−), CK20(−), CK7(−), CK5/6(−), P63(−), and Ki-67(+).
The diagnosis of small cell bronchogenic carcinoma was made; this tumor was clinically staged at T4N2M0 IIIB. Chemotherapy was promptly initiated with use of combination of carboplatin and topotecan. Shortly after the first chemotherapeutic infusion, the patient reported feeling much better. At follow-up a year later, enhanced CT scan showed that the tumour volume decreased and the patient did not experience syncope anymore.

Patient note:
A 40-year-old man with no known chronic cardiopulmonary, renal, hepatic, or hematologic illness was transported to the hospital’s medical intensive care admission bay after developing sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back while finishing a late shift at a printing warehouse, followed by several bouts of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis and a single episode of near-syncope in the break room. Coworkers reported that he had been complaining of vague upper-abdominal discomfort for two days and had taken only over-the-counter ibuprofen for what he thought was heartburn; he otherwise takes no prescription drugs, smokes fewer than three cigarettes a week, drinks beer socially on weekends, and denies illicit substances. He has never required hospitalization, systemic steroids, chemotherapy, biologic agents, or dialysis and his last employment physical twelve months earlier documented entirely normal bloodwork. Emergency medical technicians located him seated forward on a chair, clutching his mid-abdomen, diaphoretic but responsive, with portable pulse oximetry reading 88 % on ambient air; they applied a Venturi mask that the respiratory therapist later verified was delivering 40 % inspired oxygen, established a single 20-gauge peripheral line but infused no crystalloid, analgesic, antiemetic, antibiotic, or vasoactive medication during the nine-minute transport. On rolling into the resuscitation alcove—and prior to any hospital-initiated therapy—the admitting nurse obtained a first full set of vital signs: oral temperature 100.1 °F, non-invasive blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg corroborated manually, radial pulse 97 beats per minute in regular sinus rhythm, and a spontaneous respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute without accessory-muscle use. The patient was sitting upright, conversing in complete sentences, oriented to person, place, time, and circumstance, able to recall three objects after five minutes, and obeying complex commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 with no sedatives, ethanol, or recreational drugs on board. His skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic; capillary refill was brisk, and there was no cyanosis or mottling. Sclerae were anicteric, mucous membranes moist, and jugular venous pulsations were not elevated at 30 degrees. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and single physiologic S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Lungs were clear to percussion; breath sounds were mildly diminished at both bases but free of crackles, wheezes, or rubs. Abdominal examination disclosed a soft yet exquisitely tender epigastrium with voluntary guarding and hypoactive bowel sounds but no rebound, distension, or organomegaly. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness. Extremities were warm and without edema; neurologic screening showed intact strength, sensation, and reflexes throughout. Importantly, during the approximately thirty-five minutes between ambulance arrival and handoff to the ICU team he received no intravenous fluids, antibiotics, opioids, sedatives, proton-pump inhibitors, steroids, or vasopressors; therefore the physiologic and laboratory values—temperature 100.1 °F, systolic pressure 122 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 78 mm Hg, heart rate 97 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, arterial pH 7.34, serum sodium 142 mmol/L, serum potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, hematocrit 43 %, white blood cell count 11 000 / mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 40 %, and arterial oxygen tension 66 mm Hg—represent his untreated presentation at the moment of intensive care admission for presumed acute gallstone pancreatitis complicated by early hypoxemic respiratory compromise.

Patient note:
A 40-year-old gentleman presented to the emergency with chief complaints of SOB, cough, and fever for about a week. He did not have any other any other known comorbidities. He had a history of dyspnea in the past also. On examination, his heart rate was 120 b.p.m., respiratory rate was 30–35 b.p.m., oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 90% on room air, and he was febrile with temperature of 100.2° F. There were decreased breath sounds on the right side and crepitations on the left side of the chest. He was administered noninvasive ventilation (NIV), and his SpO2 improved to 99%. Chest X-ray images showed extensive left-sided infiltrates, right-sided mediastinal shift, and loss of lung volume on the right side []. Subsequently, he was shifted to Intensive Care Unit, and as his chest X-ray images worsened despite NIV and broad-spectrum antibiotics, he was intubated and ventilated. His white blood cell count was 18,700 per uL and procalcitonin was 36.5 ng/mL. Arterial blood gas showed poor oxygenation and respiratory acidosis, eventually falling into category to ARDS, according to ratio of partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood and fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2-FiO2). Echocardiography revealed pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and no other significant findings. Endotracheal tube aspirate showed Klebsiella pneumoniae, and he was administered the sensitive antibiotics. Ventilatory management of ARDS was done using 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight, keeping the plateau pressure goal of <30 cm H2O with applicable positive end-expiratory pressure. Due to nonresolution of the pulmonary infiltrates and PaO2-FiO2 despite lung protective ventilation, prone ventilation was done with adequate precautions. Prone position ventilation was administered for 16 h a day. Eventually, his oxygenation and CXR worsened. Due to this deterioration in spite of all possible lung protective ventilator measures and treatment, computerized tomography (CT) of the thorax and pulmonary angiography were done. It showed agenesis of the right pulmonary artery and hypoplasia of the right lung with hyperplastic left lung having nonhomogeneous infiltrates [Figures and ]. Three-dimensional thoracic angiogram also showed right pulmonary artery agenesis [Figures and ]. He was referred to a higher center for requirement of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for the nonresolving ARDS, but due to financial restraints, the family was unable to take him to an ECMO center. He succumbed to his condition and expired despite multimodal treatment and management.

His past medical history is notable for long-standing moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease related to a 40-pack-year smoking habit that he abandoned two decades ago; he uses inhaled tiotropium and as-needed albuterol, and his last exacerbation was over a year ago. He also describes rope-like, tortuous superficial veins coursing along both calves that first appeared in his fifties and occasionally ache after prolonged standing, though he has never sought sclerotherapy or surgical stripping. Otherwise, he remains quite active for his age, walking his dog around the neighborhood every morning without limitation and climbing the single flight of stairs to his bedroom several times daily; he does not rely on a wheelchair, and has not been confined to bed or required assistance in ambulation. He specifically reports that during the past four weeks he has not undergone any operative intervention, endured any hospital admission for heart failure, sepsis, or respiratory infection, nor received antibiotics for pneumonia. His cardiovascular history is free of myocardial infarction, and apart from mild hypertension controlled with amlodipine, he carries no diagnosis of coronary disease. He denies any prior episode of calf swelling, tenderness, or skin discoloration suggestive of deep venous clot, has never been treated for a pulmonary embolus, and recalls no family member developing an unexplained thrombosis at a young age. There is no personal or family history of inflammatory bowel conditions or malignant disease. Because the anesthesiology service plans for major arterial exposure and large-bore fluid resuscitation, a right internal jugular triple-lumen catheter was inserted under ultrasound guidance yesterday afternoon; the site is clean, dry, and secured with Bio-patch and occlusive dressing. Patient note:
A 94-year-old widower arrived at the university anticoagulation clinic for his scheduled semi-annual review of oral warfarin therapy that had been instituted two years ago after a 48-hour Holter study documented persistent, non-valvular atrial fibrillation discovered during evaluation of palpitations while raking leaves. He lives alone in a one-story cottage, ambulates without assistive devices, prepares his own meals, and keeps meticulous handwritten logs of medication intake, finger-stick international normalized ratio (INR) readings, weight, and fluid balance. The notebook shows twelve INR measurements over the past seven months ranging from 2.2 to 2.8; the anticoagulation nurse calculated a time-in-therapeutic-range of 82 %, and the most recent value obtained this morning was 2.4 prior to his usual afternoon dose of 4 mg. He reports no missed doses, no temporary holds, no rescue vitamin K, no emergency department visits for out-of-range results, and an absence of bruising larger than a coin. He has never coughed up blood, passed black or maroon stools, vomited coffee-ground material, noticed tea-colored urine, or required transfusion or endoscopic hemostasis. The past medical record is devoid of transient ischemic attack, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, intracranial bleed, peripheral embolism, myocardial infarction, or venous thromboembolism. What concerns him today is whether advancing age, long-standing kidney impairment, the assortment of tablets he swallows each morning, and the considerable quantity of liquor he still enjoys might, in combination, foreshadow a catastrophic hemorrhage. Eleven years ago he was informed by nephrology that his estimated glomerular filtration rate had fallen below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² because of presumed ischemic nephropathy in the setting of a single functioning kidney removed for renal-cell carcinoma decades earlier; recent laboratory results drawn one week ago reveal creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 52 mg/dL, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, platelet count 198 × 10⁹/L, and an intact parathyroid hormone level twice the upper limit of normal, yet he remains pre-dialysis on a low-salt, low-phosphate diet. Liver enzymes, bilirubin, and albumin have remained within reference limits throughout serial monitoring, and abdominal ultrasonography last year showed a smooth hepatic contour without steatosis or portal features. His medication list—confirmed through pharmacy reconciliation—includes warfarin as noted, enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg daily left in place by his cardiologist after a drug-eluting coronary stent was implanted five years ago, naproxen 220 mg as needed up to three times weekly for lumbar spondylosis, and sertraline 25 mg nightly prescribed by his primary physician for situational low mood after his spouse’s death. He avoids ginkgo, glucocorticoids, fish-oil supplements, and herbal preparations. Vital signs obtained after five minutes of seated rest show blood pressure 118/66 mm Hg, irregularly irregular pulse 72 beats/min, respirations 14 per min, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air. Body mass index is 24 kg/m²; he appears well nourished and animated. Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa moist with no petechiae, jugular venous pressure is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the precordial examination demonstrates the expected variable first heart sound of atrial fibrillation in the absence of murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lung fields are clear to percussion and auscultation. The abdomen is soft, nondistended, nontender, with a right-sided nephrectomy scar well healed and no hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or abdominal wall varices. Extremities are warm with 2+ distal pulses, no edema, and only a few faint yellow-green ecchymoses over the shins from recent yard work. Neurologic screening confirms full orientation, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetrical 5/5 strength, normal sensation, coordination, and a steady gait. A 12-lead electrocardiogram printed during the encounter shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response of 70 beats/min, normal axis, QRS 92 ms, and no acute ST-T changes. Social history is striking for sustained high-level ethanol intake despite repeated counseling attempts; he describes a “regimented” pattern of two 12-ounce bottles of strong ale with a late breakfast, three 5-ounce glasses of red wine alongside an afternoon crossword, and three 2-ounce pours of bourbon while listening to classical music in the evening, a schedule followed every day of the week without exception. By standard drink conversion, this totals approximately 63 alcoholic beverages each week. He denies morning shakes, visual hallucinations, seizures, pancreatitis, or prior detoxification, but he recalls two minor household falls over the past year after rising quickly from a recliner. He smoked cigarettes in early adulthood, accumulating a 15-pack-year burden before quitting at age 50, and he has never tried illicit substances. Review of systems is negative for chest pain, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, claudication, visual disturbance, aphasia, focal weakness, abdominal discomfort, pruritus, jaundice, gum bleeding, or epistaxis lasting more than a few minutes. He seeks an updated appraisal of whether his chronic kidney dysfunction, concomitant use of low-dose aspirin, intermittent non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and a weekly consumption of 63 drinks, all superimposed on advanced age, materially heighten the probability of a serious hemorrhage while he remains on a seemingly well-controlled warfarin regimen for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, and he wishes to discuss practical strategies to mitigate modifiable hazards without sacrificing cardioembolic protection.

Patient note:
A 76-year-old man with a remote cadaveric renal transplant maintained on low-dose prednisone and tacrolimus, along with well-documented lymphopenia from recent rituximab infusions for antibody-mediated rejection, was rushed from the emergency department to the surgical intensive care unit after an emergent subtotal colectomy performed overnight for a free perforation of the sigmoid colon with feculent peritonitis discovered on CT. Baseline physiology was captured in the resuscitation bay immediately after arrival to the unit, before any vasopressor agents, antibiotics, antipyretics, or additional ventilator adjustments could be started. He remained endotracheally intubated on assist-control ventilation delivering 80 % inspired oxygen because attempts to reduce the fraction in the operating room resulted in precipitous desaturation. An arterial blood gas drawn within the first five minutes of ICU handoff revealed a pH of 7.21, severe metabolic and respiratory acidemia, PaCO₂ of 52 mm Hg, PaO₂ of 70 mm Hg, and an alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient calculated at 517 mm Hg, underscoring profound impairment of gas exchange likely from a combination of systemic inflammatory response, early acute lung injury, and abdominal compartment effects after closure. Core temperature measured via a bladder probe was 35.9 °C, consistent with perioperative hypothermia despite active warming blankets, and might have contributed to slowed mentation—he opened his eyes only to spoken name, uttered incomprehensible phonations around the endotracheal tube, and withdrew purposefully to nail-bed pressure, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 10 without sedative medications running. Hemodynamics were marginal: the first arterial line tracing showed a systolic pressure of 88 mm Hg and diastolic of 48 mm Hg with a tachycardic pulse of 130 beats per minute; point-of-care ultrasound confirmed a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle and a collapsible inferior vena cava, suggesting preload dependency rather than cardiogenic failure. Respiratory rate set on the ventilator was 34 breaths per minute to clear accumulating carbon dioxide, yet end-tidal values lagged, mirroring the laboratory acidemia. Initial chemistry panel demonstrated serum sodium of 145 mmol/L and potassium 5.4 mmol/L; the latter prompted readiness with calcium gluconate and insulin-dextrose, though treatment had not yet begun. Serum creatinine was 1.7 mg/dL, only slightly higher than his outpatient baseline of 1.5 mg/dL recorded two weeks earlier and thus not representing new renal failure in the transplant graft. Hematologic indices painted a picture of active inflammation and blood loss: hematocrit had fallen to 28 %, and the white blood cell count was markedly elevated at 25 000 cells/mm³ with band forms seen on peripheral smear. Platelets were 180 000 / mm³, prothrombin time mildly prolonged at 16 seconds, and serum lactate returned at 4.1 mmol/L, all values sampled prior to any crystalloid bolus or broad-spectrum antimicrobial administration. Physical examination complemented these numbers: cool mottling of distal extremities, diminished peripheral pulses, an abdominal dressing saturated with thin serosanguinous fluid but no active hemorrhage, and diffuse coarse crackles over both lung bases without wheezes or rhonchi. The colostomy formed intra-operatively was viable, and there was no evidence of fascial dehiscence on gentle palpation. Neurologically he localized but did not follow commands, pupils were equal and reactive, and no focal deficits were elicited. Urine output collected in the operating room totaled 0.8 mL/kg/hr, and the Foley catheter now drained scant concentrated urine. He had received only 1 L of balanced crystalloid intra-operatively, no blood products, and no vasopressors. Past medical history besides the kidney transplant included coronary artery disease with prior percutaneous stent, chronic atrial fibrillation on home apixaban held for surgery, and stage 1 diastolic heart failure; he lived independently, abstained from tobacco for three decades, and consumed minimal alcohol. Medications on file comprised tacrolimus 1 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, amlodipine, low-dose aspirin, and apixaban, the latter withheld since presentation. Family at bedside confirmed that he was cognitively intact the morning prior, ambulated without assistance, and had no recent infectious symptoms. Cultures of peritoneal fluid, blood, urine, and sputum were obtained but not yet resulted. In summary, before any active postoperative resuscitation commenced, the patient presented with mild hypothermia, profound acidemia (pH 7.21), severe tachycardia (130 bpm), tachypnea (34 breaths/min), arterial hypotension (88/48 mm Hg), elevated serum sodium (145 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (5.4 mmol/L), borderline elevated creatinine (1.7 mg/dL), low hematocrit (28 %), marked leukocytosis (25 000 /mm³), depressed consciousness (GCS 10), and striking hypoxemia requiring 80 % FiO₂ with an A-a gradient of 517 mm Hg—findings consistent with septic shock and early organ dysfunction in an immunosuppressed postoperative host following emergency abdominal surgery.

Patient note:
A 52-year-old woman was seen this morning in the comprehensive pre-operative assessment unit at the request of the hepatobiliary surgery service seven days before a planned open right hepatectomy for a 4.5-cm segment VI colorectal metastasis identified on surveillance MRI; operative duration is anticipated to approach four hours with full abdominal exposure, low central venous pressure anesthesia, and postoperative admission to the surgical ICU for close fluid and hemodynamic monitoring. She walked from the visitor garage, climbed two flights to clinic without pausing, and reports that she completes a 45-minute brisk walk with her dog every evening, performs yoga twice weekly, and carries grocery bags up her kitchen stairs without shortness of breath, pressure across the chest, or leg swelling. She has never experienced exertional tightness, rest pain, radiating arm discomfort, unexplained diaphoresis, or undergone stress testing, cardiac catheterization, or coronary intervention. Past medical history includes stage 1 hypertension diagnosed in her late forties for which she takes amlodipine 5 mg nightly, and type 2 diabetes discovered three years ago during an occupational health fair; the diabetes has been managed solely with metformin extended-release 1000 mg with breakfast, and her most recent endocrinology visit four weeks ago documented a glycated hemoglobin of 6.8 %. She denies ever using injectable glucose-lowering agents and performs home capillary checks twice weekly with readings generally between 110 and 150 mg/dL. She has no personal record of stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid intervention, peripheral arterial disease, valve surgery, cardiomyopathy, chronic lung disease, or chronic kidney disease. Surgical history is limited to a laparoscopic sigmoid resection for the primary colorectal cancer two years ago and an uncomplicated cesarean section in her thirties. She quit cigarette smoking 18 years ago after a 12-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of red wine on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Several first-degree relatives carry a diagnosis of essential hypertension, but there is no early coronary or cerebrovascular disease in the family. Current medications include the amlodipine and metformin already noted, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and a daily vitamin D supplement; she reports a mild rash to sulfa antibiotics and no other drug allergies. Review of systems is negative for palpitations, syncope, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, claudication, fevers, chills, night sweats, unintended weight loss, abdominal pain beyond mild intermittent right upper-quadrant discomfort, or change in bowel habits. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs record blood pressure 118/68 mm Hg in the right arm, regular pulse 64 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99 % on ambient air, oral temperature 36.5 °C, and body mass index 26 kg/m². She appears comfortable and euvolemic. Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, the point of maximal impulse is localized in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line, and auscultation reveals crisp S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. The abdomen is soft with a well-healed left lower-quadrant laparoscopic scar, moderate tenderness to deep palpation over the right subcostal region without guarding, hepatomegaly, masses, or ascites; no palpable hernias are present. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric, with no edema or discoloration. Neurologic screening shows full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation, and steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratories drawn one hour before the visit reveal hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 198 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 6.8 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 0.88 mg/dL corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting plasma glucose obtained concurrently is 117 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase is 38 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 42 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 128 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram recorded in clinic demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute, normal intervals, axis within 25 °, and no Q waves, ST-segment deviations, or T-wave inversions; comparison with a tracing two years earlier shows no interval change. Upright posterior-anterior chest radiograph reveals clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Airway assessment by anesthesia documents a Mallampati class II oropharynx, inter-incisor distance 4.5 cm, thyromental distance 6.5 cm, and full cervical extension. The anesthesiology plan includes continuation of the calcium-channel blocker and statin through the morning of surgery, withholding metformin the evening before to reduce lactic acidosis risk, placement of a radial arterial line for beat-to-beat pressure monitoring, permissive low central venous pressure during parenchymal transection, and goal-directed crystalloid guided by stroke volume variation. The surgical team reviewed potential bile leak, hemorrhage, need for Pringle maneuver, and peri-operative cardiopulmonary complications; the patient demonstrated understanding, voiced commitment to incentive spirometry and early ambulation, and expressed readiness to proceed with definitive liver surgery.

Patient note:
A 50-year-old man with no significant past medical history beyond well-controlled seasonal allergies and a remote tonsillectomy was brought to the critical care triage bay by emergency medical services after twelve hours of rapidly worsening dyspnea, rigors, and pleuritic chest discomfort that began after two weeks of untreated “flu-like” symptoms at home. In the ambulance he was noted to be febrile, diaphoretic, and breathing through pursed lips; pulse oximetry on ambient air read in the low 70s, prompting application of a tight-fitting face mask delivering 70 % inspired oxygen. On arrival—prior to any antipyretics, antibiotics, intravenous fluids, or vasoactive agents—he sat upright on the stretcher, tachypneic at 30 breaths per minute with intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, and audible expiratory grunting. Core temperature obtained rectally registered 39.2 degrees Celsius. Cardiovascular examination revealed a bounding carotid upstroke with a regular tachycardic rhythm; manual blood pressure was 105 / 58 mm Hg, and heart rate measured simultaneously was 115 beats per minute. Capillary refill was two seconds, skin was warm without mottling, and jugular venous pressure was not elevated. He answered questions but was intermittently disoriented to the exact calendar date, opened his eyes to voice, and moved all four extremities purposefully when asked to squeeze, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13. Lung auscultation disclosed diffuse coarse crackles over the right middle and lower fields with diminished breath sounds at the right base; percussion suggested a small parapneumonic effusion. Cardiovascular auscultation was otherwise unremarkable, the abdomen was soft and nontender, bowel sounds were active, and there was no lower-extremity edema or calf tenderness. A stat arterial blood gas drawn on the current oxygen flow showed a pH of 7.28 with a moderate respiratory alkalosis partially offsetting metabolic acidosis, and the calculated alveolar-arterial gradient was 156 mm Hg, confirming significant impairment of oxygen transfer despite the elevated FiO₂. Simultaneous laboratory studies demonstrated a serum sodium of 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, glucose 136 mg/dL, and a creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL—substantially above his last outpatient value of 0.9 mg/dL from six months prior—raising concern for acute kidney injury likely related to evolving sepsis and relative hypovolemia; urine output in the emergency department holding bay had been less than 0.3 mL/kg/hr over the preceding two hours. Complete blood count revealed a white blood cell count of 21 000 /mm³ with 86 % segmented neutrophils and 10 % bands and a hematocrit of 33 %, consistent with hemodilution rather than frank blood loss. Platelets were 180 000 /mm³ and international normalized ratio was 1.1. High-sensitivity troponin was within normal limits, and serum lactate returned at 3.4 mmol/L. Chest radiography performed moments after arrival showed patchy consolidation occupying the right middle lobe with air bronchograms and blurring of the right hemidiaphragm, while point-of-care cardiac ultrasound revealed preserved left ventricular systolic function and a small, collapsible inferior vena cava. The patient denied prior organ transplantation, malignancy, chronic pulmonary disease, renal disease, or use of corticosteroids, cytotoxic agents, or biologic immunomodulators, and his vaccination history was up to date except for having skipped the most recent seasonal influenza shot. Social history was negative for tobacco or illicit drug use, and he consumed alcohol only on weekends. Family noted that he had been drinking inadequate fluids for several days and had taken over-the-counter ibuprofen for fever, with no other medications or herbal supplements. Blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and a nasopharyngeal viral panel were obtained immediately but no antimicrobial therapy had been started at the moment the above values were documented. Given the high fever, tachycardia, profound leukocytosis, elevated serum creatinine in a previously healthy individual, modest hypotension, hypoxemia requiring more than two-thirds inspired oxygen, widened A-a gradient, and moderate acidemia on admission blood gas, the decision was made to move him to the medical intensive care unit for aggressive resuscitation, hourly neurologic checks, close monitoring of renal function with consideration of early nephrology input, and rapid initiation of pathogen-directed treatment once cultures were drawn.

Patient note:
A 72-year-old Caucasian woman presented with squeezing chest pain. The pain had started 30 minutes previously and was associated with nausea, vertigo, shortness of breath and weakness. Her history was significant for hypertension and coronary artery disease. Two years before admission, she had undergone coronary angiography because of angina, which revealed three-vessel coronary disease. The examination was followed by repeated angioplasty with stent implantation. A drug-eluting stent had also been applied. The first intervention had been complicated by a haematoma at the femoral puncture site.
On physical examination, the patient had a blood pressure of 130/60 mmHg and a heart rate of 65 beats per minute. The lung and heart sounds were clear on auscultation. Her weight was 60 kg, her height was 156 cm and her body mass index was 24.65 kg/m2. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without signs of myocardial ischaemia. Laboratory testing was significant for haemoglobin at 11.4 g/dL, blood urea nitrogen at 10.45 mmol/L and creatinin at 131 μmol/L. The creatinin clearance calculated with the Cockroft-Gault equation was 26.47 mL per minute. There was no elevation of cardiac troponin-I and creatine phosphokinase-MB isoenzyme levels.
After admission, her symptoms soon subsided. Repeated electrocardiography did not show signs of ischaemia, and the troponin-I value remained in the normal range. A diagnosis of unstable angina was established. The patient received early conservative treatment with the following pharmacotherapy: 2 × 60 mg enoxaparin subcutaneously, 75 mg clopidogrel, 100 mg aspirin, 50 mg metoprolol, 20 mg atorvastatin, 0.2 mg per hour transdermal nitroglycerin, 80 mg valsartan and 12.5 mg hydrochlorothiazide.
On the fifth day of her hospital stay, an exercise stress test was performed on a bicycle ergometer where she reached 3.9 metabolic equivalent and no ischaemic response occurred. A few hours later, she experienced pain in the left side of her abdomen. On examination, a palpable, growing tender mass was detected in the lower left quadrant. An abdominal ultrasound scan demonstrated a rectus sheath haematoma with a depth of 20 mm and a width of 40 mm. The upper margin of the haematoma was at the umbilicus, the lower reached the pubic bone. As continued haemorrhage was suspected, the patient underwent surgical exploration with haematoma evacuation, and received a blood transfusion. She remained on a reduced dose of enoxaparin (1 × 60 mg). Since she was febrile and showed a decreasing haemoglobin level, on the 9th postoperative day a computed tomography (CT) scan was performed. This showed a recurrence of the rectus sheath haematoma (Figure ) and its extension in the abdominal wall. A second haematoma evacuation was performed. Subsequently, no recurrence of bleeding was observed, but the patient developed an ascending superficial thrombophlebitis on the left lower limb, which was treated with ligature. She was finally discharged in good health.

Patient note:
Our patient was a 60-year-old Caucasian male who presented in September 2019 with syncope associated with hypotension.
The patient had no previous symptoms and syncope was indeed the first clinical manifestation.
The patient had no history of previous disease and he was not taking any medications.
The only red flags were the known congenital bicuspid aortic valve and family history of congestive heart failure (sister).
When he came to the emergency department, he presented hypotensive, with tachyarrhythmic peripheral pulse. A paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) episode was diagnosed, which regressed after a few hours.
Routine laboratory tests (complete blood count, kidney function, electrolytes, liver and heart enzymes) were all in the normal ranges.
Transthoracic echocardiography showed no pathological findings.
The 24-h electrocardiogram Holter monitoring recorded frequent episodes of high-grade atrioventricular block with no further AF episodes. Upon suspicion of an ischemic aetiology, he was admitted to the cardiology unit and underwent coronarography, which indicated intermediate stenosis (50%) in the left anterior descending artery. This stenosis was not considered hemodynamically significant. Thus, the decision was to implant a dual chamber anti-bradycardia pacemaker. Given the single and short AF episode and the CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0, no anticoagulation treatment was initiated. In December 2019, he underwent a scintigraphy stress–rest test, during which he presented loss of consciousness due to the onset of sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) (Figure ), which was successfully treated with cardiopulmonary resuscitation manoeuvres and lidocaine infusion. The arrhythmia was considered to be of ischaemic origin. Therefore, the patient underwent percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty with drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation at the known coronary stenosis. During and after hospitalization, numerous non-sustained VTs were recorded, for which he was given amiodarone, with clinical benefit. After a few weeks, a treadmill stress test was also performed under antiarrhythmic therapy, which was negative for both myocardial ischemia and VTs. During the follow-up examinations, considering the patient’s clinical picture, encompassing VT, atrioventricular block, family history, and echocardiographic findings showing accentuated right ventricular apex trabeculation, the treating cardiologist decided to reassess the clinical case. He recommended that the patient undergo cardiac magnetic resonance and molecular analysis performed with a panel of 128 genes known to be associated with cardiomyopathies and channelopathies. Both tests were performed in February 2020 (6 wk after DES implantation, as indicated in the manufacturer’s data sheet). The former showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 50% without any areas of late enhancement or myocardial fibrosis (Figure ).
The results of the genetic testing took 3 mo to be validated, during which outpatient appointments with patients were suddenly stopped due to the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2-related pandemic. Considering the need to supervise the patient during this time for the possible onset of life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmia (LTVT) and AF, without the possibility of a periodic in person interrogation of the PM arrhythmias registry, as was usually done, it was decided to give the patient a remote monitoring device (Medtronic Carelink Network®). The device was configurated to transmit the data it recorded, automatically every week. At the same time, both LTVT and AF were set up as “care alerts”, which meant that an automatic alert would have been sent immediately after identification, , as long as the potential LTVT or AF onset would have required a prompt and potentially lifesaving intervention, either the upgrading the PM to an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) or the initiation of a life-long anticoagulant therapy, respectively. Fortunately, no arrhythmias were detected during that time.

A 75-year-old man with sudden melena was referred to our hospital. He had a history of cardiac infarction, atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, and Parkinson's disease. The patient always took Bayaspirin (100 mg/day) and Xarelto (15 mg/day). The patient's systolic blood pressure was 84 mmHg, and heart rate was elevated at 105 beats/min. Physical examination showed eyelid anemia, and digital rectal examination revealed attachment of bloody stool. A blood test revealed anemia with a hemoglobin level of 10.7 g/dL. In coagulation tests, prolonged coagulation time was noted, with a prothrombin time percentage (PT%) of 68%, activated partial thromboplastin time of 42.4 s, fibrin degradation product level of 6.7 μg/mL, and D-dimer level of 4.7 μg/mL. Helical computed tomographic angiography (CTA) revealed an abnormal vessel in the wall of the sigmoid colon, which was visualized as a high-density area, and a hematoma in the sigmoid colon, which was visualized as a low-density area (). Colonoscopy revealed a huge hematoma with active bleeding in the submucosal area of the sigmoid colon (). Endoscopic hemostasis procedures, such as clipping and coagulation, could not be performed, because a huge hematoma obscured the bleed point. As blood pressure did not respond to fluid administration, an emergency sigmoidectomy was performed. During the procedure, a huge submucosal hematoma was seen through the wall of the sigmoid colon. The resected specimen showed a huge submucosal hematoma, which was 180 × 70 mm in size (). Histopathological examination showed a submucosal extended vessel without elastic fibers in the hematoma (Figures and ). Therefore, he was diagnosed with colonic AD. On postoperative day 7, Hartmann's operation was performed owing to an anastomotic leak. He was discharged on postoperative day 70.
