Patient note:
A 68-year-old female non-smoker was referred to our emergency department due to progressive dyspnea. On physical examination, she exhibited tachypnea (20 breaths per minute) and her oxygen saturation was 85%, her pulse was regular at 91 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 116/70 mmHg. Chest CT revealed a 36-mm mass with a cavity in the right S9 (Fig. ), and a 10-mm nodule in the right S6. CT also revealed right middle lobe atelectasis due to bulky hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes (Fig. ). Concomitantly, a bilateral pulmonary thromboembolism was identified. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal a left ventricular function; the right ventricle was dilated with moderate tricuspid regurgitation and her systolic pulmonary artery pressure was elevated (estimated pressure: 55 mmHg); these findings were considered to have been caused by bilateral pulmonary thromboembolism. Ulthrasonography of the lower extremity veins revealed right fibular vein thrombus. Her serum D-dimer, BNP and CEA levels were elevated to 8.0 μg/mL (normal range: <1.0), 332.5 pg/mL (normal range: <18.4) and 14.6 ng/mL (normal range: <5.0), respectively.
Enhanced CT performed 1 week after the administration of intravenous heparin and oral edoxaban tosilate hydrate, which were administered immediately after the detection of the bilateral pulmonary and right fibular vein embolisms, revealed that the pulmonary artery and right fibular venin thrombus had disappeared. Subsequently, the pathological analysis of a bronchoscopy specimen led to a diagnosis of adenocarcinoma harboring an EGFR exon 19 deletion. Based on these results, she was clinically diagnosed with T3N2M0, stage IIIA adenocarcinoma. As lung cancer associated with pulmonary thromboembolism was taken into consideration, EGFR-TKI treatment was proposed as the first-line systemic therapy and afatinib (40 mg/day) was prescribed after receiving her informed consent. In spite of requiring a dose reduction to 30 mg due to grade 3 diarrhea, she became asymptomatic at 2 months after the initiation of treatment. Chest CT revealed the marked response of both tumors and lymph node metastases with the disappearance of the middle lobe atelectasis (Fig. ). Her serum CEA level decreased to within the normal range (1.4 ng/mL).
We planned surgery to remove the residual lesions. Three days after the discontinuation of afatinib and after receiving her informed consent, we performed right middle and lower lobectomy with systemic mediastinal lymph node dissection. Her postoperative course was uneventful. Complete resection was achieved, with a negative bronchial margin. A histological examination showed the prominent proliferation of fibroblasts accompanied by lymphocytes and histiocytes (Fig. ). However, residual viable tumor cells were found in a small area of the primary lesion (Ef.2a, Fig. ) because an immunohistochemical examination revealed a few small clusters of atypical cells that were positive anti-pancytokeratin (AE1/3) and thyroid transcription factor 1. There were no malignant cells in the dissected lymph nodes. Down-staging from clinical stage IIIA to pathological stage IA was established. We did not identify an exon 20 point mutation (T790 M) in any of these specimens.
Although afatinib therapy was continued after the operation, she developed spinal cord compression due to 5th cervical vertebral cortical bone metastasis with the onset of neck pain at 8 months after the operation. Direct surgical decompression with tumor debulking and spinal stabilization was performed, followed by radiotherapy. An exon 20 point mutation (T790 M) was found in the resected specimens. Thus, osimertinib is now being prescribed. She is currently alive at 15 months after surgery (18 months after the initial diagnosis).

Patient note:
A 57-year-old woman, previously active and employed as an elementary-school librarian, was brought to the emergency department by family after two days of progressive shortness of breath that acutely worsened the morning of admission when she became forgetful about the date and repeatedly paused midsentence to catch her breath. Her background includes well-controlled essential hypertension and diet-managed type 2 diabetes but no chronic pulmonary disease, renal insufficiency, cirrhosis, malignancy, or use of glucocorticoids or other immunosuppressive agents; she has never required home oxygen, dialysis, or transplantation and takes only amlodipine and metformin. She quit cigarette smoking fifteen years earlier after a total exposure of eight pack-years and drinks wine socially; there is no illicit substance use. She had visited an urgent-care clinic the prior evening, where no medications were given, and returned home with a plan for outpatient chest radiography the next day. Overnight she remained afebrile but coughed intermittently, describing scant rust-colored sputum at dawn, then became more tachypneic while walking to the bathroom, prompting relatives to call emergency medical services. Paramedics found her seated upright on the couch, speaking in short phrases with perioral cyanosis; the prehospital monitor recorded an oxygen saturation of 81 % on room air, so a venturi mask delivering 45 % inspired oxygen was applied during transport. No bronchodilators, antibiotics, fluids, or analgesics were administered en route. On arrival to the resuscitation bay, before any hospital treatment could begin, she was alert but required several seconds to state the correct month, obeyed commands briskly, and localised to pain appropriately, amounting to a Glasgow Coma Score of 14. Vital signs at that moment were temperature 37.4 °C measured tympanically, heart rate 100 beats per minute in a regular rhythm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute with shallow excursions and visible use of sternocleidomastoid muscles, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg confirmed manually, and pulse oximetry 88 % on the same 45 % oxygen delivery. She was of normal habitus, diaphoretic but without peripheral edema or jugular venous distention. Lung examination revealed diffuse coarse crackles over the right middle and lower zones with diminished breath sounds posteriorly; percussion of the right base was dull, and whispered pectoriloquy was accentuated, while the left lung fields were aerated. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; capillary refill was less than three seconds, and extremity pulses were equal bilaterally. The abdomen was soft and nontender, bowel sounds were present, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. A stat radial arterial blood gas drawn within five minutes of bed placement, still on 45 % FiO₂, showed pH 7.36, PaO₂ 55 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, reflecting moderate hypoxemia with near-normal acid–base balance. Simultaneous chemistry panel demonstrated serum sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (matching the blood gas), blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, identical to values from a primary-care visit six months earlier and therefore not suggestive of either acute or chronic renal failure. Point-of-care glucose measured 158 mg/dL without ketones, and venous lactate was 2.0 mmol/L. Complete blood count returned a white cell count of 12 500 cells/mm³ with 82 % neutrophils and a hematocrit of 40 %; platelets were 245 000/µL. Coagulation profile was normal, and high-sensitivity troponin was below the laboratory threshold of detection. Portable chest radiograph obtained before any antibiotics or diuretics demonstrated a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and mild blunting of the right costophrenic angle, without cardiomegaly or interstitial edema. Focused cardiac ultrasound revealed preserved left-ventricular systolic function and a collapsible inferior vena cava, arguing against volume overload or cardiogenic pulmonary edema, while lung ultrasound confirmed subpleural consolidations and right-sided B-lines. Family history was notable only for maternal myocardial infarction at age 70 and paternal type 2 diabetes; there were no hereditary lung disorders. Because she remained hypoxemic on moderate supplemental oxygen and exhibited radiographic and examination findings consistent with community-acquired pneumonia complicated by early respiratory compromise, the decision was made to transfer her directly to the medical intensive care unit for close monitoring of gas exchange, repeat arterial blood gases, and prompt initiation of empiric antimicrobial therapy once appropriate cultures were obtained—all pending at the moment the above physiologic measurements and laboratory results were documented, with no treatments other than supplemental oxygen and catheter placement having been started.

Patient note:
An almost asymptomatic 41-year-old woman suffering from mild dyspnoea on exertion consulted her physician for the yearly checkup. The physical examination was completely unremarkable, all laboratory testings were within normal limits, and the ECG showed sinus rhythm; only the chest X-ray revealed an enlargement of the cardiac silhouette ().
Following echocardiographic examination and contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax revealed a lipomatous mass, measuring 16 × 14 × 12 cm, located on the left side of the heart with blood supply from the left coronary artery, highly suspective of a lipoma (). Within this mass, a dense calcification (3.5 × 1.5 cm in diameter) in the cranioventral part of the tumour was seen. This large mass caused a marked shift in the midline structures, displacing the heart to the right hemithorax.
In October 2010, the patient underwent open heart surgery via median sternotomy without cardiopulmonary support. The pericardium was opened on the left side and revealed the left atrium and ventricle pushed to the right side by a lipomatous tumor. The lipoma had a stalk measuring about 5 cm in diameter connected to the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle, but it did not adhere to the pericardium. The tumour mass was completely removed, hemostasis was achieved, and the chest was closed after placing one chest tube in the pericardium. The postoperative course was uneventful and the patient was discharged from hospital on the 6th postoperative day. The patient is currently asymptomatic and has not presented with evidence of recurrence at the 6-month followup.
Gross examination revealed a homogenous yellowish vascularized tumour mass with a smooth lobulated surface limited by a fibrous capsule (). Histologically, the excised specimen showed a fatty structure of mature benign fat with some areas of increased vascularity ().

Patient note:
A 21-year-old Japanese woman who had no specific medical history consulted a primary care clinic. Although she had been aware of the edema of her lower extremities for 2 weeks, her chief complaints were palpitations and chest pain, which had started the day before. An electrocardiogram (ECG) and chest radiograph did not reveal any specific abnormality. The next day she consulted another physician but her etiology was still not clear. She was referred to the emergency division in a municipal hospital 2 days later. Arterial blood gas analysis did not reveal hypoxemia. However, computed tomography (CT) revealed thrombi in her bilateral pulmonary arteries and left iliac vein, and a laboratory examination revealed NS. She was admitted and anticoagulant therapy was initiated immediately. The next day she was referred to a nephrologist at our university hospital.
She had no family history of thromboembolism; she is a nonsmoker and not obese. She has never taken a contraceptive pill. On admission, her physical characteristics were: weight 53kg; height 166cm; body mass index 19.2kg/m2; blood pressure 110/62mmHg; pulse rate 120 beats/minute; respiratory rate 20 breaths/minute and saturation of peripheral oxygen (pulse oximetry) 97% (room air). Her physical examination was normal except for the edema of the lower extremities. The laboratory investigation data were as follows: leukocyte 9660 cells/μL; hemoglobin 14.8g/dL; platelets 329,000/μL; hematocrit 42.2%; blood urea nitrogen 19mg/dL; serum creatinine 1.26mg/dL; serum albumin 1.7g/dL; total protein 4.3g/dL; total cholesterol 497mg/dL; triglyceride 187mg/dL; the levels of serum complement C3 were 116mg/dL and C4 34mg/dL. Serum antinuclear antibody was negative. The coagulation profile revealed the following: prothrombin time 15.2 seconds; activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 84.5 seconds; D-dimer 6.9μg/mL (normal: 0 to 0.4μg/mL); fibrinogen 832mg/mL (normal: 150 to 410mg/mL); fibrin-fibrinogen degradation product 10.5μg/dL (normal: 0 to 5μg/dL); antithrombin III 70% (normal: 80% to 120%); protein C 29% (normal: 70% to 140%); and protein S 66% (normal: 65% to 135%). Urinary protein excretion was 14g/g creatinine, and microhematuria was absent. In addition, arterial blood gas analysis revealed the following: pH 7.46, carbon dioxide 35.5mmHg, partial pressure of oxygen 88.6mmHg, and bicarbonate 26.0mEq/L (room air). Her chest radiograph and ECG were normal. A CT angiogram revealed thrombi of her bilateral pulmonary arteries and left common iliac vein (Figure ). Presumably, the pulmonary thrombosis originated from the thrombi of the left iliac vein.
Treatment of thrombosis was initiated with intravenous administration of heparin and urokinase. First, 18IU/kg of heparin per hour was initiated while adjusting the dose to maintain APTT between 60 and 85 seconds, thereafter, urokinase was infused at 10,000U/hour for 24 hours. Oral warfarin administration was also started, aiming at a prothrombin time-international normalized ratio of between 1.5 and 2.5, and heparin infusion was gradually decreased. An inferior vena cava (IVC) filter was placed percutaneously to avoid further development of pulmonary thrombosis by the left common iliac vein thrombi. Furthermore, corticosteroid therapy was initiated with prednisolone at a dose of 0.8mg/kg per day. Contrast-enhanced CT performed on day 14 revealed a reduction of the pulmonary thrombi and capture of the thrombi in the inferior vena cava (IVC) filter (Figure ). The patient’s proteinuria resolved after 3 weeks of treatment. The prompt and complete response to the corticosteroid therapy suggested that minimal change disease was the etiology of NS and pulmonary artery thrombosis.

Patient note:
A 22-year-old woman with no past medical history, no chronic medication use, and up-to-date routine vaccinations was transported to the critical care receiving area twenty minutes after being pulled from a freshwater quarry where she had been swimming with classmates during a midsummer outing; witnesses reported that she inhaled water during a brief struggle to stay afloat and was unconscious for “less than a minute” before lifeguards extricated her. Paramedics arrived eight minutes after the call and documented that on ambient air her pulse oximetry registered in the low seventies, prompting placement of a tightly-fitting Venturi mask delivering 50 % inspired oxygen; during the ten-minute ride she received no intravenous fluids, no bronchodilators, no antimicrobials, no vasopressors, and no opioids, and her airway remained patent without adjuncts or positive-pressure support. Upon stretcher entry to the resuscitation bay—and before any hospital-initiated therapy—vital signs were captured: tympanic temperature 38.2 °C, regular but rapid pulse 118 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry, observed respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute with moderate accessory muscle recruitment, and a non-invasive blood pressure that cycled consistently at 122⁄70 mm Hg on both arms. She opened her eyes to spoken name, answered most orientation questions but was unsure of the exact date, and followed two-step commands, establishing a Glasgow Coma Score of 14 without sedatives, ethanol, or head trauma. Skin examination revealed flushed cheeks, warm extremities, brisk capillary refill, and no peripheral cyanosis or edema. Jugular venous pulsations were not distended at 30 degrees, carotid upstrokes were sharp, and distal pulses were bounding. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a loud S1, physiologic split S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Breath sounds were coarse bilaterally with diffuse crackles more pronounced over the mid-zones, and percussion was mildly dull at the bases, consistent with fluid-laden alveoli rather than pleural effusion. The abdomen was flat, nondistended, and nontender with active bowel sounds; no hepatosplenomegaly was appreciated. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness. Extremities displayed full range of motion without crepitus or deformity, and neurologic screen showed equal pupils, symmetric facial movement, and 5⁄5 strength in all limbs. Seven minutes after arrival, while she remained on the unchanged 50 % oxygen source, a right radial arterial sample produced a pH of 7.43, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, and an analyzer-calculated alveolar-to-arterial oxygen gradient of 480 mm Hg, indicative of severe impairment of oxygen transfer despite near-normal ventilation. Capnography showed an end-tidal CO₂ of 36 mm Hg, correlating with the arterial value. Simultaneous point-of-care basic metabolic panel revealed sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 102 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL—values matching those from a collegiate sports physical filed six months earlier, suggesting intact renal function without acute injury. A rapid complete blood count returned a white-cell count of 17 050 cells/mm³ with neutrophil predominance, hematocrit 42 %, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelets 244 000/µL. Venous lactate measured 2.4 mmol/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiography obtained before any diuretics, antibiotics, or positive-pressure ventilation demonstrated bilateral patchy infiltrates with ill-defined air bronchograms, no pleural fluid, and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Point-of-care lung ultrasound corroborated diffuse B-lines throughout both fields without discrete consolidation or pneumothorax. Focused transthoracic echocardiography revealed a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle with an estimated ejection fraction over 65 % and an inferior vena cava measuring 1.4 cm that collapsed completely with inspiration, findings consonant with euvolemia rather than fluid overload. Twelve-lead electrocardiography printed during the arterial draw showed sinus tachycardia at 116 beats per minute, PR interval 150 ms, QRS duration 88 ms, QTc 420 ms, and no acute ischemic changes. Patient note:
A 65-year-old male presented with an abrupt onset of sharp, burning, constant right lower abdominal pain after previously been feeling well. There was no history of trauma, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, chest pain, shortness of breath, syncope, dysuria, hematuria or melena. His past medical history included hypertension, atrial flutter and cardiomyopathy, and he had an implantable cardioverter/defibrillator (ICD). There was no prior history of abdominal aortic aneurysm in the patient or in his family. His past surgical history included an inguinal hernia repair. His medications included aspirin, valsartan, metoprolol and atorvastatin. He did not smoke, use alcohol or illicit drugs.
Physical exam showed vitals signs as follows: body temperature of 36.3°C, blood pressure of 140/82 mmHg, heart rate of 52 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute and pulsoximetry of 98% on room air. He was alert, but appeared in mild distress due to pain. His abdominal exam revealed tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant, with no rebound, guarding, distention or organomegaly. The remainder of the exam was normal.
The initial emergency department evaluation included an electrocardiogram that showed atrial flutter with a 4:1 block. Laboratory assessment revealed trace hematuria, no leukocytosis, creatinine of 1.3 mg/dL (normal range, 0.7–1.4 mg/dL), mildly elevated lipase to 85 U/L (normal range, 12–70 U/L), mild hyperglycemia and mildly elevated aspartate aminotransferase to 46 U/L (normal range, 7–40 U/L). The lactate and coagulation profiles were within normal limits. Lactate dehydrogenase was not ordered at presentation, but obtained 2 days after admission, and was elevated at 1,479 U/L (normal range, 100–220 U/L). Lactate dehydrogenase is present in the renal tissue and elevates in serum after kidney insult, and it is unknown whether this level correlates to the severity of the infarct.
Given the nature of the pain and the hematuria seen on urinalysis and the history of cardiomyopathy with atrial flutter, both nephrolithiasis and mesenteric ischemia were strongly considered as causes for this acute pain. Therefore, both non-contrast- and contrast-enhanced helical computed tomography (CT) images [Figures and ] were obtained, which showed extensive infarction involving the upper pole of the right kidney with multiple patchy infarcts into the lower pole, a patent right renal artery, but no visualization of the interparenchymal arterial branches within the mid and upper poles of the right kidney, suggesting arterial thromboembolic disease. There was poor opacification of the right renal vein, and, therefore, renal vein thrombus could not be ruled out. A 2-mm left renal calculus was also identified.
The urology and vascular surgery services were consulted, and both recommended conservative treatment with anticoagulation. In addition to normal saline and dilaudid for pain control, a heparin bolus of 80 mg/kg was given and an infusion at 18 mg/kg/h was initiated, with the patient being admitted to the general medicine service.
It was concluded his renal artery thrombosis was most likely embolic and a 2-D echocardiogram was ordered, which showed no intramural thrombus. He was discharged 5 days later, on coumadin. His creatinine, which was 1.3 mg/dL on admission, rose to 1.8 mg/dL and fell to 1.7 mg/dL by discharge. One month later, the creatinine levels had declined to 1.6 mg/dL.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old man with diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), and atrial fibrillation (AF) presented to the emergency room with sudden onset of left leg pain due to superficial femoral artery (SFA) thrombosis. Soon after arrival, he was scheduled to undergo emergency thrombectomy. He had been receiving metformin (850 mg/day) for DM, olmesartan (40 mg/day) for HTN, and warfarin (3 mg/day) and digoxin (0.25 mg/day) for AF. In the preoperative evaluation, chest radiography showed cardiomegaly, while electrocardiogram showed the presence of atrial fibrillation. Laboratory investigations showed no remarkable findings. Prothrombin time (PT) and international normalized ratio (INR) were within the normal range (PT, 10.5 sec; INR, 0.92), even though the patient was on warfarin therapy. A central venous catheter (CVC, 7-Fr double lumen catheter) was inserted via the left subclavian vein using the landmark technique under general anesthesia. In the first attempt, the needle was passaged twice without aspiration of blood. In the second attempt, after positioning the needle tip, blood was successfully aspirated through the needle in the third passage to confirm its location, followed by successful insertion of the CVC.
Subsequently, 5,000 U of heparin was administered 5 minutes before incision of the femoral artery for thrombectomy. The thrombectomy was performed uneventfully with an operative time of 90 minutes. The arterial blood gas analysis (ABGA) during surgery showed the following: pH, 7.337; PaCO2, 43.4 mmHg; PaO2, 112 mmHg; and oxygen saturation, 98%. Additionally, the hemoglobin (Hb) level was 15.6 g/dl. The estimated blood loss and urine output were approximately 100 ml and 300 ml, respectively. A total of 1,250 ml of Hartmann's solution was administered during surgery.
The patient was then transferred to intensive care unit (ICU) for close monitoring. Postoperatively, continuous infusion of heparin (1,000 U/hr) via CVC was maintained. The infusion rate was adjusted under the activated partial thromboplastin time of 80-120 sec. A portable chest radiograph showed proper position of the CVC in the superior vena cava and no interval changes (). At 6 hr postoperation, a small swelling and oozing were observed at the insertion site of the CVC. Consequently, CVC was removed and compressed for 30 minutes. At 15 hr postoperation, when the patient's hemodynamic values were stable and the dorsalis pedis artery was palpable, he was transferred to the general ward. On the first postoperative day (POD), the patient was started on warfarin (4 mg/day). A chest radiograph at this point showed no remarkable findings except a slightly increased opacity in the left anterior chest wall (). In addition, there were no remarkable findings from the laboratory examinations. However, 10 mg of furosemide was administered when the urine output decreased, even though the fluid intake was adequate.
On POD 2, the patient experienced syncope on his way to bathroom, possibly due to orthostatic hypotension. His vital signs were as follows: blood pressure (BP), 80/50 mmHg; heart rate (HR), 142 bpm; and SpO2, 85%. Subsequently, the patient was transferred to the ICU and a diagnostic workup was performed. The ABGA revealed severe metabolic acidosis (pH, 6.93; PaCO2, 28 mmHg; PaO2, 164 mmHg; HCO3, 5.9 mM; oxygen saturation, 98%), and the patient received 15 L/min oxygen via a reservoir mask. His Hb level decreased from 14.3 g/dl to 9.6 g/dl. After transferring him to the ICU, his BP was 61/44 mmHg. Volume resuscitation was initiated with normal saline and packed red blood cells (RBCs). However, inotropes were not administered to the patient, because his BP increased to 90/50 mmHg after volume resuscitation. His hemodynamic values returned to normal with fluid therapy (4,300 ml of normal saline) and transfusion (3 units of packed RBC). In addition, sodium bicarbonate was administered to cure the severe acidosis. A computed tomography (CT) revealed a huge hematoma between the pectoralis major and minor muscles on the left chest wall (). However, an angiogram showed no detectable extravasations from the branches of the left subclavian artery. Laboratory tests revealed multiple organ dysfunction syndrome including respiratory failure, ischemic hepatitis, and acute kidney injury due to hemorrhagic shock. The levels of serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and creatinine (Cr) were remarkably elevated: AST, 2,800 IU/L; ALT, 2,100 IU/L; LDH, 6,000 IU/L; Cr, 3.40 mg/dl. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) was started on POD 2, and tracheal intubation was performed on POD 3 when an ineffective breathing pattern was observed and the SpO2 decreased to 90%. Mechanical ventilation was applied without any intervention to the hematoma, such as insertion of the wound, use of a suction tube, or surgical removal. The patient was extubated on POD 12, and CRRT was stopped on POD 13. The patient was transferred to the general ward on POD 20, and the hospital course was uneventful thereafter.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old male with no prior medical problems, who was leading an active lifestyle, presented to our emergency department with progressively worsening shortness of breath and abdominal distension for one month. His breathlessness had gradually worsened to the point where he felt winded even upon getting out of bed. He also reported intermittent abdominal discomfort associated with a decrease in appetite for a similar duration. Initially, the patient sought medical attention from his primary care physician and was started on treatment for community-acquired pneumonia without any significant improvement. He denied any fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss. Review of systems was unremarkable including bowel habits, which were regular.
The patient had been a nonsmoker his entire life but had secondhand exposure to smoking from his wife. His alcohol consumption was limited only to social occasions and he denied any illicit drug use. He had no known allergies, nor did he take any daily medications. Family history was not significant for any malignancies. No recent travel was reported and by occupation, he was a tailor.
On examination, the patient was found lying comfortably in bed. Vital signs were significant for a pulse rate of 106 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 17 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% on 2 liters of oxygen via nasal cannula. He was normotensive and afebrile. No cyanosis, clubbing, rash, or lymphadenopathy was noted. Respiratory examination revealed decreased air entry and dullness on percussion on the right side of the chest. His abdomen was distended, non-tender with a palpable liver and spleen, and he was noted to have shifting dullness. The rest of the examination was within normal limits. Laboratory data are summarized in Table .
Upon admission, a chest x-ray showed a near-complete opacity of the right hemithorax secondary to a large pleural effusion (Figure ). A bedside thoracocentesis was performed and 600 milliliters of whitish milky pleural fluid was drained (Table ). The pleural fluid analysis was consistent with chylothorax. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast revealed a large soft tissue mass in the region of the pancreatic head with extensive diffuse lymphadenopathy and minimal perihepatic ascites (Figure ). Further review of imaging revealed soft tissue deposits in the anterior abdomen and pelvis with peritoneal enhancement concerning for peritoneal carcinomatosis. The initial impression was pancreatic adenocarcinoma with peritoneal seeding. An oncology consultation was requested and a biopsy of the peritoneum was advised due to ease of access. An ultrasound-guided biopsy of the peritoneal lesion with analysis of the peritoneal fluid (Table ) and a CT-guided placement of a right chest pleural drainage catheter was performed by interventional radiology. Analysis of the peritoneal pathology specimen revealed a mature B-cell neoplasm reported as a grade 2 follicular lymphoma (Figure ), and immunophenotype stains revealed CD20+, CD79A+, CD10+, BCL-2+, BCL-6+, CD5-, CYCLIN D1-, CD3-, CD43-, AE1/AE3-. Cytology from the previously obtained pleural fluid also demonstrated lymphomatous infiltration. Due to persistent right pleural effusion, embolization of the thoracic duct was attempted without success. The patient was eventually transferred to a tertiary center under thoracic surgery service for further management of the high output chylothorax. He eventually was enrolled in the lymphoma program of the tertiary care center and started on chemotherapy.

Patient note:
A 72-year-old woman arrived this morning to the multidisciplinary pre-operative clinic at the request of the orthopaedic service ten days before an elective left total knee arthroplasty intended to relieve debilitating tricompartmental osteoarthritis that has limited her to walking half a block with a cane and climbing stairs one step at a time; the surgeon anticipates a 90-minute tourniquet-assisted procedure through a midline parapatellar approach with routine postoperative admission to the joint-replacement unit for physical-therapy-guided mobilization beginning the same afternoon. She ambulated slowly from the valet stand, pausing once in the corridor to catch her breath but declining wheelchair assistance; during the encounter she reported that over the past two years her exercise tolerance has fallen from comfortably tending her backyard vegetable beds for several hours to becoming winded after making a single trip from the living room to the bedroom with a laundry basket. She sleeps with three pillows, awakens twice weekly with a sensation of breathlessness relieved by sitting upright, and notices bilateral ankle swelling each evening that improves by morning after taking torsemide 20 mg at breakfast. Two months ago her cardiologist obtained a transthoracic echocardiogram showing a dilated left ventricle, global hypokinesis, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35 %; right-sided pressures were mildly elevated and there was trace functional mitral regurgitation. She has never experienced chest tightness, arm or jaw discomfort, diaphoresis with exertion, or undergone coronary angiography; a pharmacologic stress SPECT performed last year for dyspnea reached the target heart rate without perfusion defects. Her medication list includes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, torsemide as noted with supplemental potassium, spironolactone 25 mg nightly, and rosuvastatin 20 mg at bedtime; she takes amlodipine 5 mg each morning for long-standing hypertension and continues a daily 81 mg aspirin recommended for primary prevention by her primary physician. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed eight years ago during screening labs and has been treated exclusively with metformin extended-release 1000 mg twice daily; the most recent glycated hemoglobin three weeks ago was 6.7 %, and home glucometer logs reviewed today show fasting values between 110 mg/dL and 145 mg/dL with no symptomatic hypoglycemia. She has stage 3 chronic kidney disease attributed to combined diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy; baseline creatinine has hovered around 1.4 mg/dL for the past year. There is no personal history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid intervention, peripheral arterial disease, chronic lung disease, or prior thromboembolism. Surgical history is limited to a remote appendectomy and uncomplicated right cataract extraction. She quit cigarette smoking 25 years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of wine on holidays only, and denies illicit drug use. Family history reveals a mother who developed heart failure in her late seventies and a brother with insulin-requiring diabetes; no early coronary events are reported. Review of systems today is negative for fever, productive cough, orthostatic dizziness, abdominal pain, claudication, or unintentional weight loss. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs were blood pressure 116/68 mm Hg in the right arm, regular pulse 64 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air, oral temperature 36.8 °C, and body mass index 30 kg/m². She appeared overweight but in no acute distress. Neck examination revealed jugular venous pulsation approximately 5 cm above the sternal angle with the head of the bed at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was palpated in the sixth intercostal space lateral to the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a soft S3 gallop and a grade 1/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex without radiation; no pericardial rub was present. Lungs were clear at the apices with faint late-inspiratory crackles at both bases. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Extremities displayed trace pitting edema to the mid-shin, warm skin, and 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally. Strength testing showed preserved quadriceps contraction but pain-limited range of motion in the left knee; neurologic examination was otherwise intact with full orientation, fluent speech, and steady tandem gait when assisted by a cane. Pre-operative laboratory studies obtained one hour before the visit revealed hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.43 mg/dL, consistent with her recent baseline and corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 48 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting glucose in the same sample measured 118 mg/dL, and aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and international normalized ratio were within reference ranges. A 12-lead electrocardiogram printed in clinic demonstrated sinus rhythm at 62 beats/min, left bundle branch block unchanged from prior tracings, and no dynamic ST-segment changes. Upright posterior-anterior chest radiograph showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette, mild pulmonary vascular congestion, and no focal consolidation or pleural effusion. Airway assessment by anesthesia documented a Mallampati class II oropharynx, inter-incisor distance of 4 cm, and adequate cervical extension. The anesthesia team plans general endotracheal anesthesia with an ultrasound-guided adductor canal block for postoperative analgesia, continuation of beta-blocker and renin–angiotensin–neprilysin inhibitor therapy through the morning of surgery, withholding the loop diuretic on the day of operation to reduce intravascular depletion, and point-of-care glucose checks every two hours with subcutaneous corrective doses of rapid-acting agent only if necessary. The orthopaedic surgeon reviewed risks including infection, stiffness, thromboembolism, and cardiac decompensation; the patient affirmed understanding, verbalized adherence to sodium restriction and daily weight monitoring, and expressed willingness to proceed in hopes of regaining independent ambulation and returning to garden work by summer.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old woman presented to the cardiology transition-of-care clinic this morning after being discharged from an outside hospital three days earlier with instructions to establish follow-up for newly diagnosed systolic pump failure; she wanted a second opinion regarding long-term management and clarification of her other chronic conditions. Six weeks ago she noticed progressive dyspnea while tending to her backyard vegetable garden, an activity she had previously performed without limitation, and this shortness of breath soon culminated in orthopnea that required her to sleep propped on three pillows as well as nocturnal episodes of awakening with a feeling of suffocation relieved by sitting upright. Her ankles began to swell to the level of her mid-calves, and her weight increased by approximately 3 kg over two months despite no change in diet. She denied crushing substernal chest discomfort, radiation to arm or jaw, diaphoresis, or presyncope, and she has never undergone emergent coronary angiography, stent placement, coronary bypass, or thrombolytic therapy. Paramedics transported her to the emergency department five days ago when she developed rapid shallow breathing at rest; a point-of-care ultrasound there reportedly demonstrated a markedly dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis and an estimated ejection fraction of 30 %, moderate biatrial enlargement, and trace mitral regurgitation. She received intravenous diuretic therapy with brisk diuresis of more than 2 L, and intravenous vasodilator infusion for afterload reduction was started briefly before oral agents were substituted at discharge. A brain-type natriuretic peptide level drawn at that admission was 1,540 pg/mL. She was told that coronary computed-tomography angiography did not show flow-limiting lesions, and troponin values remained within normal limits, making an ischemic insult unlikely. Her background illnesses include a twenty-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by symmetric involvement of metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; the disease has been stable on methotrexate 15 mg weekly and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily with infrequent flares requiring short prednisone tapers. She also has type 2 diabetes discovered eleven years ago during routine laboratory screening when fasting plasma glucose was 136 mg/dL; current management consists of metformin 1 g twice daily and dietary carbohydrate restriction, and her last documented hemoglobin A1c, obtained at her primary-care visit four months earlier, was 7.1 % with no history of retinopathy, neuropathic foot ulcers, or microalbuminuria. Two years ago she underwent left-sided lumpectomy and sentinel-node sampling for a 1.6-cm estrogen-receptor–positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma staged pathologically as pT1cN0; postoperative whole-breast radiotherapy was completed, and she has been on oral anastrozole since with surveillance mammography six months ago showing no recurrence or contralateral disease. She has never been told of chronic bronchitis, emphysema, asthma, or the need for inhaled bronchodilators, and she quit smoking cigarettes at age 35 after a 10-pack-year exposure. She consumes a glass of red wine at family gatherings only, denies recreational drug use, and maintains independent living with her spouse. Family history reveals a mother who died at 78 of congestive failure thought to be valvular in origin and a brother with long-standing insulin-dependent diabetes; there is no familial clustering of early myocardial infarction or stroke. Current medications include furosemide 40 mg each morning, lisinopril 10 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine as noted, metformin, anastrozole, low-dose aspirin 81 mg, and calcium-vitamin D supplementation; she is allergic to codeine, which causes nausea. Review of systems today is negative for paroxysmal headaches, visual field deficits, speech disturbance, unilateral weakness, transient vision loss, claudication, abdominal pain, melena, hematemesis, jaundice, pruritus, polyuria, or flank discomfort. On examination she is an elderly woman sitting comfortably, conversant, and oriented. Vital signs: temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 118/64 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 18 per minute, oxygen saturation 96 % on room air, body mass index 27 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation is noted 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, the apical impulse is displaced to the sixth intercostal space anterior axillary line, and an S3 gallop is audible without murmurs or pericardial rub. Bibasilar late-inspiratory crackles are present; no wheezes or prolonged expiratory phase is heard. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, with a liver edge palpated 1 cm below the right costal margin but smooth and non-nodular; no splenomegaly or ascites is evident. There is pitting edema to the mid-shins bilaterally, but pedal pulses are 2 + and symmetric. Hands show mild ulnar deviation and swan-neck deformities compatible with chronic inflammatory arthropathy, yet grip strength remains fair. Neurologic testing reveals intact cranial nerves, normal strength in all major muscle groups, and no pronator drift. Laboratory work drawn on arrival demonstrates sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 72 mL/min/1.73 m²), fasting glucose 128 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white cell count 7.6 × 10⁹/L, platelets 242 × 10⁹/L, AST 28 U/L, ALT 25 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 84 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.0, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein 5 mg/L. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute, QRS voltage consistent with left ventricular enlargement, and diffuse T-wave flattening but no pathologic Q waves or ST-segment elevation or depression. A chest radiograph obtained today depicts cardiomegaly, mild vascular redistribution, and small bilateral pleural effusions. She has been advised to keep a daily weight log, adhere strictly to a 2-g sodium diet, and ensure compliance with disease-modifying antirheumatic therapy to mitigate systemic inflammation that might further compromise myocardial function; additional outpatient echocardiography and discussion of potential device therapy are being arranged.

Patient note:
A 22-year-old unmarried, unemployed male, resident of urban Chandigarh, was admitted in the surgical emergency in mid-December 2019 with complaints of acute onset of chest pain (which worsened during inspiration), breathlessness, and intermittent pain in the right lower abdomen for the last one week and fever for two days. History revealed regular use of heroin for the last five years and use was predominantly via injections for the last two years; if unable to procure heroin, he would chase Smack once or twice a month. He would share injection equipment and use tap water as a re-constituent. The place of injection would largely be empty and dirty parking lots and public toilets. Urine drug screen revealed the presence of morphine and cannabis. Initial assessment revealed a pulse rate of 94/min, blood pressure 120/76 mmHg, and an axillary temperature of 101° F. The chest auscultation was unremarkable. His past medical record revealed hepatitis C seropositivity.
Initial blood investigations revealed the following: hemoglobin 12 g/dl, total leucocyte count 7300/mm3 (differential count: neutrophil 67%, lymphocyte 32%, monocyte 7%, and eosinophil 4%), platelet 2,73,000/mm3, bilirubin (total: 0.7 mg/dl; conjugated: 0.2 mg/dl), and total protein 7.1 gm/dl. He was seronegative for both hepatitis B and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV1&2). Electrocardiogram was unremarkable. A chest radiogram revealed right-sided pleural effusion. Ultrasonogram (USG) whole abdomen, done as a part of acute abdomen work-up on the same day, showed mild splenomegaly, right-sided loculated pleural effusion (2.8 cm wide, with thick septations), and appendicolith.
He was diagnosed with pleural effusion and acute appendicitis. He was treated with empirical antibiotic therapy (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole) and intravenous fluids. After one day, 10 F pigtail catheter was placed in the right pleural space under USG guidance. Pleural fluid investigations revealed the following: sugar 17 mg/dl, protein 5.7 mg/dl, adenosine deaminase 53 IU/L, and cell count 680/cmm (polymorphonuclear cells: 60%, lymphocytes: 40%). The report was indicative of exudative effusion, possibly of infective origin. Real-time polymerase chain reaction for tuberculosis was negative. Culture and sensitivity report of the pleural fluid showed Burkholderia cepacia with intermediate sensitivity to cefoperazone-sulbactam and resistance to ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and meropenem. But the antibiotic regime was not changed as the patient showed clinical improvement.
After five days, the pigtail catheter was removed, and the patient was discharged on ciprofloxacin and metronidazole (to be continued for another five days). There was a temporary resolution of fever and breathlessness. History obtained in the emergency ward revealed past treatment in a private de-addiction service with buprenorphine assisted therapy, to which he was poorly adherent. He was admitted subsequently to the addiction psychiatry ward for buprenorphine reinduction. Then the chest pain reappeared. A chest radiogram was repeated, which revealed minimal right-sided pleural effusion. After consultation with pulmonary medicine, the patient was kept under observations, with a fortnightly repeat of chest radiogram. The pain was controlled by buprenorphine. However, the level of effusion remained unchanged, and an intermittent mild right-sided chest pain, radiating to back, continued. But he did not experience breathlessness or fever. After 25 days, he was discharged on 14 mg buprenorphine and was referred to pulmonary medicine OPD. On serial monitoring with chest radiogram, the effusion gradually reduced and finally resolved in another month.

Patient note:
A 75-year-old man with a 7-year history of epithelioid mesothelioma and a right sided IPC presented to the pleural clinic with a history of 2–3 weeks of a malodourous, purulent fluid drainage via the IPC. The patient was Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0 and was under the ambulatory pleural service but managed his pleural collections independently in the community. The IPC had been inserted 3½ years ago for a right-sided loculated hydropneumothorax that had developed after a radical extended pleurectomy, decortication and diaphragmatic patch surgery for mesothelioma. The rationale for the IPC was recurrent effusions and associated infections requiring repeat chest drains in the area of the postoperative hydropneumothorax.
The patient was asymptomatic and apyrexial. The pleural fluid cultured Klebsiella oxytoca and Enterococcus faecalis. He was treated with the oral fluoroquinolone, ciprofloxacin and given advice and guidance on infection prevention strategies when handling the IPC and pleural drainage apparatus. A couple of weeks later it was decided to replace the IPC as an elective procedure due to the long duration of the IPC, a persistent low-grade purulent discharge, concerns about bacterial colonisation and history of a similar infection episode a year ago.
On the day of the procedure, the patient reported that the IPC had partially migrated out of the pleural cavity and the tunnelled subcutaneous tract due to loss of integrity of the IPC cuff and thus came out easily without any intervention. The IPC tip was sent for culture.
On clinical examination, blood pressure was 133/77 mm Hg, pulse rate was 77 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 18 breaths/min and the body temperature was 36.6°C with oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Lung auscultation revealed inspiratory crackles at the right lower lung zone. The laboratory test revealed white cell count (WCC) count 11.3×109/L, haemoglobin 108 g/L, platelets 430 x10ˆ9/L and C reactive protein 71 mg/L. Bedside thoracic ultrasound scan was consistent with a hydropneumothorax.
The same day the patient underwent an uneventful IPC insertion under local anaesthesia and mild sedation with 1 mg of intravenous midazolam. Satisfactory IPC placement was confirmed on a post procedure chest radiograph ().
One and half hours postprocedure, the patient had a witnessed sudden drop in conscious level with associated seizure like activity. The patient was immediately assessed by the cardiac arrest team where blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturations were maintained within the reference range throughout. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 4 (eyes opening 1, verbal response 1 and motor response 2). General examination did not demonstrate any peripheral stigmata of systemic air embolism and no retinal air bubbles were seen in funduscopic examination. An acute stroke was suspected and an urgent CT head was performed. Repeat blood tests revealed WCC 9.4×109/L, haemoglobin 107 g/L, platelet 408x10ˆ9/L, blood urea 4.0 mmol/L, serum creatinine 73 umol/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate >90, C reactive protein 70 mg/L, alanine transaminase 9 iu/L. ECG was in sinus rhythm and no ischaemic changes were noted. CT head revealed multiple serpiginous pockets of air along the cerebral fissure, with features that were highly suggestive of an embolism and multiple wedge-shaped areas of infarction involving the cerebral hemispheres (). CT chest revealed satisfactory positioning of the IPC with no aetiology for the acute deterioration (). The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for high flow oxygen therapy and head down ventilation.

Patient note:
A 25-year-old man who until this afternoon had been taking part in a regional mountain-bike race with no complaints was brought to the emergency department by rural emergency medical services after collapsing at the finish line with shaking chills, pleuritic right-sided chest discomfort, and a productive cough that had started the night before but had been attributed to dust on the trail. His riding partner reported the patient was previously healthy, had never required prescription medication, denied tobacco or alcohol use, and had no recent travel, steroid exposure, or recurrent illnesses; he completed a routine employment physical four months earlier with entirely normal laboratory results and a resting creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. He also had no history of chronic kidney disease, liver disease, cardiac failure, HIV infection, malignancy, transplant, or other conditions that would impair immune competence, and he was not on any immunosuppressive or nephrotoxic medications. On scene, the paramedics found him sitting forward, flushed, and sweating, answering questions appropriately but short of breath; fingertip oximetry on ambient air showed readings that drifted down into the high 80s, so a clear facemask was applied and adjusted to deliver 35 % inspired oxygen as confirmed by the portable analyzer clipped to the mask port. Transport to the nearest tertiary center took just under ten minutes, during which no intravenous fluids, antimicrobials, antipyretics, bronchodilators, vasopressors, or analgesics were administered, and the only intervention was placement of a single 18-gauge antecubital catheter capped with a heplock. Upon stretcher entry to the resuscitation bay—before any hospital-initiated therapy—the triage nurse simultaneously obtained the first complete set of observations: an oral temperature of 101.4 °F, a regular pulse of 108 beats per minute on three-lead telemetry, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute counted over sixty seconds, and a blood pressure of 123/68 mm Hg confirmed on a second cuff. The patient was awake, maintained eye contact, answered every question correctly, and grasped both examiner’s hands with equal strength, establishing a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 without sedatives, intoxicants, or head trauma. Skin was warm and flushed with a fine dew of perspiration; capillary refill was brisk, and no cyanosis or peripheral edema was present. Jugular venous pulsation remained below the angle of the mandible at 45 °, and carotid upstrokes were sharp. Cardiac auscultation revealed a slightly rapid but regular rhythm with crisp S1 and a physiologic split S2, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Pulmonary examination disclosed diminished breath sounds with crackles and faint egophony over the posterior right lower zone, resonant percussion elsewhere, no wheeze, and no tracheal deviation. The abdomen was flat, moved with respiration, and was nontender; bowel sounds were active, and no organomegaly or flank tenderness was evident. There was full active range of motion of all extremities, no migratory arthritis, no petechiae, and the patient was able to stand briefly before dizziness prompted him to sit again. Eight minutes after arrival, while he remained on the same 35 % facemask and had still received no medications or intravenous fluids, a right radial arterial sample was drawn for blood-gas analysis: pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 73 mm Hg; end-tidal CO₂ recorded concurrently was 37 mm Hg. Simultaneous point-of-care chemistry showed serum sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, matching the baseline noted on his recent physical and suggesting intact renal function. Urine output remained brisk, and the stable creatinine without rising trend indicated no current acute kidney injury. A complete blood count returned a white-cell concentration of 16 000 cells/mm³ with a left shift, hematocrit 42 %, hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, platelets 238 000/µL, and a smear showing largely mature neutrophils without toxic granulation. Venous lactate measured by handheld cartridge was 2.0 mmol/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiography, performed before antibiotics or diuretics, demonstrated a wedge-shaped opacity in the posterior segment of the right lower lobe with no pleural effusion and a normal heart silhouette. Focused cardiac ultrasound done at bedside revealed a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle with an inferior vena cava that collapsed more than 50 % with inspiration, arguing against volume overload. Lower extremity Doppler study was ordered but not yet performed. Electrocardiography printed during the arterial draw showed sinus tachycardia at 110 beats per minute with normal intervals and no ST-segment deviation. A bladder scan estimated 140 mL, and the patient produced a clear, pale yellow urine sample moments later. Up to the point of transfer to the intensive-care unit for closer respiratory monitoring and empiric antimicrobial initiation, he had still not received antipyretics, bronchodilators, IV fluid boluses, vasopressors, or narcotic analgesia, leaving the documented figures—temperature 101.4 °F, systolic pressure 123 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 68 mm Hg, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respirations 22 per minute, arterial pH 7.35, serum sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, hematocrit 42 %, white blood cell count 16 000 /mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 35 %, and arterial oxygen tension 73 mm Hg—as an accurate reflection of his untreated physiologic state during initial presentation for suspected right-lower-lobe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by early sepsis and mild hypoxemic respiratory compromise.

Patient note:
A 60-year-old man was assessed late this morning in the ambulatory anesthesia clinic three days before a planned outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy for a 1.1-cm radiolucent gallstone that has provoked three separate episodes of biliary colic during the past month despite a low-fat diet; the general surgeon anticipates four trocar sites, an operative time of under one hour, minimal blood loss, and discharge home the same evening once oral intake and ambulation are satisfactory. The patient drove himself, parked on the third level of the visitor ramp, and walked unhurriedly through two corridors to reception while conversing comfortably about postoperative activity restrictions. He reports that at home he routinely climbs the 14 steps to his bedroom without interruption, mows his quarter-acre lawn with a self-propelled mower, and carries groceries up one flight, all without chest tightness or undue dyspnea. Ten years ago he awoke with crushing substernal pressure radiating to the left shoulder; paramedics documented inferior ST-segment elevation, and emergent coronary angiography showed an occlusion in the mid-right coronary artery treated with a drug-eluting stent. He completed cardiac rehabilitation, has remained free of anginal symptoms, and follows up with cardiology annually; the most recent treadmill study performed nine months ago reached nine metabolic equivalents and revealed no inducible ischemia. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily, high-intensity atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime, and metoprolol succinate 50 mg each morning; there have been no hospitalizations for chest pain, rhythm disturbance, or fluid overload since the index event. Hypertension was first noted at age 45 and is now controlled with lisinopril 20 mg nightly, office readings averaging 122/70 mm Hg. Fasting lipid panel last month showed LDL 74 mg/dL and triglycerides 110 mg/dL. He denies diabetes, and finger-stick checks performed during his spouse’s gestational diabetes monitoring years ago typically read in the 90s; no glucose-lowering agents, injectable or oral, are prescribed. There is no personal history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid intervention, or heart-failure hospitalization, and he has never been told he has valvular disease or cardiomyopathy. Pulmonary history is limited to seasonal allergic rhinitis without wheeze or cough. Prior operations include a left inguinal hernia repair at age 30 under general anesthesia without complications. He quit smoking 18 years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks one glass of bourbon on Saturday nights, and denies recreational drug use. Family history reveals a father who underwent triple coronary bypass at 70 and a mother living with hypertension; there are no early cerebrovascular events. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-limb swelling, palpitations, presyncope, claudication, unintentional weight change, gastrointestinal bleeding, or urinary symptoms beyond the episodic right upper-quadrant discomfort for which surgery is scheduled. After five minutes seated, vital signs in the right arm registered blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, regular pulse 62 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99 % on ambient air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, height 175 cm, weight 86 kg, and body mass index 28 kg/m². He appeared well nourished and in no acute distress. Jugular venous pulse was not elevated at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the apical impulse was located in the fifth interspace at the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 without gallop, click, or murmur; no friction rub was appreciated. Lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. The abdomen was soft with mild tenderness beneath the right costal margin on deep inspiration but no rebound, guarding, or palpable mass; Murphy sign was reproduced only with firm pressure. Extremities were warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally and no edema or cyanosis. Neurologic screening demonstrated full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Laboratory studies drawn one hour prior to examination showed hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, hematocrit 43 %, platelet count 245 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.14 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose measured simultaneously was 104 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 84 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 60 beats per minute, Q waves in leads III and aVF consistent with the remote infarct, and no acute ST-segment deviations compared with a tracing from last year. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography displayed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Anesthesia airway assessment documented a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 7 cm, and full cervical extension; no loose teeth were noted. The peri-operative plan is to continue beta-blocker, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, antiplatelet therapy, and statin through the morning of surgery, permit clear liquids up to two hours before arrival, employ balanced general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, administer cephalosporin prophylaxis after induction, and use multimodal analgesia including acetaminophen and a low-dose intravenous opioid to minimize nausea. Hemodynamic monitoring will consist of non-invasive blood pressure cycling every three minutes, and crystalloid administration will be restricted to 2 mL/kg/h given his stable renal function. Sequential compression sleeves will be applied in the operating room, and early ambulation with oral hydration is anticipated four hours post-procedure. After discussing potential but unlikely cardiac events, pulmonary complications, bile-duct injury, infection, and the need for possible conversion to an open approach, the patient accurately repeated medication timing, fasting instructions, signs of postoperative concern, and voiced readiness to proceed with definitive gallbladder removal.

Patient note:
A 45-year-old man with a history of stage-1 hypertension treated only with lisinopril and hyperlipidemia managed by diet was transported by county EMS after a low-speed rollover of his pickup truck on a rural gravel road at 08:32; he had been wearing the three-point seat belt, airbags deployed, and he was found sitting upright in the driver’s seat with spidered windshield but no intrusion, speaking in full sentences although complaining of a “ringing” in his ears and frontal headache. Bystanders reported no seizure-like activity, emesis, or period of apnea. Paramedics arrived eight minutes after the 911 call, applied a rigid cervical collar, slid a scoop stretcher behind him, and secured him supine with head blocks. One 18-gauge catheter was placed in the right antecubital fossa and flushed with 5 mL of normal saline only; no crystalloid bolus, sedatives, analgesics, paralytics, hyperosmolar agents, antiemetics, anticonvulsants, or vasoactive medications were given in the field so as not to confound the neurologic survey. Capillary glucose was 118 mg/dL, and he breathed ambient air at 16 breaths per minute with an initial pulse oximetry of 98 %. During the 12-minute transport he remained hemodynamically stable and conversational, and no additional interventions were undertaken. On roll-in to the emergency department at 08:56 he is still secured to the scoop, clothing dusty from gravel but without visible blood. Pre-intervention vital signs obtained simultaneously with the first hospital examination are blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg in the left arm, heart rate 86 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min with symmetric chest excursion, oxygen saturation 97 % on 2 L/min nasal cannula placed for comfort, and tympanic temperature 36.8 °C. The oropharynx is clear with intact dentition, no pooled secretions, and a brisk gag when a Yankauer tip touches the soft palate; cough is strong and protective. Breath sounds are vesicular bilaterally without wheezes or crackles, and percussion is resonant throughout. Cardiac auscultation reveals a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses are 2 + in all extremities with capillary refill under two seconds. Abdomen is flat, soft, and non-tender; bowel sounds are present. The pelvis is stable to gentle compression, rectal tone is intact, and there is no sacral step-off. Secondary survey identifies a 4-cm superficial contusion over the right parietal scalp with no palpable step-off, scattered abrasions along both forearms, and mild tenderness over the left clavicle without crepitus; long bones are straight and nontender. Pupils measure 3 mm bilaterally, are round, and constrict briskly to direct and consensual light. During a 45-second period of silent observation his eyelids remain gently closed without fluttering, and there is no spontaneous opening. When his surname is spoken in a normal tone beside either ear, both lids part immediately to mid-palpebral height; he looks directly at the examiner and maintains fixation while answering questions, but if conversation ceases for more than ten seconds the lids drift shut again. He correctly states his full name, today’s date, the current location as “County General Emergency Department,” and recounts the event by describing “the truck fishtailed, then rolled once.” Speech is fluent, appropriate in volume and cadence, with no paraphasic errors. Cranial nerves otherwise demonstrate symmetric facial movement, midline tongue on protrusion, intact palate elevation, and a forceful cough. Extraocular movements are full without nystagmus. The upper and lower extremities lie relaxed on the stretcher with normal muscle bulk and baseline tone. Deep tendon reflexes are 2 + at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally, and no clonus is elicited. To assess nociceptive reaction, a five-second nail-bed compression is applied to the left index finger; he promptly flexes the entire arm away from the stimulus, withdrawing it across midline without attempting to grab the examiner’s hand or localize the pressure point. An identical response is observed when the right trapezius is squeezed: the ipsilateral shoulder shrugs and elbow flexes defensively, then relaxes once the stimulus ceases. Between provocations he follows simple commands such as “wiggle your toes” and “give a thumbs-up,” although he occasionally pauses to ask whether imaging will be performed soon. Based on his eye opening to voice, fully oriented speech, and withdrawal to painful stimuli, his Glasgow Coma Scale tallies 12/15 (E3 V5 M4) at this time. No myoclonus, tremor, or abnormal posturing is seen. Sensation to light touch is intact and symmetric, and coordination is acceptable for his recumbent position. Skin is warm, dry, and well perfused; no petechiae or ecchymoses other than those noted are present. Portable anterior-posterior chest radiograph obtained within five minutes shows clear lung fields, normal mediastinal silhouette, and good collar placement; pelvic radiograph reveals no fractures, and extended FAST is negative for pericardial or intra-abdominal fluid. Blood has been drawn for complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, serum ethanol, and high-sensitivity troponin, but results are pending. No pharmacologic agents, intravenous fluids beyond the pre-hospital saline lock, or hyperosmolar therapy have yet been administered, ensuring that his ocular response only after being addressed, the fully coherent orientation, and the limb withdrawal to painful stimuli described above reflect his untreated neurologic baseline at presentation. Neurosurgery and trauma surgery have been consulted; non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine along with CT angiography of the neck have been ordered stat, continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and neuro checks every fifteen minutes have been initiated, and airway equipment for rapid sequence intubation remains at the bedside should his protective reflexes decline.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old retired white female accountant was admitted to our neurology department for progressive cognitive decline, which had started insidiously, about four years prior to admission. Her symptoms were difficulty with language, sensory dysphasia, impairment of memory, and overall disorientation. According to her husband, her first symptom was the inability to form uncommon and complex words, so aphasia was the most prominent deficit at symptom onset leading to impaired daily living activities. Her condition slowly deteriorated leading to a loss of everyday activities, becoming unable to perform simple tasks related to household, then to her personal hygiene. Her husband reported that the executive performance as well as her spatial and temporal orientation varied over time and showed frequent daily alterations. She had type-2 diabetes for 4 years well controlled with diet and metformin. She had atrial fibrillation necessitating preventive apixaban treatment. She has had hypertension and hypercholesterinemia for 5 years treated with the combination of simvastatin, betaxolol, valsartan, furosemide, and digoxin. She was taking paroxetin for depression. Her body mass index was 25 with normal vital parameters apart from arrhythmia. She was passive and apathic while in hospital; lying inactively in bed the whole time, often in a sleep-like state during the day and apparently remaining so in the night. She was sometimes cheerful, tolerating and cooperating reasonably well with any queries or interventions; she seemed friendly and quiet with no interest, motivations, or denial.
Her blood screen, TSH, and coagulation parameters were normal. Her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau-level was 239 pg/ml (normal range: 341±171 pg/ml), p-tau level was 24 pg/ml (normal range: 35.84–66.26 pg/ml), amyloid-β (Aβ) level was 717 pg/ml (normal range: 797±230 pg/ml), the Aβ/tau ratio was 3, while the Aβ/p-tau ratio was 29.88. Thus, the amyloid and tau levels in the CSF were in the normal range excluding AD. CSF ubiquitin or TDP-43 testing could not be performed.
The MRI brain scan revealed moderate small vessel disease with important diffuse cerebral atrophy, mainly affecting the frontal and temporal lobes with left side dominance ().
To analyze structural results more precisely, hippocampal volumes and cortical thickness were calculated with FreeSurfer5.3 image analysis suite (freely available for download: ). The technical details are demonstrated in previous reports, no changes were made to the pipeline. The image process contains motion correction, removal of non-brain tissue, automated Talairach transformation, segmentation of deep gray matter structures and subcortical white matter, intensity normalization, tessellation of white-gray matter boundary, automated topology correction and surface deformation following intensity gradients. Following the cortical models, Freesurfer managed deformable procedures such as surface inflation, registration to spherical atlas, parcellation of cerebral cortex into units and creation of different surface based data. Cortical models and results of segmentation were quality controlled.
Average left frontal thickness (in mm) was 1.79±0.16, right frontal thickness was 2.01±0.21, left temporal thickness was 2.33±0.32, right temporal thickness was 2.45±0.36, left parietal thickness was 2.01±0.2 and right parietal thickness was 2.18±0.29. The temporal and frontal values are below the normal ranges if we compare it to data from the literature, especially on the left side, while the parietals are relatively preserved, being in line with the previous reports on FTD []. The volume of the left hippocampus was 3301 mm3, and of the right was 3997 mm3. These values are in the normal range based on our previous study with the same analysis method []. However, the left hippocampus was significantly smaller showing 17.5% asymmetry which suggests pathological changes in the volume of left hippocampus besides the normal values. Volumetric asymmetry could be considered significant above 10%. The volume of the left entorhinal cortex was 1881 mm3, while that of the right was 1811 mm3. These values and the disappearance of the difference between the two sides indicate Alzheimer or frontotemporal pathology based on previous data []. Altogether, the left dominant frontotemporal thinning and normal parietal thickness, and the involvement of the entorhinal cortex suggested the morphometry of FTD []. The routine EEG showed 20–40 uV, 9-10 Hz alpha background with frontal beta activity. We detected occasional left temporal focal slowing. No specific epileptiform activity were seen. Detailed neuropsychological analysis including Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (ACE) was performed. This test has a high sensitivity (0.9) and specificity (0.93) in the differentiation of cognitive disorders, especially in the diagnosis of AD and FTD []. Her ACE score was 32/100. The Verbal-Language/Orientation-Memory ratio of ACE, which sensitively discriminates AD and FTD [], scored 1.9 suggesting FTD. The Mini-Mental State Examination score extracted from ACE [] was 16/30. The neuropsychological results were consistent with a moderate cognitive decline. The most impaired cognitive domains were single-word retrieval in spontaneous speech and naming, reading, verbal short-term memory; whereas repetition, spatial orientation and grammar were relatively preserved. No early behavioral disinhibition, apathy/inertia, early loss of sympathy/empathy, presence of perseverative behavior and hyperorality were reported, so the diagnosis of behavior variant FTD was improbable []. Based on current diagnostic recommendations, we diagnosed primary progressive aphasia related to FTD []. Based on the caregiver’s report on the significant daily variability of her cognitive functions the presence of diffuse Lewy-body dementia was also considered. However, its core criteria as Parkinsonism or visual hallucinations were not present, therefore it was excluded. To assess the severity of cognitive fluctuation we used an easily applicable, bed-side test with high sensitivity in measuring visuo-spatial performance, the Corsi Block-Tapping Task (CBTT) []. We carried out CBTT with 2-3 items four times in one day; in better and worse cognitive periods (reported by the medical staff and her husband) and compared the number of correct answers with ANOVA analysis using the IBM SPSS20 software. We revealed significant differences in the results of the four trials (df: 3; Mean Square: 1.098; F: 4.567; p: 0.004). Based on both the neuropsychology scores and the history suggesting the possibility of non-convulsive seizure-episodes, we suspected concomitant epilepsy. Risk factors for developing epileptic seizures including definitive structural lesions on MRI, previous history of head trauma, childhood seizures, CNS infection, drug or alcohol dependency or electroconvulsive therapy were absent.
To disclose the potential epileptiform activity, we performed a 24-h Holter-EEG, followed by a 3-day-long continuous scalp video-EEG monitoring. We recorded one episode of slightly irregular rhythmic theta activity lasting for 20 s during light sleep in the right temporal leads. We also detected very rare bitemporal independent sharp waves with slight right dominance, possibly consistent with epileptiform activity []. The long-term EEG revealed disturbed sleep macrostructure with superficial night sleep, no deep sleep and very short REM sleep episodes; no sleep spindles or K complexes were found.
The EEG changes supported our suspicion that the significant fluctuations of her cognitive performance might be related to temporal lobe epileptic activity. Therefore, FO electrodes were surgically implanted () under general anesthesia; and continuous video-EEG recording using both FO and scalp electrodes were performed for 4 days.
The national and institutional ethic committees approved the FO electrode implantations and the recording; the family of the patient gave written informed consent to the procedure. The FO electrode implantation and the video-EEG monitoring period were uneventful, no surgical complications, behavioral or cooperation issues occurred. Frequent neuropsychological testing with CBTT was carried out during monitoring. The patient perfectly complied so we could perform clean, artefact-free EEG recordings. The recordings revealed bilateral independent spikes on the FO leads; in average, 30 unambiguous single spikes on the right side and 4 on the left per day (). We considered these graphoelements interictal spikes because of their paroxysmal appearance, the abrupt change in polarity, the typical spike duration (less than 70 ms) and because of their consistent temporal field distribution []. The spike activity occurred mainly during superficial NREM sleep, similarly to typical temporal epileptiform activity. We recorded runs of 11-12 Hz beta waves with or without 5 Hz theta elements and spike-like components, mostly during light NREM sleep, much less during wakefulness and none during the short REM periods, as well as >1 s long runs of sharp waves more often on the left side ( and ).
None of the epileptiform EEG events propagated onto the scalp electrodes. The spikes and sharp waves had an amplitude <l00 μV, and occurred frequently in the FO electrodes. The FO revealed 15-16 Hz, crescendo-decrescendo beta spindles during wakefulness, frequently preceding movements ().
Because of the occurrence of epileptiform discharges, we initiated clobazam treatment during the monitoring period, however there were no changes in the occurrence of epileptiform potentials and the neuropsychological performance following the drug administration in the next 2 days. According to some data, levetiracetam might be effective in AD-related epilepsy and it is easier to reach a steady state much earlier than clobazam [], therefore we started levetiracetam and we plan close follow-up.
