Patient note:
A 79-year-old Chinese Han man with a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus was treated with surgical excision 3 months before admission. He denied having any family history of digestive disease.
He presented with progressive dysphagia and esophageal metallic stent placement (20 × 70 mm, the upper edge was 24 cm from the incisors) for anastomotic stenosis (27.5 cm from the incisors) 1 month before. At this time, he was transferred to our emergency department due to hematemesis and tarry stool. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed only postoperative changes in esophageal cancer and esophageal metallic stent, which was placed close above the aortic arch (Fig. ). Upon arrival at the intensive care unit, the patient vomited approximately 500 mL of fresh blood. On physical examination, he was oriented and diaphoretic with a pale conjunctiva. He had no heart murmur, clear breathing sounds, and an old operative scar over the left chest, and the abdomen was soft without tenderness. Blood pressure (BP) was 72/56 mmHg, heart rate was 108 beats/min, respiratory rate was 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 91% in room air. Hemoglobin level was 6.8 g/dL. Large volumes of blood products were rapidly transfused, including 7.5 units of packed cells and 340 mL of fresh frozen plasma, and noradrenaline were administered simultaneously. When the patient's BP reached 90/60 mmHg, gastroscopy demonstrated large quantities of fresh blood and blood clots in the esophagus and stomach, so the source of the bleeding could not be identified. A vascular rupture was highly suspected. CT angiography (CTA) of the aorta was performed, which disclosed an aortic arch with possibly localized rupture (Fig. ). A cardiovascular surgeon performed an emergent angiography of the aorta, which showed bleeding from the wall of the aortic arch, so a diagnosis of AEF was confirmed, and an long covered stent (26 × 200 mm) was implanted (Fig. ) for thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR). The patient underwent fasting and received antibiotic treatment (intravenous cefodizime [2.0 g] once every 12 hours for 2 weeks and then replaced with intravenous combination of levofloxacin [0.5 g] once a day and piperacillin-tazobactam [4.5 g] once every 12 hours for another 2 weeks). The patient recovered well and was admitted to the department of gastroenterology on post-admission day 2. On post-admission day 9, esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed neither endoleakage nor peptic ulcer, and a jejunal feeding tube was established to provide enteral nutrition. Re-hematemesis occurred abruptly and massively on post-admission day 26, and the patient eventually died. The son of the patient provided informed consent for the publication of the case.

Patient note:
A 49-year-old woman with a background of insulin-requiring diabetes, stage-2 chronic kidney disease noted on primary-care labs six months earlier (baseline creatinine 1.2 mg/dL), and longstanding obstructive sleep apnea for which she owns a home bilevel device was discovered at 05:40 slumped against the hallway wall by her teenage son after two days of febrile chills, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and progressively labored breathing that kept her from lying flat overnight. Emergency medical technicians arrived within seven minutes to find her sitting forward on the floor, clutching her chest, drenched in sweat, and speaking in two-word gasps while an inexpensive finger oximeter flashed 72 % on ambient air. Because she repeatedly retched when a basic airway adjunct was attempted yet still maintained cough and gag, the crew elected not to place an endotracheal tube; instead they fitted a tight oronasal interface connected to their portable turbine delivering a continuous distending pressure of 12 cm H₂O and blended oxygen the inline analyzer documented at 0.67. Despite that support her saturation never climbed above the high 70s, and an automated cuff on the right arm cycled twice at 82/48 and 88/52 mm Hg, prompting early notification to the receiving hospital but no vasopressors or crystalloid during the eight-minute transport. On arrival in the resuscitation bay—and before any hospital-initiated medication, intravenous fluid, or adjustment of the noninvasive settings—she remained propped upright against the CPAP cushion, respirations shallow at 30/min with pronounced sternocleidomastoid recruitment, skin cool and pale with beads of sweat over the upper lip, and capillary refill roughly four seconds. A left radial arterial catheter was sited on first attempt; the initial gas obtained three minutes after stretcher touchdown showed pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 45 mm Hg, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, and a striking PaO₂ of 56 mm Hg while the delivered inspired fraction remained 67 %. Concurrent noninvasive blood pressure confirmed 86/50 mm Hg with a feeble radial pulse of 118 beats per minute in sinus rhythm. Neurologic appraisal revealed eyes opening to voice, slurred but comprehensible answers that failed to provide the correct date, and brisk withdrawal to supra-orbital notch pressure, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13; pupils were equal at 3 mm and reactive, corneal and gag reflexes were intact, and there was no focal asymmetry of power or tone. Chest examination demonstrated asymmetric excursion with reduced expansion over the right posterior lung field, diffuse coarse crackles more prominent at the base, and occasional bronchial breaths; percussion in that region was dull, and whispered pectoriloquy was present. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, jugular veins were flat at 30°, and no peripheral edema was appreciated. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and mildly tender in the right upper quadrant but without rebound or guarding; bowel sounds were present. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during the primary survey drained 40 mL of concentrated amber urine, and the son’s smartphone hydration app—into which she logs voids for nephrology follow-up—showed cumulative urinary output of 960 mL over the last twenty-four hours. Laboratory specimens drawn simultaneously with the arterial sample and resulted before any antibiotic, vasopressor, or fluid reached the patient revealed white blood cell count 18.2 × 10³/µL with 15 % band forms, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, hematocrit 36 %, and a platelet concentration of 101 000 /µL. Serum chemistry demonstrated sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, glucose 186 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. Hepatic indices showed aspartate aminotransferase 42 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 48 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 158 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.2. High-sensitivity troponin was 0.05 ng/mL, procalcitonin measured 11 ng/mL, and venous lactate matched the arterial at 4.3 mmol/L. A bedside lung ultrasound performed within five minutes depicted shred sign and dynamic air bronchograms in the right lower lobe with scattered B-lines elsewhere, while focused cardiac sonography revealed a small hyperdynamic left ventricle and a collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.1 cm. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained without interrupting the CPAP circuit demonstrated a dense right lower-zone consolidation, patchy infiltrates in the middle lobe, and no pneumothorax. Twelve-lead electrocardiography recorded sinus tachycardia at 118 beats/min with nonspecific ST-T changes and a corrected QT interval of 460 ms. Up to the exact moment these physiologic and biochemical data were captured, she had received neither crystalloid nor vasoactive medication, remained on face-mask continuous positive airway pressure delivering 67 % oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 56 mm Hg, continued to exhibit a systolic pressure no higher than 86 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, displayed moderate thrombocytopenia, preserved bilirubin, an elevated creatinine alongside sub-one-liter urine output for the day, and evidenced only mild encephalopathy while teetering on the verge of overt septic shock likely from multilobar community-acquired pneumonia.

Patient note:
A 55-year-old man with a remote history of injection-drug use that led to chronic hepatitis C genotype 1b—treated three years ago with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir but leaving behind biopsy-proven stage 4 fibrosis and small esophageal varices last surveyed eight months ago—walked into the emergency department at 19:10 after noticing that his last two bowel movements were a thick, jet-black paste that clung to the porcelain and produced a sharp iron odor despite multiple flushes. Earlier in the afternoon he had finished a grilled beef sandwich at work, felt a vague epigastric heaviness, then passed what he thought was unusually dark stool; when a second passage four hours later looked “like roofing tar,” co-workers urged him to seek evaluation. He drove himself the twenty-five minutes to the hospital without needing to pull over, never experienced dimming vision, ear ringing, or a sensation of impending blackout, and states he was able to unload his toolbox from the truck bed without weakness or imbalance. Past medical problems apart from the treated viral hepatitis include well-controlled hypertension managed with lisinopril 10 mg daily and dyspepsia for which he takes over-the-counter omeprazole most mornings; he has never been told he has fluid around the lungs or heart, has no exertional limitations, and bicycles eight miles every weekend without breathlessness. He denies ever having required diuretics, nitrates, or echocardiographic follow-up for a weakened ventricle. Medications are limited to lisinopril, omeprazole, and a daily multivitamin; he takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, corticosteroids, or herbal supplements. He stopped drinking alcohol five years ago, has not used illicit drugs since antiviral therapy, smokes half a pack of cigarettes per day, and works full-time as a metal fabricator. Family history reveals a father with myocardial infarction at 70 and a brother with type 2 diabetes; there are no inherited bleeding disorders. Patient note:
A 71-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with symptoms of dizziness, fatigue, and bright red bleeding per rectum. She has a past medical history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension. She started having six to seven bright red colored stools for about one week, unassociated with mucus. She reported concerns of constant right upper quadrant pain that started approximately two days before the presentation. She denied any nausea, vomiting, or subjective fever, and she had no recent travel or exposure to sick contacts and no history of hemorrhoids.
On examination, she was found to be tachycardic with a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. Her blood pressure was 98/50 mmHg, and her body temperature was 100.2°F. Her oxygen saturation was 93% on room air. She appeared thin, cachectic, and had no scleral icterus. Her lungs were clear on auscultation, and her cardiovascular examination revealed no significant murmurs.
Her laboratory investigation showed leukocytosis with white blood cell count of 29,000 per microliter (neutrophils, 88%; lymphocytes, 3.5%; monocytes, 3.7%; eosinophils, 1.2%; basophils, 0.3%). Her hemoglobin was 9 g/dl (reference range: 11.2-15.7 g/dl), and her mean corpuscular volume was 77. Urine analysis was negative for infection. Chest X-ray did not show any active consolidation (Figure ).
Her Clostridium difficile screening was negative. Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed several indeterminate hypoechoic solid masses, and both lobes of the liver had several indeterminate hypoechoic solid masses. A slight gall bladder wall thickening with no surrounding inflammatory signs was noted. MRI of the abdomen showed multiple circumscribed lesions throughout the liver compatible with metastasis (Figure ).
The patient was started on empiric antibiotics with vancomycin and cefepime for possible infection. Her blood cultures grew S. anginosus, and her antibiotic regimen was changed to ceftriaxone.
As the source of the bacteremia was unknown, and because of her microcytic anemia with a recent change in bowel habits, she underwent a colonoscopy and transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE). The colonoscopy revealed a fungating infiltrative, ulcerated, partially obstructing mass in the sigmoid colon. The biopsy results are positive for moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon (Figure ).
TTE showed thickening and possible vegetation involving the aortic and mitral valves. Subsequent transesophageal echocardiogram revealed vegetation (approximately 0.2 cm) on the aortic and mitral valves (Figures , ).
She had no signs of a perivalvular abscess, and her ejection fraction was within reference range at 55% to 60%. Her care team decided to continue treatment with antibiotics for at least six weeks. Her anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation was halted due to active gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. The patient died several days later as her family focused on comfort care measures based on the patient's wishes.

Patient note:

She walked from the drop-off area accompanied by her daughter, pausing once to catch her breath on the long corridor but conversing comfortably during registration. Daily activity includes tending a small vegetable garden, climbing eight outside steps to her porch while carrying groceries, and attending water-exercise classes twice weekly; she denies chest tightness, arm or jaw discomfort, unexplained diaphoresis, exertional presyncope, or prior cardiac testing, and she has never required nitrate prescriptions or coronary interventions. Type 2 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed twenty-one years ago; progressive fasting hyperglycemia led to initiation of basal insulin seven years ago and prandial coverage three years later. She currently injects insulin glargine 28 units subcutaneously at 2200 h and uses insulin lispro before meals employing a 1 unit per 10 g carbohydrate ratio with a correction factor of 1 unit for every 30 mg/dL above 140 mg/dL, checking capillary glucose at least three times daily. Home logs reviewed today show pre-breakfast glucose readings between 100 and 160 mg/dL and no episodes below 70 mg/dL during the past month; the most recent hemoglobin A1c, drawn by her endocrinologist five weeks ago, was 7.6 %. Long-standing systemic hypertension is treated with amlodipine 5 mg each morning and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg at bedtime, yielding home pressures in the 120s/60s. Hyperlipidemia is managed with rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributable to a 30-pack-year smoking history (cessation 18 years ago) is stable on tiotropium inhalation once daily without recent exacerbation. She reports no prior stroke or transient focal neurologic symptoms, denies claudication, and has never been told of carotid disease. Past operations include a total abdominal hysterectomy at age 54 without cardiopulmonary complications and bilateral cataract extraction. Alcohol intake is limited to an occasional glass of wine on holidays, and she does not use illicit substances. Family history is notable for a brother who died of renal failure in his seventies and a mother who developed colon cancer in her eighties; there are no premature cardiovascular deaths. Review of systems is negative for fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, orthopnea, lower-extremity swelling, intermittent vision loss, or new focal weakness. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs measured blood pressure 118/66 mm Hg in the right arm, regular pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 96 % on ambient air, oral temperature 36.5 °C, and body mass index 27 kg/m². She appeared well nourished and in no acute distress. Jugular venous pulsations were not elevated, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the apical impulse was palpated in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line without displacement. Cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and S2, no extra sounds, and no murmurs. Breath sounds were vesicular with scattered end-expiratory wheezes at both bases but no crackles. The abdomen was soft and mildly full in the right lower quadrant without tenderness, rebound, or palpable mass; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites was detected. Peripheral pulses were 2+ and symmetric, and no edema or skin color changes were observed. Neurologic screening showed full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady narrow-based gait. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour before the examination revealed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, hematocrit 36 %, white blood cell count 7.3 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 248 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.7 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 19 mL/min/1.73 m²; liver enzymes and international normalized ratio were within reference limits, and fasting plasma glucose obtained simultaneously measured 144 mg/dL. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram printed in clinic displayed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 88 ms, axis 20°, and flat inferior T waves interpreted as nonspecific, with no prior tracings for comparison. Upright posteroanterior chest radiograph showed hyperinflated lung fields, flattened diaphragms, and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette without infiltrate or effusion. Airway evaluation by anesthesiology documented a Mallampati class II oropharynx, inter-incisor gap of 4 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, full neck extension, and intact dentition. The anesthetic plan discussed includes balanced general anesthesia with epidural catheter placement for postoperative analgesia, arterial line insertion for beat-to-beat pressure monitoring given the anticipated fluid shifts and baseline renal impairment, continuation of calcium-channel blocker and statin on the morning of surgery, withholding the thiazide diuretic and reducing the night-before basal insulin dose by 25 %, point-of-care glucose on arrival with intravenous dextrose or rapid-acting insulin as needed, lung-protective ventilation with permissive low tidal volumes in view of underlying obstructive lung disease, and judicious crystalloids guided by dynamic indices. Sequential compression devices will be applied in the operating room, and subcutaneous unfractionated heparin will begin the evening after surgery to mitigate venous thrombo-embolism risk. The patient demonstrated accurate teach-back regarding medication timing, fasting instructions, and warning signs of postoperative dehydration or wound infection, voiced understanding of the possibility of temporary dialysis should renal function deteriorate, and affirmed her wish to proceed with definitive tumor resection.

Patient note:
An 81-year-old man presented to the emergency department (ED) with shortness of breath and nonproductive cough. He denied fever, chills, or chest pain. He was afebrile with blood pressure 127/68 mmHg, pulse rate 63/min, and respiratory rate 22/min. The patient's saturation was 89% in room air which improved to 97% with 2L of oxygen. He had decreased breath sounds with crackles over the right lung field. The remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. The patient had been admitted 2 weeks before with lower extremity weakness which was thought to be secondary to deconditioning from a recent upper respiratory tract infection for which he was treated with amoxicillin by his primary care physician. At that time, he was discharged with provisions for physical therapy. The patient had a past medical history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on amiodarone but not on anticoagulation, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage III. He had a 20 pack-year smoking history and had quit 57 years ago.
On arrival, the patient's WBC count was 12,500/µl with 85.9% neutrophils. ABG showed pH of 7.496 with pCO2 33.9 mmHg, pO2 80.2 mmHg, and bicarbonate 26.4 meq/l. Chest X-ray revealed new, moderately extensive, multifocal right lung pneumonia with small associated parapneumonic effusion (). CT chest further detailed a right basilar opacification with right pleural effusion and small amount of pleural gas (). The patient was started on IV vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and oral azithromycin in the ED. Azithromycin was discontinued a day later after recommendations from Infectious Disease. Blood, sputum, and pleural fluid studies were ordered. Thoracocentesis showed pH 6.9, protein 4.6 g/dl (serum protein 5.7 g/dl; reference range: 6.4–8.9 g/dl), albumin 2.1 g/dl (serum albumin 2.2 g/dl), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 4844 IU/L (serum LDH: 273 IU/L), suggestive of empyema. A 12 Fr chest tube was placed under CT guidance by interventional radiology which yielded foul-smelling, dark burgundy fluid. Pleural fluid culture was positive for pansensitive C. perfringens. Surprisingly, sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Citrobacter koseri, both of which were sensitive to piperacillin-tazobactam. We did not order a quantitative culture to differentiate between pulmonary colonization and infection. We also did not perform bronchoscopy to rule out any mass or foreign body associated with the empyema. IV vancomycin was discontinued. IV clindamycin was added but was later discontinued after stool was positive for Clostridium difficile. The patient was planned for a 4-week course of IV piperacillin-tazobactam. On day 8, the patient was noted to have right lower extremity swelling which led to the discovery of extensive DVT and submassive PE, which was treated with Eliquis. Due to bleeding risk, decortication was deferred and the patient was instead treated with intrapleural tPA and dornase alpha.
With further questioning during hospital stay, the patient mentioned that he had difficulty swallowing food due to the sensation that something was stuck in his throat. He had resting tremor of the left hand and subtle cogwheeling of the right upper extremity. The swallowing function study was positive for aspiration. MRI brain to rule out any intracranial pathology was done which showed focal acute/subacute infarction. Echocardiogram with double bubble study revealed a patent foramen ovale. For this, cardiology advised anticoagulation with consideration for closure in the event of a stroke while on Eliquis. Neurology suspected that dysphagia was due to Parkinson's disease and recommended starting Sinemet in the near future. The patient was discharged to acute rehab with a chest tube to water seal. Chest CT done a month later showed improvement of the effusion with minimal drainage from the tube. The chest tube was removed. Repeat pleural fluid cultures were negative for infection. The patient did not show any fluid reaccumulation on subsequent imaging studies (Figures and ).

Patient note:
A 57-year-old unemployed African American woman with poorly controlled hypertension, congestive heart failure, and polysubstance abuse (including crack-cocaine) presented after one month of progressive nonproductive cough and dyspnea and two weeks of anorexia and fatigue. EMS was summoned to her home after she complained of increasing dyspnea. Her oxygen saturation measured 70% on room air. She was taken to Baylor University Medical Center at Dallas and admitted. Blood pressure was 187/99 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respirations 28 breaths per minute, and temperature 98.0 degrees Fahrenheit. Initial laboratory values were significant for hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL; platelets 254 K/uL, creatinine of 1.7 mg/dL; glucose 237 mg/dL; and B-type natriuretic peptide 394 pg/mL (reference range 0–100 pg/mL). Liver function tests included aspartate aminotransferase of 103 U/L (reference range 5–35 U/L); alkaline phosphatase 129 U/L (reference range 38–126 U/L); and albumin 2.9 g/dL (reference range 3.5 to 4.8 g/dL). She had no recent long trips and she was not taking any current medications.
Physical examination found diffuse rales, rhonchi, wheezing, and generalized abdominal tenderness. No lower extremity swelling was noted. Her body mass index was 31.8 kg/m2. Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates suggesting pneumonia. Pelvic sonogram found a large mass suggestive of a fibroid uterus, posterosuperior to the bladder (). A nasal swab was positive for H1N1 influenza by PCR. She was placed on empiric antibiotics and BiPAP; however, her respiratory function continued to decline. Thirteen days after admission, she experienced sudden cardiopulmonary arrest and died.
Autopsy found a normally developed, moderately obese woman. An oral endotracheal tube was well positioned. A 1275-gram, 14.8 × 14.2 × 9.4 cm subserosal pedunculated tan-white uterine nodule extended from the fundus and filled the entire pelvis with extension into the lower abdominal cavity. A vein from the surface of the nodule anastomosed with an adjacent small bowel mesenteric vein (). The myometrium also contained smaller intramural and subserosal nodules ranging in size from 0.7 cm to 2.2 cm in diameter. Cut sections of all nodules were whorled and tan-white. Multiple laminated and focally adherent hilar and peripheral intravascular thrombi were present in all lobes of both lungs. Posterior leg dissection found thrombi in bilateral posterior tibial veins and deep gastrocnemius veins.
Microscopically, the myometrial nodules consisted of smooth muscle fascicles with areas of interstitial hyalinization (). No coagulation necrosis or mitotic figures were identified; and the masses were classified as leiomyomas. Sections from the leg veins and lungs showed laminated thrombi () with focal endothelial organization (). Additional autopsy findings included cardiomegaly (485 grams) with atherosclerotic and hypertensive cardiovascular disease and diffuse alveolar damage. Postmortem studies to investigate for hypercoagulability, including MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase), prothrombin G20210A, and factor V Leiden mutations, were performed and were negative.
The cause of death was pulmonary thromboembolism due to DVT associated with a very large uterine leiomyoma and probably contributory to death was obesity. The manner of death was natural.

Patient note:
A 66-year-old Japanese male patient had received regorafenib (160 mg/day) as an anticancer treatment for metastatic colorectal carcinoma. His medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, chronic heart failure, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and permanent pacemaker implantation due to complete atrioventricular block. His DVT had been managed with low-dose apixaban (5 mg/day; body weight: 75 kg, creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL) to avoid bleeding complications.
Two months ago, he had suffered from non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction with the high-lateral (HL) branch as the culprit lesion, accompanied by chest discomfort; the HL branch occlusion was treated with balloon dilation only to avoid the need of a long-term triple antithrombotic therapy. At the same time, coronary angiography (CAG) revealed severe stenosis in the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery. A fractional flow reserve value of 0.72 confirmed a physiologically significant lesion. After PCI for the HL branch, regorafenib was withdrawn temporarily, and a triple antithrombotic therapy (aspirin: 100 mg/day, prasugrel: 3.75 mg/day, and apixaban: 5 mg/day) was successfully continued for two months without bleeding complications. Subsequently, the patient underwent PCI for severe stenosis in the LAD lesion two months after PCI for HL, as he demonstrated good tolerance to the triple antithrombotic therapy. Other medications administered included bisoprolol (1.25 mg/day), enalapril (2.5 mg/day), furosemide (20 mg/day), esomeprazole (20 mg/day), amlodipine (5 mg/day), sitagliptin (50 mg/day), mitiglinide (30 mg/day), and insulin degludec (9 units). In addition, routine blood testing revealed an elevated level of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), normal kidney function, high value of HbA1c, and mild anemia (BNP: 191.6 pg/mL, creatinine: 0.68 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate: 89.3 mL/minute/1.73 m2, HbA1c: 8.4%, hemoglobin: 9.9 g/dL, and platelet count: 318 × 103/µL). He was classified as having a high thrombotic and bleeding risk at this time, according to the CREDO-Kyoto thrombotic and bleeding risk scores. A sirolimus-eluting stent, which is a drug-eluting stent (DES) (Ultimaster Tansei 3.5/38 mm; Terumo Corporation, Tokyo, Japan), was implanted in the LAD lesion without malapposition or significant under-expansion, as confirmed by intravascular ultrasound imaging (IVUS) analysis (Fig. ). After PCI for the LAD, regorafenib was resumed because it exhibited a clinical effect on the patient's cancer. Nevertheless, the patient was admitted to our hospital for congestive heart failure with dyspnea one month later (BNP: 1,512.5 pg/mL). Echocardiography demonstrated new severe hypokinesis of the anteroseptal wall and apex. Despite continued triple antithrombotic therapy, CAG revealed focal and eccentric contrastive defects in the previous LAD stent, and OFDI confirmed ST (Fig. a–e). A 3.5/20 mm perfusion balloon (Ryusei, Kaneka Medical, Tokyo, Japan) was inflated for 3 min using an embolic protection device (Fig. f). CAG and OFDI confirmed optimal initial gain in the ST site and thrombolysis in myocardial infarction flow grade 3, with no complications including distal emboli (Fig. g–k). Antithrombotic therapy was further enhanced temporarily to prevent the recurrence of ST; it included aspirin (100 mg/day), ticagrelor (120 mg/day), and apixaban (10 mg/day). The administration of regorafenib was discontinued after PCI for ST in the LAD, and aspirin and ticagrelor were discontinued 1 and 2 months later, respectively. No further thromboembolic events (including definite/probable ST) were observed, and heart failure was managed well. However, he died due to the progression of metastatic colorectal carcinoma about 3 months after ST onset.

question:
Patient note:
A 33-year-old Somalian man initially presented with loss of neurological function of the left arm, hazy vision, and headache. A few weeks prior to this episode he had had an episode during which he experienced chest pain, nausea, and vomiting. Our patient does not drink alcohol. He smokes tobacco and chews two bundles of khat a week for more than 10 years. No other risk factors for atherosclerosis at young age were present. The blood levels of cholesterol and triglycerides were within normal range. Family history was negative for inherited thrombophilia. His ECG on admission showed a Q wave in V1 and V2 and 2 mm ST-elevations in V1, V2, and V3 and a terminal negative T wave in I, aVL, V2, V3, and V4, consistent with a recent, evolving anterior infarction (). On admission the highly sensitive troponin T was 18 ng/L (normal value < 14 ng/L). The transthoracic echocardiogram showed a poor left ventricular function with akinesia of the anterior wall and left ventricular dilatation. No thrombus was seen.
The noncontrast enhanced CT of the brain showed ischemia in the right middle cerebral artery vascular territory. The CTA of the carotids showed no stenosis or venous thrombosis.
An MRI of the brain was performed to rule out vasculitis or other vascular malformations. The MRI showed recent ischemia in the vascular territory of the posterior division of the right middle cerebral artery (Figures –).
Coronary angiography showed a 70% stenosis with haziness of the proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) (), which disappeared after intracoronary nitroglycerine injection (). The other coronary arteries were normal.
MRI of the heart showed a poor left ventricular function, with a calculated ejection fraction of 29%. The left ventricle was dilated, with an end diastolic left ventricular diameter of 63 mm (normal value < 55 mm). There was thinning of the myocardium in the apex and the midcavitary anteroseptal, anterior, and anterolateral segments. There was hypo- to akinesia of these areas with subendocardial and transmural delayed enhancement (Figures and ) in these regions. No thrombi were seen. The signs on the MRI are consistent with infarction in the vascular territory of the LAD.
Screening for thrombophilia (lupus anticoagulants, cardiolipin antibodies, factor V Leiden, and antithrombin III deficiency) was negative. A presumptive diagnosis was made of khat induced coronary spasm with myocardial infarction and khat induced cerebral infarction. Due to hypotension treatment with calcium blocking agents was not possible. He was advised to refrain from khat use. Furthermore he underwent a percutaneous coronary intervention of the proximal LAD with stent placement to prevent stenosis in case of possible future coronary spasm. His left ventricular function remained poor, which was a reason for ICD implantation for primary prevention. During admission all neurological complaints resolved.

Patient note:

Firefighters extricated him through the windshield in ten minutes using a rapid roof flap technique. Field personnel applied a rigid Philadelphia collar, performed log-roll onto a long spine board with full body straps, placed a 16-gauge peripheral catheter in the left antecubital fossa that was flushed with 5 mL of normal saline only, and started oxygen at 15 L/min through a non-rebreather facemask; they consciously withheld crystalloid infusion, opiates, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, neuromuscular blockers, hyperosmolar agents, vasopressors, antihypertensive medication, dextrose, and antiemetics so that the neurologic examination would be unaltered on arrival. Capillary glucose in the field was 118 mg/dL, and cardiac monitor strips showed sinus tachycardia between 96 and 104 beats/min without ectopy during the thirteen-minute ground transport over smooth pavement. He rolled into our trauma bay at 10:57 still immobilized on the backboard, clothing cut away but left draped for modesty, facemask delivering oxygen, and the saline lock capped. When the trauma nurse leans close and asks, “Can you tell me what happened?” the patient produces a slurred sequence of single, context-inappropriate utterances—“truck... church... Monday”—with no coherent sentence structure, and he repeats the same pair of syllables “ba-no” twice when asked his name; volume is low but unmistakably verbal rather than a mere moan. She reports maintaining her usual routine of climbing two flights of stairs to her bedroom, preparing meals, and completing a twenty-minute neighborhood walk each evening, and she emphasizes that she has not spent entire days in bed, worn an orthopedic boot, or used crutches at any point this year. She denies recent falls, athletic injuries, insect bites, rashes, fevers, chills, night sweats, unintentional weight change beyond the five-pound fluctuation she attributes to chemotherapy-related appetite shifts, and has had no blood clots, miscarriages, strokes, or heart attacks in the past. Other chronic conditions include mild primary hypertension managed with lisinopril 10 mg daily and seasonal allergic rhinitis treated intermittently with intranasal fluticasone; she takes no estrogenic agents, glucocorticoids, or erythropoiesis-stimulating drugs and is not on prophylactic anticoagulation because platelet counts have hovered near 95 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ during recent chemotherapy cycles. Her family history is notable only for a father with coronary artery disease; no first-degree relatives have experienced venous thrombo-embolism. She quit smoking eight years ago after a 6-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of red wine on weekends, and denies illicit substance use. Review of systems is negative for chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, flank pain, dysuria, abdominal distension, or lower-back discomfort. On arrival—prior to any analgesic, intravenous fluid, or anticoagulant administration—she sat upright chatting comfortably, the right leg resting on a stool while the left foot was flat on the floor. Nursing staff documented temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 124/74 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. The neck veins were not distended; cardiac examination revealed a crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear throughout. The abdomen displayed a well-healed 8-cm portacath access scar over the right pectoral region but was soft, nontender, with no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Inspection of the lower extremities showed the right calf subtly more convex posteriorly than the left, with the overlying skin retaining normal color and temperature, without erythema, brawny discoloration, varicosities, or serpiginous venous channels. Using a flexible metric tape held exactly 10 cm distal to the inferior patellar pole, measurements were 40.7 cm on the symptomatic side and 36.5 cm contralaterally, yielding a 4.2-cm discrepancy; 15 cm above the patella both thighs measured 51.3 cm, and at the malleolar level the figures were 27.4 cm right versus 27.1 cm left. Gentle thumb pressure applied over the anteromedial tibial border of the right calf produced a 3-mm depression that lingered approximately twenty seconds before resolving, whereas identical pressure on the left rebounded immediately, indicating soft pitting confined to the involved limb. Diffuse palpation of the gastrocnemius and soleus bellies elicited only a sense of tightness without discrete nodularity, cords, fluctuation, crepitus, or warmth; range of motion at the ankle and knee was full and pain-free, and straight-leg raise provoked no radicular symptoms. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were palpable at 2 + bilaterally with capillary refill under two seconds; sensation to light touch and pinprick was intact in all dermatomes, and motor strength in ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion graded 5/5. There was no inguinal, popliteal, or femoral lymphadenopathy. A portable 12-lead ECG obtained before phlebotomy demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats min⁻¹ with no ST-T wave abnormalities. She has not undergone any operative procedures, biopsies, or radiologically guided interventions since the diagnostic bone scan performed three months ago, and her implanted port has functioned without infection or thrombosis. No cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, musculoskeletal tear, lymphedema, congestive heart failure flare, nephrotic syndrome, or systemic volume overload was evident on the current examination to convincingly explain the abrupt unilateral calf enlargement accompanied by pitting in a patient actively receiving cytotoxic therapy. Consequently, comprehensive venous duplex ultrasonography from the common femoral segment through the calf veins was ordered on an expedited basis while she remained hemodynamically stable, ambulatory within the clinic, and untreated with any antithrombotic agent.

Patient note:
Six weeks following an uncomplicated delivery via low-transverse C-section for arrest of labor (placenta not sent to pathology), a 23-year-old G3P2011 woman presented to the ED with pleuritic chest pain and severe shortness of breath for two days. The patient’s prenatal course was unremarkable. Following delivery, she was discharged home on post-operative day three with a hemoglobin (Hgb) of 10.8 g/dL and a hematocrit (Hct) of 32.4%. Her post-partum history was notable for endometritis, excessive vaginal bleeding throughout the post-partum period with evidence of increased endometrial blood flow, as well as an endometrium measuring 1.5 cm via transvaginal ultrasound. She required hospitalization for antibiotics and transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) two weeks prior, but did not have any curettage performed at that time. Upon initial evaluation, she was afebrile (37.0° C), tachycardic (145 beats per minute), hypertensive [blood pressure (BP) 156/82 mmHg], and in severe respiratory distress with a respiratory rate (RR) of 30 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 99% while breathing 100% oxygen via nonrebreather mask. A chest X-ray showed diffuse pulmonary edema and bilateral airspace disease with bilateral pleural effusions (Figure ).
Initial arterial blood gas analysis showed severe hypoxemia, metabolic acidosis, and concomitant respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.31, pO2 197, pCO2 18, base excess −8, HCO3 18 on 100% O2 via bag-valve-mask). Labs demonstrated a Hgb of 4.9 g/dL and Hct of 15.6% with gross intraperitoneal blood found on sonographic exam, leukocytosis (white blood cell count 16,700 with 82% neutrophils), elevated d-dimer (>5,000 ng/mL), normal fibrinogen, and transaminitis with aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase/alkaline phosphatase of 363/356/274 units/L, respectively. Additionally, the patient was found to have a serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) of 2,800 mIU/mL, a creatinine of 1.10 mg/dL, and a lipase of 453 units/L. The patient was transfused with three units of PRBCs, and subsequently intubated with a tidal volume (TV) of 6 mL/kg ideal body weight, a respiratory rate of 16, and a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 5 cm H2O and an inspired oxygen fraction of 60%.
Initial transabdominal ultrasound revealed a hypervascular uterus with internal echogenic material, as well as an endometrial lining measuring 3.7 cm, suspicious for GTD (Figure ).
A CT angiogram with contrast of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed free fluid in the abdomen, multiple lesions within the liver, spleen, bilateral pleural effusions, and bilateral thromboses in the gonadal veins, raising concern for septic emboli vs. disseminated GTD. The patient was transferred to a quaternary center, where she was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and cisplatin/etoposide for two cycles prior to full-dose chemotherapy with etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine due to concern of acute hemorrhage given her high tumor burden. Bacterial cultures of blood, urine, and tracheal aspirate were negative.
On hospital day seven, the patient developed massive hemoptysis with marked respiratory distress. Bronchoscopy showed active hemorrhage with predominant bleeding from the right upper lobe. The patient underwent interventional radiology-guided embolization of her right bronchial artery. She continued to have DAH (Figure ).
Recruitment maneuvers (pressure-controlled inflations of 40 cm H2O sustained for 20 s) and neuromuscular blockade failed to improve gas exchange on assist-control ventilation with a TV of 4.5 mL/kg ideal body weight, RR of 23, a PEEP of 16 cm H2O, and an inspired oxygen fraction of 100% while minimizing driving pressure. She was placed on veno-venous ECMO on hospital day eight.
Under ultrasound guidance, a 23 French drainage cannula was placed percutaneously in the left femoral vein, and a 21 F return cannula was placed into the right internal jugular vein. Blood was drained from the left femoral vein into the ECMO circuit. ECMO flows were initiated at 4 L/min with a sweep gas flow of 2 L/min, titrated to keep oxygen saturation >88% and pCO2 within normal parameters. The ECMO for Protective Ventilation (EMPROVE) protocol, a lung-protective strategy utilized at our institution, was initiated on the ventilator. The protocol has been described in detail elsewhere, but in brief, it utilizes either pressure control or airway pressure release ventilation to maintain a peak pressure ≤ 30 or a plateau pressure ≤ 25. The respiratory rate is lowered to 5-8 breaths per minute, and moderate PEEP is used to keep the lungs expanded during low TV ventilation. The FiO2 is set at ≤ 50%. ECMO provided a gradual improvement in hypercapnia over the initial 45 min (PCO2 48-42, pH 7.48-7.45). Using the EMPROVE protocol her TVs declined from ~300 to ~200 mL, reducing peak airway pressures from 46 to 30 cmH2O. Her respiratory rate was maintained at 7 and her PEEP at 14 cm H2O.
Due to the hemorrhagic nature of GTD, the patient was not anticoagulated. Partial thromboplastin time measured between 25 and 36 s while on ECMO. Platelets were transfused to maintain count > 50,000/µL, as per local hospital practice. There were no thrombotic complications. The patient’s clinical condition gradually improved and extracorporeal support was discontinued after 23 days (Figure ).
Sedation was weaned and she was alert and oriented, however, with significant debility. She underwent tracheostomy placement and was weaned to T-piece. Sadly, while nearing transfer status to a decreased level of care, the patient suffered a catastrophic hemorrhage from a brain metastasis and subsequently expired on hospital day 42.

He denied vomiting, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, pruritus, dark urine, or recent weight loss. His prior decompensations included two outpatient large-volume paracenteses last winter and a single hospital stay three years ago for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; he had not bled from varices and had never undergone transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placement. Medications reconciled from pill bottles and a printed list were furosemide 40 mg and spironolactone 100 mg each morning—both self-discontinued two weeks earlier “because my legs were cramping”—nadolol 20 mg nightly, calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, and an over-the-counter multivitamin; he was prescribed lactulose 20 g orally twice daily after his prior admission but had taken only intermittent doses because of fear of incontinence, and he had never used rifaximin. The patient was awake, answered most questions appropriately but hesitated five seconds naming the current month, and required prompting to recall two of three objects at five minutes; handwriting on the consent form was slightly shaky, and with arms extended and wrists dorsiflexed a low-amplitude flapping tremor appeared within ten seconds. Speech was fluent without dysarthria, cranial nerves II–XII were intact, strength was 5/5 diffusely, and reflexes were physiologic. Neck veins were 6 cm H₂O at 30°. Cardiac examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear. Abdominal contour was protuberant with bulging flanks that remained prominent in Fowler’s position; percussion disclosed central tympany transitioning to broad dullness over both lateral quadrants, and a pronounced fluid wave coursed from one hand to the other without the need for a third-hand stop. The umbilicus was everted but not flattened, suggesting several liters of intraperitoneal fluid; the liver edge, firm and nodular, was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, and the spleen tip was appreciable. Point-of-care ultrasound performed immediately—still prior to any therapy—revealed a shrunken heterogeneous liver with capsular nodularity, a patent portal vein with hepatopetal flow at 15 cm/s, splenomegaly measuring 16.5 cm, and anechoic free fluid accumulating to a depth of approximately 4 cm in Morrison’s pouch and layering throughout the pelvis; kidneys were normal in size and echogenicity, and no biliary dilation or focal mass was present. A bedside portable chest radiograph obtained moments later showed elevated hemidiaphragms without consolidation or pleural effusion, and a 12-lead ECG documented normal sinus rhythm at 88 beats/min with a QTc of 430 ms. Venous blood drawn through an 18-gauge antecubital catheter—documented before any intravenous albumin, diuretics, cathartics, antibiotics, vitamin K, or sedatives—returned: total bilirubin 2.37 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.58 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 55 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 78 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 162 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 210 U/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, creatinine 1.02 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.4 ×10⁹/L, platelet count 96 ×10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.68. Serum ammonia, alpha-fetoprotein, and bacterial cultures were pending at the time this note was completed. Up to this juncture the patient had received no therapeutic interventions, ensuring that all observed findings and laboratory values reflect his untreated physiologic state upon presentation for evaluation of progressive abdominal distention and new-onset cognitive slowing in the setting of advanced hepatitis C–related liver disease.

Patient note:
A 71-year-old African American male presented for routine follow-up with his primary care physician 3 months after initiating atorvastatin 80 mg and pioglitazone 15 mg daily. His lipid panel revealed a total cholesterol of 152 mg/dL, triglycerides of 83 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 59 mg/dL, and a calculated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c) of 76 mg/dL. LFTs were notable for an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 1093 U/L (upper limit of normal [ULN] 41 U/L), an alanine transaminase (ALT) of 1385 U/L (ULN 58 U/L), and an alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 265 U/L (ULN 129 U/L; R Factor 11.6; ). Total bilirubin was elevated to 1.5 mg/dL (ULN 1.2 mg/dL). The patient denied myalgias, pruritus, or abdominal pain. He was admitted for further management.
The patient denied known hypotensive episodes or recent use of alcohol, herbal supplements, antibiotics, or acetaminophen. Gamma glutamyl-transferase was elevated to 551 U/L (ULN 50 U/L). Serum acetaminophen and ethanol were undetectable. Hepatitis A virus IgM/IgG, hepatitis B virus core IgM/IgG, hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) antibodies were negative, as were hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and HIV-1 and HCV RNA. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic, anti-mitochondrial, and liver-kidney microsome antibodies were not detected. Serum IgG, copper, and ceruloplasmin levels were normal. Remaining workup was unrevealing except for a borderline-positive smooth muscle antibody titer of 1:20 (normal <1:20) and a ferritin of 1469 ng/mL (ULN 336 ng/mL). Serum albumin (3.4 g/dL) and prothrombin time international normalized ratio (1.01) were within normal limits. Liver ultrasound revealed “mildly increased echogenicity, coarsened echotexture, and attenuation of sound beam” suggestive of “hepatic steatosis and/or diffuse hepatocellular disease.” The right lobe measured 14.1 cm. A prior abdominal computerized tomography scan with contrast at age 60 years revealed only a punctate calcification, likely a granuloma, within the right lobe.
On admission, his temperature was 36.8 °C, heart rate was 67 beats per minute, blood pressure was 123/63 mm Hg, respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Physical examination revealed no scleral icterus, a soft and nontender abdomen without palpable masses or organomegaly, and normal mental status. Atorvastatin and pioglitazone were discontinued on admission with rapid improvement in LFTs (see ). Liver biopsy was therefore not performed. The patient remained asymptomatic and was discharged on hospital day 4 with normalization of LFTs within 1 month. Simvastatin 20 mg daily and pioglitazone 15 mg daily were started 3 and 10 months after discharge, respectively. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen at 3 months again showed a likely granuloma but no steatosis. Serum LFTs have since remained within normal limits.
Before starting atorvastatin, the patient had been taking simvastatin 40 mg daily for 11 years for an elevated LDL-c of 137 mg/dL and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 18.9%. Other pertinent medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease. He had no history of ASCVD. His baseline serum LFTs were within normal limits. No change in LFTs or other side effects were noted while on simvastatin. His LDL-c reached a nadir of 74 mg/dL at age 70 years.
Three months prior to this presentation, the patient’s LDL-c was elevated to 93 mg/dL, at which point simvastatin was stopped and atorvastatin 80 mg daily was started. A goal LDL-c below 70 mg/dL was targeted for secondary prevention out of concern for prior ischemic stroke resulting in bilateral superior altitudinal hemianopsia noted on visual field testing 6 months prior. Pioglitazone 15 mg daily was started simultaneously with atorvastatin for an elevated hemoglobin A1c of 8.1%. He was continued on his other medications, including gabapentin 300 mg 3 times daily for diabetic neuropathy, glipizide 20 mg twice daily, lisinopril 5 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, omeprazole 20 mg twice daily, paroxetine 20 mg daily, and trazodone 100 mg as needed. Subsequent review of medication history revealed that he had not refilled his simvastatin for almost 6 weeks before starting on atorvastatin.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old male patient was admitted to the Department of Advanced General Dentistry at Yonsei University College of Dentistry on 2014, for a chief complaint of loosening of the restoration that was covering his teeth (). The patient had experienced a stroke in 2000 and was taking warfarin, 2.5 mg PO bid, due to atrial fibrillation. In addition, the patient was taking medications for hypertension (candesartan, atorvastatin, spironolactone, and carvedilol). At the time of admission, his INR value was 4.76. Clinical examination and radiological findings indicated the presence of residual root in the maxillary right second molar while existing restoration of the maxillary left canine, first premolar, and second premolar had fallen out. The Department of Cardiology at our hospital was consulted to determine whether the patient was operable and whether warfarin could be discontinued or changed. The response to the consultation was that the patient could receive dental treatments, and, in case of a high risk of bleeding, heparinization on an inpatient basis or use of low molecular weight heparins (LMWH) on an outpatient basis would be possible. Accordingly, extraction of the maxillary right residual root and prosthetic treatment following crown lengthening on the maxillary left canine, first premolar, and second premolar was planned. The treatment plan for the maxillary and mandibular missing posterior teeth (maxillary left first and second molars and mandibular right second molar) was to be reestablished after treating the area of chief complaint.
Warfarin was discontinued from three days prior to the treatment, and from two days prior to treatment, LMWH (Enoxaparin, Clexane, Sanofi-Aventis, France), 60 mg bid. was injected subcutaneously. On the day of treatment, LMWH injection was discontinued and full-mouth supragingival scaling and extraction of the maxillary right residual root were performed. Crown lengthening was performed by ostectomy of the alveolar bone after flap elevation on the area around the maxillary left canine and first and second premolars. In addition, dental pulp extirpation was performed on the maxillary left canine and second premolar. After suturing the area with 4–0 vicryl suture, hemostasis was confirmed by gauze biting for 1 hr. Starting from the evening of the day of treatment, subcutaneous injection of LMWH and warfarin administration was initiated. LMWH was continued for two more days. On the following day, hemostatic status was confirmed while dressing the area and the stitches were removed after one week. Subsequently, endodontic and prosthetic treatments were completed without discontinuing warfarin.
About one year after treatment completion, implant placement was planned on the left maxillary first and second molars (). Since medication was switched from warfarin to 20 mg of rivaroxaban (Xarelto, Bayer HealthCare AG, Germany) two months earlier, consultation was requested on whether surgery was feasible and whether the medication should be discontinued, to which the response was to discontinue rivaroxaban from the morning of the day before the procedure and to restart as soon as possible afterwards. The day of surgery, his systolic and diastolic blood pressures were 133 and 80 mmHg, respectively. After local anesthesia on the left maxillary first and second molars using 2 ampoules of 2% lidocaine containing 1:100,000 epinephrine, two implants (diameter 5.0 mm and length 8.0 mm) were placed with full thickness flap elevation () and a healing abutment (diameter 5.5 mm) was screwed onto the implants (). After suturing with 4–0 vicryl suture, pressure was applied with gauze to stop the bleeding and the patient was discharged on the same day after confirming that the bleeding had stopped.
On the day after the procedure, since there were no signs of infection or bleeding, the patient was instructed to restart rivaroxaban. On post-operative day (POD) 6, the patient visited the dental emergency room at our hospital around 4 AM for a chief complaint of spontaneous bleeding at the surgical site. Oozing bleeding in the area was observed, and pressure was applied with a gauze to stop the bleeding for about one hour, after which the patient was discharged after confirming that the bleeding had stopped (). On the same day, the patient visited our department again at about 5 PM for re-bleeding at the surgical site that had started about an hour earlier. However, the bleeding could not be stopped, despite applying pressure with gauze; therefore, oxidized regenerated cellulose (ORC) was applied to the bleeding area. After about an hour, the bleeding had stopped, but because of the possibility of continued bleeding, the decision was made to discontinue rivaroxaban for one day. On the next day (POD 7), the patient was admitted to the dental emergency room again at about 1 AM for bleeding in the same area. Slightly pulsating oozing bleeding was observed in the same area and the existing ORC was removed and new ORC was applied while simultaneously applying pressure with gauze to stop the bleeding. On POD 8, since no further bleeding was observed, the patient was instructed to restart rivaroxaban. One week thereafter (POD 14), the stitches were removed.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old man who lives alone in a two-bedroom condominium and still clocks forty hours a week as a city-bus mechanic arrived by private car to the emergency department shortly after noon, reporting four days of progressively heavier cough that turned rust-colored overnight, intermittent rigors, and a stabbing discomfort along the right costal margin whenever he tried to inhale fully; he deliberately skipped his morning lisinopril, furosemide, and sevelamer as well as his usual pre-shift coffee in order, in his words, “to let the numbers speak for themselves.” He denies pre-hospital acetaminophen, ibuprofen, inhalers, supplemental oxygen, or any intravenous fluids. His medical record lists a five-year history of ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction last measured at 30 %, along with stage-3 chronic kidney disease attributed to long-standing hypertension; outpatient serum creatinine has hovered in the upper 1.9 to low-2 mg/dL range for the past year without dialysis discussions. He has never been hospitalized for stroke, transient neurologic attacks, or hepatobiliary disorders, and he continues to maintain his own household chores without home-health assistance. Tobacco exposure totals twenty pack-years, but he quit eight years ago; alcohol is limited to a single can of beer on Saturday evenings, and he denies illicit drug use. Vaccination registry confirms both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza shot. On arrival he sat bolt upright on the stretcher, conversing in complete sentences, correctly stating the date, location, and the outcome of the morning sports broadcast. Skin was warm, lightly diaphoretic, and capillary refill was brisk; no peripheral cyanosis or clubbing was noted. Untreated triage vital signs on ambient air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.3 °C, regular radial pulse 74 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry, automated right-arm blood pressure 129/76 mm Hg corroborated manually, respirations 25 breaths per minute with mild intercostal recruitment, and fingertip pulse oximetry oscillating between 90 % and 91 %. Jugular venous contour rose to the level of the clavicle but not above while seated at 45°, and there was trace pitting edema at both ankles consistent with baseline. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and S2 with a soft third sound already documented previously and no new murmurs. Pulmonary examination demonstrated absent breath sounds with stony dull percussion over the lower third of the right posterior hemithorax, bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles just superior to that zone, and resonant left-sided fields without wheeze. Abdomen was soft, mildly protuberant, nontender, and without organomegaly. A brief neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, 5/5 strength throughout, and steady finger-to-nose testing. A capillary glucometer performed before vascular access measured 117 mg/dL. Peripheral venous samples and a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of bay entry, before any flushes larger than 3 mL of heparinized saline, antimicrobials, bronchodilators, diuretics, or crystalloid. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 37 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, the azotemia aligning with his outpatient trend. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 14.2 × 10⁹/L with 87 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 38 %, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, and platelets 232 × 10⁹/L. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, PaO₂ 77 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, depicting mild hypoxemia without significant acid–base disturbance. Serum lactate measured 1.8 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin remained below assay threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes after arrival—before any therapy—showed dense consolidation in the right middle and lower lobes with air bronchograms accompanied by a concave fluid layer that obliterated the right costophrenic angle, findings consistent with a moderate reactive collection; cardiac silhouette matched prior imaging, and mediastinal contours were stable. Twelve-lead electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm at 75 bpm with Q waves in the inferior leads unchanged from previous studies and no acute ST-segment shifts. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an induced sputum specimen, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any antimicrobial or supportive medication was ordered. Up to the moment this narrative is entered, the patient has received no intravenous fluids, no vasoactive agents, no antipyretics, and no supplemental oxygen beyond the 21 % inspired fraction in the room, ensuring that every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding above represents his untreated state at presentation.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old man arrived to the urgent musculoskeletal clinic late this morning reporting that his right lower leg had become “tight like a sausage” over the past day and a half, causing him to loosen the straps of his walking boot and prop the extremity on a stack of pillows at night. Nine days earlier he sustained a nondisplaced Weber A fibular fracture after slipping off a curb; in the emergency department at that time a posterior splint was applied, and two days later an orthopedic office visit converted the splint to a molded, circumferential below-knee plaster cast that extends from just distal to the tibial tuberosity to the metatarsal heads with the ankle held at neutral. He has remained otherwise active—he hops short distances on the contralateral leg using crutches, prepares his own meals in the kitchen, and sleeps in an upstairs bedroom—so he has not been confined to bed for any prolonged interval. His past history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1 000 mg twice daily, mild hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and seasonal allergic rhinitis; he has never had a blood clot, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, stroke, malignancy, or surgery, and there is no family history of thrombophilia. He denies tobacco; he drinks two cans of light beer on weekends and does not use illicit substances. Current medications are limited to metformin, atorvastatin, and as-needed acetaminophen; he takes no estrogen, testosterone, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants. Since the cast was placed he has adhered to the surgeon’s advice to keep the leg elevated when seated, but beginning yesterday morning he noted diffuse fullness in the posterior calf that did not abate with rest and by last evening an imprint from the edge of his sock lingered several minutes. He denies new trauma to the limb, fevers, rigors, sweats, skin abrasions, insect bites, rash, focal redness, groin mass, chest discomfort, dyspnea, cough, palpitations, abdominal pain, flank pain, dysuria, or unintended weight change. In triage—before any analgesic, fluid, or antithrombotic administration—vital signs were temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate 90 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air; he sat comfortably in a chair with the right leg resting on a stool, the cast split along its lateral aspect by staff for inspection but still otherwise intact. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed a crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs or gallops and clear lung fields throughout. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and without organomegaly; there were no jugular vein distention or peripheral edema elsewhere. Inspection of the lower extremities showed the casted limb to be noticeably fuller at mid-calf compared with the uninjured side; after the stockinette and padding were peeled back nurses used a cloth tape to measure 44.6 cm at a point exactly 10 cm below the inferior pole of the patella versus 40.2 cm on the left, a discrepancy of 4.4 cm. Fifteen centimeters above the patella both thighs measured 55.1 cm, and ankle girths at the malleoli were 29.3 cm on the right (inclusive of minimal cast padding) versus 28.7 cm on the left. Thumb pressure over the anteromedial tibial border of the symptomatic calf created a 4-mm depression that persisted approximately twenty seconds before rebounding; identical pressure on the contralateral leg rebounded immediately. The overlying skin beneath the cast appeared uniformly pink, was neither warmer nor cooler than the examiner’s hand, and displayed no serpiginous dilated channels, varicosities, ulcers, or brawny discoloration. Palpation was limited by the recent injury, yet gentle compression along the gastrocnemius and soleus bellies elicited only a diffuse sense of tightness without discrete cords or nodularity; range of motion at the knee was full, while ankle motion was restricted by the cast. Distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were palpable at 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill to all toes was under two seconds, protective sensation was intact to light touch, and motor strength of the contralateral limb remained 5/5. No inguinal or popliteal adenopathy was appreciated. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained before phlebotomy demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 88 beats min⁻¹ with no ST-T changes. Baseline laboratory tests drawn prior to any therapy revealed hemoglobin 13.8 g dL⁻¹, white blood cells 7.2 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, platelet count 247 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 138 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.2 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 0.96 mg dL⁻¹, alanine aminotransferase 22 U L⁻¹, aspartate aminotransferase 19 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 27 s. Plain radiographs obtained immediately after cast splitting showed the original fracture alignment unchanged and no new osseous lesion or soft-tissue gas. Clinical examination disclosed unilateral calf enlargement exceeding 3 cm accompanied by grade 1 pitting confined to the immobilized limb in a patient who has remained ambulatory and possesses no prior thrombotic history, systemic edema, or inflammatory signs to suggest another clear etiology; comprehensive venous duplex ultrasonography from the common femoral segment to infrapopliteal veins was therefore requested on an expedited basis while he awaits imaging in observation, hemodynamically stable, and before initiation of any anticoagulant therapy.

Patient note:
A 63-year-old man was admitted for chest discomfort, orthopnea, and dyspnea on exertion lasting 5 days. His initial vital signs included a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, a pulse rate of 80 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 20/min, and a body temperature of 36.6℃.
The jugular vein was engorged, but no hepatomegaly or audible cardiac murmurs were detected. The laboratory tests revealed the following: a hemoglobin, 11.3 g/dL; hematocrit, 35.3%; white blood cell (WBC) count, 9,550/mm3; platelet count, 254,000/mm3; blood urea nitrogen, 14 mg/dL; serum creatinine, 1.0 mg/dL; alanine aminotransferase, 58 IU/L; aspartate aminotransferase, 40 IU/L; total bilirubin, 0.9 mg/dL; glucose, 166 mg/dL; lactate dehydrogenase, 444 IU/L; protein, 6.4 g/dL; and albumin, 3.7 g/dL. Chest radiography showed an increased cardiac silhouette with a round, flask-like appearance (). Computed tomography and transthoracic echocardiography showed a large inhomogeneous and focally-enhancing mass in the right atrium, and a massive amount of pericardial and right pleural effusion ().
While in the emergency room, the blood pressure dropped to 80/54 mmHg and the pulse rate increased to 101 beats/min; the patient complained of severe dyspnea and chest pain, suggesting cardiac tamponade. An emergency pericardiocentesis and drainage was performed. The pericardial effusion was blood-like in color; an effusion analysis showed the following: hemoglobin, 11.9 g/dL; red blood cell (RBC) count, 2.95×106/mm3; WBC, 15,210/mm3 (lymphocytes, 68%; neutrophils, 23%), glucose, 109 mg/dL; lactate dehydrogenase, 591 IU/L; and protein, 5.6 g/dL. The initial drainage of the pericardial effusion was 800 mL. There were no malignant cells in the pericardial effusion cytology. The chest pain and dyspnea were improved immediately after the pericardiocentesis. Transesophageal echocardiography showed a 5.5×5 cm mass without invasion of the inferior and superior vena cava ().
On hospital day (HD) 5, surgery was performed. After the mass was resected, the right atrium was repaired with a bovine pericardial patch. The mass was close to the tricuspid valve (only 2 mm from the resection margin). On HD 7, the patient was transferred to the general ward and on HD 13 he was discharged. The patient was scheduled to receive adjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
At the time of biopsy, a 6.8×6.5×2.5 cm gray-brown protruding endocardial mass was noted in the right atrial chamber. The pericardium was spared of malignant cells. The cut surface was diffusely hemorrhagic with a gray-white solid portion. The tumor was comprised of oval-to-spindle cells with intracytoplasmic RBCs. There were frequent mitoses (> 10/10 HPF). The tumor cells were positive for CD34 immunohistochemical staining with confirmed primary cardiac angiosarcoma ().

Patient note:
A 45-year-old man with a background of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, biopsy-proven alcoholic steato-hepatitis diagnosed two years earlier, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease last documented with a baseline creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL was brought to the emergency department by his roommate after being discovered at dawn sprawled across the living-room carpet, drenched in sweat, mumbling incoherently, and clutching his lower abdomen. According to the roommate, the patient had complained for four days of burning dysuria, suprapubic discomfort, and intermittent rigors, had taken no prescribed insulin for 24 hours because of nausea, and had produced scant dark urine despite drinking “jugs of cola.” No oral or parenteral antibiotics, antipyretics, intravenous fluids, or sedatives had been given prior to arrival. During the six-minute ambulance ride he remained un-intubated, coughing weakly yet able to clear secretions, and breathed through a tight non-rebreather mask set at 15 L/min that the crew’s built-in sensor estimated was delivering an inspired fraction of 0.64; oxygen saturations fluctuated in the mid-80s en route, and no positive-pressure device was applied. A single 20-gauge antecubital cannula was placed for a keep-open rate of lactated Ringer’s at 30 mL/h, but no bolus or vasopressor infusion was started. On stretcher entry to the resuscitation bay—before any hospital-initiated therapy—he lay semi-recumbent, diaphoretic, and tachypnoeic with shallow respirations at 32/min, accessory-muscle use of the sternocleidomastoids, and audible end-expiratory groans. Oscillometric vitals recorded immediately showed a heart rate of 132 beats/min in sinus rhythm, an initial blood-pressure reading of 81/43 mm Hg repeated manually with the same result, temperature 38.9 °C tympanic, and pulse oximetry 87 % on the unchanged facemask. Capillary refill exceeded five seconds, the fingertips were cool and mottled, and jugular venous pulsation was not visible at 45°. Pupils measured 3 mm symmetrically and were sluggishly reactive; he opened his eyes only to loud verbal stimuli, uttered inappropriate words that failed to form sentences, and withdrew purposefully from painful nail-bed pressure, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 10. A right radial arterial catheter was seated on the first attempt within three minutes of arrival; the simultaneous blood gas—drawn while he continued to breathe spontaneously on 0.64 FiO₂—demonstrated a pH of 7.25, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, lactate 5.6 mmol/L, and a PaO₂ of 121 mm Hg. Chest examination revealed coarse crackles at both bases without wheeze; percussion was dull posteriorly, and transmitted voice sounds were mildly increased. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a rapid regular rhythm with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was distended and tender suprapubically with a palpable, firm bladder edge suggesting retention; flank percussion elicited bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness. Skin survey showed spider angiomata over the upper chest, scattered ecchymoses on the shins, and no peripheral edema. A 16-French Foley catheter passed during the primary survey produced 30 mL of cloudy, malodorous urine immediately; the roommate presented a smartphone note used for blood-glucose tracking that documented only 770 mL total voided in the preceding twenty-four hours. Point-of-care ultrasound performed before any crystalloid bolus visualized a thick-walled, dilated bladder with echogenic debris, moderate bilateral hydronephrosis, an underfilled inferior vena cava measuring 0.8 cm collapsing completely with inspiration, and a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Peripheral blood obtained concurrently with the arterial sample—prior to any antibiotics, insulin, fluids, or vasoactive agents—revealed a white-blood-cell count of 24.7 × 10³/µL with 19 % band forms, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, and a platelet count of 168 000 /µL. Basic metabolic panel showed sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L, an anion gap of 22, glucose 468 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.55 mg/dL. Hepatic chemistries returned aspartate aminotransferase 98 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 84 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 246 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.4, and total bilirubin 2.15 mg/dL, predominantly conjugated. High-sensitivity troponin was <0.02 ng/mL, C-reactive protein exceeded 300 mg/L, and serum ketones were positive at 3.8 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph taken while the facemask remained in place demonstrated faint bilateral patchy opacities without focal consolidation, an elevated right hemidiaphragm, and no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Plain abdominal film showed a distended bladder pushing bowel loops aside but no free air. Twelve-lead electrocardiography recorded sinus tachycardia at 128 beats/min with diffuse peaked T waves and a corrected QT interval of 444 ms. Up to this exact juncture—before a single milliliter of resuscitation fluid, vasopressor, antimicrobial, or insulin had been administered—the patient remained spontaneously breathing through a high-flow facemask delivering 64 % oxygen with an arterial oxygen tension of 121 mm Hg, exhibited a persistently low arterial pressure of 81/43 mm Hg without pharmacologic support, displayed near-normal platelet numbers, had moderate hyperbilirubinemia on a background of chronic liver injury, demonstrated acute kidney insult superimposed on chronic disease with creatinine 2.55 mg/dL and oliguria of 770 mL/day, and showed a depressed sensorium quantified as a Glasgow Coma Score of 10 in the setting of presumed septic bladder outlet obstruction complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis and early acute lung involvement.
