Patient note:
A 49-year-old Caucasian woman presented to emergency department with sudden onset of right fronto-temporal throbbing headache for 1 day. It started as 3/10 in severity and then progressed to 10/10 in about half hour. The headache was associated with right eye pain, nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia as well as chills but no fever. She denied any vision changes, dizziness, speech difficulty, focal weakness, rash, joint pains, neck pain, or rigidity. The patient was previously healthy with no history of chronic medical problems except recurrent sinus infections as well as environmental allergies. Her medications included fexofenadine and oral combined contraceptive pills (OCPs), which she has been taking regularly for 10 years for menorrhagia. She had neither personal nor family history of blood clots, bleeding disorders, or any malignancy. She never smoked but used to drink alcohol socially. The patient had no history of abortion or difficulty getting pregnant. She had three pregnancies; last one was at the age of 35 with no complications. Her mother had three miscarriages while being on phenobarbital for epilepsy. Physical examination showed normal vital signs with blood pressure of 127/70 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats/min, temperature 98.2°F (36.8°C), respiratory rate 14 per min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She was alert, oriented to time, place, and person, and in no distress; cardiopulmonary examination revealed clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes or rhonchi, and normal heart sounds with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Abdominal exam showed no tenderness, masses, or organomegaly, and she had no edema of the lower extremities. Detailed neurological examination showed intact cranial nerves 2–12 and round, reactive pupils to light and accommodation with normal fundi. She had normal and symmetric motor power in both upper and lower extremities, intact sensation, and no focal neurologic deficit.
Complete blood count was abnormal for leukocytosis of 18.6 K/µL with higher lymphocyte differential count of 21% and no bands. Complete metabolic panel and coagulation studies were within normal limits. Infectious workup including blood cultures was negative. The patient was given ketorolac and hydromorphone, but failed to relieve her headache; so computed tomography (CT) of the head without contrast was done that showed venous sinus thrombosis involving the posterior sagittal sinus and extending into the dominant right transverse sinus (). CT head with contrast was done for confirmation (); it showed occlusive thrombus within the posterior superior sagittal sinus, extending inferiorly into the dominant right transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and superior right internal jugular vein. The diagnosis of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis was made based on the patient's presentation and CT findings. Her OCPs were stopped. Anticoagulation was started with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) that was switched to warfarin with an international normalized ratio (INR) target range of 2.0 to 3.0. She received warfarin for 3 months and then switched to low-dose aspirin. Further workup during her hospital stay including carotid artery Doppler and transthoracic echocardiogram was negative. Follow-up CT head 3 months after the initial diagnosis showed complete recanalization of the occluded cerebral sinuses and veins.
Three weeks after completion of anticoagulation, the patient underwent testing for prothrombotic conditions, including protein S, protein C, and antithrombin deficiency; antiphospholipid syndrome; prothrombin G20210A mutation; and factor V Leiden; all were negative.

Patient note:
A 54-year-old male patient without relevant medical history was referred to the emergency department (ED) due to dyspnoea with an oxygen saturation of 85%, tachypnoea, and tachycardia. He reported a general fatigue, increased stress at work as a salesman, a single episode of angina, and a flight journey of 1.25 h 7 days prior to admission. The electrocardiogram (ECG) showed new T-wave inversions in the anterior leads (V1–V5). Laboratory analysis indicated global respiratory insufficiency, troponinemia (high sensitive troponin T of 77.3 ng/L, cut-off <14.0 ng/L), elevation of the N-terminal fragment of pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), and D-Dimer. Consecutive thoracic computer tomography (CT) revealed the presence of subsegmental PE, but no pathological masses. Aetiological clarification revealed multiple DVT and elevated factor VIII in thrombophilia screening.
For cardiac assessment and additional clarification of newly observed T negativities, TTE showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50%, with hypokinesia, but no signs of intraventricular masses. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries.
To clarify ECG and laboratory abnormalities and considering also inflammatory causes and myocarditis as aetiology, we conducted a CMR, which did not show any Gadolinium enhancement nor oedema or other abnormalities in the myocardium. As an incidental finding, a partially fixed and partially floating mass measuring 32 mm × 11 mm () at the lateral wall of the right ventricle was detected. It showed hyperintense characteristics in T1w and T2w compared to the myocardium, absent mass perfusion at first-pass perfusion and no uptake of contrast with homogeneous signal suppression within the mass at EGE and LGE (), thus, according to the criteria of standardized CMR tissue characterization, indicating thrombotic nature of the mass., Hyperintense appearance of this thrombus in T1w and T2w sequences indicated its recent character.
Considering the stable cardiopulmonary condition and morphology of the thrombus, we waived surgical embolectomy, thrombolysis or percutaneous retrieval, and continued anticoagulation instead. Follow-up CMR after 3 months showed complete resolution of the thrombus.

Patient note:
A 63-year-old female patient was admitted to the Galactophore Department, Bao Ji Central Hospital with a huge lump in the left breast. The patient stated that they had identified a thumb-sized lump two years earlier, but that they had ignored it. From July 2011, the patient observed that the lump was growing rapidly; in February 2012 the lump had become so large that the patient’s left chest was entirely covered with a solid, irregularly-shaped, somewhat moveable mass of tremendous size and the patient was barely able to lie in the prone position. Family members then finally convinced the patient to seek medical attention. Upon physical examination, the patient presented with an elastic hard mass in the left breast that was 45 cm in diameter, with a circumference of 97 cm (). Rapid growth had resulted in shiny stretched skin that was translucent, showing underlying extremely enlarged veins with sections of the circuitous veins about to undergo ulceration, although no bleeding or discharge was noted. The lymph nodes in the axillary and other superficial areas were not palpable. The patient’s previous medical history revealed that they had high blood pressure, diabetes and atrial fibrillation. Moreover, the patient had suffered from a cerebral infarction; the patient’s right side was paralyzed and communicative disorders had appeared two years previously. The patient was unable to care for herself due to the cerebral infarction. The patient’s medical history was negative for allergies, smoking, drinking, contagions and serious addiction. Furthermore, there was no family history of breast cancer on either side of the patient’s family.
Due to the non-compressible nature of the mass and the size of the tumor, regular breast examinations, including mammography and ultrasound studies, could not be used, while a computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest revealed a solid mass. Total body scintigraphy was negative. Comprehensive examinations and detailed assessments were additionally performed on the patient due to the presence of high blood pressure, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and cerebral infarction. In order to ensure the long-term success of the treatment, a consultation with the Respiratory Medicine, Vasculocardiology, Neurology and Anesthesiology departments was organized. Antihypertensive, glycemic control, oxygen uptake and antiarrhythmic therapies were administered prior to surgery. The pectoris major and minor had atrophied and were tightly adhered to the tumor due to long-term compression, so the surgeon decided to resect the mass along with these muscles. The mass was resected subsequent to 3 hours of surgery (). The post-operative pathology report showed an extremely large grey mass, weighing 11 kg and measuring 36×40×18 cm, which was covered by ∼32×35 cm of skin tissue. When the tumor was cut into halves along the nipple, it was observed that the majority of the tumor tissue was a myxoid, lobulated mass with multiple hollow cavities, thick, yellow, viscous fluid and certain necrotic areas. The microscopy findings showed extensive necrosis and the majority of the tumor tissue exhibited an epithelial component with a leaf-like pattern, but no cellular atypia. The final histopathological diagnosis was PT of the benign type ().
In view of the benign nature of this tumor, no chemotherapy or radiotherapy was administered following surgery. The patient recovered well and to date there has been no evidence of local recurrence or distant metastasis.

Patient note:
A 48-year-old female patient presented to the emergency department (ED) after CPR due to VF that occurred after a seizure. Four years prior, she presented to other hospital ED and discharged after observation for a condition where her arms were raised and her limbs were stretched continually for approximately 1 min while sleeping after an episode of alcohol intake. She did not undergo any particular tests and neither was she administered any drugs, under the assumption that these symptoms were temporary and had been caused by alcohol intake. Three years prior, a similar episode occurred during sleep, for which some medical tests were conducted such as electrocardiogram (ECG), brain MRI, and electroencephalogram (EEG), but no conclusive results were reported. Drugs were also prescribed but not taken by the patient. One and a half year prior, the patient experienced another relapse again during sleep at dawn. According to the statement given by her husband who witnessed the episode at the time, for approximately 1 min while sleeping, the patient groaned with her mouth shut tightly, her arms raised, limbs stretched, and did not respond when called. Subsequently, her body collapsed, she stopped breathing for approximately 30–40 s, and then she breathed in a concentrated manner. Urination and post-ictal confusion were also noted. The patient had no family history of epilepsy or no medical history of febrile convulsion in the past, and only reported of the inability to sleep well and waking up frequently due to a burning sensation in the foot. In the previous hospital, the patient underwent video-EEG and polysomnography in an epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) for two days to investigate the cause under the putative diagnosis of restless legs syndrome and nocturnal bilateral tonic seizure – frontal lobe epilepsy. Based on EEG findings, there was no inter-ictal epileptiform discharge and an intermittent slow wave was observed in the right frontotemporal area, but it was equivocal, and therefore, no clear abnormality was reported. Subsequently, administration of pramipexole and pregabalin was started to control the rare nocturnal seizures and symptoms of the restless legs syndrome under the putative diagnosis of restless legs syndrome and unknown etiologic epilepsy – bilateral tonic seizure.
On the day before current admission, her epileptic seizure relapsed during sleep but she recovered consciousness immediately; thus, she did not come to the hospital. In the evening of the admission day, while conversing with her children, she suddenly had a general tonic-clonic type seizure for 2–3 mins and emergency medical services (EMS) were informed as she did not recover consciousness immediately after the seizure like in previous episodes and her breathing was almost negligible. Following the instructions of the EMS center, her family started CPR. After the paramedics arrived, spontaneous circulation was restored after CPR and 2 times of defibrillation as VF was indicated by the AED findings (). At the time of ED arrival, the patient was stupor and her vital signs and oxygen saturation were normal with a blood pressure of 121/82 mmHg, pulse rate of 80 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 16 breathes per minute, and body temperature of 36.2°C. ECG performed immediately after arrival showed a sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 78 beats per minute and QTc duration of 401 ms (). The initial arterial blood gas analysis (ABGA) showed a pH of 7.35, PCO2 21 mmHg, PO2 134 mmHg, HCO3 11.6 mEq/L, and a lactate level of 6.1 mg/dL. Approximately 10 min after arrival, she regained consciousness but Todd’s paralysis in the right limbs and global aphasia were shown. The repeat ABGA showed that all values had recovered to normal levels. All other blood test results were normal, including electrolyte and myocardial enzyme levels. Levetiracetam was administered intravenously in the ED. Brain diffusion MRI showed no abnormality. Thereafter, the patient was admitted to the cardiology intensive care unit (ICU) and received a full cardiologic work-up. After admission to the ICU, her consciousness was maintained in an alert state, the paralysis in the right limbs and aphasia resolved completely, and the EEG showed normal results. Transthoracic echocardiography performed on the day after admission showed that the left ventricle ejection fraction (LVEF) was reduced to 44%, and left ventricle global hypokinesia and moderate systolic dysfunction were observed. After that, consecutively performed coronary angiography (CAG), spasm provocation test, cardiac MRI, and 24-hr Holter monitoring showed normal results. For the purpose of preventing sudden cardiac death (SCD), the insertion of an implantable cardiac defibrillator (ICD) was recommended. The patient was discharged without any complications 6 days after the procedure. Currently, levetiracetam administration is being maintained by the neurology department and her condition is being periodically followed by the cardiology department under the diagnosis of aborted SCD due to VF and heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction.

question:
Patient note:
A 77-year-old man arrived by private automobile in the early afternoon after two days of progressive breathlessness that culminated in an early-morning episode in which he found himself gasping for air while seated at the kitchen table sipping coffee. He described the illness as beginning with mild chills, a dry cough, and low-grade fever the previous evening; overnight the cough became productive of tan sputum and he awoke drenched in perspiration, feeling “winded just standing up.” His spouse checked an oral temperature of 100.6 °F and, noting labored respirations, insisted on transport to the emergency department before any over-the-counter medications were taken. The patient lives in a single-story house, performs his own activities of daily living, and had walked the quarter-mile to the neighborhood mailbox without difficulty four days earlier; he has never required institutional care. His medical background is notable for long-standing systolic dysfunction with a most recent outpatient echocardiogram six months ago reporting an ejection fraction of 35 % and mild concentric hypertrophy. Nephrology follows him for Stage 4 chronic kidney disease related to decades of hypertensive nephrosclerosis; baseline serum creatinine last month measured 2.6 mg/dL and he has not yet required renal replacement therapy. He also carries a diagnosis of anemia of chronic disease for which no transfusions have been necessary, with a baseline hematocrit in the mid-20s. He denies prior transient ischemic attacks or cerebrovascular accidents, has no chronic liver disorder, and has never been treated for malignancy. Medications taken routinely include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 24-26 mg twice daily, oral furosemide 40 mg each morning, amlodipine 5 mg nightly, and low-dose aspirin; he had ingested only his usual morning pills and half a cup of oatmeal before leaving home today. He quit smoking 25 years ago after a 20-pack-year exposure, drinks one glass of wine at holiday gatherings, and denies illicit drug use. Immunizations are current, including the seasonal influenza vaccine administered at a grocery-store clinic six weeks earlier and both pneumococcal injections within the past three years. Emergency medical services were not activated, and no supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, or antipyretics were given en route. In triage he sat leaning forward with elbows on his knees, speaking in short phrases yet fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Untreated vital signs documented temperature 38.1 °C, heart rate 105 beats per minute and regular, non-invasive blood pressure 109/66 mm Hg (systolic confirmed manually), respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute with visible alae nasi flaring, and pulse oximetry 86 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic; mucous membranes were tacky. Jugular venous pulsation rose approximately 4 cm above the sternal angle, similar to cardiology notes. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid S1 and S2 with a soft third sound, no new murmurs, and no pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination showed coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower and posterior mid-lung zones without dullness to percussion, and vesicular breath sounds elsewhere; no wheezes were heard. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge was not palpable and there was no shifting dullness. Extremities were warm without cyanosis or edema, and capillary refill was brisk. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated equal, reactive pupils, intact cranial nerves, fluent speech, and full strength in all extremities. Finger-stick glucose prior to cannulation was 129 mg/dL. Venous blood samples and a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival while the patient remained on room air. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 119 mEq/L, potassium 4.9 mEq/L, chloride 93 mEq/L, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 49 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, consistent with his chronic baseline trends except for the hyponatremia. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 15.2 × 10⁹/L (88 % neutrophils), hematocrit 23 %, hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, and platelets 240 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas obtained on ambient air showed pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, PaO₂ 54 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation and significant hypoxemia. Serum lactate measured 2.6 mmol/L. A portable posteroanterior and lateral chest radiograph, performed before any therapy, demonstrated a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, clear costophrenic angles, and a cardiothoracic ratio unchanged from prior imaging, with no evidence of fluid layering. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram captured concurrently showed sinus tachycardia at 106 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave changes identical to outpatient tracings. Two sets of blood cultures, an expectorated sputum sample sent for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were collected prior to antibiotic administration. At the moment this note is completed the patient continues to breathe room air in a semi-upright position, has received no intravenous crystalloids, vasopressors, oxygen supplementation, diuretics, or antimicrobials beyond the small heparinized flush used for arterial sampling; thus all physiologic observations and laboratory data detailed above reflect his untreated baseline presentation.

question:
Patient note:
A 27-year-old man (75 kg) presented to our emergency department and was monitored by a cardiologist. Dissection occurred following weightlifting across his chest and shoulders. He described multiple episodes of faintness over the preceding hours. These were associated with sweating, dyspnea, and temporal right eye vision deficit. The first episode began during heavy weight lifting (180 kg) and lasted 10 minutes before resolving with rest and drinking fluids. The second episode began while lifting weights again, which was more intense in severity and lasted for 20 minutes. The third fainting episode occurred when he left the gym, whereby he fell over the floor outside the club. The patient was a coach and a professional bodybuilder. During the first lifting, he remembered weight training heavier than his normal regimen involving squatting with weights of around 140 kg in the supine position across the anterior chest wall. He initially denied taking illicit drugs but, upon insistence, he confessed that he took intramuscular 250 mg testosterone twice per week and human growth hormone 20 mg/day for two years. In the emergency room, the patient’s vital signs were a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, heart rate of 120 beats/min, respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min, and temperature of 36 oC. Blood chemistry revealed increased levels of cardiac troponin (up to 7.6 ng/mL) and creatine kinase (CK) (up to 597 IU/L). Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed ascending aorta dissection with severe aortic regurgitation. The patient underwent emergency cardiac surgery.

Patient note:
A 43-year-old female with no previously documented neurologic disease was transported to the emergency department by ambulance after being discovered unresponsive in her apartment by a family member approximately 45 minutes prior to arrival; empty blister packs of oxycodone and several partly consumed alcoholic beverage cans were noted at the scene, raising concern for a mixed drug ingestion. On arrival she is lying supine on the stretcher, flaccid except for intermittent posturing, with dried emesis on the right side of her face and mild perioral cyanosis. Initial vital signs are temperature 36.1 °C, heart rate 118 beats/min, blood pressure 102/64 mm Hg, respiratory rate 8 breaths/min with shallow, irregular effort, and oxygen saturation 89 % on room air, improving to 95 % after placement of a non-rebreather mask. The pupils are equal at 4 mm and sluggishly reactive; despite verbal coaxing, clapping near the ears, and a firm supraorbital notch pressure, her eyelids remain firmly closed without even a brief flutter. She does not track or fix on light. When her name is shouted and she is asked simple orientation questions, she emits only low-pitched, guttural moans devoid of recognizable words or phrases, and there is no attempt at purposeful articulation even when her family name is repeated loudly beside her ear. Airway inspection shows copious saliva mixed with gastric contents; gag reflex is present though weak. Cranial nerve exam is otherwise limited but reveals a grimace to nail-bed pressure. Motor assessment demonstrates that painful stimuli applied to the trapezius and to the ulnar nerve on the forearm elicit a stereotyped abnormal movement in which both elbows briskly flex, wrists pronate, and the arms draw toward the thorax while the lower extremities remain extended and internally rotated; no purposeful withdrawal or localization is seen. Tone is otherwise low, and deep tendon reflexes are 1+ throughout. There is no spontaneous movement of the limbs at rest. Based on these findings, her overall Glasgow Coma Scale is estimated at 6. Skin survey shows several old ecchymoses on the upper arms but no fresh trauma. Breath sounds are coarse bilaterally with scattered rhonchi; heart sounds are tachycardic but regular without murmurs. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, and bowel sounds are hypoactive. Point-of-care glucose is 92 mg/dL. Laboratory studies are pending at the time of this note; an arterial blood gas drawn on supplemental oxygen shows pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 60 mm Hg, PaO₂ 110 mm Hg, bicarbonate 28 mEq/L, base excess ‑2 mEq/L. A urinary catheter has not yet been inserted. Past medical history per family includes chronic low-back pain managed with opioids, hypertension controlled with lisinopril, and a prior episode of major depressive disorder three years ago without hospitalization. She reportedly consumed “several glasses of wine” earlier in the evening. Medications at home include lisinopril 10 mg daily and oxycodone 10 mg every eight hours as needed; no allergies are known. Social history is significant for smoking one pack-year in adolescence but none since, and occasional alcohol use. Family history is noncontributory. No prior surgeries. There is no documentation of seizures, diabetes, or intracranial events in the past. At this juncture the airway remains at risk due to depressed consciousness and possible aspiration, and anesthesiology has been paged for definitive airway management while the toxicology and neurocritical care teams are being consulted.

question:
Patient note:
Our patient was a 73-year-old female with history of Ebstein anomaly, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on home oxygen, presented to the hospital with 1-week history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion and peripheral edema. Transthoracic echocardiography performed 2 years ago revealed mild tricuspid regurgitation and a suspected patent foramen ovale with left-to-right shunt by color Doppler.
On presentation, she had severe hypoxemia with room air oxygen saturation of 66% and partial pressure oxygen of 33 mmHg. A trial of bilevel positive airway pressure led to no improvement. She was started on empiric anticoagulation for suspected pulmonary embolism until a CT scan ruled it out. After a trial of diuretics without improvement in oxygenation, the patient was intubated and nitric oxide was initiated to facilitate transfer to a tertiary care hospital.
Postintubation transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular systolic function, severely enlarged right ventricle with apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets (consistent with Ebstein anomaly) (), severe tricuspid regurgitation, and a patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunt at rest. Examination revealed an oxygen saturation of 80% on 100% fraction of inspired oxygen and high dose nitric oxide with evidence of peripheral cyanosis.
The patient underwent right heart catheterization demonstrating marginally elevated pulmonary artery pressure (mean pulmonary artery pressure 23 mmHg), elevated right atrial pressure (mean right atrial pressure 12 mmHg), and an oxygen step-down from the pulmonary veins to left ventricle. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed significant flow of the tricuspid regurgitation jet through the patent foramen ovale (Figures 
, video).
Percutaneous closure of the patent foramen ovale was undertaken with a 30 mm Gore Septal Occluder device. The defect was not measured with a sizing balloon and the 30 mm device was selected to ensure complete defect coverage. This led to resolution of shunting and instantaneously improved arterial saturations (); however, the patient had significant deterioration in overall hemodynamics (20 mmHg systolic drop in systemic pressure, central venous pressure increase from 11 to 17, and mixed venous oxygen saturation of 35%). A 10 mm smaller device (20 mm Gore Septal Occluder) was selected for partial closure of the patent foramen ovale resulting in acceptable hemodynamics and reduction in right-to-left shunting (). The patient recovered, had no evidence of worsening right heart failure or peripheral edema, and was discharged home. Transthoracic echocardiography performed 3 months after patent foramen ovale closure demonstrated a moderate residual shunt present with right-to-left passage of saline contrast at rest.

Patient note:
A 54-year-old woman with a background of insulin-treated type 2 diabetes mellitus, mild persistent asthma controlled on an inhaled corticosteroid–long-acting β₂ agonist combination, and well-documented generalized myasthenia gravis (baseline negative inspiratory force −40 cm H₂O, most recent crisis three years prior) was transported to the emergency department from an outpatient neurology infusion suite after nursing staff noticed a sudden loss of airway control during routine intravenous immunoglobulin therapy; within two minutes she developed agonal gasps and became cyanotic, prompting the clinic physician to perform rapid-sequence intubation with etomidate and rocuronium using a 7.5-mm cuffed endotracheal tube and to connect her to a transport ventilator set at a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, rate 18 breaths per minute, and an inspired oxygen fraction of 0.33 without added positive end-expiratory pressure. No sedative infusion was started en route, and no vasopressors, antibiotics, or crystalloid boluses were administered before arrival. In the resuscitation bay ten minutes later, she remained on the same ventilatory settings; the first arterial blood gas obtained from a right radial line while the ventilator parameters were untouched revealed a PaO₂ of 104 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 39 mm Hg, pH 7.37, and bicarbonate 23 mEq/L. Vital signs recorded simultaneously showed temperature 36.9 °C by temporal scanner, heart rate 82 beats per minute in sinus rhythm on telemetry, respiratory rate equal to the set 18 breaths per minute with no patient-initiated efforts, and an automated cuff blood pressure of 130/78 mm Hg that matched manual measurement, with warm extremities and brisk capillary refill suggesting intact perfusion despite the neuromuscular paralysis. A brief pause in the ventilator alarms allowed neurologic assessment; there was no spontaneous eye opening, no phonation around the endotracheal tube with cuff momentarily deflated, and no motor response to deep supra-orbital pressure, yielding a composite Glasgow Coma Score of 1. Pupils were isocoric at 3 mm and sluggishly reactive, corneal reflexes were present, and doll’s-eye movements were absent. Lung auscultation revealed equal breath sounds without wheeze or crackle, and the tube depth measured 22 cm at the incisors. Cardiac examination demonstrated a regular rhythm without murmurs, jugular veins were not distended at 30°, and no peripheral edema was appreciated. The abdomen was soft and non-tender; bowel sounds were hypoactive. Skin inspection uncovered scattered ecchymoses on the dorsal forearms from recent intravenous line attempts but no petechiae or rash. A Foley catheter inserted in triage drained clear yellow urine, and nursing documentation from her infusion unit together with the 120 mL collected in the emergency department indicated an aggregate output of approximately 1 800 mL over the prior twenty-four hours. Initial laboratory studies, all drawn before any medications were given in our facility, demonstrated white-blood-cell count 11.4 × 10³/µL, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, and a platelet count of 132 000 /µL. Serum electrolytes returned sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.65 mg/dL compared with her baseline of 1.1 mg/dL noted in the neuromuscular clinic four months earlier. Total bilirubin was 0.5 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 29 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 94 U/L. Lactate measured 1.8 mmol/L, coagulation profile showed an international normalized ratio of 1.2, and arterial carboxyhemoglobin was undetectable. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave changes but no acute ischemia. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained moments after she was transferred to the trauma stretcher showed the endotracheal tube tip 4 cm above the carina, clear lung fields, and no mediastinal widening or pleural effusion. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound revealed a mildly dilated left atrium but preserved biventricular function, with a collapsible inferior vena cava suggesting she was not volume overloaded. The patient’s spouse arrived with medication bottles confirming nightly pyridostigmine, prednisone tapered to 10 mg daily, and no recent use of fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides. She denied alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use, and there was no history of liver disease, explaining the normal bilirubin. According to family, the patient had been fully alert and conversant thirty minutes before the sentinel episode, complaining only of facial muscle fatigue, without dysphagia, fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. At the moment all the above measurements were documented, no reversal agents, corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin adjustments, or hemodynamic supports had yet been administered; she remained sedative-free and paralyzed, mechanically ventilated on 0.33 FiO₂ with an arterial oxygen tension of 104 mm Hg, hemodynamically stable at 130/78 mm Hg, with mild thrombocytopenia, modest renal insufficiency, an exceptionally low composite neurologic score of 1, negligible bilirubin elevation, and adequate urine output of 1 800 mL per day.

Patient note:
A 79-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension and mild Alzheimer’s dementia presented with acute onset loss of consciousness in the community. She was a passenger in a car and found to be unresponsive, with a family member reporting absence of a palpable pulse. She was presumed to have had a cardiac arrest and received 2 min of cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the community before the return of spontaneous circulation was noted. Paramedics arrived, and she was transported to a regional secondary hospital, triaged as a cardiac arrest. She was unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 3 and intubated on arrival. On arrival, she was in sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 84 beats/min. Her blood pressure was 140/110 mm Hg. The blood glucose reading was 6.7 mmol/L. Her neurological deficits were difficult to determine as she was unresponsive, but there was no obvious focal neurology. On examination, her lung fields were clear and she had dual heart sounds. There was no evidence of an infective aetiology on further history and examination. She was transferred to a tertiary hospital on the same day for further work-up in light of her ongoing reduced level of consciousness. The patient was extubated 24 hours later, with her GCS improving to 13–14 over the next day.

Patient note:
We describe the case of a 79-year-old woman, with a history of atrial fibrillation, who had undergone left atrial appendage (LAA) closure device implantation due to contraindication for anticoagulation because of a previous subdural haemorrhage. She was admitted for elective mitral valve replacement due to asymptomatic severe primary mitral regurgitation caused by anterior veil prolapse. An echocardiogram performed a month before showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 56% and normal LV diameters. CT-angiography prior to surgery showed absence of coronary lesions. On admission, cardiac auscultation revealed a systolic murmur in mitral focus at the apex. Lung auscultation was normal. Prior to the surgery, the patient was on acetylsalicylic acid 100 mg/day. Cardiac surgery was uneventful. Since valve repair was not considered feasible, a Magna Ease biological mitral valve was implanted, maintaining the LAA closure device. Intra-operative transoesophageal echocardiography showed normal functioning of the prosthesis and extracorporeal circulation was concluded. Only low doses of noradrenaline (0.05 μg/kg/min) were required after extracorporeal circulation.
On arrival to the intensive care unit (ICU), the patient presented with cardiogenic shock: she presented cold extremities and oliguria, systolic blood pressure was 80 mmHg and blood analysis showed metabolic acidosis and elevated serum lactate; therefore, requiring vasoactive agents (noradrenaline at 0.1 μg/kg/min and dobutamine at 5 μg/kg/min). An electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed atrial flutter with a rapid ventricular rate (150 b.p.m.), which was electrically cardioverted. An ECG performed after cardioversion showed inverted T waves in precordial leads () and pulmonary congestion was evidenced on chest X-ray (). The findings of an echocardiogram showed severe LV dysfunction (LVEF 20%) with mid to distal diffuse hypokinesia that was more severe in the anterior and septal walls, which were almost akinetic. Contractility was much better in all basal segments (, Video S). Mitral prosthesis function was normal. Owing to a suspected coronary complication secondary to cardiac surgery, the patient underwent urgent coronary angiography, which showed absence of significant coronary lesions (, Video S). Troponin I levels were elevated to 0.12 ng/mL (normal value <0.08). Her haemodynamic status was compromised for the following 48 h, during which time vasoactive drugs (noradrenaline ranging from 0.1 to 0.2 μg/kg/min and dobutamine ranging from 5 to 7 μg/kg/min, adjusted to haemodynamic status) and intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation were needed. Daily echocardiographic evaluations showed similar images that resembled the first one, with severe LV dysfunction and regional WMA in the mid to distal segments. After 48 h, the haemodynamic status of the patient suddenly improved, leading to progressive suspension of supportive measures; echocardiography at 48 h showed partial recovery of LV systolic function, with an LVEF of 45–50% and mild paradoxical septal motion (, Video S). The electrocardiographic changes also reverted (). Altogether, the clinical picture of the patient was interpreted as a stress cardiomyopathy occurring in the postoperative period of mitral valve replacement surgery. After 1 week, the patient was discharged. Treatment at discharge was acetylsalicylic acid 100 mg/day. One month later, she was asymptomatic and had low to normal LVEF (50%).

Patient note:
A 59-year-old man with hyperlipidemia managed on rosuvastatin 10 mg nightly and mild obstructive sleep apnea treated with nocturnal CPAP presented to the acute care clinic late this morning complaining that his right calf had become “tight and bulky” over the prior thirty-six hours; he first noticed difficulty zipping up his work boot yesterday and awoke today with more pronounced fullness and a vague pulling sensation behind the knee whenever he placed the limb in a dependent position. Five weeks earlier he underwent an elective open sigmoid colectomy with primary anastomosis for recurrent diverticulitis; the postoperative course was uncomplicated, he was discharged on postoperative day 4, and since returning home has resumed his usual routine of office work, dog-walking, and twice-weekly stationary cycling. He denies prolonged recumbency, long-haul travel, casts, splints, limb weakness, or neurologic deficits, and has been ambulating without assistive devices since hospital discharge. There is no prior history of clots in the legs or lungs, no known thrombophilia, and no first-degree relatives with venous thromboembolism. Current medications other than rosuvastatin include a vitamin B-complex tablet and as-needed acetaminophen; he uses no hormonal agents, corticosteroids, or anticoagulants. He quit smoking twelve years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks two beers on weekend evenings, and does not use illicit substances. Review of systems is negative for fevers, chills, night sweats, erythema of the limb, skin ulceration, trauma, low-back pain, chest discomfort, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, palpitations, syncope, hematuria, abdominal pain, or weight loss. On arrival—before receiving any analgesic, intravenous fluid, or antithrombotic—vital signs recorded temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 134/78 mm Hg, heart rate  ninety-two beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % while breathing ambient air. He sat upright and conversed comfortably, though he kept the right knee flexed and elevated on the stretcher rail. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs or gallops and clear breath sounds bilaterally. The abdomen was soft with a well-healed midline laparotomy scar, nontender, and without organomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities showed the right calf visibly fuller between the tibial tuberosity and gastrocnemius belly compared with the contralateral side, whereas both thighs, ankles, and feet appeared symmetric. A cloth tape positioned exactly 10 cm distal to the inferior pole of the patella measured 44.2 cm on the symptomatic limb and 40.1 cm on the left, a difference of 4.1 cm; 15 cm above the patella circumference measured 53.0 cm bilaterally, and ankle girths at the malleolar level differed by less than 0.5 cm, indicating that the enlargement is limited to the calf region rather than involving the entire leg. When the limb was allowed to hang over the edge of the bed for thirty seconds, a latticework of straight, blue-tinged superficial veins surfaced along the posteromedial calf and collapsed promptly with elevation; no comparable network was visible on the left. The overlying skin was normothermic and maintained uniform coloration without erythema, mottling, or brawny hyperpigmentation. Gentle but firm palpation tracing the expected course of the femoral vein distal to the inguinal ligament, through the adductor canal, into the popliteal fossa, and down the deep posterior compartment reproduced focal tenderness most pronounced in the proximal gastrocnemius just distal to the popliteal crease; similar pressure over the quadriceps, peroneal compartment, and Achilles tendon elicited only diffuse pressure. No discrete cord, fluctuance, crepitus, or mass was appreciated. Passive ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended intensified the deep ache slightly, whereas hip rotation and straight-leg raise were painless. Distal perfusion remained intact—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2+ and symmetric, capillary refill to all toes was under two seconds, and light-touch sensation as well as motor strength graded 5/5 throughout both lower limbs. There was no inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy and no posterior knee cystic fullness. Laboratory studies obtained at the bedside before any pharmacologic intervention revealed hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, platelet count 258 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.2 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 seconds. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram displayed normal sinus rhythm at 90 beats per minute without ST-T abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the tibia and fibula obtained by an urgent-care site earlier this morning demonstrated intact osseous structures with only soft-tissue prominence. No cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, muscle tear, or lymphedematous change was detected on examination to plausibly account for the unilateral calf enlargement, visible collateral veins, and localized tenderness along the deep venous path; consequently, comprehensive duplex ultrasonography of the right lower-extremity venous system has been arranged on an expedited basis while the patient remains hemodynamically stable and without anticoagulation in the observation bay awaiting imaging.

Patient note:
A 79-year-old woman, widowed and living alone in a single-story apartment, was seen this afternoon in the combined vascular–pulmonary clinic at the request of her podiatrist after she reported needing more frequent rests when walking from her driveway to the mailbox. She attributes this progressive left-calf tightness to “poor circulation” first identified ten years ago when ankle–brachial indices measured 0.62 on the right and 0.54 on the left; three years later she underwent balloon angioplasty of the superficial femoral artery but refused stent placement because the procedure restored only limited symptom-free walking distance. Since that time she has limited herself to short neighborhood strolls with a rollator and applies 30-mm Hg knee-high compression stockings each morning; she has no history of gangrene or lower-extremity amputation, yet two small fissures at the base of the left fifth metatarsal required weekly debridement last winter. She smoked one pack per day from age 18 to 68—approximately 50 pack-years in total—quitting when forced to use a short prednisone taper after an emergency department visit for wheezing and prolonged cough; pulmonary function testing afterward showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 with an FEV1 of 49 % predicted that improved by only 3 % following bronchodilator, and she now inhales tiotropium 18 µg each morning, budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 µg twice daily, and uses albuterol about four times per week when climbing the two small steps into her porch. She has never required home oxygen or non-invasive nocturnal ventilation, though she keeps a three-day “rescue pack” of doxycycline and prednisone supplied by her primary physician for winter exacerbations, of which she has needed two in the past five years without hospitalization. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 22 years ago during pre-operative blood work for cataract removal; her regimen progressed from diet to metformin, then to insulin glargine 24 units nightly combined with sitagliptin 100 mg each morning. A hemoglobin A1c measured last month was 8.4 %. She underwent pan-retinal photocoagulation six years ago for proliferative retinopathy, inserts custom molded shoe inserts for distal sensory neuropathy that causes numb toes, and urinates clear urine without foaming; a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio two weeks ago was 110 mg/g, while serum creatinine today is 1.0 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73 m². For the past decade comprehensive metabolic panels have shown borderline aminotransferase elevations—current AST 46 U/L, ALT 48 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and albumin 4.2 g/dL—attributed to biopsy-proven non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; she denies pruritus, easy bruising, abdominal distention, or encephalopathic episodes, and abdominal ultrasound last spring confirmed smooth hepatic contours without portal vein dilation or splenomegaly. She has never experienced crushing substernal discomfort, diaphoresis on exertion, or catheter-based coronary intervention, and an echocardiogram obtained for presurgical clearance two years ago demonstrated normal biventricular size and an ejection fraction of 58 % without segmental wall-motion abnormality. There is no history of sudden unilateral weakness, slurred speech, facial droop, seizures, or visual field loss, and cognitive screening with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment performed last year scored 27/30; she independently manages complex medication schedules, pays household bills online, and recalls recent news events in conversation. She abstains from alcohol, denies intravenous drug use, and her vaccination record is current through last season’s high-dose influenza formulation. Family history is notable for a brother who required aorto-bifemoral bypass at 71 and a father who died of emphysema in his early seventies; there is no familial clustering of hepatic cirrhosis, hematologic malignancy, or immunodeficiency. Current medications include aspirin 81 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily initiated after the prior angioplasty, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, insulin and sitagliptin as noted, tiotropium, budesonide–formoterol, albuterol, vitamin D 1000 IU daily, and over-the-counter fish oil; she is allergic to sulfonamide antibiotics, which caused widespread hives decades ago. On examination she sits upright, breathing comfortably in full sentences. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 138/74 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 82 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 94 % on ambient air, body-mass index 25 kg/m². Carotid pulses are brisk without bruit; the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, S1 and S2 are crisp, and no murmurs, gallops, or rubs are evident. Lungs reveal diminished breath sounds at the bases with scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, with a palpable liver edge 1 cm below the right costal margin that is smooth and non-nodular. Patient note:
A 41-year old male patient with an oligosymptomatic wide complex tachycardia was referred to the emergency department. The tachycardia was terminated by a 360 J DC-shock after unsuccessful administration of adenosine prehospitally. ECG documentation of the tachycardia was not available. The patient had no history of relevant comorbidities. Physical exam was unremarkable, the patient did not take any medication. Similar episodes with palpitations over several minutes and one syncope in the past were reported. Initial 12-lead ECG showed a shortened PR interval with prominent delta waves in I, II, aVL, V4-V6 and R/S transition at V4/V5 suggesting a right midseptal pathway (Fig. ). Diagnosis of WPW syndrome was established. Non-invasive cardiologic work-up did not show significant pathologies.
AVRT was suspected as the underlying mechanism of arrhythmia. Due to recurrent symptomatic paroxysmal tachycardias an electrophysiological study (EPS) was scheduled. An accessory pathway with bidirectional conduction in right-midseptal location was diagnosed and successfully ablated. After ablation no tachycardia could be induced by atrial and ventricular stimulation at rest and following isoprenaline infusion. The patient was discharged the next day.
Five months later the patient was admitted to the emergency department complaining about palpitations and dyspnea since the evening before. ECG showed a wide complex tachycardia (168 beats per minute (bpm); QRS duration 130 ms) with right bundle branch block (RBBB) morphology, left axis deviation and AV (atrioventricular) dissociation (Fig. ). Diagnosis of an ILVT was made. Following administration of Verapamil (cumulative: 240 mg p.o. and 40 mg i.v.) tachycardia slowed down and converted into sinus rhythm. After hospital admission the patient remained in sinus rhythm on Verapamil (120 mg sustained release b.i.d.) and was discharged 1 day later. EPS and ablation of ILVT was recommended. At scheduled ablation the patient presented the ECG of the index-tachycardia, which was terminated by DC-shock. This ECG showed the ILVT rather than the initially suspected AVRT.
In the EPS ILVT of the common type was induced by atrial burst-stimulation and radiofrequency ablation of the ILVT was performed. The patient showed normal AV conduction without signs of pre-excitation. Figure displayed ECG after ablation of WPW syndrome and ILVT. There were no palpitations or symptoms during a follow up of 18 months.

Patient note:
A 50-year-old woman with chronic systolic ventricular dysfunction secondary to a postpartum cardiomyopathy nine years earlier and a history of stage IIA right-sided breast carcinoma treated with lumpectomy, adjuvant chemotherapy, and radiation four years ago—without evidence of recurrence on surveillance imaging this past winter—came to the emergency department late in the morning after three days of progressive shortness of breath and a new productive cough. She reports that the illness began with mild rhinorrhea and a scratchy throat during a weekend hike, but by the second evening she was panting after walking from the bedroom to the kitchen, noted streaks of blood-tinged sputum, and developed a pleuritic ache beneath the right scapula that worsened when lying on her left side. She denies dizziness, loss of consciousness, confusion, seizures, dysuria, abdominal pain, or recent antibiotic exposure. The patient works as a high-school guidance counselor, drives herself to work, and jogs at a slow pace twice weekly when well; she lives with her spouse in a single-story home and performs all activities of daily living independently. She has never been institutionalized, has had no hospital admissions for the past two years, and has not required home oxygen or diuretic up-titration since her last cardiology follow-up. Medications taken the morning of presentation include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49-51 mg twice daily, low-dose furosemide 20 mg every other morning (skipped today), and a daily cholecalciferol supplement; she has no implanted cardiac devices or ports. She quit smoking more than twenty years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure, drinks red wine socially no more than once per week, and has never used recreational drugs. Immunizations are current, including the seasonal influenza shot given at her workplace two months earlier. Emergency medical services found her seated upright on her sofa, speaking in full sentences but tachypneic, and transported her without supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, or medications. On arrival to triage—and before any antipyretics, bronchodilators, antibiotics, or vasoactive agents—vital signs were temperature 36.7 °C oral, heart rate 83 beats per minute and regular, non-invasive blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg with a palpable systolic of 132 mm Hg, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute with shallow excursions and intermittent use of sternocleidomastoids, and pulse oximetry 92 % breathing ambient air at sea level. She was alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation, answered all questions appropriately, and followed commands without hesitation. Mucous membranes were moist; conjunctivae were anicteric. Jugular venous pulsation was noted 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, consistent with her cardiology baseline. Cardiac auscultation revealed a regular rhythm with a soft third heart sound but no murmurs or pericardial rub. Lung examination demonstrated markedly diminished breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion over the right posterior lower third of the thorax, with coarse crackles and egophony just superior to that zone; no wheezes were heard. The abdomen was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge was not palpable. Extremities were warm without edema or cyanosis, and capillary refill was brisk. Neurologic screening showed equal, reactive pupils, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, and steady finger-to-nose testing. A bedside finger-stick glucose registered 100 mg/dL. Venous samples and a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 153 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 108 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 11 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, consistent with her prior outpatient values. Complete blood count showed hematocrit 26 %, hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL (baseline 9.0 g/dL), leukocytes 14.8 × 10⁹/L with 87 % segmented neutrophils, and platelets 260 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated pH 7.56, PaCO₂ 29 mm Hg, PaO₂ 77 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, compatible with a primary respiratory alkalosis provoked by tachypnea. Serum lactate measured 1.4 mmol/L. A portable postero-anterior and lateral chest radiograph obtained before initiation of therapy revealed a dense consolidation involving the right middle lobe with air bronchograms and blunting of the adjacent costophrenic angle by a meniscus-shaped opacity suggestive of fluid accumulation; the cardiac silhouette was mildly enlarged but unchanged from an echocardiography-guided film six months prior, and there was no pulmonary vascular redistribution. Bedside thoracic ultrasonography confirmed an anechoic stripe approximately 1.2 cm thick overlying the right diaphragm consistent with a small free-flowing effusion. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm at 82–84 beats per minute, left ventricular hypertrophy voltage criteria, and T-wave flattening in the lateral leads identical to prior tracings. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens, and a respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched while the patient remained seated upright on room air. At the moment this note is drafted she has received no intravenous crystalloids, diuretics, bronchodilators, supplemental oxygen, or antimicrobial agents, thus all physiologic measurements and laboratory data above represent her untreated state on presentation.

Patient note:
A 68-year-old man arrived this afternoon to the comprehensive peri-operative clinic at the request of the vascular surgery service, six days before a planned open repair of a 5.8-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm discovered incidentally on surveillance ultrasound for renal insufficiency; the operative team anticipates a transperitoneal midline approach lasting four to five hours with need for aortic cross-clamping below the renal arteries, possible cell-saver autotransfusion, and immediate postoperative admission to the surgical intensive care unit for invasive hemodynamic and urine-output monitoring. He strolled slowly from the parking lot using the handrail on the front steps and requested a brief rest in the waiting area, explaining that over the past year he has become short of breath after walking two New-York-City blocks or carrying a basket of laundry up one flight. Three years ago he was hospitalized for rapid weight gain, bilateral ankle swelling, and nocturnal breathlessness; echocardiography obtained during that admission demonstrated a globally dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30 %, mild functional mitral regurgitation, and normal right-sided chamber size. He required two additional admissions for volume overload in the subsequent 18 months, most recently three months ago after a long road trip that limited his access to prescribed medications; intravenous loop diuretic therapy achieved a 4-kg net weight reduction. His current regimen includes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg with breakfast, spironolactone 25 mg at bedtime, and a 2-gram-sodium diet; he records daily morning weights in a notebook reviewed today and calls his primary clinician if he gains more than 2 lb in 24 hours. He sleeps on three pillows, awakens once or twice weekly gasping for air until he sits at the edge of the bed, and notes that his socks leave imprints by evening although the swelling subsides overnight. There have been no episodes of syncope, palpitations, or unexplained presyncope. Blood pressure has been elevated since his early fifties and is treated with amlodipine 10 mg each morning; type 2 diabetes diagnosed five years earlier is managed solely with metformin extended-release 1000 mg with supper and a carbohydrate-restricted diet taught by a nutritionist, with a glycated hemoglobin of 7.0 % at last month’s primary-care visit. He monitors capillary glucose twice weekly, reporting readings between 110 and 160 mg/dL and no hypoglycemic events. He has never experienced abrupt unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, monocular vision loss, or episodes suggestive of transient neurologic ischemia. Chronic kidney disease stage 3a, attributed to combined hypertensive and diabetic microvascular change, is co-managed with nephrology; serum creatinine has hovered in the 1.2–1.4 mg/dL range for the past two years. Surgical history is limited to a remote laparoscopic cholecystectomy without complications. He quit cigarette smoking 15 years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks two light beers on weekend evenings, and denies recreational drug use. Review of systems is negative for fever, chills, productive cough, abdominal pain, claudication, unexplained weight loss, or bleeding tendencies. After five minutes of quiet sitting, vitals are temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg in the right arm, regular pulse 62 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95 % on ambient air; body mass index is 29 kg/m². He appears comfortable at rest but breathes more heavily when turning to remove his coat. Jugular venous pulsation is visualized 5 cm above the sternal angle with the head of the bed at 45 °, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is laterally displaced in the sixth intercostal space. Cardiac auscultation reveals a quiet S1 and S2, a soft S3 gallop, and a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex consistent with functional regurgitation; no pericardial rub is present. Lungs are clear in the upper fields but have fine late-inspiratory crackles at both bases. The abdomen is soft and nontender with a palpable pulsatile mass above the umbilicus, no guarding, and intact midline scar tissue from prior surgery. Extremities exhibit bilateral 1+ pitting edema to mid-shin, warm skin, and symmetric dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. Neurologic examination shows full orientation, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength proximally and distally, normal sensation, and a steady narrow-based gait when he walks unassisted down the hallway. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour before the encounter demonstrate hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 232 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.26 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 56 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose in the same panel is 132 mg/dL, and liver transaminases as well as international normalized ratio are within reference limits. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows sinus rhythm at 60 beats/min with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes unchanged from a tracing four months ago. Upright posterior–anterior chest radiograph reveals cardiomegaly, mild pulmonary vascular congestion, and an enlarged descending aorta without pleural effusion. Airway assessment by anesthesia documents a Mallampati class II oropharynx, inter-incisor distance of 4 cm, thyromental distance of 6 cm, and full cervical extension. The anesthesiology team plans balanced general anesthesia with lumbar epidural catheter for postoperative analgesia, continuation of beta-blocker and renin-angiotensin–neprilysin inhibitor therapy through the morning of surgery, omitting the loop diuretic on the day of operation to avoid intravascular depletion, insertion of a radial arterial line and large-bore central venous catheter, and goal-directed crystalloid guided by stroke-volume variation. Sequential compression devices, subcutaneous low-dose heparin beginning the evening after surgery, incentive spirometry, and early ambulation have been reviewed; the patient verbalized understanding of peri-operative instructions, demonstrated accurate teach-back regarding medication timing and fasting, and expressed determination to proceed with definitive aneurysm repair to prevent rupture.

question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old woman was admitted to our department because of pain and limitation in motion in the left hip for 2 years after primary total hip arthroplasty with hybrid prosthesis for avascular necrosis of the femoral head 15 years ago. The patient underwent mitral commissurotomy because of mitral stenosis 30 years ago, when she complicated with atrial fibrillation, since then she had been taking aspirin 100 mg once daily. The patient presented absolute arrhythmia and uneven first heart sound on auscultation. Electrocardiogram demonstrated atrial fibrillation. X-ray film of the pelvis and the left femur revealed osteolysis around the femoral stem and subsidence of femoral component.
The patient was diagnosed as aseptic loosening of the femoral component after total hip arthroplasty and underwent revision total hip arthroplasty with cementless acetabular component and cementless modular stem and allograft for bone defects in both sides. Aspirin was discontinued 7 days before surgery. The procedure was performed uneventfully. The patient began to take rivaroxaban 10 mg 12 h after surgery, which was planned once daily for 35 days. The patient was told to start functional exercises of the left lower extremity as soon as tolerated and began to ambulate with crutches with the left lower extremity free of weight bearing on the 15th day postoperatively.
The patient felt sudden numbness, tingling in the right lower extremity, and inability to move it after having a nap on the 17th postoperative day. Physical examination: pulse 80/min and blood pressure (BP) 120/70 mmHg mentally conscious, with pupils round, symmetrical, and sensitive to light. There was loss of sensation, paresis, and decreased skin temperature for the right lower extremity, with pedis artery impalpable on the right side and normal pedis artery on the left side.
The color Doppler showed that there was insufficient blood flow with low vascular tension in the right lower extremity, which suggested stenosis or incomplete obstruction proximal to the popliteal artery. Computed tomography (CT) angiography showed that there was complete occlusion of the right common iliac artery and the beginning of internal and external iliac arteries, with no collateral circulation from the contralateral side (), which caused narrowing of arteries of the right lower extremity.
The patient underwent an emergency digital subtraction angiography (DSA; ) and catheter-directed thrombolysis combined with balloon angioplasty. The procedure was performed by a contralateral retrograde approach under regional anesthesia. Initially, catheter-directed thrombolysis was performed with urokinase 300,000 units for half an hour. Subsequent angiography showed antegrade flow with large residual thrombi. Then, a balloon was used to get patent recanalization (), followed by urokinase 500,000 units pumped into the right common iliac artery for 24 h. Post-procedure angiography demonstrated smooth blood flow without filling defects in the previously occluded arteries (). The feeling of tingling in the right lower extremity disappeared soon after balloon angioplasty. The right pedis artery got palpable and skin temperature gradually returned to normal. Sensation gradually recovered with disappearing of numbness in the right lower extremity. No presentation of ischemia-reperfusion injury, such as swelling of the right lower extremity, increased creatinine, or hyperkalemia, was detected.
After the procedure, the patient received subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin calcium 4100 units twice daily for 2–3 days, warfarin 2.5 mg once daily for half a year, and aspirin 100 mg once daily for life time. The international normalized ratio (INR) was maintained within 2–3. The procedure went uneventfully without any complications, and the patient was fine at the 2-year follow-up. Informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report. The institutional review board of The Third Hospital of Changsha does not require ethics approval for reporting individual cases.

She has been an inpatient for the past nine days, spending almost the entirety of that time supine with the head of the bed elevated to 30 degrees because standing or even dangling her legs precipitates sharp right-lower-quadrant pain and light-headedness. Nursing flow sheets document fewer than 250 cumulative steps this week, and physical therapy sessions were deferred until the infectious process was controlled. Patient note:
A 30-year-old man arrived to the emergency department by private vehicle late on a humid summer afternoon after two full days of escalating pleuritic chest discomfort and a cough that progressed from dry to the current production of small amounts of yellow-green sputum streaked with blood. He reported shivering episodes overnight that left the bedsheets damp, and measured an oral temperature of 101 °F at home with a digital thermometer an hour before presentation; he purposely avoided acetaminophen, decongestants, inhalers, or any form of supplemental oxygen in the hope that “the doctors could see the real numbers.” He lives alone in a third-floor walk-up apartment, works as a package sorter for an overnight delivery company, and routinely rides his bicycle five miles to and from work; coworkers noted he required several rest breaks on today’s morning shift and persuaded him to seek evaluation. Past medical history is notable for systolic dysfunction diagnosed after a presumed viral myocarditis during adolescence, the most recent echocardiogram nine months earlier showing a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 35 % with mild biatrial enlargement; he takes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and low-dose sacubitril-valsartan, with adherence confirmed by pharmacy fills. In addition, he follows nephrology for stage 3 chronic kidney impairment attributed to long-standing hypertension; baseline creatinine runs near 1.5 mg/dL and he has not required dialysis, transplantation, or erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy. There is no record of prior strokes, transient ischemic attacks, seizures, chronic liver disorders, or malignancies, and he has never been admitted to a long-term care facility. Immunizations include both pneumococcal formulations completed within the past five years and last season’s inactivated influenza vaccine. He smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily in college but quit six years ago, drinks craft beer socially once or twice per month, and denies recreational drug use. His only medications this morning were the usual heart-failure regimen; he had not eaten since a late night snack and drank only coffee before work. On roll-in he sat upright on the stretcher, conversed in full sentences, and accurately stated name, location, date, and the current major sporting event, answering questions briskly without confusion. Skin appeared flushed yet dry, mucous membranes were tacky, and capillary refill was brisk. Pre-intervention vital signs documented an oral temperature of 101.4 °F, a regular tachycardic pulse of 142 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead monitoring, non-invasive blood pressure 141/78 mm Hg verified manually, an extraordinarily rapid respiratory rate of 60 breaths per minute with visible alae nasi flaring, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 89 % and 91 % on ambient air at this sea-level facility. Neck veins hovered 4 cm above the sternal angle while upright, unchanged from prior cardiology notes, and trace bilateral ankle edema was again observed. Cardiac auscultation revealed a brisk S1 and S2 with a soft third sound, no new murmurs, and no pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination showed coarse inspiratory crackles throughout the right mid-and lower posterior lung fields without dullness to percussion, while the left lung remained clear; no wheezes or pleural friction sounds were appreciated. Abdomen was scaphoid and nontender with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge was smooth and could not be palpated below the costal margin. Screening neurologic assessment demonstrated equal reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, fluent speech, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. A bedside glucometer registered 149 mg/dL immediately before venipuncture. Peripheral venous samples and a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival, before any intravenous fluids or oxygen were administered. Basic metabolic panel returned a striking sodium of 166 mEq/L, potassium 3.7 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 25 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, values only modestly above his outpatient baseline except for the severe hypernatremia. Complete blood count revealed leukocytosis to 14.8 × 10⁹/L with neutrophil predominance, hematocrit 33 %, hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL, and platelets 242 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas on room air displayed an alkalemic pH of 7.69, PaCO₂ 23 mm Hg, PaO₂ 82 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, consistent with primary respiratory alkalosis from profound tachypnea and mild hypoxemia given his age. Serum lactate was 1.5 mmol/L. Troponin-I was below the assay threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph, obtained before any medication or fluid therapy, demonstrated a dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, preserved diaphragmatic and costophrenic outlines, and no layering fluid; cardiomediastinal silhouette was unchanged from prior outpatient imaging. Twelve-lead electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia at 144 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave flattening but no acute ischemic pattern. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an expectorated sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched to the laboratory before antimicrobial, diuretic, antipyretic, vasodilatory, or supplemental oxygen therapy was ordered. At this moment he remains seated upright on the gurney breathing ambient air, receiving no intravenous crystalloid, vasoactive infusion, bronchodilator, or antipyretic, thereby preserving the physiologic observations and laboratory data above as his untreated presentation.

Patient note:
A 62-year-old right-handed male with a longstanding history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with sudden-onset left-sided body weakness as well as a loss of feeling over the left side of his body. These symptoms started approximately 3 days before the presentation to the hospital. He gave a history of difficulty looking to the left side as well. There was no history of loss of consciousness, speech difficulties, seizures, headaches, or vomiting. His neurologic examination showed an intact level of consciousness, normal higher mental functions as well as normal speech. The examination of vision showed conjugate horizontal left gaze palsy. He could maintain gaze near mid-position but could not cross the midline to the left side. Doll's head maneuver brought the eyes past the midline to the left. Visual acuity was normal at the bedside near-fixation test. Visual fields were assessed by bedside confrontation methods and did not show clear defects. Examination of facial nerves showed weakness of the upper motor neuron type on the left side, and the remainder of cranial nerves was intact.
Motor system examination showed hypotonia, hemiplegia, hyporeflexia as well as extensor plantar response on the left side of the body. Sensory system examination showed left hemisensory loss of pain and temperature sensations.
Computed tomography scan of the brain showed an area of infarction over the right subcortical corona radiata region (Fig. ). He received inpatient stroke care and then was discharged home.
He was re-assessed in the neurology outpatient clinic (OPD) at 1, 3, and 6-month intervals after discharge. Neurologic examination on the first visit to the neurology clinic showed some improvement in the range of eye movements; however, he had residual partial defects of both saccadic and pursuit functions on horizontal gaze. His motor power over the left side of his body was better as compared to his baseline. Tone and deep tendon reflexes were increased over the left side as well, and the other neurologic findings were the same as his baseline.
His neurologic assessment on the second visit to the neurology OPD did not show significant changes from the first visit. However, re-assessment on the third visit (i.e., 6 months after discharge) showed complete recovery of gaze palsy, better motor power on the left side of his body with otherwise similar findings as before.
