Patient note:
A 67-year-old female with a history of poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and chronic atrial fibrillation on no anticoagulation was brought to the emergency department by advanced life support after being discovered by her neighbor lying supine beside an overturned stepladder on the laundry room tile; the neighbor reports the patient had been trimming curtains on a high window earlier in the afternoon and was last seen well about ninety minutes prior to the 911 call. Pre-hospital personnel state there was no witnessed seizure activity and that the patient did not respond to repeated verbal prompts en route; no medications or glucose had been administered in the field. On arrival she is secured to a long spine board with a foam cervical collar in place and an 18-gauge intravenous catheter in the left antecubital fossa, but no fluids have yet been started. Initial vital signs are blood pressure 196/104 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, respirations 16 per minute with shallow excursions, oxygen saturation 95 % on 4 L nasal cannula, and oral temperature 36.7 °C. The airway is patent with snoring respirations that improve when the mandible is lifted forward; pink frothy secretions are absent, and there is no blood in the oropharynx. Auscultation reveals clear lung fields bilaterally, a variable S1 and S2 without murmurs, and no carotid bruits. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender; pelvis is stable to gentle rock; distal pulses are 2+ and capillary refill is under two seconds. A focused musculoskeletal survey shows a superficial 3 cm occipital scalp abrasion with dried blood but no boggy swelling, deformity, or active hemorrhage; the remainder of the skin exam identifies scattered ecchymoses over both shins that the neighbor says are chronic from gardening. Pupils are symmetric at 3 mm, round, and briskly reactive to direct and consensual light; cranial nerve testing is otherwise limited by cooperation, though corneal reflexes are present and the gag is intact when a tongue depressor contacts the posterior pharynx. Throughout the examination the patient’s eyelids remain tightly shut and do not part when her name is called, when she is asked to open her eyes, or when periorbital pressure is applied; only after a firm trapezius squeeze does the brow briefly knit without the lids separating. When addressed loudly by first name, she produces mumbled phrases such as “I need to finish… where are we… is it morning?” in a slurred, dysarthric tone that conveys clear language yet incorrect context; she is unable to state the year, location, or reason for hospital presence and persistently drifts off midsentence. She follows no simple commands such as “show me your thumb” or “stick out your tongue.” Nail-bed pressure to the right index finger elicits brisk withdrawal of the entire right upper extremity to the level of the chest, flexing at the elbow with slight external rotation of the shoulder, but she does not reach toward or attempt to push away the examiner; a similar response is observed in the left lower extremity when the tibial shaft is squeezed, with the limb drawing back and the hip flexing. Based on her lack of eye opening to voice or pain, confused but discernible speech, and withdrawal of limbs from painful stimulus, her Glasgow Coma Scale score is calculated as 9 (E1 V4 M4). There is no abnormal decorticate or decerebrate posturing, no myoclonic jerks, and muscle tone is mildly increased in both arms. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ at the biceps and patellae, 2+ at the ankles, with bilateral plantar flexor responses. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing cannot be performed due to lack of cooperation, but passive range of motion of all joints is full without crepitus. Bedside capillary glucose reads 127 mg/dL. No odors of alcohol or ketones are detected on her breath. Electrocardiogram leads applied during the exam confirm atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate around 80 and no acute ischemic changes. No antihypertensives, sedatives, antiepileptics, or analgesics have yet been administered, and the neurologic findings recorded reflect her untreated state on presentation. A stat non-contrast head CT, cervical spine CT, baseline labs including CBC, basic metabolic panel, coagulation panel, serum troponin, and type and screen have been ordered, and neurosurgery is being paged in light of the concerning level of consciousness and focal cranial trauma risk factors.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman, previously independent in her activities of daily living but burdened by a twelve-year history of dilated cardiomyopathy (last clinic echocardiogram three months earlier showed an ejection fraction of 25 %), long-standing insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes, poorly controlled hypertension, and intermittent alcohol consumption, was found by a neighbour slumped over the armrest of her couch at 04:30 complaining she “couldn’t catch a breath” and feeling “light-headed.” According to emergency medical services, she was sitting bolt upright, speaking in short phrases between gasps, and visibly diaphoretic; a portable finger probe recorded oxygen saturation of 78 % while she breathed room air. Airway reflexes were intact, and she was able to answer orientation questions though slowly and with occasional word-finding pauses. The crew elected to apply a tight-fitting full-face circuit attached to their transport turbine, set to provide a constant distending pressure of 10 cm H₂O with an entrained oxygen concentration of 0.50, and they did not administer sedatives, paralytics, or intubate. No crystalloid bolus, vasopressor, diuretic, nitrate, or opioid was given in the field; the only intervention during the seven-minute ride was placement of a single 18-gauge antecubital cannula through which a keep-open rate of lactated Ringer’s was running. On stretcher entry to the emergency department—before any hospital-initiated therapy—the patient remained seated forward, clutching the mask cushion against her face, respiratory rate 30 min⁻¹ with visible accessory muscle use yet synchronous chest expansion, and the transport device alarmed peak pressures no higher than 22 cm H₂O. A triage automated cuff cycling on the contralateral arm displayed 99 / 61 mm Hg, heart rate registered 118 beats min⁻¹ in an irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with her known atrial fibrillation, oral temperature was 37.4 °C, and fingertip saturation stabilized at 92–93 % on the documented 50 % inspired fraction. Capillary refill was delayed to about four seconds, the hands were cool and mottled to the knuckles, and the jugular venous column flickered 6 cm above the sternal angle. She opened her eyes to voice, answered questions with confused conversation—giving the correct name but the wrong month—and withdrew briskly from trapezius pinch with both arms, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 12 without any pharmacologic influence. Pupils were equal at 3 mm and reactive, corneal and gag reflexes remained intact, and no focal motor asymmetry was noted. Lung examination revealed diffuse fine crackles to the mid-scapular line posteriorly, scattered expiratory wheezes, and markedly reduced breath sounds at the bases; percussion was dull over both lower lobes. Cardiac auscultation found a rapid irregular rhythm with a third sound but no new murmur or pericardial rub. The abdomen was soft and mildly distended with a smooth, tender liver edge palpated two fingerbreadths below the right costal margin; bowel sounds were hypoactive. Lower extremities were free of edema yet cool to touch. A right radial arterial catheter was placed within two minutes of arrival, and the first sample—drawn while ventilator settings were unchanged—revealed pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 45 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq L⁻¹, lactate 3.1 mmol L⁻¹, and a PaO₂ of 129 mm Hg on the noted 0.50 FiO₂. Simultaneous peripheral blood, obtained before administration of loop diuretics, vasodilators, or antibiotics, demonstrated white-blood-cell count 13.4 ×10³ µL⁻¹ with 6 % band forms, hemoglobin 12.1 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 36 %, and a platelet concentration of 142 300 /µL. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 132 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 5.1 mmol L⁻¹, chloride 98 mmol L⁻¹, an anion gap of 14, glucose 226 mg dL⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 44 mg dL⁻¹, and serum creatinine 2.12 mg dL⁻¹—well above her documented outpatient baseline of 1.3 mg dL⁻¹. Hepatic profile showed aspartate aminotransferase 58 U L⁻¹, alanine aminotransferase 54 U L⁻¹, alkaline phosphatase 186 U L⁻¹, an international normalized ratio of 1.4 (no anticoagulants had been taken for three days because she ran out), and a total bilirubin of 1.73 mg dL⁻¹ with the majority in the direct fraction, consistent with passive congestion. Point-of-care ultrasound performed while she remained on the non-invasive circuit revealed a severely dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis, moderate mitral regurgitation by color Doppler, bilateral B-lines coalescing diffusely, and an inferior vena cava measuring 2.5 cm with less than 5 % respiratory variation. The bladder scan showed approximately 120 mL of residual volume; a Foley catheter placed during the secondary survey produced a scant 30 mL of concentrated amber urine, and review of her home logbook—kept for nephrology follow-up—indicated only 910 mL passed over the preceding twenty-four hours. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained without interrupting CPAP support demonstrated cardiomegaly with cephalization of pulmonary vessels, bilateral perihilar alveolar infiltrates, and no overt pleural effusion; the diaphragms were low and flattened. Twelve-lead electrocardiography printed immediately afterward showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response at 122 beats min⁻¹, lateral Q waves from prior infarction, and diffuse nonspecific ST-T changes without acute elevation. Up to the exact moment these physiologic and laboratory data were captured, she had received no intravenous diuretics, nitrates, inotropes, vasopressors, antibiotics, or additional oxygen therapy beyond the 10 cm H₂O continuous distending pressure delivering a 50 % oxygen blend; she remained spontaneously breathing through the sealed mask with an arterial pressure fixed in the high nineties systolic, displayed mild thrombocytopenia at 142 300 /µL, harbored a modest direct hyperbilirubinemia of 1.73 mg dL⁻¹, demonstrated acute kidney injury with creatinine 2.12 mg dL⁻¹ and sub-optimal urine output of 910 mL per day, and showed moderate encephalopathy quantified at Glasgow Coma Score 12 while suffering a presumed acute decompensation of chronic heart failure complicated by pulmonary edema and systemic hypoperfusion.

Question: What is the patient's Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) Score?

Patient note:
A 55-year-old woman with long-standing bilateral knee osteoarthritis managed with over-the-counter ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily during the recent winter cold spell and a remote history of Helicobacter-associated duodenitis successfully treated five years ago walked into the emergency department shortly after sunrise complaining that she had passed “three bowls of pitch-black, sticky stool” since going to bed the night before and awoke feeling “drained, as if I gave blood all night.” She reported a nagging, gnawing epigastric pressure that worsened empty and eased briefly with toast, persistent metallic after-taste, and progressive fatigue over the last 48 hours but firmly denied any episode in which the room spun, her vision tunneled, or she fell, stating she remained able to drive the twenty-minute distance from her farmhouse without pulling off the road for dizziness. She has never been diagnosed with cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, cholestatic disorders, alcohol-related liver injury, or congestive heart disease, and she characteristically sleeps flat without extra pillows and wears sandals rather than compression stockings because her ankles never swell. Medications include the above ibuprofen, a daily enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg that her primary care clinician suggested last year for primary prevention, pantoprazole 40 mg each morning though she admits missing several doses this week, and an oral combined calcium-vitamin D tablet; she has never taken corticosteroids, dual antiplatelet therapy, or anticoagulants. Socially she drinks a glass of beer no more than twice per month, quit smoking fifteen years ago after a ten-pack-year history, and denies recreational drug exposure. Family history lists a father with a perforated duodenal ulcer at age 62 and a sister with rheumatoid arthritis; no relatives have cardiomyopathy or bleeding diatheses. Review of systems was otherwise negative for fever, chills, cough, hemoptysis, chest tightness, palpitations, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, unintentional weight loss, jaundice, pruritus, easy bruising, hematuria, or hematochezia. On arrival—preceding establishment of intravenous access, administration of fluids, acid suppression, antiemetics, vasoactive agents, or blood products—she sat upright on the stretcher appearing pale, lips dry, and answered questions in full sentences though pausing to catch her breath between phrases. Manual vital signs obtained with the right arm supported at heart level revealed a systolic blood pressure of 91 mm Hg with a diastolic of 58 mm Hg, a regular tachycardic pulse of 122 beats per minute verified on the cardiac monitor, respirations 22 per minute, oral temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Capillary refill was approximately three seconds; conjunctivae were noticeably blanched but anicteric, oral mucosa dry with a thin streak of coffee-ground material at the posterior oropharynx, and there were no telangiectasias, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, or pedal edema. Neck veins were not distended at 45° and carotid upstrokes were brisk. Cardiac auscultation produced a rapid but crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear throughout. The abdomen was flat, soft, and non-distended; gentle palpation elicited mild mid-epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound, the liver edge was not palpable, and spleen could not be felt below the costal margin. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. Digital rectal examination yielded a smear of tarry, malodorous stool that rendered the guaiac card a deep blue immediately. A single 18-gauge intravenous catheter was placed solely for phlebotomy, and type-and-screen was dispatched; at that instant she had not yet received crystalloid or pharmacologic therapy. Initial laboratory results returned within fifteen minutes and demonstrated hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, hematocrit 25 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, platelet count 266 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 11.2 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 57 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.05. A 12-lead electrocardiogram run simultaneously showed sinus tachycardia at 124 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic ST-T abnormalities. Upright chest radiography depicted clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette; a single supine abdominal film displayed a nonspecific gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. She remained nil per os, was connected to continuous telemetry and pulse oximetry, and gastroenterology was paged urgently for endoscopic evaluation of her ongoing upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage manifested by melena and significant anemia in the setting of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use.

Patient note:
A 63-year-old man with a fifteen-year history of alcohol-associated cirrhosis—last drink six weeks earlier after enrolling in an outpatient rehabilitation program—walked into the emergency department late this afternoon because over the prior five days his belt no longer reached the third hole, he struggled to bend forward to tie his shoes, and he noted progressive abdominal pressure that forced him to sleep propped on two pillows; he denied confusion, changes in sleep–wake cycle, tremor, personality shifts, or episodes of staring, and he continued to balance his checkbook and complete the daily newspaper crossword without difficulty. Past medical history includes remote chronic hepatitis C successfully treated with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir five years ago, staple line hernia repair following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. He takes furosemide 40 mg and spironolactone 100 mg each morning, propranolol 20 mg twice daily for portal pressure reduction, and thiamine 100 mg daily; he has no drug allergies. He smokes half a pack of cigarettes per day, quit intravenous drug use two decades ago, and lives alone in a single-story apartment. Family history is significant for a brother who died of esophageal variceal hemorrhage at 58 and a father with myocardial infarction at 60. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chills, jaundice noted by friends, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, pruritus, shortness of breath at rest, chest pain, palpitations, or recent medication changes. On arrival—before intravenous access, diagnostic paracentesis, diuretics, vitamin K, antibiotics, albumin, or any sedative—vital signs were temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 102/60 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % on ambient air. He was alert, maintained eye contact, recalled three objects after five minutes, spelled the word “world” backward quickly, and held his arms outstretched for twenty seconds without a flapping motion. Sclerae carried a deep yellow tint, conjunctivae were anemic, and the breath emitted a faint odor of stale beer. Dozens of spider angiomata peppered the upper chest and shoulders, palmar erythema was pronounced, and nail beds were pale. Neck veins were flat at 30°. Cardiac examination demonstrated a tachy-but-regular rhythm without murmurs or extra sounds; lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen ballooned into a smooth hemisphere with everted umbilicus; percussion revealed tympany centrally that shifted to broad flank dullness when he rolled, and a fluid impulse traversed the abdominal wall without the need for a second examiner’s counter-pressure, though the wall was still soft and not rock-hard. A firm, nodular liver edge was just palpable two centimeters below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, and the spleen was appreciated three fingerbreadths below the left costal margin. There was bilateral 1+ pitting edema to the mid-shins. Neurologic examination showed intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal tone, and a narrow-based gait down the corridor. He had similar complaints 9 months prior, at which time he was diagnosed with pneumococcal meningitis and pneumococcal mitral valve endocarditis (often referred to as Austrian syndrome). During that time, a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) showed mitral valve vegetation and posterior annular abscess. Blood cultures grew penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae. He underwent mitral valve repair, which consisted of P2 resection with the vegetation and repair of the posterior annular abscess at the hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (HUP). Five months later, he was again diagnosed with penicillin-sensitive pneumococcal mitral valve endocarditis; however, he responded promptly to medical therapy with ceftriaxone given intravenously over a 6-week period. He had received a pneumococcal vaccination 2 years prior to this presentation. On physical examination during this admission, he was alert but disoriented to time, place and person. The temperature was 104.3°F, blood pressure 120/74 mm Hg, heart rate 87/minute, and respiratory rate 22/minute. Cardiac auscultation revealed a soft S1 and grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the mitral area without any radiation. There were no meningeal signs, focal neurological deficits, or peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis. Laboratory data is shown in . Chest X-ray and urinalysis were normal. Electrocardiogram showed an old left bundle branch block. Computed tomography of head was normal. The patient was initially started on intravenous ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin while waiting for blood cultures. Lumbar puncture was not performed on admission due to the risk of bleeding as the patient was on coumadin (INR-2.3). Blood cultures (4/4 cultures) grew penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae. Ampicillin and vancomycin were stopped on day 3. TEE revealed severe mitral regurgitation and a small vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet without any evidence of abscess (). He finished a 6-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone therapy. During the follow-up visit at the clinic 6 weeks later, he was found to be asymptomatic and stable.

Patient note:
A 63-year-old male presented with a 2-day history of a widespread, erythematous rash covering all surfaces of his body. The rash appeared 2 days prior to admission with associated prodromal malaise and anorexia. His medical history was significant for a cellulitis of his left lower limb for which he was prescribed oral clindamycin 5 days prior. Two days before admission, the patient noted a pruritic rash on his abdomen which subsequently became erythematous. The rash then migrated to his face and the rest of his torso. Within the next 48 h, it spread to involve his back and upper and lower limbs. The patient then began experiencing subjective fever and presented to his general practitioner before being referred to hospital. On hospital presentation he was apyrexic, tachycardic (irregularly irregular pulse rate of 170 beats per min) and was tachypneoic (respiratory rate of 28). He was normotensive (126/84 mmHg) and remained alert and interactive clinical examination was remarkable for an oatmeal dermatitis of the face and perioral area ( and ) and an erythematous, blistering rash covering 80% of his total body surface area. Nikolosky sign was positive. Oral involvement was noted. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet were spared.
Potentially causative medications (including clindamycin) were stopped. Electrocardiogram confirmed atrial fibrillation. The patient was immediately isolated from other patients and increased contact precautions were taken. Fluid resuscitation was commenced as per local hospital sepsis guidelines and urinary output monitored. Paraffin gel was applied liberally two hourly and potent topical corticosteroids twice daily. Intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg) was given four times daily. Laboratory investigations on admission were significant for a moderate leucocytosis of 15.5 × 109/l and a neutrophilia of 14.5 × 109/l. C-reactive protein levels were 123 mg/l and venous lactate was markedly elevated at 6.5 mg/dl. Blood, urine and wound site cultures were sent for culture and sensitivity. Autoimmune and viral screens were taken. Skin biopsies were performed on two occasions: A 4 mm punch biopsy of affected skin was taken from the anterolateral left forearm and a repeat punch biopsy was taken from the sacral area on Day 2 of admission. The patient’s chest X-ray revealed no abnormality.
A marked improvement in the patient’s rash was seen on admission Days 3 and 4, and his clinical condition gradually improved. The patient remained apyrexic. A switch from intravenous hydrocortisone to 30 mg of oral prednisolone was made on Day 7. The patient evidenced impressive regeneration of the affected skin and corticosteroids were tapered prior to discharge 21 days after admission.

Patient note:
A 55-year-old woman with no past medical problems was referred to our ED from a local hospital with acute pulmonary edema. She was seen in that hospital twice previously with episodes of acute pulmonary edema that was treated with intravenous diuretics. She had an appointment with cardiologist after a month. Clinical examination revealed normal vital signs, normal JVP, bibasilar rales and a very faint mid-diastolic murmur heard at the apex of the heart without an opening snap. Her ECG was normal. Chest X-ray showed no cardiomegaly but there was pulmonary congestion. In view of recurrent pulmonary edema in the absence of obvious causes for pulmonary edema and a long waiting for cardiologist consultation, a bedside transthoracic echocardiographic examination of the heart was performed using the ATL HDI 5000 machine to rule out any gross abnormalities in the heart. Bedside transthoracic echocardiographic examination showed a large rounded mass protruding from the left atrium into the left ventricle [Figures and ]. This mass was relatively fixed at mitral valve causing diastolic obstruction of mitral inflow and ‘functional’ mitral stenosis leading to recurrent pulmonary edema. The mass seemed to be attached to lower part of interatrial septum and the echocardiographic appearance of the mass was pathognomic of atrial myxoma. The patient underwent urgent surgery to remove the mass. At surgery interatrial septum was intact with an 8×4 cm mass seen attached from low interatrial septum with a small pedicle and occupying whole of mitral annulus. The mass was excised from the atrial septum which was secured by a patch closure. It weighed 64 gm and the histology of the specimen showed abundant hyaline and myxoid stroma containing small groups of tumor cells, compatible with the diagnosis of atrial myxoma.

Patient note:
A 65-year-old woman who has been residing in a long-term care facility since a left middle cerebral artery infarct five years ago was transported to the emergency department by ambulance near dawn after nursing staff noted a sudden onset of productive cough streaked with yellow sputum, low-grade fever, and increased work of breathing that began the prior evening and failed to improve with an as-needed nebulized saline treatment customarily used for comfort. The paramedic crew found her sitting upright at the bedside and elected not to initiate oxygen, intravenous fluids, antipyretics, or bronchodilators en route in order to preserve an undisturbed physiologic profile for the receiving team. Before the stroke she had lived independently and remained physically active, and although she retains mild right-sided weakness she ambulates the hallway of the facility with a single-point cane and performs her own activities of daily living. Chronic medical issues include well-controlled primary hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and a remote hysterectomy for fibroids; she has never been told of heart muscle dysfunction, chronic kidney impairment, cirrhosis, chronic lung disease, or any form of malignancy. She quit a 10-pack-year cigarette habit two decades ago, drinks coffee but no alcohol, and denies use of illicit substances. Vaccination records at the facility confirm both pneumococcal formulations administered within the past five years and the current season’s influenza inoculation. Upon arrival to the bay at this sea-level hospital, she sat on the stretcher, shoulders slightly hunched forward, speaking between short clusters of words while clutching a disposable emesis bag that contained a small volume of mucopurulent sputum. Skin was warm and lightly moist with a roseate flush over the cheeks; nail beds were pink without cyanosis, and capillary refill measured less than two seconds. Neck veins were not visibly distended at 45 ° of elevation. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rhythm with a midsystolic point of maximal impulse, an unremarkable S1 and S2, no gallops, murmurs, or friction rubs. Lungs transmitted vesicular breath sounds throughout the left field; over the right mid-zone and lower posterior lung she had coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds, but percussion remained resonant and no dullness or stony note was appreciated inferiorly. The abdominal contour was flat, bowel sounds were present, and no organomegaly or tenderness could be elicited. There was trace dependent edema at both ankles attributed to prolonged sitting, and her old hemiparetic right arm displayed unchanged mild spasticity but preserved distal pulses. Triage vital signs obtained on ambient air before any therapy showed an oral temperature of 38.1 °C, a regular radial pulse of 97 beats min⁻¹ confirmed on three-lead monitor, noninvasive right-arm blood pressure 112/66 mm Hg verified manually, respirations counted for a full minute at 23 breaths min⁻¹ with modest intercostal recruitment and occasional pursed-lip exhalations, and fingertip pulse oximetry ranging 93–94 %. Point-of-care capillary glucose prior to venipuncture read 109 mg dL⁻¹. Peripheral blood drawn within ten minutes of arrival, before any flush larger than the 2 mL saline used to lock the catheter, returned a basic metabolic panel notable for sodium 137 mEq L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mEq L⁻¹, chloride 102 mEq L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mEq L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg dL⁻¹, and creatinine 0.8 mg dL⁻¹. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 14.1 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 39 %, hemoglobin 12.9 g dL⁻¹, and platelets 247 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. Patient note:
A 73-year-old female patient, who was hospitalized since 3 months, presented with complaints of paroxysmal dry cough since 2 weeks. The patient was admitted initially due to progressive dyspnea. Respiratory distress occurred 2 days later and she was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) after intubation for mechanical ventilation. Her past medical history included hypertension and diabetes mellitus for approximately 20 years; both of which were in a stable condition with regular medication. Six months before admission, she underwent a median sternotomy and thymectomy for thymoma. She denied having a recent travel history aboard but reported contact with a large pigeon population as there was a large dovecot near her residence. A series of examinations were performed for the unexplained respiratory failure, and myasthenic crisis was diagnosed based on high levels of acetylcholine receptor antibodies (> 4 nmol/L) and neurophysiological study findings. Consequently, she received several courses of plasma exchange followed by a high dose of prednisolone (30 mg daily) and azathioprine (25 mg daily) to treat the myasthenic crisis. Her respiratory condition improved after the therapy. She was transferred to the general ward after successfully weaning off mechanical ventilation. Oral prednisolone and azathioprine therapy was continued. After receiving prednisolone and azathioprine therapy for nearly 3 months, she developed dry cough. Physical examination revealed that respiratory rate was 15 breaths/min, blood pressure was 140/88 mmHg, heart rate was 80 beats/min, and body temperature was in the normal range. The remainder of the examination including cardiovascular, respiratory, and other organ systems was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation included a peripheral white blood cell count of 8870/µL; hemoglobin, 10.8 g/dL; and platelet count of 299,000/µL. Her serum alanine aminotransferase level was 9 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase level was 19 U/L; blood urea nitrogen level was 13 mg/dL; creatinine level was 0.3 mg/dL; level of procalcitonin was 0.1 ng/Ml, and level of C-reactive protein was 1.78 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis (with the patient breathing ambient air) revealed pH 7.47, PaCO2 56.9 mmHg, PaO2 66.7 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99%.
A thoracic CT scan was performed. On comparing it with the previous thoracic CT scan performed on admission (Fig. a), a newly developed 2-cm consolidative nodule was observed on the upper lobe of the left lung (Fig. b). Serum aspergillus galactomannan antigen testing, fungus stain and fungus culture of sputum, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of sputum for mycobacterium tuberculosis were all negative. The CT-guided biopsy was performed, and its pathology revealed chronic granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells engulfing thick-wall micro-organisms (Fig. a). These organisms were 4–6 microns in diameter, stains bright red with Periodic Acid Schiff (Fig. b) and black in Gomori Methenamine-Silver (Fig. c), consistent with those of cryptococcus. A subsequent serum titer of cryptococcal antigen was 1:8 using Remel Cryptococcus Antigen Test Kit (Remel, Lenexa, KS, USA). Because there were no neurologic symptoms and signs indicated cryptococcus meningoencephalitis, lumbar puncture was not performed. Immune status of the patient was then assessed. Except for recent immunosuppressive therapy for the myasthenic crisis, the patient revealed no evidence of malignancy or vasculitis, and human immunodeficiency virus testing was negative. To determine the possibility of cross transmission from infected patients, we reviewed the incidence of cryptococcal infection cases in the ICU and the general ward for up to 1 month before the patient was diagnosed, but no new cryptococcal infection cases were reported. Intravenous fluconazole, 400 mg daily, was administered for pulmonary cryptococcal infection for 14 days. Respiratory symptoms nearly resolved after treatment and the patient was discharged for outpatient follow-up with continuation of oral fluconazole 400 mg daily. The chest CT scan, 3 months after discharge, revealed complete clearance of the lesion (Fig. c) and the relevant inflammatory biomarkers were in the normal range. No recurrence of the Cryptococcal infection has occurred to date.

Patient note:
A 33-year-old man came to the hospital-based electrophysiology follow-up service this afternoon for a scheduled check-in regarding the oral vitamin K antagonist that had been prescribed six months earlier when ambulatory telemetry, ordered for episodic palpitations during marathon training, documented persistent non-valvular atrial fibrillation with an average ventricular response of 90 beats per minute; he has remained on the agent ever since and brings a neatly formatted spreadsheet showing thirteen consecutive finger-stick international normalized ratio (INR) measurements ranging from 2.2 to 2.7, with no single value outside that window and a calculated time-in-therapeutic-range above 80 percent. He has never required prothrombin complex concentrate, phytonadione rescue, hospital admission for over-anticoagulation, blood transfusion, nasal packing, endoscopic hemostasis, or iron supplementation, and he denies epistaxis, hematuria, hematochezia, melena, coffee-ground emesis, easy bruising larger than a coin, gum oozing, or subconjunctival hemorrhage. Nevertheless, he is concerned that several facets of his lifestyle might amplify hemorrhagic risk while systemic anticoagulation continues. He was told at 27 years of age, during a pre-employment physical for a commercial trucking company, that his systolic pressure was “too high”; since then two primary-care offices have documented seated readings consistently in the mid-150s systolic despite prescriptions for losartan 100 mg and chlorthalidone 25 mg daily, and in clinic today three auscultatory measurements obtained after five minutes of rest average 158/96 mm Hg with an irregularly irregular pulse of 78 beats per minute, respirations 15, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. To manage chronic lumbar pain from a collegiate weight-lifting accident he takes over-the-counter naproxen 440 mg each morning and, after evening workouts, an additional 220 mg; a cardiologist also started him on enteric-coated acetylsalicylic acid 81 mg daily one year ago after coronary artery calcium scoring landed in the 85th percentile for age. A psychiatrist initiated sertraline 50 mg nightly three months ago for generalized anxiety associated with career changes; he acknowledges that none of these agents has been reviewed in aggregate with an anticoagulation specialist. Social history reveals substantial ethanol intake: on weekdays he typically drinks two 16-ounce craft beers after work and a 5-ounce whiskey neat while preparing dinner, and on each weekend day he meets friends at a local brewery where he consumes five pints of lager followed by two mixed rum beverages during late-night gaming sessions, totaling approximately 44 standard alcoholic drinks per week. He denies morning drinking, tremors, blackouts, pancreatitis, or prior counseling to cut back, but he admits to occasional mild gastritis symptoms after late-night meals. He never smoked cigarettes, uses no recreational drugs, and follows a high-protein diet tailored for endurance sport. Past medical history is otherwise negative for transient ischemic attack, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, myocardial infarction, peripheral embolism, deep vein thrombosis, peptic ulcer disease, inflammatory bowel disease, liver cirrhosis, platelet disorders, connective-tissue disease, or hereditary coagulopathy, and there is no family history of intracranial aneurysm or hemophilia. Review of systems today is negative for chest pain, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, syncope, diplopia, visual field loss, dysarthria, unilateral weakness, abdominal distention, jaundice, pruritus, lower-extremity edema, or gross hematuria. On physical examination he appears muscular and in no acute distress with body mass index 29 kg/m²; conjunctivae are pink without pallor, sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa moist without petechiae, and the neck is supple without jugular venous distention. Cardiac auscultation reveals the expected variable first heart sound and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields are clear to percussion and auscultation. The abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender with no hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal wall varices, or spider angiomas. Extremities are warm with 2+ distal pulses, brisk capillary refill, and no ecchymoses or palpable purpura; neurologic screening shows full orientation, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation, and stable tandem gait. Laboratory studies drawn 45 minutes before the visit reveal hemoglobin 15.0 g/dL, hematocrit 45 percent, platelet count 265 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 13 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 100 mL/min/1.73 m², aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 72 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and albumin 4.4 g/dL; the point-of-care INR checked simultaneously is 2.4. A 12-lead electrocardiogram confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 80 beats per minute, normal axis, QRS duration 94 ms, and no acute ST-T abnormalities, while transthoracic echocardiography performed two months ago showed mild left atrial enlargement (4.2 cm), concentric left ventricular remodeling consistent with long-standing elevated afterload, and preserved ejection fraction of 60 percent without meaningful valvular disease. The patient requests comprehensive counseling on how persistently elevated arterial pressures, concurrent daily aspirin and frequent naproxen, regular selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use, and consumption of roughly 44 alcoholic beverages a week may influence the probability of a clinically significant hemorrhage while he remains on chronic warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation, and he is open to medication adjustments, lifestyle changes, or alternative anticoagulant strategies that might mitigate modifiable contributors to bleeding risk.

Patient note:
A 38-year-old Caribbean-Black (Afro-Trinidadian) female with a medical history of endometriosis, intermittently adherent with the oral contraceptive pill, initially presented to the adult emergency department with acute dyspnea during the preceding 2 days. Her vital signs reflected systolic blood pressures of 142 mm Hg, heart rate of 112 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. Her physical examination revealed a mildly elevated jugular venous pulse (10 cm of water), right chest stony dullness, no peripheral edema, and active menses.
A 12-lead electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia with an incomplete right bundle branch block, right ventricular hypertrophy, and subtle secondary ST-T segment changes (see ). A portable chest radiograph revealed a large-sized, right pleural effusion with mild perihilar congestion (see ). Pertinent diagnostic laboratory investigations included a D-dimer 208 ng/dL (normal ≤500 ng/mL), pro–brain natriuretic peptide (pro-BNP) 323 pg/mL (normal ≤300 pg/mL), cardiac troponin I (cTnI) 0.08 ng/mL (normal = 0.0-0.15 ng/mL). The patient’s arterial blood gas was consistent with mild hypoxia on 24% fractional inspiration of oxygen (FiO2) with an alveolar-arterial gradient (A-a gradient) of 14 mm Hg.
The patient was subsequently admitted for an inpatient hospitalization, and computed tomography (CT)-guided therapeutic thoracentesis was performed with a resultant hemorrhagic exudative effusion. Despite this intervention, the pleural effusion recurred within 48 hours, and cardiothoracic surgery was consulted for a video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) pleural biopsy, which later affirmed the presence of endometrial tissue on clinicopathological examination. The tentative diagnosis at this juncture was recurrent catamenial pleural effusions. On further interview, the patient acknowledged that she often experienced dyspneic episodes during menstruation.
During the ensuing hospitalization, she continued to experience persistent shortness of breath with an episode of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (PAF). A 2-dimensional transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed preserved left ventricular function with moderate right heart enlargement, septal flattening, and mild pHTN with estimated right ventricular systolic pressures of approximately 45 mm Hg. A 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional transesophageal echocardiogram (2D/3D-TEE) also revealed an intact interatrial septum with agitated saline “bubble” study. The PVs were incompletely visualized and hence the rationale for further advanced imaging (see ). A cardiac CT angiogram (CCTA) affirmed the presence of the suspected PAPVC of the left inferior PV to the left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein with angiographically normal coronary arteries (see ). The patient also underwent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI), which demonstrated the same aberrant connection with the remaining pulmonary venous vasculature appearing dilated in addition to the RA, right ventricle, and main pulmonary artery (see and , respectively). Left heart catheterization established angiographically normal coronary arteries with right heart catheterization revealing a significant hemodynamic left-to-right shunt with Qp:Qs ratio of 3:1, mild pHTN, and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (see for a summary of the pertinent cardiovascular investigations).
Cardiothoracic surgery was reconsulted regarding the surgical repair of the PAPVC. In the interim, the patient was instituted on an optimal cardiovascular regimen that included apixaban for her PAF, angiotensin receptor blocker with a neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), β-blocker (BB), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) for her heart failure and nitrates, tadalafil, and calcium channel blockade (CCB) for her pHTN. The rest of her hospital course was uneventful, and she was discharged home with scheduled corrective surgery in 2 months (due to our limited resource setting pending consultation from an international specialist CHD cardiothoracic surgeon).

Patient note:
A 68-year-old male with a background of long-standing hypertension and chronic systolic dysfunction of the left ventricle (most recent outpatient echocardiogram three months earlier documented an ejection fraction in the mid-30 % range) presented to the emergency department after two days of progressively worsening productive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest discomfort, and exertional dyspnea that had advanced to shortness of breath at rest during the morning of admission. He denied any previous cerebrovascular events, malignancy, chronic liver problems, or intrinsic kidney disease and reported that his baseline serum creatinine had always remained within normal limits during routine cardiology follow-up. He lives independently in a single-story home and manages his own activities of daily living without assistance. Home medications included carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg every morning, and low-dose aspirin. He had taken no antibiotics during this illness and had not sought other care prior to arrival. He denied recent travel, sick contacts, or exposure to institutional settings. On initial assessment in the triage bay he appeared mildly ill but in no distress while seated upright; he was alert, conversant, and oriented to person, place, and time without confusion or lethargy. Vital signs at that moment were temperature 38.3 degrees Celsius, heart rate 104 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute with shallow inspirations, blood pressure 110 mm Hg systolic and 68 mm Hg diastolic, and oxygen saturation of 88 % on ambient air which improved to 93 % after placement of 2 L/min nasal cannula. The jugular veins were not distended, cardiac auscultation revealed a displaced, laterally palpable point of maximal impulse and a soft S3 without murmurs, and bibasilar inspiratory crackles were more pronounced over the right lower posterior thorax. The remainder of the pulmonary examination demonstrated mildly prolonged expiratory phase but no wheezes. No peripheral edema was present. Neurologic examination was non-focal, and his speech and gait were normal when he ambulated to the restroom. A complete blood count showed a hematocrit of 40 % with mild leukocytosis; comprehensive metabolic panel revealed sodium 134 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL. Serum glucose measured 115 mg/dL on the basic metabolic panel drawn concurrently. Arterial blood gas obtained on room air before supplemental oxygen showed pH 7.45, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 60 mm Hg, yielding an A-a gradient suggestive of impaired oxygen transfer. Chest radiography demonstrated a right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and clear costophrenic angles; no blunting or layering fluid was seen to suggest an effusion. An electrocardiogram displayed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Initial lactate was 1.6 mmol/L. Given his chronic cardiac history, auscultatory S3, and borderline blood pressure, intravenous diuretics had not yet been administered so as not to compromise preload until further diagnostic clarification could be achieved. At the time the emergency physician completed her evaluation, the patient had received only supportive oxygen and antipyretics; no antibiotics, bronchodilators, or vasodilators had been started, preserving the ability to accurately document his presenting physiology.

Patient note:
An 82-year-old man was admitted to our medical center because of nausea and vomiting that occurred after the first oral anti-tuberculosis medication. One week before the admission, the patient underwent a routine-biannual health check-up at a local healthcare facility, and his chest radiograph showed consolidation in the left upper lobe (LUL). The patient received immediate medical attention owing suspected pulmonary tuberculosis. The patient had been receiving routine-biannual health check-ups, and did not have any major disease, except hypertension and diabetes mellitus. He had no history of smoking and drinking. He had been under clinidipin and sitagliptin treatments for 5 years for hypertension and diabetes, respectively.
On physical examination, his blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg, heart rate was 70 beats/min, respiratory rate was 18 breaths/min, and body temperature was 36.5℃. The findings of auscultation were insignificant. Signs of collagen vascular disease were not observed, and the remaining physical examination was unremarkable. His chest radiograph showed an increase in consolidation in the LUL as compared with the observation a week ago. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed a diffuse, patchy consolidation with ground-glass opacity in the LUL. Reticular opacities, on which our suspicion of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) was based, were found along the periphery of both the lower lobes (). No bronchiectasis or honeycombing was observed.
Laboratory findings were as follows: leukocyte count was 8,700/µL, C-reactive protein level was 103 mg/dL, and anti-nuclear antibody was not detected. Arterial blood gas analysis was not performed because the patient did not have dyspnea. The other data were within normal limits. Upon admission, 750-mg of levofloxacin was administered to the patient for the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia.
Blood and sputum cultures were negative. The results of the serologic tests for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Streptococcus pneumoniae were also negative. On day 4 after admission, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed because the lesion in the LUL had not improved. Cellular components and lymphocyte subsets were not assessed for the BAL specimen. Culture, tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction, and cytology of the BAL specimen were negative. Video-assisted thoracoscopy was performed owing to increased infiltration observed on the chest radiograph obtained on day 10. Pathological examination of the tissue samples obtained from the anterior and posterior segment of the LUL showed that DAD was at its organizing stage ().
We immediately started treatment with high doses of parenteral methylprednisolone, and found that the consolidation of LUL decreased within 3 days after the initiation of the treatment. Further, antibiotic treatment was discontinued, and the steroid therapy was maintained for 3 weeks. A follow-up examination showed almost complete disappearance of the LUL infiltration, although reticular opacities on both the lower lobes remained ().

Patient note:
A 75-year-old female presented to the emergency department with dyspnoea. She had been treated for recurrent lower respiratory tract infections by the general practitioner (GP) with oral antibiotics (12 cases in the past 14 months). Her relevant medical history included chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine 80–110 µmol/L), polymyalgia rheumatica requiring long-term steroids, asthma and chronic back pain. The pneumonia diagnosis was confirmed by a chest radiograph and CT showing multifocal nodular consolidation in the right lower lobe with cavitations and blood cultures were taken that grew Staphylococcus aureus.
Her medical history otherwise included depression, hypercholesterolaemia, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, spondylosis, glaucoma, hypertension, lacunar stroke, transient ischaemic attack, vitamin B12 deficiency and vascular dementia.
Her long-term treatment included hydromorphone, paracetamol, topiramate, paracetamol–codeine–doxylamine, doxylamine, colecalciferol, aspirin, duloxetine, pantoprazole, prednisolone, docusate, macrogol, hydroxocobalamin, salbutamol and denosumab.
On presentation, she was initially afebrile, heart rate of 95 bpm, respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation of 96%. On examination, there were crackles on the right base, dual heart sounds with no murmurs and no peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis. She was subsequently treated for pneumonia and urinary tract infection with intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam. The working diagnosis was S. aureus bacteraemia secondary to a pulmonary source.
The patient was transferred to the closest tertiary hospital as the eventual need for further investigations, including a trans-oesophageal echo, was anticipated in the context of S. aureus bacteraemia. The treatment of her bacteraemia was eventually changed to intravenous flucloxacillin (2 g four times daily) once sensitivities were confirmed. Flucloxacillin was planned to continue for a further 5 weeks via peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) on an 8 g/24 hours infuser that was monitored via hospital in the home (HITH).
Four weeks into the HITH treatment, the patient developed nausea and was investigated with blood results that showed worsening renal function associated with HAGMA. She was subsequently referred back to the regional hospital. Her heart rate was 105 bpm, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute and O2 sat 98% on room air. At that point, HAGMA was attributed to an acute kidney injury (AKI). Following adequate fluid resuscitation, HAGMA and AKI persisted. She was investigated for the AKI with a renal ultrasound which was negative and there were no eosinophils found in the urine. Interstitial nephritis secondary to flucloxacillin use was considered as another reason for her AKI but was deemed unlikely. The treatment plan was to commence sodium bicarbonate 840 mg once daily following consultation with the renal team. Ultimately, further investigations for the AKI were completed at the tertiary hospital. The HAGMA was suspected to be caused by the concurrent use of flucloxacillin and paracetamol. As a result of this, flucloxacillin was changed to cefazolin and the patient transferred again to a tertiary facility pending further investigations as well as suspected pulmonary embolism following reports of chest pain.

Patient note:
A 79-year-old male presented to the emergency department with acute left elbow pain. His past medical history was significant for diabetes mellitus, osteoarthritis, transient ischemic attack and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, for which he was prescribed warfarin. He woke on the morning of his presentation with pain and swelling in the elbow, which worsened over 6 hours before he arrived in the emergency department. He had no history of trauma and was non-ambulatory due to chronic pain from arthritis; he required assistance with all transfers from bed to a chair. There was no fever, rash, or other acute arthralgia. He reported that his most recent international normalized ratio (INR) measured 3 days ago was in the therapeutic range.
On physical examination, his temperature was 36.6°C, pulse 77 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 per minute, and blood pressure of 157/87 mmHg. His left elbow was swollen and warm posterolaterally. There was no erythema or ecchymosis. He had no bony tenderness along the joint, upper arm, or forearm. Range of motion of the elbow was markedly limited secondary to pain.
The treating physician performed point-of-care ultrasound to evaluate the swelling and suspected effusion. Using a high-frequency 10-5 MHz transducer (Sonosite, Bothell, WA, USA), both lateral longitudinal and posterior transverse images of the joint were obtained. The ultrasound images demonstrated a complex, compressible effusion with mixed hyperechoic and hypoechoic content, consistent with a hemarthrosis (, ) [-]. No layering fluid was appreciated to suggest lipohemarthrosis from an intra-articular fracture. Radiographs of the elbow were subsequently obtained, which re-demonstrated an effusion without evidence of fracture (). Laboratory studies were subsequently available, and notable for an INR of 7.9 and hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL.
Given the clinical history, absence of trauma or fever, and markedly supratherapeutic INR, a diagnosis of a spontaneous hemarthrosis was made. Although the elbow is an unusual location for a spontaneous hemarthrosis, the point-of-care ultrasound findings consistent with acute bleeding supported the diagnosis and decision to avoid arthrocentesis to further investigate the cause of the effusion. In the absence of bony tenderness or a history of trauma, the ultrasound findings of bleeding without cortical disruption helped obviate the need for computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging to evaluate for occult fracture.
The patient was managed conservatively, with a focus on symptom control. He was given oral and intravenous analgesia. The affected extremity was placed in a splint and sling for comfort, with a compression bandage applied to the elbow to facilitate hemostasis. Given the degree of pain associated with the hemarthrosis, his coagulopathy was reversed with oral vitamin K to accelerate INR normalization. He was discharged with instructions to follow up with his physician in 2 days. In serial follow-up visits, he reported progressive decrease in pain and swelling and ultimately symptom resolution. He and his primary care physician ultimately elected to discontinue anticoagulation.

Patient note:
A 38-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department in the early evening after three days of non-productive cough, mild right-sided chest tightness, and a gradual decline in her exercise tolerance from her customary 30-minute treadmill routine to feeling winded after climbing a single flight of stairs at work. She denied shaking chills, sweats, or measurable fever at home, reporting that her highest digital oral reading had been 36.6 °C earlier that morning. Her spouse, who accompanied her, stated she had remained fully alert, paid household bills online without difficulty, and drove herself to work the entire week, but had complained of “pressure” behind the sternum when taking a deep breath. She has a history of peripartum cardiomyopathy diagnosed six years ago with the most recent outpatient echocardiogram documenting a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 40 %; her symptoms have been stable on carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, low-dose sacubitril-valsartan, and a morning 20 mg furosemide tablet that she admits she skipped yesterday because she “didn’t feel puffy.” In addition, hepatology follows her for autoimmune cholangiopathy discovered on biopsy two years prior; she takes ursodiol 600 mg daily, has normal synthetic function, and has never required paracentesis or suffered encephalopathy. She has no known kidney disorder, her last office basic metabolic panel one month ago showed a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, and she has never seen a nephrologist. She denies cerebrovascular accidents, malignancies, or immune-suppressing conditions. She has never smoked, drinks an occasional glass of wine on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Vaccinations include the current season’s influenza shot given at an employer health fair and a 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate injection administered one year ago; she has not received antibiotics, corticosteroids, or inhaled bronchodilators in the past twelve months. Bronchoscopy with trans-bronchial lung biopsy revealed non- caseating granulomatous inflammation with characteristic ‘asteroid bodies’ (

With the diagnosis of sarcoidosis with coexisting Takayasu arteritis, she was treated with prednisolone 60 mg once daily (1 mg/kg/day) along with supportive treatment including oxygen, chest physiotherapy, bone protection with calcium and vitamin D, and thromboembolism prophylaxis with daily 60 mg of subcutaneous enoxaparin. Glaucoma was treated with topical timolol (0.25% twice daily) and oral acetazolamide (500 mg followed by 250 mg twice daily), and she responded well over the course of 2 weeks.

Patient note:
The patient described in this report was a woman, aged 35 years, married with two children, and had a history of relapsing episodes of paroxysmal AF, for which flecainide controlled-release was prescribed (January 2017) at the dose of 100 mg once daily. Subsequently, due to the reappearance of AF runs during the 24-h Holter recording, associated with annoying palpitations, the patient was offered the radiofrequency ablation, which she refused. The controlled-release flecainide was therefore cancelled and replaced by the addition of bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily plus amiodarone 200 mg daily. The echocardiogram () was characterized by a severely depressed (23%) left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) due to uniform dilatation of the left ventricle and moderate secondary mitral insufficiency. Thus, considering the echocardiographic picture compatible with the diagnosis of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, the therapy was supplemented by ramipril at the dose of 5 mg once a day, plus a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, i.e., canrenone 25 mg daily, plus furosemide 25 mg daily. In addition, due to the incumbent risk of cardioembolic events related to recurrent paroxysmal AF episodes, the patient was given rivaroxaban at the dose of 15 mg once daily. In January 2018, despite the patient’s close adherence to therapy, she started complaining about dyspnea related to minimal physical activity (New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III). The deterioration of the hemodynamic and clinical picture was related to the worsening of the functional mitral insufficiency and the occurrence of intermittent left bundle branch block. For the worsening mitral regurgitation the patient was offered a MitraClip procedure that she refused (February 2018). The echocardiogram revealed a severe dilation of the left ventricle with end-diastolic volume of 107 mL and end-systolic volume of 82 mL, and severely reduced LVEF (32%) with left atrial volume index (LAVI) of 38 mL/m2. During the follow-up, in July 2018, her ventricular function was still severely reduced (LVEF 32%) and LAVI was about 38 mL/m2, despite the cardioprotective therapy. Therefore, ramipril was suspended, and after 48 h sacubitril/valsartan therapy was initiated, at the dosage of 24/26 mg twice daily in add-on to therapy with furosemide 25 mg quaque altera die (qod), carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, canrenoate 25 mg once daily, and rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily. In February 2019, sacubitril/valsartan was up titrated to 49/51 mg/bis in die (bid). In May 2019, sacubitril/valsartan was up titrated to 97/103 mg/bid, but patient had symptomatic hypotension, so the dosing was reduced to 49/51 mg/bid. At the subsequent follow-up visit, sinus rhythm was restored and LVEF progressively recovered, with a marked reduction of chamber dimensions and cardiac volumes. In May 2019, LVEF was 35%, and LAVI was reduced to 30 mL/m2. At present, the patient is in good conditions and furosemide dosing has been curtailed to the 25 mg qod ().
The patient whose clinical description constitutes the subject of the present article, gave informed consent to participate in the study, and provided informed consent for publication.

She had a history of congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and hypertension; moreover, she had a history of hepatocellular carcinoma at the segment S5 caused by chronic hepatitis C, which was treated by transcatheter embolism. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) performed at 78 years of age revealed a 7 mm small, mobile, string-like mass attached to the noncoronary cusp (). Infective endocarditis was excluded on the basis of the following findings: blood chemical analyses revealed no elevation of inflammation markers, blood cultures were negative for microorganisms, and the patient's body temperature was within the normal range. A cardiac tumor, including metastasis of the hepatocellular carcinoma, was suspected, and surgical treatment was recommended to prevent thromboembolic events. However, the patient declined surgery; thus, she was carefully followed up with periodic TTE.
Thereafter, the patient was transferred to our institution with complaints of upper abdominal pain and hematemesis. Her blood pressure was 130/90 mmHg, and heart rate was 130 beats/min. Physical examination revealed mild anemia, a soft, flat abdomen with no palpable masses, and normal bowel sounds. On auscultation, her chest was clear and no abnormal murmurs could be heard. Chest radiography did not present any signs of cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion. Electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation. Blood chemical analyses revealed mild anemia (red blood cell count: 255 × 104/μL; hemoglobin levels: 8.2 g/dL), slightly low platelet count (12.5 × 104/μL), slightly elevated serum urea nitrogen levels (29.6 mg/dL), mild hypoproteinemia (6.1 g/dL), mild hypoalbuminemia (2.3 g/dL), slightly elevated C-reactive protein levels (1.3 mg/dL), and coagulation dysfunction (prothrombin time, 49%; fibrin/fibrinogen degradation products, 27.9 μg/mL; and D-dimer, 14.7 μg/mL). Upper gastroendoscopy revealed a gastric ulcer with an exposed blood vessel situated posteriorly in the body of the stomach. Anticoagulant therapy was ceased, and a proton pump inhibitor was administered.
On day 15 of admission, the patient experienced mild impairment of consciousness, disturbance of speech articulation, and left facial paralysis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed high-intensity signal lesions in the right insular cortex and right corona radiate (). Acute cerebral infarction was diagnosed and heparin sodium and warfarin potassium were administered; subsequently her symptoms improved. TTE revealed no alteration of mobile, string-like mass attached to the noncoronary cusp. Moreover, moderate mitral and mild aortic regurgitations were evident, although ejection fraction was unaffected. We considered the tumor to be the cause of acute cerebral infarction, although the possibility of atrial fibrillation causing the infarction could not be excluded. The patient consented to surgical therapy, and surgery was performed 1.5 months after the cerebral infarction occurred. Cardiopulmonary bypass was established and the ascending aorta was opened by median sternotomy. The tumor revealed attachments to the noncoronary, left, and right coronary cusps; eventually tumor resection was performed. Furthermore, after resection, the maze procedure was performed for atrial fibrillation.
Pathological examination of the resected specimen revealed that it is comprised of a core of aggregated elastic fibers and hyaline material covered with a single squamous cell layer (). There was no evidence of metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma; however, the pathologic findings were consistent with PFE. Atrial fibrillation was restored to sinus rhythm, and the postoperative course was uneventful.

Patient note:
A 67-year old right-hand-dominant male was referred to our plastic surgery department with a 3 year history of a swelling on his right middle fingertip with no prior history of trauma to the digit. The mass had been slowly enlarging over the preceding 3–4 months, was becoming increasingly tender and occasionally bled due to a superficial abrasion on the surface. The patient had a past medical history of Grave’s disease, atrial fibrillation and a perforated gastric ulcer.
Examination revealed a 2 × 1.5cm mass over the distal pulp and hyponychium of the right middle finger. The swelling was mildly tender and there was an area of superficial ulceration centrally (). The digit was neurovascularly intact with normal range of motion and no evidence of local erythema, inflammation or discolouration. The working differential diagnosis following initial consultation included glomus tumour, ganglion cyst and haemangioma, thus the patient was booked for surgery without prior imaging.
One month following referral, the patient underwent excision biopsy of the lesion which was not found to be communicating with bone, nerve or tendon and the intra-operative impression was that of a ganglion cyst (). The initial histopathology examination reported a circumscribed multinodular predominantly solid tumour () ulcerating the overlying epidermis. There were focal papillary projections with tubular/ductal structures () where ducts were lined by a double layer of epithelium consisting of inner cuboidal cells and an outer myoepithelial layer (). There was also evidence of lymphovascular invasion (), focally high mitotic activity () and the tumour was shown to abut the margins. Immunohistochemistry was performed () confirming a myoepithelial cell population expressing smooth muscle actin, calponin, D2-40 () and p63 (). The tumour was classified as digital papillary adenocarcinoma. The histopathology sections were sent to an external institution for expert opinion and the diagnosis affirmed with recommendation of complete excision and close follow-up. This recommendation was echoed when the case was discussed at the local multi-disciplinary meeting.
The patient underwent partial amputation of the digit () and computed tomography (CT) scan of thorax, abdomen and pelvis, which showed no evidence of distant disease. The histology report on the wider excision specimen confirmed no invasion of underlying bone and margins free of tumour (residual tumour in wider specimen 0.5 mm). This patient is currently 1 year disease-free and will be followed closely in the outpatient department with clinical examination, yearly chest X-ray and additional imaging as needed for at least a ten year period.

Patient note:
A 29-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-week history of progressive paroxysmal
palpitations accompanied by persistent chest tightness and dyspnea. She had no other
medical history. During her 3 years of marriage, she had encountered difficulty
achieving pregnancy naturally. When admitted, she was in the 11th week of
gestation following in vitro fertilization. Physical examination revealed a pulse of
167 beats per minute (bpm), regular heart rhythm, clear heart sounds with no
pathological murmur and no lower limb edema. Auxiliary examinations included a
12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) which showed AT at 150 bpm with a negative
P-wave in leads I, aVL and aVR, as well as a positive
P-wave in leads II, III, aVF and V1 (), and an echocardiogram which revealed
an LA of 42mm (anteroposterior diameter), left ventricular end-diastolic dimension
(LVEDD) of 55mm and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 48%. She was found
to be euthyroid and her N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide level was 4285
pg/ml. The patient was diagnosed with atrial tachyarrhythmia. An esophageal lead was
applied to confirm the diagnosis, but rapid pacing failed to terminate it. Rest ECG
showed a rate of 110 to 120 bpm. Slight movement, such as eating or going to the
toilet, caused her heart rate to exceed 150 bpm. Intravenous administration of
propafenone transiently converted the tachycardia to sinus rhythm but could not
sustain. Other medications such as metoprolol could not adequately control the heart
rate either.
Ablation was performed under local anesthesia, Multichannel EP recorder (EP
MedSystems, USA) and three-dimensional (3D) electroanatomic mapping system
(CartoSound, Biosense Webster, CA, USA). The patient still exhibited tachycardia
while undergoing the procedure. The right femoral vein was cannulated using an
8French (F) sheath, through which a saline infusion ablation catheter (ThermoCool
Electrophysiology Catheter, Biosense Webster, CA, USA) was introduced into the right
atrium (RA). A detailed electro-anatomic map of the RA and coronary sinus (CS) were
created using fast anatomical mapping (FAM). Then the right internal jugular vein
was cannulated using a 6F sheath through which a decapolar EP catheter (Rithm ID,
Synaptic Medical, CN) was introduced into the CS under the guidance of the
electro-anatomic map. The intracardiac electrogram showed a cycle length of 330-370
msec and CS activation order of CS1,2 earlier than CS9,10
(), which confirmed the AT
originating from the LA. Then the right femoral vein was cannulated using a 10F
sheath and an 8.5F long sheath, through which an EP catheter (SoundStar, Biosense
Webster, CA, USA) was introduced and a transseptal needle (St. Jude Medical, USA)
was applied to perform transseptal puncture under CartoSound guidance. Four thousand
units of unfractionated heparin were administered intravenously with access to LA to
maintain an active clotting time of approximately 350 seconds. The ablation catheter
and a circular decapolar catheter (Lasso, Biosense Webster, CA, USA) were introduced
into the LA via the transseptal site. A detailed electro-anatomic map of LA was
created and clearly demonstrated focal activation originating from the very distal
LAA (). There was no evidence of
macro-reentry. Radiofrequency (RF) ablation was performed using 20 watts, titrating
up to 25 watts, for approximately 16 times (power control mode, 40℃, 30cc/min). Each
time, ablation energy was delivered for 6-10 seconds. Ablation at this site
terminated the tachycardia with no recurrence noted during a 30-minute observation
period. No tachycardia was induced by programmed stimulation and rapid atrial
pacing. The procedure lasted for 2.5 hours with no fluoroscopy and without
complications.
At the 1-month follow-up visit, the ECG showed normal sinus rhythm and the
echocardiogram showed LA of 30 mm, LV of 48 mm, LVEF of 52%. Three months after the
procedure, a 24-hour Holter exam revealed sinus rhythm with 7987 atrial premature
beats and 903 episodes of paroxysmal AT (8.1% of the day). And the patient
complained of occasional palpitations. Six months later, a 24-hour Holter exam
conducted showed sinus rhythm with 37 atrial premature beats and 5 episodes of
paroxysmal AT (0.06% of the day). A healthy baby boy was eventually delivered by
Cesarean section. No palpitations were reported thereafter.

Patient note:
A 52-year-old Thai man presented with acute chest tightness and palpitation while rubber farming for 1 week. He had a history of hypertension and heavy smoking for 10 years. He was admitted at a local hospital, and the results of the complete blood count and lipid profile showed within normal limits. His electrocardiogram showed a normal sinus rhythm with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and his clinical signs did not improve, so he was referred to our hospital. His clinical condition was suspected to be due to coronary arterial disease by a cardiologist. However, his exercise stress test was inconclusive, so he was further investigated by CTCA.
The 64-slice CTCA findings showed no calcified coronary artery walls, and the calcium score was zero. A completely absent LCx was observed, which was associated with multiple enlarged diagonal branches of the left anterior descending artery (LAD) to supply the lateral wall of the left ventricle (). Also seen was the superdominant RCA with its posterolateral branch continuing into the territory of the LCx (Figures and ). No significant stenosis was detected. The patient was treated with antiarrhythmic drug (amlodipine 2.5 mg/day) and scheduled for follow-up visits at his district hospital.
