Patient note:
A 42-year-old man was rushed to the department by co-workers after he collapsed onto a loading dock pallet midway through his afternoon shift at a local electronics warehouse; they report he had spent the previous three days pushing through worsening chills, high-volume sweating, and a hacking cough that produced foul-tasting yellow sputum but refused to seek help because he “couldn’t afford to miss any hours.”  He normally resides in a second-floor walk-up apartment with his partner, climbs two flights of stairs multiple times a day without limitation, and commutes by bicycle when the weather allows; no family members describe baseline confusion or memory lapses.  Past illnesses are few except for chronic transaminitis discovered during a blood donation screening eight years ago and later attributed to untreated hepatitis B acquired perinatally—fibro-scan last year revealed mild portal bridging without evidence of varices, ascites, encephalopathy, or synthetic failure, and he has never required antiviral therapy or hepatology procedural interventions. He denies any prior diagnoses of cancer or congestive heart failure.  He takes no prescription medications, purchases over-the-counter ibuprofen for occasional musculoskeletal aches, drinks two bottles of beer on weekends, and has never smoked or used illicit substances.  Vaccination records in his phone show an inactivated influenza shot from a community drive in November and completion of both pneumococcal series during adolescence because of childhood asthma that resolved by high school.  Paramedics found him seated on the warehouse floor, diaphoretic and panting, alternating between mumbling incoherent phrases and staring blankly; out of concern for preserving pristine vitals they withheld oxygen, intravenous fluids, antipyretics, or nebulizers during the eight-minute transport.  In the resuscitation bay, before any intervention beyond placement of saline locks, he appeared tremulous, skin flushed and hot, pupils equal but slow to track, and answered only to loud voice, misidentifying the month and hospital; Glasgow Coma Scale scored 13 (E3 V4 M6).  Pre-treatment vital signs read: oral temperature 102.0 °F, regular pulse 119 beats per minute, automated right-arm blood pressure 134/81 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute with nasal flaring and visible abdominal displacement, and fingertip pulse oximetry 92 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude.  Neck veins were flat at 30°, the point of maximal impulse was non-displaced, and auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1/S2 without gallop or murmur.  Pulmonary examination demonstrated coarse bronchial breath sounds and inspiratory crackles spanning the entire left upper lobe and lower lobe posteriorly, with resonant percussion tones throughout and no stony dullness or succussion splash to suggest fluid accumulation; the right lung transmitted vesicular sounds with an occasional late crackle at the base.  Abdomen was soft, mildly distended, and revealed a smooth, firm liver edge palpable two centimeters below the costal margin but non-tender; no spider angiomas, caput medusae, or asterixis were elicited.  Extremities were warm without edema, capillary refill under two seconds, and fingernails stained with years of solder flux exposure.  Bedside capillary glucose obtained before phlebotomy measured 158 mg/dL.  Venous blood drawn within five minutes of arrival showed sodium 115 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 88 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 56 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, and serum glucose 154 mg/dL; complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 18.4 × 10⁹/L with 90 % neutrophils, hematocrit 62 %, hemoglobin 20.0 g/dL, and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L.  An arterial sample from the right radial artery, drawn while he continued to breathe room air, returned pH 7.65, PaCO₂ 24 mm Hg, PaO₂ 94 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 26 mEq/L, and base excess +2, consistent with a primary respiratory alkalosis driven by extreme tachypnea.  Lactate was 1.8 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin fell below the assay detection threshold.  A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes after arrival—prior to fluids, antibiotics, or oxygen—revealed a dense, homogeneous consolidation occupying most of the left upper lobe with prominent air bronchograms; both costophrenic angles remained sharp, cardiac silhouette was normal, mediastinum stable, and no meniscus or layering shadow suggested pleural fluid.  Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 118 bpm with a normal axis and nonspecific anterior T-wave flattening comparable to an occupational health tracing from two years earlier.  Two peripheral blood-culture sets, a coughed sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched before any antimicrobial or supportive therapy was initiated, ensuring that all physiologic measurements and laboratory values above represent the patient’s untreated presentation.

Patient note:
A 51-year-old lady presented with cough and shortness of breath. The symptoms started in the morning after waking up from sleeping. The cough was productive of pink-colored sputum and she was using accessory muscles to breathe. The family members noticed that she was also drowsy, confused, and not responding to them for about 30 min. Afterwards, she was fully aware of the surroundings; however, she could not recall what happened. They measured her blood glucose and it was 8.5 mmol/L. The past medical history was significant for a resected right temporal meningioma 3 years back and type 2 diabetes mellitus with well controlled HbA1c. Home medications are phenytoin 200 mg twice daily, lamotrigine 200 mg three times daily, escitalopram 10 mg once daily, and metformin/sitagliptin 1000/50 mg twice daily. The patient is known to experience seizures despite those anti-epileptic medications.
On examination, she was afebrile (37.3°C), hypotensive (89/47 mmHg), and hypoxic (82% oxygen saturation on room air). Respiratory exam showed bilateral crackles up to the mid zones bilaterally. Neurological examination did not reveal any abnormality. The initial laboratory tests ordered upon admission are shown in .
Arterial Blood Gases (ABG) on Room Air. pH 7.41 (7.35–7.45), PaO2 48.8 mmHg (83–108), PaCO2 35 mmHg (35–45), HCO3 22.5 mmol/L (21–28), PaO2/FiO2 ratio: 232 (normal ratio is approximately 500).
ABG on Room Air after 2 Days. pH 7.43 (7.35–7.45), PaO2 90 mmHg (83–108), PaCO2 36 mmHg (35–45), HCO3 24.5 mmol/L (21–28), PaO2/FiO2 ratio: 429 (normal ratio is approximately 500).
CXR on Admission. Multiple confluent and patchy air space opacities noticed diffusely involving both lung fields ().
CXR after 2 Days. Bilateral lung opacities appear significantly resolved as compared to the previous chest radiograph ().
ECG. Sinus tachycardia with premature ventricular complexes ().
Trans-Thoracic Echocardiography. Good global contractility and no resting regional wall motion abnormality. Normal Left ventricle systolic function. Ejection fraction 58%–60%.
The patient received 1.5 L of intravenous normal saline boluses, she was connected to noninvasive ventilator—Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machine with empirical IV. antibiotic to cover aspiration pneumonia and admitted to MICU for observation. There, she stayed for 2 days and showed marked improvement clinically and in the requirements of oxygen. Repeated CXR showed dramatic resolution of bilateral lung opacities without giving furosemide (). Compliance to anti-convulsant medications was emphasized, and she was maintaining oxygen saturation above 95% on room air upon discharge.

Patient note:
An 86-year-old man who spent nearly half a century maintaining diesel locomotives for the state rail line arrived to the pre-operative consultation this morning walking slowly but unassisted, carrying a thin folder that contained outside imaging reports and a neatly handwritten medication list. Over the past year he has noted a gradually intensifying morning cough productive of scant white sputum, occasional wheeze while climbing the single flight to his apartment, and two winter flare-ups that required five-day prednisone tapers from his primary physician but never emergency-department evaluation or ventilatory support. Baseline spirometry performed last month for surgical planning recorded an FEV1 of 1.05 L (55 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.45 and less than 6 % reversibility after 400 µg salbutamol; a postero-anterior chest radiograph the same day showed hyperinflated lung fields and flattened diaphragms but no infiltrates. He inhales tiotropium 18 µg each dawn and budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 µg two puffs twice daily, empties an albuterol inhaler roughly every six weeks when neighborhood sidewalks become steep, and saturates 95 % on ambient air at rest today with a respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min. A screening low-dose CT obtained for lung-cancer surveillance six months ago incidentally revealed a 2.1 cm spiculated lesion in the right upper lobe; subsequent PET–CT demonstrated avid uptake confined to that nodule without mediastinal, hepatic, adrenal, or osseous activity, and bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated non-small-cell carcinoma. Cardiothoracic colleagues plan a video-assisted thoracoscopic lobectomy and have requested clearance in view of his advanced age and pulmonary limitations. 

The patient denies ever experiencing crushing retrosternal pressure, diaphoresis with exertion, unexpected dyspnea when lying flat, awakening suddenly gasping, or bilateral ankle swelling, and he has never been hospitalized for a myocardial infarction. He walks four short city blocks at his own pace to the grocery and pauses only for breathlessness related to his chronic airway disease rather than calf discomfort, and he has never undergone lower-extremity bypass, angioplasty, or evaluation for claudication. He has no history of connective-tissue or autoimmune disorders, peptic ulcer disease, or gastrointestinal bleeding. Neurologically he recalls no episodes of facial droop, unilateral weakness, transient speech disturbance, visual blackout, seizure, or memory lapses; he still balances his checkbook without errors and recounts the dates of his grandchildren’s birthdays from memory. Routine HIV screening performed three years ago was negative, and he has never had opportunistic infections. Serial complete blood counts have remained within normal ranges, and he has no personal history of hematologic malignancy. 

His past laboratory panels have shown mildly elevated transaminases attributed to a combination of long-standing statin therapy and hepatic steatosis documented by ultrasound three months ago, which revealed a homogeneous hyperechoic liver measuring 15 cm with smooth contour, patent portal flow, and no splenomegaly. At that draw alanine aminotransferase was 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 84 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1; he has never developed jaundice, abdominal distention, encephalopathy, or required diuretics. Fasting plasma glucose recorded during last week’s comprehensive metabolic panel was 102 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.6 %, values he maintains with portion control and evening walks—he takes no hypoglycemic agents and logs carbohydrate intake on paper. Renal indices today include sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 78 mL/min/1.73 m²; urinalysis is bland with no protein, blood, or casts. Lipid profile last month demonstrated total cholesterol 208 mg/dL, LDL 118 mg/dL, HDL 46 mg/dL, and triglycerides 130 mg/dL; he takes atorvastatin 20 mg nightly without myalgias. Current medications also include low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg each morning for systolic pressures that average 130s mm Hg at home, and cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily; he reports no drug allergies. He quit cigarettes 18 years ago after accumulating 55 pack-years, drinks a single glass of red wine with Sunday dinner, and denies illicit drug use. Family history is remarkable for a brother who died from pneumonia at 90 and a father who succumbed to “old age” at 93; there are no early strokes, coronary interventions, peripheral amputations, or cirrhotic complications among first-degree relatives. 

Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, night sweats, unintentional weight loss beyond four pounds since the biopsy, hemoptysis, chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, abdominal pain, hematemesis, melena, dysuria, gross hematuria, or rash. On examination he appears lean and attentive, seated comfortably. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/68 mm Hg seated in the right arm, pulse 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate as noted, weight 69 kg, height 173 cm, and body-mass index 23 kg/m². Oral mucosa is moist without cyanosis. Neck is supple, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulsation rises to 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung percussion is hyperresonant bilaterally, and auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds with scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. The abdomen is flat and nontender; the liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, smooth and mildly tender to deep inspiration, with no shifting dullness. Extremities are warm with 2+ radial, femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses, capillary refill under two seconds, no digital clubbing, cyanosis, or edema. Neurologic screen shows orientation to person, place, and date, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady gait albeit slowed by mild exertional dyspnea. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, axis within normal limits, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, and no pathologic Q waves or ST-segment deviation. 

The surgical team seeks guidance regarding peri-operative inhaler scheduling, need for pre-habilitation to enhance postoperative pulmonary mechanics, interpretation of his mildly abnormal liver enzymes in the context of anticipated anesthesia, and recommendations for antiplatelet management around the planned minimally invasive resection.

question:
Patient note:
A 72-year-old woman was seen in the joint-replacement pre-assessment suite six days before a scheduled primary right total knee arthroplasty intended to address debilitating tricompartmental osteoarthritis that has failed topical NSAIDs, physical therapy, and three ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injections; the orthopaedic team anticipates a midline parapatellar approach lasting about 90 minutes, tourniquet inflation for less than one hour, estimated blood loss 200–300 mL, and transfer post-closure to the orthopaedic ward with plans for weight-bearing as tolerated beginning the same evening. She arrived in her daughter’s car, walked unassisted from the parking deck to reception, and spoke in full sentences without needing to pause, noting that at home she climbs the eight steps to her porch with one rest at the top because of knee pain rather than breathlessness and can fold laundry for 20 minutes before sitting. Ten years ago she was admitted with progressive ankle swelling, nocturnal cough, and a 4-kg weight gain; echocardiography revealed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 38 % with global systolic dysfunction and mild functional tricuspid regurgitation. Guideline-directed therapy—currently carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, and furosemide 20 mg each morning—has prevented any repeat hospitalization in the past year, though she occasionally awakens once per month to orthopnea that resolves after elevating the head of the bed. Five years before the heart-failure diagnosis she experienced squeezing substernal discomfort radiating to the jaw while gardening; troponin I peaked at 4.1 ng/mL, coronary angiography demonstrated an 80 % proximal left anterior descending lesion treated with a drug-eluting stent, and she completed phase II cardiac rehabilitation without recurrent angina. Follow-up stress echocardiography performed eight months ago achieved seven metabolic equivalents without inducible ischemia. Current medications in addition to those above include aspirin 81 mg daily, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, spironolactone 25 mg in the morning, and lisinopril 10 mg nightly; adherence is corroborated by pharmacy refill history. Hypertension was first noted in her forties and remains controlled, with home blood-pressure diary entries averaging 118–126/68–74 mm Hg. She has never been told she has diabetes, and fasting plasma glucose values obtained at annual wellness visits remain below 105 mg/dL; no glucose-lowering agents have ever been prescribed. She denies transient vision loss, speech disturbance, focal weakness, or carotid intervention. Pulmonary history is limited to well-controlled mild intermittent asthma treated with as-needed albuterol; she quit smoking 20 years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure and now consumes a glass of red wine twice weekly. Surgical background includes an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 50 and a left cataract extraction at 67. Family history is notable for a brother who required coronary bypass at 72 and a mother who died of heart failure at 83; no early cerebrovascular events are reported. Review of systems today is negative for fever, recent weight change, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea beyond her rare episodes, palpitations, syncope, abdominal pain, hematochezia, urinary changes, or easy bruising. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs obtained in the right arm show blood pressure 124/70 mm Hg, regular pulse 64 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, and oral temperature 36.6 °C; height 164 cm, weight 78 kg, body-mass index 29 kg/m². She appears euvolemic and in no distress. Jugular venous pulsation is estimated at 4 cm above the sternal angle with the head of bed at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is palpated in the fifth interspace slightly lateral to the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft third heart sound and a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border without radiation; lungs are clear to auscultation with symmetric excursion. Abdominal examination is soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds; no hepatosplenomegaly or pulsatile masses are appreciated. Lower extremities demonstrate trace bilateral pitting edema to the ankles and a valgus-deforming, crepitant right knee with 10° fixed flexion contracture but full motor strength distally. Neurologic screening shows intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in upper extremities, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a slightly slowed but steady gait with a cane. Laboratory studies drawn one hour prior reveal hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, platelet count 236 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.67 mg/dL corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 46 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting glucose obtained in the same sample is 102 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded today shows normal sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute, Q waves in leads V1-V2 consistent with prior infarction, and no acute ST-T changes when compared with a tracing from last year. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography displays mild cardiomegaly without pulmonary vascular congestion or effusion. Airway assessment documents a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor gap 3.5 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, and full cervical extension. The peri-operative plan includes continuing beta-blocker, renin-angiotensin inhibition, mineralocorticoid antagonist, loop diuretic, and antiplatelet therapy on the morning of surgery; withholding the diuretic if systolic blood pressure falls below 100 mm Hg on the day of admission; employing a regional anesthetic technique with ultrasound-guided adductor canal and IPACK blocks supplemented by light general anesthesia; inserting a radial arterial catheter for beat-to-beat monitoring; limiting crystalloid to 1 mL/kg/h with goal-directed boluses guided by pulse-pressure variation; and performing strict fluid balance accounting given her underlying ventricular dysfunction and reduced renal reserve. Sequential compression sleeves will be applied in theatre, chemoprophylaxis with low-dose subcutaneous heparin will commence the evening of surgery, and physical therapy will assist with dangling at the bedside within four hours of arrival to the ward. After the plan was reviewed, the patient accurately repeated medication instructions, fasting guidelines, early mobilization goals, and signs of volume overload that should prompt notification of the care team, and she voiced determination to proceed with knee replacement to regain mobility for gardening and church activities.

Patient note:
A 67-year-old woman came to the peri-operative evaluation clinic this afternoon at the request of her general surgeon five days before a planned elective laparoscopic ventral hernia repair that is expected to last under two hours, use three trocar sites, and require an overnight stay for pain control but no critical-care monitoring. She walked from the parking garage to the clinic without assistance, carrying a handbag and speaking in full sentences, and reports that during a typical day she prepares meals, vacuums her small apartment, gardens for thirty minutes, and climbs the twenty-two steps to her second-floor unit while pausing briefly at the landing to catch her breath more from deconditioning than cardiorespiratory limitation. She denies exertional chest tightness, jaw or arm discomfort, palpitations, presyncope, or lower-extremity swelling, and states she sleeps flat on one pillow with uninterrupted rest. Her medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes diagnosed twenty-three years ago; because oral agents eventually failed to keep her glucose targets in range she transitioned to a basal-bolus regimen consisting of insulin glargine 24 units subcutaneously each evening and pre-meal insulin lispro doses adjusted to carbohydrate intake three times daily. Continuous glucose sensor downloads reviewed at today’s visit show fasting values largely between 110 and 150 mg/dL with no nocturnal hypoglycemia alarms. The endocrinology note from last month documents an A1c of 7.4 %. She also recounts a small right frontal lacunar infarct four years ago that left her with a barely noticeable decrease in fine sensation over the fingertips of her left hand but no weakness; she completed a six-week course of outpatient occupational therapy, maintains independence in all activities of daily living, drives without restriction, and has had no further transient neurologic episodes. Antiplatelet prophylaxis consists of aspirin 81 mg daily, and she remains on atorvastatin 40 mg nightly for mixed dyslipidemia discovered at the same time as her stroke. Additional chronic problems include well-controlled primary hypertension treated with losartan 50 mg each morning and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease attributed to longstanding diabetic nephropathy with a baseline creatinine in the mid-1 mg/dL range. She has never been told she has coronary artery blockages, has not undergone stress testing or cardiac catheterization, and reports no hospitalizations for cardiac or pulmonary complaints. Respiratory history is limited to mild intermittent asthma requiring two puffs of albuterol perhaps once every two weeks during spring pollen season; she quit cigarette smoking sixteen years ago after a 12-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of white wine with dinner on Saturdays, and denies illicit drug use. Surgical history includes only an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy at age 30. Allergies are limited to penicillin, which caused a pruritic rash in childhood. Review of systems today is negative for fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, claudication, visual changes, or bleeding tendencies. After five minutes seated her vital signs are blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg in the right arm, pulse 68 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air, and oral temperature 36.7 °C; body mass index is 31 kg/m². Physical examination shows a well-nourished, alert individual in no distress. Jugular venous contour is not elevated at 45 degrees, carotid upstrokes are brisk with no bruits, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced. First and second heart sounds are crisp without gallops, rubs, or murmurs. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout. Abdomen displays a soft reducible midline fascial defect measuring approximately 4 cm but no tenderness, guarding, or organomegaly. Extremities are warm with 2+ radial and dorsalis pedis pulses and no edema. Neurologic screening reveals intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation except for diminished pinprick over the left distal fingertips, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn an hour before the visit demonstrate hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.9 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.48 mg/dL, unchanged from previous measurements and corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 46 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose in the same panel is 128 mg/dL; liver enzymes and coagulation profile are within reference limits. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats per minute, normal intervals, and no Q waves or ischemic ST-T abnormalities. Chest radiograph reveals clear lung fields and normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. The anesthesiology note documents Mallampati class II airway, full cervical extension, and an inter-incisor distance of 4 cm. She has been instructed to continue her evening basal insulin at 80 % of the usual dose the night before surgery, omit rapid-acting insulin on the morning of the procedure unless point-of-care glucose exceeds 200 mg/dL, take all antihypertensive and statin medications as scheduled, hold the thiazide diuretic on the day of operation to minimize intravascular depletion, and remain nil per os after midnight with sips of clear liquid allowed up to two hours before arrival. A plan for sequential compression devices and early ambulation has been reviewed, and she verbalizes understanding of postoperative incentive spirometry, wound care, and glucose monitoring goals.

Patient note:
A 63-year-old male with a history of HIV/AIDS (last known CD4 count of 279 CMM) and disseminated Cryptococcus presented to the emergency department with a painful protuberant left lower extremity cutaneous mass. He initially experienced symptoms of bilateral lower extremity lesions four months prior to presentation, during which surgical biopsy of a left lateral calf mass yielded necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with Cryptococcus. During that admission, he was treated with amphotericin and flucytosine and discharged home on oral fluconazole. These cutaneous lesions persisted and he was treated with periodic incision and drainage of these areas; however, this new lesion on his left lower extremity appeared over several weeks prior to this admission and brought him to the emergency room. His physical exam was remarkable for the following skin findings: (1) the anterolateral aspect of his right thigh had two fluctuant, well-circumscribed, circular lesions approximately 3 cm in diameter that were tender to palpation and nonmobile and (2) his left lower extremity had a fleshy-appearing, pinkish, ovular exophytic mass approximately 5 cm in diameter that was tender to palpation and appeared to be growing over an area of previous Cryptococcus infection ().

Further biopsies were not pursued, and the patient was subsequently started on his first cycle of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (CHOP). Patient note:
A 59-year-old male with hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) was referred for catheter ablation due to an increasing frequency of symptomatic AF episodes over the past year despite antiarrhythmic drug (ADD) therapy. After discussion of the risks and benefits of catheter ablation and different modalities for pulmonary vein (PV) isolation (PVI), the patient opted to undergo visually guided laser balloon (LB) ablation. A baseline transthoracic echocardiogram revealed normal left ventricular ejection fraction (55%) and left atrial (LA) volume index (32.1 mL/min).
After informed consent was obtained, the patient was brought to the electrophysiology (EP) laboratory and placed under general anesthesia for the procedure. Percutaneous femoral venous access was obtained using ultrasound guidance and modified Seldinger technique. An 8-French (Fr) intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) catheter (AcuNav™; Biosense Webster, Diamond Bar, CA, USA) was advanced into the right atrium (RA) and a three-dimensional (3D) electroanatomic shell was created of the RA, LA, superior vena cava (SVC), and coronary sinus (CS) ostium and integrated into the CARTO® 3 mapping system (CARTOSOUND®; Biosense Webster, Diamond Bar, CA, USA). A five-spline multielectrode mapping catheter (Pentaray®; Biosense Webster, Diamond Bar, CA, USA) was advanced to the inferior vena cava (IVC)–RA junction and a 3D fast anatomic map of the RA cavity, ostium, proximal body of the CS, and SVC was created. A detailed map of the course of the right phrenic nerve (PN) was also developed during high-output pacing from the mapping catheter’s distal poles beginning at the right innominate artery–SVC junction and sweeping down to the SVC-RA junction (. Next a 7-Fr decapolar catheter (Biosense Webster, Diamond Bar, CA, USA) was positioned in the CS using electroanatomic mapping (EAM) guidance and previously acquired anatomy as visual landmarks.
The multispline mapping catheter was then exchanged for a long 0.032-in J-wire, which was positioned in the SVC under ICE visualization (ie, high in the RA with a posterior tilt) without the use of fluoroscopy (. A 63-cm-long SL1 sheath (Abbott Laboratories, Chicago, IL, USA) was advanced over the long 0.032-in J-wire into the SVC under ICE visualization. The 0.032-in J-wire was then exchanged for a BRK-1 transseptal needle (Abbott Laboratories, Chicago, IL, USA), and brief fluoroscopy was used to confirm that the tip of the transseptal needle did not extend beyond the tip of the SL1 dilator. The proximal end of the BRK-1 needle apparatus was connected to alligator cables (Abbott Laboratories, Chicago, IL, USA) and a pin box to facilitate live tracking of the needle tip on the CARTO® 3 mapping system (CARTOSOUND®; Biosense Webster, Diamond Bar, CA, USA). Under EAM guidance, the transseptal assembly was pulled down from the SVC onto the fossa ovalis (. The presence of interatrial septal tenting was visually confirmed on ICE imaging in the plane of the PVs. Successful puncture of the interatrial septum with the BRK-1 needle was confirmed on ICE by the presence of bubbles within the LA, and the SL1 was advanced into the LA. The BRK-1/dilator assembly was exchanged for the multispline mapping catheter, and a 3D map of the LA and PVs was created.
The multispline mapping catheter was removed, and an Amplatz super stiff guidewire (Boston Scientific, Natick, MA, USA) was advanced through the SL1 sheath and placed into the left superior PV (LSPV) under ICE imaging (. While maintaining constant ICE visualization of this wire in the LSPV, the SL1 sheath was exchanged for a 12-Fr steerable sheath-dilator assembly (CardioFocus, Marlborough, MA, USA). The LB catheter (HeartLight Excalibur™; CardioFocus, Marlborough, MA, USA) was advanced through the 12-Fr sheath and into the LA cavity. Under ICE visualization, the soft, atraumatic tip of the LB catheter was directly advanced into an upper branch of the LSPV without tactile resistance (. The catheter’s balloon was then manually inflated under endoscopic and ICE visualization (. The ideal antral position of the equatorial surface of the LB was confirmed on ICE by the presence of the balloon’s proximal end within the LA cavity and by endoscopic landmark visualization (. If the position of the catheter’s distal end interferes with obtaining coaxial alignment of the balloon with the PV ostium, the LB can be pulled back into the LA cavity while still inflated ( and the PV can be reengaged by gently pushing forward with the LB while viewing on ICE until the tip is advanced into a different side branch.
Following delivery of a circumferential lesion set around the LSPV antrum, the LB was deflated and withdrawn from the LSPV. Under ICE visualization, the sheath was deflected until the catheter tip was pointing directly toward the ostium of the left inferior PV (LIPV) (. The LB catheter was advanced into the LIPV and inflated until antral balloon contact was confirmed with endoscopic and ICE visualization (. A similar circumferential laser lesion set was created to isolate the LIPV (.
To cannulate the right inferior PV (RIPV) under ICE visualization, we utilized a “hockey-stick” maneuver. First, the LB catheter was withdrawn until just the atraumatic tip was exposed beyond the 12-Fr sheath. While still facing the left PVs, we maximally deflected the sheath and withdrew the assembly toward the interatrial septum while maintaining a curve on the sheath. To avoid damage to the LA posterior wall during this maneuver, brief fluoroscopy was used to reconfirm that the LB catheter’s soft tip remained beyond the sheath prior to RIPV cannulation. Using ICE, the 12-Fr sheath was rotated clockwise until the sheath–catheter assembly was visualized in the same plane as the RIPV (. Following cannulation of the RIPV and inflation of the LB using the aforementioned steps, the decapolar catheter was removed from the CS and aligned with previously tagged sites of PN capture. While pacing at a suprathreshold output, an antral circumferential RIPV lesion set was created while simultaneously limiting the likelihood of PN injury by monitoring the compound motor action potential amplitude and manually assessing diaphragmatic movement.
For cannulation of the right superior PV (RSPV), the ICE catheter was advanced superiorly with slight posterior deflection until the vein was visualized. After withdrawing the LB catheter from the RIPV, deflection on the 12-Fr sheath was released and the sheath–catheter assembly was slowly clocked until the LB catheter was seen in the same plane as the RSPV on ICE (. The LB catheter was then advanced into the RSPV and circumferential ablation was performed while monitoring for PN injury as described above.
After LB ablation of all four PVs was visually completed, the LB catheter was exchanged for a multielectrode mapping catheter and a postablation high-density voltage map was created of the LA and PVs, confirming entrance block (. Pacing from the multielectrode catheter positioned at the ostium of each PV was used to demonstrate exit block. The LB catheter–sheath assembly was then removed from the LA. After checking the final activated clotting time, protamine was administered intravenously and all remaining sheaths and catheters were removed. Hemostasis was obtained with manual pressure.
There were no complications during the procedure. The final ICE images of the pericardial space revealed no evidence of pericardial effusion. The patient resumed his direct oral anticoagulation regimen the same evening and was discharged from the hospital the following day. His AAD was discontinued three months after ablation and he experienced no recurrence of AF during eight months of follow-up.
Overall, the total procedure time was 146 minutes and the LA dwell time was 59 minutes. The fluoroscopy setting was 7.5 frames per second. The fluoroscopy time required to obtain transseptal access was 0.3 minutes. The total fluoroscopy time in the LA to accomplish PVI and confirm bidirectional block of all four PVs was 0.2 minutes. Thus, the total procedural fluoroscopy time was 0.5 minutes.

Patient note:
A 24-year-old Caucasian man was hospitalised in March 2015 for renal transplantation. He had a history of spina bifida, neurogenic bladder with Bricker ileal conduit complicated by chronic renal failure requiring haemodialysis since 2011; and atopy, comprising respiratory allergy to pollens and house dust mites (asthma and rhinitis), contact allergy to latex (angioedema following inflation of a toy balloon), and vancomycin drug allergy.
The patient was undergoing renal transplantation for the first time. Surgery was performed in a latex-free operating room. General anaesthesia was induced by intravenous (IV) administration of propofol (150 mg IV push), ketamine (35 mg IV push) and sufentanil (20 µg IV push). Tracheal intubation was performed without complication and the patient received antibiotic prophylaxis by cefoxitin (2 g IV). Forty-five minutes after induction, thymoglobulin immunosuppression (12.5 mg/h of 5 mg/mL in 50 mL 5% dextrose to be administered over 8 h) was initiated. Within 3 min of the start of the thymoglobulin infusion, the patient experienced hypotension of 56/35 mmHg and extreme bradycardia (43 bpm) secondary to hypoxia, requiring resuscitation with external cardiac massage (for less than 1 min) and administration of adrenaline (0.1 mg IV push) (Table ). The thymoglobulin infusion was stopped immediately (at which point 0.625 mg had been infused). The patient concomitantly presented with generalised erythroderma and bronchospasm. He was subsequently managed in the intensive care unit and the operation was deferred. A favourable course was observed in response to adrenaline 2 mg/h, despite another episode of bronchospastic respiratory distress several hours later than required terbutaline nebulisation. A tryptase assay performed 1 h after onset of anaphylactic shock was elevated to 182 µg/L (normal 10.5 µg/L) confirming the anaphylactic origin of the shock. Histamine was also elevated to 234 nmol/L (normal < 10 nmol/L).
To explore the origin of the shock, the patient was hospitalised for allergy testing in September 2015. A clinical interview retrospectively revealed a history of atopy with asthma and allergic rhinitis and contact hypersensitivity to rabbits triggering asthma and facial oedema. Skin tests were performed. Positive (histamine dihydrochloride 10 mg/mL equivalent to 1% or 5.43 mmol/L, Stallergenes, France) and negative (glycerinate solution) controls were included. Skin prick tests (SPTs) were carried out and interpreted according to international guidelines []. The results were read after 10 min and the largest diameter was recorded. A skin reaction of ≥3 mm was considered positive. The histamine positive control response was small (wheal of 2 mm). SPTs and intradermal tests (using a sterile solution of the suspected drug serially diluted in phenolated saline) were negative for all medications used during induction of anaesthesia []: sufentanil, propofol, and ketamine at 10−3, 10−2, and 10−1 dilutions; suxamethonium, rocuronium bromide, and cisatracurium besylate at 10−3 and 10−2 dilutions; and atracurium besylate and mivacurium chloride at 10−1 dilution. An intradermal test for colloid (Voluven®) was negative at 10−3, 10−2, and 10−1 dilutions. In contrast, a SPT for thymoglobulin was positive, with an 8 mm wheal at a dilution of 10−6. Additional SPTs were performed using commercial standardised extracts and prickers (Alyostal Prick®, Stallergenes, France). The panel included the following allergenic extracts at 100 IR/mL or 100 IC/mL: rabbit, hamster, guinea pig, and horse epithelia, and latex (a known allergen for this patient). The SPTs for rabbit and horse epithelia were positive at 5 mm; the test for latex was also “positive” but was only 2 mm. A blood sample was taken for measurement of specific IgE (ImmunoCap system, ThermoFisher, Uppsala, Sweden). IgE for quaternary ammonium and suxamethonium were <0.10 kU/L and specific IgE for penicillin and cefaclor were negative. Specific IgE to rabbit dander and rabbit serum proteins were elevated at 10.2 and 2.22 kU/L, respectively. IgE specific to rabbit meat was 0.13 kU/L.
On the basis of clinical and laboratory data, we concluded that the patient had experienced a grade IV anaphylactic reaction to thymoglobulin due to rabbit protein allergy. All medications containing rabbit proteins will be permanently contraindicated for this patient and an allergy card was issued. To date, the patient has not been transplanted.

specific Haemophilus spp. PCR revealed a non-typeable strain. No sign of malignancy was

A 36-year-old man who received a deceased-donor renal transplant nine years ago for biopsy-proven focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and who continues to take twice-daily tacrolimus with low-dose mycophenolate was brought to the hospital by ground emergency medical services after waking at dawn with a tightening sensation in the chest, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea that forced him to sit upright on the edge of the bed; his spouse reported no recent changes in antirejection therapy, no missed doses, and no sick household contacts, though he had spent the previous weekend volunteering at a community animal shelter where several kittens were noted to have respiratory infections. The home blood-pressure cuff the couple keeps for tacrolimus monitoring showed numbers in the low 120s systolic, and a personal thermometer read 100 °F; because the patient felt “foggy” and was breathing faster than normal, an ambulance was summoned. Paramedics found him sitting forward, speaking in full sentences but pausing for breath; oxygen saturation on room air was 84 %, so a clear facemask connected to the portable blender was adjusted to deliver 40 % oxygen. En route he received no intravenous fluids, corticosteroids, bronchodilators, antibiotics, vasopressors, antipyretics, or analgesics, and the only intervention other than the mask was placement of a single 18-gauge antecubital catheter left capped. Transport time from front door to hospital bay was eleven minutes. On stretcher roll-in to the medical intensive care pod—and before any hospital therapy could be initiated—the clerk simultaneously documented and confirmed with a second cuff a blood pressure of 118/70 mm Hg, telemetry displayed a regular pulse of 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate counted over a full minute was 22 breaths, and an oral temperature on a digital probe registered 100.0 °F. The patient was awake, answered questions appropriately, obeyed commands, and had equal grip strength, establishing a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 without sedation or intoxicants on board. Skin was warm, lightly diaphoretic, and well perfused with capillary refill under two seconds; sclerae were anicteric, and oral mucosa moist. No jugular venous distention was seen at 30 degrees. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and distal pulses were 2+ throughout. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally with scattered fine inspiratory crackles over the mid-zones yet without wheeze; percussion was resonant, and tactile fremitus was symmetric. The abdomen was soft and nondistended; a well-healed right iliac fossa transplant scar was noted, and there was no costovertebral angle tenderness. No peripheral edema or clubbing was present, and neurological screening found intact cranial nerves, normal coordination, and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Eight minutes after bay arrival, while he remained on the same 40 % oxygen source and before any medications or fluids were started, a right radial arterial puncture yielded bright red blood with immediate analysis showing pH 7.42, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 56 mm Hg; an end-tidal capnography trace was 35 mm Hg, correlating with the arterial value. A point-of-care metabolic panel drawn from the arterial sample reported sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 94 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL—consistent with his baseline values recorded at last nephrology follow-up. Rapid complete blood count returned a white cell count of 11 600 cells/mm³ with 72 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 41 %, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, and platelets 226 000 /µL. Venous lactate on the same stick measured 1.6 mmol/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiography performed before any antimicrobial, diuretic, or corticosteroid therapy showed patchy bilateral interstitial opacities more pronounced in the perihilar regions without pleural effusion or cardiomegaly; point-of-care lung ultrasound corroborated diffuse B-lines but no consolidation. Focused cardiac echo demonstrated a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle with an inferior vena cava that collapsed approximately 50 % with inspiration, arguing against overt volume overload. Twelve-lead electrocardiography obtained concurrently revealed normal sinus rhythm at 92 beats per minute, PR 150 ms, QRS 86 ms, QTc 410 ms, and no ischemic changes. A bladder scan estimated 120 mL, and the straight catheter placed for output monitoring drained 55 mL of clear yellow urine over the first fifteen minutes in the unit. Importantly, from front-door contact through completion of initial diagnostics—a span of roughly forty minutes—the patient had not received intravenous crystalloid, antibiotics, bronchodilators, antipyretics, vasopressors, or supplemental steroids; the only intervention in place remained the facemask delivering 40 % inspired oxygen. Consequently, the contemporaneous physiologic and laboratory values of temperature 100.0 °F, systolic pressure 118 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 70 mm Hg, heart rate 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 per minute, arterial pH 7.42, serum sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, hematocrit 41 %, white-cell count 11 600 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 40 %, and arterial oxygen tension 56 mm Hg represent an accurate snapshot of his uncorrected presentation for suspected opportunistic pulmonary infection in the setting of long-term immunosuppression, necessitating admission for close hemodynamic and respiratory monitoring in the intensive care environment.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old male with a past medical history of coronary artery disease, congestive cardiac failure, permanent atrial fibrillation status-post nodal ablation, and placement of a biventricular pacemaker presented to the hospital with complaints of generalized fatigue. The patient denied other constitutional symptoms including chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or dysuria. Vitals were as follows: afebrile, blood pressure 116/80, pulse 72, respiratory rate 21, and saturating well on 3 litres/minute nasal cannula. Physical examination showed pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities till knees, decreased bibasilar breath sounds, and jugular venous distension. There was no rash, painful nodes or splinter hemorrhages. Holosystolic murmur was heard at the apex, JVD ∼18 cm H2O. Laboratory investigations showed normal WBC count, neutrophilia with 17 bands, 26 lymphocytes, and 8 monocytes. CRP was elevated at 4.3. The patient also had a troponin level of 0.22; however, this was found to be chronically elevated. Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly, but no pulmonary vascular congestion, consolidation, nor effusions. Urinalysis did not show any evidence of infection. Overnight, the patient developed fever with a maximum temperature of 39.2°C.
Blood cultures turned positive for Gram-positive rods at which time the patient was started on vancomycin. Echocardiogram was performed due to concerns of endocarditis and showed left ventricular ejection fraction 20–25%, severe diffuse hypokinesis, moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, and a 1 mm mobile strand in the left atrium attached to pacer lead concerning vegetation. Final blood cultures revealed Listeria monocytogenes, and two sets of subsequent cultures grew listeria. TEE was not performed as it would not have changed management. The patient was not a surgical candidate for pacemaker removal due to comorbidities and advanced heart failure. Antibiotic therapy with vancomycin was continued. Ampicillin was not used due to high sodium content in the infusion in setting of decreased systolic function. The patient received 6 weeks of IV vancomycin followed by oral suppression with amoxicillin. There was appropriate clinical response to the abovementioned treatment with resolution of fever and subjective improvement.

Patient note:
A 42-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department because of inability to remove an adult product from his rectum. The patient described the incidence as his first event, and he had no specific history. The patient denied homosexual identity. No abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting was observed. The patient's blood pressure was 128/82 mm Hg; pulse rate, 92/min; respiration rate, 18/min; and body temperature, 36.6℃. Abdominal examination revealed a soft and flat abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination revealed the hard plastic bottom of the object abutting the upper anal canal and normal anal sphincter tone. His laboratory data were as follows: hemoglobin level, 12.7 g/dL; white blood cell count, 8,940/mm3; and CRP level, 6.33 mg/L. The results of evaluations for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody were all negative. Radiography revealed a vibrator in the rectum, without evidence of peritoneal or perirectal free air ().
Several attempts to remove the vibrator by endoscopic snare, alligator forceps, grasping forceps, and u-turn technique with a transparent hood were made to no avail. As the endoscopic maneuvers failed to remove the foreign body, surgical removal under spinal anesthesia was planned. However, the patient refused to receive spinal anesthesia. We attempted to remove the foreign body by blindly using tenaculum forceps but could not grasp it tightly and failed (). Finally, we decided to use the forceps under endoscopic assistance. After the endoscope was inserted in the anal canal, the tenaculum forceps was inserted and proceeded along the vision obtained by the endoscope until the distal ends reached the foreign body. Under direct endoscopic guidance, the tenaculum forceps was opened and used to grasp the end of the foreign body (). Finally, the object was removed successfully. The removed object was relatively large and heavy (length, 25 cm; diameter, 5 cm; weight, 650 g). Mucosal injury was observed during endoscopic examination immediately after the removal. However, the patient did not complain of abdominal pain and therefore was discharged.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old male with a past history significant for stage 1 hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and remote tobacco use was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after being found collapsed on the garage floor approximately 35 minutes prior to arrival. According to the accompanying family member, he had been speaking normally less than an hour earlier, complaining only of a mild occipital headache after coming in from mowing the lawn, and was not known to have ingested alcohol or drugs today. Emergency medical services reported that on scene he was breathing spontaneously at a rate of 18 breaths per minute, had an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air, a radial pulse of 88 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 158/92 mm Hg. No glucose abnormalities were noted in the field (capillary finger-stick 116 mg/dL). He was transported without advanced airway placement because he maintained protective cough and gag reflexes, but paramedics noted progressive unresponsiveness and loss of spontaneous eye opening during transit. On ED arrival he is lying supine on the stretcher, head midline, with cervical collar applied; there are dried grass clippings on his clothing but no obvious signs of external trauma or bleeding. Primary survey demonstrates a patent airway with sonorous respirations, equal breath sounds bilaterally, and no chest wall instability. Secondary survey reveals no deformities of long bones, stable pelvis, and no external scalp lacerations. Rectal tone is flushed but intact. Core temperature via Foley catheter probe is 37.1 °C. Pupils are midsize at 4 mm bilaterally and sluggishly reactive; corneal reflexes are present. On neurological evaluation, he does not spontaneously open his eyes and gives no response when his name is called in a loud voice; however, when firm pressure is applied to the nailbed of his left thumb and subsequently to the trapezius, his eyelids part briefly with a slow, roving upward gaze before drifting closed again. Throughout repeated attempts at verbal engagement and with the same painful stimuli, he remains completely mute—there is no articulation, no groan, no guttural sound, and no reactive cry. Limb tone is generally increased; when supra-orbital pressure is applied, both upper extremities extend at the elbows with pronation and internal rotation of the shoulders, wrists flexed and fingers splayed, while the lower limbs remain straight with plantar-flexed feet. There is no purposeful avoidance, localization, or withdrawal noted. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk, and bilateral Babinski signs are present. No clonus appreciated. Overall, these findings correspond to a Glasgow Coma Score of 5 (E2, V1, M2). Cardiovascular examination is regular rate and rhythm with no murmurs; lungs remain clear; abdomen is soft and nondistended with normal bowel sounds. Skin is warm and dry without petechiae or purpura. Laboratory studies, head CT, and point-of-care INR are pending at the time of documentation. Given the finding of a reactive but silent airway, the critical care team is standing by for potential intubation should protective reflexes diminish. Prior to any sedative or paralytic administration, the patient is still breathing at 16–18 breaths per minute with end-tidal CO₂ reading 38 mm Hg on capnography by nasal cannula. Intravenous access has been obtained but no medications or fluids have yet been administered other than 2 mL of preservative-free saline to keep the line patent. Family denies anticoagulant usage, recent travel, or head injuries. They report a longstanding complaint of intermittent headaches for which he took over-the-counter acetaminophen; no prior seizure history. Baseline functional status: independent in activities of daily living, works as an accountant, no prior strokes. Allergies: none known. Social history: occasional whisky on weekends, last drink two nights ago. No illicit substance use according to family. Review of available outpatient records shows last documented blood pressure of 144/86 mm Hg three months ago at a routine check-up. Imaging suite has been alerted for emergent non-contrast CT brain to rule out hemorrhage versus large infarct. Neurology consultation is en-route. Until further diagnostic clarification is obtained, he will remain under close cardiorespiratory monitoring with neuro checks every 15 minutes.

Patient note:
A 90-year-old woman presented to the emergency department complaining of chest pain and syncope. Her medical history included chronic kidney disease (stage G4) and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Arrhythmia, atrial fibrillation, or atrial flutter had not been previously detected. On admission, her blood pressure (149/77 mmHg) and heart rate (68 b.p.m.) were stable, physical examination revealed no heart murmur. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm and a complete right bundle branch block, with significant ST depression in the V3–V6 leads. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed diffuse hypokinesis of the left ventricular wall with an ejection fraction of 20%; no evidence of apical thrombi, severe mitral regurgitation, and ventricular septal rupture were observed. Troponin I level was slightly elevated, at 0.039 ng/mL (normal, <0.034 ng/mL). Subsequently, the patient’s blood pressure gradually decreased, and, as cardiogenic shock was expected, catecholamines (noradrenaline 0.2 γ) were initiated, and emergency coronary angiography was scheduled for suspected ACS. Before the procedure, 200 mg aspirin and 300 mg clopidogrel were administered, in addition, 8000 units of unfractionated heparin (∼200 units per kg) were administered by intravenous bolus.
An intra-aortic balloon pump was inserted via the left common femoral artery in the catheter laboratory. The first angiogram of the left coronary artery showed filling defect in the proximal ascending aorta ( and Video 1). A guiding catheter was inserted into the left coronary artery, and the angiogram revealed no enhanced area at the LMCA or the left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) (). IVUS revealed a large thrombus ( and Video 2), extending from the ascending aorta to the proximal LAD, without dissection of the coronary artery or the proximal ascending aorta ( and Video 3). Thus, the patient was diagnosed with ACS of the LMCA caused by a floating thrombus in the ascending aorta. Although we performed thrombectomy several times, the thrombus could not be completely removed. Consequently, we deployed a drug-eluting stent, and a final Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction flow grade of 3 was obtained. The patient’s vital signs were stable after the intervention. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) confirmed a large abnormal low-density area; thus, a large thrombus in the left coronary cusp without aneurysm was suspected. Additionally, contrast-enhanced CT confirmed that the ascending aorta was not dissected (). We suggested surgical repair to remove the thrombus; however, the patient and her family opted for palliative care without invasive surgical intervention, as she was a nonagenarian. Therefore, antithrombotic (warfarin) and dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel) were initiated, together with unfractionated heparin by continuous intravenous infusion (therapeutic dosing targeting 2.0–3.0 times the activated partial thromboplastin time). Unfortunately, her general condition gradually worsened, and she died of heart failure and multiple organ failure on Day 7 of hospitalization after the percutaneous intervention. The family denied an autopsy request.

Patient note:
Mr. E. K. P was a 77-year-old Chinese gentleman who presented to our institution with 3 days history of fever associated with chills and rigors. There were no other constitutional symptoms. Prior to the current admission, he was treated for a liver abscess which had resolved. The patient's past medical history included tablet-controlled Type 1 diabetes mellitus, a previous cholecystectomy, and a previous repair of a perforated peptic ulcer.
On examination, he was found to be afebrile with stable vital signs. There were bilateral basal lung crepitations on auscultation. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Blood investigation showed elevated glucose level of 18.2 mmol/l. Full blood count revealed leukocytosis with total count of 23.7 × 109/l and mild thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 139 × 109/l. Liver function test showed mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutaryl transaminase.
A supine chest radiograph was performed on admission which was also unremarkable. Ultrasound of the hepatobiliary system was performed on admission to exclude recurrent liver abscesses, which also turned out to be negative.
The patient was admitted for blood glucose control and antibiotic treatment. Repeat physical examination in the ward revealed bronchial breathing in the right lower zone with crepitations and signs of a right pleural effusion which was confirmed on a right decubitus chest radiograph. He was then treated for community-acquired pneumonia and was started on intravenous Imipenem (Tienem®). Patient responded clinically well initially to the treatment.
However, despite treatment, C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) levels remained elevated at 17.1 mg/dl and 75 mm/h, respectively. A leukocyte labeled scintigraphy was then performed to exclude other foci of infection, which turned out to be negative except for an intense tracer uptake in the left distal thigh. A fused single-photon emitter computed tomography and computed tomography (SPECT-CT) was performed, and a diagnosis of a left popliteal vein aneurysm was made. No evidence of thrombosis was noted.

Patient note:
A 55-year-old man with a twelve-year history of biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis related to chronic hepatitis C superimposed on longstanding metabolic syndrome was transported to the emergency department after a coworker found him slumped over his desk, eyes half-open, mumbling incoherently, and unresponsive to repeated questions about the date and his name; by the time emergency medical services arrived, he was groaning only when the sternal rub was applied and could not protect his airway, prompting placement of an oropharyngeal airway but no medications or intravenous fluids before hospital arrival. According to his spouse, the patient had complained for the past week of increasing fatigue, vivid yellow discoloration of his eyes, and dark urine but had never mentioned abdominal swelling or ankle puffiness; on the morning of presentation he skipped breakfast, stared blankly at the wall for several minutes, then left for work without shaving or changing his stained shirt, behavior described as highly atypical. He had never undergone variceal ligation, was not taking lactulose or rifaximin, and had stopped his prescribed low-dose spironolactone months earlier because “it made me pee too much.” Other medications included metformin 850 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and a daily multivitamin; there was no recent antibiotic, sedative, or opioid exposure, and he reported no alcohol use for the past four years after previously drinking three to four beers nightly for two decades. Medical history also featured well-controlled type 2 diabetes, class II obesity with a baseline weight of 110 kg, and mild obstructive sleep apnea on nocturnal CPAP. He had never smoked cigarettes and denied illicit drug use since remote intravenous experimentation in his 20s. Family history was significant for a brother who died from gastric cancer at age 60 and a mother with type 2 diabetes; there was no known familial liver disease. Review of systems obtained from the spouse was negative for fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, gastrointestinal bleeding, pruritus, rash, or recent travel. In the ambulance a finger-stick glucose measured 102 mg/dL, blood pressure 108/64 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min on room air, and oxygen saturation 96 %. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—still before any therapeutic intervention—vital signs were temperature 37.0 °C, pulse 98 beats/min, blood pressure 104/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20 /min with shallow tidal volumes, and oxygen saturation 94 % on 2 L/min via nasal cannula. The patient’s eyes remained half-lidded, pupils were equal and reactive to light, corneal and gag reflexes were present, yet he uttered incomprehensible sounds and withdrew sluggishly to deep nail-bed pressure without localizing; he could not follow one-step commands, and when his arms were passively extended, a coarse irregular flap was intermittently visible before limbs drifted back to the stretcher. Breath had a faint musty odor, sclerae were brilliant yellow, and mild parotid enlargement was noted. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs and clear breath sounds. The abdominal wall was soft, scaphoid, and nontender with no flank bulging, no shifting dullness, and percussion remained tympanitic across all quadrants; no fluid wave could be elicited, and the umbilicus was slightly inverted. A firm, nodular liver edge was palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, while the spleen tip was not appreciated. There were scattered spider angiomas over the shoulders, mild palmar erythema, and multiple ecchymoses over the forearms from minor bumps, but no pedal edema. Neurologic examination showed brisk deep tendon reflexes and equivocal plantar responses without focal deficits. Point-of-care ultrasound performed prior to invasive access demonstrated a shrunken heterogeneous liver with an irregular capsule, patent portal vein with hepatopetal flow at 11 cm/s, and no free intraperitoneal fluid or biliary dilatation; the spleen measured 15 cm in longitudinal axis. Initial laboratory studies, drawn through a peripheral line placed immediately after the ultrasound and before administration of any medications or IV fluids, revealed total bilirubin 6.3 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.4 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 98 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 188 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 220 U/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.8 × 10³/µL, platelet count 82 × 10³/µL, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 2.65. Serum ammonia was sent but not yet resulted. Urinalysis showed dark amber urine with moderate bilirubin and urobilinogen, no leukocyte esterase, and no nitrites. A portable chest radiograph displayed elevated hemidiaphragms without infiltrates or effusions, and a twelve-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm at 96 beats/min with a QTc of 448 ms and no acute ischemic changes. Blood and urine cultures, hepatitis B serologies, and an acetaminophen level were obtained. Given severe jaundice, marked coagulopathy, significant hypoalbuminemia, and profound mental status depression with preserved protective reflexes rapidly deteriorating, the emergency physician activated the airway team, initiated discussions with the liver transplant service, and prepared empiric therapy for possible infection-induced decompensation once cultures were secured.

Patient note:
In February 2011, this 26-year-old Ethiopian male awoke in the morning with bilateral paralysis of his extremities. When he presented to the emergency department 4 h later he exhibited partial recovery. He had no associated swallowing or breathing difficulty, weakness of the facial muscles, sphincter disturbances, pain, sensory symptoms, or change in mental state. Two months earlier, he had undergone a similar episode, beginning after midnight, which resolved spontaneously within 3 h. He had been experiencing heart palpitations for several months, along with heat intolerance and failure to gain weight despite a good appetite. He had no other known prior medical or surgical illnesses. He denied alcohol abuse or illicit drug use and was not on any medications. No similar weakness or other remarkable diseases in the family was reported.
At presentation, his blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg and his heart rate was 114 beats/min. He had no thyromegaly, and his skin was warm and dry. He was fully oriented and cooperative. No gross cranial nerve deficits were noted. He demonstrated flaccid symmetrical proximal and distal weakness of the arms and legs (power: legs 3/5, arms 4/5). Knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes were depressed bilaterally (grade 1/4). Sensation was intact.
Blood tests showed serum K+, 2.7 mmol/L (normal range: 3.6–5.5); Mg2+, 1.8 mg/dL (normal range: 1.9–2.5); and creatine kinase-total, 223 IU/L (normal range: 38–174). Serum phosphate was not determined, but results of the remainder of the electrolyte panel, complete blood count, and blood chemistry were normal. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) was less than 0.0005 IU/mL (normal range: 0.27–4.2), free triiodothyronine (T3) was 17.72 pg/dL (normal range: 2.02–4.43), and free thyroxine (T4) was 5.33 ng/dL (normal range: 0.93–1.71). The ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 120 beats/min, U waves fused with P waves, and inferior T-wave inversions (Fig.). Results of an electromyography and a nerve conduction study conducted the following day were within normal limits. Because of logistical constraints, a thyroid radioiodine uptake scan could not be done until ≈6 weeks later, during which time the patient had been receiving antithyroid medication. The results were reported normal.

Patient note:
A 57-year-old female was referred to our hospital because of dyspnea worsening for 2 days. She had no hypertension, diabetes, or prior spontaneous abortion. At presentation, physical examination revealed that arterial pressure was 140/90 mmHg, heart rate was 110 beats/min, and respiration was 20 breaths/min. Mild pitting edema was noted in the right lower extremities. She was found to have both a lupus anticoagulant and antibodies to beta2-glycoprotein I of IgG, type. IgG and IgM anticardiolipin antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, double-stranded DNA antibodies, and venereal disease research laboratory tests were negative. Procoagulant work up including protein C, protein S, antithrombin, urine homocystine assays were normal. Factor V leiden mutation was not seen. The twelve lead electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia and non-specific ST-T segments changes in precordial leads. A chest radiography showed mild cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio, 0.55). Color Doppler and duplex-scan ultrasonography of the lower limbs presented deep venous thrombosis in right common femoral vein, superficial femoral vein, and popliteal vein. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed a dilated right ventricle associated with severely depressed systolic function ( and ). Computed tomography (CT) with contrast confirmed a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism via the disclosure of clots at the bifurcation of the common pulmonary artery and in its main branches (). In additions, the aortic valve mass, located at the non-coronary cusp, resembling papillary fibroelastoma was discovered incidentally during chest CT (). Its margin was smooth, and internal contour was homogeneous comparatively. However, the aortic mass was not diagnosed initially with TTE due to poor acoustic windows. Four hours later, her vital signs were unstable; heart rate was 110 beats/min, blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, and she was breathing at a rate of 26/min. Because of persistent right ventricular dysfunction and progressive clinical deterioration, thrombolytic therapy were immediately performed. After initial treatments, a repeat echocardiography the following day revealed clear improvement in the right ventricular (RV) dysfunction with normal RV dimension. Subsequently, a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was performed for evaluation of the aortic valve, revealing a 1 cm sized mobile cylindrical mass in the aortic valve. It attached without stalk to the non-coronary cusp annulus of the aortic valve and to extend into the ascending aorta. The aortic valve was tricuspid, without dystrophic calcification, and had no functional abnormality. In addition, there was no intracardiac shunt such as patent ductus arteriosus or atrial septal defect. The aortic valve mass was initially considered as a thrombus according to the presence of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. After 2 weeks anticoagulation, however, a repeat TEE revealed that there was still a mass over 1 cm long at the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve (, and ). Because a size change of the mass was not found after 2 weeks anticoagulation, we concluded that the aortic valve mass was thought to be a papillary fibroelastoma rather than thrombus. Therefore, surgical resection was considered as the best treatment option in this patient with mobile mass to prevent fatal embolic complications and to confirm pathologic findings. The following day, operation was performed under cardiopulmonary bypass. Aortic valve mass was easily removed and the valve was preserved. Gross inspection of cardiac mass showed a red-colored gelatinous lobulated mass measuring 1.4 × 0.9 cm. In the surgeon's opinion, the aortic mass was suggested as a diagnosis of organized thrombus. The histology of specimen revealed an organized thrombus with no evidence of papillary fibroelastoma ().
Postoperative CT showed complete removal of the thrombus (). She was diagnosed with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome based on her clinical presentation and laboratory findings. We repeated the lab tests after 12 weeks, which confirmed the diagnosis of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

Patient note:
A 72-year-old man presented to the emergency department with the complaint of palpitation, progressive dyspnea and mental status deterioration present for four days. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg and an irregular heart rate of 190-240 beats per minute. The 12 lead- electrocardiogram showed preexcited atrial fibrillation (). Urgent cardioversion was required. So transesophageal echocardiography was performed to rule out the presence of left atrial thrombus. Echocardiography revealed a mitral valve area of 1.19 cm2 with a gradient of 20/10 mmHg, moderate tricuspid regurgitation and no left atrial thrombus. A biochemical profile obtained on admission revealed high levels of serum glutamic-oxaloacetic acid transferase (SGOT), serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT), international normalized ratio (INR) and creatinine (CR) (SGOT 1800 IU/L, SGPT 3600 IU/L, INR 6.3 CR: 2.8 mg/dl) indicating hepatic and renal failure. Because of hemodynamic instability, immediate cardioversion was performed. But multiple attempts of electrical cardioversion using biphasic energy failed to restore normal sinus rhythm. Also it was not possible to control the ventricular rate medically. Because of hepatic failure, amiodarone couldn't be given to control the ventricular rate. After obtaining informed consent the patient was transferred to the electrophysiology laboratory. Because stable cannulation of coronary sinus was not possible due to anatomical reasons, two electrode catheters, one 6-French Josephson catheter, and one 7-French ablation catheter (Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN), were advanced through both femoral veins and placed at right ventricular apex, and tricuspid annulus positions. During AF, full preexcitation was present in 12-lead ECG. According to 12-lead ECG, accessory pathway was right paraseptal in location. But to exclude the possiblity of a left-sided paraseptal accessory pathway, coronary sinus was mapped by the ablation catheter. Mapping of coronary sinus revealed that earliest ventricular activation in coronary sinus was located in the ostium. Then, endocardial mapping of the tricuspid annulus during preexcited AF showed the area of earliest ventricular activation at the level of the right midseptal region (: ). Current was delivered at this site using automatic temperature control with a maximum power setting of 30 watt and a target temperature of 50ºC. Because it was impossible to follow 1:1 AV conduction during ablation, we only observed bradycardia and regularity of the rhythm to follow AV conduction. Radiofrequency current was then applied abolishing the preexcitation in the first second of the application without bradycardia and regularity of AF (). Then after 20 seconds, setting of the generator was changed to a maximum of 50 watt and a target temperature of 60ºC. Ablation was performed for total of 60 seconds. After ablation, AF was still present, but the rate was less than 100 bpm and QRS complexes were narrowed. No preexcitation was seen and there was no AV block. After ablation procedure, electrical cardioversion was reattempted and sinus rhythm was restored. But after 1 hour, atrial fibrillation resumed again. Because mitral stenosis was present and the recurrence risk of AF was high after even a successful cardioversion and rate control was perfect after ablation of accessory pathway, cardioversion was not considered. After ablation, rate control was obtained by AV nodal blocking agents easily. SGOT, SGPT, INR and CR levels reduced to normal range after sixth day of ablation.
