Patient note:
A 63-year-old man with a twenty-year history of chronic hepatitis C infection complicated by compensated cirrhosis was referred from his rural primary-care office to the regional liver clinic after his spouse noticed during the past month that his belt notch crept outward by two holes by evening and that lying flat in bed required an extra pillow to ease abdominal pressure; the patient, an electrician by trade, confirmed that his work harness felt tighter by mid-day and that he could no longer bend easily to lace his boots, yet he maintained full energy on job sites, denied daytime sleepiness, disorientation, personality changes, handwriting difficulties, or tremor, and recounted driving the two-hour distance to the clinic without missing exits. He had never bled from varices, had not undergone prior therapeutic fluid drainage, and had never been prescribed lactulose, rifaximin, or diuretic therapy. His medical background includes well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine 10 mg, stage 1 chronic kidney disease with a stable creatinine near 1.0 mg/dL, and remote right ankle open reduction for a construction injury; he drinks no alcohol since his hepatitis diagnosis, quit smoking fifteen years ago, has never used illicit drugs, and takes no herbal supplements. Medications verified through pharmacy refill records are sofosbuvir-veldaprevir completed four years earlier, amlodipine, low-dose aspirin 81 mg, and a daily multivitamin; he reports no drug allergies. Family history reveals a father with myocardial infarction at 70 and a sister with rheumatoid arthritis, but no relatives with liver disease. Review of systems elicited no fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, cough, pruritus, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, dark urine, or ankle swelling. The patient arrived at 08:10 having taken only his usual morning pills and nothing was administered prior to evaluation. Initial vital signs before venipuncture showed temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, heart rate 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. He was sitting comfortably, conversed coherently, stated the correct date and clinic location, performed serial sevens to 65 without error, and sustained outstretched arms for thirty seconds without flapping or tremor. Sclerae were faintly tawny, conjunctivae pink, oral mucosa moist without fetor, and skin survey revealed half a dozen spider telangiectasias across the upper chest and mild palmar erythema but no bruises. Jugular venous pulsation measured 6 cm H₂O at 30°, carotid pulses were brisk, heart sounds regular without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and lungs were clear throughout with good diaphragmatic excursion. The abdomen was distended in a broad dome with laterally bulging flanks and an umbilicus flattened yet not everted; the wall rose synchronously with respiration. Percussion produced central tympany transitioning to dullness along both flanks that migrated medially when the patient rolled to his left, and a fluid impulse traversed the abdominal wall despite a stabilizing hand at the midline. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, bowel sounds were normoactive, and a firm nodular liver edge was palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration; the spleen tip was not appreciated. Lower extremities were warm without pitting edema, and muscle bulk over the deltoids and temporal fossae was preserved. Capillary glucose measured 108 mg/dL. Ten minutes later antecubital venous blood—drawn before any intravenous line, vitamin K, albumin, or diuretic—returned total bilirubin 2.12 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.62 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 42 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 132 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 176 U/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL (estimated GFR 84 mL/min/1.73 m²), hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.6 ×10⁹/L, platelet count 118 ×10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 2.13. Urinalysis from a mid-stream specimen showed trace bilirubin, moderate urobilinogen, no protein, and no evidence of infection. A focused point-of-care ultrasound performed immediately—still prior to any therapy—revealed a shrunken heterogeneous liver with irregular capsule, a patent main portal vein with hepatopetal flow at 15 cm/s, a spleen length of 16 cm, and anechoic fluid surrounding abdominal viscera to a depth of approximately 4 cm in Morison’s pouch and 5 cm in the pelvis; kidneys were normal in size and echogenicity and the biliary tree was not dilated. An upright chest radiograph obtained minutes later showed elevated hemidiaphragms without infiltrate or effusion, and a 12-lead ECG recorded normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min with a QTc of 418 ms. Up to the moment this note was finalized, the patient has received no diuretics, laxatives, antibiotics, albumin, vitamin K, or paracentesis, ensuring that all observations and laboratory data presented represent his untreated physiologic state at the time of presentation for progressive abdominal distension in longstanding hepatitis C–related cirrhosis.

Patient note:
A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension controlled on amlodipine, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on apixaban, and stage-II chronic kidney disease whose last serum creatinine six months earlier was 1.1 mg dL⁻¹ was driven to the emergency department by his partner after awakening at 02:30 with shaking chills, left-sided flank pressure, and a single episode of emesis streaked with coffee-ground material. He had taken two tablets of 500 mg acetaminophen and sipped half a glass of water but no other medications, and he arrived without any ambulance personnel having placed an intravenous line, provided fluids, or administered antimicrobials. On wheelchair entry to triage—before a single intervention—he was alert, oriented to name, place, and date, able to recount the sequence of events in full sentences, and obeyed all commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 15. Initial vital signs obtained by automated monitor and confirmed manually showed a temperature of 38.6 °C orally, heart rate 98 beats min⁻¹ in an irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with chronic fibrillation, respiratory rate 22 min⁻¹ with mild splinting of the left flank, and a blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg in the right arm; capillary refill was under two seconds and the fingers were warm. Oxygen saturation on room air hovered in the high eighties, so nursing staff applied a venturi mask adjusted to deliver 32 % inspired oxygen; five minutes later an arterial puncture at the left radial artery, performed before any analgesic, antiemetic, or crystalloid could be given, revealed pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, bicarbonate 20 mEq L⁻¹, lactate 2.3 mmol L⁻¹, and a PaO₂ of 138 mm Hg on the documented 0.32 fraction. Breath sounds were vesicular with no wheezes or crackles, and chest expansion was symmetric without accessory muscle use. Cardiac examination demonstrated an irregularly irregular S₁/S₂, no murmurs, no gallop, and jugular venous pulsation at three centimetres above the sternal angle. The abdomen was soft with active bowel sounds; deep palpation of the left costovertebral angle elicited marked tenderness, whereas there was no guarding or rebound elsewhere. No stigmata of chronic liver disease were present, sclerae were anicteric, and the skin was free of petechiae or bruising. A fresh 16-gauge antecubital catheter allowed rapid sampling for laboratory tests prior to any pharmacologic therapy. The complete blood count returned white-blood-cell concentration 17.2 × 10³ µL⁻¹ with 12 % band forms, hemoglobin 13.0 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 39 %, and platelets 160 500 µL⁻¹. Comprehensive metabolic panel showed sodium 133 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.5 mmol L⁻¹, chloride 98 mmol L⁻¹, an anion gap of 15, glucose 174 mg dL⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg dL⁻¹, and a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg dL⁻¹, only marginally above his outpatient baseline. Hepatic chemistries were aspartate aminotransferase 46 U L⁻¹, alanine aminotransferase 52 U L⁻¹, alkaline phosphatase 118 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.1, and total bilirubin 1.0 mg dL⁻¹. High-sensitivity troponin measured 0.012 ng mL⁻¹ (within institutional reference). Urinalysis obtained via a midstream catch in the triage restroom before antibiotics revealed cloudy amber fluid with trace protein, large leukocyte esterase, numerous white cells, and many Gram-negative rods on unspun microscopic review; no ketones, nitrites positive. The patient uses a smartphone application to track fluid intake for his nephrologist and presented screenshots documenting 1 550 mL of urine passed over the previous twenty-four hours, consistent with normal output. Point-of-care ultrasound done immediately after labs and still prior to any treatment showed a non-dilated inferior vena cava that collapsed about 40 % with quiet inspiration, preserved left-ventricular systolic function, and a left kidney with mildly thickened pelvis and moderate hydronephrosis while the right kidney appeared normal; no perinephric collection or ascites was seen. A focused lung scan demonstrated dry pleural bases. Twelve-lead electrocardiography obtained on arrival confirmed chronic atrial fibrillation at 96 beats min⁻¹ without acute ST-T changes. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph completed while he remained seated breathing through the same venturi mask showed clear lung fields, sharp diaphragms, and normal cardiac silhouette. Up to the exact moment the above physiologic, biochemical, and imaging data were captured, the patient had received neither intravenous fluids nor vasoactive drugs, had not been connected to any positive-pressure ventilator or continuous airway support device, and remained seated upright, breathing spontaneously through a low-flow oxygen interface with stable systemic arterial pressure, a normal platelet count of 160 500 µL⁻¹, bilirubin 1.0 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 1.2 mg dL⁻¹, and preserved daily diuresis of 1 550 mL in the setting of suspected acute pyelonephritis.

Patient note:
A 48-year-old man arrived to the cardiac rhythm clinic for an initial counseling visit regarding long-term oral anticoagulation that had been prescribed three months earlier when electrocardiographic monitoring for intermittent palpitations unexpectedly demonstrated non-valvular atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. He describes himself as a full-time software engineer who bicycles to work when the weather permits and generally feels healthy, but he has been told for several years that his blood pressure trends high; his primary care clinician started lisinopril 20 mg daily two years ago, yet home cuff readings remain in the mid-140s/90s and in clinic today a seated manual measurement after five minutes of rest is 156/94 mm Hg with a repeat value of 152/92 mm Hg, heart rate irregularly irregular at 86 beats per minute, respirations 16 per minute, temperature 36.5 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. He states that at age 46 he was hospitalized overnight after passing a large, tarry stool and becoming light-headed while playing basketball; hemoglobin at that time was 6.9 g/dL, upper endoscopy revealed an actively spurting posterior duodenal ulcer that required epinephrine injection and clip placement, and he received two units of packed red blood cells before discharge on a twice-daily proton-pump inhibitor regimen. Since that episode he has experienced no further melena, hematemesis, epistaxis, hematuria, or easy bruising and his baseline hemoglobin has remained in the 14 g/dL range, but the memory of that bleeding event makes him anxious about taking “blood thinners.” He denies any prior ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid disease, or peripheral embolic phenomena and has no family history of cerebral aneurysm or bleeding diathesis. Other medical problems include borderline dyslipidemia managed with dietary modification alone and mild seasonal allergic rhinitis treated with an as-needed intranasal corticosteroid; he has never been diagnosed with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, viral hepatitis, fatty liver, cirrhosis, or pancreatitis. Review of systems is negative for jaundice, pruritus, right-upper-quadrant pain, confusion, abdominal distension, ankle swelling, or exercise limitation. He reports consuming alcohol socially—two craft beers most weeknights after work and an additional three or four drinks during weekend gatherings—totaling about 13 alcoholic drinks per week; he denies binge patterns, blackouts, withdrawal symptoms, or any counseling for alcohol reduction. He quit smoking ten years ago after a five-pack-year history and has never used recreational drugs. Current medications include apixaban 5 mg twice daily, lisinopril as noted, cetirizine 10 mg each evening during pollen season, and omeprazole 40 mg every morning; he specifically avoids over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents because of his prior ulcer and does not take aspirin, clopidogrel, dipyridamole, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, corticosteroids, or herbal supplements geared toward “natural blood thinning.” He brings a log from his community laboratory showing apixaban anti-Xa levels checked opportunistically for research enrollment have been within the expected reference range on three occasions, and routine coagulation studies obtained by his primary physician one week ago noted an international normalized ratio of 1.1, activated partial thromboplastin time 28 seconds, platelet count 245 × 10⁹/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 70 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 4.3 g/dL, and hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL. Physical examination today reveals a lean man in no distress, body mass index 24 kg/m², with anicteric sclerae, moist mucous membranes without petechiae, a supple neck absent jugular venous distention, clear lung fields, a nondisplaced point of maximal impulse, variable S1 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and a soft nontender abdomen without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites; there is no peripheral edema, cyanosis, ecchymosis, or palpable purpura, and neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves, normal coordination, and steady gait. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained during the visit confirms atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate of 82 bpm, normal axis, and no acute ischemic changes, while an echocardiogram performed last month documented normal biventricular size and function with mild left atrial enlargement and no significant valvular disease. After a detailed discussion, he expresses desire to better control his blood pressure, continue avoidance of agents that could enhance bleeding risk, moderate his alcohol consumption to below current levels, and obtain clarification from gastroenterology regarding long-term ulcer prophylaxis while he remains on anticoagulation.

Patient note:
A 43-year-old male presented with palpitations that started three hours prior to presentation. He had a similar episode three years ago at which time he was diagnosed with AF with RVR. During that episode, he was treated with diltiazem 10 mg and the rhythm converted to sinus rhythm. After that episode, he was taking metoprolol, but had stopped taking it about two years ago. He had not followed up with a cardiologist and had not had another episode in the prior two years.
The patient was alert and oriented but complained of palpitations associated with mild nausea. The patient had been generally healthy and did not take any medication. He was diagnosed with influenza A one week prior to presentation and finished a five-day course of oseltamivir. He denied illegal drug use and endorsed occasional coffee consumption. Physical examination was unremarkable except for an irregularly irregular rhythm and tachycardia. His laboratory evaluation was also unremarkable, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, and thyroid-stimulating hormone level.
Upon arrival to the ED, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure of 124/89 mmHg, pulse of 119 beats per minute (bpm), respirations of 18 breaths per minute, and saturation of 98% on room air (SpO2). Electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed AF with RVR (Figure ).
Diltiazem 10 mg was ordered, and the patient was placed under telemonitoring. The second ECG was obtained, at which time vital signs were as follows: blood pressure of 103/69 mmHg, pulse of 80 bpm, SpO2 of 98% (Figure ).
The heart rate then decreased to less than 30 bpm, and the rhythm showed a complete atrioventricular (AV) block. The patient subsequently became asystolic and unresponsive (Figure ).
Chest compressions were started, and rhythm subsequently changed from asystole to ventricular tachycardia (Figure ).
The patient had return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) within a minute without interventions such as epinephrine or defibrillation (Figure ).
Vitals at that time showed blood pressure of 124/82 mmHg, heart rate of 99 bpm, and SpO2 of 99%. The patient then woke up and was alert and oriented without any neurologic deficits, but he was unable to remember what had happened. After the rhythm was stabilized, the ECG showed a heart rate of 67 bpm and AF (Figure ).
Electrophysiology service was consulted, and the patient was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. Two-dimensional echocardiography was performed which showed normal systolic function (50-60% ejection fraction), normal diastolic function, no valve abnormalities, and no pericardial effusion. The patient had a CHADS-VASc score of 0, but given that he was in AF for several hours, he would need anticoagulation for at least 30 days to reduce his risk of thromboembolism. The patient was thus discharged home the next day with apixaban 5 mg and propafenone 150 mg both twice daily.

Patient note:
A 29-year-old woman was seen this morning in the hospital-based rhythm follow-up clinic for her first in-person review since initiation of long-term vitamin K antagonist therapy six months ago for symptomatic, non-valvular atrial fibrillation that emerged in the setting of thyrotoxicosis; the arrhythmia has persisted despite normalization of thyroid function, and rate control is maintained with metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. She rode the bus to clinic unaccompanied, reporting no chest discomfort, presyncope, focal neurologic change, or exertional limitation beyond occasional palpitations during high-intensity interval training classes. The primary purpose of today’s visit was to discuss whether her current lifestyle and medication profile might jeopardize the safety of continuing anticoagulation, particularly in light of a worrisome bleeding episode three years earlier when a posterior duodenal bulb ulcer eroded into a branch of the gastroduodenal artery, producing hematemesis, a hemoglobin fall from 12.9 g/dL to 7.4 g/dL, and necessitating endoscopic hemostasis with epinephrine injection, hemoclipping, and transfusion of three units of packed red blood cells; she completed Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy afterward and has used a daily proton-pump inhibitor ever since, with no recurrent melena or iron-deficiency anemia. She keeps a color-coded spreadsheet of finger-stick international normalized ratio (INR) readings performed every other week at a local laboratory: over the past twelve measurements the values have ranged narrowly from 2.1 to 2.6, and today’s point-of-care INR obtained before any dose adjustment is 2.3, matching the pharmacist-directed warfarin regimen of 5 mg nightly that has not required a hold or vitamin K rescue. Her only other prescriptions are escitalopram 10 mg each morning for generalized anxiety disorder and sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraines; for the latter she often takes two 220 mg naproxen tablets purchased over the counter at the first hint of prodrome, a practice occurring roughly twice weekly. She denies aspirin, clopidogrel, dipyridamole, glucocorticoids, or herbal supplements but admits to routinely ingesting an omega-3 fish-oil capsule at breakfast on the advice of a fitness coach. Blood-pressure logs from a home automated cuff display systolic readings between 106 and 118 mm Hg and diastolics in the upper 60s; three oscillometric measurements today after five minutes of seated rest are 112/70, 110/68, and 114/72 mm Hg with an irregularly irregular pulse of 78 beats/min, respirations 14/min, afebrile temperature, and oxygen saturation 99 % on ambient air. Comprehensive metabolic panel drawn the same morning shows sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 110 mL/min/1.73 m²; alanine aminotransferase is 18 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 20 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, and albumin 4.5 g/dL, matching prior baselines. Hemoglobin today is 13.5 g/dL and platelet count 245 × 10⁹/L. Patient note:
A 101-year-old retired shipyard engineer arrived at the hospital-based arrhythmia follow-up session accompanied by his grandson, seeking reassessment of the vitamin K antagonist he has taken since paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was first documented on an emergency department electrocardiogram nine years ago during evaluation of palpitations and mild dyspnea while pruning his garden. He remains mentally sharp, reads the daily newspaper without glasses, and walks unaided over short distances, though advanced osteoarthritis limits longer excursions. His principal worry today is that the combination of chronic hepatic scarring from decades of ethanol excess, wide swings in recent clotting-time measurements, and the low-dose antiplatelet tablet his cardiologist insisted he continue after a bare-metal stent four years ago might one day provoke a catastrophic bleed. A meticulously kept pocket log shows twenty-three capillary international normalized ratio values obtained by community pharmacists over the past six months: 4.5, 1.5, 3.9, 1.7, 4.2, 1.6, 3.8, 1.8, 4.1, 1.9, 3.7, 1.5, 4.3, 1.4, 3.6, 1.6, 4.0, 1.7, 3.8, 1.8, 4.4, 1.5, and 3.9. Two values above 4.5 prompted temporary dose holds and half-milligram oral phytonadione, whereas subtherapeutic readings led to bridging with three days of enoxaparin while his evening warfarin dose was titrated from 3 mg to 4 mg then back again. Although he never required transfusion or hospital admission, the erratic pattern unsettles him. Past records reveal biopsy-proven cirrhosis attributed to mixed alcoholic and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis; last week’s metabolic panel showed alanine aminotransferase 64 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 79 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 186 U/L, total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL (direct 1.4 mg/dL), albumin 3.1 g/dL, and an uncorrected prothrombin time of 17 seconds predose, findings that have been slowly drifting upward over the past three years. Ultrasound performed the same day demonstrated a coarsened, nodular liver contour with mild caudate lobe hypertrophy, trace ascites, and patent portal and hepatic veins, but no splenomegaly or focal mass. Renal indices remain reassuring for his age—creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 62 mL/min/1.73 m²—and electrolytes, calcium, and thyroid function are within reference limits. Complete blood count lists hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 146 × 10⁹/L, and mean corpuscular volume 92 fL. He denies ever coughing blood, passing black or maroon stools, vomiting coffee-ground material, seeing frank hematuria, or having nosebleeds longer than five minutes, and there is no documented intracranial hemorrhage, retinal bleeding, or joint effusion. His only surgical history is cholecystectomy at age 73. Current medications verified through brown-bag review include warfarin as noted, enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg each morning maintained for coronary protection, omeprazole 20 mg daily for reflux, acetaminophen 650 mg as needed for knee pain, and sertraline 25 mg nightly prescribed years ago after his spouse’s death; he explicitly avoids non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs but admits taking a cannabidiol tincture “now and then” for sleep. Social history is remarkable for an unwavering pattern of alcohol consumption extending back to his naval service: breakfast involves two 5-ounce glasses of fortified wine “to get the circulation moving,” mid-morning crossword puzzles are paired with three 12-ounce cans of lager, lunch features a 6-ounce bourbon on the rocks, mid-afternoon chess with neighbors brings four 1.5-ounce shots of rye, dinner is accompanied by half a 750-mL bottle of red wine, and bedtime is ushered in with three 2-ounce brandies; Sundays add several celebratory highballs after church. When the week’s intake is converted carefully during counseling, the total equals approximately 76 standard alcoholic drinks, and he cannot recall a single alcohol-free day in decades. He denies morning tremor, diaphoresis, seizures, or prior detoxification but concedes occasional memory gaps after late evening rounds. He stopped smoking pipes forty years ago and has never used illicit substances. Review of systems is otherwise negative for exertional chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, claudication, focal neurologic complaints, visual disturbance; he specifically denies any prior ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke or transient ischemic attack, and there is no abdominal distention beyond mild post-prandial bloating. In the examination cubicle he appears thin yet vigorous, body mass index 21 kg/m², converses fluently, and is oriented to person, place, and time. Vital signs after five minutes seated reveal temperature 36.5 °C, respiratory rate 14/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air, irregularly irregular radial pulse 72–78 beats per minute, and blood pressure readings of 124/62 and 126/64 mm Hg. Sclerae carry a faint icteric tinge; conjunctivae are pink, oral mucosa is moist without petechiae, and three spider angiomata are scattered over the upper chest. Neck is supple with no jugular venous distention; carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a variable first heart sound, soft systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border, no gallops, and no pericardial rub. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation. The abdomen is flat, soft, and mildly tender in the right upper quadrant; the liver edge is firm and descends 2 cm below the costal margin on inspiration, no splenic tip is felt, shifting dullness is absent, and there are no caput medusae or abdominal wall collaterals. Extremities are warm with 2+ distal pulses and scatterings of yellow-green ecchymoses 0.5–1 cm over the forearms attributed to gardening mishaps; no peripheral edema is appreciated. Neurologic screening finds intact cranial nerves, symmetric strength, normal coordination, and a gait that is slow but steady without assistive device. A point-of-care INR obtained 30 minutes before his usual evening dose registers 4.1. Twelve-lead electrocardiography printed during the encounter confirms atrial fibrillation with an average ventricular response of 74 beats per minute, normal axis, QRS 92 ms, and no acute ST-T changes. Transthoracic echocardiography performed six months earlier showed left atrial enlargement (5.0 cm), concentric left ventricular remodeling with preserved ejection fraction of 60 %, and trivial tricuspid regurgitation without pulmonary hypertension. He requests individualized guidance on how his centenarian age, biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis, substantial intake of roughly seventy-six alcoholic beverages each week, daily aspirin and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor therapy, and markedly fluctuating international normalized ratios together influence the likelihood of life-threatening hemorrhage and whether switching to a direct oral agent, tightening dietary consistency, or reducing alcohol might meaningfully mitigate risk while preserving protection against cardio-embolic events.

Patient note:
An 86-year-old Jordanian woman presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of fever, increased rash, and bilateral lower limb edema. The patient reported concerns of itchy skin lesions that first appeared three months ago on her thighs and then progressed to involve the whole body, including the intertriginous areas (i.e., the axillae, inframammary, and groin areas). The patient was diagnosed with scabies in another hospital, and she and other family members were treated topically with permethrin cream (Figure ). She and her family members improved after the anti-scabietic treatment (Figure ). Her medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, bronchial asthma, and major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease.
In the emergency room, the patient became hypotensive, and the team started her on intravenous normal saline (500 cc). Her laboratory investigations revealed high creatinine, potassium, and lactic acid levels. Other results from her laboratory investigations were unremarkable. The patient did not respond to fluid management, leading the treating team to suspect septic shock. After consulting with the intensive care unit (ICU) team, her care team admitted her to the ICU.
Her care team consulted with the dermatology team because she had multiple nonblanchable purpuric lesions and an erythematous papular rash on her trunk and upper and lower limbs with facial sparing. This rash was different from the rash for which the patient was diagnosed with scabies based on the history provided by the patient’s caregiver.
Biopsies of the lesion revealed parakeratosis and neutrophil collection in the stratum corneum of the epidermis and superficial neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermis. In addition, we noted fragmented neutrophils surrounding the blood vessels with red blood cell extravasation. There were no eggs, mites, or scybala visible. This was consistent with LCV. The patient was treated with topical corticosteroid creams after finishing two applications of permethrin cream, following which all her lesions resolved. Her caretaker provided consent to publish this case report, and identifying information has been kept confidential.

Patient note:
A 24-year-old young man was admitted to our hospital with chief complaints of high-grade fever more than 1 week. Antibiotic treatment in local hospital was ineffective. He denied a history of hypertension or a family history of cardiac disease. Six months prior to admission, the patient developed acute aortic dissection DeBakey type-1 for which he underwent complex surgery including removing autologous aortic walls of the ascending aorta and arch, David procedure, elephant trunk stenting and dacron graft repair of the total arch.
On admission, his blood pressure was 104/84 mmHg, pulse rate 96 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 19 per minute. He was febrile with temperature of 37.8 °C. There was a swelling in the superior sternum fossa, the skin temperature was higher than that of the surrounding normal skin, and the yellow turbid pus flowed out from the surface breach. Hematological findings included C-reactive protein of 59.8 mg/L (reference range<7 mg/L), hemoglobin of 102 g/L (reference range from 120 to160g/L), white blood cell count of 23.35 G/L (reference range from 4 to 10 G/L). Blood bacterial culture was negative. Transthoracic echocardiography showed (Fig. a) an echolucent area consistent with fluid or blood around the ascending aorta conduit graft concerning for perigraft leak or abscess, but the valves were not involved. Liquid dark area was found in the subcutaneous tissue above the sternum with a few flocculent echo (Fig. b). Due to the concerning findings, a total aortic arch CTA scan with contrast was ordered and showed that the lesion surrounded the ascending aortic artery, aortic arch and its branches, extending into the level of the C7 vertebral body and going down to the origin of the aortic body (Fig. c;1d).
This case was diagnosed with perigraft abscess and treated surgically. We chose a median sternotomy and saw the abscess cavity when opening the skin of the suprasternal (Fig. a). After thoracotomy, the old thrombus was cleared, and then washed repeatedly with active iodine and warm saline. No obvious bleeding was found. On surgical exploration, purulent material was drained from the wall of the aorta around the graft and microbiological cultures were obtained. The graft were normal in shape with a little old thrombus tissue (Fig. b). Intraoperatively, it was found that there was a clear demarcation between the graft and the abscess collection, and therefore, a decision was made not to explant the graft. After thoracotomy, the thrombus was cleared, then washed repeatedly with active iodine. Bacterial culture of pus and tissues collected during the surgery was negative. All surveillance culture samples collected perioperatively were also negative. Patient was still continued on intravenous antibiotics (Vancomycin mainly) for 2 weeks from the day after surgery. It based on the empirical use of antimicrobial agents in the treatment of infections. He started to defervesce postoperatively and remained afebrile upon discharge. As of 3 months postoperatively, there has been no recurrence of the infection.

Patient note:
A 66-year-old Caucasian male was referred for colonoscopy having had a positive faecal occult blood test (FOBT) as part of the national bowel cancer screening programme performed in the UK. At screening the patient was asymptomatic and denied rectal bleeding. He was not anaemic.
The endoscopist noted a past medical history of ischaemic heart disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, atrial fibrillation and hypercholesterolaemia, for which his medication included Dabigatran. The patient was a retired labourer, normally fit and well with a performance status of 1.
Colonoscopy was carried out using Olympus standard colonoscope with CO2 insufflation and pump irrigation containing simethicone, under Entonox gas. At intubation an unusual vascular pattern encompassing the entire rectum up to the rectosigmoid junction was noted. At this point a decision was taken with the patient to proceed with full colonoscopy. The lesion was characterised by confluent circumferential purple discolouration indicating venous blood supply, with heaping up of the mucosa involving the entire rectum (see Figs. & ) and rectosigmoid junction. There was a well demarcated border with normal mucosa in the distal sigmoid colon (see Fig. ). No mucosal ulceration or active bleeding was seen.
Macroscopically, the pattern within the rectum resembled extensive rectal varices, although the patient did not have liver disease or venothromboembolic disease and was not known to have any cutaneous or visceral vascular malformation.
The patient proceeded to axial imaging with computed tomography (CT) to further evaluate this abnormality. The CT demonstrated a considerably thickened rectosigmoid wall with multiple small rounded punctate calcifications seen within it (see Fig. ). There was no evidence of other visceral involvement or cutaneous lesions.
To further characterise the CT findings a magnetic resonance (MR) scan of the pelvis was performed which demonstrated extensive diffuse thickening of the rectum and lower sigmoid with intermediate to high T2 signal, and an internal architecture of multiple ‘grapelike’ lobulations. The outer margin was well-defined, largely with a low signal wall indicating that the pathology was confined by the muscularis propria. Incidentally, the abnormality extended inferiorly, into the right side of the anal canal posteriorly, between the internal and external sphincter. Following enhancement, there was initially some nodular mucosal enhancement followed by progressive enhancement of the multiple discrete lobulations with infilling (see Figs. and ). Incidentally there was also a patchy intermediate signal in the prostate with avid peripheral zone enhancement. His prostate specific antigen was normal.

Patient note:
A 59-year-old female patient presented with a personal history of non-insulin-treated diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, usually medicated with metformin, perindopril, and simvastatin.
The patient attended to emergency service (ES) due to epigastric pain and feeling of fullness, for which was submitted to dioctyl sulfosuccinate enema and later discharged. Due to the persistence of the complaints and, now, with progressive tiredness, the patient frequented the ES two days later, where she underwent an abdominal ultrasound, which revealed pericardial effusion.
Objectively, on admission, the patient was conscious, oriented, collaborative, eupneic at rest and hemodynamically stable with rhythmic heart tones, no murmurs, decreased vesicular murmur in the right pulmonary base, free and defenceless abdomen, and lower limbs without oedema.
The patient displayed on electrocardiogram a sinus rhythm, 90 bpm heart rate, low amplitude QRS complexes, and nonspecific alterations in ventricular repolarization; chest X-ray was performed with increased cardiothoracic index and bilateral pleural effusion, especially at the base of the right hemithorax; echocardiogram was with large pericardial effusion “swinging heart” and partial collapse of the right heart chambers. The patient is admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit, in the context of cardiac tamponade.
During hospitalization, the patient underwent: pericardiocentesis, with a total drainage of 1250 cc, whose fluid, according to the pathological anatomy, evidenced neoplastic cells. She also underwent a thoracic-abdominal-pelvic computed tomography which revealed bilateral pleural effusion, with adjacent parenchymal atelectasis, slight pericardial effusion (), and zones on the left side, with clear pericardial thickening suggestive of pericardial metastasis, after intravenous contrast. Several nodules in all lung lobes were indicative of metastases. The patient also underwent fine-needle aspiration biopsy of a cervical nodule, which has shown to be a melanoma metastasis. Later on, it was found out that the patient had malignant melanoma with inguinal ganglion metastasis in 1995 and completed chemotherapy, cutaneous excision, and lymphadenectomy in 1996.
During hospitalization, the patient had several periods of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, despite chemical cardioversion with amiodarone. The patient was discharged with oral anticoagulation and digoxin, as an effective heart rate management agent.

Patient note:
A 41-year-old man with an extensive medical history, including Child-Pugh B liver cirrhosis and chronic pancreatitis, consulted his family doctor with progressive dyspnea, retrosternal pain radiating to the back, repeated vomiting, and fever for 3 days. On admission at the emergency ward, the patient appeared confused and agitated. Core temperature was 38.5°C, heart rate was regular at 150 beats/min, and respiratory rate was 40 breaths/min. Physical examination revealed a supple but tender abdomen, normal peristalsis, and muffled breath sounds over the right lung. Blood analysis showed macrocytic anemia, 18500 leukocytes/mm³, normal enzymes, a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 303 mg/L, and a lactate level of 7.4 mmol/L. Chest X-ray showed a silhouette sign over the right heart border and small mediastinal radiolucent streaks of air (). A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax confirmed the pneumomediastinum () and showed a dilated oesophagus with a distal tear, bilateral pleural effusions, and heterogeneous retro- and paracardiac collections (). The diagnosis of Boerhaave's syndrome was made. Blood cultures were taken; intravenous antibiotic therapy (β-lactam + aminoglycoside) and ample fluid resuscitation were initiated. The patient was transferred to the ICU. Two hours after ICU admission, the patient became increasingly oxygen- and vasopressor-dependent. A new chest X-ray revealed a rapidly evolving right pleural effusion (). Subsequently, the patient was intubated and mechanically ventilated. A chest tube was inserted in the right pleural space. A brown, foul-smelling fluid was evacuated. The pleural fluid did not contain food particles, pH was 7, and amylase was 685 U/L. Gastroscopy confirmed an oesophageal tear in the lower one-third of the oesophagus. At that time, a severe concomitant mucosal inflammation precluded further endoscopic treatment because of a too high risk of oesophageal rupture. A control CT scan demonstrated a left-sided paravertebral encapsulated air-fluid collection and a left pleural effusion that had substantially increased in size. A pigtail catheter was inserted into the left pleural space. CT guided drainage of encapsulated pleural collections was performed. Four days after ICU admission, a self-expandable oesophageal stent was endoscopically placed. Despite stenting, continuous bilateral pleural drainage, and broad antimicrobial covering, the patient remained septic with hectic fever and persistently high leukocyte counts and CRP levels. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was performed with drainage and rinsing of the mediastinum and pleural cavities. Thereafter, fever subsided and clinical and biological parameters progressively normalised. After an ICU stay of 33 days, the patient was discharged.

Magnetic resonance venography (MRV) of the brain demonstrated dural venous thrombosis involving left transverse and sigmoid sinus with minimal cerebral edema []. In view of sudden onset diminution of vision, RAPD, severe headache and neuroimaging findings, a working diagnosis of CVT, papilledema, and auto-immune hyperthyroidism was made. Treatment with mannitol [100 ml, intravenous (IV) three times a day (TDS)], oral glycerol [four teaspoonful four times a day (QID)], oral acetazolamide (250 mg QID), enoxaparin 0.6 ml subcutaneously twice a day (BD), oral warfarin 5 mg once a day (OD), oral carbimazole 20 mg TDS, and oral cholecalciferol 60,000 U once a week, was initiated. After 1 week of initiation of this treatment, oral prednisolone in a dose of 40 mg was added and gradually tapered as documented in . demonstrates the sequential follow-up of the patient on treatment.
Repeat MRI of the brain at 12 weeks was normal [Fig. and ]. BCVA remained 6/9 OD and 6/6 OS at subsequent follow-up, the last being at 15 months after the initial presentation []. The optic disc swelling decreased over time [Fig. and ]. The free T3 and T4 levels gradually normalized over a period of 1 year, oral carbimazole was stopped after 14 months, oral warfarin continued at 1.5 mg for 8 months and the patient was advised periodic monitoring of her thyroid function tests and coagulation profile under the supervision of an endocrinologist.

Patient note:
A 65-year-old African American female with past medical history significant for noninsulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, essential hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic back pain, morbid obesity (body mass index (BMI) was 41), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), uterine fibroids, generalized anxiety disorder, and former tobacco abuse presented to the emergency department (ED) complaining of generalized abdominal pain of 3 weeks' duration with intermittent diarrhea and constipation. Upon review of systems, she complained of atypical chest pain which was pleuritic and reproducible on palpation. The chest pain was nonexertional but she had exertional dyspnea. Of note, she had no prior history of cardiovascular disease.
Past surgical history was remarkable for cesarean section and hysterectomy. Prior to admission medications included metformin, hydrochlorothiazide, propranolol, ranitidine, and acetaminophen. Family history was remarkable for diabetes. In terms of social history, she was a former tobacco smoker, drank alcohol socially, and denied illicit drug use. She had a history of allergy to hydroxyzine, propoxyphene, and zomepirac.
In the ED, measurement of vital signs showed a temperature of 37.0°C, heart rate of 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 148/82, and pulse oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Initial physical examination was normal except for obesity, depressed mood, chest wall tenderness, mild abdominal distention with tympanic note to percussion and mild generalized nonspecific tenderness to palpation. Rectal exam showed small nonbleeding external hemorrhoids. Complete blood count and basic metabolic panel were normal except for blood glucose of 240 milligrams/deciliter (mg/dL). Hemoglobin A1c was 9.3%. Troponin I was slightly elevated at 0.07 and it trended down on second measurement. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with new T-wave inversion in the inferolateral leads. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was only remarkable for fecal stasis in the rectum. Her abdominal pain and constipation was partially relieved after administration of IV morphine and senna-docusate.
She was also given aspirin for the chest pain. After her abdominal symptoms moderately improved, she was placed in the observation unit for cardiology consultation. After evaluation by the cardiologist, she was admitted to a telemetry unit for an inpatient cardiac stress test. She was receiving 81 mg aspirin daily. On day 2 of hospital admission, she underwent myocardial perfusion scan using the standard 0.4 mg regadenoson (LEXISCAN) injection. The stress test showed reversible perfusion defect involving the apex and lateral wall of the left ventricle, suggesting myocardial ischemia. At that time, clopidogrel (Plavix) was added to aspirin and the patient was started on IV heparin per ACS protocol pending cardiac catheterization. On day 4, coronary angiography was performed and it showed no significant occlusive coronary artery disease (CAD). During the catheterization procedure, the patient received IV heparin and IV nitroglycerin in addition to midazolam for sedation and fentanyl for analgesia. The radio contrast used was iohexol (OMNIPAQUE 350). Post-procedure, IV heparin was discontinued while DAPT with aspirin and Plavix were resumed.
After recovery from sedation, the patient complained of a headache which got progressively worse within a few hours. It did not improve with repeated doses of oral hydrocodone and oral/IV acetaminophen. After around 12 hours of cardiac catheterization, the patient developed acute left-sided ptosis, deviated gaze (down and outward palsy), and anisocoria with left pupillary dilation (mydriasis) consistent with acute left 3rd nerve palsy (). The patient did not complain of decreased vision and visual field testing by confrontation was normal. She had no other sensory or motor deficits. Her mental status examination did not show evidence of confusion. Her vital signs were normal. STAT CT head without contrast (per stroke protocol) was read as negative for acute intracranial process. CTA of the head and neck was negative for arterial stenosis or aneurysms. The next day, MRI head and orbit with and without contrast were done using Gadodiamide as the MRI contrast agent. The MRI report, as read in our hospital, indicated a nonenhancing heterogeneous pituitary mass measuring 1.9 × 2.0 cm in the greatest dimension and slightly compressing on the optic chiasm suggestive of pituitary macroadenoma (). There was no report of any bleed/infarction by either CT or MRI report.
A multidisciplinary team approach was undertaken with involvement of neurology, endocrinology, ophthalmology, otolaryngology (ENT), and neurosurgery. A full ophthalmological examination was normal except for complete left 3rd nerve palsy and mild cataracts. Visual field testing was normal. Hormonal studies were ordered and the results were as shown in . Of note, prolactin was lower than normal, while adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) level was above the reference range. Both follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) were considered low given the patient's postmenopausal status. The patient had normal random cortisol and free T4 level. She did not receive any IV glucocorticoids. The next day after the third nerve palsy, the patient developed a mild fever at 37.9°C with mild neutrophilic leukocytosis (white blood cell count 14.2 K/UL). The patient was transferred to a neuro step-down unit for close observation. Her vital signs remained mostly normal. Subjectively, she neither had a progression of symptoms nor developed new symptoms. Her headache was controlled with oral hydrocodone/acetaminophen. Her full neurologic examination remained normal except for isolated complete left oculomotor palsy. Leukocytosis gradually normalized over several days.
Pituitary apoplexy was highly suspected as a cause of the third nerve palsy, but the diagnosis was challenged by the fact that our radiologist's interpretation of imaging did not mention bleed or cavernous sinus extension. The diagnosis of diabetic neuropathy of the third nerve from microvascular ischemia was contemplated but it was felt less likely because it is usually pupil-sparing []. Neurosurgery requested ENT help for trans-sphenoidal pituitary resection. ENT did not feel comfortable with the plan and recommended transfer to a higher level center. The patient and her family were involved in decision making. They were truthfully told that our medical center is not a high volume center for such pituitary cases and the patient might benefit from a transfer to a more experienced center. They chose to transfer and the patient was transferred by ambulance to an academic center of excellence on day 7 of presentation.
There, neuroradiologists read the images obtained at our hospital differently. The new CT scan report indicated increased attenuation of the sella turcica and in the suprasellar cistern at the site of the patient's pituitary mass, suggestive of possible hemorrhage within the tumor (). The new MRI report indicated that there was a sellar/suprasellar mass lesion which appeared to show central intrinsic T1 shortening and hypoenhancement with peripheral right-sided enhancement. There was mass effect on the optic chiasm superiorly. The lesion appeared to extend laterally into the left cavernous sinus with mild mass effect on the cavernous internal carotid artery. The overall hypoenhancing portion measured 2.1 × 1.9 × 1.3 cm (Figures and ).
The physicians in the other hospital decided to proceed with surgical intervention hoping to relieve the pressure on the third nerve. On day 9 of symptoms, the patient underwent successful trans-sphenoidal pituitary resection. Intraoperatively, the neurosurgeon reported a typical contused apoplectic adenoma. A frozen section biopsy report, as well as final pathology report, confirmed necrotic pituitary tumor with evidence of recent hemorrhage. The apoplectic adenoma was removed and the pituitary gland was left intact. Postoperatively, the laboratory assessment indicated central hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency. Vital signs were stable. No major sodium abnormalities were noted. The patient was started on oral hydrocortisone and levothyroxine. Otherwise, the immediate postoperative course was uneventful and the patient was discharged home on day 11 of symptoms development. One-month follow-up at the neurosurgeon's office was remarkable for persistence of oculomotor palsy. A six-month follow-up is scheduled.

Patient note:
A 67-year-old woman was escorted to the surgical step-down clinic late this afternoon because over the past twenty-four hours she developed a pinpoint, linearly distributed ache that tracks from just inferior to the right inguinal ligament through the adductor canal toward the popliteal crease whenever the examiner presses directly over that trajectory, yet the surrounding quadriceps musculature feels only mildly sore from disuse; she likens the sensation to a “thin rope bruise” rather than diffuse muscular cramp. Four weeks earlier she underwent an elective cementless total right hip arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis, an operation that was uncomplicated and required a four-day inpatient stay followed by two weeks in an inpatient rehabilitation facility. She was discharged home nine days ago with instructions to ambulate short household distances using a front-wheeled walker and to perform bed exercises, but three days after arriving home she caught a tracheobronchitis that left her fatigued and couch-bound except for toileting; her activity log from the orthopedic physical-therapy app shows daily step counts well under 200 for the past six consecutive days compared with the 1500–2000 steps she had achieved during supervised rehab. She denies any plaster or fiberglass splinting, lower-limb braces, or neurologic weakness of the extremities, and confirms that she can actively dorsiflex and plantar-flex the ankle without difficulty. There has been no twisting injury, fall, insect bite, dog scratch, heat or chemical burn, vigorous exercise, or new medication except for the continuation of postoperative celecoxib 200 mg twice daily and a proton-pump inhibitor; her only other chronic drugs are lisinopril 10 mg each morning for hypertension and vitamin D 1000 IU daily. She does not take estrogen preparations, systemic steroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants, having completed the surgeon’s recommended ten-day course of apixaban two weeks ago. Family history contains no venous thromboembolism, and she has never smoked; she drinks a glass of red wine with Sunday dinner and uses no illicit substances. This morning she first noticed that stepping down from bed produced a twinge along the inner thigh, and firm palpation of that path reproduced the discomfort, prompting today’s evaluation. She denies fever, chills, night sweats, rash, erysipelas, groin lymph-node enlargement, low-back pain, sciatica, chest tightness, dyspnea, hemoptysis, palpitations, or syncope. On arrival—before any analgesic, intravenous fluid, or antithrombotic medication—vital signs were temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. She sat upright on the stretcher with the operative leg slightly abducted and externally rotated on a pillow, conversing comfortably. Cardiovascular examination revealed a crisp S₁ and S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; neck veins were flat. Lungs were clear to auscultation with occasional dry cough. The abdomen was soft and nontender, without hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower limbs showed the right mid-thigh incision well healed with no drainage. No overt size discrepancy was visible, and flexible tape positioned 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity measured 38.9 cm on the right versus 37.8 cm on the left, a difference of 1.1 cm; at 15 cm above the patella circumferences were 50.2 cm and 49.6 cm respectively. The skin over the right calf and ankle was warm but retained normal pink coloration, displayed no shiny tautness, brawny induration, stasis dermatitis, or serpiginous superficial channels, and thumb pressure along the anterior tibial crest rebounded immediately without leaving any persisting depression. With the leg dangling for thirty seconds, there was no generalized swelling of the foot or entire limb, and the shoe fit mirrored the contralateral side. Systematic palpation along the expected track of the common femoral vein under the inguinal ligament, through the proximal femoral tunnel, and into the popliteal space elicited a reproducible focal tenderness just medial to the sartorius where it crosses the adductor hiatus; pressing lateral to that line or compressing the gastrocnemius produced only mild diffuse soreness secondary to limited ambulation. No palpable cord, fluctuance, crepitus, or popliteal cyst was appreciated. Passive ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended provoked only a stretch sensation without tearing pain. Range of motion at the hip was limited by postoperative precautions but remained symmetric to prior physical-therapy notes; knee and ankle movements were full. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2+ bilaterally, and capillary refill at all toes was under two seconds. Sensation to light touch and vibration was intact, and motor strength in plantar flexion and dorsiflexion graded 5/5. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was present. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained prior to phlebotomy displayed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats min⁻¹ with no ST-segment deviation. Point-of-care laboratory testing, drawn before any medication was administered, showed hemoglobin 12.9 g dL⁻¹, platelet count 235 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, white blood cells 6.8 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, serum sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.0 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 0.93 mg dL⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 28 seconds. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph demonstrated clear lung fields and normal cardiac silhouette. Supine pelvic radiograph confirmed the prosthesis remained in satisfactory alignment with no peri-prosthetic lucency. No cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, hamstring strain, lymphatic obstruction, or congestive physiology is apparent that would more plausibly explain the new focal venous-line tenderness in the context of nearly a week of markedly reduced mobility following recent major orthopedic surgery, so a duplex Doppler ultrasonography of the right iliac, femoral, and popliteal segments was requested while she remains hemodynamically stable on room air and before any antithrombotic therapy is initiated.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman was transported to the emergency department by emergency medical services after an episode in which, according to her spouse, she suddenly became pale while brushing her teeth, slumped to the bathroom floor, and remained unresponsive for approximately twenty seconds before spontaneously awakening confused but able to recall feeling light-headed moments beforehand; she did not seize, did not experience urinary incontinence, and had no postictal disorientation beyond a brief period of grogginess. On regaining full alertness she complained of persistent nausea accompanied by two bouts of forceful vomiting containing streaks of fresh red blood mixed with partially digested food but denied expelling material resembling coffee grounds or passing black, tar-like stools during her last bowel movement earlier that morning, which she described as its usual medium brown color. She endorsed a dull burning discomfort centered in the epigastrium that had intensified over the preceding five days, substantially worsened each time she took her over-the-counter naproxen for chronic shoulder tendinopathy, and was only partially relieved by antacids. She reported no prior peptic ulcer diagnosis yet recalled undergoing an abdominal ultrasound two years ago when routine laboratory work showed mildly elevated aminotransferases; that evaluation ultimately revealed a nodular liver contour and she was informed she had early fibrosis linked to long-standing nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, for which she follows with hepatology every six months and takes vitamin E along with lifestyle modification counseling. She has never undergone upper endoscopy, has not been told she has varices, and has no history of alcohol misuse, though she admits to one glass of wine on special occasions. Her medical background otherwise includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily, hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 75 µg daily, and mild chronic kidney disease stage 2 with a baseline creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL. She denies any anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, has never smoked, and uses no illicit substances. Family history is notable for a mother with gastric ulcer disease and a father who died of a cerebrovascular accident in his sixties. On arrival to the resuscitation bay she was seated upright, alert, anxious, and clutching an emesis bag containing approximately 50 mL of bright red fluid. Initial vital signs, obtained before administration of any intravenous fluids or medications, showed a blood pressure of 112/68 mm Hg, a regular pulse of 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oral temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. She appeared pale with cool extremities but was not diaphoretic. Conjunctival pallor was mild; sclerae were anicteric. Oral mucosa was tacky. Neck veins were flat at 45 degrees. Cardiac examination revealed a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen was soft and nondistended with moderate tenderness to deep palpation in the epigastrium, no rebound or guarding, normal bowel sounds, and no palpable organomegaly. There were a few spider angiomata over the upper chest and faint palmar erythema; no ascites wave was elicited. Rectal examination produced normal brown formed stool that tested positive for occult blood but showed no visible black discoloration. Peripheral pulses were 2+ and symmetric with no edema. Neurologic screen revealed intact cranial nerves and no focal deficits; orthostatic testing was deferred given her earlier loss of consciousness. Blood samples drawn at triage prior to any intervention returned a hemoglobin of 10.9 g/dL (down from a recorded 13.4 g/dL at her primary care visit three months earlier), hematocrit 33 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, white blood cell count 7.9 × 10³/µL, platelet count 185 × 10³/µL, blood urea nitrogen 27 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, glucose 142 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 62 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 118 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.2. Electrocardiogram obtained on arrival demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 92-96 beats per minute without ischemic changes. Upright chest radiograph showed no free intraperitoneal air and clear lung fields. Two large-bore peripheral intravenous lines were placed, type and screen was sent, and she was kept nil per os while awaiting gastroenterology assessment for potential urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy to identify the source of this suspected upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

Patient note:
A 69-year-old man was evaluated this afternoon in the vascular surgery optimization suite three days before a scheduled elective transperitoneal repair of a 5.8-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm that was discovered incidentally on surveillance ultrasound for chronic kidney disease; the operating team anticipates a midline incision from xiphoid to pubis, proximal aortic clamping below the renal arteries, interposition of a Dacron tube graft, cross-clamp time of roughly 40 minutes, total operative duration approaching four hours, blood loss in the 600–800 mL range, and postoperative admission to the surgical intensive-care unit for overnight ventilatory weaning and hemodynamic monitoring. He drove himself to the hospital, walked the length of the main corridor at an unhurried pace without shortness of breath, and stated that at home he mows his quarter-acre lawn with a self-propelled mower and climbs a full flight of stairs to the bedroom while conversing comfortably on the phone. He denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, exertional chest tightness, palpitations, or syncope, and he has never required loop diuretics or echocardiography for ventricular dysfunction. Past medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed twenty years ago; oral agents sufficed until six years ago when fasting plasma glucose drifted above 180 mg/dL, prompting initiation of basal insulin glargine. Three years ago prandial insulin lispro was added when hemoglobin A1c exceeded 8.5 %. He currently injects 34 units of glargine subcutaneously each night and counts carbohydrates at meals using a 1-unit-per-10-gram ratio for lispro with a correction factor of 1 unit for every 25 mg/dL above a target of 130 mg/dL; glucometer downloads reviewed today show pre-breakfast values ranging from 112 to 168 mg/dL over the past month with no documented hypoglycemia. Five years earlier he suddenly developed right-sided facial droop and expressive aphasia while eating lunch; neuroimaging demonstrated a left frontal cortical infarct without large-vessel occlusion, intravenous alteplase was administered within the treatment window, and deficits resolved completely after three weeks of outpatient speech therapy. He has experienced no recurrent focal neurologic events, and duplex sonography last year revealed 40 % bilateral internal carotid narrowing that did not warrant intervention. Long-standing hypertension is managed with amlodipine 5 mg every morning and lisinopril 20 mg nightly; home pressures logged by the patient average 124–132/70–76 mm Hg. Hyperlipidemia is treated with atorvastatin 40 mg each evening, and the most recent low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was 78 mg/dL. He quit smoking fifteen years ago after a 30-pack-year exposure, drinks one bottle of light beer with Friday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Prior procedures include laparoscopic appendectomy at age 40 and left inguinal hernia repair at 57, both uneventful. Family history is significant for a father who died of complications of an aortic aneurysm rupture at 72 and a mother who required dialysis for diabetic nephropathy in her late sixties. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss, claudication, chronic cough, abdominal pain beyond occasional dull mid-abdominal fullness from the aneurysm, gastrointestinal bleeding, or urinary changes. After five minutes of quiet sitting, vital signs obtained in the right arm showed blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg, regular pulse 68 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, height 178 cm, weight 91 kg, and body-mass index 28.7 kg/m². He appeared well nourished and in no acute distress. Jugular venous pulsation was not visible at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was localized in the fifth interspace at the mid-clavicular line without displacement or heave. First and second heart sounds were crisp with no gallop, rub, or murmur. Lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. Abdominal examination revealed a pulsatile, nontender midline mass superior to the umbilicus consistent with the known aneurysm, no bruits, and active bowel sounds. Peripheral pulses were 2 + in radial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis distributions without asymmetry; there was no peripheral edema or skin discoloration. Neurologic screening demonstrated full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Anesthesia airway assessment documented Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor gap 4 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, and full cervical extension. Preoperative laboratory studies drawn one hour before examination revealed hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 248 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.5 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 44 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.9 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 24 mL/min/1.73 m²; simultaneous fasting glucose measured 144 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 25 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displayed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, axis 40°, and no ST-segment deviation compared with a tracing from two years ago. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography revealed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette without pulmonary congestion or pleural effusion. The perioperative plan is to continue antihypertensive and statin therapy on the morning of surgery, reduce the bedtime glargine dose by 20 % the night before, withhold prandial lispro after midnight until point-of-care glucose is checked pre-induction, employ balanced general anesthesia with invasive arterial monitoring and a triple-lumen central venous catheter, guide crystalloid and colloid replacement with stroke-volume variation to avoid both hypovolemia and fluid overload in the setting of marginal renal reserve, administer cell-salvage autotransfusion as needed, place sequential compression devices before induction, and commence subcutaneous unfractionated heparin on the evening of postoperative day 0 for thromboembolism prophylaxis. After all elements of the operative strategy, potential complications including hemorrhage, graft infection, renal deterioration, spinal cord ischemia, respiratory failure, and recurrent neurologic events were discussed, the patient accurately restated fasting and medication instructions and expressed readiness to proceed with definitive aneurysm repair.

Patient note:
An 82-year-old male presented to ED with sudden onset of drowsiness and hypotension. Previous medical history was significant for hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity, liver steatosis, benign prostatic hyperplasia and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection two months earlier. Current medication included furosemide, clopidogrel, perindopril, indapamide, metformin, silodosin, and iron.
At admission, the patient was normotensive (blood pressure (BP): 115/70 mmHg), but tachycardic (heart rate (HR): 120 bpm); had a respiratory rate of 22 cpm and showed signs of poor peripheral perfusion. He had otherwise normal cardiac and pulmonary examination, no signs of deep venous thrombosis such as unilateral leg swelling or calf tenderness. Arterial blood gas (ABG) revealed respiratory alkalemia, hypoxemia and hyperlactacidemia (pH 7.50, pCO2 29mmHg, pO2 48mmHg, SatO2 87%, lactate 3.8mmol/L). He started fluid-challenge and oxygen therapy, while further workup was ordered.
On re-evaluation, his BP dropped (70/41 mmHg), maintained tachycardia (110 bpm) and hypoxemia (pO2 50 mmHg). Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia with 120bpm.
Bedside ultrasound was performed showing right ventricular (RV) overload, severe systolic disfunction and free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing on echocardiography (McConnell sign) (Video ).
A subsequent computerized tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) was obtained confirming bilateral massive pulmonary emboli and infarction of superior lobe of the left lung. Laboratory workup was significant for high troponin 3056.16 ng/L (range 37.50-80.35), N-Terminal Pro-Brain Natriuretic Peptide (NTproBNP) concentration 1778 pg/mL (ref range <125 pg/mL), D-dimer 17436 ng/mL (range 45.0-250.0).
He started fibrinolytic treatment with alteplase 100 mg over two hours and norepinephrine.
He was admitted to the coronary intensive care unit.
Twenty-four hours later his systolic blood pressure (SBP) was 105-120 mmHg, HR 75 bpm and lactates 1 mmol/L. Bedside ultrasound showed no right heart overload, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion 20 mm, good left ventricle systolic function and no inferior vena cava (IVC) distention with inspiratory collapse.
He was discharged 11 days later with hemodynamic stability, with no dyspnea on exertion or hypoxemia.

Patient note:
We present an 11-year-old female with complex medical history consisting of developmental delay, septo-optic dysplasia, central DI, panhypopituitarism including central adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and epilepsy. Her weight at presentation was 49.5 kg. She presented to the emergency department (ED) of a tertiary care academic medical center with impending respiratory failure (approximately two months after the first confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 within the United States). She became ill eight days before presenting to the ED with fever. At that time, she was taken to a local urgent care facility where she was diagnosed with an acute otitis media. She was started on PO amoxicillin for an anticipated 10-day course of therapy. She was also given stress-dosed hydrocortisone (30 mg PO, twice daily) given her underlying panhypopituitarism. During the subsequent days, there was no reported change in oral intake or urine output (UOP). Her fevers initially improved; however, they never fully resolved. Three days prior to presentation, the patient experienced increased frequency and temperature of fevers. She again presented to a local urgent care facility where a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for the SARS-CoV-2 virus (via the PCR test). Within a few days, she developed a persistent, nonproductive cough, increased work of breathing, and shortness of breath, prompting the evaluation in the ED. Initial vital signs were remarkable for rectal temperature of 40.8°C, heart rate of 163 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 34 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 89%. Physical exam revealed an alert female in a moderate amount of respiratory distress as evidenced by tachypnea and intermittent grunting. Dry oral mucosa was noted indicating a mild amount of dehydration. The remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. Laboratory results were remarkable for hyperosmolar hypernatremia (serum sodium of 156 mmol/L and serum osmolality of 321 mOsm), mild hyperglycemia (serum glucose of 146 mg/dL), and elevated ESR (21 mm/hr), CRP (2.3 mg/dL), and procalcitonin (6.9 ng/dL). Her respiratory distress acutely worsened within hours of her ED arrival, and she was intubated for acute hypoxic and hypercarbic respiratory failure (immediate postintubation arterial blood gas with pH 7.20, PCO2 78, PO2 132, HCO3 30, and BD 1.7).
The patient was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). She was transitioned from her home regimen of subcutaneous desmopressin to a 0.5 mU/kg/hr Vasopressin infusion. Review of her baseline condition revealed that her DI was well controlled on her home regimen. She was continued on stress-dosed steroids (methylprednisolone 20 mg q6h IV). The patient had acute lung injury (SaO2/FiO2 = 120). Mechanical ventilator settings were adjusted to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury. Arterial and central venous lines were placed to promote more accurate determination of oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 ratios) and venous monitoring. She was started on ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and hydroxychloroquine in addition to receiving one dose of tocilizumab. Ceftriaxone was used to treat presumed bacterial superinfection based on the severity of the patient's clinical status. At the time of the patient's presentation, our institutional protocol for the treatment of severe COVID-19 infection was based on current literature suggesting that the combination of azithromycin and hydroxychloroquine may achieve antiviral and anti-inflammatory effects against SARS-CoV-2 []. Additionally, at this time, tocilizumab was suggested to have beneficial effects against “cytokine storming” in SARS-CoV-2 patients []. The patient had hypotension that was unresponsive to fluid resuscitation. An epinephrine infusion was started to maintain adequate blood pressures. Given the patient's underlying conditions and critical state, chemistry panels were drawn every six hours on day one of admission. These panels quickly revealed a steady worsening of hypernatremia to a maximum value of 171 mmol/L associated with increasingly abundant UOP of more than 4 L on the first day of hospitalization (Figures and ). These changes occurred despite a maximum Vasopressin infusion rate of 8 mU/kg/hr along with appropriate, simultaneous adjustments in both the sodium concentration and rate of administered IV fluids.
By the second day of hospitalization, a net positive fluid balance of 2.8 L was noted and severe hypernatremia persisted (serum sodium of 160 mmol/L). Her moderate ARDS continued (PaO2/FiO2 = 132) []. When the hypernatremia persisted into the third day of hospitalization, a trial of Furosemide (10 mg IV) in addition to decreasing the Vasopressin dose from 8 mU/kg/hr to 6 mU/kg/hr was attempted. After five doses of IV Furosemide over a 48-hour period along with reduction in the Vasopressin dose, successful diuresis along with resolution of hypernatremia was achieved (net balanced fluid balance of -497 mL and reduction in serum sodium to 138 mmol/L, respectively) (Figures and ). Her ARDS gradually improved. The patient was extubated on hospital day 10. She remained hospitalized in the PICU for a total of 29 days during which time she was weaned from supplemental oxygen and was gradually weaned from sedative medications. She had normal serum sodium levels and UOP throughout the remainder of her PICU stay. She was discharged to her home with an outpatient subspecialist follow-up.
