Patient note:
A 69-year-old man presented to the musculoskeletal peri-operative clinic four days before a scheduled arthroscopic repair of a chronic full-thickness supraspinatus tear that has limited overhead reach and interrupted sleep despite dedicated physical therapy, activity modification, and three ultrasound-guided subacromial corticosteroid injections; the orthopedic sports service anticipates a beach-chair position, three small portal sites, approximately 90 minutes of anesthesia time, minimal blood loss, and a single night of observation on the orthopedic ward with sling immobilization and formal physiotherapy beginning the following morning. He drove himself from a neighboring town, opted for the stairs rather than the elevator from the parking deck, and spoke in complete sentences at the registration desk, noting that shoulder pain—not breathlessness—forces him to rest after mowing half of his quarter-acre lawn, although he remains able to climb one flight of stairs to his bedroom while carrying a laundry basket without pausing. Twelve years ago he experienced sudden substernal pressure radiating to the left arm while shoveling heavy snow; peak troponin I rose to 7.6 ng/mL, emergent coronary angiography identified a 95 % proximal right-coronary-artery lesion that was treated with a drug-eluting stent, and dual antiplatelet therapy was continued for one year. He has had no recurrent chest discomfort, and a treadmill stress echocardiogram performed nine months ago reached 8 metabolic equivalents without ischemia or arrhythmia while he remained on his usual dose of metoprolol succinate 50 mg each morning. He has never been hospitalized for lower-extremity edema, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or weight gain suggesting ventricular failure, and serial transthoracic echocardiograms ordered by his cardiologist during annual visits have demonstrated a stable left-ventricular ejection fraction of 55 % with normal diastolic parameters. Type 2 diabetes mellitus, diagnosed at age 55 when fasting plasma glucose exceeded 140 mg/dL, is currently managed with insulin glargine 28 units at 2200 h and insulin lispro dosed at a 1-unit-per-12-gram carbohydrate ratio before meals; finger-stick logs displayed on his smartphone show pre-breakfast readings between 100 and 160 mg/dL during the past month with no documented hypoglycemia, and the most recent hemoglobin A1c three months earlier was 7.4 %. Hypertension first identified two decades ago is controlled with lisinopril 10 mg nightly in addition to the beta-blocker, yielding home pressures that average 124/72 mm Hg. Hyperlipidemia is treated with rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly; his last lipid panel revealed an LDL of 78 mg/dL. He denies transient monocular blindness, speech disturbance, focal weakness, carotid intervention, seizure, or syncope. Pulmonary history is limited to mild seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with intranasal fluticasone; he quit cigarette smoking 25 years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure and now drinks a 12-ounce light beer with weekend dinners, denying recreational drug use. Previous operations include an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 50 and a right inguinal hernia repair at 63 without anesthetic difficulties. Family history is notable for a father who required coronary bypass at 68 and a mother who lived to 86 with diet-controlled diabetes; no close relatives suffered early stroke. Review of systems today is negative for fever, night sweats, paroxysmal cough, wheeze, palpitations, exertional dizziness, claudication, abdominal pain, melena, dysuria, or unintentional weight change. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs in the right arm read 126/70 mm Hg, regular pulse 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, and oral temperature 36.7 °C; he measures 175 cm in height, weighs 84 kg, and has a body-mass index of 27.4 kg/m². He appears well nourished and in no acute distress. Jugular venous pulsation is not visible at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is palpable in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line without displacement. First and second heart sounds are crisp with no gallop or murmur. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. The abdomen is soft and nontender with well-healed laparoscopic scars and no hepatosplenomegaly. Extremities are warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally and no edema. Examination of the right shoulder shows atrophy of the infraspinatus fossa, painful arc from 90° to 120°, positive Jobe test, and intact distal neurovascular status; gait is steady. Airway assessment documents Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor gap 4 cm, thyromental distance 7 cm, and full cervical range of motion. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour prior reveal hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.71 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 47 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose drawn in the same sample measures 118 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 23 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats per minute, Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF consistent with the prior infarction, and no acute ST-segment deviation compared with a tracing from last year. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography demonstrates a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette and clear lung fields without pleural effusion. The anesthesia plan reviewed with the patient includes balanced general anesthesia supplemented by an ultrasound-guided interscalene block, continuation of metoprolol and lisinopril on the morning of surgery, reduction of the glargine dose by 20 % the preceding evening, withholding rapid-acting insulin and solid food after midnight with hourly intra-operative point-of-care glucose checks, and application of sequential compression stockings with postoperative low-dose subcutaneous heparin to mitigate venous thromboembolism risk. After teach-back, he accurately repeated fasting instructions, insulin adjustments, and early mobilization goals and voiced willingness to proceed with repair to regain pain-free overhead function.

A 63-year-old retired postal clerk, gravida 3 para 3, walked into the emergency department at 11:15 complaining that for the last 18 hours every bowel movement “looked like tar spilled on the pavement,” coated the porcelain, emitted a pungent metallic odor, and was difficult to rinse away despite multiple flushes; the most recent episode occurred in the triage lavatory only minutes before her vital signs were obtained and again produced a thick, shiny, coal-black stool that clung to the bowl and turned the test card positive for occult blood within seconds. She reports mild crampy discomfort in the epigastrium radiating toward the left costal margin and an acrid taste at the back of her throat but denies regurgitating blood of any color, denies seeing coffee-ground material in vomitus, and denies red streaks on toilet paper, bright red blood per rectum, or hematochezia. She explicitly states she has not felt dizzy, had tunnel vision, or actually fainted at any point today; she drove herself from home after calling her daughter for advice, parked in the visitor lot without difficulty, and ambulated briskly to the check-in window. The patient has a past medical history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1 000 mg twice daily, long-standing essential hypertension treated with amlodipine 10 mg each morning, chronic knee osteoarthritis for which she takes over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg three times daily “for the last couple of weeks” because spring gardening aggravated her joints, and hyperlipidemia on rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly. She has no prior endoscopic evaluations, has never required hospitalization for gastrointestinal complaints, and her last primary-care laboratory panel obtained eight months ago reportedly showed normal creatinine and hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL. She has never been prescribed anticoagulants, antiplatelet therapy beyond a baby aspirin that she stopped two years ago due to reflux, corticosteroids, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and she uses no herbal supplements or energy drinks. She quit smoking 12 years ago after a 20-pack-year history and drinks a single lager on Saturday evenings while watching televised baseball; she denies recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a brother with celiac disease and a mother who died of stroke at 80; there is no known family history of bleeding disorders or gastric malignancy. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, weight loss, night sweats, pruritus, jaundice, cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-extremity edema, skin bruising, hematuria, or dark urine. She has been nil per os since a light dinner of grilled chicken and rice the evening before because of queasiness. On arrival—prior to intravenous access, crystalloid infusion, vasoactive medication, acid suppression, antiemetic, or blood transfusion—she was seated upright on the stretcher, conversant and oriented, with cool dry skin and an occasionally furrowed brow. Manual vital signs taken with her left arm supported at heart level revealed a systolic blood pressure of 151 mm Hg, diastolic 86 mm Hg, and a narrow pulse pressure; the cardiac monitor displayed a regular sinus tachycardia at 147 beats per minute that matched her rapid radial pulse; respirations were 18 per minute and unlabored; oral temperature measured 36.7 °C; oxygen saturation was 97 % while breathing ambient air. Capillary refill was three seconds, palpebral conjunctivae appeared pale, sclerae were anicteric, and oral mucosa was moist without telangiectasias or petechiae. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated at 30°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruits, and peripheral pulses were rapid but symmetric without pitting edema. Cardiac auscultation noted tachycardic S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal excursion. The abdomen was flat, not distended, tympanitic to percussion; gentle palpation produced modest tenderness in the mid-epigastrium without guarding, rebound, hepatosplenomegaly, or palpable masses. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. Skin examination revealed no spider angiomas, palmar erythema, purpura, or ecchymoses. Focused neurologic screening showed alert mentation, equal reactive pupils, intact extraocular movements, symmetric facial strength, 5/5 power in all extremities, and steady finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements. Digital rectal examination produced a copious smear of glossy black stool with characteristic tarry consistency and pungent iron odor. A single 18-gauge peripheral catheter was then placed exclusively for diagnostic blood sampling and type-and-screen; at that precise snapshot she had received no therapeutic interventions. Stat laboratory studies resulted 14 minutes later—still before any treatment—including hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, hematocrit 27 %, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, platelet count 214 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 10.1 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 78 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.04; alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and albumin were pending at note time. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained concurrently confirmed sinus tachycardia at 146 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Upright portable chest radiography displayed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette; a single-view supine abdominal radiograph revealed a nonspecific bowel gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air or obstructive features. She remains fasting, connected to continuous telemetry and pulse-oximetry monitoring, while expedited esophagogastroduodenoscopy is being arranged to localize and control the presumed upper gastrointestinal source of her profuse black stools and anemia.

Patient note:
A 49-year-old woman arrived for a scheduled visit in the outpatient cardiac rhythm suite to revisit the risks and benefits of continuing systemic anticoagulation that had been started nine months ago after non-valvular atrial fibrillation was detected incidentally on a pre-employment ECG. She describes herself as generally healthy and still working full-time as a veterinary technician, lifting animal carriers and walking large dogs without dyspnea, chest discomfort, presyncope, or exercise intolerance. Over the past three months she has experienced only occasional awareness of an irregular heartbeat lasting a few minutes at a time, but no episodes of dizziness, focal weakness, visual loss, dysarthria, or transient neurologic phenomena. She has never been told her blood pressure is elevated; in fact, she keeps a wrist cuff at home for her employer’s wellness incentive and recent logs show resting values consistently between 112/68 mm Hg and 118/72 mm Hg. At today’s appointment, after five minutes of seated rest, three manual measurements average 114/70 mm Hg with an irregularly irregular pulse of 78 beats per minute. She denies diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, peripheral vascular disease, chronic pulmonary disease, connective-tissue disorders, or malignancy and has never required hospitalization except for the birth of her two children. She reports no prior episodes of epistaxis, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hematuria, or anemia and has never needed blood product transfusion or endoscopic intervention. The review of systems is negative for unintentional weight change, fever, night sweats, pruritus, jaundice, abdominal swelling, dark urine, flank pain, foamy urine, easy bruising, petechiae, or prolonged bleeding from cuts. She maintains a balanced diet, exercises with yoga videos three evenings per week, and drinks roughly three 5-ounce glasses of red wine spread across the entire week, usually one glass with dinner on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; she has never engaged in binge drinking, experienced blackouts, or been counseled for alcohol misuse. She quit smoking socially in her early twenties after a cumulative seven-pack-year exposure and denies recreational drug use. The medication list verified through her community pharmacy includes apixaban 5 mg twice a day for stroke prophylaxis, over-the-counter naproxen sodium 220 mg up to three times daily as needed for recurrent tension-type headaches and trapezius muscle pain from animal handling, and sertraline 100 mg every morning for generalized anxiety disorder started two years ago by her primary care clinician. She also takes an oral combined contraceptive pill for menstrual regulation and a daily multivitamin but no herbal preparations or dietary supplements. Family history is pertinent only for coronary artery disease after age 60 in both parents; there is no familial bleeding diathesis, hemochromatosis, chronic hepatitis, chronic kidney disease, or early cerebrovascular accident. Physical examination reveals an alert, well-nourished woman in no distress, body mass index 24 kg/m², afebrile, respiratory rate 14 per minute, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. Sclerae are anicteric, conjunctivae pink, oral mucosa moist without petechiae, and the neck is supple with brisk carotid upstrokes and no jugular venous distention. Cardiac auscultation discloses the variable first heart sound characteristic of atrial fibrillation without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields are clear to percussion and auscultation. Abdominal examination demonstrates a soft, non-tender abdomen with no palpable hepatosplenomegaly, shifting dullness, spider angiomata, or abdominal wall collateral veins. Extremities are warm with 2+ radial and dorsalis pedis pulses, capillary refill <2 seconds, and no edema, ecchymoses, or purpura. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric strength, normal sensation, intact coordination, and steady tandem gait. Laboratory studies drawn 30 minutes prior to the visit document hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 13 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 93 mL/min/1.73 m², aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 72 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and albumin 4.4 g/dL; a point-of-care prothrombin time measured about twelve hours after the last apixaban dose yields an international normalized ratio of 1.1. Urinalysis is unremarkable for protein, blood, or casts. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic confirms atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response, normal axis, QRS duration 94 ms, QTc 432 ms, and no acute ST-T wave changes. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed six weeks earlier shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60 %, normal chamber dimensions except for a mildly enlarged left atrium measuring 4.2 cm, and no clinically significant valvular stenosis or regurgitation. The patient seeks guidance on how her age of forty-nine years, normal blood pressure profile, absence of prior hemorrhage, modest wine intake, and concurrent use of naproxen and sertraline might influence the likelihood of a major bleeding event while she remains on long-term anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation.

Patient note:
We present a 53-year-old female with a past medical history significant for right breast cancer, status-post lumpectomy followed by completion of six rounds of chemotherapy (Taxotere [Sanofi-Aventis, France], Herceptin [Genentech, USA], and carboplatin) and 36 rounds of radiation six years prior and currently in remission, hypertension, and bilateral lower extremity varicose veins, status-post phlebectomy 14 years prior complicated by a post-operative right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis treated successfully with three months of Coumadin (Bristol Myers Squibb, USA). She presented to the hospital with complaints of sudden onset sharp, constant, and non-radiating substernal chest pain while eating dinner with her husband at home. Her symptoms were not associated with nausea, diaphoresis, haemoptysis, palpitations, or syncope. She denied any symptoms suggestive of acid reflux; however, she did endorse shortness of breath and dyspnoea on exertion. There were no provoking factors. She denied any recent history of recent immobilization, trauma, calf/leg pain or swelling, long car rides, or air travel. There was no surgical history of prior lobectomies, lung transplants, or atrial fibrillation ablations. Her family history is negative for blood dyscrasias or blood clots and her social history is negative for tobacco or illicit drug use. She has no active cancer disease.
Her initial investigations in the emergency department demonstrated completely unremarkable parameters in regards to her complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, prothrombin time, troponin-I, d-dimer, and electrocardiogram. Her physical examination was unrevealing. The chest radiograph did not demonstrate evidence of acute disease. A computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram was performed which did not demonstrate evidence of pulmonary arterial embolism; however, there was evidence of significant thrombosis of a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary vein without an obvious visualizable aetiology (Fig. ). Her transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated normal left ventricular systolic function without evidence of right heart strain or elevated right ventricular systolic pressure. There was no evidence of mitral stenosis and no presence intra-atrial or ventricular thrombus formation. A hypercoagulable workup, consisting of anti-cardiolipin IgG/M, lupus anticoagulant, and proteins C and S, was performed and found to be negative. No identifiable source was determined to be the underlying culprit; therefore, her pulmonary vein thrombus was determined to be idiopathic in nature.
The rest of her hospital course was unremarkable after the initiation of intravenous therapeutic anticoagulation via unfractionated heparin. She was discharged home with instructions to continue apixaban for three months followed by re-evaluation in the outpatient setting. During her follow-up visit in our outpatient pulmonary clinic, she was found to be in good health with complete resolution of all prior presenting symptoms and normoxic on ambient air. A follow-up CT scan was offered to evaluate for resolution of the thrombus; however, due to the risk of further radiation, the patient declined.

Patient note:
A 47-year-old woman arrived to the rheumatology infusion suite this morning at the request of her primary physician to review persistent polyarticular pain, confirm baseline organ status, and discuss escalation from weekly subcutaneous methotrexate to a biologic agent if warranted. She recalls that aching and morning stiffness in the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and knees began at age 33, at which time serologies revealed a rheumatoid factor of 132 IU/mL and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies of 86 U/mL; radiographs two years later showed marginal erosions at the second proximal interphalangeal joints. Over the past decade she has managed fatigue, episodic low-grade fevers, and symmetric synovitis with a combination of methotrexate 20 mg weekly, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, and low-dose folic acid, supplemented twice yearly with intramuscular methylprednisolone when flares limited her ability to type at work. She denies sicca symptoms, malar rash, photosensitive eruptions, or serositis, and there has been no history of interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, or exertional dyspnea; she jogs three miles three times weekly without wheeze or prolonged cough and has never carried an inhaler. Five years ago she was admitted overnight for coffee-ground emesis after a week of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use during a hand-swelling flare; esophagogastroduodenoscopy at that time demonstrated a 1.5-cm posterior duodenal ulcer with a clean base and negative rapid urease test. She completed a two-week course of amoxicillin, clarithromycin, and omeprazole for empiric Helicobacter eradication, and since then remains on pantoprazole 40 mg each morning; she reports no subsequent dyspepsia, melena, or iron-deficiency anemia. Endocrine review reveals that a routine employment screening six years ago uncovered a fasting plasma glucose of 152 mg/dL; she initiated lifestyle modification and later began metformin extended-release 1 g nightly. Finger-stick readings at home typically range 110–160 mg/dL, her last glycated hemoglobin measured two months ago was 7.1 %, and she has never experienced blurred vision, paresthesias, pedal ulcers, proteinuria, or ketoacidosis. Cardiovascular history is unremarkable: she comfortably climbs four flights of stairs to her office, has never had chest pressure, diaphoresis, left-arm radiation, or emergency evaluation for suspected infarction, and her most recent exercise treadmill study performed before marathon training last year was negative for ischemia. Blood pressure has been stable near 118/72 mm Hg without antihypertensives, and lipid profile last week showed total cholesterol 182 mg/dL, LDL 96 mg/dL, HDL 58 mg/dL, and triglycerides 122 mg/dL. She denies intermittent claudication, toe discoloration, or non-healing wounds, and ankle pulses have remained full and symmetric on routine examinations. Neurologic inquiry brings no episodes of sudden speech disturbance, unilateral weakness, facial droop, or gait imbalance; she continues to perform complex spreadsheet analysis at work, balances household finances, and has had no memory lapses reported by family. She drinks one glass of wine on Friday evenings, abstains from tobacco and illicit drugs, and has received three previous negative HIV tests as part of infertility evaluations. Family history includes a mother with hypothyroidism and a father who underwent cholecystectomy; no early coronary disease, stroke, or malignancy is noted among first-degree relatives. Current medications, in addition to those mentioned, include calcium 600 mg with vitamin D₃ 800 IU twice daily and acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for headaches; she does not take biologics, anticoagulants, or herbal supplements. On examination today she is alert, appropriately groomed, and in no acute distress with a body-mass index of 27 kg/m². Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 120/74 mm Hg seated in the left arm, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. Hands reveal mild ulnar deviation, fusiform swelling of the second through fourth proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally, and a tender, boggy right wrist; elbow and shoulder motion are full without effusion. No jugular venous distention is visible; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout, and diaphragmatic excursion is intact. Abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds; there is no epigastric tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, or palpable masses, and the liver edge is not appreciated. Distal pulses are 2 + at the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries, and there is no edema, cyanosis, or skin ulceration. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, and symmetric sensation to light touch and vibration in all extremities. Laboratories drawn this morning reveal hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white-cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, platelets 314 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 98 mL/min/1.73 m²), fasting glucose 156 mg/dL, HbA1c as noted 7.1 %, AST 26 U/L, ALT 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.4 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0. Urinalysis is negative for protein, blood, and ketones. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, axis within normal limits, and no Q waves or ST-segment abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the hands confirm mild progression of juxta-articular osteopenia and small erosions without new joint-space narrowing. She seeks counsel on risks and benefits of adding a tumor-necrosis-factor inhibitor, strategies to minimize gastrointestinal relapse given her prior ulcer, and guidance on maintaining glycemic control while her physical activity fluctuates with joint inflammation.

Patient note:
An 81-year-old woman who until this week ambulated the halls of her retirement complex with a rolling walker and managed her own morning antihypertensive and phosphate-binder tablets was brought in by emergency medical services after a night of progressive breathlessness that she first attributed to “a chest cold” spreading through the facility; she has long-standing hypertension, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, and stage 3 kidney dysfunction that has hovered near a serum creatinine of 1 mg/dL for several years but takes no corticosteroids, chemotherapy, or other agents that would blunt her immune response, and she has never required dialysis, transplantation, or chronic oxygen at home. According to the paramedic run sheet, fingertip oximetry on ambient air registered in the mid-60 percent range, prompting application of a Venturi mask that the respiratory therapist later measured to be delivering 53 % inspired oxygen; no bronchodilator, vasopressor, diuretic, antibiotic, or crystalloid bolus was administered during the ten-minute ride, and the only intravenous access placed was a single 20-gauge catheter in the left forearm through which nothing had yet flowed. On entry to the high-acuity bay—before any emergency department therapy could be started—a triage nurse documented a tympanic temperature of 37.3 °C, blood pressure 131/69 mm Hg confirmed manually, pulse 83 beats per minute in a regular rhythm on the monitor, and a respiratory rate counted at 26 breaths per minute with mild intercostal retractions. The patient opened her eyes when addressed but seemed uncertain of the month and misidentified the location as her old farmhouse, though she followed two-step commands and localized discomfort to a trapezius pinch, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13 without sedatives, ethanol, or head trauma. Skin was warm and dry with brisk capillary refill; sclerae were anicteric, and oral mucosa appeared tacky. Jugular venous pulsations were not distended. Cardiac examination revealed a normal S1 and physiologic split S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Pulmonary auscultation disclosed diffuse crackles more pronounced at the bilateral bases and faint bronchial breath sounds over the right mid-lung field, and percussion over those areas was mildly dull compared with the anterior apexes. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender; a healed midline cholecystectomy scar was noted, and bowel sounds were present. No peripheral edema was observed, and a focused neurologic screen showed symmetric strength and intact sensation of the extremities. Nine minutes after stretcher placement, while she remained on the same 53 % oxygen source, a right radial arterial sample returned a pH of 7.23, and the blood-gas analyzer calculated an alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient of 533 mm Hg in the setting of persistently elevated end-tidal CO₂, indicating severe impairment of gas exchange likely from an evolving lower respiratory infection. Simultaneously drawn basic metabolic studies revealed a serum sodium of 147 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 105 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 132 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.24 mg/dL—essentially at her historical baseline, suggesting no acute worsening of her chronic kidney condition. A complete blood count demonstrated a white-cell concentration of 13 400 /mm³ with a neutrophil predominance and scant bands, hematocrit 36 %, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, and platelets 219 000 /µL. Venous lactate checked at the bedside was 2.3 mmol/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before any antimicrobial or diuretic therapy showed patchy right lower-lobe consolidation and increased interstitial markings bilaterally without pleural effusion or cardiomegaly; bedside lung ultrasound corroborated these findings with multiple B-lines and a small subpleural consolidation. Focused cardiac ultrasound revealed a vigorously contracting left ventricle, normal valvular motion, and an inferior vena cava measuring 1.5 cm in expiration that collapsed more than half with inspiration, arguing against frank fluid overload. Electrocardiography printed during the arterial puncture displayed normal sinus rhythm at 82 beats per minute, normal intervals, and no acute ischemic changes. A straight catheter placed for urinary monitoring produced 60 mL of clear yellow urine in the first fifteen minutes. Importantly, throughout the thirty-minute interval between ambulance arrival and acceptance by the medical intensive care unit, the patient received no intravenous fluids, antimicrobials, bronchodilators, vasopressors, antipyretics, or bicarbonate, ensuring that the documented physiology—temperature 37.3 °C, systolic pressure 131 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 69 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats per minute, respirations 26 per minute, arterial pH 7.23, serum sodium 147 mmol/L, serum potassium 4.4 mmol/L, creatinine 1.24 mg/dL, hematocrit 36 %, white-cell count 13 400 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 53 %, and calculated alveolar–arterial gradient 533 mm Hg—faithfully represents her untreated presentation for what appears to be community-acquired pneumonia complicated by marked hypoxemic respiratory failure on a background of stable chronic kidney insufficiency.

Patient note:
A 27-year-old man with no previous medical history presented to the emergency department with 1 hour of acute onset of left-sided chest pain, shortness of breath, and diaphoresis. He reported active tobacco smoking but denied other drug use. He used nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications for back pain. There was a family history of coronary artery disease in an uncle who underwent coronary revascularization. He had also recently been using energy drinks (Rockstar, Rockstar, Inc., Las Vegas, NV), sometimes 4-5 beverages in a 12-hour period, in order to stay awake during his evening work shift in a warehouse. He denied any previous episodes of chest pain, exertional symptoms, previous thromboembolic disease, nausea or vomiting, or syncope. On examination, his blood pressure was elevated at 155/100, pulse was 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 100% on 2 liters of supplemental oxygen. His cardiac examination was normal, including a normal first and second heart sound and no appreciable murmur or pericardial friction rub. His laboratory values were notable for hemoglobin of 15.4 g/dL, white blood cell count of 5.8, platelet count 254,000, normal blood chemistry, and an elevated troponin T of 0.41 (normal reference range < 0.01 ng/mL) and CK-MB of 123.4 (normal reference range < 7.8 ng/mL). His electrocardiogram demonstrated ST-segment elevations in leads V2–V6, I, and aVL along with reciprocal changes in leads III and aVF, concerning for an acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) (). He was treated with sublingual nitroglycerin, unfractionated heparin, and aspirin in the emergency department which improved but did not completely alleviate his symptoms and brought urgently to the cardiac catheterization laboratory. Coronary angiography was performed from a radial approach and symptom relief was documented after intra-arterial injection of a radial antispasmodic cocktail (i.e., 200 mcg nitroglycerin, 2.5 mg verapamil, and 5,000 units of heparin). Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries with TIMI III flow without any angiographic evidence of stenosis, dissection, embolism, or plaque rupture (). A repeat electrocardiogram after his coronary angiogram demonstrated normalization of his ST-segment abnormalities (). An echocardiogram was performed and demonstrated significant akinesis of the left ventricular apex (Figures and ), findings that were confirmed with abnormal longitudinal strain in the apical segments (). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI) also documented akinesis in the left ventricular apex, similar to the wall motion abnormalities present on echocardiography. In addition, cMRI confirmed areas of abnormal delayed gadolinium enhancement in both a patchy and full-thickness configuration along the mid and distal anterior wall and the mid septum (Figures and ). A formal toxicology examination was not requested given that the patient rapidly recovered after his initial presentation. The absence of the toxicology leaves the question as to whether other potential substances could have been associated with the acute cardiac presentation. A urine drug screen at the time of admission was negative for cocaine, amphetamines, and barbiturates. The patient was treated with long acting nitrates and calcium channel blocker, though he continued to have occasional episodes of chest discomfort. Given the concern of recurrent spasm and given that the presumed etiology of his ST-elevation myocardial infarction was coronary vasospasm, he was referred for repeat coronary angiography, including a functional protocol to test the response of the coronary endothelium and the coronary microcirculation. His coronary angiogram was normal, with no evidence of atherosclerosis or vasospasm. Intracoronary adenosine was administered at a dose of 60 mcg and coronary flow reserve (CFR) was normal at 3.0 using intracoronary Doppler study in the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. These findings suggested normal microcirculatory function. Subsequently, increasing concentrations of intracoronary acetylcholine were administered with no significant change in the Doppler-derived average peak velocity, CFR, symptoms, angiographic appearance of the LAD, or electrocardiographic parameters, all consistent with normal endothelial function. Based on these results, he was not felt to have any functional coronary or endothelial abnormalities. He was advised to abstain from any further use of energy drinks.

Patient note:
A 70-year-old man was referred from primary care to the renal-medicine clinic for progressive azotemia identified on routine laboratory monitoring; he arrived accompanied by his spouse and was able to provide a coherent, detailed history without prompting. He reports that type 2 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed at age 48 after an employment physical revealed a fasting plasma glucose of 168 mg/dL, and over the ensuing two decades he has escalated from diet and metformin to a multi-dose basal–bolus insulin regimen. Approximately eight years ago ophthalmology documented multiple microaneurysms with focal laser photocoagulation to the right eye, and podiatry follows him for distal symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy manifesting as diminished vibration and occasional burning discomfort in the forefeet for which he takes nightly gabapentin; despite these issues he remains fully independent in activities of daily living. Three years prior to today’s visit he was admitted elsewhere for sudden-onset right-sided facial droop and slurred speech that resolved within 36 hours; brain MRI at that time demonstrated a small left pontine diffusion-positive lesion consistent with an acute lacunar infarct, and subsequent carotid duplex studies and cardiac telemetry failed to identify a high-risk embolic source. He completed six weeks of outpatient speech therapy and has had no further neurologic events, no residual limb weakness, and denies episodes of transient monocular blindness, transient aphasia, or focal sensory loss. He has never experienced crushing substernal pain, diaphoresis with exertion, emergency catheterization, or hospital admission for fluid overload; a resting transthoracic echocardiogram performed last winter in the course of pre-operative clearance for cataract surgery showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 62 % with no regional wall-motion abnormalities, normal chamber sizes, and trivial tricuspid regurgitation. He walks his dog briskly for 20 minutes twice daily without chest discomfort or calf cramping, and distal pulses have been described as palpable and symmetric during podiatry examinations. He has no chronic cough, wheeze, orthopnea, or requirement for inhalers, has never been intubated, and chest imaging obtained within the past year for a pulmonary nodule screening protocol was unremarkable apart from mild age-related basilar atelectasis. He denies dyspepsia, hematemesis, melena, or prior endoscopic findings of gastric or duodenal ulceration. Patient note:
On March 5, 2020, a-58-year-old woman was transferred to our intensive care unit (ICU) due to acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. The patient was previously diagnosed with COVID-19 on a screening test for throat discomfort 12 days earlier. The patient lived in Daegu, the epicenter of COVID-19 in Korea, and had acquired the infection through community spread. Seven days before ICU admission, the patient was diagnosed with pneumonia and started lopinavir/ritonavir 400 mg/100 mg tablets twice a day and supplemental oxygen was started 3 days ago. Vital signs on presentation to the ICU were: blood pressure 145/90 mmHg, pulse rate 90/min, respiratory rate 32/min, and body temperature 36.9°C. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.383, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) 33.5 mmHg, partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2) 83.9 mmHg, and bicarbonate (HCO3-) 19.5 mmol/L on high-flow nasal cannula (fraction of inspired oxygen [FiO2], 0.95; flow rate, 50 L/min). The patient was intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation with elaborate lung-protective strategies. The PaO2 improved to 229.1 mmHg on FiO2 0.9, and we initiated intravenous methylprednisolone 60 mg. A chest radiograph showed bilateral, multifocal, patchy consolidations in the lungs (). The C-reactive protein level was 22.9 mg/dL. Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs as well as sputum specimens were obtained for retesting at our hospital and reported positive for infection with the novel severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) by real-time reverse-transcriptase–polymerase-chain-reaction (RT-PCR) assay.
From the evening on Day 1 of hospitalization, the patient's body temperature began to increase, reached approximately 40°C on Day 2, and was followed by tachycardia and desaturation (). The fever was refractory to repeated administration of antipyretics. The body temperature increased up to 41.6°C, heart rate to 156 per min, and oxygen saturation decreased to 88% on FiO2 of 1.0. Nitric oxide (NO) inhalation was initiated and raised to 40 ppm, and injection of methylprednisolone 60 mg was repeated. However, arterial blood gas analysis showed PaO2 of 77.6 mmHg, and the troponin I level increased to 6.22 ng/mL. Considering extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) as the last resort for treatment, we applied a surface cooling device (Arctic Sun®) with a target temperature of 37°C. From an initial core temperature of 41.8°C, the target temperature was rapidly attained within 4.5 hours. PaO2 was markedly improved to 318.2 mmHg, and tachycardia resolved after a few hours. The norepinephrine requirement that had increased up to 16 µg/min during the shock phase was tapered off. Echocardiography on Day 4 showed mid-to-apical-segment akinesia and depressed left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 26%. The patient was extubated on Day 6 and TTM was stopped on Day 9. Other treatment details including antibiotics and steroid use are summarized in . On Day 12, SARS-CoV-2 RT PCR results converted negatively in all nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, and sputum specimens. Supplemental oxygen was discontinued on Day 16, and the patient's cardiac function was confirmed to have recovered on Day 19 with an ejection fraction of 54%. A coronary computed tomographic angiography was also normal. A chest radiograph on Day 22 showed considerable improvement compared to the previous ones ().

Patient note:
A 57-year-old man was admitted to the Pneumology Department of the Affiliated Hospital of Medical School, Ningbo University in December 2016 for cough and sputum production for half a month and hemoptysis for 1 day. He had a medical history of pulmonary aspergillosis and type 2 diabetes.
On admission, blood pressure was 125/76 mm Hg, the body temperature was 36.6°C, respiratory rate was 19 breaths/min, and heart rate was 79 beats/min. Results of laboratory tests included the following values: urea nitrogen 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 139.7 μmol/L, uric acid 539 μmol/L, potassium 4.43 mmol/L, glucose 7.83 mmol/L, leukocytes 12 × 109/L, with 75.6% neutrophils, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, lactic acid 1.9 mmol/L, and pH 7.37.
Intravenous voriconazole (200 mg q/12 h, first dose doubling) was used to treat pulmonary fungal infection. The results of a sputum smear examination showed gram-positive cocci+, gram-positive bacilli+, and gram-negative bacilli++. According to the results of sputum smear examination and the clinical manifestations, community-acquired pneumonia cannot be excluded and moxifloxacin (400 mg q/d) was added on day 3. Five days later, the patient presented with shortness of breath and became febrile up to 38.8°C. Chest radiography showed aggravated infection. Intravenous imipenem and cilastatin sodium (500 mg q/8 h) was substituted for moxifloxacin.
The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit on day 10 for severe pneumonia-induced respiratory failure. The antibiotic therapy was escalated to vancomycin. Because of poor renal function (estimated renal clearance 36 mL/min), intravenous linezolid (600 mg q/12 h) was introduced as an alternative treatment to vancomycin. After 3 doses of linezolid, the patient's blood lactate had risen up to 10.0 mmol/L, blood pressure was 50/40 mm Hg, heart rate was 42 beats/min, and creatinine was 335.8 μmol/L. Noradrenaline and dopamine were administered with a minipump to maintain a relatively normal pressure. As linezolid was implicated as a possible cause of the lactic acidosis, the agent was discontinued.
The patient required mechanical ventilation because of respiratory failure and continuous renal replacement therapy for 6 days to normalize his blood pH and clear linezolid from his plasma. However, the lactic acidosis improved only marginally, and his blood pressure decreased to 30/22 mm Hg. The patient died on day 17.
We searched for cases of linezolid-induced lactic acidosis reported in English in PubMed from their inception until April 2017. Literature searches included keywords for “linezolid” or “Zyvox” and “lactic acidosis” or “hyper-lactatemia.”
Two reviewers (Yiyang Mao and Danping Dai) independently screened all titles and abstracts for eligible articles. Cases presented in the articles were included if the lactic acidosis was induced by linezolid and the data were extractable.
Two authors extracted data independently (Yiyang Mao and Danping Dai). Any dispute was settled by discussion or by a third investigator. Study characteristics were extracted from each case, including first author identification, gender, age, comorbidities, reason for use, duration of linezolid, dosage, lactate concentration before linezolid, peak lactate concentration after linezolid, treatment for lactic acidosis, and outcome.
Seven, fourteen, and twenty-eight days were selected to be the cut-off points in statistics according to the treatment duration recommended in the drug instruction. The treatment duration of linezolid was expressed in days in the calculations. The dosage of linezolid was assumed to be 600 mg/bid, when it was not reported according to the drug instruction. Only the lactic acidosis-related deaths were included when analyzing and evaluating the data. Patients ≥65 years were defined as elderly according to the WHO's definition.
All statistical analyses were conducted using the SPSS software package (version 18.0). Statistical evaluations were carried out using the chi-squared tests with P values of <.05 considered to be statistically significant. All statistical tests were 2-sided. Fisher exact test was used when the sample size was <40.

Patient note:
A 74-year-old woman was seen in the perioperative medical clinic this morning at the request of her orthopedic surgeon seven days before a scheduled elective right total knee arthroplasty intended to relieve progressive tricompartmental osteoarthritis that has limited her walking radius to two blocks and forced reliance on a cane; the surgical team anticipates a 90-minute tourniquet time under spinal anesthesia with postoperative admission to the regular ward for pain control and physical-therapy mobilization beginning later the same day. She arrived by taxi, slowly negotiated the fifteen-meter hallway to the examination room, and asked to sit for a minute to catch her breath, noting that over the past year she has required pauses when climbing a single flight of stairs or carrying groceries from the driveway. Five years ago she was hospitalized for sudden weight gain and bilateral leg swelling; echocardiography at that admission showed a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30 % in the absence of wall-motion abnormalities, and coronary angiography performed to exclude atherosclerotic disease revealed angiographically normal epicardial vessels. Since that index hospitalization she has had two additional emergency department visits for volume overload treated with intravenous diuretics, the most recent eleven weeks ago after dietary indiscretion at a family gathering. Her heart-failure regimen now includes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril–valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, torsemide 40 mg each morning, spironolactone 25 mg nightly, and a low-sodium diet, with daily weights recorded in a notebook reviewed today. She sleeps on three pillows, reports mild orthopnea if she tries to lie flat, and experiences occasional nocturnal awakenings relieved by sitting on the edge of the bed, yet denies any episodic chest pressure, arm or jaw discomfort, palpitations, or syncopal spells. Endocrine history is significant for type 2 diabetes diagnosed at age 52; oral agents were discontinued eight years ago when HbA1c values drifted above 9 %, and she has since followed a basal-bolus plan of insulin glargine 26 units at bedtime and insulin aspart with meals dosed according to a 1:10 carbohydrate ratio. Glucose logs reviewed in clinic show fasting levels between 100 and 165 mg/dL with only one recorded hypoglycemic reading (62 mg/dL) in the prior month. Hypertension is well controlled on amlodipine 5 mg daily, and hyperlipidemia is treated with atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. She has never experienced a stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid procedure, peripheral revascularization, or episodes suggestive of vasospasm. Past surgical history includes an uncomplicated laparoscopic oophorectomy at age 60 and cataract extraction at 68. She quit cigarette smoking three decades ago after a 20-pack-year exposure, drinks half a glass of wine with Sunday dinner, and denies illicit drug use. Review of systems is negative for fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, abdominal pain, intermittent claudication, or bleeding tendencies. After five minutes of quiet sitting her vital signs are blood pressure 116/68 mm Hg in the right arm, regular pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95 % on ambient air, and oral temperature 36.6 °C; body mass index is 31 kg/m². Neck examination reveals jugular venous pulsation 6 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the apical impulse is displaced laterally in the sixth intercostal space. Cardiac auscultation detects a soft third heart sound and a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex consistent with functional mitral regurgitation; no pericardial rub is present. Lungs are clear in the upper zones with fine late-inspiratory crackles at both bases. Abdomen is soft and nontender with no organomegaly. Lower extremities show bilateral 1+ pitting edema to mid-shin and well-healed varicose vein ablations; distal pulses are palpable. Sensory and motor examination of the lower limbs is intact aside from pain-limited range of motion at the right knee. Laboratory studies drawn one hour before the visit demonstrate hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.7 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.37 mg/dL, unchanged from her baseline and corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 48 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose in the same panel measures 128 mg/dL, and liver enzymes as well as coagulation indices are within reference limits. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes unchanged from prior tracings. Posterior-anterior chest radiograph reveals a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette and vascular congestion without pleural effusion. Airway assessment by anesthesia documents a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor distance of 3.5 cm, and full cervical extension. The plan is to continue beta-blocker, renin–angiotensin–neprilysin inhibitor, and mineralocorticoid antagonist therapy through the morning of surgery, withhold the loop diuretic that day to minimize intravascular volume shifts, reduce the evening basal insulin dose by 20 %, omit prandial insulin while NPO, perform point-of-care glucose testing on arrival in the operating suite, and utilize goal-directed fluid therapy with arterial line monitoring. Sequential compression devices, early postoperative ambulation, incentive spirometry, and physical-therapy evaluation for gait training with the new prosthesis were reviewed extensively; the patient verbalized understanding, expressed motivation to regain mobility, and agreed to strict adherence to sodium and fluid recommendations during the perioperative period.

Patient note:
A 38-year-old male presented to the emergency department with worsening chronic right lumbar pain associated with legs and scrotum edema. He also had itchy and erythematous cutaneous lesions on the abdominal wall over the last 8 months, with no remission despite numerous therapeutic attempts, and complained of diffuse mild to moderate abdominal pain. He denied weight loss, fever, or night sweats. He was a smoker, and his past medical history included unilateral (right) polycystic kidney disease with functional renal exclusion and a left vicariant kidney (he was waiting for a right nephrectomy) and pulmonary tuberculosis in 2003. He frequently used diclofenac, paracetamol, caffeine, and carisoprodol for his chronic lumbar pain.
On admission, he had a good general appearance, no signs of respiratory distress, no alterations in skin color. His heart rate was 95 bpm, blood pressure 166 x 104 mmHg, and room air oximetry were 96%. There were eczematous desquamating skin lesions on his thighs and legs. There were no enlarged lymph nodes. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right lung base. On abdominal palpation, the liver was enlarged, palpable up to 5 cm below the costal margin and was slightly tender. His legs had 2+ symmetrical pitting edema extending from his feet to just above his knees. Laboratory workup revealed mild anemia (Hb 10.8 g/dl), normal white blood cell, and platelet count. The hepatic enzymes, bilirubin, creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, uric acid, and electrolytes were within the normal range. However, the creatinine was 1.47 g/dL (RR: 0.70 - 1.20 g/dL) and the creatinine clearance estimated by the CKD-EPI equation was 69 mL/min/1.73m2. C-reactive protein (32 mg/L; RR: < 3 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (46 mm/1h) were increased. HIV, HCV, syphilis, and Hepatitis B virus serologies yielded negative results. The rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies were negative, and the complement was normal. Urinalysis revealed 1+ of protein and 150 x 103 red blood cells/mm3.
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed a large, contrast-enhanced mass (10 x 8 x 4cm) involving the abdominal infrarenal aorta and the iliac arteries and compressing the inferior vena cava with dilated iliac veins and the left ureter (), raising the hypothesis of the lymphoproliferative disease. The liver had normal size but had a heterogeneous attenuation.
The chest CT showed a diffuse pleural thickening in the right hemithorax with a small loculated pleural effusion, and enlarged mediastinal and peri-esophageal lymph nodes.
The patient was admitted with the working diagnosis of a lymphoproliferative disease for a confirmatory diagnostic workup. A double J ureteral stent was placed in the left ureter. A CT-guided biopsy of the right pleural thickening was performed, which lacked a precise diagnosis. The patient was submitted to a laparoscopic-guided biopsy of the peri-aortic mass. This biopsy showed a fibro-connective tissue exhibiting fibrosis, obliterating phlebitis, and moderate mixed inflammatory infiltrates with few eosinophils, histocytes, and small lymphocytes and frequent plasma cells (
).
The immunohistochemical examination () showed an increased number of IgG4 positive plasma cells. The IgG4/IgG ratio of 30% and approximately 80 IgG4 positive-plasma cells per high-power field (HPF) in areas of more density. This examination, together with the morphological and clinical findings, is highly suggestive of IgG4-RD.
The patient was started on 1.0 mg/kg/day of prednisone for 2 weeks and then tapered for 0.6 mg/kg/day for two months, and to 20 mg/day for 3 months, afterward. The outcome was favorable and he gradually recovered his previous health status. The abdominal and lumbar pain ceased in about 3 weeks after starting treatment, his hemoglobin level returned to normal and his inflammatory markers decreased. Five months after initiation of corticotherapy, a new abdominal CT scan was done (), and the initial contrast-enhanced mass had almost disappeared, but it showed an inferior vena cava thrombosis extending to bilateral external iliac veins. He was started on warfarin. The double J ureteral stent was removed, and the patient remains asymptomatic with a good urine output with no renal function impairment. At the closure of this manuscript, he was asymptomatic and taking only 5 mg/day of prednisone.

Patient note:
An 85-year-old man with a medical history significant for ASH, hypertension,
hyperlipidaemia, and severe aortic stenosis presented to our centre for worsening dyspnoea
with the New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III symptoms with no reported angina nor
syncope. On physical examination, his blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, heart rate was 76
b.p.m. Cardiac auscultation was remarkable for an aortic systolic murmur best heard at the
second intercostal space with a significant decrease in S2. The transthoracic echocardiogram
(TTE) showed ASH with a diastolic septal diameter of 17 mm, a fixed LVOT gradient of
11 mmHg, moderately calcified aortic valve associated with severe stenosis (mean gradient of
42 mmHg, the maximal velocity of 4.05 m/s, the continuity equation was not applicable to
calculate aortic valve area due to accelerated jet in the LVOT), an ejection fraction (EF)
of 60%, and normal systolic pulmonary artery pressure. Cardiac catheterization revealed
normal coronary angiogram. He had a low risk for open-heart surgery (Logistic Euro score
7.96%, STS score 2.9%) with a frail physical state for which the Heart team decided to refer
him for TAVI. Computed tomography and angiography showed ASH with a moderately calcified
aortic valve, mild LVOT calcifications (), and an accessible femoral route.
The TAVI procedure was performed with a 26 mm Sapien 3 bioprosthetic valve (Edwards
Lifesciences, Irvine, CA, USA). The initial result was acceptable, with no PVL nor coronary
obstruction. We noticed an upward movement of the valve during implantation (). There was no pre- nor post-dilations required. No
electrical or access site complications were encountered. The patient was transferred to the
cardiac ward.
Later that day, the patient developed chest discomfort associated with atrial fibrillation
with a rapid ventricular response at 130 b.p.m. and non-specific ST-T changes. A TTE showed
normal EF, a mean aortic gradient of 8 mmHg, a fistula jet reaching from the LVOT to the RA,
no right ventricular dilation, no right atrial dilation, and no pericardial effusion.
Transoesophageal echocardiogram showed mild PVL, and an LVOT pseudo-aneurysm, that is
associated with an LVOT to the RA fistula. The fistula's jet was lining the tricuspid valve
plane with a maximal gradient of 123 mmHg (). A post-procedure computed
tomography (CT) scan showed that the bioprosthesis was well placed with no significant PVL,
no coronary artery obstruction. At the level of the LVOT, there exists a small
pseudo-aneurysm of 5 mm, immediately upstream of the valve prosthesis. It is extended by a
fistulous track towards the RA of an ∼2 mm diameter, where the jet flushes parallel to and
outlining the tricuspid valve plane ().
The patient remained asymptomatic during the course of the hospitalization and was
discharged home on Day 7 post-TAVI. The follow-up TTE was done 1 month later showed a
persistence of the fistula with an increase in size (from 2 to 2.95 mm) and an increased
colour jet and gradient (maximal gradient 166 mmHg) ( and ).

Patient note:
A 38-year-old woman with a background of poorly controlled autoimmune hepatitis on intermittent prednisolone, stage-3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine around 1.9 mg/dL, and recent admission three weeks earlier for culture-negative ascites was discovered by a visiting social worker slumped sideways on her living-room sofa, eyes half-open, drenched in vomitus, and groaning incomprehensibly while clutching her abdomen; 9-1-1 was called immediately. First responders arrived within seven minutes to find her airway partially obstructed by residual gastric contents, respirations agonal at 6–8 per minute, peripheral oxygen saturation unreadable, and a thready carotid pulse of 132 beats/min. After a single 0.3-mg dose of etomidate and 100 mg of succinylcholine administered in the field, she was endotracheally intubated on the second attempt with a 7.5-mm cuffed tube; no continuous sedative infusion was started en route, and the ventilator of the transport unit was set to deliver 28 cm H₂O peak inspiratory pressure, tidal volume 460 mL, rate 18 breaths/min, and an inspired oxygen fraction measured by the in-line analyzer at 0.69. No intravenous fluids, vasopressors, or antibiotics were given during the 11-minute transfer, and the only running line was a 22-gauge catheter infusing lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate. On arrival to the emergency department—before any hospital-initiated therapy could be instituted—she remained mechanically ventilated on the same settings, breathing asynchronously but generating some spontaneous effort; peak airway pressures were unchanged, and end-tidal CO₂ averaged 28 mm Hg. A cuffless non-invasive blood-pressure reading registered 68/42 mm Hg, prompting immediate placement of a right radial arterial catheter that confirmed 75/45 mm Hg with a calculated mean of 55 mm Hg. Heart rhythm on the monitor was sinus tachycardia at 126 beats/min with occasional premature ventricular complexes, temperature was 38.4 °C via esophageal probe, and pulse oximetry on the ventilator’s digital screen fluctuated between 89 % and 91 % on the documented 69 % inspired oxygen. Neurologic assessment, conducted after verifying that no sedation drips were running and with train-of-four monitoring showing recovery from paralytic, revealed pupils 4 mm bilaterally sluggish to light, no eye opening to verbal stimulus, incomprehensible guttural sounds around the tube when sternal rub was applied, and extension of the right arm with flexion of the left to supra-orbital pressure, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 6. The skin was jaundiced with florid spider angiomas over the upper chest, sclerae were icteric, and the conjunctivae were pale; capillary refill exceeded five seconds and the distal extremities were cool and mottled. Chest auscultation disclosed coarse crackles over the right mid-zone and diminished breath sounds at the left base, while cardiac examination detected no murmurs but a faintly audible S3. The abdomen was markedly distended, tense, and diffusely tender without guarding or rebound; a bedside tap drawn under sterile conditions yielded cloudy straw-coloured fluid, but analysis results were pending at the time physiologic data were captured. A 16-French Foley catheter inserted during primary survey produced 25 mL of dark amber urine, and the family member who maintains the patient’s medication diary reported only about 560 mL of urinary output in the preceding twenty-four hours. Arterial blood gas obtained two minutes after line placement—while ventilator settings remained unchanged—showed pH 7.19, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L, lactate 7.2 mmol/L, and PaO₂ 131 mm Hg on 0.69 FiO₂. Concurrent laboratory studies drawn before any crystalloid bolus, broad-spectrum antibiotic, corticosteroid, or vasopressor infusion revealed white-blood-cell count 23.1 × 10³/µL with 18 % band forms, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, hematocrit 31 %, and a platelet concentration of 96 000 /µL. Comprehensive metabolic panel documented sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L, an anion gap of 20, glucose 142 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 64 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 3.6 mg/dL. Liver profile returned aspartate aminotransferase 112 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 98 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 215 U/L, international normalized ratio 2.1, albumin 2.4 g/dL, and a total bilirubin of 3.4 mg/dL with a predominantly conjugated fraction. High-sensitivity troponin was negative, procalcitonin measured 18 ng/mL, and serum ammonia was elevated at 87 µmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph, taken without interrupting ventilatory support, displayed patchy right-middle-lobe consolidation, moderate left pleural effusion, correctly positioned endotracheal tube, and no free sub-diaphragmatic air. Focused cardiac ultrasound performed at the bedside revealed a small hyperdynamic left ventricle, flattened inferior vena cava measuring 0.9 cm with complete inspiratory collapse, and no pericardial effusion. Abdominal ultrasound visualized massive ascites with swirling echogenic debris, coarse heterogeneous hepatic parenchyma, and patent portal and hepatic veins. Twelve-lead electrocardiography recorded sinus tachycardia at 124 beats/min, low-voltage limb leads, and nonspecific ST-T changes without acute ischemia. Up to the precise moment these physiologic and biochemical data were acquired she had received neither crystalloid resuscitation nor pressor medication, no antimicrobial therapy, no continuous sedation, and remained dependent on the endotracheal tube delivering 69 % oxygen while sustaining an arterial pressure of 75/45 mm Hg, a markedly depressed mental status quantified as a Glasgow Coma Score of 6, thrombocytopenia at 96 000 /µL, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia of 3.4 mg/dL, severe renal impairment with creatinine 3.6 mg/dL and oliguria limited to 560 mL over the prior day, and laboratory and imaging findings pointing toward decompensated chronic liver disease complicated by fulminant septic physiology likely originating from infected ascitic fluid.

Patient note:
A 24-year-old native Japanese man presented to our hospital after developing high-grade fever. He had travelled to Vietnam and Cambodia for 14 days. After leaving Japan, he visited the beach in Halong Bay, the forest region near the border of China, and Siem Reap in Cambodia. During his stay, he had participated in forest trekking tourism and had stayed in a youth hostel. For dietary intake, he ate home-cooked food and drank beverages with ice, in a similar manner to local people. Fourteen days after he returned to Japan, he developed a mild headache, chills and malaise, and 2 days later, he developed a high fever with chills and rigors. He did not have any abdominal pain or diarrhoea. His past medical history, family history and social history were unremarkable. On examination, his temperature was 39 ℃, his blood pressure was 128/68 mmHg, his pulse was 101 beats per minute, his respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute and his oxygen saturation was 98 % with room air. He did not present a rash, lymph node swelling, abdominal tenderness, or hepatosplenomegaly. His laboratory examination demonstrated elevated serum C-reactive protein (5.1 mg dl−1; normal range, 0–0.3 mg dl−1). The blood cell counts and the other biochemical tests were normal (WBC 6900 µl−1, AST 20 U l−1, ALT 19 U l−1). The HIV test result was negative, while contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed ileocecal lymphadenopathy. We did not detect enterocolitis, arthritis, or abscesses. We also did not detect an aneurysm or abscess via brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Based on his travel history and clinical findings, we suspected primary bacteraemia from typhoid fever. He was admitted to our hospital for observation and treated with antibiotics. On the day of admission, ceftriaxone (2 g/day) and minocycline (200 mg/day) were administered. On hospital day two, the initial blood cultures yielded Gram-negative bacilli, which were identified as by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry. The bacterial subspecies could not be identified by biochemical testing at our hospital. Antibiotic susceptibility testing revealed that the organism was not resistant to the following antibiotics: ampicillin, piperacillin, cefotiam, cefotaxime, ceftizoxime, ceftazidime, cefepime, imipenem, meropenem, azythromycin, levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin and fosfomycin. Only minomycin had an MIC90 value of >8 µg ml−1.
After 1 day of ceftriaxone and minocycline, his fever, malaise and headache remitted. We discontinued minocycline, and ceftriaxone was continued for 14 days. The patient was discharged on day 10 and had an uneventful recovery with no recurrence of fever.
Further testing using commercial O and H antisera (Denka Seiken Co. Ltd, Tokyo, Japan) according to the Antigenic Formulae of the (9th ed.) [] identified the organism as serovar Corvallis (at Hokkaido Institute of Public Health, Sapporo, Japan). Thus, serovar Corvallis was likely to have caused the primary bacteraemia in this patient, as described.

Patient note:
A 91-year-old Japanese woman presented to our hospital with hypoxia of unknown origin. She had a medical history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation. Eight years before, when she was 82, an advanced atrioventricular block was diagnosed after a syncopal episode and she received a permanent dual chamber pacemaker implantation. She underwent coronary computed tomography (CT) and radioisotope examination at this time, but there was no evidence of cardiomyopathy or of ischemic heart disease. The tip of the pacemaker lead was observed to pass through a PFO at the left ventricular apex; she received a follow-up examination because of no serious adverse event. She had no history of lung disease or tobacco smoking. She had no subjective symptoms associated with cardiovascular disease after pacemaker implantation. There was no evidence of a decline in oxygen saturation levels at that time, which were measured by pulse oximetry.
Her physical examination findings on admission were as follows: clear level of consciousness and severe hypoxia and cyanosis observed only in the right lateral decubitus position. These symptoms were immediately improved in the left lateral decubitus, the supine, and the upright position. Arterial blood gas values were consistent with her symptoms. Partial arterial oxygen pressure (PaO2) and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) decreased only in the right lateral decubitus position (Table ). These observations were reproducible. There was no evidence of lung rales or cardiac murmur.
Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, thyroid function tests, and D-dimers were almost normal. A chest X-ray showed a significant elevation of her right diaphragmatic dome.
An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed an atrium-sensing, ventricular-pacing rhythm with a complete right bundle branch block (RBBB) pattern (Fig. ). In general, when the pacemaker lead is set on the right ventricle correctly, the pacemaker first stimulates the right ventricle, and next the left ventricle. Because of this, the expected ECG pattern with right ventricle pacing should show a left bundle branch block (LBBB) pattern. A RBBB pattern suggests that the pacemaker first stimulates the left ventricle, and next the right one. Only this ECG pattern could indicate the possibility of inadvertent left ventricle pacing. This patient’s ECG pattern also suggested left ventricle pacing. However, we could not assess a malposition of the pacemaker lead from only an ECG pattern because sometimes we find a RBBB pattern although the pacemaker lead is set correctly. Contrast-enhanced CT excluded the diagnosis of cerebral infarction, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, and lung parenchymal abnormalities and revealed giant liver cysts and compression of the right atrium by one of cysts (Fig. ). A chest X-ray and CT scan revealed right hemidiaphragmatic elevation that was probably compressing the right atrium. This finding was suspected in the case of right hemidiaphragmatic paralysis []. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, left atrial dilatation, and compression of the right atrium due to the giant liver cyst. In addition, the pacemaker lead probably ran abnormally to the left atrium and ventricle through PFO, but shunt flow across the PFO on color Doppler image was not apparently observed. Pulmonary perfusion imaging with 99mTc-macroaggregated albumin (MAA) was performed in the right lateral decubitus position. MAA accumulated in her kidneys and brain, which suggested the presence of a right-to-left shunt. The estimated shunt ratio was 26.3%.
A transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) with intravenously administered agitated saline contrast solution was performed in both right and left lateral decubitus (Fig. ). TEE showed a compressed right atrium and shunt blood flow in both directions: from the left to the right atrium and vice versa. The shunt flow was exacerbated by postural changes from the left to the right lateral decubitus (Fig. ). TEE also confirmed that the giant liver cyst was compressing the right atrium and the pacemaker lead was abnormally running to the left atrium through PFO (Fig. ).
Considering these results, we concluded that the cause of hypoxia was POS with right-to-left interatrial shunt through PFO. POS can be treated with the closure of the interatrial shunt by thoracotomy or percutaneous cardiac catheterization []. Surgical closure of PFO was not performed due to the age of our patient, surgical difficulties, and failure to obtain informed consent. For these reasons she was discharged after receiving medical advice about her posture.

He explained that he first observed an unusual charcoal hue when he wiped early this morning but dismissed it as dietary until the smell and stickiness became unmistakable after lunch; alarmed, he drove himself to the hospital. He specifically denied dizziness, blurred vision on rising, presyncope, actual loss of consciousness, chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea. Over-the-counter analgesics have been his only medications: he estimates taking 600 mg of ibuprofen every six hours for four consecutive days to ease a right ankle sprain sustained during recreational basketball. He has no prior history of peptic ulcer disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, hematologic disorders, pancreatitis, or chronic viral infections, and he has never undergone endoscopy.
