Patient note:
A 36-year-old Iranian man was admitted to our emergency department on 31 August 2006, presenting with epigastric and retrosternal pain of two and a half hours duration. His detailed medical history revealed that he had no risk factors for coronary artery disease, however, BD had been diagnosed 10 years earlier and he was on colchicine 1 mg/day. Oral aphthous ulcers were exacerbated during coronary artery events. Eye examination was normal. He had an episode of thrombophlebitis of his left leg in 2004 and had been taking warfarin but had discontinued the medication.
Medical examination revealed blood pressure of 130/70 mmHg and heart rate of 85 beats/minute and the patient was pale and perspiring. Chest auscultation revealed no abnormalities. His electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed normal sinus rhythm with ST segment elevation on II, III and aVF and reciprocal ST segment depression on V1-V6. Laboratory tests showed elevation of plasma total creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and CPK-MB activities. There were no findings consistent with coagulation and fibrinolysis disorders. He was diagnosed as having an acute inferior wall myocardial infarction, therefore nitroglycerin, heparin, aspirin and beta blocker therapies were started immediately followed by thrombolytic therapy with streptokinase within 1 hour. After 40 minutes, his chest pain was relieved and there was a significant reduction of ST segment elevation along with increased cardiac enzyme levels. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed mild apical hypokinesia and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50%.
On the third day of hospital admission, he underwent coronary angiography. Coronary angiography revealed an 8 mm giant aneurysm of the proximal left anterior descending artery, an 8 mm aneurysm of the proximal left circumflex coronary artery (Figure ) and a 9 mm aneurysm of the proximal right coronary artery (Figure ). Based on clinical evidence, electrocardiogram and coronary angiography, we considered that the acute myocardial infarction in our patient was due to a coronary aneurysm. Therefore, we did not attempt any coronary intervention and decided to continue with medical therapy including azathioprine, colchicine, prednisolone, aspirin, beta blocker, nitroglycerin and enalapril. On 25 November 2006, the patient experienced another episode of chest retrosternal pain which lasted for 7 hours. His ECG revealed significant ST segment depression on V1-V6. Cardiac enzymes did not rise so he was diagnosed with unstable angina. No changes in ECG were noticed after 5 days. The patient was not adhering to drug therapy and when his coronary events occurred drug therapy was restarted. The next episode of retrosternal pain occurred on 28 February 2007 and lasted for 5 hours. His ECG showed tall T waves on precordial leads. Laboratory tests showed elevation of plasma total CK and CK-MB activities. He was diagnosed with an acute anterior wall myocardial infarction. Medical treatment was started but since he had received thrombolytic therapy 5 months earlier, streptokinase was not administered. The echocardiogram showed septal, apical and anterior wall hypokinesia with an estimated left ventricular ejection fraction of about 25-30%. He was discharged 10 days later with his previous medication plus digoxin, warfarin, frusemide, and spironolactone. On 2 August 2007, he experienced another bout of retrosternal pain that lasted for 7 hours. ECG showed ST segment elevation on precordial leads. Laboratory tests showed elevation of plasma total CK and CK-MB activities. This time, a new anterior myocardial infarction was diagnosed, medical treatment was started and azathioprine was switched for pulse cyclophosphamide 10 mg/kg, but the patient then discharged himself. At the time of writing, the patient is well with pulse cyclophosphamide every 2 months and prednisolone 7.5 mg/day, but unfortunately, he is non-compliant to drug therapy and so it was not possible to switch him to oral medication.

Patient note:
We describe the case of an 18-year-old woman with chest pain radiating to the left arm at rest. Her past medical history was unremarkable, apart from Graves’ disease on treatment with methimazole at a dosage of 5 mg/die. She came to our attention in 2020, when she was admitted to the emergency department (ED) for the onset of sharp chest pain radiated to the left arm and to the trapezius ridge. Pain was less severe when in a seated position and more severe when in a supine position, when breathing deeply or during coughing. No episodes of fever, diarrhoea, respiratory symptoms, or myalgia were reported in the previous days. In the ED, the pain was persistent; laboratory findings showed no significant abnormalities. In particular, cardiac markers, D-dimer, complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin were normal. The ECG () showed tachycardia at 128 b.p.m. and diffuse, concave (‘saddle-shaped’) and non-specific ST-segment elevations in all leads except aVR and V1, and PR-segment depression except aVR. Analgesic drugs were administered and the patient was then hospitalized in the Cardiology Department for further diagnostic and therapeutic assessment. On physical examination, blood pressure was 141/63 mmHg and body temperature 36.5°C. On cardiac auscultation, S1 and S2 heart sounds were normal and no pathological murmur was reported; no friction rub was heard. Absence of jugular vein distension and no pulsus paradoxus was reported. Laboratory tests were repeated and showed no significant abnormalities: serum Beta 2 microglobulin, electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase, and transaminases (ALT, AST) were normal and renal function was not impaired, thus ruling out uraemic pericarditis. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) was suppressed (<0.0008 mIU/L, local lab normal reference range: 0.4–4 mIU/L) and serum-free thyroxine 4 was increased (61.24 pg/mL, reference range: 8–19 pg/mL); cardiac markers and acute-phase proteins were still negative. Antithyroid therapy was optimized, increasing methimazole dosage to 10 mg TID, and oral propanolol 10 mg TID was introduced. Laboratory tests for autoimmune diseases were performed and the antinuclear antibody panel, lupus anti-coagulant, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies were negative. Additionally, anti-mitochondrial (AMA, M2), anti-extractable nuclear antigens, anti-actin smooth muscle antibodies, and anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies were negative, excluding systemic autoimmune and auto-inflammatory causes of pericardial diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma and vasculitis. Tests for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) (nasopharyngeal swab), Epstein–Barr virus, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis C virus, Enterovirus, Parvovirus B19, and Adenovirus were also negative, so that the main viral infectious causes of pericarditis were excluded. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular ejection fraction (EF = 65%), absence of valvular diseases, no pericardial effusion, and normal right ventricular dimensions and function. Thoracic non-ECG-gated CT angiography was then performed () and acute aortic and pulmonary diseases were ruled out. The CT showed the presence of a pericardial effusion with slightly increased density (with radiological characteristic not consistent with blood nature) having a maximum thickness of 15 mm in the upper mediastinum. To characterize this effusion, gadolinium cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed and the effusion turned out to be an extrapericardial mass of 73 × 51 mm () located in the upper mediastinum. A minimal pericardial effusion was found near the anterior mid-basal wall of the left ventricle where the mass had contact with the pericardium. The pericardium, however, showed no signs of infiltration by the mass and no late gadolinium enhancement was described. In view of this and in the absence of surrounding lymphadenopathies, the haematology specialist indicated biopsy of the mass, which was then performed through video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery. Histological analysis showed true thymic hyperplasia and, from an anatomopathological point of view, prevalence of thymic cortex with various Hassall’s bodies in the absence of lymphoid infiltration was described. After the improvement of the symptoms, the patient was discharged and ambulatory follow-up was planned. At the 1-month follow-up visit on 4 November 2020, the patient was asymptomatic, TSH levels were normal (3 mIU/L), anti-TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) were 10 IU/L (vs. 35.50 IU/L on admission; reference range <0.55 IU/L), and a 12-month cardiac MRI was planned.

Patient note:
A 61-year-old female former smoker presented with increasing dyspnea and productive cough with white expectoration for a few days. She denied fever, chest pain, palpitation, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and edema. She had unintentional weight loss of 20 lbs along with loss of appetite. She had past medical history of bronchial-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT) lymphoma and was treated with rituximab. A positron emission tomography (PET) scan two months prior to the admission showed left lower lobe mass with obstruction of the left mainstem bronchus, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules with moderate left pleural effusion. Subsequently, she received chemotherapy with obintuzumab and bendamustine.
On admission, she was afebrile, sinus tachycardia 110/min, normotensive, respiratory rate 25/min and oxygen saturation 96% on 2 L nasal cannula oxygen. There was neither jugular venous distension nor pedal edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmur or added sound. Lung auscultation revealed diminished breath sound over the left hemithorax. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
Her electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with the rate of 109/min. Complete blood count showed normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 9 g/dl which was stable compared to that two months ago. Blood chemistry was within normal limits. Chest X- ray showed opacification of the left hemithorax (Figure ).
Given these observed findings along with the elevated risk of thrombosis in active cancer, computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram was performed (Figure ). CT chest ruled out pulmonary embolism but revealed a large filling defect within the left atrium, left inferior and superior pulmonary veins. It was suspected to be a thrombus since it was not reported on earlier PET scan. Apixaban was initiated given the concern for thromboembolism.
A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 3 x 3 cm, mobile, echogenic mass in the left atrium best seen in the parasternal long axis view (Figure ). Her left atrial size was reported to be normal. Her left ventricular size and function were also within normal limit. Further evaluation with transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was considered. However, the patient did not provide consent for TEE after being informed about the risks of the procedure.
To offer the best characterization of soft tissue cardiac masses, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) was performed (Figure ). It confirmed a bulky left lung mass suggestive of carcinoma invading the left atrium via the left pulmonary veins. There was bulky intraluminal tumor thrombus and extensive mediastinal invasion by tumor. CT-guided biopsy of left lung mass was suggestive of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC). A diagnosis of dual synchronous cancers, BALT lymphoma and NSCLC, adenocarcinoma to be exact, with cardiac invasion was made. As of now, we are not sure about the relationship between these two tumors. We do not know which one had invaded the left atrium. She continued to receive palliative chemotherapy. After discussion with the hemato-oncology, the anticoagulation was stopped due to the risk of internal bleeding.

Patient note:
A 35-year-old woman visited the emergency department with a 2-day history of increasingly worsening abdominal pain. She had no history of serious illnesses. Physical examination showed that her blood pressure was 113/72 mmHg, pulse was 97 b.p.m., and body temperature was 37.7 °C. She presented with epigastralgia (sometimes intermittent abdominal colics without muscle guarding). Laboratory examination showed that her haemoglobin level was 13.0 mg/dl, haematocrit level was 39.2%, white blood cell count was 10 870 mm–3 (74.6% segmented neutrophils) and C-reactive protein level was 0.07 mg/dl. An enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of her abdomen showed the presence of a large intraluminal mass located in the transverse colon with signs of intussusception (Fig. a and b). There were no findings of intestinal ischaemia. Abdominal findings indicated no peritonitis or ischaemic change; therefore, colonoscopy was performed to release the intussusception and diagnosis the lead point lesion. There was an oval-shaped, 4-cm mass in the transverse colon, indicating ileocecal-type intussusception (Fig. ). The clinical impression was that intussusception was due to a non-epithelial tumour, such as a gastrointestinal stromal tumour, which could be pushed back into the ileum easily using pressurized air. It was difficult to obtain a biopsy given its movement.
Two days later, a laparoscopic-assisted operation was performed. Her intussusception was almost improved. There was no movable caecum or intestinal oedema; the laparoscopic-assisted operation was performed uneventfully. The ileocecal segment was resected, and functional end-to-end anastomosis was performed.
Results of the histopathological examination showed a 3.5 × 4.5 cm IFP composed of oedematous stroma containing spindle-shaped stromal cells, lymphoid nodules and eosinophils (Fig. a and b). Results of immunohistochemical analysis indicated that the spindle cells were negative for smooth muscle actin, C-kit, desmin and CD34 (Fig. a–d). A diagnosis of IFP of the ileum was made.
The patient has had no specific post-operative complications; she was discharged 11 days post-operatively. There was no recurrence at the 8-month follow-up.

A 43-year-old man presented to the emergency department reporting sudden-onset feeling of palpitations and near syncope after strenuous heavy lifting. He was pale and diaphoretic; blood pressure was measured 90/70 mmHg, oxygen level 99%, heart-rate 210–230 b.p.m., and body temperature 36.6°C. Past medical history was clear for cardiac disease, syncope, or pre-syncope. No history of sudden cardiac death (SCD) or cardiomyopathy into his family was stated. He denied recent flu-like symptoms, smoking, illicit drug use, or excessive alcohol consumption. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial electrocardiogram (ECG) depicted an irregularly irregular, broad QRS complex tachycardia (). No previous ECG recordings were handed. Direct current (DC) cardioversion restored sinus rhythm with manifest ventricular pre-excitation and clear ‘delta’ waves () confirming our initial clinical suspicion for underlying WPW syndrome. Shortest pre-excited RR interval (SPERRI) during AF was estimated at 160 ms (), indicating an AP with extremely short antegrade effective refractory period (ERP) at risk for mediating SCD. Echocardiography ruled out abnormalities associated with WPW, including Ebstein’s anomaly, valve lesions, cardiac hypertrophy, atrial aneurysms, and septal defects. Cardiac ischaemia was also excluded on the basis of clinical, electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and laboratory data. The patient was put on enoxaparin 80 mg b.i.d. and propafenone 150 mg t.i.d. and his clinical course remained uneventful. Electrophysiological study (EPS) was performed at a tertiary centre on Day 10 post-diagnosis; programmed atrial stimulation induced pre-excited AF with markedly increased SPERRI = 264 ms and a left anterolateral AP with antegrade only conduction properties was ablated (). The patient was scheduled for routine cardiologic follow-up and advised to abstain from intense physical activity for at least 1-month post-discharge. In case of palpitations, ECG and 24-h Holter monitoring were suggested. CHA2DS2-VASc Score was calculated zero, so 1 month of rivaroxaban 20 mg daily was deemed sufficient post-ablation. Family members were also screened for pre-excitation. The patient remained symptom free without pre-excitation on surface ECG on his latest follow-up visit 3 months after the procedure.

Patient note:
We report the case of a 32-year-old Indian woman admitted to our institute with angina on exertion. This symptom first appeared 2 years prior to her presentation, with gradual onset and progressive worsening from class I to class III associated with multiple episodes of pre-syncope. She had no history of diabetic mellitus, arterial hypertension, palpitation, or syncope and no family history of similar complaints or sudden death. On physical examination, our patient appeared generally well. Her blood pressure and pulse rate were 128/84 mmHg and 57 beats per minute, respectively.
Electrocardiography revealed a sinus rhythm and left ventricular hypertrophy by Sokolow–Lyon criteria, with secondary ST depression and biphasic T-waves in leads I, aVL, and V4–V6. A chest X-ray was normal. A Holter study was not suggestive of any significant arrhythmias or pause as a plausible cause of the pre-syncope. Her biochemical blood parameters were also within normal ranges. Echocardiography revealed HOCM (Fig. ) with systolic anterior movement. Pulsed wave Doppler showed a dagger-shaped spectral profile with a peak sub-aortic velocity of 287 cm/s and a maximum pressure gradient of 33 mmHg (Fig. ), with mild eccentric mitral regurgitation. After an initial evaluation, our patient underwent cardiac catheterization to exclude concomitant coronary artery disease and to rule out other coexisting congenital coronary anomalies. Coronary angiography showed no significant stenosis due to coronary artery disease. However, angiography revealed multiple coronary microfistulas originating from both her left coronary artery system (Fig. , Additional file 1) and her right coronary artery (Fig. , Additional file 2). Our patient also underwent a cardiac catheterization study with oximetry analysis to confirm that the microfistulas originated from her left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD), left circumflex artery (LCX), and right coronary artery (RCA). The rapid filling of her pulmonary artery after dye was injected into her left coronary artery during the catheterization study demonstrated that the microfistulas were all draining into her right ventricle (RV) (Fig. , Additional file 3). Further confirmation came from an oxygen step up of 15 % (from 65 % to 80 %) from her right atrium (RA) to her RV during oximetry analysis.
Our patient was discharged 5 days after the completion of her clinical investigation on medical therapy including metoprolol and nicorandil. At a follow-up 1 month later, her angina grade had decreased from class III to class II.

Patient note:
A 28-year-old woman presented to our center complaining of a sudden onset of right-side lower abdominal pain with slight vaginal bleeding. She had undergone a thawed ET with two embryos 23 days before, following IVF. She had a history of right salpingectomy for an ectopic pregnancy during ovulatory cycle downregulation for IVF–ET 1 year previously. On physical examination, she was hemodynamically stable with a blood pressure of 97/65 mm Hg and heart rate of 80 bpm. A physical examination demonstrated a distended abdomen with diffuse abdominal pain that was maximal in the right iliac fossa with rebound pain and signs of peritonitis. Transvaginal sonography demonstrated one intrauterine gestational sac with an uneven mass measuring about 9.2 × 5.0 cm at the right adnexa (Fig. ). The intrauterine gestational sac measured 1.0 × 1.1 × 0.8 cm with a yolk sac about 0.3 cm in diameter (Fig. ). Ultrasonographic evidence of hemoperitoneum was present, with a large amount of free fluid within the pouch of Douglas (Fig. ). The patient underwent emergency laparoscopy that confirmed a ruptured right interstitial pregnancy and hemoperitoneum (Fig. ). This ectopic pregnancy tissue was removed and effective hemostasis achieved. The amount of hemoperitoneum was approximately 1.0 L, which was evacuated followed by peritoneal lavage. Histopathology of the tissues confirmed a tubal stump pregnancy. Medical treatment of progesterone and estrogen was used to prevent abortion of the intrauterine pregnancy. However, on day 10 after the operation, the patient had an incomplete abortion and underwent uterine curettage.

Patient note:
A 29-year-old woman with no significant past medical history walked into the urgent evaluation bay early this evening because her entire left lower limb had become “tight and huge” since yesterday morning. She recalls waking up for an early laboratory class, noticing that her favorite pair of skinny jeans would not slide up past mid-thigh on the left side, and assuming it was post-workout soreness from a light jog two days earlier. By lunchtime the same day she could see a visible difference between the two legs when seated at her desk, and climbing one flight of stairs to the anatomy lab caused a dull, throbbing discomfort that radiated from the medial calf toward the groin. She denies recent falls, twists, insect stings, penetrating injuries, or soft-tissue infections and has not noticed fevers, chills, night sweats, rigors, or weight change. There has been no chest pain, pleuritic discomfort, cough, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, abdominal pain, or urinary complaints. She completed a 5 km charity run five days ago without incident and has maintained her usual routine of walking across campus between classes, stating that she has not required crutches, braces, casts, or walking boots at any point. She has never been diagnosed with clotting disorders, has no prior thromboembolic events, and takes no estrogen-containing contraception, glucocorticoids, or anticoagulants; her only medication is an as-needed ibuprofen tablet for menstrual cramps. There is no personal or first-degree family history of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, premature myocardial infarction, or stroke, and she specifically denies malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, nephrotic syndrome, or chronic heart failure. She has never been pregnant, does not smoke cigarettes, drinks wine socially once or twice per month, and has never used illicit substances. On arrival, before any therapeutic intervention, she appeared alert, oriented, and mildly uncomfortable when shifting position on the stretcher. Vital signs were temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 114/74 mm Hg, heart rate 94 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; lungs were clear on auscultation. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, and nontender with no palpable masses. Inspection of the lower extremities showed striking asymmetry: the left limb was globally enlarged from proximal thigh to ankle with a faint glossy sheen to the skin yet preserved normal color. Tape measurements taken 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 45 cm on the symptomatic side versus 40 cm on the right, confirming a 5 cm discrepancy; at mid-thigh the left measured 56 cm and the right 51 cm. Palpation along the course of the common femoral vein in the inguinal crease, through the adductor canal, and across the popliteal fossa elicited localized tenderness most pronounced in the distal posterior thigh and upper calf, whereas similar pressure on the contralateral limb was painless. No palpable cords, fluctuance, crepitus, or masses were appreciated, and the skin temperature was marginally warmer over the tender track than over the right side. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2 + bilaterally with brisk capillary refill; sensory examination to light touch and pinprick was intact, and motor strength graded 5/5 throughout both legs. Active and passive ranges of motion of the hip, knee, and ankle were full, though she winced slightly when the knee was flexed against resistance, correlating with the deep pathway discomfort. There were no varicosities, telangiectasias, or serpiginous superficial channels visible, and inguinal nodes were not enlarged. No erythematous streaks, bullae, or ulcerations were present, and Homan’s sign was not specifically elicited to avoid provoking unnecessary pain. Baseline laboratory testing obtained prior to any anticoagulation showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, platelet count 248 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.9 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 0.82 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, INR 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 seconds; hepatic enzymes fell within reference limits. An electrocardiogram displayed normal sinus rhythm at 92 beats/min without ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities, and plain radiographs of the femur and tibia—ordered by the triage physician to exclude occult fracture—showed only soft-tissue fullness without osseous injury or gas. Given the abrupt onset of unilateral enlargement involving the entire length of the extremity, objective confirmation that the calf exceeds the contralateral side by more than 3 cm, focal tenderness precisely over the expected deep venous route, absence of a prior clotting history, lack of neurologic weakness or immobilization devices, and no competing infectious, traumatic, or orthopedic explanation on examination, an intraluminal obstruction within the deep venous system of the left lower limb is considered the leading concern, and duplex ultrasonography from the iliac segment to the ankle has been arranged on an urgent basis while therapeutic decisions await imaging confirmation.

Patient note:
A 59-year-old healthy male presented for an assessment of nonhealing painful necrotic lesions of the left leg. His past medical history included anemia with intermittent pancytopenia diagnosed 10 years ago. Previous specialist hematologic assessment did not reveal an etiology. Two weeks prior, he believed that he sustained a spider bite while mowing the lawn during the month of August. The lesion began as a small papule less than 1 cm and then developed into a large blister on the left lower calf. Oral cloxacillin was initiated for one week; however, the lesion rapidly increased in size, began to ulcerate, and was extremely painful. He presented to the emergency room at a community hospital, febrile (38 degrees Celsius) with otherwise stable vitals. The documented area of necrosis measured 10 cm × 13 cm. Blood work showed ongoing pancytopenia (white blood cell count of 1.8 × 109/L, hemoglobin 100 g/L, platelets 88 × 109/L). He underwent urgent surgical debridement due to clinical concerns of a necrotizing process. Empiric ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and clindamycin were initiated. There was no intraoperative evidence of necrotizing fasciitis, purulence, or foul odour. Tissue cultures yielded methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), and the antibiotics were narrowed to cefazolin. Necrosis developed at the surgical margins and rapidly extended a further 3 cm over the next 3 days. A second surgical debridement was completed with the addition of a negative pressure dressing over the wound. The intraoperative tissue cultures yielded MSSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Ciprofloxacin was added to cefazolin. During the subsequent three days, the patient developed severe calf pain with an expanding hematoma and required urgent surgical exploration. No significant abnormalities were noted. Tissue cultures yielded the same mixture of organisms. Further extension of necrosis again was observed at the surgical margin, and a fourth surgical debridement extended his wound up to the popliteal fossa and down to the ankle. Microbiology yielded commensal flora. Histopathology showed skin necrosis, ulceration and inflammation of subcutaneous tissues, and neutrophilic dermal infiltration with abscess formation. All bacterial and fungal stains were negative, and there was no evidence of vasculitis. New necrotic lesions developed on the left medial malleolus and the plantar aspect of his first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. He was subsequently transferred to our centre for evaluation of an infectious etiology of progressive nonhealing necrotic skin lesions and assessment for potential limb amputation.
On initial assessment, the lesions were violaceous, painful, and necrotic with raised, irregular borders. The largest lesion extended circumferentially from the left tibial tuberosity to the ankle. Satellite lesions were noted at the medial and lateral malleoli and the base of the first MTP joint (). Investigations showed ongoing pancytopenia (leukocytes 2.3 × 109/L, hemoglobin 72 g/L, and platelets 64 × 109/L). His C-reactive protein level was 225 mg/L. A nuclear bone scan indicated osteomyelitis of the left first MTP joint. A bone marrow biopsy showed pancytopenia with possible hairy cells. Flow cytometry revealed a pattern consistent with hairy cell leukemia (HCL).
Based on the clinical course of leg lesions exhibiting a pathergic phenomenon in response to skin trauma and nonresponse to multiple adequate courses of antimicrobial therapy and pathology showing sterile neutrophilic infiltration, combined with diagnosis of underlying hematological malignancy, we diagnosed him clinically with pyoderma gangrenosum. All further debridement was suspended, and negative pressure dressings were stopped. Due to the open nature of the wound, imaging consistent with osteomyelitis and impending chemotherapy, empiric piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin were initiated. A bone biopsy of the left MTP grew E. coli (Amp C) and P. aeruginosa. Antibiotics were switched to ertapenem and ciprofloxacin. He received seven days of cladribine chemotherapy plus prednisone for HCL and continued antibiotics for osteomyelitis of his left MTP. Six months after diagnosis of PG, the lesions showed significant clinical improvement, but severe scarring ().

Patient note:
A 48-year-old woman with a history limited to diet-controlled hyperlipidemia and seasonal allergic rhinitis was transported by rural EMS after being discovered collapsed on the living-room carpet by a coworker who stopped by for a scheduled ride to work; the witness reports hearing a loud thud, finding her lying prone and snoring faintly, but observing no convulsive activity, emesis, or obvious trauma to furniture or fixtures. Paramedics arrived nine minutes later, rolled her supine onto a backboard, applied a cervical collar because the exact mechanism of the fall was uncertain, obtained a finger-stick glucose of 112 mg/dL, started a single 18-gauge IV in the left antecubital vein, and provided 6 L/min oxygen by simple face mask after noting shallow respirations, yet administered no crystalloid, analgesic, anxiolytic, paralytic, or vasoactive medication during the twelve-minute transport. On entry to the emergency department resuscitation bay she remains on the EMS board in street clothing flecked with pet hair, purse still slung over one shoulder, and has not been repositioned or suctioned since leaving the scene. Initial pre-intervention vitals show blood pressure 164/96 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 102 beats/min in a regular rhythm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min with occasional irregular sighs, peripheral oxygen saturation 97 % while still receiving face-mask oxygen, and a tympanic temperature of 36.9 °C. The airway is presently patent; the oropharynx contains no blood, dentures, or foreign material, and a brief sweep with a Yankauer catheter triggers an intact gag and brief cough. Inspection of the head reveals a 2-cm superficial abrasion on the left frontal scalp without active bleeding; pupils are 3 mm, equal, round, and briskly reactive. At baseline her eyelids are fully closed and lashes still, yet the moment her first name is spoken firmly near either ear the lids part to mid-palpebral height, gaze centers on the ceiling for roughly two seconds, then drifts inferiorly as the lids fall even though no painful stimulus is applied, allowing repeated confirmation that ocular opening is reproducible with voice alone but absent when the room is silent. Throughout multiple cycles of voice prompting she produces no phonation, mouth movement, or articulation—there is not even a muffled groan or vowel, and her tongue remains motionless behind closed teeth unless the Yankauer again brushes the palate. Cranial nerve assessment is otherwise limited but notable for symmetric corneal reflexes, intact blink to threat once the lids are lifted manually, and midline uvula. The extremities rest flaccid at her sides; deep tendon reflexes are 2 + and symmetric in biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles, plantar responses mute. When firm pressure is applied to the trapezius or to the nail bed of either index finger, both upper arms abruptly flex at the elbows, wrists curl inward, and shoulders adduct toward the sternum in a stereotyped pattern lasting three to four seconds before the limbs relax back to neutral—no purposeful withdrawal or localization is observed, and the lower extremities remain motionless except for a slight internal rotation at the hips during the same noxious stimulus. No extension, flailing, or cycling motions occur. Taken together, her observed eye opening to voice, absence of any verbalization, and flexion of the upper extremities to painful stimulus yield a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 (E3 V1 M4). Cardiovascular examination reveals a regular S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; peripheral pulses are 2 + radially and dorsalis pedis, and capillary refill is under two seconds. Lungs are clear to auscultation with equal breath sounds and resonant percussion; there is no accessory muscle use. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender with active bowel sounds; the pelvis is stable on gentle compression, and rectal tone is preserved on digital exam. Skin survey identifies scattered ecchymoses over both knees consistent with a fall forward but no long-bone deformity or step-off along the spine. Point-of-care arterial blood gas obtained on the current oxygen flow shows pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 39 mm Hg, PaO₂ 128 mm Hg, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, and base excess −2 mEq/L. Rapid chemistry panel returns sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, calcium 9.0 mg/dL, and serum glucose 114 mg/dL; hemoglobin by co-oximetry is 13.6 g/dL. A 12-lead ECG demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 100 beats/min with normal intervals. Portable AP chest radiograph taken on the board shows clear lung fields, intact clavicles, and the cervical collar in satisfactory position; pelvic and lateral cervical spine radiographs are pending. Two additional peripheral IV lines have been placed but remain saline-locked, and no intravenous fluid bolus, sedative, anticonvulsant, antiplatelet, or antihypertensive therapy has yet been initiated, ensuring the neurologic responses described above represent her untreated presentation. Computed tomography of the head without contrast and CT angiography of the neck have been ordered stat, and neurosurgery as well as neuro-critical care have been paged; in the interim, continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, supplemental oxygen, and serial neurochecks at fifteen-minute intervals have been instituted, with intubation equipment readied at bedside should her airway reflexes deteriorate.

A 59-year-old woman presented to the pre-operative anesthesia and medicine consultation suite this morning in anticipation of an open right hemicolectomy that is scheduled for tomorrow; the resection is being undertaken for a recently diagnosed, non-metastatic adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon discovered on colonoscopy after several months of iron-deficiency anemia and a positive fecal occult blood test. She arrived walking independently without the aid of a cane or walker, greeting staff comfortably and climbing two flights of stairs to the clinic without shortness of breath, which attests to her baseline, unrestricted mobility. The patient describes a remote cholecystectomy fifteen years ago but no other operative interventions in the recent past, and she has not required any emergency procedures, limb casts, or prolonged bed rest over the last month. She denies chest pain, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, pedal swelling, or prior episodes of venous clots in herself or close relatives. Her cardiovascular history is notable only for well-controlled hypertension; she has never been told she suffered a heart attack or heart failure. Neurologically she reports no prior stroke, transient ischemic attack, or spinal cord injury, and she cannot recall any episode of pneumonia, sepsis, or disseminated infection within the past several weeks. Respiratory review is significant for longstanding tobacco-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; she quit smoking five years ago after a 35-pack-year habit and currently uses a twice-daily long-acting bronchodilator with an as-needed rescue inhaler. She has not required hospitalization, oxygen supplementation, or oral steroids for pulmonary exacerbations during the last year. Gastrointestinal history is negative for inflammatory bowel disorders. Endocrine, renal, and rheumatologic reviews are unremarkable. She takes lisinopril 10 mg daily, tiotropium inhalation once daily, and over-the-counter multivitamins; she has never received heparin products that triggered thrombocytopenia, and she does not use hormonal replacement or oral contraceptives. Family history is pertinent only for coronary artery disease in her father; there is no recollection of close relatives developing blood clots or inheritable coagulation defects. Socially, she lives with her spouse, remains active by gardening, and performs light aerobic exercise three times weekly. Physical examination reveals a well-nourished female in no distress, body mass index 27 kg/m², blood pressure 134/78 mm Hg, pulse 78 beats/min, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air. Cardiovascular exam is normal with a regular rhythm and no murmurs. Pulmonary exam demonstrates mildly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with occasional end-expiratory wheeze but no accessory muscle use. Abdomen is soft with mild right-sided tenderness but no palpable masses. Of note, inspection of the lower extremities shows clusters of dilated, tortuous superficial veins along the posterior aspect of both calves; the skin is intact, calf circumferences are symmetric, and there is no pitting edema, erythema, warmth, or tenderness. No indwelling venous catheters, ports, or peripherally inserted central lines are present. Neurologic and musculoskeletal examinations are otherwise normal, and plantar flexion against resistance is strong without pain. Pre-operative laboratory studies obtained earlier today reveal hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, hematocrit 33 %, platelet count 280 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and normal electrolytes. Baseline coagulation profile shows prothrombin time 12.4 seconds and activated partial thromboplastin time 28 seconds. Chest radiograph demonstrates hyperinflated lungs consistent with her chronic bronchitis but no acute infiltrate, and ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. She has been instructed to remain NPO after midnight and to continue her bronchodilator until the morning of surgery. Given her cancer diagnosis, impending extensive intra-abdominal operation, chronic pulmonary disease, and visible superficial venous varicosities, peri-operative strategies to lower thrombotic risk—including early ambulation, pneumatic compression stockings, and pharmacologic prophylaxis once hemostasis is assured—will be discussed with the surgical team.

Patient note:
An 88-year-old man with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and extensive peripheral artery disease was referred to our cardiovascular department for elective valvular treatment. He reported a progressive worsening of his exercise tolerance (effort dyspnoea) in the last 6 months leading to a significant limitation in daily life activity in the last month (NYHA Class III).
Physical examination at admission revealed mild systolic hypertension (140/85 mmHg), rough systolic murmur radiating to both the carotid arteries, with no signs of peripheral or pulmonary oedema. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm (60 b.p.m.) with left axis deviation and moderate ST-segment depression in lateral leads. Medical therapy at the time of admission included furosemide 50 mg/die, cordarone 200 mg/die, bisoprolol 2.5 mg/die (maximum tolerated dose), ramipril 2.5 mg/die, and apixaban 5 mg/die (paroxysmal atrial fibrillation).
Transthoracic echocardiogram showed left ventricle hypertrophy with normal systolic contractility (EF 60%) but moderate diastolic dysfunction (E/E′ 28), left atrial enlargement with mild mitral regurgitation, and calcified severe aortic stenosis (valve area of 0.5 cm2 with mean gradient of 52 mmHg, VTIr 0.16). Coronary angiography excluded the presence of concomitant coronary artery disease.
Due to his advanced age and multiple co-morbidities, the patient was judged not suitable for traditional surgical valve replacement (Society of Thoracic Surgeons mortality 7.9%) and scheduled to TAVI (TAVI Score 6.42%).
Pre-procedural multislice computed tomography confirmed a bilateral calcific disease of both iliac-femoral axes with tortuosity and inadequate lumen diameters (). Conversely, the subclavian-axillary axes showed adequate dimensions (i.e. diameters 5.1 mm) and an acceptable degree of kinking and calcification (). Thus, to minimize access-related complications and facilitate peri-procedural management, a completely percutaneous TAVI was planned using an angio-guidewire-ultrasound (AGU) technique by both arms.
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation procedure was performed under conscious sedation, in a hybrid operating suite by a multidisciplinary team including cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, and anaesthesiologists. After local anaesthesia of both wrists, left and right radial arteries were cannulated with 6-Fr glide sheath (Terumo) introducers. By means of a multipurpose 6-Fr diagnostic catheter, a 0.35″ guidewire was retrogradely advanced from the left radial artery into the left axillary artery up to an angiographically ideal point (i.e. adequately large extra-thoracic segment). Ultrasound guidance was then used to scan the vessel wall and exclude the presence of any calcific plaque. Merging data from both imaging techniques, the optimal axillary access point was identified and flagged by the J-tip of the guidewire ( and ).
After local anaesthesia of the left delto-pectoral groove, puncture of the anterior surface of the left axillary artery was assured by AGU technique and a 9-Fr sheath was inserted with a standard Seldinger technique. Two Perclose ProGlide™ (Abbott Vascular Devices) were implanted immediately before sheath introduction according to the pre-close technique.
From the right radial access, a left Judkins 6-Fr diagnostic catheter was used to obtain selective antegrade left subclavian cannulation, and a 0.14″ guidewire 300 cm in length (ChoiceTM extra-support, Boston Scientific Corp., Natick, MA, USA) was positioned distally in the left forearm to ensure axillary artery access in case of acute vascular complication (i.e. vessel rupture) () and to facilitate end-procedural haemostasis.
Using the left radial access, a second 0.14″ guidewire 300 cm in length (ChoiceTM extra-support, Boston Scientific Corp., Natick, MA, USA) was then positioned distally up to ascending aorta to ensure also homolateral rescue axillary artery access.
At this point, heparin was administered intravenously to achieve an activated clotting time >250 s, a stiff guidewire (Innowi®, Symedrix GmbH, Deisenhofen) was positioned into the left ventricle and used to obtain a rapid pacing during preliminary valvuloplasty with 18 mm balloon diameter (True Balloon BARD peripheral vascular, Inc., Tempe, AZ, USA) ().
Finally, a 14-Fr equivalent 29 mm self-expanding Evolut R transcatheter aortic valve (Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA) was successfully implanted with trivial residual para-valvular regurgitation ().
During valve introducer pulling out, a percutaneous transluminal angioplasty balloon (6.0 mm × 20 mm) was simultaneously advanced into the subclavian artery via the right radial access. This assured a temporary blood flow blockade during percutaneous vessel closure manoeuvres (). Finally, anticoagulation was reversed with protamine infusion, the introducer device was removed, and axillary haemostasis was immediately obtained with the vascular closure systems.
The Choice ES guidewires remained in situ to secure access into the vessel at any procedural phase. The final angiography check of the puncture site from the right radial route revealed a complete haemostasis but with a significant pinching of the lumen artery at the site of vascular sutures (). After a failed first attempt to cross the iatrogenic stenosis antegradely due to low support, the suture-caused pinching was successfully crossed retrogradely by left radial access and corrected by a gentle prolonged angioplasty (). The final angiographic check excluded residual bleeding or major vessel injury ().
Post-procedural course was uneventful (); the patient was mobilized after 24 h and transthoracic echocardiography showed a transvalvular gradient of 5 mmHg with trivial para-valvular regurgitation. At 1-month follow-up, the patient described a sensible subjective improvement in activity tolerance and echocardiogram re-evaluation confirmed the pre-discharge findings.

Patient note:
A 78-year-old Caucasian woman with no known past medical history presented to the emergency department with complaints of bilateral lower extremity edema and erythema with a clear serous discharge. The patient first noticed some small blisters on her left lower extremity which subsequently opened with some clear serous drainage. She also experienced progressively worsening swelling first of the left lower extremity and then her right lower extremity which prompted her to come into the hospital. Except for a cough, the patient had no other symptoms.
Preliminary evaluation at the emergency department indicated the patient had cardiomegaly and bilateral pleural effusions with a BNP of 1260. She also had atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. The patient was not complaining of any chest pain, fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. Her chest x-ray showed evidence of cardiac enlargement with interstitial densities and bilateral air-space processes possibly associated with asymmetric pulmonary edema. Large bilateral pleural effusions were noted, with the left greater than the right side. Incidentally, some evidence indicating a compression fracture of indeterminate age involving the upper lumbar/lower dorsal spine was observed.
The patient had no known medical history. In fact, she had not been seen by a physician for the last 15 years. Besides taking aspirin occasionally, she was not on any medications. She did not use alcohol, tobacco or illicit drugs. Physical examination did not reveal any specific concerns other than bilateral lower extremity edema.
CT angiogram of the chest showed large bilateral pleural effusions with bilateral lower lobe enhancing volume loss and worse on the left. Cardiomegaly was noted and there was no evidence for a pulmonary embolus. In addition, there was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis in the venous Doppler studies of her lower extremities bilaterally.
Echocardiogram indicated the left ventricle with some mild hypertrophy. Systolic function was normal with an ejection fraction estimated at about 60%. The right ventricle was mildly enlarged and mildly hypokinetic. The left atrium showed marked enlargement and the right atrium was moderately enlarged as well. The aortic valve was mildly sclerotic and trileaflet. The pulmonic valve was unremarkable. The mitral valve showed flail motion of the posterior leaflet and there was a small mobile echo seen in the left atrium which strongly indicated endocarditis as the cause for pulmonary edema. Doppler examination showed severe mitral regurgitation that tracked underneath the anterior leaflet along the interatrial septum. There was mild aortic insufficiency. The inferior vena cava was dilated indicating elevated right atrial pressure and the pulmonary systolic pressure was estimated at about 50 mmHg.
Gram positive cocci in diploids, tetrads, and clusters were isolated from three sets of blood cultures. The organism was catalase positive and produced a negative coagulase reaction by SlidexTM (BioMérieux, NC). The Vitek 2 GP card (BioMérieux, MO) identified the bacterium as Staphylococcus warneri. It produced acid from trehalose and lacked phosphatase enzyme, two key characteristics that differentiate this species from S. epidermidis - one of the most recognized CoNS [].
The patient was initially treated with Unasyn, 3 grams IV every 6 hours for presumed bilateral lower extremity cellulitis. After the diagnosis of bacterial endocarditis was made and supported by the echo-cardiographic results, the patient was started on nafcillin with gentamicin following consultation with the infectious diseases specialist. In addition, congestive heart failure was treated initially with lasix IV and subsequently with lasix orally. Atrial fibrillation was rate controlled with diltiazem. Gentamicin was later discontinued due to acute renal failure, and the patient was discharged with a PICC line for treatment with 2 grams Nafcillin intravenously every 4 hours for a total of 6 weeks. Repeat blood cultures were negative for 48 hours prior to discharge.

Patient note:
A 52-year-old woman with a five-year history of biopsy-confirmed steatohepatitis-related cirrhosis was transported to the academic hospital’s emergency department after her spouse found her shortly after dawn seated on the bathroom floor, eyes half-closed, mumbling incoherently, and unable to be roused to stand; emergency medical personnel noted that during the twenty-minute transit she intermittently moaned, grabbed at the stretcher rails without purpose, and never formed intelligible words, yet maintained spontaneous respirations and protective cough. The family reports that over the prior fortnight she had grown progressively somnolent, sleeping through midday meals and requiring verbal prompts to finish sentences; two evenings ago she attempted to brush her teeth with an eyeliner pencil and last night mistook a coat closet for the front door. For months she had complained of a subtle “water slosh” in her lower abdomen that forced loosening of her belt by one notch but denied overt distention, frank pain, orthopnea, lower-extremity swelling, hematemesis, melena, or recent alcohol—she quit drinking eight years earlier after social use only. Her background includes type 2 diabetes managed with insulin glargine 18 units nightly and metformin 1000 mg twice daily, class III obesity (body mass index 42 kg/m²), hypertension on lisinopril 20 mg, and obstructive sleep apnea treated with nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure; no variceal bleeding, large-volume paracenteses, or previous episodes of altered mentation have been documented. Surgical history consists solely of laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy three years prior, and she has no known drug allergies. She never smoked, denies illicit drug use, and works remotely as an accountant. Family history reveals a father with coronary artery disease and a mother with type 2 diabetes but no known hereditary liver disorders. At triage—before any intravenous lines, medications, fluids, or oxygen beyond room air—vital signs registered temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg, heart rate 106 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95 % breathing ambient air. The patient lay in the supine position with eyes partially open, pupils equal and reactive, absent gagging on gentle oral suction, and emitted a sweet, musty odor on exhalation; she withdrew slowly to painful trapezius squeeze, uttered unintelligible syllables, and did not follow commands, while motor examination showed intermittent decorticate posturing of the upper limbs when noxious stimuli were applied. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk yet symmetric, plantar responses flexor, and asterixis could not be tested because she could not sustain arm extension. Sclerae were deeply icteric, conjunctivae anemic-tinged, and fewer than twenty spider nevi peppered the upper thorax. The neck was supple without jugular venous distention. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs; lungs were clear. Inspection of the abdomen showed a gentle outward curve with an umbilicus that remained slightly indented; percussion produced tympany centrally and a slender rim of dullness low in both flanks that migrated medially when the stretcher was tilted, and a transmitted impulse was felt across the abdominal wall only when an assistant’s hand pressed firmly along the midline. The abdominal wall was soft, nontender, and the liver edge was nodular and firm 3 cm below the right costal margin on deep palpation, while the spleen tip was not appreciated. There was trace pitting edema at the ankles. Point-of-care capillary glucose measured 112 mg/dL. Bedside ultrasound performed before blood sampling demonstrated a shrunken, coarsely echogenic liver with capsular irregularity, patent hepatopetal portal flow at 15 cm/s, a spleen length of 18 cm, and a thin anechoic fluid stripe up to 1.5 cm deep in Morison’s pouch without free fluid layering around bowel loops; hepatic and portal veins were unobstructed, and the gallbladder showed no calculi or wall thickening. Chest radiograph obtained immediately afterward displayed elevated diaphragms with clear fields and no pleural effusion, while a 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia at 108 beats/min with a QTc of 440 ms but no acute ischemic changes. Peripheral venous blood drawn through an 18-gauge antecubital catheter prior to any therapy revealed: total bilirubin 11.4 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.2 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 95 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 198 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 244 U/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.2 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 88 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 3.3. Serum ammonia, blood cultures, and acetaminophen level were sent but pending. Urinalysis demonstrated dark amber urine with 2+ bilirubin, moderate urobilinogen, and no leukocyte esterase or nitrites. At the moment of this documentation the patient had not yet received lactulose, rifaximin, diuretics, albumin, antibiotics, vitamin K, or any sedatives, thereby reflecting her untreated physiologic state on arrival while plans were underway for airway evaluation, diagnostic paracentesis, and expedited transplant consultation given profound jaundice, severe coagulopathy, and advanced alteration of consciousness.

Patient note:
A 70-year-old woman with a history of stage II hypertension controlled on amlodipine, osteoarthritis of both knees, and remote cholecystectomy was brought to the emergency department by her neighbor after she was discovered sprawled on the kitchen floor approximately fifteen minutes before arrival; according to the neighbor she had been heard moving about normally moments earlier, then a loud thud followed by unintelligible shouting prompted investigation. No seizure-like activity, tonic-clonic movements, or tongue biting were witnessed, and no medications, glucose, oxygen, or intravenous fluids were administered in the interim. On entry to the critical care bay she lies supine on the EMS cot with a loose blanket draped over her shoulders, spectacles skewed on the bridge of her nose, and fragments of broken ceramic plate scattered in her hair and on the collar of her housecoat. The airway is currently patent: oropharynx clear of secretions, uvula midline, and no dentures present. Respiratory effort is regular at 18 breaths per minute with symmetrical chest rise and audible bilateral vesicular breath sounds; oxygen saturation registers 99 % on room air. Cardiac monitor reveals sinus tachycardia at 108 beats per minute, peripheral pulse equally rapid but strong; blood pressure obtained by automated cuff on the right arm is 154/88 mm Hg. Rectal temperature reads 37.4 °C. Skin is dry, warm, and well-perfused; capillary refill <2 seconds. A 4 cm crescent-shaped superficial laceration is noted over the left parietal scalp with oozing venous blood, but no active arterial spurting; digital pressure dressing has been applied in transit only. Pupils are 3 mm bilaterally, briskly reactive to direct and consensual light, and the extra-ocular range appears full as her gaze roams around the resuscitation suite without prompting, occasionally tracking personnel who pass within her field of vision. She maintains lid elevation continuously and blinks spontaneously every few seconds without any verbal or tactile stimulus. When addressed by first name she turns her head toward the speaker yet responds with phrases such as, “Pick up the telephone… blue apples on Tuesday… stop sprinkling salt,” delivered in normal volume and clear articulation but lacking coherence or relevance; she is unable to state her name, location, or the current year despite repetition of questions. Cranial nerve assessment reveals intact corneal reflexes, a symmetric grimace when the angle of the jaw is pressed, and shoulder shrug present on command; gag reflex is brisk when a Yankauer tip brushes the posterior pharynx. No overt dysarthria, aphasia, or slurring is identified; the content, not the clarity, of speech is abnormal. On motor examination she lies with arms resting at her sides and lower limbs loosely flexed at the knees. When asked to lift either hand, squeeze fingers, or wiggle toes, she offers no purposeful movement. However, application of firm supra-orbital pressure on the right provo­kes a deliberate reach of her ipsilateral hand toward the examiner’s knuckles; fingers grasp at the offending hand and attempt to push it away, after which the limb returns to baseline. Identical targeted movements occur when nail-bed pressure is applied to the left index finger and when trapezius squeeze is performed over the right shoulder. No decorticate or decerebrate posturing, no generalized withdrawal, and no asymmetry in strength are observed during these maneuvers. Between stimuli her extremities exhibit normal axial tone without rigidity or flaccidity, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar stimulation produces downgoing toes on both sides. Sensory testing to pinprick and light touch elicits grimace and brisk hand withdrawal diffusely, though formal mapping is limited by cooperation. Cervical spine is manually stabilized during assessment; no midline tenderness is appreciated along the spinous processes, and there is full passive range of motion of all four limbs without crepitus. Cardiovascular exam reveals regular tachycardic rhythm with normal S1 and S2, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; peripheral pulses palpable 2+ in radial, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial arteries. Lungs are clear to auscultation, abdominal contour is flat and soft, bowel sounds present, and there is no guarding or rebound. Pelvis is stable to gentle compression, and rectal tone is preserved. A bedside glucose obtained by EMS two minutes before departmental arrival measured 112 mg/dL; repeat in the bay confirms 109 mg/dL. Point-of-care hemoglobin is 13.9 g/dL and hematocrit 41 %. No alcohol odor is detected on breath, and the neighbor reports the patient consumed only tea and toast at breakfast with no alcohol intake. Medications at home include amlodipine 10 mg daily and acetaminophen 650 mg as needed; no anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or psychoactive drugs. She lives alone, performs her own activities of daily living, and has no prior strokes or cognitive impairment per neighbor statement. Two 18-gauge peripheral IVs have been inserted but left heparin-locked; no crystalloid or pharmacologic agents have been infused. Full trauma panel labs, serum electrolytes, coagulation profile, ethanol, and urine toxicology have been sent, and a non-contrast head CT along with cervical spine imaging is pending. Throughout this initial evaluation—conducted before any sedatives, analgesics, or paralytics—she continues to keep her eyes effortlessly open, speak sentences devoid of contextual meaning, and consistently reach with the stimulated limb to ward off localized painful pressure, all observations capturing her untreated neurologic status on presentation.

Patient note:
A 59-year-old man was brought to the acute care clinic this morning by his partner because, over the preceding forty-eight hours, he noticed that the lower half of his right leg had become visibly larger and increasingly sore whenever he stood up to walk to the bathroom. He recounts that five days ago he developed a febrile influenza-like illness that left him exhausted; aside from getting up to drink water or use the toilet, he remained propped on pillows in bed from Sunday evening through Thursday morning—roughly four and a half consecutive days—streaming television and sleeping for long stretches. By the time the fever and myalgias subsided yesterday, he felt well enough to shower but realized his jogging pants clung tightly around the upper portion of the right calf while hanging loosely on the left. He denies stumbling, weight-lifting, long-distance driving, air travel, insect bites, joint sprain, or localized infection of either lower limb and reports no back pain, groin pull, foot swelling, plantar fasciitis, or recent episodes of cellulitis. He has not felt short of breath, experienced chest discomfort, coughed up blood, had palpitations, or fainted. Review of systems is otherwise unremarkable for fever recurrence, chills, night sweats, unintended weight change, abdominal pain, flank pain, dysuria, or neurologic deficits. His medical history includes well-controlled hyperlipidemia managed with atorvastatin 20 mg nightly and seasonal allergic rhinitis treated with loratadine as needed; he has never been hospitalized for vascular disease, never required anticoagulation, and no first-degree relative has been diagnosed with a clotting disorder before age sixty. He underwent arthroscopic meniscal debridement of the left knee nine years ago without complications and has had no casts, walking boots, or braces since. He does not smoke, drinks two beers on weekend evenings, and denies illicit drug use or testosterone supplementation. Current medications are limited to atorvastatin and loratadine; he has never taken estrogen, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, glucocorticoids, or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. On arrival—and prior to administration of any analgesic, antipyretic, or anticoagulant—he was seated upright with the right ankle elevated on a pillow. Initial vital signs recorded temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % while breathing ambient air. The abdomen was soft and nontender with no organomegaly. A flexible tape placed 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity measured 42.6 cm on the symptomatic side versus 38.8 cm on the left, establishing a 3.8 cm difference; circumferential assessment 15 cm above the patella revealed symmetric measurements of 55 cm bilaterally, and ankle girth at the malleoli was 24 cm on each side. The skin over the enlarged calf appeared normally pigmented and slightly glossy yet maintained temperature comparable to the contralateral limb. Firm thumb pressure held for five seconds along the anterior tibial crest produced immediate recoil without persistent indentation, and identical pressure on the left leg gave the same result. Gentle but systematic palpation along the course of the femoral canal, popliteal fossa, posterior tibial track, and peroneal corridor elicited a distinct, localized tenderness deep in the medial aspect of the gastrocnemius and along the upper popliteal groove, whereas palpation of adjacent muscle bellies and tendons produced only mild soreness likely related to recent inactivity; no discrete palpable cords, masses, or fluctuant collections were detected. Passive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee extended reproduced a dull ache in the posterior calf but no sharp tearing sensation. Hip, knee, and ankle joints moved through full active range without crepitus or effusion, and straight-leg raise did not provoke back or radicular pain. Distal pulses—posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis—were 2+ and symmetric, capillary refill at all toes was under two seconds, sensation to light touch remained intact, and motor strength in ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion graded 5/5 bilaterally. There were no inguinal or popliteal lymph nodes enlarged on careful palpation. Twelve-lead electrocardiography demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 82 beats/min without ST-T segment abnormalities. Patient note:
A 57-year-old man visited Inje University Ilsan Paik Hospital after experiencing abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for 3 weeks. He had visited our emergency room for the same symptoms 2 weeks prior, where he was suspected of having paralytic ileus. However, he was discharged against our medical advice, insisting that his symptoms were not severe. His symptoms had not improved since this visit. He had chronic renal disease for 10 years. Instead of taking prescription drugs, he had been using self-manufactured herbal medication for over 6 months. The herbal medication included more than 10 herbal ingredients such as sansisi (Gardenia jasminoides), hua shi (magnesium silicate), long gu (Mastodi ossis fossilia or talc), and mu li (Ostrea gigas). He had been taking no other medication except for the herbal medicine. He was a 15-pack-year current smoker, and did not drink alcohol.
The patient looked acutely ill; his blood pressure was 132/71 mmHg, pulse rate 97/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and body temperature 36.2℃. The patient's abdomen was distended and tympanic, and showed tenderness without rebound tenderness. In addition, his bowel sounds were decreased. Laboratory tests were as follows: white blood cell 6,970/mm3, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, platelet count 372,000/mm3, BUN 43 mg/dL, creatinine 4.52 mg/dL, and CRP 0.3 mg/dL. The electrolyte levels were within normal limits.
A plain radiograph showed diffuse small bowel distension and colon wall calcification along the colonic area (). Because of his reduced renal function, a non-contrast-enhanced CT scan was taken, which showed diffuse fluid-filled distension of the small bowel with colonic wall thickening and calcifications in the colon wall and at the mesocolon, suggesting atherosclerotic changes (). Paralytic ileus was suspected, and the patient was initially managed with supportive care including hydration, bowel rest, and nasogastric drainage. However, a follow-up CT taken on hospital day 7 did not show any improvement in bowel distention. Colonoscopy without bowel preparation performed on hospital day 8 showed diffuse bluish edematous mucosal change, multiple scarring, and loss of vascularity from the distal sigmoid to the transverse colon. There was a pinpoint stricture in the transverse colon, 65 cm from the anus, and scope passage was not possible (). A biopsy taken from the stricture site showed chronic inflammation and fibrosis with mild regenerative change (). Under the supposition of a PC diagnosis, a contrast-enhanced CT scan with delayed phase angiography was performed, which showed extensive calcifications along the colonic wall, mesenteric, and portal veins (). Total colectomy was recommended, but the patient refused. Fortunately, on the day after the colonoscopy, the patient's symptoms dramatically improved, and the ileus disappeared (). Presumably, this was due to the dilatational effect from the scope passage attempt, or dislodgement of a fecalith. Based on radiologic, endoscopic, and histologic findings, we diagnosed the patient with PC. After several days of a soft diet, the patient remained asymptomatic, and was discharged. The patient is currently symptom-free, after 2 months of follow-up.

Patient note:

The onset of pain had been approximately 2-3 days before presentation. He did not have a remarkable past history. He complained of frequency but denied recent trauma or any problems moving his bowels. Although he had visited the outpatient department 2 days before coming to the ED, he was discharged because of normal urine examination and intravenous pyelography results. Because of discomfort with frequency, he visited the ED for medical attention. In the ED, the urine analysis was redone. Similarly, urinalysis did not detect red blood cells in the urine. Serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine levels, and white blood cell count were normal. Kidney sonography did not show obvious hydronephrosis. Although he did not complain of dysuria, he did mention increased micturation frequency. He did not seem anxious or hypochondriatic, and he went to the toilet several times during observation.
The MEAD device was then used to record the data in the ED. The meridian electrical conductance was low (14.9 μA; normal range, 30–64 μA). The index of sympathovagal balance was high (3.75; normal range, 1.0–1.5). The ratio of electrical conductance of the left side to the right side bladder meridian was obviously abnormal (L/R: 2.09) (). A urologist was consulted at this time. Unenhanced helical computed tomography (CT) was performed and depicted a tiny calculus at the left ureterovesical junction (). The patient was admitted to the urological service and started on an aggressive hydration regimen in an attempt to “flush” the stone. One day later, with his pain worsening, he was taken to the operating room to perform ureteroscopy. A ureteral stone (about 4 mm) was removed, and the patient's pain was relieved (meridian electrical conductance: 14.6 μA; index of sympathovagal balance: 3.31; ratio of electrical conductance of left to right side bladder meridian: 3.26). The subsequent hospital course was uncomplicated. The patient was discharged the following day and instructed to follow up as an outpatient. At the same time, he was encouraged to drink sufficient amounts of fluid to prevent the recurrence of ureteral calculi. The follow-up measurements of the meridian parameters (meridian electrical conductance: 47.8 μA; index of sympathovagal balance: 2.0; ratio of electrical conductance of left to right side bladder meridian: 1.19) returned to normal 1 month after treatment.

Patient note:
A 71-year-old man with a remote cadaveric renal transplant maintained on tacrolimus and a daily tapering dose of prednisone for chronic rejection prophylaxis was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after suddenly collapsing at home with profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal distention, and rapidly progressive obtundation; his spouse reported that for the preceding forty-eight hours he had complained of diffuse cramping, low back discomfort, and dizziness but refused to call his transplant clinic because he was “just a little dehydrated.” The paramedic crew arrived to find him moaning, clutching his abdomen, with vomitus on his clothing and a faint radial pulse; they performed rapid sequence intubation for airway protection, placed a large-bore arterial catheter, and ventilated him through a transport ventilator set to deliver 85 % inspired oxygen without positive end-expiratory pressure. No crystalloids, vasopressors, antibiotics, or antipyretics were given in the field, and the transport time was under fifteen minutes. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—and before any hospital-based therapy—his temperature registered 35.5 °C rectally, heart rate was 135 beats per minute in sinus tachycardia, respiratory rate generated on the ventilator was 36 breaths per minute with shallow excursions, and cuff blood pressure read 82/45 mm Hg, confirmed by the arterial line tracing. The skin was cool, mottled over the knees, and capillary refill exceeded four seconds; jugular veins were flat at 30 degrees. Mechanical ventilation delivered a tidal volume of 450 mL and an end-tidal carbon dioxide of 28 mm Hg. Neurologically he opened his eyes only to painful trapezius squeeze, emitted incomprehensible sounds against the endotracheal tube, and attempted to localize but not follow commands, producing a Glasgow Coma Score of 8; there were no lateralizing motor deficits. Abdominal examination disclosed a rigid, distended abdomen with board-like guarding and absent bowel sounds, raising concern for perforated viscus. A stat portable plain film demonstrated free subdiaphragmatic air, and the surgical team proceeded with an emergent midline laparotomy that revealed a 2-cm jejunal perforation with feculent peritonitis; a damage-control resection and stapled ends were fashioned in under an hour with two liters of warmed crystalloid administered in the operating room, but no vasopressors or blood products were started because systolic pressure briefly climbed above 90 mm Hg toward the end of the procedure. At the conclusion of anesthesia the patient remained intubated, deeply sedated, and was transferred directly to the surgical intensive care unit, where the following laboratory results obtained within ten minutes of arrival were signed out to the receiving team: arterial blood gas on the same 85 % FiO₂ showed pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 35 mm Hg, PaO₂ 142 mm Hg, corresponding to an alveolar–arterial gradient of 225 mm Hg; serum sodium 125 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, glucose 168 mg/dL, and a creatinine of 3.0 mg/dL, markedly higher than his documented baseline of 1.3 mg/dL three weeks earlier, consistent with new oliguric injury that meets accepted criteria for acute kidney injury; prior outpatient evaluations had shown stable graft function without chronic renal insufficiency. Point-of-care ultrasound performed by the intensivist showed a slit-like inferior vena cava and no pericardial effusion. Urine output since catheter insertion in the operating room totaled only 5 mL despite aggressive bladder palpation. Hematology returned a white blood cell count of 30 000 cells/mm³ with 18 % bands, hematocrit 27 %, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, and platelets 210 000/µL; peripheral smear demonstrated toxic granulation but no schistocytes. Coagulation panel revealed an international normalized ratio of 1.4 and fibrinogen of 310 mg/dL. Electrocardiography at bedside continued to show sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. No antimicrobial agents, vasopressor infusions, corticosteroid stress doses, or renal replacement therapies had yet been started at the moment the above physiologic and biochemical data were documented; preparations for broad-spectrum antibiotics, norepinephrine, and possible continuous veno-venous hemofiltration were under way while the nursing staff completed central venous catheter insertion and repeat arterial sampling. The patient’s profound leukocytosis, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, elevated creatinine, metabolic acidemia, hypothermia, severe tachycardia, rapid ventilatory rate, low hematocrit, and persistent hypotension despite initial intraoperative fluid resuscitation were all noted to portend a high likelihood of septic shock superimposed on immunosuppressed status from chronic antirejection therapy, prompting the team to initiate sepsis protocols immediately after the initial ICU assessment was finalized.
