Patient note:
A 66-year-old female with ESRD secondary to hypertensive nephrosclerosis presented to our hospital complaining of bilateral lower extremity pain. Her past medical history included coronary artery disease, diastolic congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, and chronic atrial fibrillation on warfarin for 3 years. She had progressed to ESRD and had been started on thrice-weekly HD 5 months prior to presentation. Physical examination was notable for several tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules with necrosis on her thighs and calves bilaterally (Fig. ).
The monthly biochemical data and dialysis clearance profiles are shown in Table . Her outpatient dialysis clearance was inadequate and her bone mineral parameters were uncontrolled prior to presentation. Other pertinent laboratory findings on presentation included a C-reactive protein level of 25.90 mg/L (normal, <10 mg/L) and homocysteine >50 µmol/L (normal, 5–15 µmol/L). Notably, she was taking calcium acetate as a phosphate binder and receiving intravenous paricalcitol, a 1,25-vitamin D analog, with each outpatient dialysis treatment.
She underwent an extensive investigation during the index admission for presumed CUA. A magnetic resonance imaging scan, without use of intravenous gadolinium, demonstrated areas of abnormal signal intensity within the thigh muscles highly suggestive of soft-tissue calcification. Echocardiography showed severe mitral valve calcification with restriction of both leaflets, as well as severe sclerosis of the aortic valve; both had advanced compared with echocardiography performed 6 months prior to admission. A non-iodinated contrast computerized tomography scan of the chest revealed extensive atherosclerotic calcification of the coronary arteries, mitral valve, aorta, bronchial walls, and small arteries supplying the breasts, axillae, and chest wall.
A punch skin biopsy was performed − instead of a wedge biopsy, to avoid complications such as infection, bleeding, and pain − on the periphery of the subcutaneous lesion on her left thigh corresponding to the increased signal intensity on the MRI. This yielded a mural calcification of a single deep dermal blood vessel without microvascular thrombosis, necrosis, or extravascular calcium and phosphate deposits (Fig. ).
Serial bone scintigraphy demonstrated metastatic pulmonary CUA. Five months prior to admission, a bone scintigraphy was obtained to evaluate the cause of her rib pain (Fig. ); it showed no activity in the lungs or soft tissues. The bone scintigraphy at the time of CUA diagnosis, however, demonstrated extensive increased activity throughout the lungs and lower extremities (Fig. ).
The clinical diagnosis of CUA was made based on the physical characteristics of the lesions, risk factors, and bone scintigraphy, despite having no histological evidence of microvessel thrombosis or necrosis on the punch skin biopsy. We excluded other differential diagnoses of CUA, such as warfarin necrosis, cholesterol embolization, atherosclerosis, ischemic ulcers, and early stages of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
After CUA was diagnosed, lanthanum carbonate (Fosrenol®) 500 mg 2 tablets with meals, in lieu of calcium-containing oral phosphate binders, was initiated to control her bone mineral parameters. Warfarin was discontinued, due to its ability to inactivate vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of matrix Gla protein (MGP). There were no alternative anticoagulants offered, since the patient was deemed at high risk for bleeding after the skin biopsy. HD was optimized to improve her dialysis clearance.
Despite adequate dialysis clearance and optimal control of bone mineral parameters, a repeat bone scintigraphy performed 1 month after the diagnosis showed no changes in metastatic CUA (Fig. ). Because of the lack of clinical improvement, we initiated treatment with STS after each HD session, beginning at a dose of 5 g intravenously with titration to 10 g. The patient did not experience gastrointestinal side effects or develop metabolic acidosis from STS. Clinically, we observed slight improvement of the localized CUA on the patient's thighs, but the metastatic pulmonary CUA on the last bone scintigraphy obtained 2 months after the diagnosis remained unchanged (Fig. ).
Severe pain from CUA and depression marked her hospital course. Poor nutrition, as evident by her low serum albumin and phosphorus, failed to heal her CUA lesions. She requested cessation of all treatment 2 months after the diagnosis, and she expired shortly thereafter. There was no autopsy performed.

Patient note:
A 69-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by her partner late this afternoon after three days of progressive shortness of breath and a new productive cough that yielded thick yellow sputum beginning yesterday evening; she reports that earlier today even slow conversation left her winded and she felt “light-headed” when walking from the bedroom to the kitchen. Home medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, low-dose furosemide taken most mornings for ankle swelling, aspirin 81 mg, and atorvastatin 40 mg at night. She was diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction two years ago after an admission for pulmonary edema, and an outpatient echocardiogram six months ago noted an ejection fraction of 30 %. Ten years earlier she suffered a left frontal ischemic stroke that left only a subtle right-hand clumsiness without speech or cognitive deficits; she completes crossword puzzles daily and drives herself to the grocery store once a week. She denies any chronic kidney disorder, has never required dialysis, and recalls her most recent creatinine being “around one.” There is no history of chronic liver problems, cancer, or residence in an extended-care facility; she and her partner live independently in a single-story home, climb the eight porch steps without assistance, and handle all activities of daily living themselves. She quit cigarette smoking 18 years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks wine once or twice a month, and has never used illicit substances. Vaccination records show receipt of both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza injection. Prior to arrival she took her usual morning medicines and a single 500 mg acetaminophen tablet but no diuretic beyond her routine dose, no antibiotics, steroids, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen. In triage, before any therapeutic intervention, she was seated upright, conversing in full sentences, and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Vital signs recorded an oral temperature of 37.7 °C, regular pulse 95 beats per minute, blood pressure 99/58 mm Hg confirmed by manual reading, respiratory rate 39 breaths per minute with shallow accessory muscle use, and pulse oximetry 83 % on ambient air that improved only to 86 % when she was asked to purse-lip breathe. Mucous membranes were dry, jugular venous pulsation was difficult to appreciate with the head of bed at 30°, and mild bilateral ankle pitting edema to 2 mm was present—unchanged from her baseline, according to the patient. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid but regular S1 and S2 with a faint third heart sound similar to prior clinic notes, no new murmurs or rubs. Pulmonary examination produced coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower posterior chest with dullness to percussion in that area, while the remainder of the fields were vesicular without wheeze; there was no stony dullness, egophony, or asymmetry of diaphragmatic motion to suggest fluid accumulation. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended; the liver edge was not palpable below the costal margin. Neurologic screening demonstrated equal and reactive pupils, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 motor strength except for slightly slowed rapid fine movements of the right hand, and unremarkable sensation, coordination, and gait (tested briefly with assistance). Capillary finger-stick glucose measured 107 mg/dL. Venous and arterial samples were obtained within ten minutes of arrival prior to fluids, diuretics, vasodilators, or antimicrobials. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 126 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 98 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, glucose 107 mg/dL (matching the point-of-care value), blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Hemogram showed hematocrit 54 % with hemoglobin 18.0 g/dL and white blood cell count 14.0 × 10⁹/L predominated by neutrophils; platelets were 260 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas obtained while she remained on room air demonstrated pH 7.53, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, PaO₂ 57 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, and lactate 1.4 mmol/L, consistent with primary respiratory alkalosis accompanying significant hypoxemia. Upright posteroanterior and lateral chest radiographs obtained immediately thereafter revealed a dense consolidation filling the right lower lobe with air bronchograms; the heart was mildly enlarged but unchanged from prior films, the mediastinum midline, costophrenic angles sharp, and no layering fluid or meniscus sign was visualized. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 96 bpm with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria but no acute ischemic ST-T changes. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, urinary antigens for common bacterial pathogens, and a respiratory viral panel were sent to the laboratory. At the moment this note was completed, the patient had not received intravenous crystalloids, vasoactive agents, supplemental oxygen beyond brief pulse-oximetry measurement on room air, bronchodilators, diuretics, or antibiotics, ensuring that the physiologic and laboratory data detailed above reflect her untreated state at presentation.

Patient note:
A 56-year-old man who resides on the medical wing of a long-term care facility was transferred to the emergency department in the early afternoon after staff noticed that he had developed a harsh, productive cough overnight accompanied by shaking chills and a single recorded tympanic temperature of 39.4 °C despite scheduled acetaminophen being held for the past twenty-four hours. According to the hand-off note, he is normally able to propel his own wheelchair to meals and recreational activities, manages bathing with minimal assistance, and routinely converses clearly with staff and other residents; no baseline cognitive impairment is documented, and the nurse accompanying him reported that he was “his usual self” during the ambulance ride. His medical background is notable for biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis with bridging fibrosis diagnosed three years earlier; he sees hepatology every six months, has never experienced ascites or encephalopathy, and his most recent outpatient laboratory panel eight weeks ago showed preserved synthetic function except for mildly elevated transaminases. He has long-standing hypertension treated with amlodipine 10 mg daily and lisinopril 5 mg, but he has never been told he has weak heart muscle, valve disease, or fluid overload and he remains free of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity edema. He denies any prior kidney problems, has never required nephrology consultation, and his serum creatinine has been stable around 0.8–0.9 mg/dL on facility checks; he has also never undergone chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or tumor resection, and no family member has mentioned concern for malignancy. He quit smoking cigarettes two decades ago after a 12-pack-year exposure, drinks no alcohol because of his liver condition, and has never used illicit drugs. He received both pneumococcal vaccines last year and the current season’s influenza vaccine, and he has not taken antibiotics in the preceding twelve months. Medications taken with breakfast this morning included the two antihypertensives noted above, vitamin D, and lactulose 10 g as bowel regulator; he had not ingested any antipyretics, steroids, bronchodilators, or diuretics before presentation. On arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences, oriented to name, location, date, and current events, and he answered all questions appropriately without slurred speech or hesitation. Triage vital signs recorded prior to any intervention revealed an oral temperature of 39.4 °C, heart rate 86 beats/min with a regular rhythm, non-invasive blood pressure 121/74 mm Hg, respiratory rate 36 breaths/min with shallow excursions and faint intercostal retractions, and pulse oximetry 92 % breathing ambient air. His skin was warm and flushed, conjunctivae were anicteric, and capillary refill was brisk; jugular venous contour was not distended at 45°. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Pulmonary examination revealed markedly reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the left posterior lower third of the thorax with coarse crackles just above that level; no wheezes were heard on forced expiration. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with a firm but nontender liver edge palpable two centimeters below the right costal margin; there was no shifting dullness or peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease other than mild palmar erythema. Extremities were warm, without edema, and distal pulses were symmetric. Screening neurologic assessment showed equal pupils, intact extraocular movements, fluent speech, 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups, normal sensation to light touch, and steady finger-nose-finger testing. Point-of-care capillary glucose measured 117 mg/dL. Venous blood was drawn and an arterial sample obtained from the radial artery within ten minutes of stretcher placement, both prior to any intravenous fluids, antimicrobials, or supplemental oxygen. Initial laboratory results demonstrated sodium 150 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 26 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and hematocrit 32 %. White blood cell count was 13.1 × 10⁹/L with 85 % neutrophils, and platelet count was 220 × 10⁹/L. Liver panel showed AST 74 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, albumin 3.5 g/dL, and INR 1.2, consistent with his chronic hepatic condition. An arterial blood gas obtained on room air revealed pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, PaO₂ 81 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 25 mEq/L. Portable postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs taken before any therapy displayed a dense consolidation involving the left lower lobe with a meniscus-shaped opacity blunting the left costophrenic angle, suggestive of an accompanying pleural fluid collection; the heart appeared normal in size, mediastinum was midline, and the right lung fields were clear. Electrocardiography performed immediately afterward showed normal sinus rhythm at 84 beats/min, normal intervals, and no ischemic changes. Two sets of blood cultures, expectorated sputum for Gram stain and culture, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were collected before antibiotics were ordered. At the moment this note is written, he has received no intravenous fluids other than the small heparinized flush used for the arterial line, no antipyretics, no oxygen beyond ambient air, and no antimicrobial agents, thereby preserving the above measurements as his untreated baseline.

Patient note:
A 19-year-old man with relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia who completed his second cycle of blinatumomab two weeks ago and remains on daily oral prednisone 40 mg as graft-versus-host prophylaxis after a matched-sibling stem-cell transplant six months earlier was brought by ambulance from his university dormitory after his roommate found him curled on the bathroom floor complaining of shaking chills and a pounding headache; they reported that over the preceding 24 hours he had felt progressively febrile, vomited twice, and grown short of breath walking the ten yards to the communal sink. Paramedics arrived eight minutes after the 911 call and recorded an axillary temperature of 104.2 °F, a thready radial pulse in the 130s, and oxygen saturation in the low 80s on room air; they applied a high-flow nasal cannula set to 60 L min⁻¹ with a blender dialed to 70 % but administered no intravenous fluids, antibiotics, antipyretics, steroids, vasopressors, bronchodilators, or insulin en route. Within the emergency department resuscitation bay—before any hospital therapy was started and with the oxygen device unchanged—triage documented a core temperature measured rectally at 40.1 °C, non-invasive blood pressure cycling reproducibly at 108⁄61 mm Hg, a sinus tachycardia of 136 beats min⁻¹ on three-lead telemetry, and a visibly labored respiratory rate counted over a full minute at 39 breaths min⁻¹ with pronounced intercostal retractions. The patient opened his eyes only to loud verbal stimulus, uttered clipped phrases that were occasionally confused for time, and withdrew purposefully from painful nail-bed pressure, establishing a Glasgow Coma Score of 12 in the absence of sedatives, alcohol, or head trauma. Skin examination revealed flushed cheeks, generalized diaphoresis, and scattered petechiae over both shins; capillary refill was roughly three seconds, distal pulses were rapid but palpable, and there was no peripheral edema. Neck veins were flat at 30°, carotid upstrokes were brisk, and heart auscultation uncovered a rapid regular rhythm with no murmurs or rubs. Lung fields transmitted coarse crackles most prominently over the right middle zone, and percussion was mildly dull at the posterior bases; breath sounds were diminished but present throughout. The abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness and active bowel sounds, and the transplanted right iliac crest scar from marrow harvest was well healed without erythema. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness, and bladder palpation was unremarkable. A right radial arterial puncture performed six minutes after stretcher placement while the fraction of inspired oxygen remained 73 % yielded a pH of 7.32; the blood-gas analyzer displayed an alveolar-to-arterial oxygen gradient of 167 mm Hg and a PaCO₂ of 34 mm Hg. End-tidal capnography read 32 mm Hg, validating effective ventilation despite tachypnea. Concurrent point-of-care chemistry returned sodium 118 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 5.9 mmol L⁻¹, chloride 92 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 20 mmol L⁻¹, glucose 132 mg dL⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg dL⁻¹, and serum creatinine 1.2 mg dL⁻¹—the latter matching his oncology clinic baseline from the previous week and arguing against renal injury; he likewise carries no prior diagnosis of chronic kidney disease or need for renal replacement therapy. A complete blood count drawn from the same syringe demonstrated white blood cells 24 200 mm³ with 85 % neutrophils and 3 % bands, hematocrit 43 %, hemoglobin 14.2 g dL⁻¹, and platelets 68 000 µL⁻¹. Venous lactate measured 3.6 mmol L⁻¹ at the bedside. Plain-film chest radiography obtained before any antimicrobial or steroid dosing revealed patchy right-perihilar consolidation with blurring of the right heart border and no overt effusion; the mediastinal silhouette was normal, and there were no lines or tubes present. Focused cardiac ultrasound showed a small but vigorously contracting left ventricle and an inferior vena cava measuring 1.3 cm that collapsed more than 50 % with inspiration, suggesting relative intravascular depletion rather than overload. Twelve-lead electrocardiography printed during the arterial draw depicted sinus tachycardia at 136 beats min⁻¹, PR interval 150 ms, QRS 86 ms, QTc 430 ms, and no acute ischemic changes. A urine sample obtained by straight catheterization produced 40 mL of concentrated amber fluid with a specific gravity of 1.027; dipstick was negative for ketones, leukocyte esterase, or nitrites. Importantly, from dormitory discovery through the conclusion of the initial intensive-care handoff—a span of roughly thirty minutes—the patient received no crystalloid infusion, no empiric antibiotics, no antipyretics, no vasopressors, no insulin, and no bronchodilators; the only ongoing intervention remained the high-flow nasal cannula delivering 73 % oxygen. Because there had been no operative procedure preceding this episode, the forthcoming intensive-care admission was categorized as a nonoperative medical transfer of an immunosuppressed host with presumed community-acquired pneumonia complicated by marked hyperpyrexia, profound hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, leukocytosis, and early hypoxemic respiratory compromise reflected by the contemporaneously captured values—temperature 40.1 °C, systolic pressure 108 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 61 mm Hg, pulse 136 beats min⁻¹, respirations 39 min⁻¹, arterial pH 7.32, serum sodium 118 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 5.9 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 1.2 mg dL⁻¹, hematocrit 43 %, white blood cell count 24 200 mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 73 %, and alveolar-to-arterial gradient 167 mm Hg.

Patient note:
A 69-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the emergency department of our hospital after returning from a one-month vacation to Myanmar that included horseback riding. The patient had not taken malaria prophylaxis and did not receive any vaccinations prior to his departure. The patient's medical history was remarkable for gout, ciguatera, and neurosurgical reconstruction of the skull after a basilar skull fracture. The latter occurred 5 years before this event (after a fall from a horse), and it was complicated by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage and right-sided glossopharyngeal and vagal nerve damage, which resulted in right-sided vocal cord paralysis with hoarseness and sporadic aspiration. The patient did not take any medications and did not smoke, but he drank wine regularly.
For the last few days, the patient had been increasingly tired and somnolent, with complaints of headache, left-sided ear pain, and night sweats. One day prior to admission, the patient had become increasingly confused. On the day of his admission, he was found by his wife lying on the floor of his home, confused, agitated, shivering, and incontinent of urine. At the emergency department, the patient's temperature was 39.2 °C, and his heart rate was 111 beats per minute, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute and a blood pressure of 161/88 mmHg. The patient's peripheral oxygen saturation was 87%, and his Glasgow Coma Scale was scored as 9 (E2 M5 V2). Clinical examination revealed fasciculations of the face and lower legs and crepitation over the right lower lung on pulmonary auscultation. There was no purpura or nuchal rigidity.
At that time, blood results revealed a leukocyte count of 34 900 × 109/l (normal: 4 300–10 000) (>95% being neutrophils) and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 204 mg/l (normal value <3). A chest X-ray revealed no abnormalities. A CT scan of the brain showed only nonspecific white matter lesions but no haemorrhage or oedema. Lumbar puncture examination revealed a leukocyte count of 1160/mm3 (almost all neutrophils), a normal glucose level, and a total protein level of 128 mg/dl (normal value 15–40) accompanied by an elevated lactate level of 6.1 meq/l. Gram stain showed irregularly shaped cocci. Bacterial meningitis was suspected, and after obtaining two sets of blood cultures, empirical therapy with 2 g of intravenous ceftriaxone every 12 h, 2 g of ampicillin every 4 h and 10 mg/kg of acyclovir every 8 h was initiated. Shortly after starting the antibiotic therapy, the patient became more somnolent and developed a left-sided hemiplegia, left-sided central facial palsy, and right-sided head and eye deviation, and the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Because of increasingly obstructive respirations and an increasing oxygen need by the next day, the patient was intubated and ventilated.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures showed β-hemolytic colonies; blood and CSF cultures were positive for Streptococcus equi. Intravenous treatment with 2 g of ceftriaxone every 12 h was continued for 21 days, while ampicillin and acyclovir were discontinued. In vitro testing confirmed a sensitivity to ceftriaxone. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images (FLAIR) showed a “dirty CSF” appearance in the right parietal region (, white arrow). Axial () and sagittal () T1-weighted images after the intravenous administration of gadolinium-chelate revealed a focal area of superficial contrast enhancement overlying the cerebral cortex, presumably representing a thickened pia mater and opacification of the left mastoid. In view of the MRI lesions and the left hemiplegia, one gram of intravenous methylprednisolone once daily was added to the treatment for 3 days with gradual tapering afterwards because meningoencephalitis with accompanying cerebral vasculitis was suspected []. After 4 days, the patient was weaned from the ventilator and extubated. Initially, the patient remained very agitated and disoriented and was temporarily treated with 25 mg of twice daily quetiapine and 100 mg of daily trazodone. Nine days after admission to the ICU, the patient was transferred to the neurology department. Later, this Streptococcus equi was identified as S. equi subspecies equi (at the National Reference Center for Invasive Non-Group B Beta-Hemolytic Streptococci, Belgium).
The patient initially recovered completely and had no complaints apart from mild gait disturbances and light-headedness at a follow-up appointment 3 months after discharge. Because of the patient's prior medical history of basilar skull fracture and opacification of the left mastoid on brain MRI, despite a lack of clinical evidence of acute otitis or mastoiditis, an additional CT scan of the base of the skull was performed to rule out possible portals of entry for central nervous system (CNS) infection. The CT scan revealed only an asymmetrical widening of the left squamosal suture; therefore, we opted for a conservative approach.
One month later (5 months after the initial referral), the patient was readmitted with intracranial bleeding, and consecutive CT scans showed multiple right-sided cerebral haemorrhages, with the largest located precentrally in the frontal lobe with small perilesional parietal and temporal haemorrhages accompanied by a left hemiparesis and aphasia (). CT angiography examination (, para-axial MPR) showed multiple tortuous, engorged pial veins of the right hemisphere. Cerebral angiography confirmed the presence of a suspected superficial dural arteriovenous fistula (, lateral projection of right internal carotid artery injection, large black arrow) in the right parietal region. The arterial feeders were mainly meningeal branches originating from the right ophthalmic artery and transosseous feeders from the right superficial temporal and occipital arteries (, lateral projection right external carotid artery injection); in addition, there was limited arterial supply to the fistula from the left middle meningeal artery across the midline (not shown). Venous drainage was through a large, right temporal draining vein (large white arrow) with reflux into multiple tortuous, superficial frontotemporal veins, as shown in , indicating a fistula with high risk of haemorrhage.
Comparison of the axial T2-weighted images of MRI examinations at initial admittance () and at the second admission () showed the new finding of dilated pial veins (encircled), demonstrating de novo development of the dural AV fistula.
The dural AV fistula was excised by the neurosurgeon. Microscopy of the resected dura showed a previously damaged vein with inflammatory remnants and granulation tissue in its wall (Figures and ). The patient was discharged to home with a hemiparesis that was still present. Seven months later, after this second event, the patient's GCS was 15/15, and the hemiparesis had almost completely disappeared.

Patient note:
We present the case of a 62-year-old gentleman, who was brought into the emergency department (ED) by ambulance with a history of dry cough, low grade fever, worsening shortness of breath for 4 days, and pleuritic sounding chest pain, which was different to when he had a pulmonary embolism approximately ten months ago. His past medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, treated malignant neoplasm of the base of tongue, diverticular disease, essential hypertension, and previous provoked pulmonary embolism. Before admission, he was living independently with his wife. His exercise tolerance was restricted to 10 yards with the assistance of a walking stick. He was an exsmoker and used to smoke 5 cigarettes a day but stopped smoking a few years previously.
On admission, he was pyrexial with a temperature of 38.2°C, oxygen saturations 98% on 28% FiO2, blood pressure 73/35 mmHg, and pulse rate 92 bpm. Initial treatment included oxygen 28% FiO2 via a venturi mask and fluid resuscitation for hypotension. Physical examination revealed bibasal crepitations on auscultation of chest and a swollen and tender right leg. Initial investigations revealed deranged biochemical markers () and opacification affecting the right midzone of the lung ().
Initial laboratory workup summarised in .
In view of the clinical presentation and raised d-dimer, a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) was performed which reported right upper lobe consolidation with subtle peripheral ground glass opacification in the left upper lobe and both lower lobes, suggestive of early COVID-19 infection (). Moreover, his troponin I levels were markedly elevated and electrocardiogram (ECG) showed ST segment depression and T-wave inversion in the anterolateral chest leads. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed moderately impaired left ventricular systolic function with an akinetic and rounded apical septal wall.
On account of the history, examination, and investigations, he was treated as suspected COVID-19, community-acquired pneumonia (CURB-65 score = 2, moderate severity), COVID-19 myocarditis, and sepsis, leading to multiorgan failure. In view of poor physiological reserve and comorbidities, the ceiling of care was decided to be ward level care and noninvasive ventilation if needed. However, he began to improve clinically, became normotensive, and was able to be weaned off oxygen day 3 after admission. By that time, his swab detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA which confirmed the diagnosis of COVID-19.
Following initial improvement, he suddenly developed a new, increased oxygen demand, requiring titration of humidified oxygen up to 10 litres. Chest physiotherapy helped him bring up copious volumes of thick sputum, and he was stable for most of the day with oxygen saturations of 93%. Later that day, he suddenly deteriorated and becoming cyanotic and critically unwell. Oxygen saturations were 80% on 15 litres nonrebreathe mask, and he was significantly tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 40/minute. An urgent portable chest X-ray revealed a large right-sided pneumothorax causing mediastinal shift ().
An intercostal drain was inserted on an emergency basis and the patient improved slightly over the next 24 hours though he still required oxygen via a high flow nasal cannula system to maintain oxygen saturations of 92% or more. Despite the chest drain and the addition of thoracic suction, the lung did not reexpand. He continued to deteriorate rapidly, was unable to tolerate further pleural procedures, and died.

Patient note:
A 25-year-old male graduate student in architectural design presented to the academic arrhythmia clinic for his first comprehensive discussion of long-term anticoagulation after ambulatory telemetry worn during a recent evaluation for sustained palpitations captured several prolonged episodes of non-valvular atrial fibrillation with ventricular rates up to 180 beats per minute; rate control was initiated with low-dose diltiazem, and the electrophysiology team advised oral anticoagulation based on his risk profile, which the patient wishes to understand in granular detail before committing to therapy. He has had elevated blood pressures since late adolescence when sports physicals repeatedly documented readings in the 140s/90s, and three months ago an automated pharmacy kiosk logged values as high as 162/94 mm Hg; despite a trial of lifestyle modification, the visiting family physician recently placed him on lisinopril 20 mg daily, but self-recorded measurements entered into a phone application still average 148/92 mm Hg over the past four weeks. The social history reveals striking ethanol consumption: every weekday he begins with two 16-ounce cans of hard cider during a late breakfast while drafting digital models, follows lunch with three 12-ounce bottles of India pale ale, sips four 1.5-ounce shots of tequila during afternoon studio critiques, and unwinds after evening lectures with two 8-ounce whiskey-cola mixes; Fridays add a brewery “flight” of six 5-ounce pours, Saturdays feature a gaming marathon accompanied by eight 12-ounce lagers, and Sunday brunch brings six 5-ounce mimosas plus three night-cap bourbon neat pours. Meticulously added together with the patient during brief motivational interviewing, the tally comes to 69 standard alcoholic drinks each week, with no alcohol-free day in the prior six months. He denies morning tremor, seizures, pancreatitis, or prior detoxification attempts but admits occasional blackouts after multiple shots. Past medical records also list chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to biopsy-proven focal segmental glomerulosclerosis diagnosed at age 17 after persistent microscopic hematuria on sports urinalyses; he has never required dialysis, but the most recent laboratory panel drawn yesterday shows serum creatinine 2.6 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 28 mL/min/1.73 m²), blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, calcium 9.1 mg/dL, phosphorus 4.5 mg/dL, and hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL. Liver chemistries remain within reference ranges—alanine aminotransferase 25 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 71 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and albumin 4.3 g/dL—and he has never experienced jaundice, pruritus, ascites, or hepatic encephalopathy. There is no personal history of cerebrovascular accident, systemic embolism, gastrointestinal ulceration, hematuria beyond baseline microscopic findings, melena, hematochezia, hemoptysis, epistaxis lasting more than five minutes, joint bleeding, blood product transfusion, thrombocytopenia, hereditary coagulopathy, or malignancy. The medication list is intentionally short: lisinopril as noted and 1,000 mg acetaminophen taken sporadically for tension headaches; he expressly avoids aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thienopyridines, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, glucocorticoids, fish-oil supplements, ginkgo, garlic, or other herbal preparations because “they might thin my blood more.” Family history is negative for premature coronary disease, aneurysm, or hemorrhagic stroke. He has never smoked tobacco or used illicit drugs. Review of systems is negative for chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, claudication, visual disturbance, speech difficulty, focal weakness, easy bruising larger than a dime, dark urine, foamy urine, abdominal distention, or peripheral edema. In the examination bay the patient appears lean, body mass index 23 kg/m², dressed in casual studio clothing, and conversant. Vital signs after five minutes seated reveal blood pressure readings of 150/94, 152/92, and 148/96 mm Hg by calibrated sphygmomanometer, irregularly irregular radial pulse averaging 94 beats per minute, respirations 14 per minute, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. Sclerae are anicteric, conjunctivae pink, oral mucosa moist without petechiae, and dentition intact. Neck is supple with no jugular venous distention and brisk carotid upstrokes without bruit. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a variable S₁ with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation. The abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender; the liver edge is not palpable, there is no splenic tip, and no shifting dullness or abdominal wall collateral veins are seen. Extremities are warm with 2+ distal pulses and no edema; a few faint yellow-green ecchymoses less than 0.5 cm on the shins are attributed to inadvertent contact with drafting stools. Neurologic screening shows the patient to be alert and oriented with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal rapid alternating movements, and a steady tandem gait. A point-of-care capillary INR obtained before any anticoagulant initiation is 1.0, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, and urinalysis again shows 1+ blood but no proteinuria. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram printed during the visit confirms atrial fibrillation with variable ventricular response 92–110 beats per minute, normal axis, QRS duration 86 ms, and no acute ST-T wave abnormalities; transthoracic echocardiography performed last week revealed left atrial enlargement (anteroposterior diameter 4.2 cm), normal left ventricular size with ejection fraction 60 %, and no valvular stenosis or regurgitation. The patient seeks detailed counseling on how his persistent hypertension, advanced chronic kidney impairment, and consumption of 69 alcoholic beverages per week might intersect with upcoming anticoagulation and requests guidance on lifestyle modification, alcohol reduction strategies, optimization of blood-pressure control, and whether his renal function influences the selection or dosing of a specific oral agent.

Patient note:
A 67-year-old man presented with a mass on the intergluteal cleft and lymphadenopathy in both inguinal regions. There was no history of pain, fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting, constipation, bloody diarrhea, or abdominal distension. Past medical history included Systemic arterial hypertension in treatment. He first noticed it 1 year before and it had progressively increased in size to 2.5 × 2.5 cm. The mass was soft, non-tender, and freely mobile in the subcutaneous tissue with normal-appearing overlying skin. Examination revealed bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy (right of 1 cm and a ganglionic conglomerates of 4.5 × 7 cm in left inguinal region). Mohs surgery was performed, and a tumor and ganglion biopsy was taken, histopathological examination revealed high-grade malignancy of primary cutaneous appendages of skin with basaloid differentiation of squamous cells, glandular and alveolar tubule, in some areas myxoid degeneration, microcalcifications, lymphatic and vascular permeation; the tumor was less than 1 mm from the edges of the section and from the surgical bed and ganglion right inguinal lymphatic with metastasis of malignant neoplasm mixed with high skin grade (Fig. and ).
An abdominal computed tomography (CT) with intravenous contrast was performed in which a solid tumor lesion in intergluteal cleft of 2.3 cm, as well as a giant adenopathy in left inguinal region (4.5 cm conglomerate) was reported. Contrast chest CT reported bilateral pulmonary nodules (right 6.4 mm and left basal 1.1 cm) and bilateral axillary and cervical adenopathies. The diagnosis was EPC with areas of epidermoid, basal cell and sebaceous differentiation. No perineural lymphatic invasion, lymph node with carcinoma metastasis (Fig. and ). He started chemotherapy based on etoposide, vincristine, carboplatin.

Patient note:
A 28-year-old man with no significant past medical or surgical history arrived at the acute care clinic just before closing time because his left lower leg had become “tight and sore” since waking that morning, roughly eighteen hours after an evening indoor-soccer match in which he recalled no direct blow, sprain, or collision worthy of note. He works as a graphic designer, commutes by bicycle, and had ridden the 4 km route to his studio without difficulty the previous day; he reports climbing two flights of stairs to his workstation several times daily and completes a 5 km jog three times each week, thus having spent no recent interval confined to bed, a couch, or a wheelchair, nor has he worn a cast, immobilizer, or rigid boot at any time. He denies earlier episodes of clots in the legs or lungs and has never required anticoagulation. Medications consist only of a daily over-the-counter omega-3 supplement and as-needed ibuprofen for post-exercise aches; he takes no hormonal agents, corticosteroids, erythropoietin, or chemotherapy. Family history is free of venous thromboembolism, hemophilia, or malignancy, and he quit social smoking during college after a cumulative two-pack-year exposure; alcohol is limited to an occasional weekend beer, and he denies recreational drug use. The patient specifically notes that, aside from some delayed-onset muscle fatigue typical after soccer, nothing else felt abnormal until he noticed fullness in the posteromedial calf while stepping out of the shower this morning. Over the course of the day the discomfort sharpened whenever he pointed the toes or pressed along the back of the knee but remained absent at the ankle, thigh, and hip. There has been no fever, chills, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, rash, insect bite, break in the skin, groin mass, chest pain, dyspnea, cough, palpitations, syncope, abdominal pain, flank pain, or urinary complaint. On presentation—before any analgesic or heparin was offered—vital signs were temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. He ambulated into the examination bay with a minimally antalgic gait favoring the left side. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and without organomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities showed that the proximal thigh, knee joint, and ankle contours were symmetric bilaterally, but the left calf appeared visibly fuller and the overlying skin glistened slightly in fluorescent light while retaining normal color and temperature. A tape measure placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 40.2 cm on the symptomatic side versus 36.4 cm contralaterally, a discrepancy of 3.8 cm; at mid-thigh the girths were 51.6 cm bilaterally, and around the malleoli the difference was less than 0.3 cm. When the limb was placed in a dependent position for thirty seconds, a latticework of straight, bluish, non-tortuous superficial veins emerged along the course of the small saphenous vein and posteromedial calf, emptying promptly upon elevation. Firm but gentle palpation following the anticipated line of the popliteal and posterior tibial vessels elicited a distinct, focal tenderness midway between the popliteal crease and the medial Achilles origin; pressing on surrounding gastrocnemius muscle bellies or the anterior compartment produced only diffuse dull pressure without focal jump response, and no palpable cord or fluctuant collection was appreciated. Thumb indentation over the pretibial area rebounded immediately without leaving a residual pit, confirming the absence of persistent indentation. Passive ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended provoked only a mild stretch sensation, and straight-leg raise reproduced no radicular symptoms. Hip, knee, and ankle joints moved through full range of motion and were painless; distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were 2 + and equal, with capillary refill at the toes under two seconds, intact light-touch sensation, and motor strength graded 5/5 throughout. There was no inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy, no erythema or streaking to suggest cellulitis, and no palpable cyst in the popliteal fossa. Point-of-care laboratory studies, drawn prior to any pharmacologic therapy, revealed hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, platelet count 248 × 10⁹/L, leukocyte count 7.0 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.93 mg/dL, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 27 seconds; hepatic enzymes were within reference limits. A resting twelve-lead electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm at 88 beats per minute without ST-T changes. Plain radiographs of the tibia and fibula obtained by triage to rule out occult fracture or exostosis were unremarkable. With the measured unilateral calf enlargement exceeding three centimeters, the conspicuous network of non-varicose superficial veins draining the region, the sharply localized deep posterior tenderness, and the lack of pitting, cast immobilization, prolonged recumbency, recent surgery, prior thrombotic history, or another more plausible musculoskeletal or infectious explanation on examination, duplex ultrasonography of the entire left lower-extremity venous system has been requested on an urgent basis while the patient remains hemodynamically stable seated in the observation pod awaiting imaging.

Patient note:
In late June, a 51-year-old male presented to the ED with a chief complaint of shortness of breath. The patient reported sporadic fevers and chills at home over the past two weeks, but denied current fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, or any urinary symptoms. The patient reported no past medical history and was not on any medications. His son, however, was diagnosed with COVID-19 two weeks prior, with a cough, fever, and typical viral syndrome type symptoms. The patient reported that he did not quarantine from his son even after the positive COVID-19 diagnosis, as they lived in the same house.
The patient’s vital signs were temperature 99.1°F, blood pressure 111/76 mmHg, pulse rate 87 beats per minute, respiration rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Physical examination revealed significantly decreased breath sounds bilaterally. The remainder of physical examination was unremarkable, including cardiovascular and neurological examination. Laboratory analysis showed signs of leukopenia (white blood cell count of 3,000 per cubic mm) but was negative for neutrophilia or lymphocytopenia. All electrolytes were within normal limits. The D-dimer count was elevated at 2.05 mg/L. Radiological examination included a chest x-ray that demonstrated scattered opacities throughout both lungs suggestive of multifocal atypical pneumonia (Figure ).
Chest CT showed multifocal ground glass opacities (GGO) throughout both lungs typical of underlying SARS-CoV-2 infection. There was no evidence for pulmonary embolism (Figure ).
He appeared well throughout the remainder of his stay in the ED with stable vitals. The patient was ambulated in the ED with no decrease in oxygen saturation noted. Although the patient had imaging findings typical of COVID-19 pneumonia and a corroborating history of present illness, the patient was nonetheless treated with 500 mg intravenous azithromycin and 1 g of ceftriaxone as empiric treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. Given that the patient had no other comorbidities, and wanted to go home, he was discharged home with a course of oral antibiotics. During a telephone follow-up three days after being discharged, the patient reported that he continued to feel better while at home.

Patient note:
A 58-year-old woman arrived this morning to the pre-operative intake area in anticipation of an open total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and selective pelvic lymph node dissection for a recently staged, grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma that was discovered on dilation and curettage three weeks ago after several months of abnormal uterine bleeding. She parked in the garage, walked the length of the hallway without assistance, and climbed one flight of stairs to the registration desk, describing her usual baseline as fully independent with twice-weekly water aerobics and daily dog-walking; she denies limitations with household chores, yardwork, or climbing two flights of stairs. Her surgical history includes only an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed eight years earlier, and she has not been admitted to a hospital or undergone any operative or invasive procedure within the last several months. She specifically reports no recent casting, fractures, blunt trauma, strokes, or spinal injuries, and she has not required prolonged bed rest or mechanical ventilation. Medical history is notable for a pulmonary embolus diagnosed seven years ago after she experienced sudden pleuritic chest discomfort and shortness of breath on the final day of a vacation flight from Asia; computed-tomography angiography at that time demonstrated segmental clot in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery without right-heart strain. She completed a six-month course of warfarin, had no recurrence, and has not used chronic anticoagulation since. During that episode, a hematology consultation obtained a thrombophilia panel that revealed moderately elevated IgG anticardiolipin antibody on two occasions twelve weeks apart; the remainder of the panel was unrevealing. Since then, repeat antibody titers have remained above reference range but she has experienced no additional venous or arterial events, no unexplained pregnancy losses, and no livedo, ulcers, or neurologic symptoms. She has no chronic lung disease, obstructive airway symptoms, or baseline oxygen requirement and discontinued a 10-pack-year smoking habit more than 20 years ago. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exertional chest pain, ankle swelling, or prior cardiology evaluations for ventricular dysfunction. Review of systems is negative for fevers, shaking chills, productive cough, dysuria, abdominal pain beyond her gynecologic complaints, or weight loss apart from a deliberate 5-pound reduction since diagnosis through dietary changes. She takes letrozole 2.5 mg daily as part of neoadjuvant hormonal therapy initiated by gynecologic oncology two weeks ago, as well as vitamin D and calcium; she uses no glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or hormonal contraception, and has never received heparin products that resulted in platelet drops. There is no tunnelled catheter, port, or peripherally inserted central line in place. Family members are generally healthy, and she is unaware of clotting problems in close relatives. On examination she is seated upright, conversant, and appears her stated age. Vital signs: blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14, temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Body mass index is 26 kg/m². Conjunctivae are pink; oropharynx clear; neck supple without jugular venous distension. Heart sounds are crisp, S1 and S2 normal without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation with good air movement bilaterally. Abdomen is soft and nondistended; a palpable, mobile, nontender uterine fundus extends just above the pubic symphysis; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites is appreciated. Extremities are warm with palpable radial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+ bilaterally. Calves are symmetric without pitting, tenderness, erythema, cord-like structures, or superficial varicosities. No edema is present at the ankles, and there is full active range of motion of hips, knees, and ankles without discomfort. Neurologic exam shows intact sensation and 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups, normal gait, and negative Romberg; cranial nerves II–XII are grossly intact. Skin inspection reveals surgical scars in the right upper quadrant from prior cholecystectomy but no bruises or ulcerations elsewhere. Pre-operative laboratories obtained yesterday show hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 243 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 6.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL, AST 21 U/L, ALT 19 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, PT 12.3 seconds, INR 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 31 seconds. Electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm without ST-segment changes, and a recent chest radiograph is unremarkable. An anesthesia airway assessment graded a Mallampati II with good mouth opening and thyromental distance; no predictors of difficult intubation were identified. She has remained fasting since midnight, has taken her morning antihypertensive but held the aromatase inhibitor as instructed, and currently has a single 20-gauge peripheral intravenous catheter in the dorsum of the left hand for fluids and peri-operative medications. The surgical team anticipates an operative duration of approximately three hours under general endotracheal anesthesia with lower-abdominal midline incision, estimated blood loss under 300 mL, and post-procedure admission to the surgical floor for recovery and early ambulation.

Patient note:
A 78-year-old female with a past medical history significant for breast cancer and moderate COPD presented to Emergency Department with syncope. Nine months prior to admission, she underwent left total mastectomy for invasive ductal carcinoma and was started on Tamoxifen 20 mg daily. Home medications included GB 50 mcg once daily, Salbutamol, calcium and a multi-vitamin. GB was started 3 months prior to her presentation for syncope.
The day prior to admission, she received an IV vitamin infusion consisting of a mixture of thiamine, folic acid, multivitamin and magnesium sulfate at a naturopath clinic. Shortly after completion of the IV infusion, she developed emesis and took 2 tablets of dimenhydrinate. The following day, she reported dizziness as she walked across the kitchen and passed out after sitting in a chair. The patient reported no palpitations, chest discomfort, nausea, warm sensation or diaphoresis prior to the syncope event. She was not witnessed to have any seizure like activity and when she regained consciousness, reported immediate awareness of surroundings with no neurological deficits, no tongue biting, bowel or urinary incontinence. There was no previous history of syncope and no family history of sudden cardiac death. Her initial blood pressure in the ambulance was 70/50 mm Hg. Hemodynamics normalized after administration of intravenous fluid and her symptoms resolved. Oxygen saturation was above 97 % and telemetry revealed normal sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 77. Precordial examination was unremarkable with regular normal heart sounds and no murmurs. In the Emergency Department, blood tests including complete blood count (CBC), serum electrolytes (potassium, calcium, magnesium), glucose, creatinine and thyroid stimulating hormone were normal. Electrocardiogram (ECG) showed a corrected QT interval using Fridericia (QTcF) and Bazett’s formula (QTcB) of 603 and 631 ms respectively (Fig. ) and she was admitted to the cardiology service for further investigation of the etiology for her QT prolongation.
Prior to starting Tamoxifen her QTcF and QTcB were 439 and 440 ms respectively (Fig. ), however no ECG was obtained after initiation of Tamoxifen and prior to starting GB. Her last dose of Tamoxifen and GB were the day of admission with both medications discontinued at presentation.
An echocardiogram revealed that her left ventricular ejection fraction was >60 % with no valvular or regional wall motion abnormalities. Serial electrocardiograms demonstrated corrected QTcF and QTcB respectively of 603 and 631 ms day 0, 496 and 514 ms day 1, and 446 and 455 ms on day 2 and 442 and 460 ms on day 3 (Fig. ). There were no arrhythmias seen on telemetry. Syncope was felt to be secondary to orthostatic changes and she was discharged on day 3 after admission.

Patient note:
We report a case of 12 years old boy, black, student who was admitted to our department for a 1 year progressive slowly growing of not painful abdominal mass occupying the right flank and right-lower quadrant. The patient had history of chronic constipation of 2 years referring 1 bowel movements every third-fourth day with hard stools. He denies symptoms of vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, fever, hematocquezia, hematuria, anorexia, lost weight. Not learning or mental disabilities were reported from his parents.
The patient was hospitalized previously four times during his life by history of constipation treated with laxatives and enemas and discharged with food recommendations. Only family history of diabetes in his grandmother.
On initial evaluation, the patient had a temperature of 37°C, blood pressure of 100/70 mm Hg, a heart rate of 85 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, with weight 30 kg and height 133 cms (BMI = 16.5, 18th centile).
Physical examination revealed a good general condition, cardiac and lungs examination were unremarkable. Abdomen without scars, soft, not distended, tympanic in 4 quadrants, normoactive bowel sound, palpation revealing an abdominal mass smooth, mobile, nontender in the lower right flank and quadrant of ± 13 cm of diameter. Rectal examination revealed no palpable stool in the rectal vault and was hemoccult negative. No malformations were finding during the examination.
The laboratory test parameter during admission were: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dl, hematocrit of 39.5%, WBC 5.500, platelets 374.000 mm3; creatinine 0.8/BUN 70, Na:142, K:4.3, urinalysis and liver function tests were normal. Stool samples for parasites were negative.
Intravenous pyelogram revealed a large rounded mass of approximately 12 cm. in diameter at the colon which seemed to have an irregular mottled texture. The right ureter seemed to be somewhat displaced by the mass that produce a slightly enlargement of the renal pelvis (Fig. ). Roentgenologic examination of the colon after barium enema showed an intraluminal mass having a smooth contour and without any mucosal attachment (Fig. ).
Ultrasound of the abdomen showed a mass arising probably from the intestine with no evidence of hydronephrosis.
The flexible rectosigmoidoscopy was done and only passed through 25 cm of rectum which presented a normal rectum with a roomy sigmoid colon and a large, firm fecal ball. Sigmoidoscopic rectal biopsies were not performed and fragmentation was attempted but abandoned because of pain during the procedure. Repeated enemas and laxatives were unsuccessful in evacuating the fecal mass.
The patient underwent elective laparotomy. Preoperative bowel cleaning was performed with phosphosoda solution and lavage with warm saline until evacuations were liquid without fecal residue. A 20-cm midline incision (infraumbilical with supraumbilical extension) was made. During the procedure we founded an enlarged sigmoid colon lateralized to the right showing a large, rock-hard mass, smooth and ovoid in shape, measuring about 14 cm, which appeared to be a hardened mass of feces. The rest of the colon appeared normal and empty.
The sigmoid colon with the mass was resected (Fig. ) and an end-to-end anastomosis was done. The patient recovered for the surgical procedure and had an uneventful convalescence. After six months our patient refers 1 bowel movement per day performing soft stools with no recurrence of his symptoms leading a completely normal healthy life.
Examination of the gross specimen after incision of the intestinal wall showed a firm fecal mass covered with a white material (barium) which filled the lumen but was unattached to the wall of the colon (Fig. ). No lesions were observed at the sigmoid wall. Microscopic examination of the colon demonstrates normal intestinal mucosa without ulcers. Myenteric plexus shows nerve fibers with lack of ganglion cells (Fig. ).

Patient note:
A 47-year-old woman with a documented history of poorly controlled hypertension, migraine with aura, and recent initiation of topiramate for weight-neutral mood stabilization was transported by air ambulance from a rural hiking trail at 14:22 after fellow trekkers heard her collapse against a granite outcrop and strike the left parietal scalp; no witness observed seizure activity, vomiting, or limb jerking, and according to companions she had complained only of a “splitting visual snow” before losing posture. Forest-service medics arrived within nine minutes, applied a rigid cervical collar, placed a 16-gauge intravenous catheter in the right antecubital vein but infused only a 5-mL saline lock, secured her to a scoop stretcher, and administered no analgesics, benzodiazepines, paralytics, anticholinergics, opioids, dextrose, vasopressors, or antihypertensives. Finger-stick glucose on scene measured 112 mg/dL and there was no odor of alcohol or ketones on breath; pupils were said to be symmetric, and spontaneous respirations were present without accessory muscle use. On arrival to our emergency bay at 15:03 the patient remains immobilized on the original backboard with helmet cut free but fragments still taped to her backpack; dusty trail clothes are intact, damp near the shoulders from melted sleet, and no dressings have yet been applied to a 2-cm superficial laceration at the scalp impact site. Pre-intervention vital signs obtained simultaneously with the neurologic exam reveal blood pressure 152/88 mm Hg in the left brachial artery, pulse 86 beats per minute and regular in rhythm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute with equal chest excursion, oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air, and core temperature 36.5 °C obtained rectally. The airway is patent, dentition complete, tongue midline, and a Yankauer tip brushing the soft palate provokes an immediate gag followed by a single cough. Throughout silent observation her eyelids remain firmly shut, lashes motionless; calling her first name at conversational and then shouted volume produces no flutter, and a bright penlight directed at the closed lids fails to elicit any parting. A supraorbital notch pressure of ten seconds as well as deep nail-bed compression on the right index finger similarly leave the lids sealed. Pupils, examined after gentle manual separation of the lids, measure 3 mm bilaterally and briskly constrict to direct and consensual light; extra-ocular movements appear full and conjugate when the globes are rotated manually, and corneal reflexes are intact. No spontaneous speech is generated, yet intermittent guttural phonation occurs: when the charge nurse palpates a radial pulse she utters isolated, unrelated utterances such as “keys… riverbank… kitchen” in clear articulation but without context, orientation, or response to questions about name, location, or event. Cranial nerves V through XII are otherwise grossly preserved: symmetrical nasolabial folds at rest, tongue protrusion midline when the jaw is passively opened, and a strong trapezius shrug elicited by painful stimulation. Upper and lower extremities lie in neutral with mild baseline flexion at the elbows and knees; tone is normal to passive range. Patient note:
We describe the case of a 63-year-old man, Caucasian, affected by non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy who did not drink alcohol, did not smoke tobacco, and did not have diabetes. He had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator implanted, in New York Heart Association (NYHA) IV class, and left bundle branch block (LBBB; QRS duration of 145 ms). He was referred for CRT-D upgrade, awaiting cardiac transplantation, despite optimal medical therapy: b-Blockade, loop-diuretic, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, K-sparing agent, and ivabradine. Standard clinical imaging protocol revealed a dilated left ventricle with an end-systolic volume (ESV) of 380 ml, an ejection fraction (EF) of 4.8% as measured by the modified Simpson’s method, and severe FMR, assessed by qualitative estimation with two-dimensional color flow Doppler approach, showing a very large central jet and reaching the posterior wall of the left atrium (see Fig. and Additional file 1: Video S1).
He underwent the implant of a CRT-D device with a quadripolar left ventricular (LV) lead placed in the posterolateral branch of the coronary sinus. After recording the right ventricle (RV)-to-LV electrical delay at each of the four LV rings, we chose the A1 unipolar vector for LV pacing (greatest electrical delay 80 ms).
At 13-day post-implant follow-up, he showed worsening heart failure (HF) symptoms and only A2 unipolar LV vector configuration, with interventricular (VV) interval of 0 ms, was suitable for simultaneous biventricular activation (Fig. ).
Echo-PIV was then used, during the acute study with contrast agent bubbles, to evaluate the orientation and relative magnitude of blood-induced intraventricular forces in correspondence of different pacing settings.
Without pacing stimulation (CRT OFF, Fig. a, and Additional file 2: Video S2) the intraventricular flow was dominated by rotation without evident inflow–outflow dynamics. As a result the intraventricular forces were predominantly transverse and not aligned along the LV axis (Fig. a1) as quantified by the large value of their mean angle φ (φ = 55.6°, this angle ranges from 0°, when forces are aligned with the LV axis, to 90°). A first setting option (CRT ON, VV delay 0 ms, Fig. b and Additional file 3: Video S3) changed the orientation of intraventricular forces (Fig. b1) reducing the angle (φ = 45°), and increasing the delay (CRT ON, VV delay − 30 ms, Fig. c and Additional file 4: Video S4) improved the alignment (Fig. c1) reducing the angle (φ = 40.3°). Eventually, the sequential biventricular activation with delay − 50 ms (Fig. d and Additional file 5: Video S5) provided the best alignment of intraventricular forces (Fig. d1, φ = 38.8°).
No reduction of FMR by three-dimensional FVCD, during the same acute study with shutdown versus reactivation of device, was demonstrated, as shown in Figure and by comparing Additional file 6: Video S6 and Additional file 7: Video S7.
The data acquisition time, by three-chamber apical view, for each three-dimensional color Doppler data set was approximately 5 seconds, and it took less than 3 minutes to analyze the average regurgitation volume, with automated anatomy detection of the LV endocardial border, mitral annulus (MA), LV outflow (LVOT), and placement of three-dimensional hemispheric flow sampling planes in the MA and LVOT. The software of three-dimensional FVCD computed the flow volumes as the area under the curve of both the MA and LVOT flow in three cardiac cycles, and FMR volume was calculated by subtracting LVOT stroke volume from MA stroke volume.
Our patient showed an improvement of NYHA class (III versus IV) and LV EF (26.6% versus 4.8%). Significant reduction of ESV (288 ml versus 380 ml) and persistent improvement of diastolic function were obtained. The regularized function is noticeable in Additional file 8: Video S8 (to be compared with Additional file 1: Video S1) and it is summarized in Fig. . At follow-up, a significant reduction of FMR (mean value regurgitant volume, 42.2 ml versus 65.3 ml) was estimated (Fig. , Additional file 9: Video S9, Table ).
The intraventricular forces estimated by echo-PIV were still partially dominated by the longitudinal path of pressure gradient (Fig. and Additional file 10: Video S10) with φ = 43.1°.

Patient note:
An 84-year-old Italian woman presented to our hospital with a stroke and was referred to our cardiology unit for cardiologic evaluation. She had a history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and pulmonary embolism and was using warfarin for pulmonary embolism during our evaluation: international normalized ratio (INR) 2.3; time in therapeutic range (TTR) >63%. She reported palpitations and dyspnea that started 1 week before our evaluation. An electrocardiogram showed AF with a heart rate of 96 beats per minute. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal left ventricle (LV) diameters and volume, left ventricular ejection fraction of approximately 60%, and a dilated left atrium (LA) with dense spontaneous echo contrast. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed a round, partially mobile, disorganized and weakly hypoechogenic mass (12 × 12 mm) that resembled a thrombus in the LAA (Fig. a). We examined the following in regard to thrombophilia: prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen, activated protein C resistance, factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A mutation, homocysteine, ATIII, protein C, protein S, antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus-like anticoagulant), anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I antibodies, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, factor VIII, and methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase C677T mutation. Testing revealed heterozygosity for both factor V Leiden and methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase C677T mutation, which created resistance to activated protein C [].
We started anticoagulant treatment with unfractionated heparin administered intravenously. After 1 week of therapy, we performed a second TEE that showed that the LAA thrombus remained unchanged (Fig. b). Her treatment was then switched to rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily for long-term treatment and stroke prevention []. A third TEE performed at the 3-month follow-up visit revealed no thrombotic mass (Fig. c). No major or clinically relevant bleeding occurred during follow-up. At the 6-month and 12-month follow-up visits, she continued to be in good clinical condition. After thrombus resolution, because our patient was at high risk for thromboembolism and had a history of pulmonary embolism, we recommended LAA percutaneous occlusion; however, she refused this option.
For rate control, because our patient had a first diagnosed AF with mean ventricular response, we treated her with a beta blocker (bisoprolol) at low dosages (1.25 mg twice daily).

Patient note:
A 69-year-old man who carries a long-standing diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy with a baseline serum creatinine in the upper 1 mg/dL range, along with hypertension and coronary artery disease treated with percutaneous stenting five years earlier, was brought to the emergency department from an assisted-living facility after staff noticed a sudden onset of rigors, productive cough with yellow-green sputum, and increasing shortness of breath over the preceding twelve hours; he had been fully vaccinated against influenza and pneumococcus, had not received corticosteroids or chemotherapy, and had never undergone solid-organ or stem-cell transplantation. Paramedics reported an oxygen saturation in the mid-70s on ambient air, so they placed a Venturi mask delivering 50 % inspired oxygen for transport, started no intravenous fluids or antibiotics, and administered no analgesics, antipyretics, or bronchodilators en route. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—before any hospital-initiated therapy—he was seated upright, leaning forward, and speaking in short phrases between breaths. Initial vital signs recorded an oral temperature of 38.3 °C, radial pulse 102 beats per minute in a regular rhythm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute with moderate accessory muscle use, and noninvasive blood pressure 110/62 mm Hg confirmed by repeat cuff on the opposite arm. His skin was warm and diaphoretic; capillary refill was brisk. He opened his eyes to voice, was oriented to person and place but not date, and followed commands sluggishly, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13 without sedatives or intoxicants on board. Conjunctivae were injected but not icteric, pupils were equal and briskly reactive, and extraocular movements were full. Neck veins were not distended. Cardiac auscultation revealed a soft S1, normal S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses were bounding. Lung examination demonstrated diffuse coarse crackles over the right middle and lower fields and diminished breath sounds at the left base without wheezes; percussion was dull posteriorly. The abdomen was protuberant yet soft with mild epigastric tenderness but no rebound or guarding; bowel sounds were present. There was no flank tenderness, peripheral edema, or skin mottling. A radial arterial blood gas obtained within ten minutes of arrival while he remained on the 50 % mask showed a pH of 7.33, PaCO₂ 46 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 68 mm Hg, corresponding to an alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient of 321 mm Hg. Simultaneous serum chemistry demonstrated sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 106 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, the latter modestly above his usual baseline but unchanged from a nephrology visit two months earlier. Point-of-care glucose measured 168 mg/dL. Complete blood count revealed a white blood cell count of 14 500 cells/mm³ with 88 % neutrophils, hematocrit 35 %, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, and platelets 212 000/µL. High-sensitivity troponin was negative, and serum lactate returned at 2.2 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph taken before any antimicrobial therapy or intravenous bolus demonstrated patchy consolidation throughout the right lung with a subtle parapneumonic effusion and low lung volumes on the left but no overt cardiomegaly. Bedside cardiac ultrasound showed preserved left ventricular systolic function and a collapsible inferior vena cava suggestive of relative hypovolemia rather than congestive state. Electrocardiogram revealed normal sinus rhythm at 100 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-segment flattening but no ischemic changes. A urinary catheter placed shortly after room entry produced 20 mL of dark yellow urine over the first half-hour. No crystalloid boluses, vasopressors, antipyretics, bronchodilators, or antibiotics had yet been administered when the above physiologic measurements, arterial blood gas, laboratory values, and imaging findings were documented, thus reflecting his untreated status at the moment the intensive care team accepted him for admission for management of presumed severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by marked hypoxemia, mild acidemia, and decompensation on a background of chronic kidney dysfunction.

Patient note:
The patient was a 63-year-old white Turkish male living in Istanbul, Turkey who presented to the clinic with increasing chest pain on exertion, which had progressed in the last six months. He was 169 cm tall and weighed 74 kg. He had been a smoker for more than 45 years, and on an average smoked 1-1.5 packs per day. His family history was negative for cardiovascular disorders. He was not hypertensive (blood pressure of 128/76 mmHg on left arm and 132/77 mmHg on right arm at rest) and did not have diabetes mellitus (overnight fasting blood glucose of 98 mg/dL, normal range: < 100 mg/dL). Blood lipid profile indicated total cholesterol and low density lipoprotein levels of 193 mg/dL (normal range: < 200 mg/dL) and 124 mg/dL (normal range: < 130mg/dL), respectively. Cardiologic check up protocol was considered and the patient underwent stress electrocardiography which resulted positive. Myocardial thallium perfusion scintigraphy indicated ischemic zones at the inferior, inferolateral and inferoapical zones of the heart. According to the results, coronary angiography was performed and it revealed triple vessel disease with subtotal occlusion of left anterior descending artery (LAD) at the midportion, midportion 80% stenosis at the circumflex coronary artery (Cx) and 70% stenosis at the right coronary artery (RCA). Echocardiography was normal with preserved left ventricular functions (65% ejection fraction) and left ventricular hypertrophy. Following the consent of the patient, coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) was planned.
During the preparatory phase for surgery, the patient complained of acute first toe pain. The first toe looked swollen, hyperemic and painful on palpation. Laboratory findings including complete blood count, blood lipid profile, renal and hepatic enzymes, clotting times, were normal except increased serum uric acid levels (10.74 mg/dl, Normal: 3.4-7 mg/dl) and slighly elevated C-reactive protein (6.72 mg/L, Normal: 0-5 mg/L). He was consulted with internal medicine department and diagnosed as Gout arthritis. He was prescribed allopurinol 300 mg twice daily and scheduled for surgery when the circulating uric acid levels returned to normal. Following four days of treatment, uric acid levels returned to normal limits, and he underwent triple vessel CABG (Left internal mammarian artery to LAD, aorta-first obtuse marginal artery and aorta-posterior descending branch of the right coronary artery bypasses with separate saphenous veins) with the use of cardiopulmonary bypass on arrested heart at 33-34°C. Cross clamp and cardiopulmonary bypasses were 35 minutes and 47 minutes, respectively. After the operation, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and extubated there on the post-operative 4th hour. He was taken to the ward the next day and discharged on the 6th day. Blood and blood product usage was 1 units of erythrocyte suspension and 2 units of fresh frozen plasma in total.
Immediately after the surgery, there was a slight increase in serum uric acid levels (7.4 mg/dl) detected in the blood drawn in the intensive care unit. As soon as the patient was extubated and oral intake was started, allopurinol was initiated at the same pre-operative dosage, and this returned the serum uric acid levels to normal. Post-operative course was otherwise uneventful. He has been followed symptom free for more than 9 months and is on allopurinol treatment in addition to anti-aggregant (aspirin, 100mg daily), anti-lipidemic (atorvastatin, 20mg daily) and low dose beta-blocker (metoprolol 25 mg daily) medications and a low calori diet.
